provenance.rightsNote: Lectio Edition (SDIT): clear modern English of Plato's Republic, synthesized from the public-domain translation tradition (Jowett 1871) and checked against the Greek; modern translations consulted, not quoted. In progress, book by book.
sourcesCited: Greek, the original text of the Politeia
Benjamin Jowett, The Republic of Plato (1871, public domain)
Paul Shorey, Loeb Classical Library (consulted, not quoted)
G. M. A. Grube / C. D. C. Reeve (1992, consulted, not quoted)

character: Plain modern English — the sense of the original, made to read with ease today.
overview: The Lectio Edition renders Plato's Republic in plain modern English that keeps the drive of the dialogue and the force of its argument — justice, the just city, the Cave, the philosopher-king — while dropping the Victorian formality.
introduction: The Republic begins with a simple question — what is justice, and is it worth having? — and builds, step by step, an entire ideal city to answer it. Along the way come its most famous images: the Cave, the divided line, the philosopher-king. It is a conversation, so read for the back-and-forth, not just the conclusions.

divergences.phrase: τὸ τοῦ κρείττονος συμφέρον (338c)
divergences.older: I proclaim that justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger.
divergences.lectio: I say that justice is nothing other than the advantage of the stronger.
divergences.note: Sympheron is what profits or benefits someone. In modern English 'interest' has drifted toward finance and polite concern; 'advantage' keeps Thrasymachus's thesis as blunt as he makes it — justice is whatever serves the man on top.

divergences.phrase: τί εὐηθίζεσθε πρὸς ἀλλήλους ὑποκατακλινόμενοι; (336b–c)
divergences.older: And why, sillybillies, do you knock under to one another?
divergences.lectio: Why are you playing the fool, bowing and deferring to each other?
divergences.note: Jowett turns the Greek verb euēthizesthe ('to play the simpleton') into a nursery insult, making Thrasymachus quaint at the very moment Plato makes him terrifying. The Lectio keeps it a verb, and keeps the wrestling image in hypokataklinomenoi — deliberately taking a fall for an opponent.

divergences.phrase: τίτθη σοι ἔστιν; (343a)
divergences.older: Tell me, Socrates, have you got a nurse?
divergences.lectio: Tell me, Socrates — do you still have a wet nurse?
divergences.note: A titthē is specifically a wet nurse. Thrasymachus's taunt is that Socrates is an unweaned, sniveling infant; the generic 'nurse' blunts an insult that is meant to draw blood.

divergences.locus: II.359d — the finder of the ring
divergences.phrase: Γύγῃ τῷ τοῦ Λυδοῦ προγόνῳ
divergences.older: the power... which is said to have been possessed by Gyges, the ancestor of Croesus the Lydian (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: the kind of power they say once came to the ancestor of Gyges the Lydian
divergences.note: In the manuscripts the shepherd who finds the ring is an unnamed ancestor of Gyges, not Gyges himself; Jowett smooths the oddity away by renaming him 'Gyges, the ancestor of Croesus.' The Lectio keeps the manuscript reading — even though Plato himself, at the end of the Republic (612b), calls it 'the ring of Gyges.' The wobble is Plato's own, and it changes nothing in the thought experiment: whoever wears the ring, the question is what you would do if no one could see you.

divergences.phrase: ἐπιστατητέον τοῖς μυθοποιοῖς
divergences.older: the first thing will be to establish a censorship of the writers of fiction (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: our first job, it seems, is to stand watch over the makers of stories
divergences.note: Jowett's 'censorship' imports a Victorian institution — boards, stamps, banned books — into a Greek phrase that says only that the founders must 'stand over' (epistatein) the myth-makers, the way a foreman stands over a crew. What Socrates proposes is editorial oversight of the city's nursery tales, severe enough on its own terms; the Lectio lets it be exactly that, without the anachronism.

divergences.locus: II.379a — the first pattern for the gods
divergences.phrase: ὁ θεός (ho theos)
divergences.older: God is always to be represented as he truly is... God, if he be good, is not the author of all things (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: however the god actually is, that is how he must always be rendered... neither can the god, since he is good, be the cause of everything
divergences.note: Jowett's capital-G 'God' quietly turns Plato's theology into something like Victorian Christianity. The Greek says ho theos — 'the god' — and slides freely between singular and plural: Socrates is laying down rules for talking about Zeus, Hera, and Apollo, not anticipating monotheism. The Lectio keeps the lowercase god and the plural gods, which makes the argument more startling, not less: even Homer's gods, rightly understood, cannot cause evil, cannot change shape, and cannot lie.

divergences.phrase: γενναῖόν τι ἓν ψευδομένους πεῖσαι (gennaion ti hen pseudomenous peisai)
divergences.older: How then may we devise one of those needful falsehoods of which we lately spoke—just one royal lie which may deceive the rulers, if that be possible, and at any rate the rest of the city?
divergences.lectio: Then how, I said, might we contrive one of those lies we spoke of earlier — the lies told at need? One noble lie, to persuade, in the best case, the rulers themselves; and failing that, the rest of the city?
divergences.note: Gennaios means well-born, noble — the word you would use of a pedigreed hound or an aristocrat. Jowett's 'royal lie' quietly relocates the scandal: it names the audience of the lie rather than its breeding. Plato's phrase is a deliberate oxymoron — a lie of noble stock — and Socrates can barely bring himself to say it. The Lectio keeps 'noble lie,' discomfort intact: the founding myth of the ideal city is admitted to be a falsehood by the man proposing it.

divergences.phrase: χαλκόν τε καὶ σίδηρον (chalkon te kai sidēron)
divergences.older: others again who are to be husbandmen and craftsmen he has composed of brass and iron
divergences.lectio: and iron and bronze into the farmers and the other craftsmen
divergences.note: Chalkos is bronze — the alloy of heroic-age weapons and armor — not modern brass; 'brass' is an old English habit that runs from the King James Bible through the Victorians. Bronze restores the myth's metallurgy: gold, silver, bronze, iron, a descending scale that deliberately echoes Hesiod's races of men, which Plato's first readers would have heard at once.

divergences.phrase: μίμησις (mimēsis)
divergences.older: And narration may be either simple narration, or imitation, or a union of the two?
divergences.lectio: And don't they carry it off either by plain narration, or by imitation — impersonating their characters — or by a mix of the two?
divergences.note: Mimēsis here means something closer to impersonation — the poet acting a part, speaking as Chryses rather than about him. The Lectio keeps the traditional 'imitation' because the word is load-bearing: this passage plants the concept Book X will use to put poetry itself on trial. But it glosses the first occurrence with 'impersonating,' so the modern reader hears what Adeimantus heard — role-play, not copying.

divergences.phrase: σωφροσύνη (sōphrosynē)
divergences.older: temperance (Jowett, and most of the tradition)
divergences.lectio: self-command
divergences.note: The Greek names a mind in right order — self-mastery, soundness — and has nothing to do with abstaining from drink, which is what 'temperance' has come to smell of since the temperance movement. Plato's own handle on the word is the strange phrase 'stronger than himself' — the better part of a man holding the worse in hand — and 'self-command' keeps that engine visible every time the word appears.

divergences.phrase: τὸ τὰ αὑτοῦ πράττειν καὶ μὴ πολυπραγμονεῖν (to ta hautou prattein kai mē polypragmonein)
divergences.older: doing one's own business, and not being a busybody (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: doing your own work, and not meddling in another's
divergences.note: This formula is the engine of the whole book: justice in the city and justice in the soul are both defined by it. Jowett's 'busybody' makes polypragmonein sound like gossip over a fence; the Greek is graver — grabbing at work, and rule, that belongs to another. 'Doing your own work' is kept word-for-word constant at every appearance, so the reader can watch the definition travel from cobblers and carpenters to the parts of the soul.

divergences.phrase: ἰδοὺ ὑμῖν, ὦ κακοδαίμονες, ἐμπλήσθητε τοῦ καλοῦ θεάματος
divergences.older: Look, ye wretches, take your fill of the fair sight (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: There, you wretches — drink your fill of the beautiful sight!
divergences.note: Leontius is shouting at his own eyes — he has just pried them open with his fingers to stare at the corpses. Jowett's 'Look, ye wretches' lets a reader miss the addressee entirely. The self-directed rage is the whole point: it is Plato's proof that spirit (thumos) is a third thing in the soul, distinct from appetite, that can take reason's side against it.

divergences.phrase: ean me e hoi philosophoi basileusosin en tais polesin... (473c-d)
divergences.older: Until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy... cities will never have rest from their evils (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: Unless philosophers become kings in our cities, or the men now called kings and rulers become philosophers — genuinely, thoroughly... there will be no rest from evils for our cities
divergences.note: The book's famous sentence. Plato's ean me is a hard conditional — 'unless' — that promises nothing; Jowett's 'until' quietly assures the reader the day is coming. And his 'kings and princes of this world' borrows a King James cadence (cf. 1 Corinthians 2:6) that wraps the sentence in a Christianity Plato never heard of. Lectio keeps the condition stark and the politics plain: power and philosophy in the same hands, or no rest from evils.

divergences.phrase: auto to kalon (476b); pantelos on (477a)
divergences.older: absolute beauty; absolute being (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: the beautiful itself; what fully is
divergences.note: Plato's phrase is disarmingly plain — 'the beautiful itself,' set against the many beautiful things. Jowett's 'absolute beauty' and 'absolute being' dress the argument in nineteenth-century idealism ('the Absolute' belongs to Hegel, not Plato) and make it sound more mystical than it is. Book V's closing argument — knowledge is set over what is, opinion over what tumbles between being and not-being — stays sharper when the vocabulary stays Plato's own.

divergences.phrase: daimones hagnoi epichthonioi (Hesiod, quoted at 469a)
divergences.older: They are holy angels upon the earth, authors of good, averters of evil (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: they become pure spirits dwelling upon the earth, noble beings, protectors against evil, guardians of mortal men
divergences.note: Hesiod's daimones are not angels — that word imports a Christian cosmology some five centuries early. The glorious dead of the golden race become watchful spirits of the earth itself, a pagan idea whose strangeness is worth keeping. Lectio restores 'spirits' and lets Hesiod sound like Hesiod.

divergences.phrase: ναύκληρος (nauklēros)
divergences.older: Imagine then a fleet or a ship in which there is a captain who is taller and stronger than any of the crew, but he is a little deaf and has a similar infirmity in sight...
divergences.lectio: The shipowner is bigger and stronger than everyone else on board, but a little deaf, a little short-sighted, and his knowledge of seafaring runs about as deep.
divergences.note: Jowett's 'captain' collapses the parable's cast. The nauklēros is the shipowner — the people, who own the ship of state but are strong, half-deaf, and short-sighted — while the quarreling sailors are the politicians and the true helmsman (kybernētēs) is the philosopher. Keeping owner and pilot distinct keeps the allegory exact: the crew fights over a helm that belongs to neither of them, and the one man who studies the sky is called a useless stargazer.

divergences.phrase: οὐκ οὐσίας ὄντος τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ, ἀλλ' ἔτι ἐπέκεινα τῆς οὐσίας (epekeina tēs ousias)
divergences.older: the good is not essence, but far exceeds essence in dignity and power
divergences.lectio: the good is not being. It stands beyond being, surpassing it in rank and in power.
divergences.note: Ousia is 'being' — what it is for a thing to be — not 'essence' in the later scholastic sense, and Jowett's 'far exceeds' softens epekeina, which means flatly 'beyond.' The claim is that the good is not the topmost item on the scale of being but the source of the scale itself, off the map it makes possible. Presbeia is literally an elder's seniority — rank, precedence — not vague 'dignity.' Stated plainly, the sentence is startling enough; it needs no mystification, and Glaucon's burst of laughter in the next line ('Apollo! What an unearthly exaggeration!') only lands if the statement stays as bald as Plato made it.

divergences.phrase: νόησις, διάνοια, πίστις, εἰκασία (noēsis, dianoia, pistis, eikasia)
divergences.older: reason answering to the highest, understanding to the second, faith (or conviction) to the third, and perception of shadows to the last
divergences.lectio: intelligence for the highest; thought for the second; assign conviction to the third; and to the last, imaging — the reading of shadows and likenesses
divergences.note: Jowett's 'faith' for pistis drags in a religious sense Plato doesn't intend: pistis is everyday confidence in solid things — the trust that the chair will hold you. The four are conditions (pathēmata) that arise in the soul, one per segment of the line, and the geometry is part of the argument, not decoration: a line cut in two unequal parts, each part cut again in the same ratio, so that clarity tracks truth by strict proportion. The Lectio keeps the four names parallel and plain — intelligence, thought, conviction, imaging — so the scale reads as the piece of mathematics Plato drew.

divergences.phrase: καταγείῳ οἰκήσει σπηλαιώδει (katageio oikesei spelaiodei)
divergences.older: human beings living in an underground den (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: people in a home under the earth, a kind of cave
divergences.note: Jowett's 'den' makes the most famous image in Western philosophy sound like an animal's burrow. The Greek says cave — spelaiodes, 'cave-like' — and the force of the allegory depends on its being a human dwelling: a place people live in and mistake for the world. We say 'cave' throughout, which is also the name the tradition itself settled on — the allegory of the Cave.

divergences.phrase: ἡ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ἰδέα (he tou agathou idea)
divergences.older: the idea of good (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: the form of the good
divergences.note: To a modern ear 'idea' means a thought in someone's head — exactly what Plato does not mean. The idea is what is most real: the good itself, seen last and with effort at the top of the climb, not anyone's notion of it. 'Form' has become the settled English for this, and we keep it, so the summit of the ascent reads as a reality to be seen, not an opinion to be held.

divergences.phrase: περιαγωγή (periagoge)
divergences.older: conversion (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: the turning around of the soul
divergences.note: Jowett's 'conversion' pulls the passage toward religious experience. The Greek word is physical — a wheeling-about, the same motion as the prisoner forced to turn his neck from the wall toward the fire. Education, Socrates says, is not putting sight into blind eyes but turning an eye that already sees. 'Turning around' keeps the cave's own image doing the work.

divergences.phrase: γεωμετρικὸς ἀριθμός (geōmetrikos arithmos)
divergences.older: Jowett (1871) interleaves his own arithmetic — parenthetical equations and conjectures — into the Muses’ speech on the ‘nuptial number’
divergences.lectio: renders the riddle as a riddle, without the editorial mathematics
divergences.note: The Muses’ ‘geometric number’ that governs better and worse births is the most disputed passage in Plato, and it is written to be oracular — Socrates says outright that the Muses are teasing, speaking in mock-tragic high style. Jowett folded a reconstruction of the math into the text itself; Lectio keeps the high style and the obscurity, which is the point.

divergences.phrase: ἀκράτου ἐλευθερίας μεθυσθῇ (akratou eleutherias methysthē)
divergences.older: ‘has drunk too deeply of the strong wine of freedom’ (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: ‘drinks past the point of drunkenness on freedom taken neat’
divergences.note: Greeks diluted their wine with water; drinking it akratos — unmixed, neat — was the mark of a barbarian. Plato’s image is precise: freedom is not the poison; freedom taken without any admixture of restraint is. Lectio keeps the drinking custom visible so the metaphor keeps its edge.

divergences.phrase: προστάτης (prostatēs)
divergences.older: ‘protector’ (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: ‘the people’s champion’
divergences.note: The prostatēs tou dēmou was a real role in Athenian politics — the man who ‘stands in front of’ the people, their front-man and defender. ‘Protector’ sounds institutional; ‘champion’ catches how the crowd feels about him, which is what makes the wolf-story land. Every tyrant in this book begins as the man the people loved.

divergences.phrase: the lawless desires that wake in sleep
divergences.older: no conceivable folly or crime—not excepting incest or any other unnatural union, or parricide (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: it does not shrink, in fantasy, from trying to sleep with a mother — or with anyone else, man, god, or beast; it is ready for any bloodshed
divergences.note: The Greek is specific: the dreaming appetite tries to lie with its own mother (mētri epicheirein mignysthai) and stops at no bloodshed. Jowett wraps this in Latinate abstraction — ‘incest or any other unnatural union’ — which blunts the point of the passage: that these lawless desires exist in everyone, even the most measured. The specificity is the argument, so the Lectio keeps it.

divergences.phrase: the 729-times calculation
divergences.older: living 729 times more pleasantly (Jowett, with an inserted explanatory parenthesis)
divergences.lectio: the king lives seven hundred and twenty-nine times more pleasantly — the arithmetic kept step by step
divergences.note: The calculation is deliberately odd: the tyrant is third from the oligarch and the oligarch third from the king, so his phantom pleasure is nine times removed; square and cube that ‘length’ and you get 729 — a number with Pythagorean prestige, close to the days-plus-nights of a year. It is half proof and half joke, and Plato plainly enjoys its mock precision. The Lectio keeps every step of the sum rather than smoothing it into a vague ‘immeasurably worse.’

divergences.phrase: en ouranōi paradeigma — the pattern laid up in heaven
divergences.older: which he who desires may behold, and beholding, may set his own house in order (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: for the man who wants to see it — and, seeing it, to found that city in himself
divergences.note: Jowett’s famous ‘set his own house in order’ domesticates the Greek. The verb is katoikizein — to found a settlement, to plant a colony: the man founds the ideal city in himself and becomes its citizen. The book’s last word is political through and through, not a homily about tidy living; the Lectio keeps it exact and unsentimental.

divergences.locus: Book X, 597e (and throughout the argument about painters and poets)
divergences.phrase: tritos apo tes aletheias (τρίτος ἀπὸ τῆς ἀληθείας)
divergences.older: thrice removed from the truth
divergences.lectio: third from the truth / at the third remove
divergences.note: Jowett's famous 'thrice removed' suggests three steps beyond the truth — fourth in line. Plato counts inclusively: the form is first, the craftsman's bed second, the painter's image third. We keep his arithmetic exact — the imitator is 'third from the king and from the truth' — because the whole argument hangs on that count.

divergences.phrase: daimon (δαίμων)
divergences.older: genius
divergences.lectio: guardian spirit
divergences.note: Jowett renders daimon as 'genius' — correct in the old Latin sense of a tutelary spirit, but to a modern ear it means intellect or talent. The daimon is the spirit that accompanies and guides a life. We say 'guardian spirit' so the herald's point lands as Plato wrote it: 'No guardian spirit will draw you by lot; you will choose your guardian spirit.' The life is chosen, not assigned — which is why the blame belongs to the chooser, and god is blameless.

divergences.locus: Book X, 621a–c (the plain and the river; the last word of the Republic)
divergences.phrase: to tes Lethes pedion / ho Ameles potamos (τὸ τῆς Λήθης πεδίον / ὁ Ἀμέλης ποταμός)
divergences.older: the plain of Forgetfulness; the river of Unmindfulness
divergences.lectio: the plain of Forgetting; the river of Heedlessness
divergences.note: Plato names two distinct places: the plain of Lethe (Forgetting) and the river Ameles — literally 'Careless,' the water of not-paying-attention, which no vessel can hold. Jowett's 'Forgetfulness' and 'Unmindfulness' blur into each other. We keep them separate and plain: every soul must drink a measure of Heedlessness, but those not saved by good sense drink past the measure — and it is that excess, not the drink itself, that erases everything.
divergences.phrase: justice is the advantage of the stronger
divergences.older: I proclaim that justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: I say that justice is nothing but the advantage of the stronger
divergences.note: Thrasymachus's thesis is the hinge of the whole Republic, so the wording has to land hard and plain. Jowett's 'interest' is a fair rendering of the Greek 'sympheron' (what is advantageous, what brings profit), but to a modern ear 'interest' is cool and abstract. 'Advantage' keeps the cynical edge of the claim, that the powerful simply call whatever benefits them 'justice', and renders the same phrase consistently every time it returns so the reader can track the argument.

divergences.phrase: giving each what is owed; helping friends and harming enemies
divergences.older: justice is the giving to each man what is proper to him... an art which gives good to friends and evil to enemies (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: justice is giving each person what's appropriate to him... doing good to friends and harm to enemies
divergences.note: Polemarchus inherits the conventional Greek morality, do good to friends, harm to enemies, and Socrates reduces it to absurdity (the just man as expert thief). The crux is 'to opheilomenon', what is owed/due. Jowett's 'what is proper to him' is accurate but stilted; 'what's appropriate to him' keeps the same idea while letting the everyday sense of 'owing' a debt stay audible, which the argument needs, since Socrates plays on the slide from 'owed money' to 'owed treatment'.

divergences.phrase: the shepherd and the sheep
divergences.older: you fancy that the shepherd or neatherd fattens or tends the sheep or oxen with a view to their own good and not to the good of himself or his master (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: you imagine that shepherds and herdsmen look after the good of their sheep and cattle for any reason other than the good of their masters and themselves
divergences.note: This is Thrasymachus's most vivid image: rulers tend their subjects exactly as a shepherd fattens sheep, for the slaughter, not the sheep's sake. The line answers Socrates' craft-analogy (an art serves its subject, not the practitioner), so the translation has to keep the sneer and the bite. 'Neatherd' is dead Victorian vocabulary; 'herdsmen' carries it. The cynicism, that care for subjects is only ever a means to exploiting them, is preserved without softening.

divergences.phrase: the Ring of Gyges
divergences.older: he turned the collet of the ring inside his hand, when instantly he became invisible to the rest of the company... no man can be imagined to be of such an iron nature that he would stand fast in justice (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: he happened to turn the setting of the ring toward the inside of his hand, and at once he became invisible... No one, it seems, would be made of iron enough to stay on the path of justice
divergences.note: This is the most famous thought-experiment in the book, and it has to read as a story a modern person can fall into, not as an antique fable. Jowett's 'collet' is dead jewelry-vocabulary; 'setting' is the live word for the part of a ring that holds the stone, and it keeps the mechanical detail (turn it in, you vanish; turn it out, you reappear) perfectly clear, which matters because the whole argument rests on the man being able to act unseen. 'Made of iron enough' keeps Plato's metaphor of an iron, unbending nature rather than flattening it to 'adamant' or paraphrasing it away. The point preserved is the sting: give the just man the same impunity and he walks the very same road as the unjust one.

divergences.phrase: justice as a social contract
divergences.older: hence there arise laws and mutual covenants; and that which is ordained by law is termed by them lawful and just... it is a mean or compromise (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: That's where laws and contracts come from, and people call what the law commands lawful and just... It stands midway between the best case, doing wrong and getting away with it, and the worst case, being wronged with no power to strike back
divergences.note: Glaucon's account is the ancestor of every social-contract theory, so the logic of the bargain must be exactly trackable, not draped in Victorian abstraction. Jowett's 'mutual covenants' and 'a mean or compromise' are accurate but archaic and vague; 'contracts' and 'midway between the best case... and the worst case' lay the deal out as the cold cost-benefit calculation Plato intends: people accept justice not because it's good but because they're too weak to do wrong safely, and it's the lesser evil. Nothing is added or softened; the cynicism that justice is merely a grudging truce is kept intact.

divergences.phrase: the perfectly just man, reviled and impaled
divergences.older: the just man who is thought unjust will be scourged, racked, bound—will have his eyes burnt out; and, at last, after suffering every kind of evil, he will be impaled (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: the just man, with his reputation for wrongdoing, will be whipped, racked, and chained; they'll burn out his eyes; and in the end, after suffering every torment, he'll be impaled
divergences.note: This is the dark heart of Glaucon's challenge, the portrait of perfect justice stripped of every reward and crowned only with suffering. The catalog of tortures has to land with full physical force, not be muffled by 'scourged' and other Sunday-readings; 'whipped,' 'racked,' 'chained,' 'they'll burn out his eyes' keep the brutality concrete and present-tense. The Greek anaskhinduleuthesetai ('impaled,' often heard by readers as the crucifixion of the righteous man) is kept exact, not blurred, because the whole power of the thought-experiment is that the just man gets the unjust man's fate and we still have to ask whether his life is the better one.

divergences.phrase: God is good and the cause only of good
divergences.older: God, if he be good, is not the author of all things, as the many assert, but he is the cause of a few things only... of the evils the causes are to be sought elsewhere, and not in him (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: the god, since he's good, can't be the cause of everything, as most people say. He's the cause of only a few things that happen to us, and not of most... for the bad we must look for some other cause, not the god
divergences.note: This is the founding principle of Socrates' 'patterns for tales about the gods' and one of the earliest statements of the problem of evil. Jowett's capital-G 'God' silently imports Christian monotheism; the Greek ho theos is the god / a god within a polytheistic frame, and keeping the lowercase definite article (alongside 'the gods' elsewhere) is the honest rendering, it lets the reader hear Plato reforming Greek religion rather than preaching a later creed. 'Author' becomes 'cause' (aitios) to keep the argument's causal logic exact: the good produces only good, so a good god cannot be the source of the many evils of human life, which must be traced elsewhere.

divergences.phrase: the noble lie / myth of the metals
divergences.older: How then may we devise one of those needful falsehoods of which we lately spoke—just one royal lie which may deceive the rulers, if that be possible, and at any rate the rest of the city?... in the composition of these he has mingled gold... others he has made of silver... of brass and iron (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: how could we contrive one of those necessary lies we were talking about a while ago, a single noble lie that might convince even the rulers, or at least the rest of the city?... he mixed gold into those of you fit to rule... silver into the auxiliaries; and iron and bronze into the farmers and the other craftsmen
divergences.note: This is the most famous and most contested phrase in the book: 'gennaion pseudos.' Jowett's 'royal lie' is wrong on the Greek (he conflated it with the earlier 'medicine' line and with the later loose talk of the rulers' privilege), and his 'needful falsehoods' buries the scandal. 'Gennaion' means well-born, noble, of good stock, with a touch of irony; 'pseudos' is flatly a lie or fiction, not a mere story. The standard English title 'the noble lie' has to stand, because that is what every reader has come to argue over, and softening it ('myth,' 'fiction,' 'tale') would conceal exactly the difficulty Plato wants us to feel. Socrates' own visible embarrassment ('I hardly know how to find the nerve') is preserved so the reader sees the author flagging the problem, not smuggling it past us. The metals are kept exactly as named (gold, silver, iron and bronze) and tied to the three classes, since the whole political point rides on them.

divergences.phrase: simple narration vs. imitation
divergences.older: And narration may be either simple narration, or imitation, or a union of the two?... this assimilation of himself to another... is the imitation of the person whose character he assumes (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: the narrating is done either by plain narration, or by impersonation, or by a mix of the two?... making yourself like someone else, in voice or gesture, is impersonating the one whose character you've taken on
divergences.note: The crux is 'mimesis,' which Jowett renders 'imitation' throughout. 'Imitation' is defensible and is the traditional term, but in modern English it drifts toward 'copying' or 'forgery' and loses the theatrical force Plato needs: the poet (or guardian) actually becomes the character, speaks in his voice, takes on his bearing. Rendering the verb as 'impersonate' where the act is described keeps that bodily, performative sense (the danger is that you turn into what you act out), while 'imitation' is retained for the abstract noun where the tradition expects it. The distinction between the poet speaking 'in his own voice' (plain narration) and speaking 'as' a character is kept sharp, because the whole argument about which characters a guardian may impersonate depends on it.

divergences.phrase: guardians without private property; gold in the soul
divergences.older: none of them should have any property of his own beyond what is absolutely necessary... Gold and silver we will tell them that they have from God; the diviner metal is within them... ought not to pollute the divine by any such earthly admixture (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: none of them should own any private property beyond what's absolutely necessary... we'll tell them they have the divine kind always in their souls, given by the gods... it would be sacrilege to defile their store of the divine metal by mixing it with mortal gold
divergences.note: The austere communism of the guardians is one of the Republic's hardest doctrines, and the passage works by a deliberate pun that ties it back to the myth of the metals: the guardians own no earthly gold precisely because they already carry divine gold in their souls. Jowett's 'the diviner metal is within them' and 'pollute the divine by any such earthly admixture' are accurate but abstract; the modern rendering keeps the concrete image ('defile their store of the divine metal by mixing it with mortal gold') so the reader hears the echo of 414e and feels the force of the prohibition: these men alone may not touch, wear, or drink from gold. Nothing is softened, the consequence Plato spells out, that property would turn the guardians into 'masters and enemies' of the citizens, is rendered in full.

divergences.phrase: justice is doing one's own work and not meddling
divergences.older: we affirmed that justice was doing one's own business, and not being a busybody (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: justice is doing one's own work and not meddling in other people's
divergences.note: This is the definition the whole book has been driving toward, the principle that turns out to have been operating since the city was founded. The Greek is 'ta hautou prattein', to do/practice what is one's own. Jowett's 'doing one's own business... not being a busybody' is accurate but the word 'busybody' has shrunk in modern English into something almost comic, the nosy neighbor. Plato means something graver: a part or a person stepping outside its proper function and seizing work that isn't its own. 'Not meddling in other people's' keeps the everyday sense audible while preserving the structural force the argument needs, since the same word governs both the just city (each class doing its own) and the just soul (each part doing its own).

divergences.phrase: temperance is the agreement about who should rule
divergences.older: temperance... is the agreement of the naturally superior and inferior, as to the right to rule of either, both in states and individuals (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: temperance... is the agreement between the naturally worse and the naturally better about which of them should rule
divergences.note: Sophrosyne is the hardest of the four virtues to carry into English; 'temperance' now suggests only abstaining from drink, and 'moderation' loses the political and musical sense Plato builds here. The crux is that, unlike wisdom and courage which each sit in one class or part, sophrosyne is a relation that runs through the whole, the agreement of ruler and ruled about who rules. Jowett's 'naturally superior and inferior' is faithful, but I render it as 'naturally worse and better' to keep the same plain pair Plato uses for the soul's parts, so the reader can hear that the harmony in the city and the harmony in the soul are literally the same thing. I keep 'temperance' as the headword but lean on 'harmony' and 'agreement' to carry the weight.

divergences.phrase: the thirsty soul pulled two ways
divergences.older: if you suppose something which pulls a thirsty soul away from drink, that must be different from the thirsty principle which draws him like a beast to drink (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: if something ever pulls it back when it's thirsty, that must be something in it different from the thirsty part, the part that drives it like a beast to drink
divergences.note: This is the engine of the tripartite-soul proof: the principle of opposites applied to the thirsty man who refuses to drink. The whole argument rests on the same thing not doing opposite things in the same respect at the same time, so the two pulls must come from two distinct parts. The fidelity risk is softening 'drives it like a beast' (the Greek has the appetite hauling the soul like an animal driven to water) or blurring the strict logical conditions ('in the same respect, toward the same thing, at the same time') that license the conclusion. I keep the beast-image hard and preserve the conditions verbatim throughout the passage, because if those slip, the proof that the soul has parts collapses, and with it justice-in-the-soul as 'each part doing its own'.

divergences.phrase: women as guardians; the difference of the sexes
divergences.older: if women are to have the same duties as men, they must have the same nurture and education... women must be taught music and gymnastic and also the art of war, which they must practise like the men (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: if women are to do the same work as men, they have to be given the same upbringing and the same education... we'll have to give women music and physical training too, and train them in war as well, and put them to the same use as the men
divergences.note: The first wave is the most easily blunted in older English, where 'the same duties' and 'practise like the men' sound like a mild concession. Plato's point is sharper: the female guardians are to be trained for war and worked exactly as the males are, the only difference being strength. 'Do the same work,' 'train them in war,' and 'put them to the same use' keep the equality of role unmistakable, which the whole nature-versus-task argument that follows depends on. Softening it here would let a reader miss why Glaucon thinks the proposal will look 'ridiculous.'

divergences.phrase: the community of women and children
divergences.older: the wives of our guardians are to be common, and their children are to be common, and no parent is to know his own child, nor any child his parent (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: these women are all to be shared in common among these men, and none is to live privately with any man; and the children too are to be shared in common, and no parent is to know his own child, nor any child his parent
divergences.note: Jowett's 'the wives... are to be common' reads, to a modern ear, as merely odd or quaint, and 'wives' smuggles in the very private marriage the proposal abolishes. The Greek 'koinas' means held in common, shared by the group; the radical claim is precisely that there are no private wives and no private families among the guardians. Rendering it 'shared in common... none is to live privately with any man' restores the shock and the logic, since the unity of the city ('mine' and 'not mine' said by all of the same things) hangs on there being nothing privately one's own. The eugenic and child-rearing machinery that follows only makes sense once this is stated plainly, not prettified.

divergences.phrase: the philosopher-king (the third and greatest wave)
divergences.older: Until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy... cities will never have rest from their evils (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: Unless philosophers become kings in their cities, or those we now call kings and rulers take genuinely and adequately to philosophy, so that political power and wisdom meet in the same person... there will be no rest from evils... for cities, nor I think for the human race
divergences.note: This is the hinge of the whole Republic, the 'greatest wave,' and the sentence has to land with full force and full rigor. Jowett's 'have the spirit and power of philosophy' is graceful but loosens the Greek 'philosophesosi gnesios te kai hikanos', that they take to philosophy genuinely and adequately, really and sufficiently, not as a hobby. The conditional must stay strictly bilateral (philosophers become rulers OR rulers become philosophers) and the consequence must keep its sweep ('no rest from evils for cities, nor for the human race'). Spelling out 'political power and wisdom meet in the same person' preserves the exact identity-claim, the coincidence of power and wisdom, that makes the proposal so extravagant and so famous.

divergences.phrase: knowledge, ignorance, and opinion (being, not-being, and the in-between)
divergences.older: knowledge corresponded to being and ignorance of necessity to not-being, for that intermediate between being and not-being there has to be discovered a corresponding intermediate between ignorance and knowledge (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: knowledge was set over what is, and ignorance, necessarily, over what is not, then for this in-between thing we'll have to find something in between ignorance and knowledge
divergences.note: The argument that divides the philosopher from the lover of sights and sounds is the most technically demanding stretch in the book, and its force depends on three terms staying rigidly aligned: knowledge / being, ignorance / not-being, opinion / the in-between. Jowett's 'corresponded to' is vaguer than the Greek 'epi' (set over, ranged upon, assigned to its object), which makes each faculty correlate to a definite field. Rendering it consistently as 'set over what is / what is not / the in-between thing' keeps the parallelism visible so the reader can track the inference step by step, ending in the conclusion that the many beautiful things (which both are and are not beautiful) are objects of opinion, while the Beautiful itself is the object of knowledge.

divergences.phrase: the ship of state and the true pilot
divergences.older: Imagine then a fleet or a ship in which there is a captain who is taller and stronger than any of the crew, but he is a little deaf... the sailors are quarrelling with one another about the steering (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: Picture, then, a fleet, or a single ship, set up like this. There's a shipowner, taller and stronger than anyone else aboard, but a little deaf... The sailors are all quarreling with one another over the steering
divergences.note: The simile is the heart of Socrates' answer to why philosophers look useless, so the picture has to read like a scene, not a parable in costume. The Greek 'naukleros' is the ship's OWNER, not its working captain; Jowett's 'captain' blurs the very point, since the owner stands for the demos (the people who own the ship of state but can't steer it) while the despised stargazer is the real 'kybernetes', the navigator who alone knows the art. Lectio keeps 'shipowner' distinct from the 'navigator/pilot' throughout so the allegory's two roles never collapse, and renders the mutineers' contempt ('prater, star-gazer, good-for-nothing') as plain modern jeers that still sting.

divergences.phrase: the Good is beyond being (epekeina tes ousias)
divergences.older: the good is not essence, but far exceeds essence in dignity and power (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: the good is not itself existence, but lies even beyond existence, surpassing it in dignity and power
divergences.note: This is the single most famous and most contested line in the Republic, the claim that the Good is 'beyond being'. Jowett's 'essence' renders 'ousia' technically but, to a modern reader, sounds like a perfume or an extract rather than the sheer fact of a thing's existing. 'Existence/being' keeps the metaphysical force audible: the Good is the source of being yet is not on the same level as the things that have being. The matching pair earlier ('their very being and existence') is rendered consistently so the reader can feel the deliberate escalation 'beyond' it. Glaucon's almost comic outburst is kept ('What a staggering height!') because Plato plants it precisely to register how extreme the claim is.

divergences.phrase: the Divided Line and its four states of the soul
divergences.older: reason answering to the highest, understanding to the second, faith (or conviction) to the third, and perception of shadows to the last (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: reason answering to the highest, understanding to the second, conviction to the third, and the perception of images to the last
divergences.note: The Divided Line has to stay rigorous, since everything in Book VII (the Cave) hangs on it. The four faculties are noesis (reason/understanding), dianoia (the 'understanding' of the mathematician, working from hypotheses), pistis (belief/conviction about visible objects), and eikasia (the grasp of images/shadows). Jowett's 'faith' for pistis is misleading to a modern ear (it suggests religious faith); 'conviction' keeps the sense of a settled belief about the seen world. For eikasia, 'perception of images' is kept rather than the narrower 'perception of shadows', since the line's lowest objects are explicitly shadows AND reflections. The crucial mechanics, dianoia descending from hypotheses to a conclusion versus noesis ascending past hypotheses to an 'unhypothetical first principle' and moving 'through Forms, by way of Forms, to Forms', are rendered to stay trackable step by step.

divergences.phrase: the prisoners and the shadows on the wall
divergences.older: Jowett pictures an "underground den" with prisoners who from childhood have "their legs and necks chained," watching shadows thrown by a fire, with "a low wall built along the way, like the screen which marionette players have in front of them, over which they show the puppets."
divergences.lectio: We keep every concrete part of the machinery (the long entrance, the fire behind and above, the raised path, the low wall like a puppeteer's screen, the carried statues of men and animals) but trade Victorian stage-words like "den" and "marionette players" for a scene a modern reader can build in the mind's eye, so the apparatus reads as the deliberately strange contraption Plato designed and not as a quaint diorama.
divergences.note: The image's power depends on the reader actually visualizing the rig: who is chained, what casts the shadows, where the fire sits. We were careful to add nothing (no extra symbolism) and drop nothing (the echo, the talking carriers, the puppet-screen), so the allegory does the interpreting later, on its own terms.

divergences.phrase: education is not putting sight into blind eyes
divergences.older: Jowett: "certain professors of education must be wrong when they say that they can put a knowledge into the soul which was not there before, like sight into blind eyes," whereas "the instrument of knowledge can only by the movement of the whole soul be turned from the world of becoming into that of being."
divergences.lectio: We render Plato's periagōgē as "turning the whole soul," and frame education flatly as "the art of turning this power around": not filling an empty mind but re-aiming a power of sight the soul already has. The contrast (not inserting sight, but turning the eye the right way) is kept sharp and is stated as the book's thesis, not buried in a clause.
divergences.note: This is the conceptual heart of Book VII and the point the cave exists to make. Greek periagōgē is literally a "turning around," and the surrounding argument (the leaden weights of appetite, the clever rogue whose keen sight is aimed at evil) all turns on direction, not capacity. We were careful to keep "the whole soul" (holē hē psychē) rather than softening it to "the mind."

divergences.phrase: they must be made to go back down into the cave
divergences.older: Jowett: "they must be made to descend again among the prisoners in the den, and partake of their labours and honours"; the objection that this is "unjust" is answered by the legislator's aim that "the happiness was to be in the whole State."
divergences.lectio: We keep the compulsion blunt: the philosophers "must go down" again to live with the prisoners and "get used to seeing in the dark," and Glaucon's protest that this wrongs them is left fully in force before Socrates answers it. We resisted any softening that would make the return sound like a privilege rather than an imposed duty.
divergences.note: The required descent is what distinguishes Plato's philosopher-ruler from a contemplative who escapes the world; it is also the quiet echo of Socrates' own fate (the returned prisoner is mocked and, if he frees others, killed). Faithfulness demands that the return read as a genuine cost reluctantly accepted, which is exactly why the best rulers are the ones least eager to rule.

divergences.phrase: dialectic rises by reason alone to the first principle
divergences.older: Jowett: "dialectic, and dialectic alone, goes directly to the first principle"; it is "the coping-stone of the sciences," reached only by one who can "give and take a reason" and "abstract and define rationally the idea of good."
divergences.lectio: We render dialektikē as the power to "give and take an account" and to grasp "what each thing itself is" by reason alone, without the senses, until one reaches the Good itself. We keep Plato's architectural image ("coping-stone") and the demand that the dialectician "fight his way through every objection, as in a battle," rather than flattening dialectic into mere clever conversation.
divergences.note: Plato is precise that the mathematical sciences only "dream about" being because they leave their assumptions unexamined; dialectic alone "does away with its assumptions" and climbs to the unhypothetical first principle. We were careful to preserve that the lower studies are a prelude (prooimion) and dialectic the song itself (nomos), and to keep the four-part scale (knowledge, thought, belief, imagination) intact as the frame the ascent is measured against.

divergences.phrase: the nuptial number — the secret law of human breeding
divergences.older: the period of human birth is comprehended in a number in which first increments by involution and evolution (or squared and cubed) obtaining three intervals and four terms... (Jowett, with pages of bracketed arithmetic)
divergences.lectio: the cycle of human births is governed by a more elusive one — a number reached by raising the base figures to higher powers, working through three intervals and four terms... (this is the famous "nuptial number," a knot of arithmetic and geometry whose exact value has never been agreed; the point of it for the argument is simply that the timing of breeding is governed by a hidden law)
divergences.note: This is Book VIII's most notorious crux — the Muses' riddling "geometrical number" that supposedly sets the right times for the guardians to breed, and whose miscalculation begins the city's decline. The Greek is genuinely obscure, and Jowett floods the line with bracketed conjectures (216, 12,960,000, Pythagorean triangles) that have never been settled and that stop a modern reader cold. Lectio keeps Plato's actual claim — that there is a hidden mathematical cycle governing fertility, and that the rulers will lose track of it — and folds in a single plain gloss naming the "nuptial number," rather than reproducing competing arithmetic. Nothing in the argument turns on the exact figure; everything turns on the idea that the decline starts from a failure of knowledge about breeding, and that is preserved intact.

divergences.phrase: excess of liberty passes into excess of slavery
divergences.older: The excess of liberty, whether in States or individuals, seems only to pass into excess of slavery... liberty, getting out of all order and reason, passes into the harshest and bitterest form of slavery (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: Excess of liberty, whether in a state or in an individual, seems only to turn into excess of slavery... So liberty, breaking out of all measure and all reason, passes into the harshest and bitterest slavery there is
divergences.note: This is the hinge of Book VIII's politics and the line the whole sequence of regimes is built to deliver: democracy's defining good, freedom, pursued without limit, swings round into its opposite. The point must land hard and stay verbally consistent both times the thought appears (the diagnosis at 564a and the verdict at the book's close), so the reader can feel the argument close like a trap. Jowett's "getting out of all order and reason" is accurate but slack; "breaking out of all measure and all reason" keeps the Greek sense of metron (due measure, the limit that excess violates) audible. The pendulum image — too much of anything provokes a violent swing the other way — is preserved exactly, in weather, plants, animals, and above all in governments.

divergences.phrase: insolence they term breeding, anarchy liberty, waste magnificence, impudence courage
divergences.older: insolence they term breeding, and anarchy liberty, and waste magnificence, and impudence courage (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: insolence they rename good breeding, anarchy they call liberty, extravagance they call magnificence, and shamelessness they call courage
divergences.note: This is the moral core of the democratic man's formation: the appetites don't just win, they rebrand the vices as virtues, renaming each fault with the name of the quality it counterfeits. The crux is that this is a deliberate corruption of language — the same move Thucydides describes in the Corcyra passage — so the translation has to keep the one-for-one swap audible and the verbs of renaming explicit ("rename," "call") rather than letting it blur into a list. "Insolence ... good breeding" and "shamelessness ... courage" preserve the sting; nothing is softened, because the whole indictment of democratic liberty depends on the reader seeing that liberty here is a flattering new name for anarchy.

divergences.phrase: the lawless desires that wake in sleep; the master passion as a winged drone
divergences.older: those which are awake when the reasoning and human and ruling power is asleep; then the wild beast within us, gorged with meat or drink, starts up... a sort of monstrous winged drone (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: The ones that wake up when the rest of the soul is asleep, the reasoning, gentle, ruling part of us. Then the wild beast inside, gorged with food and drink, stirs... a kind of monstrous winged drone
divergences.note: This is the engine of the whole portrait of the tyrant, the bestial desires that surface in dreams and, once a master passion (Eros) is bred to lead them, take over the waking man. The crux is that these desires are present in everyone, even the decent, so the horror is psychological, not just political. Jowett's 'meat or drink' narrows the Greek (which is food generally), and his 'human power' for to logistikon is stilted; 'the reasoning, gentle, ruling part' keeps the three-part-soul vocabulary we've used since Book IV so the reader tracks that it's reason being lulled. 'Winged drone' is kept verbatim as a fixed image, since Plato is recalling the drone from Book VIII; softening it to 'parasite' or the like would break the thread.

divergences.phrase: the three pleasures, and the philosopher as the only competent judge
divergences.older: what ought to be the criterion? Is any better than experience and wisdom and reason?... pleasures which are approved by the lover of wisdom and reason are the truest (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: What ought we to judge by, if we want to judge well? Isn't it by experience, by intelligence, and by reasoning?... the pleasures the philosopher, the lover of reasoning, approves are the truest
divergences.note: The first of the three proofs that the just life is the happiest turns on a procedural point: the philosopher alone has tried all three lives (gain, honor, wisdom) and alone owns the instrument of judgment, reasoning, so his verdict on which life is most pleasant is the only trustworthy one. The argument has to read as a clean checklist, experience / intelligence / reasoning, because Plato applies each criterion in turn. Jowett's 'wisdom' for phronesis blurs into the later 'lover of wisdom'; 'intelligence' keeps them distinct. Rendering the three standards consistently every time they recur lets the reader see the proof close like a trap, which the Victorian phrasing obscures.

divergences.phrase: the many-headed beast, the lion, and the man; ruling the human creature within
divergences.older: model the form of a multitudinous, many-headed monster... a second form as of a lion, and a third of a man... give the man within him... the most complete mastery over the entire human creature (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: mold one form of a many-colored, many-headed beast... a second form, of a lion, and a third, of a man... give the inner man the firmest possible control over the whole human creature
divergences.note: The closing image is the payoff of the book and arguably of the whole work: the soul as a composite creature whose outer human shell hides a many-headed beast (the appetites), a lion (spirit), and a small inner man (reason), and justice is the inner man, with the lion as ally, ruling and taming the beast. The pun that injustice means feeding the monster and starving the human part has to land plainly. 'Multitudinous monster' is dead Victorian diction; 'many-colored, many-headed beast' restores the literal poikilon kai polykephalon. We keep 'human creature' for the whole composite and 'inner man' for the reasoning part, so the reader can feel the sting of the paradox, that to be unjust is to starve the very thing that makes you human. This sets up the 'city within himself' that the just man, not the politician, actually governs.

divergences.phrase: the three beds; the imitator thrice removed from the truth
divergences.older: the tragic poet is an imitator, and therefore, like all other imitators, he is thrice removed from the king and from the truth (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: the tragic poet, since he's an imitator too, is like all the rest of them: three removes from the king and from the truth
divergences.note: This is the philosophical engine of Book X: the Form of the bed that the god makes, the carpenter's bed copied from it, and the painter's bed copied from that, so the imitation stands at the third remove. Jowett's 'thrice removed' is accurate but reads as an antique fixed phrase; 'three removes from' keeps the exact count (which the whole argument rides on, the painter and poet are two steps below the carpenter, three below the truth) while letting a modern reader feel it as distance rather than incantation. The Greek triton apo tes aletheias, 'third from the truth,' is preserved without softening, and the god is kept as maker of the single natural Form (Jowett's capital-G 'God' is rendered lowercase 'a god' / 'the god' to keep Plato's Greek frame rather than importing later monotheism, matching how 'the god' is handled in the Book II divergence).

divergences.phrase: the ancient quarrel between philosophy and poetry
divergences.older: there is an ancient quarrel between philosophy and poetry; of which there are many proofs, such as the saying of 'the yelping hound howling at her lord' (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: there's an old quarrel between philosophy and poetry. There are plenty of signs of it: 'the bitch that yelps and snarls at her master'
divergences.note: This line names the rivalry the whole book has been staging, the reason the city must exile imitative poetry. The crux is the tone of the quoted slanders that poets throw at philosophy: Jowett's 'yelping hound howling at her lord' is genteel and blurs the insult. The Greek kuon is bluntly a dog (a bitch, with the contemptuous force the image carries), snapping at its master, so 'the bitch that yelps and snarls at her master' keeps the sneer the quarrel needs. 'Old quarrel' for palaia diaphora is plainer and harder-edged than 'ancient quarrel,' which has gone soft with overuse. The fragments are rendered as live taunts, not curiosities, so the reader hears an actual feud, not a footnote.

divergences.phrase: the blame is the chooser's; God is blameless
divergences.older: Virtue is free, and as a man honours or dishonours her he will have more or less of her; the responsibility is with the chooser—God is justified (Jowett)
divergences.lectio: Virtue has no master; each will have more of it or less according as he honors or dishonors her. The blame belongs to the one who chooses. God is blameless.
divergences.note: This is the moral hinge of the Myth of Er and arguably of the whole Republic: souls choose their own lives, so the responsibility is theirs and not heaven's. The Greek aitia helomenou; theos anaitios is a tight, almost legal antithesis, aitia (blame, cause, guilt) set against anaitios (blameless, without cause). Jowett's 'God is justified' subtly shifts it toward a defense of God (theodicy), whereas Plato simply removes God from the dock: the cause lies with the chooser. 'The blame belongs to the one who chooses; God is blameless' keeps the bald antithesis and the courtroom ring, and 'virtue has no master' (arete adespoton, literally 'ownerless') renders the radical claim that virtue answers to no one and is in each soul's own power. Nothing is softened: the point is that we cannot pin our ruined lives on the gods.

segments.text: I went down to the Piraeus yesterday with Glaucon, the son of Ariston, to offer my prayers to the goddess — Bendis, the Thracian Artemis — and to see how they would put on the festival, this being the first time it was held. I thought the procession our own people made was beautiful, though the one the Thracians marched in looked every bit as good. We said our prayers, watched the spectacle, and set off back toward the city. And just then Polemarchus, the son of Cephalus, caught sight of us from a distance, starting on the road home, and sent his slave running ahead to tell us to wait for him. The boy caught my cloak from behind and said: Polemarchus asks you to wait.

spine.text: Yesterday I went down to the Piraeus with Glaucon, the son of Ariston. I wanted to say my prayers to the goddess, and I was also curious to see how they would run the festival, since this was the first time it was being held. The local procession struck me as fine, but the one the Thracians put on was just as good, if not better. When we had finished praying and watching, we turned back toward the city.
I turned around and asked where his master was.

Just then Polemarchus, the son of Cephalus, spotted us from a distance, heading home, and sent his slave running ahead to ask us to wait. The boy caught me by the cloak from behind. 'Polemarchus wants you to wait,' he said.
There he is, said the boy — coming up behind you. Just wait.
I turned and asked him where his master was.

Of course we'll wait, said Glaucon; and in a few minutes Polemarchus came up, with Adeimantus, Glaucon's brother, Niceratus the son of Nicias, and several others, all on their way from the procession.
'Right behind you,' said the boy. 'He's coming. Just wait.'
Polemarchus said: Socrates, it looks to me as if you two are heading back to the city.

'Of course we'll wait,' said Glaucon. A moment later Polemarchus arrived, and with him Adeimantus, Glaucon's brother, and Niceratus, the son of Nicias, and several others, all of them coming from the procession.
A fair guess, I said.
'Socrates,' said Polemarchus, 'it looks to me as if the two of you are already on your way back to the city.'
But do you see how many of us there are? he said.
'You're not wrong,' I said.
Of course.
'Well, do you see how many of us there are?' he said.
Well then, he said, either prove yourselves stronger than all of us, or stay where you are.
'Obviously.'
Isn't there one option left, I said — that we persuade you to let us go?
'Then either you're stronger than all of us,' he said, 'or you're staying here.'
And could you persuade us, he said, if we refused to listen?
'Isn't there another option?' I said. 'We might persuade you to let us go.'
Not a chance, said Glaucon.
'And how could you persuade us,' he said, 'if we refuse to listen?'
Then you'd better make up your minds to it: we won't be listening.
'There's no way,' said Glaucon.
Adeimantus added: Hasn't anyone told you there's a torch-race on horseback this evening, in honor of the goddess?
'Then take it for granted that we won't be listening.'
On horseback! I said. That's something new. You mean riders carrying torches and handing them on to one another as they race?
Adeimantus put in, 'Don't you know about the torch race tonight, on horseback, in honor of the goddess?'

Exactly, said Polemarchus — and there's an all-night celebration besides, which will be worth watching. We'll go out after dinner and see it. There will be crowds of young men there, and we'll talk. So stay — don't be difficult.
'On horseback?' I said. 'That's something new. You mean the riders will carry torches and pass them to each other as they race?'
It looks as if we'll have to, said Glaucon.

'Exactly,' said Polemarchus, 'and there'll be an all-night festival too, which is worth seeing. We'll get up after dinner and go watch, and there'll be plenty of young men there to talk with. So stay. Don't make this difficult.'
Then it's settled, I said.
'It seems we have no choice,' said Glaucon.

So we went home with Polemarchus, and there we found his brothers Lysias and Euthydemus, and with them Thrasymachus of Chalcedon, Charmantides of Paeania, and Cleitophon the son of Aristonymus. Polemarchus's father Cephalus was there too. I hadn't seen him in a long while, and he seemed to me to have grown very old. He was sitting on a cushioned chair with a garland on his head — he had just been sacrificing in the courtyard — and other chairs stood around the room in a half-circle, so we sat down beside him. The moment he saw me, Cephalus greeted me warmly, and then he said:
'If that's how it is,' I said, 'then that's what we'll do.'

Socrates, you don't come down to see us as often as you should. If I were still strong enough to make the trip up to town easily, you wouldn't need to come here — I would come to you. But as things are, you must visit the Piraeus more often. I want you to know: in my case, as the body's pleasures wither away, the appetite for conversation and the delight I take in it grow in exact proportion. So don't refuse me. Keep company with these young men, and come here to us as to old friends — as to your own family.

So we went along with Polemarchus to his house, and there we found his brothers Lysias and Euthydemus, along with Thrasymachus of Chalcedon, Charmantides of the deme Paeania, and Cleitophon, the son of Aristonymus. Polemarchus's father, Cephalus, was there too. I hadn't seen him in a long while, and I thought he looked quite old. He was sitting on a cushioned chair with a garland on his head, since he had just been performing a sacrifice in the courtyard. There were other chairs arranged in a half-circle, and we sat down beside him. The moment he saw me, Cephalus greeted me warmly.

And I enjoy it, Cephalus, I said. I like talking with the very old. They have gone ahead of us on a road that we too will probably have to travel, and I think we ought to ask them what it's like — rough and hard going, or smooth and easy. You have reached the point the poets call ‘the threshold of old age,’ and I would especially like to hear what you make of it. Is it a hard stretch of life? What is your report?

'Socrates,' he said, 'you don't come down to see us in the Piraeus nearly often enough. You really should. If I still had the strength to travel up to the city to see you, I wouldn't ask you to come to me. But at my age that's hard, so you must come here more often. I'll tell you, the more the pleasures of the body fade, the more I crave good conversation and the more I enjoy it. So don't refuse me. Make this house your second home, and spend time with these young men. We're old friends, and you'll be at ease with us.'

I'll tell you, Socrates, he said, exactly how it looks to me. Several of us of about the same age often gather together — birds of a feather, as the old proverb has it. And when we meet, most of the company do nothing but grieve. They miss the pleasures of their youth — the sex, the drinking, the feasts and everything that goes with them — and they carry on as though they had been robbed of great things: life was good then, and what they have now is no life at all. Some of them complain of the insults an old man suffers from his own family, and on that theme they recite the whole litany of miseries old age has caused them. But in my view, Socrates, they are blaming the wrong thing. If old age were the cause, it would have done the same to me and to every other man who has grown old. In fact I have known others who don't feel that way at all — above all the poet Sophocles. I was with him once when someone asked him: How is it with you and sex, Sophocles? Can you still be with a woman? Quiet, man, he said. It is the sweetest relief to have escaped all that — like escaping from a raging, savage master. I thought it a good answer then, and I think so still. For in old age comes a deep peace and freedom from such things. When the appetites slacken and loosen their grip, then what Sophocles said comes true exactly: we are set free from a whole crowd of raving masters. But of all these complaints, including the grievances about family, there is one true cause — not old age, Socrates, but a man's character. For someone with an orderly and contented nature, old age weighs only moderately. For the other sort, youth is as heavy a burden as age.

'There's nothing I'd like better, Cephalus,' I said. 'I love talking with men who are well along in years. They've traveled a road I may have to travel myself, and it seems right to ask them what the going is like, whether it's smooth and easy or rough and hard. So I'd like to ask you, now that you've reached the stage the poets call "the threshold of old age," how does it look from there? Is the last stretch of life a hard one? What's your report?'

I was delighted with him, and because I wanted to keep him talking, I prodded: Cephalus, I suspect most people don't believe a word of this. They think you carry old age lightly not because of your character but because of your money. The rich, they say, have many consolations.

'I'll tell you exactly how it seems to me, Socrates,' he said. 'Men of my age get together often, like birds of a feather, as the old saying goes, and when we meet, most of them are full of complaints. They miss the pleasures of their youth, the eating and drinking, the love affairs, and they mourn for them as if they'd lost something enormous. In those days, they say, life was really living, and now it's no life at all. Some of them grumble about how their own families slight them in their old age, and they go on and on about all the miseries that age has brought them. But it seems to me, Socrates, that these men are blaming the wrong thing. If old age were really the cause, then I would feel the same way, and so would every other old man. But that hasn't been my experience, nor that of others I've known. I remember the poet Sophocles being asked once, "Sophocles, how are you doing with love? Can you still make love to a woman?" And he answered, "Quiet, man! It's the greatest relief in the world to have escaped that. It's like getting free of a savage and raging master." I thought that was well said then, and I think so still. Old age brings real peace and freedom from things like that. When the appetites loosen their grip and finally let go, you're released, exactly as Sophocles said, not from one mad master but from many. The truth is, Socrates, that all these complaints, and the family troubles too, come from the same source, and it isn't old age. It's a man's character. If a man is decent and even-tempered, age is no great burden to him. But if he's the opposite, then youth was hard on him and old age is hard on him too.'

You're right, he said; they don't believe me. And there is something in what they say — only not as much as they think. Themistocles' answer fits here. A man from Seriphus was needling him, saying his fame came from his city and not from himself; and he replied that he himself would never have become famous had he been born in Seriphus — but neither would the Seriphian, had he been born in Athens. The same answer fits men who aren't rich and find old age hard to bear: a decent man wouldn't carry old age easily in poverty, but a bad man, however rich he got, would never be at peace with himself.

I admired what he said, and because I wanted to draw him out further, I pushed back a little. 'Cephalus,' I said, 'I suspect most people won't believe you when you talk like that. They'll think old age sits lightly on you not because of your character but because you're rich, and wealth, as everyone knows, brings plenty of consolation.'
Cephalus, I said, tell me — did you inherit most of what you have, or did you make it yourself?

'You're right,' he said, 'they don't believe me, and there's something in what they say, though not as much as they think. There's a good answer to them, the one Themistocles gave to the man from Seriphos who was insulting him, saying his fame came not from himself but from his being an Athenian. "True," said Themistocles, "if I'd been born in Seriphos I'd be nobody, but neither would you, even if you were an Athenian." The same answer fits men who aren't rich and find old age hard. A good man who is poor won't find old age easy, but a bad man won't be at peace with himself no matter how rich he is.'

Make it, Socrates? he said. As a man of business I've fallen somewhere between my grandfather and my father. My grandfather — whose name I carry — inherited about the fortune I hold now and multiplied it many times over; my father, Lysanias, drew it down below what it is today. As for me, I'll be content to leave these boys here not less than I received — and a little more.
'And the money you have, Cephalus,' I said, 'did you mostly inherit it or make it yourself?'

The reason I asked, I said, is that you never seemed to me to care much for money, and that is generally the mark of a man who didn't make it himself. The self-made are twice as attached to it as anyone else. They love their money the way poets love their poems and fathers love their children — as their own creation — on top of loving it for what it can do, the way the rest of us do. It makes them hard company: they have no good word for anything but wealth.

'Make it?' he said. 'As a money-maker, Socrates, I fall somewhere between my grandfather and my father. My grandfather, whose name I have, inherited about as much as I own now, and multiplied it several times over. My father, Lysanias, cut it down to less than it is today. As for me, I'll be satisfied if I leave to my sons here not less than I received, and maybe a little more.'
That's true, he said.

'I asked,' I said, 'because you don't strike me as someone who's especially attached to money, which is usually the way with men who've inherited their wealth rather than made it. People who've made their own fortunes are twice as fond of it. Just as poets love their own poems and parents love their own children, money-makers love their wealth as something they themselves created, on top of the ordinary love everyone has for it because it's useful. They're tiresome company for it, too, since they can't talk about anything but the praises of money.'
It certainly is, I said. But tell me this much more: what do you think is the greatest good you have enjoyed from having a large fortune?
'That's true,' he said.

Something, he said, that most people would never take my word for. Understand this, Socrates: when a man begins to face the thought that he will die, fear and worry come over him about things that never touched him before. The stories told about the world below — how the man who did wrong here must pay for it there — stories he once laughed at, begin to torture his soul with the thought that they might be true. And whether from the weakness of age, or because he now stands closer to that other place and sees it more distinctly, he fills up with doubt and dread, and starts running his accounts, asking whether he has wronged anyone. The man who finds a life full of injustices in his ledger wakes from his sleep in terror, again and again, the way children do, and lives in dark foreboding. But the man who knows he has done no wrong has sweet hope always at his side — as Pindar so charmingly says, the kind nurse of his old age. His words are these:
'It certainly is,' I said. 'But let me ask you one more thing. What would you say is the greatest benefit you've gotten from being wealthy?'

‘Hope,’ he says, ‘keeps warm the heart of the man who lives in justice and holiness — hope, the nurse of his old age, the companion of his road; hope, which more than anything steers the veering, restless mind of mortals.’

'It's something most people wouldn't easily believe,' he said. 'I'll tell you, Socrates. When a man begins to think he may die soon, fears and worries crowd into his mind that were never there before. The old stories about the world below, about punishment there for wrongs done here, that he used to laugh at, now begin to torment his soul, in case they should be true. Whether it's the weakness of age or because he's nearer to that other world and sees it more clearly, he becomes full of suspicion and dread. He starts going over his life, reckoning up the wrongs he has done. And if he finds them many, he wakes in the night like a frightened child, and lives in dark foreboding. But the man with nothing on his conscience has sweet hope always at his side, a kind nurse to his old age, as Pindar so beautifully puts it.

Marvelously well said — wonderfully well. And it is just here that I set the great worth of having money — not for every man, but for the decent one. Wealth does a great deal to keep a man from cheating or lying, even against his will, and from leaving for that other world afraid — still owing sacrifices to a god, or money to a man. It has many other uses too. But weighing one thing against another, Socrates, I would say that for a man of sense, this is what wealth is best for.
For Pindar says, with real charm, that whoever lives a just and holy life has "hope to nurse his old age and keep his heart company, hope that more than anything steers the restless mind of mortals."

You put it beautifully, Cephalus, I said. But this very thing, justice — what shall we say it is? Simply telling the truth and giving back whatever you have taken from anyone? Or can those very acts be sometimes just and sometimes unjust? Here is what I mean. Everyone would surely agree that if you borrowed weapons from a friend while he was in his right mind, and he went mad and demanded them back, you shouldn't return them — the man who returned them would not be doing right, nor would a man determined to tell the whole truth to someone in that state.

How well he says it! And this, to my mind, is where wealth is most valuable, not to everyone, but to a decent man. If you've never had to cheat or deceive anyone, even unintentionally, then you won't depart for the next world in terror, owing sacrifices to a god or debts to a man. Wealth helps a great deal here, because it lets you settle your accounts. It has many other uses, but for a sensible man, this, I think, is what it's chiefly good for.'
You're right, he said.

'Beautifully put, Cephalus,' I said. 'But this thing you mention, justice, are we to say it's simply telling the truth and paying back whatever you've taken? Or can even these acts sometimes be just and sometimes not? Suppose a friend, while in his right mind, leaves his weapons with me for safekeeping, and then comes back for them out of his mind.
