A true prophecy, he said.

'Now you've taken a harder, sturdier line,' I said, 'and it's not so easy to answer. If you'd only said that injustice pays but still admitted, as most people do, that it's a vice and something shameful, we could have replied to you on the usual assumptions. But as it is, you'll plainly call injustice fine and strong, and you'll grant it all the qualities we used to assign to justice, since you've dared to class it with intelligence and goodness.'

Still, I said, I must not flinch from following the argument through, so long as I take you to be saying what you actually think. Because I believe you are genuinely not joking now, Thrasymachus — you are saying what you take to be the truth.
'You read my mind perfectly,' he said.
What difference does it make to you, he said, whether I believe it or not? Refute the position.

'Still, I shouldn't shrink from following the argument through,' I said, 'as long as I believe you're really saying what you think. For now I'm convinced, Thrasymachus, that you're in earnest and not just toying with us.'
None at all, I said. But try to answer me this one thing more: does the just man want to get the better of another just man?
'What does it matter to you,' he said, 'whether I'm in earnest or not? Just refute the argument.'
Not at all, he said. Otherwise he wouldn't be the charming innocent he is.
'You're right, it doesn't,' I said. 'But try to answer one more question. Do you think the just man would ever want to outdo another just man, to get more than his fair share against him?'
And would he try to go beyond what a just action allows?
'Not at all,' he said. 'If he did, he wouldn't be the charming simpleton he is.'
No.
'And would he want to outdo a just action, to go beyond it?'
And getting the better of the unjust man — would he think that just, or unjust?
'No, not that either.'
He would think it just, he said, and he would try — but he wouldn't have it in him.
'But would he claim it's right to outdo the unjust man, and want to do it? Would he think that just or not?'
That is not my question, I said. My question is whether the just man refuses to get the better of his like, another just man, while thinking it right to get the better of his unlike, the unjust?
'He'd think it just,' he said, 'and he'd want to do it, but he wouldn't be able to.'
Yes — that's how it is.
'That's not my question,' I said. 'I'm only asking whether the just man refuses to outdo another just man but claims the right to outdo the unjust one.'
And the unjust man? Does he claim to get the better of the just man and the just action?
'Yes,' he said, 'that's right.'
Of course, he said — he claims to get the better of everyone.
'And the unjust man, does he claim the right to outdo the just man and the just action?'
So the unjust man will also strive to get the better of another unjust man and his action — he will fight to take the most of everything for himself?
'Of course,' he said. 'He claims the right to outdo everyone.'
True.
'So the unjust man will try to outdo even another unjust man and another unjust action, struggling to grab the most of everything for himself?'
Then let's put it this way, I said: the just man does not try to get the better of his like, but of his unlike; the unjust man tries to get the better of both his like and his unlike.
'Yes.'
Nothing could be better put, he said.
'Then let's put it this way,' I said. 'The just man doesn't try to outdo his like but only his unlike; the unjust man tries to outdo both his like and his unlike.'
And the unjust man is intelligent and good, and the just man neither?
'Beautifully put,' he said.
Good again, he said.
'And the unjust man is intelligent and good, the just man neither?'
And doesn't the unjust man also resemble the intelligent and the good, while the just man does not resemble them?
'That's good too,' he said.
Naturally, he said — being the kind of man he is, he resembles others of that kind; the just man doesn't.
'And so the unjust man resembles the intelligent and good man, while the just man doesn't?'
Fine. Then each of them is of the same character as those he resembles?
'Of course,' he said. 'A man of a certain character resembles others of that character, and a man who isn't, doesn't.'
Certainly, he said.
'Good. So each of them has the character of the people he resembles?'
Very good, Thrasymachus. Now, do you call one man musical and another unmusical?
'Naturally,' he said.
I do.
'Very well, Thrasymachus. Now, do you grant that one man is musical and another unmusical?'
Which of the two is intelligent, and which is not?
'I do.'
The musical man is intelligent, obviously, and the unmusical one is not.
'And which is intelligent and which is foolish?'
And where he is intelligent, he is good at it; where he is unintelligent, bad?
'Clearly the musical man is intelligent, and the unmusical one foolish.'
Yes.
'And insofar as he's intelligent, he's good; insofar as he's foolish, bad?'
And the same for a doctor?
'Yes.'
The same.
'And the same for a doctor?'

Then tell me, my friend: does a musician tuning a lyre want to get the better of another musician — to outdo him in the tightening and loosening of the strings — or claim to deserve more than another musician?
'The same.'
I don't think so.
'Now, my good man, do you think a musician, in tuning a lyre, would want to outdo another musician, to claim the right to more in the tightening and loosening of the strings?'
But the better of the unmusical man — yes?
'I don't think so.'
Of course.
'But he'd want to outdo a non-musician?'
And a doctor — in prescribing food and drink, would he want to get the better of another doctor, or of the medical art itself?
'Of course.'
He would not.
'And the doctor? In prescribing food and drink, would he want to outdo another doctor, or the medical art itself?'
But the better of the non-doctor — yes?
'No.'
Yes.
'But he'd want to outdo a non-doctor?'

Now look at knowledge and ignorance in general. Does any man who knows — whatever his field — want to choose to do or say more than another man who knows? Wouldn't he rather do the very same as his like in the same situation?
'Yes.'
Well — perhaps that must be so, he said.

'Now think about all knowledge and ignorance generally. Do you think any man who has knowledge would want to outdo another knowledgeable man, to get more than him in what he says or does? Wouldn't he rather do and say the same as someone like himself in the same situation?'
And the ignorant man? Wouldn't he try to get the better of the knower and the ignorant alike?
'Perhaps that has to be so,' he said.
Perhaps.
'And the ignorant man? Wouldn't he want to outdo both the knowledgeable man and the ignorant one alike?'
And the man who knows is wise?
'Maybe so.'
Yes.
'And the man with knowledge is intelligent?'
And the wise man is good?
'Yes.'
True.
'And the intelligent man is good?'
Then the good and wise man will not want to get the better of his like — only of his unlike, his opposite?
'Yes.'
So it seems, he said.
'So the good and intelligent man won't want to outdo his like, but only his unlike, his opposite?'
While the bad and ignorant man will try to get the better of both?
'So it seems,' he said.
Apparently.
'While the bad and ignorant man wants to outdo both his like and his unlike?'
Now, Thrasymachus, I said: didn't we find that the unjust man tries to get the better of both his like and his unlike? Weren't those your words?
'Apparently.'
They were, he said.
'Now, Thrasymachus,' I said, 'didn't we say that the unjust man tries to outdo both his like and his unlike? Weren't those your words?'
And the just man will get the better of his unlike, but not of his like?
'They were.'
Yes.
'And that the just man won't try to outdo his like, but only his unlike?'
Then the just man resembles the wise and good, I said, and the unjust man the bad and ignorant.
'Yes.'
It looks that way.
'So the just man resembles the intelligent and good man, and the unjust man resembles the bad and ignorant one.'
But we agreed that each of them is of the same character as the one he resembles.
'It looks that way.'
We did.
'And we agreed that each has the character of the one he resembles.'
Then the just man stands revealed to us as good and wise, and the unjust as ignorant and bad.
'We did.'

Thrasymachus agreed to all of this, but not the easy way I'm telling it now — he was dragged to it, step by step, sweating tremendously, for it was a summer's day. And then I saw something I had never seen before: Thrasymachus blushing. Anyway, once we had agreed that justice is virtue and wisdom, and injustice vice and ignorance, I moved on:
'So the just man has turned out to be good and intelligent, and the unjust man ignorant and bad.'
Fine, I said; let's call that settled. But we also said that injustice is strong — powerful. Do you remember, Thrasymachus?

Thrasymachus conceded all this, but not as easily as I now relate it. He had to be dragged to it, sweating, for it was a blazing summer day. And then I saw something I'd never seen before: Thrasymachus blushing. Once we'd agreed that justice is virtue and intelligence, and injustice vice and ignorance, I went on.

I remember, he said. But I'm not satisfied with what you're saying now either, and I have plenty to say about it. Of course, if I said it, I know perfectly well you would accuse me of making speeches. So either let me talk as long as I like, or, if you insist on asking questions, ask away — and I will do for you what we do for old women telling their tales: I'll say ‘very good,’ and nod, and shake my head.
'Good,' I said. 'Let's take that as settled. But we also said that injustice is strong. Do you remember, Thrasymachus?'
Only never against your real opinion, I said.

'I remember,' he said, 'but I'm not happy even with what you just said, and I have something to say about it. Only, if I said it, I know you'd accuse me of making speeches. So either let me speak my piece, or, if you'd rather keep asking questions, go ahead and ask, and I'll do what one does with old women telling tales: I'll say "Fine," and nod yes and no.'
To please you, he said — since you won't let me speak. What more do you want?
'But don't do it against your real opinion,' I said.
Nothing, by God, I said. If that's what you're going to do, do it. I'll ask my questions.
'I'll answer to please you,' he said, 'since you won't let me make a speech. What else do you want?'
Ask, then.
'Nothing, by Zeus,' I said. 'If that's what you'll do, do it, and I'll ask the questions.'

Then I ask what I asked before, so that our examination of justice and injustice can proceed in order — what each of them really is, compared with the other. It was said at some point that injustice is more powerful and stronger than justice. But now, I said, if justice is wisdom and virtue, it will easily be shown, I think, to be stronger than injustice, since injustice is ignorance — no one could still miss that. But I don't want it settled so flatly, Thrasymachus; I want to look at it another way. You would say that a city can be unjust — that it can try to enslave other cities unjustly, and succeed, and hold many of them enslaved under itself?
'Then ask away.'
Of course, he said. And the best city — the one most completely unjust — is precisely the one that will do it.

'I'll ask what I asked before, so we can go through our inquiry into justice and injustice in order. The claim was that injustice is stronger and more powerful than justice. But now that justice has turned out to be intelligence and virtue, it'll easily be shown to be stronger than injustice, since injustice is ignorance, as no one can now deny. But I don't want to leave it there, Thrasymachus. I want to look at it differently. Would you say that a city can be unjust, and can try to enslave other cities unjustly, and succeed, and hold many of them in subjection?'
I understand, I said — that was your argument. But here is what I am examining: will the city that becomes master of another hold that power without justice, or will it need justice to do it?
'Of course,' he said. 'And the best city will do this best, the one that's most perfectly unjust.'
If it is as you were just saying, he said — justice is wisdom — then with justice. But if it is as I said, with injustice.
'I understand that's your position,' I said. 'But here's what I want to examine: when one city becomes master of another, can it hold that power without justice, or must it have justice too?'
I'm delighted, Thrasymachus, I said — you are not just nodding and shaking your head; you are giving beautiful answers.
'If you're right that justice is intelligence,' he said, 'then it needs justice. But if I'm right, then it doesn't.'
I'm indulging you, he said.
'I'm delighted, Thrasymachus,' I said, 'that you're not just nodding yes and no, but giving fine answers.'

Kind of you. Then indulge me this far too, and tell me: do you think a city, or an army, or a gang of bandits or thieves, or any other group that goes after some common purpose unjustly, could accomplish anything at all if its members wronged one another?
'I'm doing it to please you,' he said.
Certainly not, he said.

'How kind of you. Now please me with one more. Do you think a city, an army, a band of robbers or thieves, or any group out to do wrong together, could accomplish anything if its members wronged one another?'
And if they didn't wrong one another? They would do better?
'No, they couldn't,' he said.
Certainly.
'And if they didn't wrong one another, they'd accomplish more?'
Because injustice, Thrasymachus, breeds factions and hatreds and fighting among them, while justice brings concord and friendship. Isn't that so?
'Certainly.'
Let it be so, he said — I don't want to quarrel with you.
'Because injustice, Thrasymachus, breeds factions and hatreds and fighting among them, while justice brings unity and friendship. Isn't that so?'

Very generous of you, my friend. Now tell me this: if the work of injustice is to plant hatred wherever it goes, then whenever it turns up — among free men or among slaves — won't it make them hate one another and split into factions, until they are incapable of doing anything together?
'Let it be so,' he said, 'I don't want to quarrel with you.'
Certainly.

'And good of you not to, my friend. But tell me this. If it's the nature of injustice to plant hatred wherever it's found, then when it springs up among free men or slaves, won't it make them hate one another, split them into factions, and leave them unable to act together?'
And if it turns up in two people? Won't they quarrel, and hate each other, and be enemies to each other and to the just alike?
'It will.'
They will.
'And even between just two men, if injustice arises, won't they fall out, hate each other, and become enemies both to one another and to the just?'
And if injustice takes up residence in a single man, my remarkable friend — will it lose its power, or keep it undiminished?
'They will.'
Let's say it keeps it, he said.
'And suppose injustice takes up residence in a single man. Will it lose its power, or keep it intact?'

Then its power appears to be something like this: whatever it enters — a city, a family, an army, anything at all — it makes that thing, first, incapable of acting as one, because of the factions and quarrels it stirs up, and second, an enemy — to itself, to everything that opposes it, and to the just. Isn't that so?
'Let's say it keeps it,' he said.
Certainly.

'Then doesn't its power work like this: wherever it settles, in a city, a family, an army, or anything else, it first makes that thing incapable of acting as one, because of the internal strife and division injustice breeds, and then it makes it an enemy to itself and to everything opposed to it, and to whatever is just? Isn't that how it works?'

Then in a single man too, I suppose, it will do everything it is its nature to do. First it will make him incapable of action, at faction and war with himself, divided against himself; and then it will make him an enemy — to himself and to the just. Yes?
'Certainly.'
Yes.

'And in a single man, I imagine, it will do exactly the same. It will make him incapable of acting, because he's at war within himself and not of one mind, and it will make him his own enemy, and an enemy to the just. Won't it?'
And the gods too, my friend, are just?
'Yes.'
Let's say so, he said.
'And the gods, my friend, are they not just?'
Then the unjust man will be an enemy of the gods, Thrasymachus, and the just man their friend.
'Granted,' he said.
Feast yourself on the argument, he said — enjoy it, don't hold back. I won't cross you; I don't want these people turning against me.
'So the unjust man will be an enemy of the gods, Thrasymachus, and the just man their friend?'

Then come, I said — serve me the rest of the banquet by answering as you have been. We have shown that the just are wiser and better and more capable of action, and that the unjust can't act together at all. In fact, when we speak of unjust men ever pulling off some vigorous piece of work together, we aren't speaking quite truly: they could never have kept their hands off each other if they were wholly unjust. Clearly there was some justice in them — enough to stop them from wronging each other at the same time as their victims — and it was by that justice that they did what they did. They set out on their crimes only half-corrupted by injustice; for those wholly corrupted, the perfectly unjust, are also perfectly incapable of getting anything done. That, I take it, is how things stand — not as you laid it down at first. But there remains the question we set aside for later: whether the just also live better than the unjust, and are happier. To me they obviously are, even from what we have said so far. Still, we must look at it more closely. This is no idle topic — it is how a man ought to live.
'Feast on the argument all you like,' he said. 'I won't fight you, for fear of offending the company.'
Look, then, he said.

'Then finish the feast for me,' I said, 'by going on answering as you've been doing. We've shown that the just are wiser and better and more capable of action, while the unjust can't even act together. In fact, when we talk about men who are thoroughly bad acting effectively as a group, we don't speak quite accurately. If they'd been completely unjust, they could never have kept their hands off one another. Clearly there was some remnant of justice left in them that kept them from wronging each other as they wronged their victims. That's what got them as far as they got, but they were only half-villains in their crimes, because men who are utterly unjust and bad through and through are also utterly incapable of doing anything. That much I now see is true, and not what you said at first. But there was a further question we set out to examine: whether the just live a better and happier life than the unjust. I think they clearly do, from what we've already said, but let's look at it more carefully, because this is no trivial matter. It's nothing less than the question of how one ought to live.'
I am looking, I said. Tell me: would you say a horse has a function?
'Go on, then,' he said.
I would.
'I will. Tell me, would you say a horse has some function?'
And would you take the function of a horse — or of anything else — to be the work that can be done only with it, or done best with it?
'I would.'
I don't follow, he said.
'And would you call the function of a horse, or of anything else, that work which can be done only with it, or best done with it?'
Try this: can you see with anything except eyes?
'I don't follow,' he said.
Certainly not.
'Let me put it this way. Can you see with anything but your eyes?'
Or hear with anything except ears?
'Certainly not.'
No.
'Or hear with anything but your ears?'
Then we would rightly call these their functions?
'No.'
We would.
'So we'd be right to call seeing and hearing the functions of these?'
Now, you could cut a vine-shoot with a carving knife, or a chisel, or plenty of other tools?
'Yes.'
Of course.
'And again: you could cut off a vine shoot with a carving knife or a chisel or many other tools.'
But with nothing so well, I think, as the pruning-hook made for the job?
'Of course.'
True.
'But with none of them so well as with a pruning knife made for the job?'
Then shall we set that down as its function?
'True.'
We shall.
'So shall we call that the pruning knife's function?'
Now I think you will see better what I was asking before: whether the function of each thing is the work it alone can do, or the work it does more finely than anything else.
'We shall.'
I see it, he said — and I think that is a thing's function.
'Now I think you'll grasp what I meant when I asked whether the function of a thing is what can be done only with it, or best done with it.'
Good, I said. And doesn't everything that has a function assigned to it also have an excellence — a virtue of its own? Back to the same examples: eyes have a function, we say?
'Yes,' he said, 'I understand, and I agree.'
They do.
'And does each thing that has a function also have a virtue, an excellence? Let's go back to our examples. We said the eyes have a function?'
So eyes have an excellence as well?
'They do.'
They have.
'And do the eyes have a virtue too?'
And ears too have a function and an excellence?
'Yes.'
True.
'And the ears have a function and a virtue?'
And the same for everything else? Each thing has a function and an excellence of its own?
'Yes.'
That is so.
'And the same for everything else?'
Hold on, then: could eyes ever perform their function well if they lacked their own proper excellence and had, instead of it, the corresponding defect?
'The same.'
How could they? he said. You mean blindness instead of sight, I suppose.
'Now then, could the eyes ever do their work well if they lacked their own proper virtue and had its defect instead?'

Whatever their excellence may be, I said — I'm not asking about that yet. I'm asking whether it is by their own proper excellence that things perform their function well, and by the defect that they perform it badly.
'How could they,' he said, 'if they were blind and couldn't see?'
That much is true, he said.

'You mean if they lacked their proper virtue, which is sight. But I'm not at that point yet. I'm only asking, more generally, whether things do their work well by their own proper virtue and badly by their own proper defect.'
So ears too, deprived of their excellence, will do their work badly?
'That's true,' he said.
Certainly.
'And the ears, deprived of their proper virtue, can't do their work?'
And we may bring everything else under the same rule?
'True.'
So it seems to me.
'And the same goes for everything else?'

Then next, consider this: does the soul have a function — something you could not accomplish with anything else in the world? Take managing, ruling, deliberating, and everything of that kind: is there anything but the soul to which we could rightly assign this work and say it is proper to it?
'I think so.'
Nothing else.
'Then consider this. Doesn't the soul have a function that nothing else could perform? Managing, ruling, deliberating, and the like. Could we rightly assign these to anything but the soul?'
And what about living? Shall we count that a function of the soul?
'To nothing else.'
Very much so, he said.
'And living? Isn't that one of the soul's functions?'
And so the soul has an excellence too?
'Absolutely,' he said.
It has.
'And do we say the soul has a virtue too?'
And will the soul ever accomplish its functions well, Thrasymachus, if it is deprived of its own excellence — or is that impossible?
'We do.'
Impossible.
'And could the soul ever perform its functions well if deprived of its own virtue, or is that impossible?'
Then a bad soul necessarily rules and manages badly, and a good soul does all these things well.
'Impossible.'
Necessarily.
'So a bad soul will necessarily rule and manage badly, and a good soul will do all these things well?'
Now, we agreed that justice is the soul's excellence, and injustice its defect?
'Necessarily.'
We did.
'And we agreed that justice is the virtue of the soul and injustice its defect?'
So the just soul — the just man — will live well, and the unjust man will live badly?
'We did.'
Apparently, he said — by your argument.
'So the just soul, and the just man, will live well, and the unjust will live badly?'
And whoever lives well is blessed and happy, and whoever does not is the opposite?
'So your argument shows.'
Of course.
'And the man who lives well is blessed and happy, and the one who lives badly is the opposite?'
So the just man is happy, and the unjust man miserable?
'Of course.'
So be it.
'So the just man is happy and the unjust man wretched?'
But it doesn't pay to be miserable. It pays to be happy.
'Let it be so,' he said.
Obviously.
'But being wretched isn't profitable; being happy is.'
Then never, blessed Thrasymachus, is injustice more profitable than justice.
'Of course.'
Enjoy it, Socrates, he said — consider it your feast at the festival of Bendis.
'So injustice, my dear Thrasymachus, is never more profitable than justice.'

A feast you provided, Thrasymachus, I said — once you turned gentle with me and stopped being fierce. And yet I have not feasted well — my own fault, not yours. I have behaved like one of those gluttons who snatch a taste of every dish as it is carried past, before they have properly enjoyed the one before. Before we found the thing we were looking for first — what justice actually is — I dropped that and rushed off to ask whether it is vice and ignorance or wisdom and virtue; and when the claim fell in our laps later that injustice is more profitable than justice, I couldn't keep myself from that one either. So the result of the whole conversation, for me, is that I know nothing. For as long as I don't know what justice is, I am hardly going to know whether it is a virtue or not — or whether the man who has it is unhappy or happy.
'Let this be your feast at the festival of Bendis, Socrates,' he said.

'For which I have you to thank, Thrasymachus,' I said, 'now that you've grown gentle with me and stopped being harsh. And yet I haven't feasted well, though that's my own fault, not yours. Like a glutton who grabs at each new dish as it's brought round, snatching a taste before he's properly enjoyed the last, I think I've rushed from one thing to the next before finding the answer to what we first set out to discover, namely what justice is. I dropped that and went chasing after whether it's vice and ignorance or virtue and wisdom. Then another question came up, whether injustice is more profitable than justice, and I couldn't keep myself from leaving the first to follow that. So the upshot of the whole conversation is that I know nothing. As long as I don't know what justice is, I'm hardly likely to know whether it's a virtue or not, or whether the man who has it is happy or unhappy.'
spine.label: Book II
spine.title: The Ring of Gyges
The Challenge Renewed, and a City in Speech
spine.text: With that, I thought I was free of the argument. But it turned out, apparently, to be only a prelude. For Glaucon, who is the boldest of men in everything, wouldn't accept Thrasymachus's surrender; he wanted the fight fought to a finish. Socrates, he said, do you want to really convince us, or just to seem to have convinced us, that it is better in every way to be just than unjust?

I thought that with these words I had brought the discussion to an end, but it turned out to be only the beginning. Glaucon, who is the most combative man alive, refused to accept Thrasymachus's surrender. He wanted the fight to go on. 'Socrates,' he said, 'do you really want to convince us that being just is always better than being unjust, or only to seem to have convinced us?'
Really, I said — if it were up to me.
'I'd genuinely want to convince you,' I said, 'if it were up to me.'

Well then, you're not doing what you want. Tell me: do you think there is a kind of good we would welcome not for what comes of it, but for its own sake — glad simply to have it? Joy, for instance, and the harmless pleasures that lead to nothing afterward beyond the delight of the moment we have them.

'Well, then you've failed,' he said. 'Let me ask you something. Aren't there some goods we welcome for their own sake, regardless of any consequences? Take harmless pleasures, the kind that simply delight us in the moment, with nothing further coming of them.'
Yes, I said, I think there is a good of that kind.
'Yes,' I said, 'I think there's a class of goods like that.'
And a second kind, that we love both for itself and for what comes of it — knowing, say, and seeing, and being healthy? Goods like that we welcome on both counts, I suppose.
'And isn't there a second class, things like understanding, sight, health, which we want both for themselves and for what comes of them?'
Certainly, I said.
'Certainly,' I said.

And do you also see a third kind — exercise, say, and medical treatment when you're sick, and doctoring itself, and moneymaking in general? These we would call burdensome but good for us; nobody would choose them for their own sake, only for the pay and the other things that come out of them.

'And don't you recognize a third class as well? Physical training, being treated when you're sick, the practice of medicine, all the ways of making money. These do us good, but we find them tiresome, and no one would choose them for their own sake. We put up with them only for the wages and the results that come of them.'
There is that third kind too, I said. But what's your point?
'Yes,' I said, 'there's that third class too. But what are you driving at?'
In which of the three do you place justice?
'In which of the three would you put justice?'
In the finest one, I'd say — the class of goods that anyone who means to be truly happy must love both for their own sake and for what comes of them.
'In the finest one,' I said. 'Among the goods that anyone hoping to be happy must love both for themselves and for what comes of them.'

That's not where most people put it, he said. They file justice under the burdensome kind — the goods a man practices for the pay, and for the standing a good reputation brings, but which in themselves are hard, and to be avoided.

'Then most people disagree with you,' he said. 'They'd put justice in the tiresome class, among the goods you pursue for the wages and the reputation they bring, but which in themselves are a nuisance, something to avoid if you can.'
I know they think that, I said; Thrasymachus has been running justice down on exactly those grounds for a while now, and singing the praises of injustice. But it seems I'm a slow learner.

'I know that's how they see it,' I said, 'and it's exactly on these grounds that Thrasymachus has been running justice down and praising injustice. But I'm too slow, it seems, to be convinced by him.'

Then listen to me too, he said, and see whether you still feel the same. Thrasymachus, it seems to me, gave in too soon — charmed by your voice like a snake by a piper. But to my mind neither justice nor injustice has been shown for what it is. What is each of them? What power does each have, all by itself, when it's in the soul? Never mind the pay and the consequences — that's what I want to know. So here is what I'll do, if you agree: I'll bring Thrasymachus's argument back to life. First I'll tell you what people say justice is, and where it comes from. Second, that everyone who practices it practices it unwillingly — as a necessity, not as a good. Third, that this is reasonable of them, since the unjust man's life, they say, is far better than the just man's. None of it is what I think, Socrates. But I'm at a loss. My ears are ringing with Thrasymachus and ten thousand voices like his, and the case for justice — that it is better than injustice — I have never yet heard made the way I want to hear it. I want to hear justice praised for what it is, in itself; and you are the man I most expect to hear that from. So I am going to praise the unjust life with everything I have, and my performance will show you exactly how I want to hear you, in your turn, condemn injustice and praise justice. See whether the plan suits you.

'Then listen to me as well,' he said, 'and see whether you still agree with me afterward. Thrasymachus strikes me as a snake you've charmed into giving up too soon. As far as I'm concerned, neither justice nor injustice has yet been shown for what it really is. I want to set the rewards and consequences aside and hear what each of them is in itself, and what it does inside the soul of the man who has it. So, if you'll let me, here's what I'll do. I'll bring Thrasymachus's argument back to life. First, I'll explain what people say justice is and where it comes from. Second, I'll argue that everyone who practices it does so unwillingly, as something they have to do, not as something good. And third, I'll show why that view makes sense, because the life of the unjust man is, they say, far better than the life of the just. I don't actually believe any of this myself, Socrates. But my ears are full of Thrasymachus and a thousand others, and I've never once heard anyone defend justice, and show that it beats injustice, in a way that satisfied me. I want to hear justice praised for what it is in itself, and you're the man I most expect to hear it from. So I'll throw everything I have into praising the unjust life, and the way I argue will show you exactly the way I want to hear you argue back, praising justice and condemning injustice. Will you let me try it like that?'
Nothing could suit me better, I said. What subject would a man with any sense rather return to, again and again, than this one?
'Nothing could please me more,' I said. 'It's the kind of subject a sensible man would want to talk about again and again.'
Wonderful, he said. Then hear the first point — what people say justice is, and where it comes from.
'Good,' he said. 'Then listen, while I keep to my plan and start with the nature and origin of justice.'

By nature, they say, doing wrong is good and suffering wrong is bad — but the bad of suffering it outweighs the good of doing it. So once men have tasted both — dealing out wrong and taking it — those who lack the power to seize the one and dodge the other decide it pays to strike a deal: no one wrongs anyone. From there they begin laying down laws and contracts with one another, and whatever the law commands they call lawful and just. That, they say, is the origin of justice, and its very being: a compromise, halfway between the best case — doing wrong without paying for it — and the worst — being wronged without the power to hit back. Justice sits in the middle, and men settle for it not as a good but as the lesser evil; it gets its honor from weakness, from men's inability to do wrong and get away with it. For any real man, one who actually had the power, would never strike such a deal with anyone — never agree to neither wrong nor be wronged. He'd be out of his mind. There, Socrates, is the going account of the nature of justice, and of how it came into the world.

'People say that doing wrong is by nature a good thing and suffering wrong a bad thing, but that the harm of suffering it outweighs the good of doing it. So once men have tried both, once they've done wrong and been wronged in turn, those who can't manage to grab the one and dodge the other decide it pays to make an agreement: no one does wrong, and no one suffers it. That's where laws and contracts come from, and people call what the law commands lawful and just. This, they say, is the origin of justice and what it really is. It stands midway between the best case, doing wrong and getting away with it, and the worst case, being wronged with no power to strike back. Justice sits between these two, and people put up with it, not because it's good, but as the lesser evil, prized only because they're too weak to do wrong with impunity. No real man, no one with the power to do wrong, would ever make such a bargain. He'd be mad to. That, Socrates, is the standard account of what justice is and where it comes from.'

Now, that those who practice justice practice it unwillingly — for lack of the power to do wrong — we would see most plainly if we tried something like this in imagination. Give each of them, the just man and the unjust alike, license to do whatever he pleases, then follow along and watch where desire leads each one. We would catch the just man red-handed, headed down the very road the unjust man travels, driven by the craving to get ahead of others — the thing every nature naturally pursues as its good, until law drags it by force to honor equality. The license I mean would be most complete if they had the kind of power they say once came to the ancestor of Gyges the Lydian. He was a shepherd, the story goes, serving the man who then ruled Lydia. One day a great storm broke, and an earthquake tore the earth open at the very spot where he grazed his flock. Astonished at the sight, he climbed down into the chasm — and there, among other wonders the story tells of, he saw a hollow bronze horse fitted with little doors. Stooping to look in, he saw a corpse inside, larger, it seemed, than any man, and wearing nothing but a gold ring on its finger. He slipped the ring off and climbed back out. Now, when the shepherds held their usual monthly meeting, to send the king their report on the flocks, he came wearing it; and as he sat among the others, he happened to twist its bezel around toward himself, into his palm — and the instant he did, he became invisible to the men beside him, and they began talking about him as if he had left. He couldn't believe it. Feeling for the ring again, he twisted the bezel outward — and reappeared. After that he put the thing to the test, to see whether the ring really held this power, and it came out the same every time: bezel in, invisible; bezel out, visible. The moment he was sure, he arranged to be one of the messengers sent to the king; and once there, he seduced the king's wife, plotted with her against him, killed him, and took the throne. Suppose, then, there were two such rings — the just man wearing one, the unjust man the other. No one, it would seem, could be made of stuff so adamant that he would hold to justice. No one would keep his hands off what wasn't his when he could lift whatever he liked out of the market without fear, walk into any house and sleep with anyone he chose, kill anyone or spring anyone from prison at will — moving through the world, in short, like a god among men. And in all of it he would do exactly as the other man does; the two of them would be headed for the same place. Surely this is powerful evidence that no one is just willingly — only under compulsion, because justice is no private good to him: wherever a man believes he can get away with wrong, he does it. For every man believes, in his heart, that injustice pays far better than justice — and believes it rightly, says the maker of this argument. Because if a man got hold of a license like that and refused ever to do wrong, refused to lay a finger on other men's things, those who noticed would think him the most pathetic fool alive — though they'd praise him to each other's faces, lying to one another out of fear of being wronged themselves. So much for that.

'And the proof that people act justly only under compulsion, because they lack the power to do wrong, comes through most clearly if we try a thought-experiment. Give both the just man and the unjust man the freedom to do whatever they please, and then follow them and watch where their desires lead. We'll catch the just man red-handed, heading down the very same road as the unjust one, driven by the appetite to have more, which every nature pursues as its good, though law forces it back into line and makes it respect equality. The clearest way to give them this freedom would be to grant them the power that once belonged, so the story goes, to Gyges, the ancestor of Croesus the Lydian. Gyges was a shepherd in the service of the Lydian king. One day there was a great storm, and an earthquake split open the ground where he was pasturing his flock. Amazed, he climbed down into the chasm, and there, among other wonders, he saw a hollow bronze horse with little doors in its side. Stooping to look inside, he saw a corpse, larger than human, it seemed, wearing nothing but a gold ring on its hand. He slipped the ring off and climbed back out. Now, the shepherds held their usual monthly meeting to send the king a report on the flocks, and Gyges came wearing the ring. As he sat among the others, he happened to turn the setting of the ring toward the inside of his hand, and at once he became invisible, and the others started talking about him as though he'd left. Astonished, he fingered the ring again, turned the setting back outward, and reappeared. He tested it again and again, and the result was always the same: setting turned in, he vanished; turned out, he reappeared. As soon as he was sure of this, he arranged to be one of the messengers sent to the king. Once at court, he seduced the queen, plotted with her against the king, killed him, and seized the throne. Now suppose there were two such rings, and the just man put on one and the unjust man the other. No one, it seems, would be made of iron enough to stay on the path of justice and keep his hands off other people's things when he could take whatever he wanted from the market stalls without being seen, walk into any house and sleep with anyone he liked, kill or free whomever he chose, and in every way act like a god among men. The two of them would end up behaving exactly alike, both walking the same road. And surely this is strong evidence that no one is just willingly, but only under compulsion, because no one believes justice is any good to him personally. The moment a man thinks he can get away with doing wrong, he does it. Everyone, deep down, believes that injustice pays far better than justice, and on this account they're right to believe it. If a man got hold of such a power and then never once used it to do wrong or to lay a hand on what wasn't his, anyone watching would think him utterly pathetic, an idiot, though of course they'd praise him to his face, lying to one another out of their own fear of being wronged. So much for that.'

As for the judgment itself — the actual lives of the two men we're discussing — we can only make it if we set the perfectly just man and the perfectly unjust man side by side; there's no other way. And how do we manage that? Like this. Subtract nothing from either: let the unjust man be perfectly unjust and the just man perfectly just, each of them complete at his own pursuit. First, then, the unjust man: have him operate the way the masters of a craft do — a first-rate pilot, say, or a doctor, who knows exactly what his art can and cannot do, attempts the one and lets the other alone, and can recover himself if he ever slips. Just so, the unjust man attempting his crimes in the right way must go undetected, if he's to be great at injustice; the one who gets caught is a bungler. For the summit of injustice is to seem just without being it. So to the perfectly unjust man we must give the most perfect injustice — nothing deducted — and allow him, while committing the greatest wrongs, to have secured the greatest reputation for justice. If he ever slips, he can recover: he can talk his way out, persuasively, should any of his wrongdoing come to light, and force his way through where force is called for — he has the courage and strength for it, and a good supply of friends and money. So there he stands. Now set beside him, in the argument, the just man: simple and noble, a man who wants, as Aeschylus says, not to seem good but to be it. So strip away the seeming. If he seems just, honors and rewards come with the seeming, and then no one could tell whether he's just for justice's sake or for the honors and rewards. Strip him bare of everything but justice, and make his condition the exact reverse of the other man's: let him do no wrong and carry the greatest reputation for wrongdoing — that way his justice is tested, proof against ill fame and everything it brings — and let him walk on unchanged until death, seeming unjust his whole life long while being just. Then both men have reached the extremes, one of justice, one of injustice, and we can judge which of the two is the happier.

'Now, if we're going to judge between the lives of the just and the unjust man, we have to set each of them apart in his pure form. There's no other way to do it. And how do we manage that? Like this. We strip nothing away from the unjust man's injustice or the just man's justice. We make each of them perfect in his own line of work. First, the unjust man. Let him operate like a real master of his craft. A top pilot or doctor knows exactly what his skill can and can't do; he attempts what's within his reach and, if he slips, he can recover. So let the unjust man commit his crimes the right way, and stay hidden if he means to be great at injustice, because the man who gets caught is a bungler. The highest reach of injustice is to seem just while being the opposite. So we must grant our perfectly unjust man his perfect injustice, taking nothing away: while committing the worst crimes, he has secured for himself the finest reputation for justice. If he ever stumbles, he can set himself right; he's persuasive enough to talk his way clear if any of his deeds come to light, and forceful enough to get his way where force is needed, backed by his courage, his strength, his money, and his friends. Now set beside him the just man, plain and noble, who wants, in Aeschylus's words, not to seem good but to be it. So we have to take away the seeming. If he seems just, he'll get honors and rewards for it, and then we won't be able to tell whether he's just for justice's sake or for the sake of the rewards. Strip him bare, then, of everything but his justice, and put him in the opposite situation from the other man. Though he does no wrong, give him the worst reputation for wrongdoing, so that his justice is put to the ultimate test and we can see whether it bends under disgrace and all that disgrace brings. Let him hold his course, unchanging, to his dying breath, being just while seeming unjust his whole life long. Then, when both have reached the very limit, one of justice and the other of injustice, let us decide which of them is the happier.'
Good lord, my dear Glaucon, I said — how vigorously you scour your two men clean for the judging, first one and then the other, like a pair of statues.
'Good heavens, Glaucon,' I said, 'how vigorously you scrub the two of them down for judgment, like a man polishing a pair of statues!'

I'm doing the best I can, he said. And with the two of them as I've described, it should be no trouble now to trace out the life that waits for each. Let me say it — and if it comes out coarsely, Socrates, remember that it isn't me speaking, but the men who praise injustice over justice. This is what they'll say: the just man in that condition will be whipped, stretched on the rack, chained, both his eyes burned out — and at the end, when he has suffered everything there is to suffer, he will be impaled on a stake, and learn at last that a man should want not to be just but to seem it. So that line of Aeschylus turns out to apply far more truly to the unjust man. He's the one, they'll say, pursuing the real thing; he's the one who refuses to live for appearances — who wants not to seem unjust but to be it,

'I'm doing my best,' he said. 'And now that we know what each of them is like, there's no trouble describing the life that awaits them. Let me do it, then. And if what I say sounds harsh, Socrates, remember that the words aren't mine. Put them in the mouths of the men who praise injustice. They'll tell you that the just man, with his reputation for wrongdoing, will be whipped, racked, and chained; they'll burn out his eyes; and in the end, after suffering every torment, he'll be impaled. Then he'll learn that one should want not to be just but to seem so. In fact, Aeschylus's line fits the unjust man far better than the just: it's the unjust man who pursues reality, who lives for what truly is and not for appearances. He wants to be unjust, not merely seem it.'
'harvesting the deep furrow of his mind, / where sound counsel takes root and grows.'
'"Deep is the soil of his mind, and from it / the harvest of his shrewd designs springs up."'

And the seeming wins him everything: first, rule in the city, since he's thought just; then a wife from whatever house he likes, and his children married into whatever house he likes; deals and partnerships with whomever he pleases — and profit from all of it, because cheating doesn't turn his stomach. Enter any contest against him, private or public, and he comes out on top, ahead at his rivals' expense. Being ahead, he's rich; being rich, he does his friends good and his enemies harm; and to the gods he offers sacrifice and dedicates gifts on the grand scale, magnificently, serving heaven — and whatever men he cares to serve — far better than the just man can. So the odds are, they say, that the gods love him better too. And that is how, Socrates, gods and men alike are said to conspire in making the unjust man's life better than the just man's.

'First, because he's thought to be just, he holds office in the city. He can marry into any family he likes and give his own children in marriage where he pleases. He can do business and form partnerships with anyone, and since he has no scruples about doing wrong, he comes out ahead in every dealing and grows rich. He helps his friends and harms his enemies. He makes lavish, magnificent sacrifices and offerings to the gods, and serves them, and serves any man he wishes to honor, far better than the just man can, so it's likely the gods will love him more than the just man too. And so, Socrates, men say, and the gods agree, that a better life is laid up for the unjust man than for the just.'
I had an answer for Glaucon on the tip of my tongue, but his brother Adeimantus got in first: Socrates, he said, surely you don't think the case has been fully stated?
I was about to answer Glaucon when his brother Adeimantus broke in. 'Surely you don't think the case has been fully made, Socrates?'
Why — what's missing? I said.
'Why, what's left?' I said.
The very thing that most needed saying, he replied, hasn't been said.
'The single most important point hasn't even been mentioned,' he said.

Well then, I said, as the proverb goes — let brother stand by brother. If Glaucon has fallen short anywhere, back him up. Though for my part, what he has said already is enough to flatten me and leave me helpless to come to justice's rescue.

'Well,' I said, 'as the proverb has it, let a man's brother stand by him. So if Glaucon has left anything out, you come to his aid, though I have to admit he's already floored me as it is, and left me no strength to defend justice.'

Nonsense, he said. Hear this much more. To bring out what I take to be Glaucon's real meaning, we have to go through the opposite speeches too — the ones that praise justice and condemn injustice. When fathers lecture their sons — when anyone with someone in his charge does it — they urge them to be just; but it isn't justice itself they praise. It's the respectability that comes of it: the hope that a reputation for being just will bring the offices, the marriages, all the advantages Glaucon just counted out as coming to the unjust man from his good name. And this crowd runs the reputation argument even further: they throw in good standing with the gods, and can list blessings by the armful, which heaven, they say, showers on the pious — just as the good Hesiod tells it, and Homer too. For the one says the gods make the oak trees, for men who are just,

'That's nonsense,' he said. 'But hear me out, because there's another side to Glaucon's argument that needs saying if we're to bring out his full meaning. When fathers tell their sons to be just, and tutors tell their charges the same, what is it they praise? Not justice itself, but the good name it brings. They want the boy, by being thought just, to land the offices and marriages and all the rest of the advantages that Glaucon listed as flowing from a reputation for justice. In fact these people pile even more onto the rewards of reputation. They throw in the favor of the gods, and they'll tell you of the showers of blessings the heavens rain down on the pious, just as the good Hesiod and Homer say. Hesiod says the gods make the oaks of the just'
'bear acorns at the crown and bees at the middle, / while the wool-heavy sheep sag under their fleeces,'
'"bear acorns at the top and bees in the middle, / and their woolly sheep stagger under the weight of their fleeces,"'
with plenty of other good things in the same vein. And the other sings much the same song — a man whose fame is
'and many other blessings of the kind. Homer says much the same, speaking of a man whose fame is'

'like some flawless king who, godfearing, / upholds what is just: for him the black earth bears / wheat and barley, his trees hang heavy with fruit, / his flocks lamb without fail, and the sea yields him fish.'

'"like the fame of a blameless king who, godlike, / upholds justice, and the black earth bears him / wheat and barley, his trees are heavy with fruit, / his flocks bring forth without fail, and the sea yields him fish."'

Musaeus and his son promise the just even racier goods than these, on heaven's behalf: in their account they lead them down into Hades, recline them on couches, lay on a banquet of the blessed, and leave them there garlanded and drunk for all eternity — as if the finest wage virtue could earn were an everlasting drinking party. Others stretch the gods' payroll even longer: the pious man who keeps his oaths, they say, leaves children's children and a whole line running on behind him. That is the style in which they praise justice — that, and more like it. But the godless and unjust get the other treatment: these they bury in mud down in Hades, and set them hauling water in a sieve; they drag them through infamy while they're still alive; and every torment Glaucon described falling on the just man who seems unjust, they assign to the unjust — that's their whole list; they have nothing else. So there you have it: the praising of the one, and the blaming of the other.

'And Musaeus and his son promise the just even grander gifts from the gods. In their telling, they bring the just down to the next world, lay them on couches, set a feast going, and crown them with garlands, so that they spend all eternity drunk, as though everlasting drunkenness were virtue's finest reward. Others stretch the rewards still further: the children and grandchildren of the pious and just, they say, will survive to the third and fourth generation. That's how they praise justice. But the wicked they bury in mud down in Hades and set to carrying water in a sieve; and while these men are still alive, they drag their names through the dirt, and load on them all the punishments Glaucon described as falling to the just man who's thought unjust. That's the whole of their repertoire. So that's how the one is praised and the other condemned.'

Beyond all that, Socrates, consider yet another way of talking about justice and injustice — you meet it in ordinary speech and in the poets alike. With one voice they all chant that self-restraint and justice are fine things, yes — but hard, and full of drudgery, while indulgence and injustice are sweet, easy to come by, and shameful only in reputation and by convention. Wrongdoing pays better than justice, they say, on the whole; and they're perfectly ready to call bad men happy and to honor them, in public and in private, provided they're rich or otherwise powerful — while the weak and the poor they slight and look past, even while admitting these are the better men. But the most astonishing of all is what they say about the gods and virtue: that the gods themselves deal misfortune and misery to many good men, and hand the opposite lot to the opposite sort. And begging priests and prophets come to rich men's doors and persuade them that they hold a power from the gods, procured through sacrifices and incantations, to heal — with feasting and pleasure — any wrong the man or his ancestors have done; and if he wants an enemy hurt, then for a small fee they will injure just and unjust alike, with certain summonings and binding-spells; for the gods, so they claim, can be persuaded to do their bidding. And for all of it they call the poets as witnesses. Some, on the ease of vice, quote Hesiod —

'And now, Socrates, here's yet another way of talking about justice and injustice, one you find not only in the poets but in ordinary speech. With one voice everyone keeps saying that justice and self-control are admirable, yes, but hard and full of toil, while loose living and injustice are sweet and easy to come by, and only convention and reputation hold them to be shameful. They say injustice usually pays better than justice, and they're perfectly willing to call wicked men happy, and to honor them in public and private, so long as they're rich or otherwise powerful, while they look down on and ignore the weak and poor, even while admitting these are the better men. But the strangest thing of all is what they say about the gods and goodness. They claim the gods hand out hardship and misery to many good men, and the opposite lot to their opposites. And then there are the begging priests and fortune-tellers who knock on rich men's doors and convince them that the gods have given them a power, worked through sacrifices and spells amid feasting and festivity, to absolve any wrong the man or his ancestors have done; and that if he wants to ruin some enemy, just or unjust, a small fee will do it, since with their incantations and binding spells they can press the gods into their service. And for all of this they call the poets to witness. Some smooth the path of vice by quoting Hesiod:'
'Vice you can have in heaps, and easily: / smooth is the road, and she lives very near. / But in front of virtue the gods have set sweat,'
'"Wickedness is easy to get in plenty: the road is smooth and she lives close by. / But in front of virtue the gods have set sweat,"'
and a road that is long and steep. Others call Homer to witness that men can bend the gods, since he too said —
'and a long, steep, uphill road. Others cite Homer to prove that the gods can be swayed by men, since he too says:'

'Even the gods themselves can be moved by prayer: / with sacrifice and gentle vows, / with libations and the smoke of burnt fat, / men turn them, praying, whenever someone / has crossed the line and done wrong.'
'"The gods themselves can be moved. With sacrifices and gentle prayers, / with offerings and the savor of burnt fat, men turn them aside / when they have transgressed and done wrong."'

And they produce a whole stack of books by Musaeus and Orpheus — offspring, so they say, of the Moon and of the Muses — and by these books they run their rites, persuading not only private men but whole cities that there is release and cleansing from injustice, through sacrifices and the pleasures of festival, for the living and for the dead alike. These last they call initiations — rites that deliver us from the evils of the world below; and terrible things wait, they say, for those who die without them.

'And they produce a heap of books by Musaeus and Orpheus, children of the Moon and the Muses, so they claim, and they conduct their rituals from them. They persuade not only individuals but whole cities that there are absolutions and purifications for wrongdoing, available to the living through sacrifices and pleasant games, and available to the dead too, through what they call initiations, which release us from the torments of the next world, while those who skip them, they warn, face horrors no one can name.'

Now, Socrates, he went on: when the young hear all this said about virtue and vice, and about how gods and men regard them, what do we suppose it does to their souls? I mean the gifted ones — the quick ones, who light like bees on everything they hear, gathering from it their conclusions about what kind of man to be and which road to take through life. A young man like that would most likely put Pindar's question to himself:

'Now, my dear Socrates,' he went on, 'when the young hear all of this said about goodness and badness, and how gods and men regard them, what do you suppose it does to them, especially the quick-witted ones, who flit like bees from one of these sayings to the next and try to work out from all of it what sort of person to be and which road to take to make the most of life? Such a youth will surely ask himself, in Pindar's words,'
'By justice, or by crooked deceit, do I climb / the higher wall' — and live my life fenced safe behind it?
'"Shall I climb to the higher rampart by justice, / or by crooked deceit, and so fortify myself for life?"'

For what the world tells me is this: if I am just but don't seem it, the being profits me nothing — there is only toil in it, and losses in plain view. But unjust, with a reputation for justice secured — that, they say, is a life fit for the gods. Well then: since the wise keep showing me that seeming overpowers even the truth, and is what happiness hangs on, I should hand myself over to it entirely. I should paint a facade of virtue around me — a shadow-picture of it, for a porch and a frontage — and haul along behind it the fox of Archilochus, wisest of sages: greedy, shifty, quick. 'But it's hard to be wicked and stay hidden forever,' someone objects. Nothing great was ever easy, we'll answer; and either way, if we're to be happy, this is the road that everything we've heard points down. To stay hidden, we'll form conspiracies and clubs; and there are teachers of persuasion for hire, selling the wisdom of the assembly and the courtroom — so partly by persuasion and partly by force, we will keep taking more than our share and never pay for it. 'But the gods can't be fooled, and can't be forced.' Come now: if there are no gods, or if human affairs are beneath their notice, why should we trouble to hide at all? And if they exist and do notice — well, everything we know of them we know from the stories and from the poets who traced their genealogies; and those same poets tell us the gods can be swayed and brought around 'by sacrifice and gentle vows and offerings.' Believe the poets in both things or in neither. If we believe them: do the injustice first, and sacrifice out of the proceeds. Stay just, and we merely escape heaven's punishment while pushing away injustice's profits. Go unjust, and we keep the profits — and by praying our way through every trespass and transgression, we talk the gods around and get off free. 'Ah, but in Hades we'll pay for what we did here — we, or our children's children.' My friend, the calculating young man will say, the initiations can do a great deal, and so can the gods of absolution. The greatest cities say so; and the children of the gods — the poets, heaven's own prophets — reveal that it is so.

'What they tell me is this. If I'm really just but don't seem so, there's no profit in it, only pain and loss, by all accounts. But if I'm unjust and yet build up a reputation for justice, a heavenly life is promised me. Very well: since the wise tell me that the look of a thing overpowers the truth of it and is the master of happiness, that's clearly where I must turn. I'll paint a front of virtue around myself, a facade for show, but behind it I'll trail the cunning, twisting fox of Archilochus. "But it's hard," someone objects, "to keep wickedness hidden forever." Nothing great is easy, I answer. Still, if happiness is the goal, this is plainly the road the argument points to. To stay hidden we'll form secret societies and political clubs; and there are teachers of persuasion who pass on the skills of the law courts and the assembly. So, partly by persuasion and partly by force, I'll get the better of others and not be punished. "But you can't outwit or overpower the gods." Well, suppose there are no gods, or suppose they take no interest in human affairs. Then why should we care about staying hidden from them? And if the gods do exist and do care, we know of them only from tradition and from the poets who trace their family trees, and these are the very people who say the gods can be swayed and turned aside by sacrifices, gentle prayers, and offerings. We should believe them on both points or neither. If we believe them, then the thing to do is commit injustice and offer up sacrifices from the proceeds. If we're just, we'll only escape punishment by the gods while forfeiting the profits of injustice; but if we're unjust, we'll keep the profits and, by praying as we sin and sinning as we pray, we'll talk the gods round and get off free. "But in the world below we'll pay, we or our descendants, for the wrongs we do here." My friend, the youth will reason, that's what the initiations and the absolving gods are for, and they have great power. The greatest cities tell us so, and so do the children of the gods, the poets and prophets, who say the same.'

On what ground, then, should we still prefer justice to the greatest injustice? If we wear a counterfeit front of decency over it, we shall do exactly as we intend, with gods and with men, in this life and after it — so runs the account of the many, and of the highest authorities. Given all of that, Socrates, by what device could a man be brought to honor justice — any man with real resources of mind or money, of body or of birth — rather than laugh out loud when he hears it praised? Truly: even a man who can refute everything I've said, and who is fully satisfied that justice is best, is remarkably forgiving toward the unjust; he feels no anger at them. He knows that apart from the rare man whom some divine instinct turns sick at wrongdoing, or the one who has won real knowledge and holds back, no one is just of his own free will. Men denounce injustice out of cowardice, or old age, or some other weakness — because they cannot manage it. The proof is plain: the first of them who comes into the power to do wrong does it — precisely as much of it as he can.

'So on what grounds would we still choose justice over the worst injustice, when, if we wrap that injustice in a convincing show of virtue, we'll do exactly as we please with gods and men, in this life and the next, as the most numerous and the highest authorities assure us? Given all this, Socrates, how could any man with some advantage of mind, looks, birth, or wealth bring himself to honor justice, instead of laughing out loud whenever he hears it praised? Even a man who could prove what I'm saying false, and who is convinced that justice is best, feels no anger at the unjust; he forgives them readily, because he knows that no one is just willingly, unless some god-given disgust at injustice holds him back, or he's come to know the truth. Apart from such a man, no one is just by choice. It's only cowardice or old age or some other weakness that makes a man condemn injustice, namely, his own inability to commit it, as is shown by the fact that the moment he gets the power, he uses it to do wrong as much as he can.'

And the cause of all this, Socrates, is nothing but the fact my brother and I set before you at the start, when we told you how astonished we were: of all of you who call yourselves champions of justice — from the heroes of old, wherever their words survive, down to the men of today — not one has ever condemned injustice or praised justice except for the reputations, the honors, and the rewards that flow from them. What each of them is in itself, by its own power, inside the soul of the man who has it — hidden from gods and hidden from men — no one has ever adequately worked out, in verse or in prose: that injustice is the greatest of the evils a soul can carry within it, and justice the greatest good. If you had all been saying that from the beginning — if you had persuaded us of it from our childhood up — we would not be standing guard over one another against injustice; each man would be his own best guard, afraid that in doing wrong he'd be taking the worst of housemates into his own soul. All this, Socrates, and perhaps more besides, is what Thrasymachus — or anyone else — might say about justice and injustice, crudely turning their true powers upside down, as I see it. And I — I'll hide nothing from you — have argued it at the top of my strength precisely because I want to hear the opposite from your lips. So don't merely demonstrate to us that justice is stronger than injustice: tell us what each of them does, all by itself, to the man who has it, that makes the one an evil and the other a good. And strip out the reputations, as Glaucon asked you to. For unless you take the true reputation from each and hand each the false one, we'll say you are not praising justice but the appearance of it, not blaming injustice but the look of it — that your real advice is to be unjust and stay hidden, and that at bottom you agree with Thrasymachus: justice is another man's good, the advantage of the stronger, and injustice one's own advantage and profit, won at the weaker man's expense. You have agreed that justice belongs among the greatest goods — the ones worth having for what comes of them, but worth far more for their own sake: sight, hearing, understanding, health, all the goods that are fruitful by their own nature and not by repute. Then praise that in justice: the good it does the man who has it, by itself, and the harm injustice does him, by itself. The wages and the reputations — leave those to others to praise. From other men I could stomach that kind of case, hymning the reputations and the pay; from you I cannot — unless you order me to — because you have spent your whole life examining this one question and nothing else. So do not merely show us that justice is stronger than injustice: show us what each one does to the man who carries it — whether gods and men see it or not — that makes the one a good and the other an evil.

'And the root of all this, Socrates, is the very thing my brother and I told you at the start, when we said how astonished we were that, of all of you who profess to champion justice, from the ancient heroes whose words survive down to the men of today, not one has ever condemned injustice or praised justice except in terms of the reputations, honors, and rewards that come of them. What none of you has ever done, in verse or in prose, is to describe what each of them, by its own power, does within the soul of its possessor, unseen by any eye, god's or man's; to show that injustice is the greatest of all the evils a soul can carry inside it, and justice the greatest good. If you had all said this from the beginning, and persuaded us of it from childhood, we wouldn't be standing guard over one another to prevent wrongdoing. Each man would be his own best guard, terrified that by doing wrong he'd be taking the greatest of evils to live inside him. Thrasymachus, or anyone else, might say all this and more about justice and injustice, crudely turning their true natures upside down, as I think. But I've put it so forcefully, and I'll be honest with you, precisely because I want to hear you argue the other side. So don't just show us that justice is stronger than injustice. Show us what each of them does to the man who has it, in himself, that makes the one a good and the other an evil. And do as Glaucon asked: leave reputations out of it. Because if you don't strip each man of his true reputation and saddle him with a false one, we'll say you're praising not justice but the appearance of justice, and not condemning injustice but only the appearance of it; we'll conclude you're really telling us to be unjust on the sly, and that you secretly agree with Thrasymachus that justice is someone else's good, the advantage of the stronger, while injustice is a man's own profit and gain, at the weaker man's expense. You've granted that justice belongs in the highest class of goods, the ones worth having for their results but far more for themselves, like sight, hearing, understanding, health, and every other good that's genuinely good by its own nature and not merely by convention. So praise that side of justice, the good it does the man who has it just by being in him, and let others praise the wages and the reputation. From other men I'd accept that kind of praise, but not from you, who've spent your whole life on this single question. Don't just prove to us that justice beats injustice. Show us what each does to its possessor, unseen by gods or men, that makes the one good and the other evil.'

Now, I had always thought well of the natures of Glaucon and Adeimantus, but hearing all this I was purely delighted, and I said: Sons of that great man — Glaucon's admirer opened his elegy for you well, after you had distinguished yourselves in the battle at Megara, when he wrote:

I had always admired the natural gifts of Glaucon and Adeimantus, but hearing them now, I was delighted, and I said, 'Sons of a distinguished father, the man who admired Glaucon made a fitting start to his verses when, after the two of you had won glory at the battle of Megara, he wrote:'
'Sons of Ariston: godlike line of a famous man.'
'"Sons of Ariston, divine offspring of a famous man."'

That seems exactly right, my friends. There is something truly godlike in your condition if you can argue like that for injustice and remain unconvinced that it is better than justice. And I believe you really are unconvinced — my evidence is the whole rest of your character; from the speeches alone, I admit, I would have doubted you. But the more I trust you, the more I am at a loss what to do. I cannot defend her — I don't think I'm equal to it; and my proof is that I thought what I said to Thrasymachus had shown that justice is better than injustice, and you two would not accept it from me. Yet I cannot refuse to defend her either. I am afraid it would be a kind of impiety to stand by while justice is slandered — to give up, and not come to her aid while I still have breath in me and a voice. So the best course is to help her in whatever way I can.

'The epithet fits, my friends. There's something truly godlike in your being able to argue so well for the superiority of injustice and yet remain unconvinced by your own case. And I do believe you're unconvinced. I judge that from the rest of your characters; from the speeches alone I'd have had my doubts. But the more I trust you, the harder I find it to know what to say. I can't see how I'm to defend justice. I feel I'm not up to it, and the proof of that is that you weren't satisfied with the answer I gave Thrasymachus, where I thought I'd shown justice better than injustice. Yet I can't refuse my help, not while there's breath in me and a voice to speak with. I'm afraid it would be a kind of impiety to stand by while justice is slandered and not come to her defense as long as I'm able to draw breath. So I'd better defend her as best I can.'

At that, Glaucon and the others begged me to come to her aid every way I could — not to let the argument drop, but to track the matter down: what each of the two really is, and where the truth lies about their benefits. So I told them what seemed true to me: The inquiry we're attempting is no small thing; it wants sharp eyes, in my judgment. And since we are no great geniuses, I said, I think we should search the way men with weak eyesight would, if they were told to read small letters at a distance and then one of them noticed that the same letters existed somewhere else — larger, on a larger field. It would look like a godsend, surely, to read the big ones first, and then check the small ones against them, to see whether they really are the same.

Glaucon and the others begged me not to let the question drop, but to press on with the inquiry, to get at the truth about what justice and injustice each are, and about their relative advantages. So I told them what I really thought. 'This inquiry we're undertaking is no light one,' I said. 'It needs sharp eyes, and since we're not especially clever, I think we should go about it the way you'd ask someone short-sighted to read small letters from far off. If someone realized the same letters appeared elsewhere in a larger size on a larger surface, it would be a godsend to read the big ones first and then check the small against them.'
Certainly, said Adeimantus. But Socrates, what's the parallel in our search for justice?
'No doubt,' said Adeimantus. 'But what's the parallel to our inquiry into justice?'
I'll tell you, I said. There is a justice of one man, we say; but there is also, surely, a justice of a whole city?
'I'll tell you,' I said. 'We speak of justice as belonging to a single man, and also as belonging to a whole city, don't we?'
Certainly.
'We do,' he said.
And a city is bigger than one man?
'And a city is larger than one man?'
It is.
'It is.'

Then justice may well exist on a larger scale in the larger thing, and be easier to read there. So, if you're all willing, let's first search out what justice is in cities; then let's examine it in the individual too, looking in the shape of the smaller for the likeness of the larger.

'Then maybe there's more justice in the larger thing, and it's easier to make out there. So if you agree, let's first look for justice in a city, and afterward look for it in the individual, comparing the smaller likeness to the larger.'
That seems a fine proposal, he said.
'That's an excellent idea,' he said.
And if we watched a city coming into being — in speech — wouldn't we also see its justice coming into being, and its injustice?
'And if we watched a city coming into being in our discussion,' I said, 'we'd see its justice and its injustice coming into being too?'
We probably would.
'Probably,' he said.
And once the city is complete, we can hope to spot what we're hunting more easily?
'And once that's done, we can hope to find what we're after more easily?'
Yes — much more easily.
'Yes, far more easily.'
Then should we attempt it? I warn you, I said, it's no small job. So think it over.
'Then should we try to carry it through? It's no small task, I think, so consider it carefully.'
It's been thought over, said Adeimantus. Go on — don't hold back.
'We have considered it,' said Adeimantus. 'Go ahead.'

Well then, I said: a city comes into being, I'd say, because none of us is self-sufficient. Each of us falls short of that — we all need many things. Or can you think of any other root for a city to grow from?
'Well then,' I said, 'a city comes into being, I think, because none of us is self-sufficient; we each need many things. Can you think of any other reason a city gets founded?'
None.
'No,' he said, 'none.'

So one man calls in a second for one need, and a third for another; and since we need many things, many of us gather into a single settlement as partners and helpers — and to that shared settlement we give the name city.
