'So because we have many needs, and one man calls in a second to meet one need and a third to meet another, a crowd of people gather in one place as partners and helpers, and we give this settlement the name "city." Right?'
True, he said.
'Yes.'
And each gives to another, or takes from him, whenever they trade — each believing the exchange leaves him better off.
'And one man shares with another, giving and taking, because each thinks the exchange is better for himself?'
Very true.
'Just so.'
Come, then, I said — let's build a city in speech, from its beginning. Though what really builds it, it seems, is our need.
'Then come,' I said, 'let's build our city from the beginning, in our discussion. Though its real builder, it seems, will be our need.'
Of course.
'Of course.'
And the first and greatest of needs is providing food — the thing our existence and our life depend on.
'Now the first and greatest of our needs is food, since without it there's no living and no being alive at all.'
Absolutely.
'Certainly.'
The second is shelter; the third, clothing and things of that kind.
'The second is shelter, and the third clothing and the like.'
True.
'True.'

Well then, I said: how will our city keep up with all that supply? Won't it take one man who's a farmer, another the housebuilder, and someone else a weaver? And should we add a shoemaker, or somebody else who tends to the body's needs?
'Now, how will our city manage to supply all this? Won't one man be a farmer, another a builder, another a weaver? And should we add a shoemaker, or someone else to look after our bodily needs?'
We should.
'Yes.'
So the city at its barest minimum would come to four or five men.
'So the most basic city would consist of four or five men.'
So it appears.
'It seems so.'

Now, how should they work? Should each man put his labor into the common pool — the one farmer, say, raising food for all four, spending four times the hours and four times the sweat on food, and sharing it out with the others? Or should he ignore them and produce a quarter of that food, for himself alone, in a quarter of the time — and spend the other three quarters getting himself a house, a coat, and a pair of shoes, troubling himself with no one, seeing to his own needs with his own hands?

'And what then? Should each of them throw the product of his work into a common pool, the farmer, say, producing enough food for four and spending four times the labor and time growing it, to share with the others? Or should he ignore the rest, grow only a quarter of the food in a quarter of the time, and use the other three quarters to build himself a house, make his own clothes, make his own shoes, never bothering to share with anyone but supplying all his own needs himself?'
Adeimantus's view was that he should keep to raising food for everyone, rather than try to produce everything himself.
Adeimantus said, 'The first way, I'd think, Socrates. He should produce only food.'

Probably right, I said. Because the moment you say it, it strikes me that, to begin with, no two of us are born quite alike. Our natures differ; different natures suit different work. Don't you think?
'And that's probably the better way,' I said. 'Hearing you say it reminds me that we're not all born alike. We differ in our natures, and different natures suit different kinds of work.'
I do.
'True.'
Well: when does a man do finer work — when he spreads himself across many trades, or when he keeps to one?
'And is a job done better when one man works at many trades or when he sticks to one?'
When he keeps to one, he said.
'When he sticks to one.'
And this, I think, is clear as well: let the right moment for a piece of work slip past, and the work is spoiled.
'And surely it's clear too that work is spoiled if you let the right moment for it pass?'
Clear enough.
'Clearly.'
Because the work won't wait on the worker's leisure. The worker has to follow the work's own schedule, and not treat it as a thing for his spare time.
'Because the work won't wait around for the worker to have spare time. The worker has to keep at it as his main business, not treat it as a sideline.'
He has to.
'He must.'

So it comes to this: everything is produced more plentifully, more easily, and better, when one man does one job — the job his nature fits him for — at the right moment, with his hands free of all the rest.

'So the conclusion is that more of everything is produced, and produced better and more easily, when each man does the one thing he's suited to by nature, does it at the right time, and leaves the other trades alone.'
No question.
'Absolutely.'

Then we'll need more than four citizens, Adeimantus, to cover the supplies we named. The farmer, it seems, won't be forging his own plough — not if it's to be a good one — or his hoe, or the rest of his field tools. Neither will the builder make all of his, and he needs plenty too; and the same goes for the weaver and the shoemaker.

'Then we'll need more than four citizens, Adeimantus. The farmer, if he wants a decent plow and hoe and the rest of his tools, won't make them himself. Neither will the builder, who needs plenty of tools of his own. And the same for the weaver and the shoemaker.'
True.
'True.'
So carpenters and smiths and many other craftsmen of that kind will come to share our little city, and start to crowd it.
'So carpenters and smiths and a whole crowd of such craftsmen will join our little settlement and make it bigger.'
True.
'They will.'

Still, it wouldn't be very large yet — not even once we add the cowherds and shepherds and the rest of the herdsmen, so that the farmers have oxen for the plough, the builders and farmers both have teams for hauling, and the weavers and shoemakers have fleeces and hides.

'Still, it won't be a huge place even if we add cowherds and shepherds and the other herdsmen, so that the farmers have oxen for plowing, the builders have draft animals to haul with, and the weavers and shoemakers have fleeces and hides.'
Not very small either, he said, with all of those in it.
'Yet it won't be a small city either,' he said, 'once it holds all of them.'
And then there's the site itself: to plant the city in some spot where it will need no imports at all — that's close to impossible.
'And then there's the question of location,' I said. 'It's nearly impossible to set up a city where it needs to import nothing.'
Impossible.
'Impossible.'
So it will need still more people, to fetch in what it needs from other cities.
'So we'll need still another set of people to fetch from other cities what ours lacks.'
It will.
'We will.'
But if our agent goes out empty-handed — carrying nothing that the people he needs things from happen to need themselves — then empty-handed he'll come home. Won't he?
'But if our agent shows up empty-handed, with nothing the other city wants, he'll come home empty-handed too.'
So it seems.
'That's right.'
Then what they make at home must be not just enough for themselves, but of the kind, and in the quantity, to serve the people they'll be trading with.
'So our people must produce at home not only enough for themselves but enough, in kind and quantity, to satisfy the people they're getting things from.'
It must.
'They must.'
So our city needs more farmers, and more of the other craftsmen.
'So we'll need more farmers and more craftsmen in our city.'
More of them, yes.
'Yes.'
And more agents too, presumably — the men to handle each import and export. And those men are merchants, aren't they?
'And other agents besides, to handle the importing and exporting. These are the merchants, aren't they?'
Yes.
'Yes.'
Then we'll need merchants as well.
'So we'll need merchants too.'
Certainly.
'Certainly.'
And if the trading runs over the sea, we'll need a whole crowd more — men who know the work of ships.
'And if the trade goes by sea, we'll need a good many more people skilled in seafaring.'
A whole crowd of them, yes.
'A good many.'
Now, inside the city itself: how will they share out what each of them makes? That sharing, remember, was the very reason we formed a partnership and founded a city at all.
'Now, within the city itself, how will people exchange what each produces? That, after all, was our whole reason for forming a partnership and founding a city in the first place.'
Obviously, he said, by buying and selling.
'Plainly they'll buy and sell.'
That gives us a marketplace, then — and money, a token that stands in for goods, for the sake of exchange.
'Then we'll need a marketplace and a currency, a token, for exchange.'
Certainly.
'Certainly.'

But suppose the farmer, or one of the other craftsmen, hauls what he's made to market and doesn't arrive at the same moment as the people who want to trade with him. Is he to sit idle in the marketplace, while his own work goes wanting?
'Now suppose a farmer, or some other producer, brings his goods to market, but arrives when there's no one there to trade with him. Is he to sit idle in the marketplace, away from his own work?'

Not at all, he said — there are men who see that opening and station themselves to fill it. In well-run cities they're generally the weakest in body, useless for work of any other kind. Their business is to stay planted in the market, paying money for goods to those who come wanting to sell, and handing over goods for money to those who come wanting to buy.

'Not at all,' he said. 'There are people who notice this and step in to serve as middlemen. In well-run cities these are usually the ones too weak in body to do anything else. Their job is to wait in the market, take money from those who want to buy, and hand over money to those who want to sell.'

So that need, I said, brings retailers into our city. Isn't that what we call the men who sit fixed in the marketplace to serve the buying and the selling — retailers — while the ones who rove from city to city are merchants?
'So this need creates a class of shopkeepers in our city. Don't we call the ones who sit in the market buying and selling shopkeepers, and the ones who travel between cities merchants?'
Just so.
'Yes.'

And there are still other workers, I think — men whose minds don't quite earn them a place as partners, but whose bodies are strong enough for heavy labor. They sell the use of their strength; the price they get for it is called a wage; and so, if I'm not mistaken, they're called wage-earners. True?

'And there's still another class, I think, of people who aren't much as partners in thought, but who have the bodily strength for heavy work. They sell the use of their strength, and since they're paid a wage, or hire, for it, we call them hired laborers, don't we?'
True.
'True.'
Then wage-earners, too, help fill out our city.
'So hired laborers help fill out the city too.'
I think so.
'They do.'
Well then, Adeimantus — has our city grown to its full size now?
'Then, Adeimantus, has our city grown to its full size now? Is it complete?'
Perhaps it has.
'Perhaps so.'
Then where in it is justice? And where is injustice? At what point did they come in, among all the things we've been moving in?
'Then where in it is justice, and where injustice? Along with which of the parts we've described did they come in?'
I can't see it, Socrates, he said — unless it's somewhere in the dealings of these people with one another. I can't imagine where else they'd be found.
'I can't see it, Socrates,' he said, 'unless it's somewhere in the dealings these people have with one another.'
You may well be right, I said. We'd better look straight at it, then, and not flinch.
'You may well be right,' I said. 'Let's look into it and not give up.'

First, let's consider how people provided for in this way will live. Won't they raise grain and make wine, weave clothes, cobble shoes? They'll build their houses; in summer they'll work mostly stripped down and barefoot, in winter clothed and shod well enough. For food they'll grind their barley and their wheat — kneading the one, baking the other — and heap their handsome flatcakes and loaves on reeds or on clean leaves. They'll dine reclining on beds of strewn briony and myrtle, they and their children with them, drinking their wine after, wearing garlands, singing hymns to the gods, delighting in one another's company; and they'll have no more children than their means can carry, keeping a wary eye on poverty and on war.

'First, then, let's think about how people will live in the city we've set up. Won't they produce grain and wine and clothes and shoes, and build themselves houses? In summer they'll mostly work stripped and barefoot, and in winter they'll be well clothed and shod. They'll live on barley meal and wheat flour, kneading and baking it into fine cakes and loaves, which they'll lay out on a mat of reeds or on clean leaves. They'll stretch out on couches strewn with bryony and myrtle, and feast with their children, drinking the wine they've made, wearing garlands and singing the praises of the gods, enjoying one another's company. And they'll be careful not to have more children than they can afford, keeping an eye on poverty and on war.'
But Glaucon broke in: You've served these men their dinner, it seems, with nothing to put on the bread.
Here Glaucon broke in. 'It seems,' he said, 'you give your men a feast with no cooked dishes.'

True enough, I said — I forgot. They'll have relish too, of course: salt, obviously, and olives and cheese, and the bulbs and greens that country people boil into their pots; and for dessert we'll set them figs and chickpeas and beans, and they'll roast myrtle-berries and acorns at the fire, sipping wine in moderation as they go. And so, in peace and in health, they'll live out their lives to a good old age, as you'd expect, and hand down the same kind of life to their children after them.

'You're right,' I said. 'I forgot they'll have something to go with their bread, salt, of course, and olives and cheese, and they'll boil up the kinds of roots and greens you get in the country. For dessert we'll set out figs, chickpeas, and beans, and they'll roast myrtle berries and acorns at the fire, drinking in moderation as they go. And living like this, in peace and good health, they'll most likely reach old age and pass a life of the same kind on to their children.'
And if you were fitting out a city of pigs, Socrates, he said — isn't that exactly the feed you'd fatten them on?
'Socrates,' he said, 'if you were founding a city of pigs, isn't this exactly the fodder you'd feed them?'
Well, how should it be done, Glaucon? I said.
'Then how should they live, Glaucon?' I asked.
The way it's usually done, he said. If they're not to live like animals, people recline on couches, dine off tables, and eat the cooked dishes and sweets that people eat today.
'In the usual comfort,' he said. 'They should recline on proper couches, I'd think, and eat off tables, and have the sauces and sweets people have nowadays.'

Ah, I said — now I understand. So we're examining not just how a city comes into being, but how a luxurious city does. Maybe that's no bad thing: watching that kind, we might spot sooner where justice and injustice take root in cities. Still, the true city — the healthy one, so to speak — is, to my mind, the one we've just described. But if you all want to look at a city with a fever, nothing stands in our way. Plainly the simple life won't satisfy some people. There will have to be couches, and tables, and the rest of the furniture; cooked delicacies, naturally, and perfume and incense, courtesans and pastries — and every variety of each. And the things we first counted as bare necessities — houses, clothes, shoes — plain versions will no longer do: now painting and embroidery must be set in motion, and gold and ivory and everything of that sort must be procured. Yes?

'I see,' I said. 'So it's not just a city we're examining now, but a luxurious one. Well, there may be no harm in that. By looking at such a city we may all the sooner spot where justice and injustice take root in a community. The true city, the healthy one, is the one I described. But if you'd like, let's look at a fevered city too. Plenty of people, it seems, won't be content with the simple fare and the way of life I laid out. They'll want couches and tables and other furniture added, and fancy dishes, and perfumes and incense, and call girls and pastries, every kind of each. And we can't restrict ourselves any longer to the bare necessities I started with, the houses and clothes and shoes. We'll have to set painting and embroidery going, and get hold of gold and ivory and all the rest.'
Yes, he said.
'True,' he said.

Then the city has to swell again; the healthy one is too small now. It must be stuffed with a mass and multitude of occupations that answer to no natural need — the whole tribe of hunters, to start, and all the imitators: the many who work in shapes and colors, and the many who work in music — the poets and their train of servants, reciters, actors, dancers, producers; and the makers of gear of every description, the gear of women's finery included. And we'll need many more servants besides. Won't there be a call for tutors, wet-nurses, nannies, ladies' maids, barbers — and then for sauce-cooks and chefs? And swineherds too: we had none in our earlier city — there was no need — but in this one we'll need them; and herds upon herds of every other animal, if people are going to eat them. Won't we?

'So we'll have to enlarge the city, because the healthy one isn't big enough now. We have to swell it with a whole crowd and a great mass of people who aren't there to meet any real need: hunters of every kind, and imitators, droves of them, some working with shapes and colors, others with music, poets and their assistants, reciters, actors, dancers, producers, and makers of all sorts of goods, including the ones for women's adornment. And we'll need more servants too. Don't you think we'll want attendants for boys, wet nurses and dry nurses, hairdressers, barbers, and cooks and butchers besides? And we'll need swineherds as well. There were none in our earlier city, which didn't need them, but this one will. And it will need vast herds of other animals, if people are going to eat them, won't it?'
Certainly.
'Of course.'
And living this way, we'll need doctors far more often than we did before?
'And living this way, we'll need far more doctors than before, won't we?'
Far more.
'Far more.'
And the land, which was enough to feed everyone then, will now be too small. True?
'And the land that was enough to feed the original population will now be too small. Wouldn't you say so?'
Quite true.
'Yes.'

Then we'll have to carve ourselves a slice of our neighbors' land, if we're to have pasture and plough-land enough — and they'll want to carve a slice of ours, if they too have let themselves slip past the limit of the necessary, into the endless getting of money.

'So we'll have to carve off a piece of our neighbors' land if we mean to have enough to pasture and plow, and they'll want a piece of ours, if they too have given themselves over to grabbing endless wealth, past the limit of what they really need.'
There's no avoiding it, Socrates, he said.
'That's bound to happen, Socrates.'
And after that we go to war, Glaucon. Or how does it play out?
'So the next step is war, Glaucon. Isn't it?'
We go to war, he said.
'It is,' he said.

Now, let's say nothing yet about whether war works harm or good, I said — only this much: we have found where war is born. It grows out of the same soil that most of a city's evils grow from, private evils and public ones alike.

'We needn't yet say whether war does good or harm,' I said. 'But we can say this much: we've found the origin of war, and it lies in the very things that breed nearly all the evils a city suffers, in private and in public alike.'
No doubt of it.
'Yes.'

Then, my friend, the city must be bigger yet again — and not by a little, but by a whole army: one that will march out and fight the invaders for all the city's wealth, and for everything and everyone we were just describing.

'So the city must grow larger again, my friend, and not by a little but by a whole army, which has to march out and fight any attackers in defense of all the city's wealth and the people we were just describing.'
Why? he said. Aren't the citizens enough by themselves?
'Why?' he said. 'Can't the citizens defend themselves?'
Not if the bargain we all struck was sound, I said, when we were shaping the city. And we agreed, if you remember, that one man cannot practice many crafts well.
'No,' I said, 'not if the principle we all agreed on when we were founding the city was right. We agreed, you'll remember, that one man can't do many crafts well.'
True, he said.
'True,' he said.
Well then — doesn't fighting a war look to you like a craft?
'Well, isn't fighting a war a craft?'
Very much so.
'Very much so.'
One deserving as much attention as shoemaking?
'And should we care more about the craft of shoemaking than the craft of war?'
It certainly does.
'Not at all.'

But we stopped the shoemaker from trying to be a farmer at the same time, or a weaver, or a builder; a shoemaker he stayed, so that the shoemaking would be done well. To every other worker, the same way, we assigned one job — the job his nature fitted him for, the one he'd work at all his life, kept clear of the others, never letting the right moments slip — and so do fine work. Now, is anything more important than that the work of war be done well? Or is war so undemanding a business that a farmer can be a soldier on the side — or a shoemaker, or the practitioner of any trade you like — when nobody on earth can so much as become a decent player of checkers or dice by taking the game up as a pastime instead of working at it from childhood? Does a man just pick up a shield, or whatever the weapon or tool of war may be, and turn that same day into a competent fighter in heavy armor, or in any other kind of combat — when no other tool in the world makes a craftsman or an athlete of the man who merely grabs hold of it, and is worth nothing to anyone who hasn't gained the knowledge of it and put in the practice?

'Now, we wouldn't let the shoemaker try to be a farmer or a weaver or a builder at the same time. We kept him to shoemaking so that the work would be done well. We assigned each man the single trade he was suited to by nature, and had him work at that one thing his whole life, leaving the others, so as not to miss the right moments and to do good work. And surely nothing matters more than that the work of war be done well. Or is soldiering so easy a craft that a man can be a farmer or a shoemaker or a tradesman and a soldier on the side, when no one can become even a decent checkers or dice player by picking it up casually and not practicing it from childhood? Can a man pick up a shield, or any other weapon or tool of war, and become a competent fighter in the heavy infantry, or any other unit, that very same day? No other tool makes a craftsman or a champion of the man who takes it up without knowledge of it and without practice.'
Tools that could teach a man their own use, he said, would be beyond price.
'If it did,' he said, 'tools would be worth a great deal.'
Then the greater the guardians' work is, I said, the more it demands: the most freedom from every other business, and the greatest skill and dedication in its own.
'So the higher the guardians' task is, the more it will demand of them, more freedom from other work, and more skill and care than anything else.'
I'd certainly think so, he replied.
'I should think so.'
And a nature, too, fitted to that very calling?
'And won't it demand a nature suited to that very calling?'
Of course.
'Of course.'
Then it would seem to be our job — if we can manage it — to pick out which natures, and what kind of natures, are fit to guard a city.
'Then our job, it seems, is to pick out, if we can, which natures are fit for guarding the city.'
Our job indeed.
'Yes, that's our job.'
My god, I said — then it's no light thing we've shouldered. Still, no flinching: we do what our strength allows.
'By Zeus,' I said, 'it's no light task we've taken on. Still, we mustn't lose our nerve. We have to do the best we can.'
No flinching, he agreed.
'We do.'
Now — do you think, I said, that when it comes to keeping guard, the nature of a well-bred pup differs much from the nature of a well-born young man?
'Now,' I said, 'don't you think that, for the purpose of guarding, the nature of a well-bred young dog and a noble young man are alike?'
How do you mean?
'What do you mean?'
I mean each of them needs senses sharp enough to spot the enemy, speed enough to run down what he's spotted, and strength enough, if he catches it, to fight it out.
'I mean that each of them must be keen-sighted, quick to spot an enemy, fast enough to chase him down once spotted, and strong enough to fight him if he has to give battle.'
They'll need all of that, yes.
'Yes,' he said, 'they need all of that.'
And courage, surely — if he's going to fight well.
'And brave, if he's to fight well.'
Of course.
'Of course.'

And will any creature be brave without spirit — a horse, a dog, anything alive? Have you never noticed what an irresistible, unbeatable thing spirit is? Let a soul have it, and that soul stands fearless before anything, and gives way to nothing.

'But will any creature, horse or dog or whatever, be brave if it has no spirit? Haven't you noticed how irresistible and unbeatable spirit is, how its presence makes a soul utterly fearless and proof against everything?'
I have noticed.
'I have.'
So what our guardian has to be in body is clear enough.
'So much, then, for the bodily qualities our guardian needs.'
Yes.
'Yes.'
And in soul as well: he must be spirited.
'And as for the qualities of soul, he must be full of spirit.'
That too.
'That too.'
Then here's the problem, Glaucon, I said. With natures like that, what is to keep them from turning savage — against one another, and against the rest of the citizens?
'But, Glaucon,' I said, 'won't natures like that be fierce toward one another and toward everyone else, if that's what they're like?'
By god, he said — it won't be easy.
'That,' he said, 'will be hard to deal with.'
And yet they must be gentle to their own people and hard on the enemy. Otherwise they won't wait for somebody else to destroy the city; they'll get there first themselves.
'And yet they have to be gentle to their own people and dangerous to the enemy. Otherwise they won't wait for an enemy to destroy them; they'll do it to themselves first.'
True, he said.
'True,' he said.
So what do we do? I said. Where do we find a character at once gentle and great-spirited? A gentle nature is the opposite of a spirited one, after all.
'So what are we to do?' I said. 'Where will we find a nature that's gentle and high-spirited at once, when the two seem to be opposites?'
So it appears.
'I don't know.'
And yet take away either quality, and a good guardian is out of the question. The combination looks impossible — from which it follows, apparently, that a good guardian is impossible too.
'And yet without both of these he can't be a good guardian. So it looks impossible, and we seem forced to conclude that a good guardian can't exist.'
I'm afraid so, he said.
'I'm afraid so,' he said.
Stuck there, I looked back over what we'd been saying. We deserve to be stuck, my friend, I said — we've wandered off from the very image we set up.
I was stuck, but turning the thing over in my mind, I said, 'We deserve to be stuck, my friend, because we've let go of the comparison we set up.'
Meaning what?
'How so?'
Meaning we failed to notice that there really are natures with these opposites in them — natures we were assuming couldn't exist.
'We've overlooked the fact that there really are natures with these opposite qualities together.'
And where would one find them?
'And where?'

In plenty of animals, actually — but best of all in the very one we matched our guardian with. You know how it is with well-bred dogs: their disposition is to be as gentle as can be with the people they know and are used to, and the very opposite with strangers.

'In several animals,' I said, 'but you can see it in the one we compared our guardian to. You know, surely, that a well-bred dog is by nature as gentle as can be with the people it knows and the opposite with strangers.'
I know it well.
'I do know that.'
So the thing is possible, I said — and in looking for a guardian built this way, we're not looking for anything against nature.
'So it's not impossible after all. We're not asking anything against nature in looking for a guardian like that.'
Apparently not.
'It seems not.'
Now, would you say our future guardian needs one thing more — that along with the spirit, he needs something of the philosopher in his nature?
'And don't you think the guardian's nature needs something more, on top of being spirited? It needs to be philosophical, a lover of wisdom.'
How so? he said. I don't follow.
'How do you mean? I don't follow.'
It's another thing you'll see in dogs, I said — something to wonder at in a mere animal.
'This too,' I said, 'you'll notice in dogs, and it's a thing worth wondering at in the animal.'
What thing?
'What thing?'

That the sight of a stranger angers a dog before the man has done him any harm at all, while the sight of someone he knows delights him, though the man has never done him a moment's good. Has that never struck you as strange?

'When a dog sees a stranger, it turns angry, though the man has done it no harm; and when it sees someone familiar, it greets him warmly, though he's never done it any good. Did you never find that remarkable?'
I'd never paid it much attention before, he said. But that's certainly what they do.
'I never really thought about it before,' he said, 'but yes, that's plainly what a dog does.'
Well, it's an exquisite touch in his nature, that — genuinely philosophic, in fact.
'Well, it's a fine trait in the dog, and a truly philosophical one.'
How so?
'How so?'

Because the one test he uses, I said, to tell a friendly face from a hostile one is that he knows the first and doesn't know the second. Now, how could a creature be anything but a lover of learning, when it defines what is its own and what is foreign by knowledge and by ignorance?

'Because the dog tells friend from enemy by nothing but this: it knows the one and doesn't know the other. And how could a creature that draws the line between what's its own and what's alien by knowledge and ignorance be anything but a lover of learning?'
How indeed.
'It couldn't,' he said.
And the love of learning and the love of wisdom — philosophy — are the same thing?
'And isn't loving learning the same as loving wisdom, the same as being philosophical?'
The same, he said.
'It is.'
Then may we say it of a man too, and say it with confidence: if he's to be gentle toward his own and toward the people he knows, he must be by nature a lover of wisdom and of learning?
'So shall we say with confidence that for a man too, if he's to be gentle toward his own people and those he knows, he must by nature be a lover of wisdom and of learning?'
We may.
'Yes,' he said.
So there is our man: philosophic, spirited, swift, and strong by nature — the one who is going to make a fine and good guardian of our city?
'Then the man who's going to be a truly fine and good guardian of our city will be philosophical, spirited, fast, and strong, all at once.'
Nothing surer.
'Absolutely,' he said.

That is what he'd be to start with, then. But now, how do we rear these men, and how do we educate them? And will working through that question move us toward the goal this whole inquiry is aimed at — how justice and injustice come to be in a city? I don't want us to skip what matters, or to drag through what doesn't.

'So that's what he'll be like to begin with. But how are these men to be raised and educated? And does looking into that help us with the larger question we set out to answer, namely, how justice and injustice arise in a city? We don't want to leave anything important out, but we don't want to drag the discussion out endlessly either.'
Adeimantus answered: I fully expect the question will serve us well.
Adeimantus said, 'I certainly expect the inquiry into education to help with that.'
Then by god, my dear Adeimantus, I said, we mustn't drop it — even if it proves a long road.
'Then by all means, my dear Adeimantus,' I said, 'we mustn't drop it, even if it turns out to be a bit long.'
No, we mustn't.
'No, we mustn't.'
Come then — like men with time on their hands, telling stories to pass it — let's educate these men of ours in speech.
'Come, then, and let's educate these men in our discussion, as if we were telling a story at our leisure.'
By all means.
'Let's do it.'
So what will the education be? Or is it hard to find better than the one long time has already worked out — gymnastics for the body, and for the soul, music: everything that belongs to the Muses?
'What will their education be? It's hard to find anything better than what tradition has already worked out: physical training for the body, and the arts, music and poetry, for the soul.'
It would be hard.
'True.'
And we'll begin the education with music, before gymnastics?
'And shall we start with the arts, before we get to physical training?'
Of course.
'Of course.'
And under music, I said, you count stories, don't you?
'And when you say "the arts," do you include stories and literature, or not?'
I do.
'I do.'
And stories come in two kinds — the true and the false?
'And there are two kinds of these, the true and the false?'
Yes.
'Yes.'
And our men must be educated in both — but in the false ones first?
'And our education should use both, beginning with the false?'
I don't see what you mean, he said.
'I don't understand what you mean,' he said.

You don't see, I said, that we start our children on myths before anything else? And a myth, taken as a whole, is false — though there's truth in it too. And we set children to myths before we ever set them to gymnastics.

'Don't you see,' I said, 'that the first thing we do with children is tell them stories? And these are, on the whole, false, though there's some truth in them too. And we tell children stories before we put them to physical training.'
That's so.
'That's so.'
That's what I meant by taking up music before gymnastics.
'That's what I meant by starting with the arts before physical training.'
Quite right, he said.
'You're right,' he said.

And you know that in any work the beginning is what matters most — above all with anything young and tender. That's when a creature is most easily molded; that's when whatever stamp you choose to press into it sinks in and holds.

'Now, you know that in any undertaking the most important part is the beginning, especially with anything young and tender. That's when it's most malleable, and takes whatever stamp you want to impress on it.'
Exactly.
'Quite so.'

Then shall we carelessly let our children hear whatever myths whoever happens along has happened to make up — and take into their souls opinions that are, for the most part, the very opposite of the ones we'll think they should hold when they're grown?

'Then shall we casually let children hear just any stories, made up by just anyone, and take into their souls beliefs that are mostly the opposite of the ones we think they should hold when they grow up?'
We will not allow that at all.
'We certainly won't allow that.'

So our first job, it seems, is to stand watch over the makers of stories: to approve any story they make well, and to reject the rest. The approved ones we'll persuade the nurses and mothers to tell the children — shaping their souls with stories with far more care than they give to shaping their bodies with their hands. Most of the stories they tell now will have to be thrown out.

'So our first job, it seems, is to supervise the storytellers. We'll approve the good stories they tell and reject the bad ones, and we'll have the mothers and nurses tell the children only the approved ones, and shape their souls with these stories far more than they shape their bodies with their hands. But most of the stories they now tell will have to be thrown out.'
Which ones do you mean? he said.
'Which ones?' he asked.
The great stories will show us the pattern for the smaller ones too, I said. Great and small are necessarily cut from the same cloth, and carry the same stamp. Don't you think so?
'If we look at the great stories,' I said, 'we'll see the pattern of the small ones too, since great and small are bound to share the same type and have the same effect. Don't you think so?'
Very likely, he replied — but I still don't know which ones you're calling great.
'I do,' he said. 'But I don't even know which you mean by the great stories.'

The ones Hesiod and Homer told us, I said — those two, and the rest of the poets. They have always been mankind's great storytellers; and the tales they composed were false, and they told them to men, and men tell them still.
'The ones Homer and Hesiod told us,' I said, 'and the other poets. They've always been the great storytellers of mankind, telling the tales men still tell.'
But which stories? he said. What is the fault you find in them?
'Which stories do you mean,' he said, 'and what fault do you find with them?'
The fault that deserves the first and gravest blame, I said: telling lies — and what's more, telling them badly.
'The fault one should mind most of all,' I said, 'especially when the lie is an ugly one.'
And when does that happen?
'And what's that?'
Whenever a story draws the nature of gods and heroes falsely — the way a painter fails whose portrait carries no likeness at all to the thing he set out to paint.
'Misrepresenting, in speech, what the gods and heroes are really like, the way a painter paints a portrait with no likeness at all to what he meant to paint.'
Yes, he said — that kind of thing certainly deserves blame. But how do they do it? What sort of thing do you mean?
'Yes,' he said, 'we're right to object to that. But which stories do you mean exactly?'

First, I said, the greatest lie of all, told about the greatest beings — and an ugly lie at that: Hesiod's tale of what Uranus did, and how Cronus took his revenge on him. As for Cronus's own deeds, and what his son did to him in turn — even if they were true, I wouldn't think they should be told so freely to the young and unformed. Far the best would be silence; and if they simply had to be told, then let a chosen few hear them in secret rite, after sacrificing not a pig but some great victim, hard to procure — so that the circle of hearers stays as small as it possibly can.

'First of all,' I said, 'the biggest lie about the most important things, the one whose teller told it badly: how Uranus did the things Hesiod says he did, and how Cronus took his revenge on him. As for the deeds of Cronus, and what his son in turn did to him, even if they were true I'd say they shouldn't be told so lightly to the young and foolish. Better to keep silent. But if there were some need to tell them, only a tiny few should hear them in secret, after sacrificing not an ordinary piglet but some huge victim almost no one could afford, so that as few people as possible would ever hear them.'
You're right, he said — those stories are hard ones.
'Yes,' he said, 'those stories are indeed hard to defend.'

And they are not to be told in our city, Adeimantus, I said. No young listener is to be told that in committing the most extreme crimes he'd be doing nothing shocking — or in punishing an unjust father by whatever means came to hand — that he'd only be doing what the first and greatest of the gods have done before him.

'And they shouldn't be told in our city, Adeimantus,' I said. 'A young man mustn't be told that in committing the worst of crimes he's doing nothing out of the ordinary, nor that if he punishes a father who's done wrong, by any means whatever, he's only doing what the first and greatest of the gods did.'
God, no, he said. I don't think those things are fit for telling either.
'No,' he said, 'I quite agree those tales aren't fit to be repeated.'

Nor a word about gods warring on gods — the plots, the pitched battles — none of which is true anyway — not if the future guardians of our city are to believe that hating one another over trifles is the ugliest thing there is. The last thing we should do is tell them tales of the battles of the giants, or work those battles into embroidered robes — or all the other quarrels, so many and so various, of gods and heroes against their own kith and kin. No: if we mean to persuade them that no citizen has ever been at odds with another citizen, and that such a thing is unholy, then that is the note the old men and old women must strike from the children's first days; and as the children grow, the poets must be made to compose along the same lines for them. But Hera bound by her own son; Hephaestus flung from heaven by his father for trying to shield his mother from a beating; and every battle of the gods that Homer composed — these must not be admitted into our city, whether they were meant as allegory or not. The young can't judge what is allegory and what isn't; whatever opinions get in at that age tend to set — hard to wash out, and immovable ever after. Which is exactly why the first stories they hear should be, perhaps, the finest things they could possibly hear — stories composed to turn them toward virtue.

'Nor should we have any talk at all of gods warring on gods, plotting against them, and fighting them, none of it true, if we mean the future guardians of our city to think that turning on one another is the most shameful thing there is. Far less should we tell them, or have them embroidered on tapestries, the battles of the giants and all the many other feuds the gods and heroes had with their own kin and kindred. If we mean to convince them that no two citizens have ever quarreled and that to quarrel is unholy, then that's the sort of thing the old men and women should tell the children from the start, and the poets must be compelled to compose in the same spirit once the children are older. As for the tale of Hephaestus being chained up by his mother Hera, or Hephaestus flung out of heaven by his father for trying to defend his mother when she was being beaten, and all the battles of the gods that Homer has composed, we mustn't admit them into the city, whether they're written with a hidden meaning or without one. A young person can't tell what's hidden meaning and what isn't, and the beliefs he takes in at that age tend to become fixed and hard to shift. That's why we should do everything to make sure the first stories they hear are composed as finely as possible to lead them toward virtue.'
That stands to reason, he replied. But if someone pressed us — which stories are those, exactly? — what would we say?
'That makes sense,' he said. 'But if someone pressed us on this and asked which stories we mean and what they are, what could we tell him?'

Adeimantus, I said, you and I are not poets, not today; we are founders of a city. Founders need to know the patterns their poets must build stories on, and the lines past which those poets can't be allowed to go. But composing the stories is not the founders' work.

'Adeimantus,' I said, 'you and I aren't poets right now; we're founding a city. And the founders of a city should know the patterns the poets must follow in telling their stories, and forbid them to depart from those; but the founders don't have to compose the stories themselves.'
Fair enough, he said. But that's just it: these patterns for speaking of the gods — what would they be?
'True,' he said. 'But these patterns for stories about the gods, what would they be?'
Something like this, I said. However the god actually is, that is how he must always be rendered — whether the rendering is done in epic, in song, or in tragedy.
'Something like this,' I said. 'Whatever the poetry, epic, lyric, or tragic, the god must always be portrayed as he really is.'
So he must.
'He must.'
Well then: the god is truly good, and must be spoken of as such?
'And isn't the god in fact good, and so to be described as good?'
Certainly.
'Of course.'
And nothing good is harmful, is it?
'And nothing good is harmful, is it?'
I think not.
'I think not.'
Does what isn't harmful do harm?
'And what isn't harmful does no harm?'
Never.
'Not at all.'
And what does no harm — does it do any evil?
'And what does no harm does no evil?'
No again.
'No.'
And what does no evil could hardly be the cause of any evil?
'And what does no evil couldn't be the cause of any evil?'
How could it be?
'How could it be?'
Go on: the good is beneficial?
'Well then, is the good beneficial?'
Yes.
'Yes.'
The cause, then, of well-being?
'So it's the cause of doing well?'
Yes.
'Yes.'
Then the good is not the cause of everything. Of what goes well it is the cause; of what goes badly it is blameless.
'Then the good isn't the cause of everything. It's the cause of the things that go well, but not of the things that go badly.'
Entirely so, he said.
'Absolutely,' he said.

Then neither can the god, since he is good, be the cause of everything, as most people say. Of what befalls human beings he is the cause of only a little; for the greater part he bears no blame — for our goods are far fewer than our evils. The goods we must credit to no one but the god; but for the evils we have to hunt out some other cause — anything but him.

'So the god, since he's good, can't be the cause of everything, as most people say. He's the cause of only a few things that happen to us, and not of most, since the good things in human life are far fewer than the bad. The good things we can attribute to no one but the god, but for the bad we must look for some other cause, not the god.'
That seems to me, he said, as true as it gets.
'That seems perfectly true to me,' he said.
Then we must not accept it — not from Homer, not from any other poet — when they blunder about the gods, foolishly, and tell us that two jars
'So we mustn't accept it from Homer, or any other poet, when he foolishly makes this mistake about the gods and says that two jars'
'stand on Zeus's floor, filled with fates — one jar / of good, the other of evil,'
'"stand on the threshold of Zeus, full of fates, one of good ones, the other of bad,"'
and that the man to whom Zeus deals a mixture of the two
'and that the man to whom Zeus gives a mixture of the two'
'meets now with evil, and now again with good,'
'"meets now with evil and now with good,"'
while the man who gets the second jar unmixed —
'while the man Zeus gives only from the second jar, the unmixed bad,'
'gnawing hunger drives him across the shining earth.'
'"is driven by ravening hunger over the bright earth."'
Nor this, either:

'Nor will we accept that Zeus is for us "the steward of good and evil alike." And if anyone says that the breaking of the oaths and truces, which was really Pandarus's doing, was brought about by Athena and Zeus, we won't praise him for it; nor that the strife and judgment among the goddesses came from Themis and Zeus. Nor again may our young men hear what Aeschylus says, that'
'Zeus, who deals out the good and the evil to us.'
'"a god plants guilt in men when he wants to ruin a house utterly."'

And whoever says that the breaking of the oaths and the truce — which was Pandarus's doing — was brought about by Athena and Zeus, will not have our approval; nor the strife and the trial of the gods, laid to Themis and Zeus. Nor may the young be allowed to hear what Aeschylus says, that

'If a poet writes of the sufferings of Niobe, the subject of the play those lines come from, or of the house of Pelops, or of the Trojan war, or anything like it, either we won't let him say these things are the work of a god, or, if he does, he must find just the kind of account we're now demanding: he must say the god did what was just and good, and that the people were better off being punished. But we won't let the poet say that those who pay the penalty are made wretched, and that a god did it to them. We'll allow him to say that the wicked were wretched because they needed punishing, and that in paying the penalty by the god's hand they were benefited. But that the god, who is good, became the cause of evil to anyone, this we must fight against with all our strength. No one, young or old, is to say it or hear it, in verse or in prose, if our city is to be well governed. Such things are unholy to say, harmful to us, and out of tune with themselves.'
'god plants the guilt in mortal men / when he wills to ruin a house, root and branch.'
'I'm with you,' he said, 'and I'd happily vote for this as a law.'

And if anyone composes the sufferings of Niobe — the play those lines come from — or the house of Pelops, or the Trojan war, or anything in that vein, then either he must not be allowed to call these things the work of a god; or, if a god's work they are, he must find in them some such account as we are seeking now: he must say that what the god did was just and good, and that the punished were the better for their punishment. What the poet cannot be permitted to say is that those who paid the penalty were miserable, and that a god was the cause. If he said that bad men were miserable because they needed punishing, and that the god's punishment did them good — that we would allow. But that a god, who is good, becomes the cause of evil to anyone — that claim must be fought with everything we have: no one is to say it in his own city, if that city is to be well governed, and no one is to hear it, young or old, in verse or out of it. Said aloud, such things are impieties; they profit no one; and they do not even agree with themselves.
'So this will be one of our laws and patterns about the gods, the one our speakers and poets must work within: the god is not the cause of everything, but only of the things that are good.'
You have my vote for that law, he said. It suits me well.
'And that's good enough,' he said.
Then let this stand as the first of our laws and patterns for the gods, which all speaking and all composing will have to fit: the god is not the cause of everything — only of the good.

'Now, what about a second pattern? Do you think the god is a sorcerer, able to appear treacherously in one form at one time and another at another, sometimes by actually changing himself and passing into many shapes, sometimes by deceiving us and making us think we see him so? Or is he simple, one being, less likely than anything else to step outside his own form?'
Quite satisfactory, he said.
'I can't answer offhand,' he said.

Now for a second one — see what you think of this. Is the god a sorcerer? Would he appear by design now in one shape and now in another — sometimes actually changing, trading his own form for a crowd of others, sometimes only fooling us into thinking he had? Or is he single and simple — of all beings the least likely to step out of his own form?
'Then answer this. If something steps outside its own form, mustn't the change come either from itself or from something else?'
I can't say, he replied — not on the spot.
'It must.'
Then try it this way. If a thing steps out of its own form, mustn't the change come either from itself or from something else?

'And aren't the things in the best condition the least altered and disturbed by anything outside them? A body, for instance, by food and drink and exertion, or a growing plant by sun and wind and the like, isn't it the healthiest and strongest that's least changed by these?'
It must.
'Of course.'

And things in the best condition are the ones least changed or shifted by anything outside them. Take the body: the healthiest and strongest is least altered by food and drink and hard labor; take any plant: the most vigorous is least altered by sun and wind and everything of that kind. Isn't it so?
'And wouldn't an external blow least confuse and disturb the soul that's bravest and wisest?'
Of course.
'Yes.'
And the braver and wiser a soul is, the less any outside force can shake it or warp it?
'And the same goes, I'd say, for all manufactured things, furniture, houses, clothing: the well-made and well-conditioned ones are least altered by time and by anything else that happens to them.'
Yes.
'That's so.'
And the same holds, I'd suppose, even for made things — furniture, houses, clothes: when they're well made and in good condition, time and wear alter them least.
'So everything that's in good condition, whether by nature or craft or both, admits the least change from outside itself.'
That's so.
'It seems so.'
So whatever is in a fine state — whether nature made it so, or craft, or both — admits the least change from outside.
'But surely the god, and everything that belongs to the god, is in every way in the best condition.'
So it seems.
'Of course.'
But the god, and everything that belongs to the god, is in every way in the finest state?
'So on this score the god would be the least likely of all things to take many shapes.'
Of course.
'The least likely indeed.'
Then on that side, the god is the last thing in the world to take many shapes.
'Then would he change and alter himself?'
The very last.
'Clearly,' he said, 'if he's altered at all.'
But might he change and transform himself?
'And would he change himself into something better and finer, or into something worse and uglier than himself?'
Clearly he must, he said — if he changes at all.
'It would have to be into something worse,' he said, 'if he changes at all, since we can't say the god is lacking in any beauty or goodness.'
Then which way? Does he make himself better and more beautiful by the change, or worse and uglier?
'Quite right,' I said. 'And given that, do you think anyone, god or man, would willingly make himself worse in any way?'
Worse — it could only be worse, if he's altered at all. For surely we won't say the god is lacking in beauty or in goodness.
'Impossible,' he said.
Exactly right, I said. And that being so, Adeimantus, do you think anyone — god or man — willingly makes himself worse in any way at all?
'Then it's impossible for a god to want to alter himself. Being, it seems, as beautiful and as good as can be, each of them stays forever, simply, in his own form.'
Impossible.
'That follows absolutely, I'd say.'
Then it is impossible that a god should even want to change himself. Each of them, it seems — being as beautiful and as good as it is possible to be — remains forever, simply, in his own form.
'Then let none of the poets tell us, my friend, that'
That has to follow, he said — in my judgment at least.
'"the gods, disguised as strangers from far-off lands, / take every sort of shape and roam our cities."'
Then let none of the poets tell us, my friend, that
'And let no one tell lies about Proteus and Thetis, or bring on, in tragedy or any other poetry, a Hera disguised as a priestess collecting alms'
'the gods, disguised as strangers out of far countries, / take every shape, and pass through the cities of men;'
'"for the life-giving children of Inachus, the river of Argos."'
and let no one lie to us about Proteus and Thetis, or bring Hera on — in a tragedy or in any other kind of poem — transformed into a priestess collecting alms

'And spare us many other lies of that kind. Nor should mothers, taken in by these poets, frighten their children with twisted versions of them, telling how certain gods prowl about by night in the likeness of all sorts of strangers, both blaspheming against the gods and turning their children into cowards.'
'for the life-giving children of Inachus, the river of Argos.'
'Heaven forbid,' he said.

No more lies of that sort, please. And no mothers, either, taking the poets at their word and terrifying their little children with the bad version of these tales — how certain gods, mind you, go roaming by night, got up as strangers of every description. That way they blaspheme the gods and turn their children into cowards at a single stroke.
'But might the gods, though they don't change in themselves, still make us imagine they appear in all sorts of forms, by deceiving us and working sorcery on us?'
God forbid, he said.
'Perhaps,' he said.
But maybe, I said, though the gods themselves are incapable of changing, they make us think they appear in all these different forms — tricking us, bewitching us?
'What?' I said. 'Would a god be willing to lie, in word or deed, by putting some illusion before us?'
Maybe, he replied.
'I don't know,' he said.
What! I said. Would a god be willing to lie — to pass off falsehood in word or in deed, by holding up a phantom of himself?
'Don't you know,' I said, 'that the genuine lie, if I may call it that, is hated by all gods and men?'
I don't know, he replied.
'What do you mean?'
Don't you know, I said, that the true lie — if that phrase can be spoken — is a thing every god and every man hates?
'I mean that no one willingly wants to be lied to in the most important part of himself, about the most important things. There, above all, a man dreads having a lie take hold.'
What do you mean? he said.
'I still don't follow,' he said.
I mean this, I said: no one willingly accepts a lie in the most sovereign part of himself, about the most sovereign things. There, above everywhere else, everyone dreads to harbor it.

'That's because you think I'm saying something grand,' I said. 'I only mean that to be lied to in the soul about reality, to be left ignorant there and to hold the lie in possession, is the thing all men least want; they loathe a lie in that place above all.'
I still don't follow, he said.
'Yes,' he said, 'they certainly do.'

That's because you think I'm saying something deep, I said. All I mean is this: to be lied to in one's own soul about the things that are — to be deceived there, to be left ignorant there, to have the lie and to hold it there — that is what no one would ever stand for. In that place, human beings hate the lie beyond everything.

'And as I was just saying, this ignorance in the soul of the man who has been deceived, the lie lodged in the soul itself, is what would most truly be called a real lie. The lie in mere words is only a kind of copy of a state already in the soul, an image that comes after it, not the pure thing itself. Isn't that so?'
Beyond everything — yes.
'Quite so.'

And this is what most exactly deserves the name I gave it just now — the true lie: that ignorance in the soul of the man who has been deceived. For the lie in words is only a copy of that condition in the soul, an image that comes after it — not the pure, unmixed lie itself. Isn't that so?
'So the real lie is hated not only by the gods but by men.'
Perfectly so.
'I think so.'
And the real lie is hated by men just as much as by gods?

'But what about the lie in words? When and for whom is it useful enough not to deserve hatred? Isn't it useful against enemies, or when one of the people we call friends, in a fit of madness or folly, is about to do some harm, and the lie becomes a kind of remedy that turns him aside? And in those stories we were just discussing, the ones about long ago, because we don't know the truth about how things were, we make our falsehood as much like the truth as we can, and so make even that useful.'
Yes.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's just how it is.'

The lie in words, on the other hand — there are times when it's useful, and earns no hatred. Against enemies, for one. Or when the people we call friends, in some fit of madness or folly, are set on doing harm: then the lie becomes a kind of medicine — a way of turning them back. And in the storytelling we were discussing a moment ago: since we don't know how the truth stands about those ancient things, we make the false resemble the true as closely as we can, and so put it to use.
'Well, in which of these ways is a lie useful to a god? Would he make his falsehood resemble the truth because he doesn't know the distant past?'
That's exactly how it is, he said.
'That would be absurd,' he said.
Then in which of these ways would a lie be useful to the god? Would he falsify for lack of knowledge — making his lie resemble a truth about ancient days he doesn't know?
'So there's nothing of the lying poet in a god.'
That would be laughable, he said.
'I think not.'
So there is no lying poet in the god.
'Would he lie, then, out of fear of his enemies?'
I should say not.
'Far from it.'
Would he lie, then, out of fear of enemies?
'Because of the folly or madness of his friends?'
Out of the question.
'But no fool or madman,' he said, 'is a friend of the gods.'
Because those close to him are fools, then, or madmen?
'So there's no reason a god would lie?'
But no fool or madman is a friend of the gods.
'None.'
Then there is nothing left — no motive at all for a god to lie.
'Then the divine, the spiritual, is in every way free of falsehood.'
None whatever.
'Completely.'
So everything divine, everything of god and spirit, is free of falsehood through and through.
'So the god is altogether simple and true, in deed and in word. He doesn't change himself, and he doesn't deceive others, in waking life or in dreams, by signs, words, or visions.'
Through and through.
'That's just how it strikes me too, now that you put it this way,' he said.

Then the god is altogether simple and true, in deed and in word. He does not change in himself, and he does not deceive others — not by apparitions, not by speeches, not by the sending of signs, to the waking or to the dreaming.

'Then you agree,' I said, 'that this is our second pattern for speaking and composing about the gods: that they aren't sorcerers who change their shape, and they don't mislead us with lies, in word or deed.'
That is how it looks to me too, he said, as you say it.
'I agree.'
Then you grant our second pattern, I said, for all speaking and all composing about the gods: they are no shape-shifting sorcerers, and they do not mislead us with lies, in word or in deed.
'So while we praise much in Homer, we won't praise the dream Zeus sends to Agamemnon. And we won't praise Aeschylus when he has Thetis say that Apollo, singing at her wedding,'
I grant it.

'"dwelt on the children she would bear, their freedom from sickness, their long lives, / and, calling my whole lot blessed by heaven, / he sang a song of triumph and gladdened my heart. / I trusted that Phoebus's mouth, brimming with prophecy, / could not speak false. And yet he, the very one who sang, / who sat at the feast, who said all this, is the one / who killed my son."'

So, though there is much in Homer we praise, this one thing we will not praise: Zeus sending the lying dream to Agamemnon. Nor will we praise Aeschylus, where Thetis tells how Apollo sang at her wedding, dwelling on the happiness of the child she would bear:

'When a poet says such things about the gods, we'll be angry, refuse him a chorus, and not let the teachers use his work to educate the young, if our guardians are to grow up god-fearing and godlike, as far as that's possible for a human being.'

'how he would know no sickness, how his days would be long, and every blessing would be his; and over my fortunes, so favored of heaven, he raised the victory-song, and gladdened my heart. And I believed the divine mouth of Phoebus could not lie — brimming as it was with the prophet's art. But the very god who sang, the guest at that very table, the god who promised all of it — he is the one who has killed my son.'

When a man says things like that about the gods, we will be angry with him; we will refuse him a chorus; and we won't allow teachers to use his lines in the education of the young — not if our guardians are to grow up god-revering and godlike, as far as that lies in human power.
I am in complete agreement with these patterns, he said — and I would make them my laws.
'I'm wholly with you on these patterns,' he said, 'and I'd make them my laws.'
spine.label: Book III
spine.title: The Noble Lie
The Education of the Guardians
spine.text: So that, I said, is where we stand on the gods — the kinds of stories men should and should not hear, from childhood on, if they are going to honor the gods and their parents, and take their friendships with one another seriously.

So those, I said, are our principles about the gods: the sort of tales to be told, and the sort never to be told, to our pupils from childhood on, if we want them to honor the gods and their parents, and to value friendship with one another.
Yes, he said — and I think we have it right.
'Yes,' he said, 'and I think our principles are right.'

Now, what if they are also to be brave? Don't they need, on top of this, the kind of stories that will make them fear death as little as possible? Or do you think anyone can ever be brave with the fear of death inside him?
'But if they're to be brave, don't they need other lessons besides these, lessons of the kind that take away the fear of death? Can any man be brave with the fear of death inside him?'
No one could, he said.
'Certainly not,' he said.
And a man who believes the underworld is real and full of horrors — will he be unafraid of death? Will he choose to die in battle rather than lose and be enslaved?
'And can a man be fearless of death, can he choose death in battle over defeat and slavery, if he believes the world below is real and terrible?'
Impossible.
'Impossible.'

Then it seems we must supervise the tellers of these stories too, and ask them not to run down the underworld wholesale but rather to speak well of it — because what they say now is not true, and not useful to men who are going to have to fight.

'So we'll have to keep a watch over the storytellers in this department too, just as in the others, and ask them to stop simply running down the world below and instead to speak well of it. Their gloomy descriptions aren't true, we'll tell them, and they'll do harm to men who are meant to be warriors.'
We must, he said.
'Yes, that will be our task,' he said.
Then we'll strike out everything of that sort, I said, beginning with these lines:
'Then we'll have to strike out a great many offending passages,' I said, 'starting with lines like these:'
'I would rather work the fields, hired out to some landless man with barely enough to live on, than be king over all the dead who have gone down to nothing.'
'"I'd rather be a serf, bound to the soil of some poor, landless man, than rule as king over all the dead who are gone."'
And this must go too — the lines where Hades himself panics,
'And we'll have to cut the verse that tells how Pluto dreaded',
'terrified that the halls of the dead would lie open to mortals and immortals — ghastly, moldering places that even the gods shudder at.'
'"lest those grim and moldering halls, which even the gods abhor, be laid open to the eyes of mortals and immortals alike."'
And again:
'And again:'
'So it's true — even in the house of Hades something survives: a soul, a shadow-image; but there is no mind left in it at all.'
'"Good god — so even in the house of Hades there is something, a soul, a phantom shape, but no real mind in it at all!"'
And this, about Tiresias:
'And the line about Tiresias:'
'To him alone, even dead, Persephone has granted mind; the others flit about, mere shadows.'
'"To him alone, even in death, Persephone granted understanding, that he alone should keep his wits; the rest are flitting shadows."'
Or this:
'And again:'
'His soul fled from his limbs and went down to Hades, wailing its fate, leaving behind its manhood and its youth.'
'"The soul flew from his limbs and was gone to Hades, mourning its fate, leaving manhood and youth behind."'
And this:
'And again:'
'and the soul, with a thin cry, vanished under the earth like smoke.'
'"And the soul, with a thin cry, slipped away like smoke beneath the earth."'
And:
'And:'
'As bats in the depths of an eerie cave fly squeaking when one drops from the chain of them clinging to the rock, and they hold fast to one another — so the souls went down together, squeaking.'
'"As bats in the depths of some eerie cave, when one of them drops from the cluster on the rock, fly squeaking and cling to one another, so did the souls go squeaking on their way together."'

We'll ask Homer and the other poets not to take it personally when we strike these lines and everything like them. It isn't that they aren't poetry, or that most people don't enjoy hearing them. Just the opposite: the more poetic they are, the more dangerous they are for boys and men who are meant to be free — who should fear slavery more than they fear death.

'We'll ask Homer and the other poets not to be angry if we cross out these passages and others like them. It isn't that they aren't fine poetry, or that the crowd doesn't enjoy them. It's the opposite: the more beautiful the poetry, the less fit it is for the ears of boys and men who are meant to be free, and who ought to fear slavery more than death.'
Absolutely.
'No doubt about it,' he said.

And we must also throw out all the dreadful, shuddering names of that world — Cocytus, the river of wailing; Styx, the river of hate; 'those under the earth'; 'the sapless dead' — every phrase of the kind that makes the listener's flesh crawl. Perhaps such horrors have a use of some sort; but we are afraid for our guardians — afraid the shudder will leave them more feverish and softer than they ought to be.

'And we'll also have to throw out all the dreadful, hair-raising names for the world below: Cocytus and Styx, ghosts beneath the earth, withered shades, all those words whose very mention sends a shudder through the soul of anyone who hears them. I'm not saying such horror stories don't serve some purpose. But there's a danger that they'll leave our guardians too jumpy, too soft.'
And that fear is justified, he said.
'Yes, that's a real danger,' he said.
So they must go.
'Then no more of them.'
They must.
'Right.'
And we should tell stories, and sing, in exactly the opposite key.
'We need a different note struck instead, a nobler one to compose and sing.'
Clearly.
'Clearly.'
Then do we also cut the weeping and wailing of famous men?
'And shall we also get rid of the wailing and lamenting of famous men?'
That has to follow, he said, from everything so far.
'They'll have to go with the rest.'
But look — are we right to cut it? Think about it. We hold that a good man will not consider death a terrible thing for another good man — for his friend.
'But are we right to get rid of them? Think it through. Our principle is that a good man won't regard death as a terrible thing for another good man, his comrade.'
We do hold that.
'Yes, that's our principle.'
Then he won't mourn for him as though something terrible had happened to him.
'So he won't grieve for his friend's death as though something terrible had happened to him.'
No.
'He won't.'
And we also say that such a man is the most self-sufficient of anyone when it comes to living well — that he, of all men, has the least need of others.
'We also hold that a man like this is sufficient unto himself for living well, and so, more than anyone, he doesn't depend on others.'
True, he said.
'True,' he said.
So for him, least of all men, is it a catastrophe to lose a son, or a brother, or his money, or anything else of the kind.
'So losing a son or a brother, or losing his money, is less terrible to him than to any other man.'
Least of all.
'Far less.'
So he, least of anyone, will collapse in grief when such a loss comes; he will bear it more calmly than any other man.
'So he'll be the least likely to mourn, and he'll bear it with the greatest calm when some such loss falls on him.'
Far more calmly.
'Yes, he'll feel it much less than the rest.'

Then we're right to cut the laments of famous men. Hand them over to women — and not to the serious ones, at that — and to the cowardly sort of men, so that the men we say we are raising to guard this country will be disgusted at the thought of carrying on like that.

'So we'll be right to strip away the laments of famous men, and hand them over to women, and not even respectable women at that, and to second-rate men, so that those we're training to guard our country will be ashamed to behave like that.'
Quite right.
'Quite right.'

So once again we'll ask Homer and the other poets not to show us Achilles, a goddess's son, lying now on his side, now on his back, now face down; then on his feet, pacing the shore of the barren sea, out of his mind with grief; or scooping black ash in both hands and pouring it over his head, weeping and wailing in all the ways Homer wrote it. And not to show Priam, near kin of the gods, begging and groveling,

'Then once again we'll beg Homer and the other poets not to show us Achilles, the son of a goddess, tossing from his side to his back to his face, then leaping up and pacing in a frenzy along the shore of the barren sea, or scooping up the black ashes in both hands and pouring them over his head, weeping and wailing in all the ways Homer describes. And not to show Priam, a kinsman of the gods, begging and pleading,',
'rolling in the dung, calling out to each man by name.'
'"rolling in the dung, crying out to each man by name."'
And we'll beg him harder still not to make the gods grieve out loud, crying,
'Still more earnestly we'll beg them at least not to bring the gods on stage in mourning, saying things like',
'Ah, my misery — I bore the best of men, and bore him for sorrow.'
'"Misery, misery — that I bore the bravest of men to my sorrow."'
And if he must have grieving gods, at least let him not dare to travesty the greatest of them — not make Zeus say,
'And if they must bring the gods on at all, at least let them not dare to misrepresent the greatest of the gods so badly as to make him say:'
'What a sight for my eyes — a man I love hunted around the city walls, and my heart grieving with him.'
'"With my own eyes I see a man I love chased round and round the city walls, and my heart aches for him."'
Or:
'Or again:'
'Ah me — Sarpedon, whom I love best of men, is fated to fall to Patroclus, son of Menoetius.'
'"Alas, that Sarpedon, the man I love best of all, is fated to fall at the hands of Patroclus, the son of Menoetius."'

Because, my dear Adeimantus, if our young men took things like that seriously — instead of laughing them off as unworthy of the gods — hardly one of them would think such behavior beneath him. He is only a man, after all. He would never catch and rebuke the impulse to say and do the same. Instead, at the smallest setback, with no shame and no endurance, he would be singing dirges and wailing his heart out.

'Because, my dear Adeimantus, if our young men take such things seriously and don't laugh them off as unworthy, then none of them will think it beneath himself, a mere man, to behave the same way. He'll feel no shame, no restraint, at wailing and moaning over the smallest setback.'
That's completely true, he said.
'That's very true,' he said.
And it must not happen — the argument just showed us so, and we should trust that argument until someone persuades us with a better one.
'It is. But, as our argument has just shown us, that's exactly what shouldn't happen, and we have to stand by that until someone gives us a better argument.'
No, it must not.
'No, it shouldn't happen.'
And they shouldn't be men who crack up laughing, either. When a man surrenders to a violent fit of laughter, it tends to trigger just as violent a swing in him.
'And our guardians shouldn't be too fond of laughter, either. As a rule, when a man gives way to violent laughter, a violent reaction follows.'
So I believe.
'I think that's so,' he said.
So we can't accept poets showing men of worth helpless with laughter — and gods, even less.
'So we won't allow worthy men, even ordinary mortals, to be shown overcome with laughter, and still less the gods.'
Even less indeed, he said.
'Much less the gods,' he said.
Then we won't accept lines like Homer's about the gods, where
'So we won't accept lines like Homer's, where he tells how',
'unquenchable laughter broke out among the blessed gods as they watched Hephaestus puffing up and down the hall.'
'"unquenchable laughter broke out among the blessed gods, when they saw Hephaestus puffing and limping about the hall."'
If we follow your argument, he said, we can't accept them.
'By your principles, we can't allow it.'
Mine — if you want to call it mine, I said. Either way, we can't accept them.
'Call them my principles if you like,' he said. 'Either way, we certainly can't allow it.'

And truth must be prized above almost everything. If we were right before — if a lie really is useless to the gods, and useful to men only as a kind of medicine — then clearly medicine like that belongs in the hands of doctors. Ordinary people have no business touching it.

'And then there's truth, which we must value highly. For if we were right earlier that a lie is useless to the gods and useful to men only as a kind of medicine, then plainly that medicine should be left to doctors. Private citizens have no business with it.'
None, he said.
'No business at all,' he said.

So if lying is a privilege at all, it belongs to the rulers of the city — to be used against enemies, or on their own citizens, for the city's good. No one else may touch it. And for a private citizen to lie to these rulers, we'll say, is a worse offense than for a patient to lie to his doctor, or an athlete to his trainer, about the state of his own body — or for a sailor to hide from the helmsman how things actually stand with the ship and the crew, what he and his shipmates are doing.

'So if anyone is to have the privilege of lying, it should be the rulers of the city, lying for the good of the city in dealings with enemies or even with their own citizens. No one else may touch it. For a private man to lie to the rulers is as grave a fault, worse, even, than for a patient to lie to his doctor about his own body, or an athlete to his trainer, or a sailor to fail to tell the captain the true state of the ship and the crew, how he and his shipmates are really doing.'
Very true, he said.
'Very true,' he said.
So if the ruler catches anyone else in the city lying —
'So if the ruler catches anyone else in the city lying, any of the craftsmen,',
'any of the craftsmen who serve the people — prophet, or healer of sickness, or worker in wood' —
'"prophet, healer of the sick, or worker in wood,"'
he will punish him for bringing in a practice that can capsize and sink a city as surely as a ship.
'he'll punish him for introducing something as ruinous and destructive to the city as it would be to a ship.'
He certainly will, he said — if actions ever follow our words.
'He certainly will, if our city is ever actually built,' he said.
Next: won't our young men need self-discipline?
'Next, our young men have to be self-controlled.'
Of course.
'Of course.'
And for most people, doesn't self-discipline come down mainly to this — obey those in command, and be in command of yourself, of the pleasures of drink and sex and food?
'And aren't the main elements of self-control, broadly speaking, obeying those in command and ruling oneself in the pleasures of food, drink, and sex?'
I'd say so.
'I think so.'
Then we'll approve of lines like the one Homer gives Diomedes,
'Then we'll approve of words like Diomede's in Homer:'
'Sit down, friend. Be quiet, and do as I say,'
'"Friend, sit still and do as I tell you,"'
and the lines near it,
'and the lines that follow,'
'the Greeks came on breathing fury, silent, in fear of their commanders,'
