'"the Greeks marched on, breathing fury, in silent awe of their commanders,"'
and everything else in that spirit.
'and other passages of that kind.'
We will.
'We will.'
But what about this one —
'But what about a line like this:'
'You wine-sack — with a dog's eyes and a deer's heart' —
'"You drunk, with the eyes of a dog and the heart of a deer,"'
and what comes after it? Are these good things to hear — all the insolent speeches, in verse or prose, that ordinary men have flung at their rulers?
'and the words after it? Are such things, and any other backtalk that private men in poetry or prose throw at their rulers, well said or badly said?'
They are not.
'Badly.'
They may be entertaining, I don't doubt it. But they do nothing for a young man's self-discipline, and that makes them dangerous. Do you agree?
'They may be amusing enough, but they do nothing for self-control, and so they're likely to harm our young men. You'd agree with that?'
Yes.
'Yes.'
Then again — having the wisest of men say that the finest thing he knows is when
'And then to make the wisest of men say that, to his mind, nothing is finer than',
'the tables are loaded with bread and meat, and the steward draws wine from the bowl and carries it round and fills the cups' —
'"when the tables are loaded with bread and meat, and the steward draws wine from the bowl and carries it round and fills the cups"',
is that the right thing for a young man to hear, if he is learning to rule himself? Or this:
'is that a fit thing, or good for self-control, for a young man to hear? Or the verse',
'the most pitiful death of all is to die of hunger.'
'"the saddest of fates is to die and meet your doom from hunger"?'

And what about the story of Zeus — how, while the other gods and men slept and he alone lay awake making plans, he forgot them all in one rush of desire; how the sight of Hera struck him so hard that he wouldn't even go inside, but wanted to take her right there on the ground, saying no craving had ever seized him like this — not even when they first went to each other,

'And what about the tale of Zeus? While the other gods and men slept and he alone lay awake, plotting his schemes, he forgot them all in an instant out of lust, and was so undone at the sight of Hera that he wouldn't even go inside, but wanted to take her right there on the ground, saying he'd never wanted her so much, not even the first time they came together',
'behind their parents' backs.'
'"in secret from their parents."'
Or the one where Hephaestus throws a chain around Ares and Aphrodite over the same kind of business?
'Or that other tale, of how Hephaestus chained up Ares and Aphrodite for the same sort of carrying-on?'
No, by Zeus, he said — none of that strikes me as fit for them to hear.
'No,' he said, 'I'm strongly of the opinion that they shouldn't hear that kind of thing.'
But acts of endurance against all odds, done and spoken of by famous men — those they should see and hear. Like this:
'But where famous men show real endurance, in word or deed, those passages they ought to see and hear. For instance the lines:'
'He struck his chest and called his own heart to heel: Bear up, my heart. You have borne worse than this.'
'"He struck his chest and rebuked his own heart: 'Endure, my heart; you have endured far worse than this.'"'
Absolutely.
'Yes, certainly,' he said.
And we can't allow our men to take bribes, or to love money.
'And we mustn't let them be men who take bribes or love money.'
Certainly not.
'Certainly not.'
So no singing to them that
'So we won't sing them lines like',
'gifts persuade the gods, and gifts persuade the mightiest kings.'
'"gifts win over gods, and gifts win over revered kings."'

And Phoenix, Achilles' old tutor, can't be praised as giving sound advice when he tells him to defend the Greeks if they bring gifts, but without gifts to stay angry. Nor will we believe it of Achilles himself — we won't grant that he was ever so greedy that he took Agamemnon's presents, or that he gave back Hector's body for a ransom and would not have done it otherwise.

'Nor will we praise Phoenix, Achilles's tutor, or call him a wise counselor for telling Achilles to take the Greeks' gifts and help them, but to hold on to his anger if no gift came. Nor will we believe, or admit, that Achilles himself was such a lover of money that he accepted Agamemnon's gifts, or that he gave back Hector's corpse only for a ransom and wouldn't have done it otherwise.'
No, he said — that kind of thing deserves no praise.
'No,' he said, 'those aren't sentiments anyone could approve.'

I love Homer, I said, so I hesitate to say it: but it is downright impious to say these things about Achilles, or to believe them when others say them. The same goes for the passage where he tells Apollo,

'Much as I love Homer,' I said, 'I'm reluctant even to say it, but to fasten these feelings on Achilles, or to believe others who do, comes close to outright impiety. The same with the story of his insolence to Apollo, when he says,',
'You have crossed me, Far-shooter, deadliest of all the gods; and I would pay you back, if I had the power,'
'"You have cheated me, far-shooter, cruelest of the gods. I would pay you back, if only I had the power."'

and where he defies the river — a god — and is ready to fight him; and where he offers his hair, already vowed to the other river, Spercheius, saying, 'let the hero Patroclus carry these locks with him' — a corpse — and we're told he did it. None of it is true. And the dragging of Hector around Patroclus's tomb, and the slaughter of living captives on the pyre — we will say all of that is false. We will not let our citizens believe that Achilles — son of a goddess and of Peleus, that most self-possessed of men, third in line from Zeus, raised by the wise Cheiron — was such a chaos inside that he carried two diseases that contradict each other: a money-grubber's stinginess, and arrogant contempt for gods and men.

'And his defiance of the river-god, on whom he was ready to lay hands; and his cutting off his own hair for the dead Patroclus, hair already vowed to another river, Spercheius, and actually going through with it; and his dragging Hector around Patroclus's tomb, and butchering captives on the pyre. None of this can I believe he really did. Nor can I let our citizens believe that Achilles, the pupil of the wise Cheiron, son of a goddess and of Peleus, the gentlest of men and third in line from Zeus, was so disordered in his mind as to be torn at once between two contradictory diseases, a mean streak shot through with greed, and at the same time an arrogant contempt for gods and men alike.'
You're right, he said.
'You're quite right,' he said.

Then let's not believe it either — or let anyone repeat it — that Theseus, son of Poseidon, and Peirithous, son of Zeus, set out to commit those monstrous abductions, or that any other hero and child of a god would dare the terrible, impious deeds now falsely pinned on them. Let's force the poets to say either that the deeds weren't theirs, or that they weren't children of gods — but not both at once. And let them stop trying to convince our young men that gods breed evil, and that heroes are no better than ordinary men. As we said before, that is neither pious nor true — for we proved that evil cannot come from gods.

'And let's equally refuse to believe, or to let anyone repeat, the tale of Theseus, son of Poseidon, and Pirithous, son of Zeus, setting out to commit terrible abductions, or of any other hero or son of a god daring to do the dreadful, unholy things they now slanderously pin on them. Let's force the poets either to deny that these were the gods' deeds, or to deny that the men were the sons of gods. They can't have it both ways. And we won't let them try to convince our young men that the gods are the source of evil and that the heroes were no better than ordinary men. As we said before, that's neither holy nor true, since we already proved that evil can't come from the gods.'
Impossible.
'No, it can't.'
And such stories do real damage to those who hear them. Every rotten man will forgive himself his rottenness once he's convinced that the same things are done, and always were done, by
'And besides, such stories do real damage to those who hear them, because every man will start excusing his own vices once he's convinced that this is just how things are done by',
'the close-sown kin of the gods, near to Zeus, whose ancestral altar stands high in the open air on Ida's peak,'
'"the gods' own kindred, the close relatives of Zeus, whose ancestral altar of Zeus stands high in the air on the peak of Ida,"',
men in whom
'and in whom',
'the blood of the gods has not yet died out.'
'"the blood of the gods still runs."'
So let's shut these stories down, before they breed in our young men an easy conscience about being bad.
'So let's put a stop to such tales, before they breed a slack and lawless spirit in the young.'
By all means.
'By all means,' he said.
Now then, I said — what kind of speech is left, while we're marking out what may and may not be said? We've covered how to speak of gods, and demigods, and heroes, and the world of the dead.

'Now, since we're deciding which kinds of subject may and may not be spoken of, let's check whether we've left anything out. How gods, demigods, heroes, and the world below are to be handled, we've already settled.'
We have.
'We have.'
What remains would be speech about men, wouldn't it?
'And what should we say about men? That's plainly the part left over.'
Obviously.
'Plainly.'
But it's impossible for us to settle that one right now, my friend.
'But we can't answer that yet, my friend.'
Why not?
'Why not?'

Because, if I'm not mistaken, we're going to say that poets and storytellers get the most important things about men wrong. They tell us that plenty of unjust men are happy, and plenty of just men miserable; that injustice pays, so long as no one catches you; that justice is another man's gain and your own loss. We'll forbid them to say any of that, and order them to sing and tell the opposite — won't we?

'Because, unless I'm mistaken, we'd have to say that poets and storytellers go badly wrong about men, in claiming that plenty of unjust men are happy and just men miserable; that injustice pays, as long as you aren't caught; and that justice is another man's good and your own loss. We'll forbid them to say such things and order them to sing and tell the opposite.'
We certainly will, he said.
'We certainly will,' he said.
But if you grant me that, I'll say you've already granted the very thing we've been hunting all along.
'But if you grant I'm right about that, then I'll say you've conceded the very thing we've been arguing for all along.'
You're right, he said — I see the inference.
'I accept that this follows,' he said.
So we can't settle what should be said about men until we've discovered what justice is, and whether by its nature it profits the one who has it — whether he looks just to the world or not.

'Whether such things are to be said about men is a question we can't settle until we've discovered what justice is, and how, by its very nature, it benefits whoever has it, whether or not he seems just to others.'
Very true.
'Very true,' he said.
That's enough, then, about the content of stories. Now we should look at the style — the how of the telling — and then we'll have covered both what should be said and the way of saying it.
'So much for the content of poetry. Now let's talk about its style or manner, and once we've done that, we'll have covered both what to say and how to say it.'
Adeimantus said: I don't understand what you mean.
'I don't follow you,' said Adeimantus.
Well, you'd better, I said. Maybe this will make it clearer. Everything the storytellers and poets tell is a narrative of things past, present, or to come. Isn't it?
'Then I'll have to make you follow,' I said. 'Maybe I can put it this way. You know, I take it, that all storytelling and poetry is a narrative of things past, present, or to come?'
What else could it be?
'Of course,' he said.
And don't they carry it off either by plain narration, or by imitation — impersonating their characters — or by a mix of the two?
'And the narrating is done either by plain narration, or by impersonation, or by a mix of the two?'
That, he said, I still don't follow.
'There again,' he said, 'I don't quite follow.'

Then I must be a ridiculous teacher, I said — I can't make myself clear. Like a man who's no good at speaking, I'll give up on the whole and break off a piece to show you what I mean. You know the opening of the Iliad, where the poet tells how Chryses begged Agamemnon to release his daughter; how Agamemnon exploded at him; and how Chryses, having failed, prayed the god down on the Greeks. Now, as far as these lines —

'I must be a laughable teacher,' I said, 'if I'm having this much trouble making myself clear. Like a poor speaker, then, I won't take the whole subject at once. I'll break off a piece of it to show you what I mean. You know the opening of the Iliad, where the poet tells how Chryses begged Agamemnon to release his daughter, and how Agamemnon flew into a rage, so that Chryses, failing in his plea, called down the god's anger on the Achaeans. Now up to the lines',
'and he begged all the Greeks, but above all the two sons of Atreus, marshals of the armies' —
'"and he begged all the Greeks, but the two sons of Atreus above all, the marshals of the host,"'

the poet speaks in his own voice; he never tries to make us think the speaker is anyone but himself. But after this he speaks as Chryses — he does everything he can to make us believe it isn't Homer talking but the old priest himself. And that's how he built virtually the whole narrative: the events at Troy, the events in Ithaca, the whole of the Odyssey.

'the poet speaks in his own voice. He never tries to make us think he's someone else. But after that he speaks as if he were Chryses himself, doing everything he can to make us believe the speaker isn't Homer but the old priest. And he's cast nearly the whole of the Iliad and the Odyssey in this double form.'
So he did.
'Yes.'
And it's all narrative, isn't it — both the speeches he delivers and the stretches in between?
'And it's all narrative, both in the speeches he gives us and in the passages between them?'
Of course.
'Of course.'
But when he delivers a speech in someone else's character, doesn't he make his own voice as much as possible like the person he has announced as the speaker?
'But when he delivers a speech in someone else's character, don't we say he makes his style as much like that person's as he can?'
He does.
'We do.'
And to make yourself like someone else in voice or in bearing — that is imitating the person you become?
'And making yourself like someone else, in voice or gesture, is impersonating the one whose character you've taken on?'
Yes.
'Certainly.'
Then in passages like that, it seems, he and the other poets build the narrative through imitation.
'So in these passages the poet's narrative works by impersonation?'
Exactly.
'Just so.'

But if the poet never hid himself anywhere, his whole poem would be narration without imitation. So that you don't tell me again you don't understand, I'll show you how that would go. If Homer had said that Chryses came bringing his daughter's ransom, as a suppliant to the Greeks and above all to their kings — and had then gone on speaking not as Chryses but still as Homer — there would be no imitation in it, just plain narration. It would run something like this (I'll drop the meter; I'm no poet): The priest came and prayed that the gods let them take Troy and come home safe, and asked them to accept the ransom and free his daughter, out of reverence for the god. When he finished, the others were respectful and ready to consent; but Agamemnon flew into a rage and ordered him to leave now and never come back — or the staff and the god's garlands might not protect him. Before he would free the daughter, he said, she would grow old beside him in Argos. He told the old man to go and stop provoking him, if he wanted to get home in one piece. Hearing this, the old man was afraid, and left in silence; and once clear of the camp he prayed and prayed to Apollo, calling the god by all his names, reminding him of every gift that had ever pleased him — temples built, offerings burned — and asking one favor in return: that his tears fall back on the Achaeans, paid for by the god's arrows. That, my friend, is how it becomes plain narration, without imitation.

'But where the poet never hides himself, the impersonation drops away and his poetry becomes plain narration. So that you can't say once more, "I don't follow," let me show how this would work. If Homer, after saying the priest came with his daughter's ransom to plead with the Achaeans and above all the kings, had gone on speaking in his own voice instead of as Chryses, the result wouldn't be impersonation but plain narration. It would run something like this, in prose, since I'm no poet: "The priest came and prayed that the gods would grant the Greeks the capture of Troy and a safe return home, but begged them, out of reverence for the god, to release his daughter and accept the ransom. The other Greeks heard him with respect and approved. But Agamemnon was furious and ordered him to leave and not come back, or his staff and the god's garlands would do him no good. The girl, he said, would not be freed; she'd grow old in Argos at his side. He told the priest to go away and not provoke him, if he wanted to get home safe. The old man was afraid and went off in silence, and once clear of the camp he prayed long to Apollo, calling on all his titles and reminding the god of every temple he'd built and every sacrifice he'd made, and asked that in return his tears be paid back by the god's arrows on the Achaeans." That's how the whole thing becomes plain narrative.'
I understand, he said.
'I understand,' he said.
Then you can also see the reverse of it, I said — cut everything the poet says between the speeches, and leave only the exchanges.
'Now picture the opposite case: the connecting passages cut out, and only the dialogue left.'
I see that too, he said. That's what tragedy is.
'That I understand too,' he said. 'You mean the way it's done in tragedy.'

You've got it exactly, I said. And now I think I can make plain what I couldn't before: one kind of poetry and storytelling works wholly through imitation — tragedy, as you say, and comedy; another through the poet's own report — you'll find that above all in the dithyramb; and a third uses both, as epic does, and plenty of other forms too. Am I making sense?

'You've got my meaning exactly,' I said. 'And now I think what you couldn't grasp before is clear: poetry and storytelling come in three kinds. One is wholly impersonation, as in tragedy and comedy. Another is the poet speaking throughout in his own voice, best seen in the dithyramb. And the third combines the two, as in epic and in several other forms. Are you with me?'
Yes, he said — now I see what you were getting at.
'Yes,' he said, 'now I see what you meant.'
Then remember what came before all this: we had settled what should be said, and still had to examine how.
'Then remember what I said when we started, that we were finished with the content and ready to move to the manner.'
I remember.
'I remember.'

What I meant was just this: we need to decide whether we'll allow the poets to build their narratives through imitation, or partly through imitation and partly not — and in that case, where each belongs — or whether they're not to imitate at all.

'What I was getting at is that we have to come to an agreement about impersonation. Should we allow the poets to tell their stories by impersonation? And if so, should it be all impersonation, or only part, and if part, which parts? Or should impersonation be banned altogether?'
I can guess what you're weighing, he said: whether we'll admit tragedy and comedy into the city, or not.
'I suspect,' he said, 'you're asking whether we'll admit tragedy and comedy into our city.'
Perhaps, I said — and perhaps something bigger still. I honestly don't know yet. But wherever the argument carries us, like a wind, there we must go.
'Perhaps,' I said. 'But there may be more to it than that. I don't quite know yet. Wherever the argument blows us, like a wind, there we'll go.'
Well said, he replied.
'And go we will,' he said.

Then here's the question, Adeimantus: should our guardians be imitators, or not? Or does the answer follow from what we said earlier — that one man does one job well, not many; and that if he tries his hand at many, he'll grasp at all of them and distinguish himself in none?

'Then tell me this, Adeimantus. Should our guardians be impersonators or not? Hasn't this already been settled by the rule we laid down, that one man can do one thing well, not many, and that if he tries his hand at many he'll fail to make his mark at any?'
It follows.
'It has.'
And doesn't the same argument hold for imitation — one man can't imitate many things as well as he imitates one?
'And the same goes for impersonation: no one man can imitate many things as well as he can imitate one.'
He can't.
'No, he can't.'

Then he'll hardly manage to practice a calling worth anything and at the same time imitate many things — be an imitator by trade. Even two forms of imitation that look like next-door neighbors — comedy and tragedy — can't be written well by the same people. You did just call those two imitations?

'So a man will hardly be able to live a serious life and at the same time impersonate a whole range of characters. Even two closely related kinds of imitation, like writing tragedy and writing comedy, are beyond the same person, aren't they? You did just now call these imitations?'
I did — and you're right, the same men can't do both.
'I did, and you're right that the same men can't do both.'
Any more than a man can recite epic and act on stage at once.
'No more than they can be both reciters and actors at once?'
True.
'True.'
Even tragic and comic actors are different people — and all of these are imitations, aren't they?
'And the same actors don't play in both comedy and tragedy, though all of these are imitations?'
They are.
'They don't.'
And it seems to me, Adeimantus, that human nature is minted in even smaller coin than this — too small to imitate many things well, or to do well the many real things the imitations copy.

'Human nature, Adeimantus, seems to me to be minted into still smaller coins than that, so that no one can imitate many things well, any more than he can actually do well the many things the imitations are copies of.'
Quite true, he said.
'Very true,' he said.

Then if we're to keep our first principle — that our guardians must be released from every other craft to be craftsmen of the city's freedom, precise ones, practicing nothing that doesn't lead to that end — they should neither do nor imitate anything else. And if they do imitate, let them imitate, from childhood on, what fits their calling: men who are brave, self-disciplined, pious, free — all that family of qualities. But what is servile and shameful they should neither do nor be good at imitating — nor anything else that is vicious — or from the imitation they'll catch the reality. Haven't you noticed how imitations, kept up from youth onward, settle into habits and a second nature — in the body, in the voice, in the mind itself?

'So if we hold to our original idea, that our guardians must set everything else aside and devote themselves wholly to keeping the city free, making this their one craft and taking up no work that doesn't serve that end, then they shouldn't do or imitate anything else. Or if they do imitate, let them imitate from childhood only what's suited to their calling: the brave, the self-controlled, the holy, the free, and so on. But meanness they shouldn't imitate, or anything else shameful, in case the imitation breeds the reality. Have you noticed how imitations, kept up from youth far into life, settle into habits and become a man's second nature, in body, voice, and mind?'
I certainly have, he said.
'I certainly have,' he said.

Then we won't allow the men we care for — men who have to become good — to imitate a woman, young or old: berating her husband, or trading defiance with the gods and bragging because she thinks herself blessed, or drowning in misfortune and grief and lament. Much less one who is sick, or in love, or in labor.

'Then we won't let those we care about, the men we say must be good, imitate a woman, young or old, railing at her husband, or quarreling with the gods and boasting because she thinks herself so happy, or sunk in grief and mourning; and we'll certainly forbid them to imitate a woman in sickness, in love, or in childbirth.'
Quite right.
'Quite right,' he said.
And no imitating slaves, women or men, doing what slaves do.
'Nor may they imitate slaves, male or female, doing slaves' work.'
No.
'No.'

Nor bad men, it seems — cowards, and men doing the opposite of everything we just prescribed: mocking and jeering at one another, trading filth, drunk or sober, and all the other ways such men wrong themselves and other people in word and deed. Nor should they get into the habit of making themselves over into madmen, in speech or action. They must recognize madness and badness, in men and in women — but do none of it, and imitate none of it.

'Nor, surely, bad men, cowards and the rest, who do the opposite of all we've prescribed, jeering and mocking and abusing each other, drunk or sober, sinning against themselves and others in word and deed, as such men do. And they shouldn't be trained to imitate the words or actions of the mad, either. They have to recognize madness and badness, but not act them out or imitate them.'
Very true.
'Very true,' he said.
What about smiths at their trade, or any other craftsmen, or the rowers of warships, or the men who call the stroke for them — should they imitate any of that?
'And may they imitate smiths or other craftsmen at their work, or rowers, or the men who keep time for them, or anything of that sort?'
How could they, he said, when they're not even permitted to give those trades their attention?
'How could they,' he said, 'when they aren't even allowed to turn their minds to any of those trades?'
And horses neighing, bulls bellowing, rivers rushing, the sea booming, thunder — will they imitate things like that?
'And may they imitate horses neighing, bulls bellowing, the rush of rivers, the roar of the sea, thunder, and all the rest of it?'
They've already been forbidden, he said, to be mad or to act like madmen.
'No,' he said, 'if they're forbidden to be mad, they can't go acting like madmen either.'

If I follow you, I said, you mean there's one style of speaking and narrating that a genuinely good man uses when he has something to say, and another style — nothing like it — that the man of the opposite nature and upbringing will always favor.
'If I follow you,' I said, 'there's one kind of narrative style a truly good man will use when he has something to say, and another that a man of the opposite character and upbringing will use.'
And what are they? he asked.
'And what are these two?' he asked.

This, I said. When a decent man comes, in the course of a story, to a speech or an action of another good man, I think he'll be willing to deliver it as if he were that man, and feel no shame in the imitation — most of all when the good man is acting steadily and wisely; less so, and less willingly, when he has been shaken by sickness or desire or drink or some other stumble. But when he comes to a character unworthy of him, he'll refuse to shape himself in earnest after his inferior — except briefly, perhaps, when the character does something good. He'll be ashamed: partly because he has no practice imitating such people, partly out of disgust at stamping and fitting himself into the molds of worse men. In his mind he holds the whole business beneath him, unless it's done as a joke.

'Suppose,' I said, 'that a good and decent man, in the course of a story, comes to some speech or action of another good man. I imagine he'll be glad to deliver it as if he were that man, and won't be ashamed of imitating him, least of all when the good man is acting steadily and sensibly, less so when illness or love or drink or some other misfortune has overtaken him. But when he comes to someone unworthy of him, he won't be willing to model himself on a worse man in earnest. He'll do it, if at all, only for a moment, when the worse man happens to do something good, and even then he'll be ashamed, since he's never practiced shaping himself to baser models, and his whole nature rebels against it, unless it's all in fun.'
That sounds likely, he said.
'That's what I'd expect,' he said.

So he'll use the kind of narration we walked through a moment ago with Homer's lines: his style will draw on both imitation and plain narrative, but with a small share of imitation in a long stretch of story. Or is that nothing?
'So he'll use the kind of narrative we found in Homer, both impersonation and plain narration, but with very little of the first and a great deal of the second. Do you agree?'
It's exactly right, he said. That has to be the pattern for such a speaker.
'Certainly,' he said. 'That has to be the model for such a speaker.'

Then take the other kind of narrator. The worse he is, the more he'll imitate everything and count nothing beneath him — in dead earnest, in front of a crowd, he'll try to do it all. What I mentioned just now: thunder, the racket of wind and hail, of axles and pulleys, the voices of trumpets and flutes and pan-pipes and every instrument there is — even the sounds of dogs and sheep and birds. His whole style will be imitation in voice and gesture, with maybe a thin thread of narration through it.

'But there's the other sort of man, who'll narrate anything, and the worse he is the less he'll hold back. Nothing is beneath him. He'll set out to imitate everything, and in dead earnest, before a big crowd. As I said, he'll try to give us the crash of thunder, the howl of wind and hail, the creak of axles and pulleys, the blare of flutes and pipes and trumpets and every other instrument. He'll bark like a dog, bleat like a sheep, crow like a rooster. His whole art will be imitation, of sound and gesture, with hardly any narration at all.'
That has to be the other kind, he said.
'That'll be his way of telling a story,' he said.
So those, I said, are the two styles I meant.
'So these are the two kinds of style?'
So they are.
'Yes.'

Now, the first of the two involves only small variations. Give the speech the musical mode and rhythm that fit it, and a speaker who does it right stays close to a single mode from start to finish — the changes are small — and keeps, likewise, to much the same rhythm.

'And you'll agree that one of them allows only slight changes, so that if you also pick a harmony and a rhythm to match its simplicity, a man who speaks it correctly stays nearly the same throughout, keeping to a single harmony, since the changes are small, and to roughly one rhythm?'
That's exactly so.
'Quite true,' he said.
But the other style needs the opposite: every mode and every rhythm, if it's to be delivered as it demands — because it holds every possible shape of change.
'Whereas the other kind needs every harmony and every rhythm, if the music is to fit the words, because it's full of changes of every sort.'
Emphatically so.
'That's perfectly true too,' he said.
And every poet, every speaker of anything, hits one of these two patterns of style, or the other, or some blend of the two. There's nowhere else to land.
'And don't all poets, and everyone who speaks at all, use one or the other of these styles, or a mix of both?'
Nowhere, he said.
'They cover everything,' he said.
Then what do we do? Admit all of them into our city, or one of the two unmixed styles, or the blend?
'So shall we admit all of them into our city, or just one of the two unmixed kinds, or the mixed one?'
If my vote carries, he said: the unmixed imitator of the good man.
'If it were up to me,' he said, 'I'd admit only the pure imitator of the good man.'
And yet, Adeimantus, the blended style is delicious too. In fact, the style children and their tutors love best — and the crowd, by a wide margin — is the exact opposite of the one you chose.
'And yet, Adeimantus, the mixed style is very charming, and the one most opposite to your choice, the all-imitating style, is what children and their attendants and the mass of people love best.'
It is what they love.
'I don't deny it,' he said.
But maybe you'd say it doesn't fit our constitution — because with us no man is double or multiple. Every man does one job.
'But I suppose you'd say it doesn't suit our city, where no man is two men or many, but each plays one part only?'
It doesn't fit.
'Yes, it doesn't suit us.'

And isn't this why ours is the only city where we'll find the shoemaker a shoemaker, and not a ship's pilot on the side; the farmer a farmer, and not a juror on the side; the soldier a soldier, and not a businessman on the side — and so on all the way down?

'And that's why ours is the only city where you'll find a shoemaker who's a shoemaker and not also a ship's pilot, a farmer who's a farmer and not also a juror, a soldier who's a soldier and not also a trader, and so on right through.'
True, he said.
'True,' he said.

So then: suppose a man arrives in our city who is clever enough to become anything — to imitate everything under the sun — and he wants to show himself off, poems and all. We'll bow down to him as someone sacred and wonderful and delightful; and then we'll tell him that there is no man like him in our city, and no law that permits there to be one. We'll pour myrrh on his head, crown him with wool like a holy image, and escort him to another town. For our own souls' health we'll settle for the plainer, less delightful poet and storyteller — the one who imitates the way a decent man speaks, and keeps to the patterns we laid down at the start, when we first set out to educate our soldiers.

'So if one of these clever, do-anything men, who can imitate the whole world, came to our city and offered to put himself and his poems on show, we'd bow down to him as a holy and marvelous and delightful creature, but we'd tell him there's no place for a man like him in our city, the law won't allow it, and then we'd anoint his head with myrrh, crown him with wool, and send him off to some other city. For our own souls' sake we'll keep the plainer, sterner poet and storyteller, the one who imitates only the style of the good man, and who keeps to the standards we laid down at the start when we began educating our soldiers.'
We certainly will, he said — if it's up to us.
'That's certainly what we'll do,' he said, 'if it's in our power.'
Then, my friend, I said, the part of music that deals with stories and legends looks finished. We've said what is to be told, and how to tell it.
'Then, my friend,' I said, 'that part of education in music and poetry that has to do with story and myth seems to be finished. We've covered both the content and the manner.'
So it seems to me too.
'I think so too,' he said.
What's left, then, is the manner of song and melody.
'Next in line comes the matter of melody and song.'
Obviously.
'Obviously.'
And by now anyone could work out what we'll have to say about those — if we're going to stay consistent with ourselves.
'And by now anyone can see what we should say about them, if we mean to be consistent.'
Glaucon laughed. Then I'm afraid, Socrates, he said, that 'anyone' leaves me out. I can't quite work out, right at this moment, what we ought to say — though I have my suspicions.
Glaucon laughed. 'I'm afraid I may not count as "anyone,"' he said, 'because at this moment I can't quite say what we should hold, though I have a guess.'
You can say this much at least, I said: a song is made of three things — words, mode, and rhythm.
'Well, at any rate,' I said, 'you can certainly say this much: a song has three parts, the words, the harmony, and the rhythm.'
That much, he said, yes.
'Yes,' he said, 'that much I can.'
Well, as far as the words go, a song's words are no different from words unsung, are they? They should follow the same patterns we laid down just now, and in the same spirit.
'And as for the words, there'll be no difference between words set to music and words not set to music. Both have to obey the same rules we've already laid down.'
True.
'Yes.'
And the mode and the rhythm have to follow the words.
'And the harmony and rhythm have to follow the words.'
Of course.
'Of course.'
Now, we said we have no use for dirges and lamentation in our stories.
'And we said we had no need of dirges and laments. So which are the harmonies that express grief? You're musical; tell me.'
We did.
'The mixed Lydian,' he said, 'and the high-pitched Lydian, and others of that sort.'
So which are the mourning modes? Tell me — you're the musician.
'Then those must be banished,' I said. 'They're useless even to women who are to be of any worth, let alone to men.'
The Mixolydian, he said, and the taut Lydian, and others in that vein.
'Certainly.'
Out they go, I said. They're useless even to women — the ones expected to be decent — let alone to men.
'And drunkenness, softness, and idleness are wholly unbecoming in our guardians.'
Agreed.
'Wholly.'
Next: drunkenness, softness, and laziness are about the last things that suit a guardian.
'Which are the soft, drinking-party harmonies?'
The very last.
'The Ionian,' he said, 'and certain Lydian modes that are called "slack."'
Then which modes are soft — the drinking-party modes?
'And are these any use to fighting men?'
The Ionian, he said, and the Lydian again — the ones they call 'loose.'
'Quite the opposite,' he said. 'So you're left with the Dorian and the Phrygian.'
And will you find any use for those, my friend, in men of war?

'I know nothing about the harmonies myself,' I said. 'But leave me one that will fittingly imitate the voice and the bearing of a brave man in the thick of battle and in every grim necessity, when his cause is going badly and he faces wounds or death or some other disaster, and in all of it stands firm and endures. And leave me another for a man at peace, acting freely, under no compulsion: persuading a god by prayer or a man by teaching and advice, or, on the other side, opening himself to another's appeal or instruction or warning, and so, by good sense, getting his way, not carried off by success but acting soberly and moderately throughout, content with how things turn out. Those two harmonies, the strain of necessity and the strain of freedom, of the unfortunate man and the fortunate, of courage and of self-control, those I ask you to leave us.'
None at all, he said. Which seems to leave you the Dorian and the Phrygian.
'But those,' he said, 'are exactly the two I was just speaking of, the Dorian and the Phrygian.'

I don't know the modes, I said. Just leave me the one that would rightly imitate the voice and cadence of a brave man in war, or in any forced and dangerous work — a man who, when it goes against him, when he's headed into wounds or death or has fallen into some other disaster, in every one of those moments stands his ground in good order and endures whatever fortune sends. And leave me one more, for a man at peaceful work — work not forced on him but freely chosen — persuading someone or asking for something, whether praying to a god or teaching and correcting a man; or the reverse, holding himself open to another's request or instruction or persuasion; a man acting as his own mind sees fit, never arrogant, moving with self-discipline and measure through all of it, and at peace with the outcome. These two modes — the forced and the free, the mode of the unlucky and the mode of the lucky, the brave man's and the self-disciplined man's — leave me those.
'Then if these and only these are to be used in our songs and melodies,' I said, 'we won't need a great range of notes or an instrument that runs through every scale.'
Then you're asking, he said, for exactly the two I named: the Dorian and the Phrygian.
'It seems not.'
In that case, I said, our songs and melodies won't need a forest of strings, or every scale at once.
'So we won't keep the makers of three-cornered harps and many-stringed instruments, or anyone who builds instruments tuned to every mode.'
Apparently not.
'Apparently not.'
So we won't be supporting the craftsmen who build triangular harps and Lydian zithers and every many-stringed, many-scaled contraption.

'And what about flute-makers and flute-players? Will you admit them, when you consider that the flute is the most many-noted instrument of all, and that the instruments tuned to every mode are really only imitations of it?'
It appears not.
'Clearly not,' he said.

And flute-makers, flute-players — will you take those into the city? Isn't the flute the most 'many-stringed' instrument of them all — isn't the every-scale instrument itself just an imitation of the flute?
'So you're left with the lyre and the kithara for use in the city, and out in the country the herdsmen can have some sort of pipe.'
Clearly it is, he said.
'That's certainly what the argument suggests,' he said.
That leaves you the lyre and the cithara as useful in town, I said; and out in the fields, the herdsmen can have some kind of pipe.
'And we're doing nothing strange,' I said, 'in preferring Apollo and Apollo's instruments to Marsyas and his.'
So the argument tells us, at least.
'Nothing strange at all,' he said.
We're doing nothing radical, my friend, I said — just choosing Apollo and Apollo's instruments over Marsyas and his.
'By the dog of Egypt,' I said, 'without noticing it we've been purging the city we called luxurious a little while ago.'
By Zeus, he said, no — nothing radical at all.
'And very sensibly too,' he said.
And look at that — by the dog! — without noticing, we've been purging the city we called bloated with luxury a little while ago.

'Then let's finish the purge. After harmonies comes rhythm, which should follow the same rules. We shouldn't go chasing complicated systems of meter, or every kind of measure, but should find out which rhythms express a brave and orderly life, and then fit the meter and the tune to words of that spirit, not the words to the meter and the tune. As for what those rhythms are, that's for you to tell me, the way you told me about the harmonies.'
And very sensibly too, he said.

'I really can't,' he said. 'I do know there are roughly three basic kinds of rhythm out of which the meters are built, just as there are four notes in sound out of which all the harmonies come, and I've observed that much. But which of them imitate which sort of life, I can't say.'

Then let's finish the purge, I said. After the modes comes rhythm, and the same rule holds: we shouldn't chase intricate rhythms or every kind of foot, but look for the rhythms that belong to an orderly and courageous life — and once we've found them, make the foot and the melody follow that kind of speech, not the speech follow the foot and the melody. Which rhythms they are is your job to say, as it was with the modes.

'Then we'll have to bring Damon into the discussion,' I said, 'and let him tell us which rhythms suit meanness, or arrogance, or madness, or other base things, and which should be kept for their opposites. I have a vague memory of him mentioning a complex marching rhythm, and a dactylic or heroic one, which he arranged somehow I don't quite grasp, balancing the rise and fall of the foot equally, long against short. And I think he spoke of an iambic and a trochaic, assigning short and long quantities to them. In some cases I believe he praised or blamed the tempo of the foot as much as the rhythm itself, or perhaps a combination of the two, I'm not sure. But as I say, let's leave all this to Damon, since untangling it would take a long argument. Don't you agree?'

Honestly, he said, I can't. That there are three basic forms out of which the meters are woven — the way four notes underlie all the modes — that much I've observed and can tell you. But which kind of life each one imitates, I cannot say.
'I certainly do,' he said.

Then on that, I said, we'll consult Damon: which feet fit meanness and insolence, or madness and the rest of what's bad, and which rhythms are left for their opposites. I have a hazy memory of hearing him name a composite war-march rhythm, and a dactyl — the heroic foot — which he arranged in some way I don't quite follow, rise and fall made equal, resolving into short and long; and, I think, an iambus, and a trochee too, with their longs and shorts assigned. And with some of these I believe he praised or blamed the tempo of the foot as much as the rhythm itself — or the two together; I can't say exactly. As I said, all of this can go to Damon. Settling it would take us more than a little talk. Or do you think otherwise?
'But this much you can see without any trouble: gracefulness, or its absence, goes with good or bad rhythm.'
By Zeus, no — I don't.
'Of course.'
But this much you can settle now: that gracefulness and gracelessness follow good rhythm and bad.

'And good rhythm naturally goes with a fine style, and bad rhythm with its opposite, and the same with harmony and discord, since rhythm and harmony, as we said, follow the words, not the other way around.'
Of course.
'Yes,' he said, 'they should follow the words.'

And good rhythm follows on beautiful speech, shaped to match it, and bad rhythm on the opposite kind; and the same goes for what sounds harmonious and what sounds off — since, as we just said, rhythm and mode follow the words, and not the words them.
'And don't the words and the style depend on the character of the soul?'
Yes, he said — they have to follow the speech.
'Naturally.'
And the manner of the speech, I said, and the speech itself — don't they follow the character of the speaker's soul?
'And everything else follows the style?'
Of course.
'Yes.'
And everything else follows the speech?

'So fine speech, fine harmony, gracefulness, and good rhythm all follow from a good character, by which I don't mean the silliness we politely call good nature, but a mind and character truly well and nobly ordered.'
Yes.
'Quite so,' he said.

Then fine speech, fine harmony, fine grace, and fine rhythm all follow from simplicity of soul — not the simple-mindedness we politely excuse with that name, but the real thing: a mind whose character is genuinely good and fine.
'And mustn't our young men aim at these everywhere, if they're going to do their proper work?'
Entirely so.
'They must.'
Then if our young men are going to do their own work, mustn't they chase these qualities everywhere?

'And surely painting is full of these same qualities, and so is every other craft of making, weaving, embroidery, building, the making of any object at all, and nature too, in living bodies and growing things. In all of them there's gracefulness or its lack. And ugliness, bad rhythm, and discord are close kin to bad speech and bad character, while their opposites are kin to, and copies of, the opposite: a sober and good character.'
They must.
'Absolutely,' he said.

And they are everywhere. Painting is full of them, and every craft like it; weaving is full of them, and embroidery, and architecture, and the making of every kind of furnishing; so is the nature of our bodies, and of every growing thing. In all of these there is grace or gracelessness. And gracelessness, bad rhythm, disharmony — these are sisters of bad speech and bad character; while their opposites are sisters, and imitations, of the opposite — a self-disciplined and good character.

'So is it only the poets we have to oversee, forcing them to put the image of good character into their poems or else not work among us? Or should we keep watch over the other craftsmen too, and stop them from setting the stamp of bad character, of intemperance, meanness, and indecency, on their paintings and buildings and other works? Anyone who can't do this shouldn't be allowed to practice his craft in our city, so that our guardians won't be raised among images of vice, as if in some poisoned pasture, where day after day they'd graze and feed on much that is harmful, a little at a time, until without noticing they piled up one great festering corruption in their souls. We should look instead for the craftsmen with the gift to track down the nature of the beautiful and graceful, so that our young men, living as in a healthy place, will take good from every quarter, wherever some fine work strikes their eyes or ears, like a breeze off clean ground bringing health, and from earliest childhood will be drawn, without their knowing it, into likeness and friendship and harmony with the beauty of reason.'
Completely, he said.
'Yes,' he said, 'that would be far the finest upbringing.'

Then is it only the poets we have to stand over, forcing them to plant the image of good character in their poems or else not write among us at all? Or do we stand over the other craftsmen too, and stop them from putting bad character — undisciplined, mean, graceless — into their images of living things, or into their buildings, or into anything else they make? And the one who can't comply is barred from working here — so that our guardians aren't raised among images of vice like cattle in a poisoned pasture, cropping and grazing a little from many places, day after day, until without noticing it they've collected one great evil in their souls. Shouldn't we look instead for the craftsmen with a native gift for tracking down the nature of the beautiful and the graceful — so that our young men live as if in a healthy country, where everything does them good, and from every side beautiful sights and sounds strike their eyes and ears like a breeze bringing health from good places, tilting them from childhood on, unawares, into likeness and friendship and harmony with the beauty of reason?

'And isn't this why education in music and poetry is so powerful, Glaucon? Because rhythm and harmony sink deepest into the soul and take the firmest hold of it, bringing gracefulness in their train, so that they make a man graceful if he's rightly brought up, and graceless if he isn't. And the man rightly educated in this way will have the sharpest eye for what's left out or badly made in any work of craft or of nature. His distaste will be just; he'll praise and welcome into his soul the beautiful things and be nourished by them and grow noble and good, while still a child, before he can give the reason, he'll rightly condemn and hate the ugly ones, and when reason comes at last, he'll greet it as a friend, because his upbringing has made him familiar with it all along.'
There could be no finer upbringing, he said.
'Yes,' he said, 'I think that's just why education in music and poetry matters so much.'

And isn't that, Glaucon, I said, why the upbringing in music matters most? Rhythm and mode sink deeper into the inmost soul than anything else; they take hold of it with the strongest grip, bringing gracefulness with them; and they make a man graceful — if he's raised rightly; if not, the opposite. And the man properly raised on music will feel it sharpest when something has been botched or stunted by craft or by nature — his disgust will be the right disgust. He'll praise beautiful things, take joy in them, receive them into his soul, feed on them, and become noble and good; the ugly he'll rightly condemn and hate while he is still young, before he can grasp the reason why. And when reason arrives, the man raised this way will recognize it and embrace it — no one will greet it like family the way he does.

'It's like learning to read,' I said. 'We weren't satisfied until we could pick out the letters, few as they are, in all their combinations, never treating them as beneath notice whether they appeared in something large or small, but everywhere eager to make them out, knowing we wouldn't be readers until we could.'
Yes, he said — that's my view too: those are the reasons for an education in music.
'True.'

Then think of reading, I said. We only had it down when we stopped missing the letters — few as they are — in all the combinations where they circulate; when we never dismissed one as beneath notice in a small word or a large one, but strained to make it out everywhere, knowing we wouldn't be readers until we did.
'And we can't recognize the reflections of letters in water or in a mirror until we know the letters themselves, since both belong to the same skill and the same study.'
True.
'Exactly.'
And if letters showed up reflected in water or in a mirror, we wouldn't recognize them there before we knew the letters themselves — it's one and the same skill and practice.

'Then, by the same token, neither we nor the guardians we're educating can become musical until we can recognize the basic forms of self-control, courage, generosity, greatness of soul, and their kindred, and their opposites too, wherever they turn up, in things great or small, knowing that all of it belongs to one and the same skill and study.'
Exactly.
'That must be so,' he said.

Then by the gods, I say it's the same here: we will never be musical either — nor will the guardians we say we must educate — until we recognize the forms of self-discipline, courage, generosity, greatness of spirit, and all their siblings, and their opposites too, everywhere they circulate; until we notice them wherever they turn up, themselves and their images, and never dismiss them in small things or great, but hold it all one and the same skill and practice.
'And when a beautiful character in the soul agrees with a beautiful form in the body, both cast in one mold, won't that be the fairest sight of all to anyone with eyes to see it?'
It must be so, he said.
'The fairest of all.'
So when a beautiful character in the soul and a matching, harmonizing beauty in the body are cast from the same mold — wouldn't that be the fairest sight there is, for anyone who has eyes to see it?
'And the fairest is also the most lovable?'
By far.
'Naturally.'
And what is fairest is what we love most?
'So the truly musical man will love such people most, but won't love anyone whose soul is out of tune.'
Of course.
'No,' he said, 'not if the flaw is in the soul. If it's only some bodily defect, he'll be patient and willing to love the person all the same.'
Then the truly musical man would love people like that most of all — and where the harmony was missing, he would not love.
'I see,' I said, 'that you have, or have had, a beloved of that kind, and I won't argue. But tell me this: does extravagant pleasure have anything in common with self-control?'
Not if the flaw were in the soul, he said. If it were something in the body, he'd bear with it and love anyway.
'How could it,' he said, 'when pleasure throws the mind off balance as much as pain does?'
I understand, I said — you have, or once had, a beloved like that. Fine; I'll grant it. But tell me this: does extravagant pleasure have anything in common with self-discipline?
'And anything in common with virtue generally?'
How could it? he said. Pleasure like that unhinges the mind as thoroughly as pain does.
'Nothing at all.'
Anything in common with the rest of virtue?
'But with violence and lack of control?'
Nothing.
'More than anything.'
With outrage and dissipation, then?
'And can you name a greater or keener pleasure than sex?'
More than with anything else.
'No,' he said, 'nor a more frenzied one.'
And can you name a pleasure bigger or sharper than sex?
'But the right kind of love is a love of what's beautiful and orderly, a self-controlled and harmonious love.'
I can't, he said — nor a madder one.
'Quite true,' he said.
But the right kind of love is loving what is orderly and beautiful — a disciplined, musical love?
'So nothing frenzied, nothing akin to a lack of self-control, should come anywhere near the right kind of love.'
Very much so.
'No, it shouldn't.'
Then nothing manic, nothing that borders on dissipation, may come near the right kind of love?
'So this mad, intemperate pleasure must never come near the lover and the one he loves; neither of them can have any share in it, if their love is the right kind.'
It may not.
'No, Socrates,' he said, 'it must never come near them.'
Then that pleasure may come nowhere near it, and lover and beloved who love rightly can have no share in it?

'So it seems you'll lay down a law, in the city we're founding, that a lover may show his beloved no greater intimacy than a father would show a son, and that only for a fine end, and only with the other's consent. This is to govern all his dealings with the boy he cares for, and he must never be seen going further. If he does, he'll be branded as coarse and without taste.'
No, by Zeus, Socrates, he said — nowhere near.
'I quite agree,' he said.

So it seems you'll lay down a law in the city we're founding: a lover may kiss his favorite, keep his company, touch him as a father would a son — for beauty's sake, and only if he consents. Beyond that, his dealings with anyone he cares for must never appear to go further; otherwise let him bear the reproach of a man with no music and no taste in him.
'And there, I think, our talk of music and poetry comes to its proper end, since it has ended where talk of these things should end, in the love of the beautiful.'
Just so, he said.
'I agree,' he said.
Well then, I said — do you see our account of music coming to an end? It ended where an ending belongs: music should end in the love of beauty.
'After music and poetry, our young men must be trained in physical exercise.'
I agree, he said.
'Of course.'
After music, our young men get physical training.

'And here too the training should start in childhood and go on carefully through life. My own view, and I'd like to hear yours to confirm it, is that it isn't a good body that makes the soul good by its own excellence, but the other way around: a good soul, by its own excellence, makes the body as good as it can be. What do you say?'
Naturally.
'I agree,' he said.

Here too the training must be strict, starting in childhood and running through the whole of life. The truth of it, I believe, is this — see what you think. I don't believe that a sound body makes the soul good by its own goodness. It's the other way around: a good soul, by its own goodness, makes the body as good as a body can be. What do you say?
'So if we give the mind a thorough training and then hand over to it the detailed care of the body, we'll be doing the right thing. To keep this short, let me just sketch the outline.'
I think so too.
'Go ahead.'
Then if we tend the mind properly and hand over to it the detailed care of the body — keeping ourselves to the general patterns, so as not to run long — we'd be doing it right?
'We already said the guardians must keep off drink. Of all men a guardian is the last who should get drunk and not know where on earth he is.'
Quite right.
'Yes,' he said, 'it would be absurd for a guardian to need another guardian to look after him.'
Drunkenness we've already ruled out. A guardian is the last man on earth who can afford to be drunk and not know where he is.
'And what about their food? These men are athletes in the greatest of all contests, aren't they?'
It would be absurd, he said — a guard who needs a guard.
'They are.'
What about food, then? These men are athletes in the greatest contest there is. Aren't they?
'Would the regime of our ordinary athletes suit them?'
They are.
'Perhaps.'
Then would the conditioning of our professional athletes suit them?

'I'm afraid that's a drowsy sort of training,' I said, 'and risky for the health. Haven't you noticed how these athletes sleep their lives away, and how they fall dangerously ill the moment they stray even slightly from their fixed routine?'
Perhaps.
'I have.'

It's a sleepy sort of conditioning, I said, and it makes health a fragile thing. Haven't you noticed? These athletes sleep their lives away, and if they step even slightly outside their prescribed routine they come down with serious, violent illnesses.

'Then our warrior-athletes need a finer kind of training. They have to be like wakeful watchdogs, with the keenest sight and hearing, and on campaign they'll have to put up with every change of water and food, with summer heat and winter cold, without their health giving way.'
I've noticed.
'That's my view too.'

Our war-athletes need something subtler: wakeful as watchdogs, seeing and hearing at the keenest pitch, and able to take all the changes a campaign throws at them — strange water, strange food, blazing heat, winter storms — without their health giving way.
'And the best physical training is the twin sister of the simple music we were just describing.'
So it seems to me.
'How so?'
Then wouldn't the best physical training be a close sister of the music we described a moment ago — the simple kind?
'I mean there's a kind of physical training that's simple and good, just as our music was, and especially the training for war.'
Meaning what?
'What do you mean?'
A simple, honest training — and above all, the training for war.

'You can learn it from Homer. You know how he feeds his heroes on campaign: no fish, even though they're camped on the shores of the Hellespont, and no boiled meat, only roast, which is what suits soldiers best, since all they need is a fire, and they don't have to lug pots around.'
How does that go?
'True.'

You could learn it from Homer, I said. You know that when his heroes are on campaign he doesn't feast them on fish — though they're camped on the Hellespont, right beside the sea — or on boiled meat, only roasted, which is what soldiers can manage most easily: a fire is nearly always to hand, and it beats hauling pots and pans around.
'And I think I'm right that Homer nowhere mentions rich sauces. In fact every athlete in training knows that a man who wants to stay in condition must keep off that sort of thing.'
True.
'Yes,' he said, 'they know it, and they're right to keep off it.'
And Homer, I think I'm right in saying, never once mentions sweet sauces. Every athlete in training knows that much, in fact: a body that means to be in condition keeps away from all such things.
'Then you wouldn't approve of Syracusan dinners and the elaborate dishes of Sicilian cooking?'
They know it, he said, and they're right to keep away.
'I think not.'
Then you won't approve of Syracusan dining, my friend, or Sicilian fancy cooking, if all this seems right to you.
'Nor would you let a man who means to stay in condition keep a Corinthian girl as his sweetheart?'
I won't.
'Certainly not.'
Then you'll also frown on a Corinthian girlfriend for a man who means to keep his body in shape.
'Nor would you approve of those famous Athenian pastries?'
Absolutely.
'No.'
And on those famous delights of Athenian pastry.
'All such food and such living we can fairly compare to a song and a melody composed in every mode and every rhythm at once.'
Necessarily.
'Exactly.'
Because all this kind of eating and living, I think, we'd rightly compare to the songs written in every scale and every rhythm at once.
'There the complexity bred license, and here it breeds disease; whereas simplicity in music bred self-control in the soul, and simplicity in physical training breeds health in the body.'
Exactly.
'Very true,' he said.
There, elaborateness bred indiscipline; here, it breeds disease. Plainness in music breeds self-discipline in souls; plainness in physical training breeds health in bodies.

'And when license and disease multiply in a city, don't they keep throwing open more courtrooms and clinics, so that law and medicine start giving themselves airs, when even free men, not just slaves, take them so seriously?'
Very true, he said.
'Of course.'

And when indiscipline and disease multiply in a city, don't the law courts and the clinics throw their doors wide? Don't law and medicine start to swagger, once even large numbers of free men are taking them terribly seriously?

'And what greater sign could there be of a bad, disgraceful education than this: that not only the laborers and common people need first-rate doctors and judges, but men who claim to have had a liberal upbringing need them too? Isn't it shameful, a glaring mark of bad breeding, that a man should have to go to others for his justice, as if to lords and masters, having none of his own inside him?'
It can hardly go otherwise.
'The most shameful thing of all,' he said.

And can you find better proof that a city's education is bad and shameful than this — that first-rate doctors and judges are needed not just by tradesmen and the poor, but by the very people who boast they were raised as free men? Isn't it disgraceful — doesn't it argue a stunning lack of cultivation — to be forced to import your justice from other men, as your lords and judges, because you're bankrupt of your own?

'Would you call it "the most" shameful,' I said, 'when there's a worse stage still? When a man not only spends his whole life in the courts, suing and being sued, but is so devoid of taste that he actually prides himself on his skill at wrongdoing, sure that he's a master at it, able to twist every which way, slip through any loophole, bend like a reed to dodge a verdict, all to win paltry points not worth mentioning, not knowing how much finer and nobler it is to order one's life so as never to need a drowsy judge at all?'
The most disgraceful thing of all, he said.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's still more shameful.'

Are you sure it's the most? I said. What about this, which is worse: a man who not only spends most of his life in the courts as defendant and plaintiff, but is vulgar enough to preen himself on it — proud of being slick at wrongdoing, able to twist through every turn, to wriggle out through every loophole, bending like a willow shoot to slip past justice — and all for the sake of small, worthless stakes. He has no idea how much finer and better it is to arrange your life so that you never need a drowsing juror at all.

'And to need medicine,' I said, 'not for a wound or one of the seasonal illnesses, but just because, through idleness and the kind of living we've described, a man fills himself up with fluids and gases like a stagnant marsh, and forces the clever sons of Asclepius to invent names for diseases, "flatulence" and "catarrh" and the rest, isn't that a disgrace too?'
You're right, he said — that is worse.
'It is,' he said. 'Those really are strange new-fangled names for diseases.'

And to need medicine, I said — not for a wound, or one of the seasonal sicknesses that visit everyone, but because idleness and the regimen we described have filled a man with gases and humors like a swamp, forcing the clever sons of Asclepius to invent names like 'flatulence' and 'catarrh' for his diseases — doesn't that strike you as a disgrace?

'The kind, I think, that didn't exist in Asclepius's day,' I said. 'I infer this from the fact that at Troy, when Eurypylus was wounded, no one objected to the girl who gave him Pramnian wine sprinkled with barley meal and grated cheese to drink, things you'd think highly inflammatory, and the sons of Asclepius there didn't blame Patroclus, who was treating him.'
It does, he said. Those really are strange, newfangled names for diseases.
'It was certainly an odd drink,' he said, 'for a man in that state.'

The kind of thing, I said, that didn't exist, I suspect, in Asclepius's own day. I take my evidence from Troy: when Eurypylus was wounded, and a woman gave him Pramnian wine thickly sprinkled with barley meal and grated cheese — a recipe you'd call inflammatory — the sons of Asclepius found no fault with the girl who served it, and none with Patroclus, who was managing his treatment.

'Not so odd,' I said, 'if you remember that before Herodicus's time the school of Asclepius didn't practice our present kind of medicine, the kind that nurses diseases along. Herodicus was a trainer who fell sick, and by mixing training with doctoring he found a way to torment first himself and then the rest of the world.'
It certainly was a strange drink, he said, for a man in that state.
'How so?' he asked.

Not if you remember, I said, that the old guild of Asclepius — before Herodicus, as they say — didn't practice today's medicine, this system that chaperones diseases through life. Herodicus was a trainer who turned sickly, so he blended training with doctoring — and wore down first and worst himself, and then plenty of others after him.

'By inventing the lingering death. He had a fatal illness, and by tending it endlessly, since there was no cure, he dragged out his whole life as an invalid. He could do nothing but nurse himself, in agony whenever he strayed from his routine, and so, by his cleverness, he died hard, and slowly, all the way into old age.'
How? he said.
'A fine reward for his skill,' he said.

By making his dying long, I said. He had a fatal disease, and he waited on it hand and foot. Recovery was impossible, so living became nursing: no time for anything else, tortured the moment he strayed from his routine. His expertise made death slow for him — he struggled all the way to old age.

'Just what you'd expect,' I said, 'for a man who never understood that Asclepius left his descendants no instruction in this invalid's art, not out of ignorance, but because he knew that in a well-run city every man has his own work to do and no leisure to spend a lifetime being ill. We see this clearly in the case of the craftsman, but, absurdly, we don't apply it to the rich.'
A fine prize his art won him, he said.
'How do you mean?' he said.

The prize you'd expect, I said, for a man who never understood why Asclepius left this branch of medicine untaught to his heirs. It wasn't ignorance or inexperience. It was knowing that in every well-run city each man has one job to do — and no one has the leisure to spend his life being sick and doctoring himself. We see this clearly enough in the working man; absurdly, we can't see it in the rich and supposedly fortunate.

'I mean this. When a carpenter falls ill, he asks his doctor for a quick remedy: something to make him vomit, or move his bowels, or a cautery, or the knife. If the doctor prescribes a long course of diet, wrapping his head up and all the rest, he says at once that he has no time to be ill, and sees no point in a life spent nursing his disease while his proper work goes neglected. So he says goodbye to that kind of doctor, goes back to his ordinary life, and either gets well and lives and does his work, or, if his body can't take it, dies and is out of his troubles.'
How so? he said.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's the right way for a man in his station to use medicine.'

When a carpenter falls sick, I said, he expects his doctor to hand him a drug to vomit the illness up or purge it out below, or to reach for cautery or the knife and be done with it. If someone instead prescribes him a long regimen — felt caps for his head and all the rest of it — he says straight out that he has no time to be sick, and that there's no profit in living like that, minding a disease while his proper work goes undone. Then he waves that sort of doctor goodbye, goes back to his usual routine, and either recovers and gets on with his business or, if his body can't carry it, dies and is quit of his troubles.
'Because he has work to do,' I said, 'and there's no profit in living if he can't do it.'
And for a man like that, he said, that seems the right way to use medicine.
'Quite true,' he said.
Because he has work, I said — and if he can't do it, life doesn't pay?
'But the rich man is different. We don't say he has any appointed task he must do or else not live.'
Obviously.
'No, he's generally supposed to have nothing to do.'
But the rich man, as we tell it, has no work assigned to him that would make life unlivable if it were taken out of his hands.
'Then you've never heard the saying of Phocylides, that a man should practice virtue once he has a living?'
None that anyone mentions.
'I'd say he should start sooner than that,' he said.
Then you haven't heard Phocylides' saying — that once a man has a living, he should practice virtue.

'Let's not quarrel with Phocylides about that,' I said. 'Let's just ask ourselves: is the rich man, too, obliged to practice virtue, and is his life worthless without it? And if he is obliged, does this fussing over the body get in the way of practicing virtue, just as it gets in the way of carpentry and the other trades?'
Even sooner, I'd have thought, he said.
'It certainly does,' he said. 'Excessive care of the body, beyond plain exercise, is about as great a hindrance to virtue as anything could be.'

Let's not fight him over that, I said. Let's settle it for ourselves: is this practice the rich man's work, so that life without it is no life at all? Or does nursing a disease, which blocks a man from applying himself to carpentry and the other trades, block the road to Phocylides' advice just as thoroughly?

'Yes,' I said, 'and it's just as incompatible with managing a household, serving in the army, or holding office in the city. Worst of all, it makes any kind of study or thought or quiet self-examination impossible, since the man is forever suspecting that his headaches and dizziness come from too much philosophy, so that wherever virtue in this higher sense is being practiced or tested, he's a hindrance, always imagining himself ill, always anxious about his body.'
By Zeus, it does, he said — there's hardly a worse obstacle than this over-tending of the body, this fussing that goes beyond plain physical training.
'Very likely,' he said.

And it's just as bad, I said, for running a household, an army, or a public office. Worst of all, it makes any kind of study or thought or work on one's own mind nearly impossible. The man is forever suspecting headaches and dizziness and blaming philosophy for causing them — so that wherever virtue is being practiced and tested, this body-coddling blocks the way. It keeps him convinced he is perpetually ill; it keeps him perpetually in labor over his own body.

'So we'll say that Asclepius knew all this, and showed his art only to people who were generally sound in body and habits but had some specific complaint. These he cured with drugs or surgery and then told to go on living as usual, so as not to harm the city. But bodies riddled with disease all the way through he wouldn't try to patch up with slow drainings and infusions, drawing out a useless life and letting weak fathers breed still weaker sons. He thought a man who couldn't live the normal span of life shouldn't be treated, since such a cure would do no good to the man himself or to the city.'
It would.
'So you make Asclepius a statesman,' he said.

So shouldn't we say Asclepius knew all this — that for people whose constitutions and habits were healthy but who came down with some specific ailment, he showed what medicine could do: drugs and surgery to drive the disease out, then the usual regimen, so the city's business wouldn't suffer. But bodies riddled through and through with disease he wouldn't touch. He wouldn't drain and dose by slow degrees to give a man a long, bad life, and let him father children in all likelihood just like himself. A man who couldn't live in his ordinary rounds, Asclepius judged, wasn't worth treating — no profit in him, to himself or to the city.

'Plainly he was one,' I said, 'and you can see it in his sons too. Notice that at Troy they fought bravely and practiced medicine the way I've described. You remember how, when Pandarus wounded Menelaus, they',
Asclepius the statesman, he said.
'"sucked out the blood and sprinkled soothing drugs on the wound,"'

Clearly, I said. And because he was, look at his sons: at Troy they showed themselves good men in the fighting, and they practiced medicine exactly the way I've described. Remember — when Pandarus's arrow wounded Menelaus, they

'but never told him afterward what to eat or drink, any more than they did with Eurypylus. The remedies were enough to heal any man who'd been sound and orderly in his habits before the wound, even if he did happen to drink Pramnian wine. But men whose bodies were sickly and intemperate, whose lives were no use to themselves or anyone else, they thought medicine wasn't meant for, and they wouldn't treat them, not even if they were richer than Midas.'
'sucked out the blood, and sprinkled gentle remedies on the wound,'
'Very shrewd men, those sons of Asclepius,' he said.

but what he should eat or drink afterward they no more prescribed for him than for Eurypylus. The remedies were enough, they judged, to heal men who had been healthy and orderly in their lives before the wound — whatever they happened to be drinking at the moment. But a man diseased in his constitution and undisciplined in his habits — his life was no profit to himself or anyone else; the art was not made for men like that, and they wouldn't treat them if they were richer than Midas.

'As you'd expect,' I said. 'And yet the tragic poets and Pindar, ignoring us, while they admit that Asclepius was Apollo's son, also say he was bribed into healing a rich man already at the point of death, and was struck by lightning for it. But by our principle we won't believe both claims. If he was a god's son, we'll say he wasn't greedy for money; and if he was greedy for money, he wasn't a god's son.'
Sharp fellows, he said, these sons of Asclepius — the way you tell it.

'That part is excellent, Socrates,' he said. 'But here's a question for you. Shouldn't a city have good doctors? And aren't the best doctors the ones who've handled the greatest number of cases, healthy and sick alike? And aren't the best judges, likewise, those who've dealt with every kind of character?'

As they should be, I said. And yet the tragedians and Pindar won't listen to us: they call Asclepius Apollo's son and then claim that gold bribed him into healing a rich man who was already dying — for which the thunderbolt struck him down. We, keeping to our earlier rule, won't believe them on both counts. If he was a god's son, we'll say, he was not greedy; and if he was greedy, he was no son of a god.
'Yes,' I said, 'I do want good doctors and good judges. But do you know which ones I think are good?'

On all that, Socrates, he said, you're right. But here's a question. Doesn't a city need good doctors? And wouldn't the best be the ones who've handled the most bodies, healthy and diseased alike — just as the best judges would be men who've dealt with natures of every kind?
'Tell me.'
Good ones — I certainly want them, I said. But do you know which ones I count good?
'I will, if I can. But notice that you've lumped together two things that aren't alike.'
If you'll tell me, he said.
'How so?' he asked.
I'll try, I said. But your one question bundled together two things that aren't alike.

'You've put doctors and judges side by side. Now the most skillful doctors are the ones who, from youth up, have added to their knowledge of the art the widest experience of disease, and who'd do better not to have been robust in health themselves but to have suffered every illness in their own bodies. For they don't cure the body with the body; if they did, we couldn't let them be, or ever have been, sickly.
