They cure the body with the mind, and a mind that's become and stayed sick can cure nothing.'
How so? he asked.
'Very true,' he said.

Doctors, I said, would become most skilled like this: starting in childhood, along with learning their art, they should handle as many bodies as possible, and the most diseased ones — and ideally suffer every illness themselves, and come to the work with less than iron constitutions. Because it isn't body that heals body — if it were, we could never allow a doctor's body to be sick or to fall sick — it's soul that heals body, and a soul that has gone bad, or is bad, can't heal anything well.

'But with the judge it's the other way around, since he governs mind with mind. He shouldn't have been brought up among vicious minds and kept company with them from youth, running through the whole catalog of crime himself, just so that he can quickly infer other people's wrongs from his own, the way a doctor might infer a disease. No, the honest mind that's to judge soundly should have had no taste of bad habits, no infection from them, when young. That's why good men, when young, often seem naive and are easily taken in by the dishonest, because they have no pattern of wickedness in themselves to match against it.'
Right, he said.
'Yes,' he said, 'that happens to them all the time.'

But a judge, my friend, rules soul with soul. And a soul must not be reared from youth among vicious souls, keeping their company, running the whole catalogue of crimes itself so that it can sharply infer other men's wrongdoing from its own — the way a doctor infers from his own body. If a soul is to be fine and good, and judge soundly of what is healthy, it must come to the work with no experience of bad character, uncontaminated by it while it was young. That's exactly why decent people look naive when they're young — easy marks for the unjust: they carry no working models of evil inside themselves.

'So the good judge mustn't be young,' I said. 'He should be old, having learned late and slowly what evil is, not from his own soul but from watching it for a long time in others. Knowledge should be his guide, not personal experience.'
It's true, he said — it happens to them constantly.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's the noblest kind of judge.'

That's why a good judge can't be young, I said. He must be old — a late learner in what injustice is, who studied it not as a resident in his own soul but as a foreign thing in the souls of others, over long years, until he knows exactly what kind of evil it is — by knowledge, not by personal acquaintance.

'And a good man, too,' I said, 'which is the answer to your question, since a man is good who has a good soul. But that clever and suspicious type, the man who's done a great deal of wrong and thinks himself a master of cunning, is impressive at taking precautions among men like himself, because he measures them by his own standard. But when he comes among good and older men, he looks a fool again, with his unseasonable suspicions, because he can't recognize an honest man, having no pattern of honesty in himself. And since the bad outnumber the good and he meets them more often, he thinks himself wise, and others think so too, rather than foolish.'
A judge like that, he said, would be the noblest kind there is.
'Very true,' he said.

And a good one, I said — which was your question. A man with a good soul is good. Whereas that other type — the clever, suspicious one, the veteran of his own many crimes, who fancies himself shrewd and wise: among his own kind he looks formidable, because the patterns inside him keep him on guard. But when he comes among good men, older men, he looks a fool instead — suspicious out of season, unable to recognize a sound character, since he has no sound pattern of his own to check it against. Still, since he runs into the bad more often than the good, he passes for wise rather than foolish — in his own eyes, and in the eyes of most other people.

'So this isn't the wise and good judge we're after, but the other,' I said. 'For badness can never know both virtue and itself, while a virtuous nature, educated over time, will come to know both virtue and vice. So it's the virtuous man, not the vicious one, who has wisdom, in my view.'
Completely true, he said.
'And in mine too,' he said.

Then that's not the man we want for a good and wise judge — it's the first one. Vice can never know both virtue and itself; but virtue, in a nature educated by time, can come to knowledge of itself and of vice together. The virtuous man, not the bad one — he's the one who becomes wise, as I see it.

'Then this is the kind of medicine and the kind of law you'll establish in your city. They'll care for the citizens whose natures are sound in body and soul, but those whose bodies are unsound they'll let die, and those whose souls are rotten and incurable they'll put to death themselves.'
As I see it too.
'That's clearly best,' he said, 'both for the men themselves and for the city.'

Then this is the medicine, and this the judging, you'll write into law in our city: arts that will care for the citizens who are sound in body and soul. As for the rest — those unsound in body they will let die; those with evil-natured, incurable souls the judges themselves will put to death.
'And plainly your young men,' I said, 'brought up on that simple music that breeds self-control, will be slow to need the courts.'
Well, he said, that's clearly best for the ones it happens to — and for the city.
'Clearly.'
As for your young men, then — trained on that simple music which we said breeds self-discipline — they'll obviously be wary of ever needing a courtroom.
'And the man trained in music, following the same path with simple physical training, will want nothing to do with medicine except in dire need.'
Clearly.
'I believe that,' he said.
And the man educated in music, hunting fitness along the same track, will choose to need no medicine except in a real emergency.

'In fact he'll undergo his exercises and labors to rouse the spirited part of his nature rather than to build up strength. He won't, like ordinary athletes, use food and exercise just to put on muscle.'
So I believe.
'Quite right,' he said.

Even his workouts and his exertions aim at the spirited part of his nature — that is what he'll be rousing as he trains — not at raw strength. He won't spend his food and toil on muscle like the ordinary athletes.
'And the two arts, music and physical training, aren't really meant, as people suppose, one for the soul and the other for the body.'
Exactly right, he said.
'Then what are they for?' he asked.
Then, Glaucon, the men who established education in music and physical training didn't do it for the reason people think — the one to tend the body, the other the soul.
'I believe,' I said, 'that whoever teaches them aims chiefly at the soul.'
Then why? he said.
'How can that be?' he asked.
It's likely, I said, that both were established chiefly for the soul.
'Have you never noticed,' I said, 'what an exclusive devotion to physical training does to a man's character, and what the opposite, an exclusive devotion to music, does?'
How so?
'In what way?' he said.
Haven't you noticed, I said, what happens to the mind itself when a man spends his whole life on physical training and never touches music? Or when he does the opposite?
'The one breeds hardness and savagery, the other softness and weakness.'
Noticed what, exactly?
'Yes,' he said, 'I'm well aware that men who train only their bodies turn out too fierce, and those who give themselves only to music turn out softer than is good for them.'
Savagery and hardness in the one case, I said; softness and over-tameness in the other.
'And yet,' I said, 'this fierceness comes from the spirited part of a man's nature, which, rightly trained, would be courage, but stretched too tight turns hard and brutal.'
I have noticed, he said. Pure athletes come out cruder than they should be, and pure musicians softer than is good for them.
'I quite think so,' he said.
And yet the savage part is the spirited part of our nature: rightly reared, it would be courage; strained past its pitch, it hardens, as you'd expect, into brutality and bad temper.
'And gentleness belongs to the philosophic nature. Indulged too far it becomes softness, but rightly trained it's gentle and orderly.'
So it seems to me.
'True.'
And gentleness — doesn't that belong to the philosophic nature? Slacken it too far and it goes softer than it should; rear it beautifully and it stays gentle and orderly.
'And our guardians, we say, need both these natures?'
Just so.
'They do.'
Now, we say our guardians need both natures.
'And the two must be in harmony with each other?'
They do.
'Of course.'
And the two must be tuned to each other?
'And the man whose soul is in harmony is both self-controlled and brave.'
Beyond question.
'Yes.'
And where they are tuned, the soul is self-disciplined and brave?
'And the man whose soul is out of harmony is cowardly and coarse.'
Certainly.
'Very true.'
And where they aren't, it is cowardly and coarse?

'So when a man lets music play over him and pours into his soul through his ears all those sweet, soft, mournful tunes we spoke of, and spends his whole life humming and lost in song, then at first, if he had any spirit, it's tempered like iron and made useful, instead of brittle and good for nothing. But if he keeps on, never letting up, the music begins to melt him down, until it dissolves his spirit and cuts the very sinews out of his soul, and he becomes a feeble warrior.'
Very much so.
'Very true,' he said.

So: when a man hands himself over to music, and lets it pour into his soul through his ears as through a funnel — those sweet, soft, mournful modes we described a moment ago — and spends his whole life humming, besotted with song, then at first whatever spirit is in him is tempered like iron: made useful, where it had been brittle and useless. But if he keeps at it, never letting up, spellbound — after a while he begins to melt and run, until the spirit has dissolved out of him and the sinews of his soul are cut away, and he is left 'a feeble spearman.'

'If his nature was short on spirit to begin with, this happens quickly. But if he had plenty of spirit, the music weakens it and leaves him touchy, flaring up over nothing and as quickly going out, peevish and irritable instead of spirited, and impossible to deal with.'
Very true.
'Exactly.'

If he started with little spirit by nature, this happens fast. If with a lot, the music weakens his spirit until it's trigger-touchy: flaring at trifles, then guttering out just as fast. Instead of spirited, such men come out short-fused and irritable — brimming with bad temper.

'Now suppose instead a man works himself hard at exercise and eats well, but never touches music or philosophy. At first, with his body in fine condition, he's full of confidence and spirit and becomes twice the man he was.'
Exactly so.
'Certainly.'

Now the reverse: a man who works himself hard in the gym and eats like a champion, and never touches music or philosophy. At first, with his body in high condition, he fills up with confidence and spirit, and becomes braver than he was.

'But what happens next? If he does nothing else and never keeps company with the Muses, then even whatever love of learning was in him, getting no taste of any study or inquiry or argument or culture, grows feeble and deaf and blind, since nothing wakes it or feeds it or clears its senses.'
He certainly does.
'True,' he said.

But what if he does nothing else — never exchanges a word with any Muse? Whatever love of learning was in his soul gets no taste of study or inquiry, no share in reasoned talk or in the rest of music. Doesn't it grow feeble, and deaf, and blind — never wakened, never fed, its perceptions never cleared?

'And such a man ends up hating reasoned argument and uncivilized, never using persuasion to get anything, but going at everything by brute force and fierceness, like a wild beast, living in ignorance and clumsiness, with no sense of measure or grace.'
It does, he said.
'That's exactly right,' he said.

And such a man ends up hating argument, I think, with no music in him at all. He gives up persuading with words altogether and drives at everything like an animal, with violence and savagery; he lives in ignorance and clumsiness, without rhythm and without grace.

'So for these two parts of human nature, the spirited and the philosophic, some god, I'd say, has given men two arts to match them, music and physical training, and only incidentally for soul and body, so that the two parts may be tightened and slackened, like strings, until they're tuned to the proper pitch.'
That's exactly how it is.
'It does look that way,' he said.

So for these two parts of us, it seems, I would say some god gave men the two arts — music and physical training — for the spirited part and the philosophic. Not for soul and body, except incidentally, but for those two: so they could be tuned to each other, slackened and tightened until each holds its proper pitch.

'So the man who blends music and physical training in the finest proportion and applies them most measuredly to his soul, he's the one we'd rightly call truly musical and harmonious, far more than the man who merely tunes a lyre.'
So it appears.
'You're quite right, Socrates,' he said.

Then the man who blends physical training with music in the finest proportion, and brings them to bear on his soul in the truest measure — he's the one we should call the complete musician, the real master of harmony, far more than the fellow who tunes strings against each other.
'And won't we always need someone like that to preside over our city, Glaucon, if its constitution is to last?'
And with reason, Socrates, he said.
'We'll need him more than anyone.'
And won't our city always need a supervisor of that kind, if its constitution is going to survive?

'So much, then, for the patterns of upbringing and education. There's no need to go into every detail, the citizens' dances, their hunting and coursing, their athletic and equestrian contests. It's pretty clear that these follow from the principles we've laid down, and once we have the principles, working out the rest won't be hard.'
It will — as much as it needs anything.
'No, it won't be hard,' he said.

So those are the patterns of their education and upbringing. Why should we spell out their dances too, their hunts with and without hounds, their athletic games and horse races? It's fairly obvious that the details follow the patterns; finding them won't be hard anymore.
'Good,' I said. 'Then what's the next question? Isn't it which of these men are to rule and which to be ruled?'
Probably not, he said.
'It is.'
Good, I said. Then what do we settle next? Isn't it which of these same people will rule, and which be ruled?
'And clearly the older must rule the younger.'
Obviously.
'Clearly.'
Well, it's plain the rulers should be older and the ruled younger.
'And the best of the older must rule.'
Plain enough.
'That too is clear.'
And that the rulers should be the best of them.
'Now, aren't the best farmers the ones most devoted to farming?'
That too.
'Yes.'
Now, the best farmers — aren't they the ones with the most farming in them?
'So since we want the best of our guardians to rule, mustn't we pick the ones who have most the character of guardians of the city?'
Yes.
'Yes.'
Then since these must be the best of the guardians, won't they be the ones with the most guarding in them?
'And for that they need to be intelligent and capable, and to care for the city.'
Yes.
'True.'
For that, they'll need to be intelligent, and capable, and — above all — to care about the city.
'And a man cares most for what he loves.'
So they will.
'Necessarily.'
And a man cares most for what he loves.
'And he loves a thing most when he believes its interests are the same as his own, and that when it does well or badly, he does well or badly with it.'
Necessarily.
'Just so,' he said.
And he'd love most whatever he believes shares his own interests — the thing whose flourishing he takes for his own flourishing, and whose failure for his own failure.

'So we'll have to pick out, from among the guardians, the kind of men who, all their lives, show the greatest eagerness to do whatever they think is good for the city, and the greatest unwillingness to do anything against it.'
Just so, he said.
'Those are the right men,' he said.

Then we must select, out of all the guardians, the men who strike us most, over a whole lifetime of watching, as doing wholeheartedly whatever serves the city — and as refusing, under any conditions, to do what harms it.

'And we'll have to watch them at every age, to see whether they hold on to this conviction and never, under the pull of force or enchantment, forget or throw off the belief that they must do what's best for the city.'
They're the ones we want.
'What do you mean, throw off?' he said.

And I think we have to watch them at every age, to see that they guard this conviction — that no spell and no force can make them forget it, or throw overboard the belief that they must do what is best for the city.
'I'll explain,' I said. 'A belief leaves a man's mind either willingly or unwillingly: willingly when he gives up a false belief and learns better, unwillingly whenever he loses a true one.'
What do you mean, throw overboard? he said.
'The willing loss I understand,' he said, 'but not the unwilling one.'

I'll tell you, I said. It seems to me a belief leaves the mind either willingly or unwillingly: willingly, when the belief is false and the man learns better; unwillingly, whenever the belief is true.

'Well, don't you think men lose good things against their will and bad things willingly? And isn't losing the truth a bad thing, and holding it a good one? And don't you agree that to hold the truth is to think things as they really are?'
The willing kind I understand, he said. The unwilling I still need explained.
'Yes,' he said. 'I agree that men are robbed of the truth against their will.'

Really? I said. Don't you agree that men part with good things unwillingly, and with bad things willingly? And isn't being cheated of the truth a bad thing, and holding the truth a good one? Or don't you count believing things as they are as holding the truth?
'And doesn't this unwilling loss come about by theft, by force, or by enchantment?'
You're right, he said — men do lose a true belief against their will.
'Now I don't follow you again,' he said.
And when it happens, isn't it by theft, by force, or by bewitchment?

'I must be talking like a tragic poet,' I said. 'By those whose belief is stolen, I mean the ones who are talked out of it or who simply forget, argument quietly carrying it off from one set of men, time from the other. Now do you understand?'
Now I'm lost again, he said.
'Yes.'

I must be talking like a tragic chorus, I said — in riddles. By 'the robbed' I just mean men who get argued out of a belief, or who forget it: time lifts it from the one, argument from the other, and they never notice. Now do you see?
'And by those forced, I mean the ones whom some pain or grief compels to change their minds.'
Yes.
'I understand that too,' he said, 'and you're right.'
By 'the forced' I mean the ones that pain or grief drives into changing their minds.
'And the enchanted, I think you'd agree, are those who change their minds either under the gentler spell of pleasure or the harsher spell of fear.'
That I understand too, he said. You're right.
'Yes,' he said. 'Everything that deceives works a kind of enchantment.'
And 'the bewitched' — I think you'd say so yourself — are the ones who change their opinion under the sweet spell of pleasure, or the pressure of some fear.

'So, as I was saying, we have to find out who are the best guardians of their own conviction that they must always do what they judge best for the city. We'll watch them from childhood and set them tasks in which a man would be most likely to forget such a conviction or be tricked out of it, and we'll pick the one who keeps it and isn't deceived, and reject the one who fails. Does that sound right?'
Yes, he said. Everything that deceives, bewitches.
'Yes.'

So, as I was just saying, we must find out who are the best guardians of this conviction inside themselves — that at every moment they must do whatever they judge best for the city. We have to watch them from childhood on: set them the tasks in which a man is most likely to forget such a conviction or be tricked out of it, and then select the one who keeps it in memory and stays hard to deceive, and reject the one who doesn't. Agreed?
'And we'll set them labors and pains and contests too, where they'll have to show the same qualities.'
Yes.
'Quite right,' he said.
And we should set them labors and pains and contests too, and watch for the same things there.

'And then,' I said, 'we'll test them with enchantments, that's the third kind of trial, and watch how they hold up. Just as colts are taken into noise and uproar to see whether they're skittish, we'll put our young men into terrors of some kind and then into pleasures, testing them harder than gold is tested in the fire, to see whether each stands proof against every enchantment, keeps his dignity throughout, guards himself well and guards the music he's learned, and shows himself, in all of it, rhythmical and harmonious, the kind of man most useful to himself and to the city. And the one who comes through the test pure, as boy and youth and grown man, we'll make a ruler and guardian of the city, and we'll honor him alive and dead, with the finest tombs and memorials we can give. The one who fails, we'll reject. That, I think, is roughly how our rulers and guardians should be chosen and appointed, in outline, without any claim to exactness.'
Rightly so, he said.
'In outline,' he said, 'I agree with you.'

Then, I said, we must hold a third kind of trial — against bewitchment — and watch them under it. Like men who lead colts into noise and uproar to find out if they spook, we must take our guardians young into terrors, then plunge them straight into pleasures — testing them harder than gold in the fire — to see whether a man resists the spell, keeps his composure through everything, guards himself well and the music he was raised on, and bears himself with rhythm and harmony in all of it: the kind of man who would be most useful to himself and to the city. And whoever is tested as a boy, as a youth, and as a man, and comes out clean, should be made a ruler of the city and a guardian; he should be given honors while he lives and in death, receiving the greatest prizes we have in burial and remembrance. The one who doesn't come out clean, we set aside. That, Glaucon, I said, is roughly how I think rulers and guardians must be selected and installed — an outline, not the fine print.

'And perhaps it's truest to reserve the word "guardian" in its fullest sense for this higher class, the ones who protect us from enemies abroad and keep the peace among our citizens at home, so that the one group won't have the will to harm us and the other won't have the power. The younger men we were calling guardians we'd more properly call auxiliaries, the ones who support the rulers' decisions.'
I see it much the same way, he said.
'I agree,' he said.

And these men are truly what we should call guardians, in the fullest sense: guarding against enemies outside and friends inside — so that the ones will lack the will to do harm, and the others the strength. The young men we've been calling guardians until now are better named auxiliaries: enforcers of what the rulers decide.
'Now, how could we contrive one of those necessary lies we were talking about a while ago, a single noble lie that might convince even the rulers, or at least the rest of the city?'
I think so too, he said.
'What sort of lie?' he said.

Then how, I said, might we contrive one of those lies we spoke of earlier — the lies told at need? One noble lie, to persuade, in the best case, the rulers themselves; and failing that, the rest of the city?

'Nothing new,' I said. 'An old Phoenician tale, the kind of thing that has happened before in many places, so the poets say and have persuaded men to believe, though it hasn't happened in our time, and I don't know whether it could happen again, or whether anyone could even be made to believe it.'
What kind of lie? he said.
'How you hesitate to come out with it,' he said.

Nothing novel, I said — a Phoenician thing. It has happened before in many places, or so the poets say, and the world has believed them; but it hasn't happened in our time, and I doubt it could. It would take a great deal of persuading.
'You won't be surprised at my hesitation,' I said, 'once you've heard it.'
You sound like a man very reluctant to say it, he said.
'Speak,' he said, 'and don't be afraid.'
Once I've said it, I replied, you'll understand the reluctance.

'Then I'll speak, though I hardly know how to find the nerve, or the words, for so bold a fiction. I'll try to persuade first the rulers themselves, then the soldiers, and after them the rest of the city, that all the upbringing and education we gave them was a kind of dream, something they only seemed to undergo, while in reality, during all that time, they were being formed and raised deep within the earth, they themselves and their weapons and all their gear made down there. When they were finished, the earth, their mother, sent them up into the light. And so they must think of the land they live in as their mother and nurse, and defend her if anyone attacks her, and regard their fellow citizens as brothers, born of the same earth.'
Out with it, he said. Don't be afraid.
'No wonder,' he said, 'you were ashamed to come out with your lie.'

Then I'll speak — though I don't know where I'll find the nerve, or the words. I will try to persuade first the rulers themselves and the soldiers, and then the rest of the city, that all the rearing and education we gave them — everything they thought was happening to them — was a kind of dream. In truth, all that time, they were under the ground, being formed and nourished inside the earth — they, their weapons, and the rest of their gear being worked and made. When they were finished, the earth, their mother, sent them up. And so they must treat the land they live on as their mother and their nurse: defend her if anyone attacks, and plan for her good; and they must treat the other citizens as their brothers, born of the same earth.

'I had good reason,' I said. 'But there's more, so hear the rest. "You are all brothers in the city," we'll tell them in our tale, "but when the god fashioned you, he mixed gold into those of you fit to rule, which is why they're the most precious; silver into the auxiliaries; and iron and bronze into the farmers and the other craftsmen. Now, since you're all of one stock, you'll generally have children like yourselves, but sometimes a golden parent will have a silver child, or a silver parent a golden one, and so on through all the metals. So the god commands the rulers, before and above everything else, to be the finest guardians of nothing so much as the mixture of metals in their children's souls. If a child of theirs has bronze or iron in him, they must show no pity, but assign him the rank his nature deserves and push him out among the craftsmen or farmers. And if a child of those classes is born with gold or silver in him, they must honor him and raise him up to the guardians or the auxiliaries. For there's an oracle that the city will be destroyed on the day a man of iron or bronze becomes its guardian." That's the tale. Is there any way to make our citizens believe it?'
No wonder, he said, you took so long to bring yourself to tell your lie.
'No way at all,' he said, 'with these men. But their sons might believe it, and their sons' sons, and the generations after them.'

There was good reason, I said. All the same, hear the rest of the story. 'All of you in the city are brothers,' we'll tell them, telling the tale, 'but the god who formed you mixed gold into those of you fit to rule — which is why they carry the greatest honor. Into the auxiliaries he mixed silver, and iron and bronze into the farmers and the other craftsmen. Since you are all one family, you will mostly breed children like yourselves; but sometimes a golden parent will have a silver child, or a silver parent a golden one, and so on, any from any. So the god commands the rulers, first and above all, to keep watch over nothing so carefully as the children — over which metal is mixed into their souls. If their own child is born with bronze or iron in him, they must show no pity: they must assign him the honor his nature is owed, and push him out among the craftsmen or the farmers. And if a child born to those classes carries gold or silver, they must honor that, and raise the one to guard and the other to assist. For there is an oracle that the city is destroyed when a man of iron or bronze stands guard over it.' That's the story. Can you think of any device to make them believe it?

'I see the difficulty,' I said. 'Still, even that would make them care more for the city and for one another. But enough of the tale; let it fly abroad on rumor's wings. Let's arm these earthborn men of ours and lead them out under their commanders. Let them look about and pick the best spot in the city for a camp, one from which they can best keep down any rebellion within, if anyone refuses to obey, and best beat off enemies who might come down on the fold like wolves from outside. And once they've made their camp and sacrificed to the proper gods, let them see to their quarters.'
None at all, he said — not these men themselves. But their sons might, and their sons' sons, and the rest of the people who come after.
'Yes,' he said.

Even that, I said, would do some good — it would make them care more for the city and for one another. I take your point about how it might spread. But enough: let the story go wherever rumor carries it. Our job now is to arm these earth-born men and march them out with the rulers at their head. Let them come and look for the best campsite in the city — the spot from which they can best control anyone inside who refuses to obey the laws, and beat back anyone outside who comes down on the fold like a wolf. Once camped, let them sacrifice to the right gods and build their sleeping quarters. Yes?
'And these quarters must be the kind that will shield them against winter's cold and summer's heat.'
Yes, he said.
'You mean houses, I suppose,' he said.
Quarters that will keep out winter cold and summer heat, presumably.
'Yes,' I said, 'but the houses of soldiers, not of moneymakers.'
Of course, he said. You mean houses.
'What's the difference?' he asked.
Yes, I said — soldiers' houses, not businessmen's.

'I'll try to explain,' I said. 'Surely the most monstrous and shameful thing a shepherd could do would be to keep, as sheepdogs, dogs so badly disciplined, or so starved, or of such bad habits, that they'd turn on the sheep themselves and worry them like wolves instead of guarding them.'
What's the difference? he said.
'Monstrous indeed,' he said.

I'll try to tell you, I said. Surely the most dreadful and shameful thing a shepherd can do is to raise sheepdogs to help with the flock that turn — through indiscipline, or hunger, or some other bad habit — and try their teeth on the sheep themselves, behaving like wolves instead of dogs.
'So we have to take every care that our auxiliaries, being stronger than the other citizens, don't treat them like that, turning from friends and allies into savage masters.'
Dreadful, he said. Of course.
'Yes,' he said, 'great care.'
Then we must guard by every means against our auxiliaries doing that to the citizens — since they are the stronger — and becoming savage masters instead of friendly allies.
'And wouldn't a really good education be the best safeguard?'
We must.
'But they have it already,' he said.
And wouldn't the best insurance be a truly good education?

'I wouldn't be so sure, my dear Glaucon,' I said. 'I'm surer of this: that they ought to have it, and that a true education, whatever it turns out to be, has the greatest power to make them gentle and humane toward one another and toward those in their care.'
But they have that already, he said.
'Very true,' he said.

Let's not swear to that yet, dear Glaucon, I said. What we can swear to is what we were just saying: that they must have the right education, whatever it turns out to be, if they're to have the thing that matters most for being gentle with each other and with the people they guard.

'And besides their education, any man of sense would say their housing and everything else about their lives should be such as won't spoil their virtue as guardians or tempt them to prey on the other citizens.'
That's right.
'He would,' he said.

And besides the education, a thinking man would add this: their housing, and their property in general, should be set up so as never to blunt their excellence as guardians — and never to tempt them into preying on the other citizens.

'Then consider whether this is the way they must live and be housed, if they're to be the men we want. First, none of them should own any private property beyond what's absolutely necessary. None should have a house or storeroom that isn't open for anyone to enter. Their food should be the rations of disciplined warriors, self-controlled and brave, which they'll receive from the other citizens as the fixed wage of their guardianship, enough to cover the year with nothing left over. They'll dine together at common messes and live together like soldiers in camp. As for gold and silver, we'll tell them they have the divine kind always in their souls, given by the gods, and have no need of the human kind besides; that it would be sacrilege to defile their store of the divine metal by mixing it with mortal gold, since that common coin has been the cause of many unholy deeds, while their own is unalloyed. To them alone, of all the people in the city, it's forbidden to handle or touch gold or silver, to come under the same roof with it, to wear it as ornament, or to drink from cups of it. This will be their salvation, and the city's. But the moment they come to own land and houses and money of their own, they'll be householders and farmers instead of guardians, the other citizens' masters and enemies instead of their allies. They'll spend their whole lives hating and being hated, plotting and being plotted against, in far more fear of enemies within than of enemies without, themselves and the whole city racing toward ruin. For all these reasons, shall we say that this is how our guardians are to be housed and provided for, and lay it down as law?'
He'd be right.

Then consider, I said, whether something like this is the way they must live and be housed, if that is what they're to be. First: no private property, none, beyond the barest necessity. Second: no house, no storeroom, that isn't open to anyone who cares to walk in. Their food — everything men need who are athletes of war, self-disciplined and brave — they'll receive from the other citizens as a fixed wage for their guarding, measured so that a year leaves them neither surplus nor shortfall. They'll live in common, eating at shared mess tables like soldiers in camp. As for gold and silver, we'll tell them they have the divine kind from the gods, always, in their souls — they have no need of the human kind on top of it; and it would be sacrilege to pollute the divine possession by mixing it with mortal gold, because the coin of the crowd has bred many unholy deeds, and the coin inside them is clean. Alone of the city's people, they are forbidden to handle or touch gold and silver, to be under one roof with it, to wear it, or to drink from it. This is how they'd save themselves and save the city. The moment they own private land and houses and money, they'll be householders and farmers instead of guardians — hostile masters of the other citizens instead of their allies. Hating and hated, plotting and plotted against, they'll spend their whole lives far more afraid of the enemies inside the walls than of the ones outside — and by then they and the rest of the city are already racing toward destruction. For all these reasons, I said, let's say this is how the guardians must be provided for in housing and everything else, and write it into law. Shall we?
By all means, said Glaucon.
'Yes, by all means,' said Glaucon.

spine.title: Justice Found
The Virtues of the City and the Soul
spine.text: Here Adeimantus broke in with a question. Socrates, he said, how would you defend yourself if someone charged that you aren't making these men very happy — and that it's their own fault? The city really belongs to them, and they get nothing good out of it. Other men acquire land, build big beautiful houses, furnish them to match, offer their own sacrifices to the gods, entertain their guests, and own the things you just mentioned — gold and silver and everything that's supposed to come with a blessed life. Your guardians, he'd say, sit in the city like hired garrison troops, doing nothing but standing watch.

Here Adeimantus broke in with a question. 'How would you answer, Socrates,' he said, 'if someone objected that you're making these men miserable, and that it's their own fault? The city really belongs to them, and yet they get nothing out of it. Other men buy up land, build big handsome houses, fill them with fine things, offer their own sacrifices to the gods, entertain guests, and on top of that own the gold and silver and everything else that goes with what people call good fortune. But your guardians might as well be hired mercenaries posted in the city with nothing to do but stand guard.'

Yes, I said — and add this to the charge: they serve for their food alone. On top of their keep they draw no pay, the way other men do, so they can't take a trip abroad at their own expense even if they want one, can't keep a mistress, can't spend money on any of the other things that men who are counted happy spend it on. These accusations, and plenty more of the same kind, you've left out of the indictment.

'Yes,' I said, 'and you can add that they only get their keep, with no wages on top of their food the way other men have, so they can't even take a trip abroad if they wanted to, or spend on a mistress, or on any of the other luxuries that people think make for happiness. You could pile up a good many more charges of the same kind.'
Well, he said, take all of that as part of the charge.
'All right,' he said, 'let's count all of that as part of the accusation.'
And you're asking how we'll answer it, I said?
'You want to know what our answer will be?' I said.
Yes.
'Yes.'

I think we'll find the answer, I said, by staying on the road we've been traveling. Our answer is this: it would be no surprise if even these men, living as they do, were the happiest men anywhere. But in any case, we did not found this city to make one class in it outstandingly happy — we founded it to make the whole city as happy as it can be. We thought we'd find justice most surely in a city like that, and injustice most surely in the worst-run one, and that by looking at both we could settle the question we've been chasing all along. Right now we're modeling the happy city — not carving out a few people and setting them up happy inside it, but shaping the whole. We'll examine the opposite kind in due course. Suppose we were painting a statue and a man walked up and objected: why aren't you putting the most beautiful colors on the most beautiful parts? The eyes are the finest feature of the body, and you've painted them black instead of purple. We'd think it a fair reply to tell him: don't ask us, sir, to paint eyes so beautiful that they no longer look like eyes — the same for the other features. Look instead at whether, by giving each part what suits it, we're making the whole thing beautiful. So don't force us now to fasten onto the guardians the kind of happiness that would make them anything but guardians. We could do it, you know. We could dress our farmers in embroidered robes, hang gold on them, and invite them to work the land whenever the mood took them. We could stretch our potters out on couches by the fire, feasting and passing the cup, with the wheel parked at their elbow for whenever they felt like making a few pots. We could hand out that kind of blessedness to everyone, so that the whole city would be happy. Don't ask it of us — because if we listen to you, the farmer will be no farmer, the potter no potter, and no one will keep any of the shapes out of which a city is made. For most of the city it matters less. If cobblers go bad, and rot, and pretend to be cobblers when they're not, a city survives it. But when the guardians of the laws and of the city are guardians in appearance only, you can see that they destroy the whole city from the ground up — and they alone hold the key to governing it well and making it happy. We are making true guardians, then, the men least likely to harm the city. Our objector, it seems, is thinking of farmers at a fair — happy feasters at a festival, not citizens in a city. If so, he and we mean different things, and he's talking about something other than a city. So the question we have to face is this: are we planting our guardians with an eye to giving them the greatest happiness we can, or is our eye on the whole city, watching to see that happiness grows there? Because if it's the whole, then the guardians and the auxiliaries — and everyone else with them — must be pressed, and persuaded, to become the best possible workers at their own work. And with the whole city growing that way and in good order, each class can be left to take the share of happiness its nature allows.

'I think we'll find it if we keep to the road we've been on,' I said. 'Our answer will be this: it wouldn't surprise us if these men, even as they are, turned out to be the happiest of all. But that was never the point. When we founded the city, we weren't aiming to make any one class outstandingly happy. We were aiming at the greatest happiness of the city as a whole. We supposed that in a city ordered for the good of the whole we'd be most likely to find justice, and in a badly ordered one, injustice; and once we'd found them, we could decide which kind of life is the happier. Right now we're shaping the happy city, not by picking out a few people and making them happy, but as a whole. We'll look at the opposite kind of city later. Suppose we were painting a statue, and someone came up and complained, "Why don't you put the most beautiful colors on the most beautiful parts? The eyes are the finest feature, and you've painted them black instead of purple." We'd have a fair answer for him: "My friend, you wouldn't have us paint the eyes so beautifully that they stopped looking like eyes at all. Look instead at whether, by giving each part its proper color, we make the whole thing beautiful." So don't force us to give the guardians the kind of happiness that would turn them into anything but guardians. We could just as easily dress our farmers in fine robes and crowns of gold and tell them to work the land only when they felt like it; we could let our potters lie back on couches by the fire, passing the wine around, with the wheel beside them to turn whenever the mood took them. We could make every class happy that way, and then, as you imagine, the whole city would be happy. But don't put that idea into our heads. If we listened to you, the farmer would stop being a farmer, the potter would stop being a potter, and no one in the city would keep the character of his own role. With most trades it doesn't matter much. If shoemakers go soft and pretend to be what they're not, the city survives. But when the guardians of the laws and of the city only seem to be guardians and aren't, you can see how they'd bring the whole city to ruin, since they alone hold the power to govern it well and keep it happy. If we mean our guardians to be the true saviors of the city and not its destroyers, then the man who's objecting is thinking of peasants at a feast, enjoying a holiday, not of citizens doing their work in a city. So we're talking about two different things, and what he has in mind isn't a city at all. The question we have to settle, then, is whether in setting up our guardians we should aim at the greatest happiness of each of them taken alone, or whether we should look to the happiness of the city as a whole, and so compel or persuade these men, and all the others, to do their own work as well as it can be done. The whole city would then grow up in good order, and each class would get the share of happiness its nature allows.'
Well said, I think, he replied.
'I think you're quite right,' he said.
Then I wonder, I said, whether you'll also think me right about that remark's twin brother.
'I wonder whether you'll agree with something else that strikes me,' I said.
What is it?
'What's that?'
Consider whether there are two things that corrupt the rest of the workmen, until they turn bad at their work.
'It seems to me there are two things that ruin a craft.'
What two things?
'And what are they?'
Wealth, I said, and poverty.
'Wealth and poverty,' I said.
How do they do it?
'How do they ruin it?'
Like this. When a potter gets rich, do you think he'll still care about his craft?
'Like this,' I said. 'When a potter gets rich, do you suppose he'll still take the same care with his craft?'
Not at all, he said.
'Certainly not.'
He'll grow lazier and more careless by the day?
'He'll get lazier and more careless?'
Much more.
'Much.'
And so he becomes a worse potter?
'And so he'll become a worse potter?'
Yes — far worse.
'Far worse.'
And from the other side: if poverty keeps a man from buying tools or anything else his craft needs, his work will come out worse, and his sons and apprentices will learn the work worse from him.
'But on the other hand, if he's so poor he can't even afford tools and the rest of his equipment, his own work will suffer, and he'll train his sons and apprentices to work just as badly.'
Of course.
'Of course.'
So both of them — poverty and wealth — make the craftsman's work degenerate, and the craftsman with it?
'So under both, poverty and wealth, the craftsman's work declines, and so does the craftsman himself?'
Evidently.
'Plainly.'
Then we've found a second set of enemies, I said, that the guardians must watch for in every way, so they never slip into the city unseen.
'Then here's another pair of evils for the guardians to watch out for,' I said, 'and to keep from slipping into the city unnoticed.'
What enemies?
'What evils?'
Wealth, I said, and poverty. One breeds luxury, idleness, and revolution; the other breeds servility and shoddy work — and revolution all over again.
'Wealth and poverty,' I said. 'The one breeds luxury and idleness and the urge to change things; the other breeds the same urge along with meanness and bad workmanship.'
True enough, he replied. But tell me this, Socrates: how will our city be able to fight a war if it has no money laid up — especially against an enemy that is big and rich?
'True,' he said. 'But here's something I'd like to understand, Socrates. How will our city manage to make war, if it has no money, especially against a rich and powerful enemy?'
Obviously, I said, fighting one such enemy is hard. Fighting two is easier.
'It would obviously be hard,' I said, 'against a single such enemy. Against two, it's easier.'
How do you mean?
'How can that be?' he asked.
First of all, I said, if fight they must, won't they be trained men of war going up against rich men?
'In the first place,' I said, 'if it comes to a fight, won't our men be trained soldiers facing an army of rich men?'
Yes, that much is true.
'Yes, that's true,' he said.
Well then, Adeimantus — don't you think one boxer, trained to the peak of the art, could easily handle two rich, fat men who don't box?
'Well then, Adeimantus, don't you think a single boxer, in peak condition and trained in his art, could easily handle two well-fed gentlemen who don't know how to box?'
Maybe not both at once, he said.
'Not if they both rushed him at once,' he said.
Not even if he could give ground, then wheel and hit whichever one came at him first — and do it again and again, under a scorching sun? Couldn't a man like that take down more than a pair of them?

'What if he could give ground,' I said, 'and then turn and land a blow on whichever one came at him first, and do this again and again under a blazing sun? Couldn't a man like that, an expert, take down more than two of them?'
No wonder in that, he said — none at all.
'No wonder if he did,' he said.
And don't you think the rich know more of boxing, in skill and in practice, than they know of making war?
'And don't you think rich men have more skill and practice in boxing than they do in the art of war?'
I do.
'Probably,' he said.
Then in all likelihood our athletes will fight double and triple their own number with ease.
'So our athletes will be able to fight two or three times their own number.'
I'll grant you that, he said; I think you're right.
'I'll grant you that. I think you're right.'

Now suppose that before the fighting starts they send an embassy to one of the two enemy cities and tell them the plain truth: Gold and silver are no use to us — we aren't permitted to have them. But you are. Fight beside us, and take the other city's wealth for yourselves. Do you think anyone who heard that offer would choose to fight against lean, hard dogs rather than stand with the dogs against fat and tender sheep?

'And suppose, before fighting, our men sent envoys to one of the two enemy cities to tell them the simple truth: "We have no silver or gold and we're not even allowed to have any, but you are. Come fight on our side, and you can keep the spoils of the other city." Who, hearing that, would choose to fight lean, wiry dogs rather than join the dogs against fat, soft sheep?'
No, I don't. But if the wealth of the other cities piles up in one of them — watch that it doesn't become a danger to the city that has none.
'No one would,' he said. 'Still, if all that wealth got gathered into a single city, that might be dangerous for the poor one.'
What an innocent you are, I said, to think anything deserves the name city except the kind we've been founding.
'How naive of you,' I said, 'to call any of them a city but ours!'
What should I call the rest?
'What do you mean?'

Something bigger, I said. Each of them is not one city but many cities — like the joke in the board game. Whatever else it contains, every one of them holds two cities at war with each other: the city of the poor and the city of the rich. And inside each of those, many more. Approach them as one city and you'll miss everything. Approach them as many — offer one side the other side's money, power, even its people — and you will always have plenty of allies and few enemies. As long as your city keeps the sober order we've just set down, it will be the greatest of cities. I don't mean the greatest in reputation — I mean genuinely greatest, even if it can field only a thousand fighting men. One city as great as that you will not easily find, among Greeks or barbarians, though you'll find plenty that look many times its size.

'You should use the plural for the others,' I said, 'because none of them is one city. Each is many cities, like the cities on a game board. At the very least, any city, however small, is really two cities at war with each other, the city of the poor and the city of the rich, and within each of those are many more divisions. Treat them as one and you'll miss the mark completely. But treat them as many, and offer the wealth or power or people of one faction to another, and you'll always have plenty of allies and few enemies. And as long as our city holds to the wise order we've laid down, it will be the greatest of cities. I don't mean greatest in reputation, but in fact and in truth, even if its fighting men number no more than a thousand. You won't easily find a single city to match it, Greek or barbarian, though plenty look as great, and many times greater.'
Very true, he said.
'That's perfectly true,' he said.
Then wouldn't this, I said, be the best boundary-stone for our rulers — fixing how big the city should grow, and how much land to mark off for that size before they let the rest alone?
'And what,' I said, 'is the best limit for our rulers to set when they decide how large the city should be, and how much territory to take in, before they stop?'
What boundary?
'What limit would you propose?' he asked.
This one, I said: let it grow as long as growing leaves it one city — that far, and no farther.
'I'd let the city grow as far as it can without losing its unity,' I said, 'and no further. That, I think, is the right limit.'
Excellent, he said.
'Good,' he said.
So here is one more order we'll lay on the guardians: guard in every way against the city seeming small or seeming grand; let it be one city, and enough.
'So here's another order for our guardians,' I said. 'See to it that the city is neither large nor small, but one and self-sufficient.'
A light enough burden, he said, to put on them.
'That's hardly a hard order to lay on them,' he said.

Lighter still, I said, is the one we mentioned earlier — that if a child of the guardians is born inferior, he must be sent down to the other classes, and if a child of the others is born superior, he must be raised up among the guardians. The point of that was this: every citizen in the whole city is to be set to the one work nature fitted him for — one man, one work — so that each man stays one man and not many, and the whole city grows to be one city and not many.

'And here's one even lighter,' I said, 'the one I mentioned before, that if a guardian's child turns out inferior, it should be sent down to the other classes, and if a child of the lower classes turns out naturally superior, it should be raised up among the guardians. The point was that each citizen should be put to the single work that suits his nature, so that, by doing his own one thing, each man becomes one and not many, and the whole city likewise becomes one and not many.'
Yes, he said — that one is even easier.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's not so hard either.'

These orders we're giving them, my good Adeimantus, are not the long list of heavy burdens someone might imagine. They are all small things, so long as the guardians guard the one great thing, as the saying goes — though I'd rather call it not great but sufficient.

'My good Adeimantus,' I said, 'these rules we're laying down aren't, as you might think, a long list of grand principles. They're all trivial, provided we take care, as the saying goes, of the one great thing, though I'd rather not call it great, only sufficient.'
And what is that?
'And what is that?' he asked.

Education, I said, and upbringing. If our citizens are well educated and grow into reasonable men, they will see their own way through all of this easily — and through the things we're passing over for now: the marrying of wives, and marriage itself, and the getting of children — seeing that all of it should follow, as far as possible, the proverb that friends hold everything in common.

'Education and upbringing,' I said. 'If our citizens are well educated and grow into sensible men, they'll see their own way through all of this easily enough, and through everything I'm leaving out too, like marriage, and the having of wives, and the bearing of children, all of which should follow the principle that, as the proverb says, friends hold everything in common.'
Yes, he said, that would be the straightest way.
'That would be the best way to arrange it,' he said.

And once a city gets a good start, I said, it rolls on and grows like a circle. Sound upbringing and education, faithfully kept, breed good natures; and good natures, taking hold of that same education, come out better than the generation before them — better in every way, including for breeding, as with the other animals.

'And once a city gets a good start,' I said, 'it gathers momentum like a turning wheel. A good upbringing and education breed good natures, and good natures, taking in turn a good education, grow better still, in people as in the other animals.'
Likely enough, he said.
'Very likely,' he said.

To put it briefly, then: the overseers of the city must hold fast to this one thing, so that it is never corrupted behind their backs — they must guard it beyond everything else. No innovation in physical training or in music against the established order. Let them guard that order with all they have, and be afraid when they hear someone say that people praise most warmly

'So, to sum up, this is what our rulers must guard above everything: that education in music and physical training is kept from being tampered with, and not the slightest change made. They must do all they can to preserve it as it is. And when someone praises a song by saying that what people most prize is "the newest song the singers have," they should be afraid he's praising not new songs but a new kind of music, which is not what the poet meant and should not be praised. To bring in a new kind of music is to risk the whole city, and it should be forbidden. So Damon says, and I believe him: when the modes of music change, the fundamental laws of the city always change with them.'
"the newest song that hovers about the singers' lips,"
'Count me in too,' said Adeimantus, 'on the side of Damon and yourself.'

For they should be afraid that the poet will be taken to mean not new songs but a new way of singing, and that this is what gets the praise. It should not be praised, and that is not what the line means. Changing over to a new form of music is a thing to beware of as a danger to the whole — for the modes of music are never shaken anywhere without the city's greatest laws shaking with them. So Damon says, and I believe him.
'Then our guardians,' I said, 'must build the outpost of their defense here, in music.'
Count me among the convinced as well, said Adeimantus — add my vote to Damon's and yours.
'Yes,' he said, 'lawlessness slips in there all too easily.'
Then it's here in music, I said, so it seems, that the guardians must build their guard-post.
'It does,' I said, 'in the form of play, where at first it looks harmless.'
Yes, he said — lawlessness of that kind creeps in easily, without being noticed.

'And it would be harmless,' he said, 'except that little by little it settles in and quietly works its way into people's manners and habits. From there it spills, stronger now, into their dealings with one another, and from their dealings it moves on, recklessly, into the laws and the constitution, until in the end, Socrates, it overturns everything, public and private alike.'
It does, I said — dressed as play, as though it did no harm at all.
'Is that so?' I said.

And it does none, he said — except that little by little it settles in, and seeps quietly into a man's character and habits. From there it swells and spills over into his dealings with other men; and from those dealings it moves against the laws and the constitution, Socrates, with real insolence, until it ends by turning everything upside down, private life and public alike.
'I believe it,' he said.
Really, I said — it goes that far?

'Then as I was saying, our young people must be brought up from the start under a stricter discipline. For if their play becomes lawless, and they grow up lawless along with it, they can never become law-abiding, serious men.'
I think so, he replied.
'True,' he said.

Then, as we were saying at the start, our children's play must be lawful play from the very beginning — because if play turns lawless, and the children with it, there is no growing law-abiding, serious men out of them.

'But when children begin their play in the right way and take in good order through music, then, unlike the lawless children, that orderliness goes with them in everything they do, and makes them grow. And if anything in the city has fallen into decay, men like these will set it right again.'
Certainly, he said.
'Very true,' he said.

But when children begin their play right, and take good order in through their music, then order — the very opposite of what happens to those others — follows them into everything, and grows as they grow, and sets upright whatever in the city had fallen before.
'Men brought up this way,' I said, 'will rediscover for themselves even the small customs that their predecessors let drop.'
True, he said.
'Which ones do you mean?'
And so those men rediscover the rules that look small, the ones the generation before them had let die out entirely.

'Things like these,' I said. 'When the young should keep silent before their elders, how they should give up their seats and stand to show respect, how they should care for their parents, how they wear their hair and what clothes and shoes they put on, their whole bearing, and so forth. Don't you agree?'
Such as?
'I do.'

Things like this: when the young should keep silent in front of their elders; giving up your seat to them, and rising when they enter; the care owed to parents; how to wear your hair; what clothes to put on, what shoes; the whole carriage of the body — all of that. Don't you agree?
'But I think it would be foolish to make laws about such things. They never really stick that way, and no written rule about them is likely to last.'
I do.
'It couldn't,' he said.
But to legislate about them would be naive, I think. It isn't done anywhere, and no rule about such things, spoken or written down, ever holds.
'It seems, Adeimantus,' I said, 'that the direction a person is started off in by his education shapes everything that comes after. Doesn't like always call out to like?'
How could it?
'It does.'
At any rate, Adeimantus, I said, the direction a man's education launches him in is likely to decide everything that comes after. Doesn't like forever call to like?
'And it leads, I suppose, to some single decisive outcome, for good or for the opposite of good?'
Of course.
'No doubt,' he said.
Until at last, I suppose, it arrives at some single, finished, vigorous result — good, or the opposite of good.
'So for my part,' I said, 'I wouldn't try to legislate any further about these small matters.'
No denying it.
'And reasonably so,' he said.
That, I said, is why I wouldn't try to legislate any further about such things.

'Well then, what about the business of the marketplace, the ordinary dealings between one man and another, and the contracts with craftsmen, the cases of slander and assault and the filing of lawsuits, the seating of juries, and any duties that have to be paid or collected at the market or the harbor, and the regulation of markets and harbors and the city police, and all the rest of it? Should we really stoop to making laws about any of these?'
Fair enough, he replied.
'There's no need to dictate such laws to good men,' he said. 'They'll find out for themselves easily enough whatever rules are needed.'

Then what about business in the marketplace — the deals people cut with one another there, and contracts with tradesmen if you like, and slander and assault, the filing of lawsuits and the seating of juries, whatever dues need collecting or paying at the markets and the harbors, and in general the whole regulation of market, city, and port? In god's name, are we going to bring ourselves to legislate any of that?
'Yes, my friend,' I said, 'provided a god grants them the survival of the laws we've already given.'
No, he said — there's no need to dictate to good men. Most of what wants regulating they'll find for themselves easily enough.
'Otherwise,' said Adeimantus, 'they'll spend their lives endlessly passing laws and amending them, always thinking they're about to reach perfection.'
Yes, my friend, I said — provided a god grants them the safekeeping of the laws we've already laid down.
'You make them sound,' I said, 'like sick men too undisciplined to give up a way of life that's bad for them.'
And if not, said he, they'll spend their whole lives passing rules of that kind and then amending them, expecting to lay hold of what's best.
'Exactly.'
You mean, I said, they'll live like the sick men who lack the self-command to give up a rotten way of living?
'And what a charming life they lead!' I said. 'They doctor themselves and only make the trouble worse and more complicated, forever hoping that some new remedy somebody recommends will cure them.'
Exactly.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's just how it goes with that kind of invalid.'

And what a charming life those men have! Forever at the doctor's and getting nowhere — except that their illnesses grow bigger and more elaborate — and forever hoping that the next drug someone recommends will be the one that makes them well.

'And the delightful part,' I said, 'is that they treat as their worst enemy anyone who tells them the plain truth, which is that until they stop their drinking and overeating and womanizing and idleness, no drug or cautery or charm or amulet will do them any good.'
Yes, he said — that's exactly how it goes with invalids of that sort.
'There's nothing charming about it,' he said. 'There's nothing pleasant in flying into a rage at a man who tells you what's right.'

And here's another charm of theirs, I said: they treat as their worst enemy the man who tells them the truth — that until they quit the drinking and the stuffing and the whoring and the idleness, no drug will do them a bit of good, no cautery and no surgery, no charm chanted over them, no amulet, nothing of the kind.
'You don't seem to think much of these people,' I said.
Charming indeed! he said. There's nothing charming about raging at a man for telling you what's right.
'I certainly don't.'
You are no admirer, I said, it seems, of men like that.

'Then you won't praise a whole city that behaves the same way. Aren't there badly governed cities that warn their citizens, on pain of death, not to disturb the established order, and yet the man who serves that order most sweetly, who flatters and indulges and panders to it, anticipating its every whim and gratifying it, is held up as a great man and a fine statesman? Don't such cities behave just like those sick men?'
By god, no.
'They do,' he said. 'I have no praise for them at all.'

Then neither will you praise it when a whole city behaves the same way — as we just described. Isn't that exactly what the badly governed cities do? Their citizens are warned not to touch the constitution as a whole — to tamper with that is death. And meanwhile, whoever serves the city just as it is, and most sweetly — who flatters it, runs ahead of its wishes, and is clever at filling them — he is counted a good man, wise in great affairs, and the city heaps its honors on him.
'But what about the men who eagerly serve such cities? Don't you admire their nerve and their cleverness?'
Yes, he said, they act just like those invalids — and I have no praise for them whatever.
'I do,' he said, 'except for the ones the crowd's applause has fooled into thinking they're real statesmen. Those I can't admire.'
But the men who are willing, even eager, to serve such cities — don't you admire their courage, and how lightly they take it?

'What do you mean?' I said. 'Have a little sympathy. When a man can't measure, and a crowd of others who can't measure either keep telling him he's six feet tall, how is he supposed to help believing it?'
I do, he said — except for the ones the crowd's applause has fooled into believing they're statesmen in earnest.
'No,' he said, 'in that case he can't.'

What do you mean? Have you no sympathy for them? I said. When a man can't measure, and a crowd of others who can't measure either keep telling him he's six feet tall, do you think he can help believing it of himself?

'Then don't be angry with them. They're as good as a comedy, these men, with their petty reforms of the kind I was describing. They keep imagining that by passing laws they'll put an end to fraud in contracts and all the other rackets I mentioned, never realizing that they're really just lopping the heads off a hydra.'
No, he said — not that.
'That's exactly what they're doing,' he said.

Then don't be hard on them — they're the most charming of the whole breed. They pass laws about the things we just listed, and amend them, always convinced that this time they'll put a stop to cheating on contracts and the rest of what I was describing — never seeing that all the while they're only hacking heads off a Hydra.

'So I'd say the true lawmaker shouldn't bother with this class of laws and constitutional details, in a badly run city or a well-run one. In the badly run city they're useless, and in the well-run one some of them anyone can figure out, while the rest follow naturally from what we've already laid down.'
It's true, he said — that's all they're doing.
'Then what's left of the work of legislation for us?' he asked.

So I, for one, I said, wouldn't have thought the true lawgiver needs to bother with laws and government of that class at all, in a badly run city or a well-run one — in the one because it's useless and changes nothing, in the other because anyone could find some of those rules for himself, and the rest follow of their own accord from the practices already in place.
'For us, nothing,' I said. 'But for Apollo, the god at Delphi, there remain the greatest and finest and most important laws of all.'
Then what's left for us, he asked, in the way of lawgiving?
'And which are those?' he asked.
For us, I answered, nothing. But for Apollo, the god at Delphi, there remain the greatest of the laws, the finest and the first.

'The founding of temples, the sacrifices, and the whole service of the gods, the spirits, and the heroes; and likewise the burial of the dead and all the rites we owe the powers of the world below to keep them favorable. These are things we don't understand ourselves, and in founding a city we'd be unwise to trust them to any guide but our ancestral one. And this god, seated at the center of the earth, on its very navel, is the ancestral guide who interprets such things for all mankind.'
Which are those?
'Well said,' he replied. 'And that's what we'll do.'

The founding of temples, and sacrifices, and the whole service of gods, spirits, and heroes; and the burial of the dead, and the rites owed to those who dwell in the world below, if we want them gracious to us. These are things we don't understand ourselves; and in founding our city we will trust no other interpreter of them, if we have any sense, than the god of our fathers. For this god is the interpreter of such matters, by inheritance, to all mankind, and he interprets them seated at the center, on the very navel of the earth.

'So now,' I said, 'son of Ariston, our city has been founded and made fit to live in. Bring a light and search it, and call in your brother and Polemarchus and the rest, and let's see if we can spot somewhere in it where justice lies and where injustice, how they differ from each other, and which of the two the man who means to be happy must have, whether gods and men see him have it or not.'
Well said, he replied — that's what we must do.
'Nonsense,' said Glaucon. 'You promised to do the searching yourself. You said it would be an act of impiety to fail to come to justice's aid when you could.'

So there it stands, son of Ariston, I said: your city is founded. Now look inside it. Get yourself a light from somewhere and search — call in your brother and Polemarchus and the rest of them — and let's see whether we can spot where the justice in it is and where the injustice, how the two differ from each other, and which of them a man must possess if he means to be happy, whether every god and every man sees him possess it or not.
'You're right, I did say that,' I replied, 'and since you remind me, I'll keep my word. But you'll have to help.'
Nonsense, said Glaucon. You promised to do the searching yourself — you said it would be impious of you not to come to justice's rescue with everything you had, every way you could.
'We will,' he said.
So I did, I said — you're right to remind me. I'll be as good as my word. But all of you have to help.
'Then here's how I hope to find it,' I said. 'I'll start from the assumption that our city, if it's been rightly founded, is completely good.'
We will, he said.
'It must be,' he said.
Then here's how I hope to hunt it down, I said. I take it that our city — if it has been founded rightly — is completely good.
'And if it's completely good, then it's wise and brave and temperate and just.'
It has to be.
'Clearly.'
Then clearly it is wise, it is brave, it has self-command, and it is just.
'Then if we find some of these qualities in it, whatever's left over will be the one we haven't yet found?'
Clearly.
'Of course.'
So whichever of these we find in it first, won't the remainder be what's not yet found?

'Suppose there were four things in something, and we were looking for one of them. If we spotted the one we wanted first, that would settle it. But if we recognized the other three first, that would settle it too, since the one we were after would obviously be the one left over.'
Very good.
'True,' he said.

Take any four things, I said, and suppose we were hunting for one of them in something. If we spotted it first, that would be enough. But if we identified the other three first, by that alone we'd know the thing we were hunting — clearly it could only be whatever was left.
'And since the virtues we're looking for also happen to be four, don't we follow the same method?'
That's right, he said.
'Plainly.'
So with these virtues, since there are four of them, shouldn't we hunt the same way?
'Well, the first of them I think I can see in the city is wisdom, and there's something peculiar about it.'
Obviously.
'What's that?'
Well, the first of them I think I see plainly is wisdom. And there's something odd about it.
'The city we've described is called wise, I take it, because it's sound in its deliberations?'
What?
'Yes.'
The city we've described really is wise, I think — for it's sound in judgment, isn't it?
'And sound deliberation is clearly a kind of knowledge. Men deliberate well by knowledge, not by ignorance.'
True.
'Obviously.'
And sound judgment is clearly some kind of knowledge — it's by knowing, not by ignorance, that people judge well.
'But there are many different kinds of knowledge in a city.'
Clearly.
'Of course.'
Now the city holds knowledge of many different kinds.
'Is it because of the carpenters' knowledge, then, that we call the city wise and well-advised?'
Of course.
'Not at all,' he said. 'That would only make it good at carpentry.'
So is it because of its carpenters' knowledge that a city should be called wise and sound in judgment?
'So a city isn't called wise because of the knowledge that gives the best advice about wooden furniture?'
Hardly, he said — that makes it good at carpentry.
'No.'
Then it's not the knowledge that deliberates about how wooden implements can be made best, I said, that earns a city the name of wise.
'And not because of knowledge about bronze ware, or any knowledge of that sort?'
No, certainly not.
'None of those,' he said.
Nor knowledge about vessels of bronze, nor anything else of that sort?
'And not because of the knowledge of how to grow crops from the soil? That would only make it good at farming.'
Nothing of that sort, he said.
'I think so.'
Nor the knowledge of raising crops from the soil — for that, a city gets called good at farming.

'Well then,' I said, 'is there some knowledge, in this city we've just founded, possessed by some of its citizens, that advises not about any one particular thing in the city but about the city as a whole, how it should best conduct itself toward itself and toward other cities?'
So I'd say.
'There certainly is.'

Then is there, I said, in this city we've just founded, a knowledge held by some of its citizens that deliberates not about any one thing in the city, but about the city as a whole — what course is best for it, within itself and toward other cities?
'And what is that knowledge,' I asked, 'and who has it?'
There is.
'It's the knowledge of the guardians,' he said, 'found in those we called the perfect guardians.'
What is it, I said, and where does it live?
'And what name do we give the city because it has this knowledge?'
It's the guardians' knowledge, he replied, and it lives in those rulers we were just now calling the perfect guardians.
'Sound in counsel,' he said, 'and truly wise.'
And what do you call the city on account of that knowledge?
'And do you think there'll be more of these true guardians in our city, or more metalworkers?'
Sound in judgment, he said, and truly wise.
'Far more metalworkers,' he said.
Now which do you think our city will hold more of, I said — smiths, or these true guardians?
'And of all the groups that get a name from the kind of knowledge they have, won't the guardians be the smallest of all?'
Smiths, he said — far more.
'Much the smallest.'
Of all the groups who take a name from the knowledge they hold, wouldn't the guardians be the smallest?

'So it's because of the smallest part of itself, and the knowledge in the part that presides and rules, that the whole city, founded according to nature, is wise. And this part, which alone has the knowledge that deserves to be called wisdom, is by nature the smallest of all.'
By a wide margin.
'Perfectly true,' he said.

Then it's from its smallest class and part — from the knowledge living in the part that presides and rules — that a whole city founded according to nature is wise. And this class, it seems, whose portion is the one knowledge that of all knowledges deserves the name wisdom, is by nature the smallest class there is.
'So there it is. One of the four, somehow or other, we've found, both what it is and where in the city it sits.'
Very true, he said.
'And found it well enough to satisfy me,' he said.
So here — though how, I can't say — we've found one of our four, both the thing itself and the seat it occupies in the city.
'Now courage,' I said, 'is no harder to make out, both the quality itself and the part of the city in which it sits and gives the city its name.'
Found well enough for me, he replied.
'How do you mean?'
And courage next — the thing itself, and the part of the city it lives in, the part that gets the whole city called brave — isn't very hard to see.
'Anyone who calls a city brave or cowardly,' I said, 'will be thinking of the part that fights and goes to war on the city's behalf.'
Why not?
'No one,' he said, 'would think of anyone else.'
Who would call a city cowardly or brave, I said, by looking at any part of it except the part that defends it and takes the field on its behalf?
'I'd say the rest of the citizens can be as brave or as cowardly as you like, and it won't make the city itself one or the other.'
No one, he said, would look anywhere else.
'No.'
Because the rest of the people in it, I take it, could be cowards or brave men without the city being the one thing or the other on their account.
