'A city is brave, then, by a part of itself, the part that holds onto, through everything, the right belief about what is to be feared and what isn't, the belief the lawmaker instilled in their education. That, I take it, is what you call courage.'
They could.
'I'd like to hear that again,' he said. 'I don't think I quite followed.'

So a city is brave, too, by a part of itself — because in that part it has a power that will preserve, through everything, its judgment about what is to be feared: that the fearful things are exactly those things, and of exactly that kind, which the lawgiver declared them to be in the education. Isn't that what you call courage?
'I'm saying that courage is a kind of preservation,' I said.
I didn't quite follow, he said. Say it once more.
'Preservation of what?'
I mean, I said, that courage is a kind of preserving.

'Of the belief, planted by the law through education, about what things are to be feared and what their nature is. And by saying "through everything" I mean holding onto that belief and never letting go of it, whether under the pull of pleasure or pain, of desire or fear. Shall I give you a comparison?'
A preserving of what?
'Please.'

Of the judgment, bred by law through education, about what is to be feared — what things they are, and of what kind. And by preserving it 'through everything' I meant holding onto it in pain and in pleasure, in desire and in fear, and never throwing it away. I'll give you a picture of it, if you like.

'You know how dyers work,' I said. 'When they want to dye wool a true sea-purple, they first pick out the white wool from all the rest, then prepare and treat it with great care so it will take the dye in full, and only then dip it. Whatever is dyed that way takes a fast color, and no washing, with or without soap, can strip the brightness out of it. But if the wool isn't prepared first, you know what happens, whether they use purple or any other color.'
Please.
'Yes,' he said, 'it comes out washed-out and ridiculous.'

You know, I said, that when dyers want to dye wool that true sea-purple, they begin by choosing, out of all the colors of wool, the one natural ground — the white. Then they prepare it, working it over with no small preparation, so that it will take the color at its fullest bloom. Only then does the dyeing begin. Wool dyed that way holds fast; no washing, with soap or without it, can strip the bloom out of it. Done the other way — well, you know what it looks like, whether it's purple or anything else laid onto an unprepared ground.

'Then you'll see what we were trying to do when we chose our soldiers and trained them in music and physical exercise. We were working out how to get them to take the dye of the laws as thoroughly as possible, so that their belief about what to fear, and every other belief, would be fixed fast by their upbringing and training, and no soap, no matter how strong, would wash it out, not pleasure, which is a more powerful solvent of the soul than any soda or lye, and not pain or fear or desire either, the strongest solvents of all. This power to hold onto, through everything, the right and lawful belief about what is and isn't to be feared, this is what I call courage, unless you object.'
I do, he said — washed-out, and ridiculous.
'I don't object,' he said. 'I take it you mean to exclude the raw, untaught courage of a wild animal or a slave. That, in your view, isn't lawful courage and ought to have some other name.'

Then understand, I said, that we were doing the very same thing, as best we could, when we chose our soldiers and educated them in music and physical training. Don't imagine we designed all that for anything else but this: that, persuaded, they should take the laws into themselves the way wool takes dye, so that their judgment about what's to be feared — and about everything else — would be fixed fast in them, nature and rearing having both been right, and so that no solvent could scour the dye out: not pleasure, which works at that harder than any potash or lye, and not pain, fear, or craving, which outscour every soap there is. This power, then — the preserving, through everything, of right and lawful judgment about what is and is not to be feared — is what I call courage, and I'll stand by it unless you say otherwise.
'Exactly right,' I said.

I say nothing against it, he replied. For I take it that when right opinion about these same things arises without education — in an animal, say, or a slave — you don't count it truly lawful at all, and you'd call it something other than courage.
'Then I accept that this is courage.'
Exactly right, I said.

'Accept it,' I said, 'at least as the courage of a citizen, and you won't be far wrong. We'll come back to it later and go into it more fully if you like, but for now we're after justice, not courage, and we've said enough for that.'
Then I accept this as your account of courage.
'Fair enough,' he said.

Accept it as an account of civic courage, I said, and you'll accept rightly. We'll go through it more fully another time, if you like. Right now the hunt is for justice, not courage, and for that purpose I think we've said enough.
'Two virtues are left to find in the city,' I said, 'temperance, and then justice, which is the whole point of our search.'
Well said, he replied.
'True.'
That leaves two things, I said, still to be seen in the city: self-command, and then the one for whose sake we've been searching through all the rest — justice.
'Now, could we somehow get to justice without bothering with temperance?'
Yes, exactly.
'I don't see how,' he said, 'and I wouldn't want justice brought to light at the cost of leaving temperance in the dark. So please, do me the favor of taking up temperance first.'
Is there any way we could find justice and spare ourselves the trouble of self-command?
'I could hardly refuse you,' I said.
I don't know one, he said — and I wouldn't want justice to show itself first if it means losing sight of self-command. If you want to please me, look into self-command before the other.
'Then go ahead,' he said.
Of course I'm willing, I said. I'd be wrong not to be.
'I will,' I said. 'And as far as I can see at this point, temperance is more like a harmony, a tuning, than the two before it.'
Then look into it, he said.
'How so?' he asked.
I will, I said. And seen from where we stand now, it's more like a concord, a harmony, than the two that came before it.

'Temperance,' I said, 'is a kind of order and a mastery over certain pleasures and desires. People hint at this when they call a man, in that odd phrase, "master of himself," and there are other traces of the same idea scattered through the way we talk.'
How so?
'No doubt,' he said.

Self-command is a kind of good order, I said — a mastery over certain pleasures and appetites. That's what people are pointing at when they say a man is 'stronger than himself,' an odd expression, I admit; and other sayings of the kind are tracks of the same thing. Aren't they?

'But isn't "master of himself" a ridiculous phrase? If he's master of himself, then he's also slave to himself, and if he's slave to himself, master of himself, since it's the same man we're talking about throughout.'
Certainly.
'Of course.'

But 'stronger than himself' is absurd on its face. A man who's stronger than himself is also, presumably, weaker than himself, and the weaker one is the stronger — it's the same man being talked about the whole time.

'What the phrase means, I think, is that within the same person, in his soul, there's a better part and a worse part, and when the part that's naturally better controls the worse, we say the man is master of himself, as a kind of praise. But when, through a bad upbringing or bad company, the better part, which is also the smaller, is swamped by the larger mass of the worse, then we reproach the man and call him a slave to himself and undisciplined.'
Of course it is.
'And rightly,' he said.

What the phrase means, I think, is this: in the man himself — in his soul — there is a better part and a worse part; and when the naturally better part holds the worse in hand, that is what 'stronger than himself' points to. It's praise. But when bad rearing, or bad company, leaves the better part small and overrun by the sheer mass of the worse — that draws blame and reproach. A man in that state is called weaker than himself, a slave of himself, a man without restraint.

'Now look at our newly founded city,' I said, 'and you'll find one of these two conditions in it. You'll agree it can fairly be called master of itself, if a thing in which the better part rules the worse deserves to be called temperate and master of itself.'
That sounds right.
'I'm looking,' he said, 'and what you say is true.'

Now look at our young city, and you'll find one of those two conditions in it. You'll admit the city deserves to be called master of itself — if a thing in which the better rules the worse deserves to be called self-commanded, and master of itself.
'And the many complicated pleasures and pains and desires you'll find mostly in children and women and slaves, and in the great majority of so-called free men, the lowest sort.'
I'm looking, he said, and what you say is true.
'Certainly.'

Notice, too, that desires of every shape and number — and the pleasures and pains that ride with them — turn up mostly in children, in women, in household servants, and, among the so-called free, in the many of the common sort.
'While the simple, moderate desires, the ones guided by reasoning and by right belief and intelligence, you'll find in only a few, those born with the best natures and given the best education.'
Certainly.
'True.'
While the simple and measured desires — the ones that go where reasoning leads, guided by intelligence and right opinion — you'll meet in few people: the ones born best and educated best.
'And don't you see both of these in our city, with the desires of the worse and more numerous part held in check by the desires and the wisdom of the better and fewer?'
True.
'I do,' he said.
And you can see both of these in our city — where the desires of the common many are mastered by the desires, and the wisdom, of the decent few.
'So if any city deserves to be called master of its own pleasures and desires, and master of itself, ours does.'
I can.
'It does indeed,' he said.
So if any city deserves to be called master of its pleasures and appetites — master of itself — this one does.
'And temperate too, for the same reasons?'
Absolutely.
'Yes.'
And self-commanded too, on all these counts?
'And if there's any city in which the rulers and the ruled agree about who should rule, it's ours.'
Yes, very much.
'Beyond a doubt.'
Then again: if there's any city where the rulers and the ruled hold the same conviction about who ought to rule, it's this one. Don't you think?
'And with the citizens in such agreement, in which group will temperance reside, the rulers or the ruled?'
Without question.
'In both, I'd say,' he replied.
And when the citizens agree like that, where would you say the self-command lives — in the rulers, or in the ruled?
'You see we weren't far off,' I said, 'when we guessed temperance was a kind of harmony.'
In both, I suppose, he said.
'How do you mean?'
You see? I said. Our hunch just now was a good one — that self-command is like a kind of harmony.

'Because, unlike courage and wisdom, each of which sat in one part of the city and made it brave or wise, temperance isn't like that. It stretches across the whole, making the weakest and the strongest and those in between all sing the same note, whether you rank them by intelligence, or strength, or numbers, or wealth, or anything else. So we'd be quite right to call temperance this agreement, this harmony between the naturally worse and the naturally better about which of them should rule, in a city or in a single man.'
How so?
'I agree completely,' he said.

Because it doesn't work the way courage and wisdom do. Each of those lives in one part, and yet the one makes the whole city wise and the other makes it brave. Self-command isn't like that. It's strung through the whole city, straight through the octave, and it sets the weakest and the strongest and those in the middle all singing the same song — weakest and strongest in judgment, if you like, or in muscle, or in numbers or money or whatever you please. So we'd be exactly right to say that self-command is this unison: a concord between the naturally worse and the naturally better about which of the two should rule — in a city, and in each single person.
'Good,' I said. 'So three of the four are in view in our city. What's the last kind, the one that makes a city good? Clearly it must be justice.'
I entirely agree.
'Clearly.'
Good, I said. Three of them are now sighted in our city — as far as this kind of judgment goes. So what would the last form be, the one still needed to make the city good? Justice, clearly.

'So now, Glaucon, like hunters, we have to surround the thicket and keep a sharp watch so justice doesn't slip away and vanish on us. She's in here somewhere, no doubt about it. So look hard, strain to catch sight of her, and if you spot her first, give me the word.'
Clearly.
'I wish I could,' he said. 'But really you should treat me as a follower, someone with just enough sight to make out whatever you point to. That's about all I'm good for.'

Now, Glaucon — now we do like hunters ringing a thicket. Close in and keep your eyes open, so that justice doesn't slip out somewhere and vanish and get clean away. She's here somewhere; that much is plain. Look hard — and if you catch sight of her before I do, sing out.
'Then say a prayer with me,' I said, 'and follow.'
I wish I could, he said. What I'm really good for is following — a man with eyes just sharp enough to see what he's shown. Take me for that, and you have me right.
'I will,' he said, 'only lead the way.'
Then follow, I said, and pray with me as we go.
'There's no path here,' I said, 'and the wood is dark and hard to see through. Still, we have to push on.'
I will, he said — just lead.
'Then let's push on,' he said.
The ground here looks bad, I said — thick shade, hard going. Dark, and not easy to beat through. But on we go all the same.
And just then I caught something. 'Look!' I cried. 'I think I see a track. I believe the quarry won't get away from us after all.'
On we go.
'Good news,' he said.
And then I saw something. Aha, Glaucon! I called out. I think we have a track — I don't believe she's going to get away from us after all.
'We really are slow-witted,' I said.
Good news, he said.
'How so?'
Honestly, I said, what a pair of fools we've been.

'My good man, it's been right under our feet from the start, ages ago, tumbling about there in front of us, and we never saw it. Nothing could be more absurd. It's like people hunting all over for something they're already holding in their hand. We kept staring off into the distance instead of at the thing in front of us, and that's probably how we missed it.'
How so?
'What do you mean?' he said.

All this time, my friend — from the very beginning — the thing has been rolling around in front of our feet, and we never saw it. We've been completely ridiculous. You know how people sometimes hunt for the very thing they're holding? That was us. We never looked at it. We kept peering off into the distance — which is probably exactly how we missed it.
'I mean that all this time, I think, we've been talking about justice and saying what it is without realizing that's what we were doing.'
What do you mean?
'I'm getting impatient with this long preamble,' he said.
I mean, I said, that I think we've been saying it, and hearing it said, all along — without ever grasping that in a way we were the ones saying it.

'Then tell me whether I'm right,' I said. 'You remember the principle we kept coming back to from the very founding of the city, that each man should do the one thing his nature best suits him for. Well, justice is that principle, or a part of it.'
A long prelude, he said, for a man who's eager to hear the song.
'Yes, we kept saying each man should do one thing.'

Then listen, I said, and see whether there's anything in it. The thing we laid down at the very start, when we were founding the city — the rule everything else had to follow — that, I think, or some form of it, is justice. And what we laid down, and repeated again and again if you remember, was that each one man should practice one occupation in the city: the one his own nature is best suited for.
'And we said, again and again, that justice is doing one's own work and not meddling in other people's. Plenty of others have said the same.'
Yes, we said that.
'We did say that.'
And that doing your own work, and not meddling in another's, is justice — that we've heard from plenty of other people, and said ourselves, over and over.
'Then it seems, my friend, that doing one's own work, in a certain way, is justice. Do you know what makes me think so?'
We have.
'No, tell me.'
Then this, my friend, I said — done in a certain way — is likely to be what justice is: doing your own work. Do you know where I get my evidence?

'I think it's because this is the one thing left over in the city once we've set aside the others we examined, temperance, courage, and wisdom. It's what made all of those possible in the first place, and once they're there it keeps them safe as long as it stays in them. And we did say that if we found the other three, justice would be the one remaining.'
No — tell me.
'That follows of necessity,' he said.

This, I think, is what's left over in the city after the ones we've already examined — self-command, courage, and wisdom: the thing that gave all three of them the power to arise in it, and that keeps them safe, once arisen, for as long as it remains. And we said that whatever was left, once we'd found the other three, would be justice.

'Now, if we had to decide which of these four does most, by being present, to make the city good, it wouldn't be easy. Is it the agreement of rulers and ruled? Or the soldiers' preservation of the lawful belief about what's truly to be feared? Or the wisdom and watchfulness in the rulers? Or is it this other thing, present in child and woman, slave and free, craftsman, ruler, and ruled, the doing of one's own single work and not meddling? Which deserves the prize? It's hard to say.'
It would have to be.
'It is,' he said.

And suppose we had to judge, I said, which of these does our city the most good by being in it. It would be a hard call. Is it the agreement of rulers and ruled? Or the soldiers' keeping, unbroken, of lawful judgment about what is and is not to be feared? Or the wisdom and watchfulness of the rulers? Or is the city's greatest good this — found in child and woman, in slave and free man and craftsman, in ruler and ruled alike — that each of them, being one person, did his own work and didn't meddle in anyone else's?
'So this power, each man in the city doing his own work, seems to compete with the other three virtues, wisdom and temperance and courage, for making the city good.'
A hard call, he agreed — no question.
'It does,' he said.
So as a power making a city good, it seems, each person doing his own work goes head to head with the city's wisdom, its self-command, and its courage.
'And we'd call this competing virtue justice?'
It certainly does.
'Exactly.'
And the rival of those three in making a city good — wouldn't you name that justice?
'Look at it another way, and see if you agree. Won't you assign your rulers the job of judging lawsuits?'
Absolutely.
'Of course.'
Now look at it from this side too, and see if you agree. It's the rulers you'll assign to try the city's lawsuits, isn't it?
'And when they judge, what will they aim at but this, that no one take what belongs to another or be deprived of his own?'
Certainly.
'Yes, that's the principle.'
And when they judge, will they aim at anything more than this — that no man have what belongs to another, and no man be stripped of what is his own?
'Because that's just?'
No — that's exactly what they'll aim at.
'Yes.'
Because it's just?
'So on this view too, justice turns out to be the having and doing of what is one's own and belongs to one.'
Yes.
'That's right.'
So from this angle too, justice would be agreed to be the having and the doing of what is one's own — of what properly belongs to you.

'Now see whether you agree with this. Suppose a carpenter set about doing the shoemaker's work, or the shoemaker the carpenter's, and they swapped their tools and their jobs, or suppose one man tried to do both at once. Would the city take much harm from that?'
That's so.
'Not much,' he said.

Now see whether you agree with me on this. Suppose a carpenter tries his hand at a cobbler's work, or a cobbler at a carpenter's — they trade tools, they trade standing, or one man takes on both trades, and swap whatever else you please. Do you think that does the city much harm?

'But suppose a man who's a craftsman by nature, or some other money-maker, gets puffed up by his wealth or his strength or the number of his supporters, and tries to force his way into the soldier class, or a soldier into the class of the rulers and guardians when he isn't fit for it, and they trade their tools and their jobs around; or suppose one man tries to do all of these at once. I think you'll agree that this swapping and meddling among the three classes is the ruin of the city.'
Not much.
'Absolutely.'

But when a man nature meant for a craftsman or some other kind of money-maker gets puffed up — on wealth, or a following, or muscle, or anything else of the sort — and pushes his way into the warriors' class; or a warrior pushes into the class of counselors and guardians without being worthy of it; when these men trade tools and standing between them, or when one man grabs at all of it at once — then I think you'll agree with me that this swapping and this meddling is the destruction of the city.
'So the meddling and exchange among these three classes is the greatest harm to the city, and we'd be most justified in calling it the worst of crimes against it.'
It is — absolutely.
'Just so.'
So with three classes in the city, meddling and switching from one into another is the greatest injury to it, and could most rightly be called the worst kind of wrongdoing.
'And the worst crime against one's own city, wouldn't you call that injustice?'
Precisely.
'Of course.'
And the worst wrongdoing against your own city — won't you call that injustice?
'So this is injustice. And turn it around: when the money-making class, the soldiers, and the guardians each do their own work in the city, that is justice, and it makes the city just.'
Of course.
'I'd say that's exactly so,' he said.

That, then, is injustice. Now say it the other way around: when the money-making class, the auxiliaries, and the guardians each keep to their own work — each doing its own in the city — that is justice, and that is what makes the city just.

'Let's not be too sure just yet,' I said. 'If this idea of justice holds good when we apply it to the individual man as well as the city, we'll grant it; there'll be nothing more to say. But if it doesn't fit the individual, we'll have to look again. First, let's finish what we set out to do. We took it that if we examined justice on the larger scale first, in something bigger that has it, we'd find it easier to make out in the single man. The city seemed to be that larger thing, so we built the best one we could, sure that justice would be found in a good city. Now let's carry over what we found there to the individual. If it matches, good. If the individual shows us something different, we'll go back to the city and test the idea again. Maybe, by rubbing the two cases together like fire-sticks, we'll make justice flash out, and once we've seen it we can fix it firmly in our minds.'
I see it exactly that way, he said.
'That's the right way to go about it,' he said. 'Let's do as you say.'

Let's not set it in stone quite yet, I said. If this same form, carried into each single human being, is agreed to be justice there too, then we'll concede the point — what more could we say? If not, we'll look elsewhere. For now let's finish the inquiry we began with this thought: that if we first tried to watch justice in something larger that contains it, it would be easier to see what it is in one man. The larger thing, we agreed, was a city, so we founded the best city we could, knowing well that justice would be in a good one. Now let's carry what showed itself there back down to the individual. If it agrees, all is well. If something different turns up in the individual, we'll go back to the city and test again — and maybe, examining the two side by side and rubbing them against each other like fire-sticks, we can make justice flash out; and once it has shown itself, we'll fix it firm in ourselves.
'Now,' I said, 'when you call two things by the same name, one larger and one smaller, are they alike or unlike in respect of the thing the name refers to?'
That's the right road, he said. Let's take it.
'Alike,' he said.
Well then, I said: when a bigger thing and a smaller thing are called by the same name, are they unlike in the respect the name fits them, or alike?
'So the just man, in respect of justice itself, won't differ at all from the just city; he'll be like it.'
Alike, he said.
'He will,' he said.
So a just man, in respect of the very form of justice, will be no different from a just city — he'll be like it.

'And we decided a city is just when each of its three kinds of nature does its own work, and that it's temperate and brave and wise because of certain other conditions and states of those same three.'
He will.
'True.'

Now, the city seemed to us just when each of the three kinds of natures in it did its own work; and self-commanded, and brave, and wise, through certain other conditions and habits of those same three kinds.
'So we'll expect the individual to have these same three kinds in his soul, and to deserve the same names as the city because he's in the same conditions as it is.'
True.
'That must be so,' he said.
Then, my friend, we'll expect the same of the individual: that he has these same three forms in his own soul, and that the same conditions in them rightly earn him the same names we gave the city.
'Once again, then, my friend, we've stumbled into an easy little question about the soul, whether it has these three kinds in it or not.'
It has to follow.
'It doesn't look so easy to me,' he said. 'But maybe the proverb's right, Socrates, that fine things are hard.'
Well, here's another trivial little question we've tumbled into, I said: does the soul have these three forms in it, or not?

'Apparently,' I said. 'And I'll tell you frankly, Glaucon, that in my opinion we'll never get a precise answer to this by the methods we've been using. The road that leads there is another and a longer one. Still, we may reach an answer that's up to the standard of what we've already said.'
It doesn't look so trivial to me, he said. But maybe, Socrates, the old saying is true: fine things are hard.
'Won't that do?' he said. 'For now it would satisfy me.'

So it seems, I said. And I'll tell you plainly, Glaucon: in my judgment we will never grasp this precisely by the kinds of methods we're using in the argument now. There is another road to it, longer and larger. Still, we can perhaps reach an answer worthy of what we've said and examined so far.
'And me,' I said.
Isn't that enough, then? he said. For me, for the present, it would do.
'Then don't give up,' he said. 'Press on with the inquiry.'
And it will more than do for me, I said.

'Well,' I said, 'we have to admit, don't we, that each of us has in himself the very same kinds and characters that are in the city? Where else could the city have got them from? It would be absurd to think that the spirited, high-tempered quality came to be in a city from any source but the individuals who have it, the people we credit with it, the Thracians and Scythians and the northern peoples generally. Or take the love of learning, which one might especially credit to our part of the world, or the love of money, which you could fairly attribute to the Phoenicians and the Egyptians.'
Then don't flag, he said — go on and look.
'Exactly,' he said.

Well, isn't it strictly necessary, I said, to admit that the same forms and habits that are in the city live in each of us? They certainly didn't arrive there from anywhere else. It would be laughable if someone imagined that the spirited element in cities didn't come from the individual citizens who bear that reputation — the peoples of Thrace and Scythia, say, and generally of the north; or the love of learning, which you'd credit chiefly to our own part of the world; or the love of money, which you'd say is found not least among the Phoenicians and the people of Egypt.
'So this much is plain enough,' I said.
Quite so, he said.
'Quite plain.'
That's how it stands, then, I said, and there's nothing hard in knowing it.

'But here's where it gets harder. Do we do each of these with the same part of ourselves, or with three different parts? Do we learn with one part, get angry with another, and with a third desire the pleasures of food and sex and the like, or do we do each of these with the whole soul? That's what's hard to settle.'
No, nothing.
'I agree,' he said. 'That's the difficulty.'

But here's what is hard: do we do each of these things with the same one thing in us, or are there three, and we do a different thing with each — learn with one, grow angry with another part of ourselves, and with some third crave the pleasures of food and sex and everything of their family? Or is it the whole soul acting, all of it, in every one of them, once we've set ourselves going? That is what will be hard to mark off in any way worthy of the argument.
'Then let's try this way to decide whether they're the same or different.'
I think so too, he said.
'How?' he asked.
Then let's try to draw the line this way — to see whether these things are the same as each other or different.

'It's clear,' I said, 'that the same thing can't do or undergo opposite things in the same respect and in relation to the same thing at the same time. So if we find that happening here, we'll know we're dealing not with one thing but with more than one.'
How?
'All right.'

Clearly the same thing will not consent to do or undergo opposites in the same respect, in relation to the same thing, at the same time. So if we ever find that happening in these elements of ours, we'll know we were dealing not with one thing but with several.
'Take this case. Can the same thing be at rest and in motion at the same time, in the same part of itself?'
All right.
'Of course not.'
Then consider what I ask: can the same thing, in the same respect, be standing still and moving at the same time?

'Let's be even more precise, so we don't fall out over words later. If someone said of a man who's standing still but moving his hands and his head that the same man is both at rest and in motion at once, we wouldn't accept that way of speaking. We'd say one part of him is at rest and another in motion.'
No way.
'True.'

Let's agree on it more precisely still, so we don't fall to quarreling later. Suppose someone said of a man standing still, but moving his hands and his head, that the same man is at rest and in motion at once. We wouldn't accept that way of putting it, I think. We'd say that one part of him is at rest and another part moving. Isn't that right?

'And if our objector got cleverer still and pointed out that a spinning top, whirling with its point fixed in one spot, is at rest and in motion as a whole at the same time, and said the same of anything that turns in place, we wouldn't accept it, because such things aren't at rest and in motion in the same part of themselves. We'd say they have an axis and a circumference; with respect to the axis they're at rest, since they don't lean off it, and with respect to the circumference they're moving. But if the axis itself tips to the right or left, forward or back, while it spins, then it's not at rest in any respect.'
It is.
'And we'd be right to say so,' he replied.

And suppose our objector turned wittier still and refined the point: tops, he says, stand still and move as wholes, whenever they spin with the peg planted in one spot — and so does anything else that circles in place. We wouldn't take it — because in those cases it is not in respect of the same parts of themselves that the things stand and turn. We'd say each has an axis in it and a circumference: in respect of the axis it stands still, since it leans to no side, and in respect of the circumference it goes round and round. But if the upright tilts right or left, forward or back, while the thing spins, then it isn't standing still in any way at all.
'So no objection of that kind will throw us off or persuade us that one and the same thing could ever, in the same respect and toward the same thing, at the same time, do or undergo opposites.'
That's correct, he said.
'It won't, not as far as I'm concerned,' he said.

Then no objection of that kind will scare us, or come any nearer to persuading us that anything, while remaining the same thing, could ever undergo, or be, or do opposites at the same time, in the same respect, toward the same thing.

'Still,' I said, 'so we don't have to wade through every such objection and prove each one false, let's assume this principle is sound and go ahead, agreeing that if it ever turns out to be false, everything we build on it falls with it.'
It won't persuade me, at least, he said.
'That's the best way,' he said.

All the same, I said, to spare ourselves the tedium of walking through every such quibble and proving each one false, let's assume this is so and push on — with the understanding that if it ever looks otherwise to us, everything we've concluded from it comes undone.

'Now then,' I said, 'wouldn't you put nodding yes and shaking the head no, reaching for something and pushing it away, drawing toward and thrusting off, all in the class of opposites, whether they're things you do or things done to you? That makes no difference to their being opposites.'
Yes, he said, that's what to do.
'Yes,' he said, 'they're opposites.'

Now then, I said: nodding yes and shaking no; reaching for a thing and refusing it; drawing it toward you and pushing it away — wouldn't you set all these down as opposites to one another, whether they count as doings or as undergoings? For that makes no difference here.

'And what about thirst and hunger, and the desires generally, and willing and wishing? Wouldn't you put all of those somewhere among the things we just mentioned? Wouldn't you say the soul of a man who desires is reaching for the thing it desires, drawing toward itself what it wants to have, or that, insofar as it wills something to be given to it, it nods yes to itself, longing for that, as if someone had asked it a question?'
Yes, he said — opposites.
'I would.'

And thirst, I said, and hunger, and the appetites generally — and again willing and wishing — wouldn't you place all of these somewhere in the classes we just named? Won't you say, for instance, that the soul of a man in desire either reaches for what it desires or draws toward itself what it wants to have; or again that, insofar as it wills that something be handed to it, it nods assent to itself, as though someone had asked it a question, straining toward the getting of the thing?
'And not-willing, refusing, not desiring, wouldn't we put those with the soul's pushing away and thrusting off, the opposite class?'
I would.
'Of course.'
And what of not-wanting, not-wishing, not-desiring? Won't we put those with the soul's pushing-away and driving-off — with all the opposites of the first class?
'That being so, let's say there's a class of desires, and the clearest of them are the ones we call thirst and hunger.'
Of course.
'Let's say so,' he said.
That being so, shall we say there is a class of the appetites, and that the sharpest examples in it are the two we call thirst and hunger?
'And one of these is for drink, the other for food?'
Let's say it, he said.
'Yes.'
One of them is desire for food, the other for drink?

'Now, insofar as it's thirst, is it a desire in the soul for anything more than what we said, for drink? Is thirst, just as thirst, a thirst for hot drink or cold, for much or little, for any particular kind of drink at all? Or is it that if heat goes along with the thirst, that adds the desire for something cold, and if cold, for something hot; and if the thirst is great because of some added largeness, the desire is for much, and if small, for little? But thirst itself will never be a desire for anything but its natural object, drink, just as hunger is for food.'
Yes.
'That's right,' he said. 'Each desire, in itself, is just for its own natural object, and the desire for a particular kind of thing comes from something added on.'

Then here's the point. Insofar as it is thirst, is it a desire in the soul for anything more than that? Is thirst, as thirst, a thirst for hot drink or cold, for much drink or little — in a word, for drink of any particular kind? Isn't it rather that if heat is present along with the thirst, it adds on the desire for something cold, and if cold is present, for something hot; and if the thirst is great, the drink desired will be much, and if slight, little — but thirst by itself will never be a desire for anything but its natural object, drink by itself, as hunger is for food?

'Let's be careful here,' I said, 'so that no one catches us off guard with the objection that no one desires drink as such, but good drink, or food as such, but good food, since everyone desires good things, and so, thirst being a desire, it must be a desire for good drink, and the same with every other desire.'
Just so, he said: each desire, taken by itself, is only of its natural object taken by itself; desire for an object of this or that kind is something added on.
'There might be something to that objection,' he said.

Now let's not be caught off guard, I said, by someone springing up with the objection that no one desires drink, but good drink, and not food, but good food — because everyone, after all, desires good things; so if thirst is a desire, it must be a desire for good drink, or good whatever-it-is, and the same for the other desires.

'But surely,' I said, 'with things that are relative to something, the qualified ones are relative to a qualified object, while the thing taken by itself is relative only to its object taken by itself.'
Well, he said, the man who says that might seem to have a point.
'I don't follow,' he said.

But surely, I said, with all things that are relative to something, the ones that are qualified are relative to a qualified object, while each thing taken just by itself is relative to its object taken just by itself.
'You understand that the greater is what it is in relation to the less?'
I don't follow, he said.
'Certainly.'
Don't you know that the greater is such as to be greater than something — than a less?
'And the much greater to the much less?'
Certainly.
'Yes.'
And the much greater than the much less?
'And the once-greater to the once-less, and the going-to-be-greater to the going-to-be-less?'
Yes.
'Of course,' he said.
And the once-greater than the once-less, and the greater-that-will-be than the less-that-will-be?
'And so with more in relation to fewer, double to half, and all such pairs, and heavier to lighter, faster to slower, and again hot to cold, and everything of that kind?'
Of course, he said.
'Yes.'

And the same again for the more and the fewer, the double and the half and everything of that stamp; and the heavier and the lighter, the faster and the slower; and again the hot and the cold, and every other pair like them — doesn't each go with its own correlate?

'And isn't it the same with the branches of knowledge? Knowledge as such is knowledge of what can be learned, or whatever we should call its object, while a particular knowledge of a particular kind is knowledge of a particular object. Take the building of houses: it's a kind of knowledge, marked off from the others, and so it's called architecture.'
Yes.
'Certainly.'

And what about the branches of knowledge — doesn't the same principle hold? Knowledge, taken just as itself, is knowledge of the knowable taken just as itself, or of whatever we should say knowledge is of; but a particular knowledge, of a particular kind, is of a particular object of a particular kind. I mean this sort of thing: when a knowledge of making houses arose, didn't it differ from the other knowledges, and so get called house-building?
'And it's called that because it has a particular character that none of the others has?'
Certainly.
'Yes.'
And wasn't that because it's a particular kind of knowledge, different from all the others?
'And it has that character because it has an object of a particular kind, and the same goes for all the other arts and branches of knowledge?'
Yes.
'It does.'
And it became a particular kind because its object was of a particular kind? And the same holds for the rest of the arts and knowledges?

'Well then,' I said, 'take that as what I meant before about relatives, if you understand me now. I meant that whenever one term is taken just by itself, it's relative to its object just by itself, and whenever it's qualified, to a qualified object. I'm not saying it's relative to an object of its own kind, that knowledge of health is itself healthy or knowledge of disease diseased, or that knowledge of good and bad is itself good or bad. I'm only saying that once knowledge becomes knowledge not of its object as such but of a qualified object, in this case of health and disease, it gets a particular character itself, and so it's no longer called just knowledge but, with the qualification added, medicine.'
It does.
'I understand,' he said, 'and I think you're right.'

Well then, I said, say that this is what I meant before — if you've now got hold of it: with everything that is relative to something, the thing taken alone goes with its object taken alone, and the thing qualified goes with its object qualified. I'm not saying the relative shares the quality of its object — that the knowledge of health and sickness is itself healthy or sick, or the knowledge of good and evil is itself good or evil. I mean that when a knowledge arose whose object was not the bare thing knowledge is of, but an object of a particular kind — namely health and sickness — the knowledge itself came out qualified in turn; and that is why it's no longer called simply knowledge but, with the kind added on, medicine.
'And thirst, won't you put it among the things that are relative to something, being what it is in relation to something?'
I understand, he said, and I think you're right.
'I will,' he said. 'Thirst is relative to drink.'
Then take thirst again, I said. Won't you set it among the things that are what they are in relation to something? Thirst, presumably, is thirst —
'So a particular kind of thirst is for a particular kind of drink, but thirst itself isn't for much or little, good or bad, or any particular kind of drink at all, but simply for drink itself.'
Yes, he said — for drink.
'Absolutely.'

So a particular kind of thirst is for a particular kind of drink; but thirst by itself is not for much drink or little, not for good drink or bad — in a word, not for drink of any kind at all. Thirst by itself is, by nature, only for drink by itself.
'So the soul of the thirsty man, insofar as he's thirsty, wants nothing but to drink. That's what it reaches for and strains toward.'
Absolutely.
'Plainly.'
Then the soul of a thirsty man, insofar as he thirsts, wants nothing else but to drink — that is what it strains after, that is what it starts toward.

'Then if something ever pulls it back when it's thirsty, that must be something in it different from the thirsty part, the part that drives it like a beast to drink. For we agreed the same thing can't, with the same part of itself, at the same time, in relation to the same object, do opposite things.'
Plainly.
'No, it can't.'

So if something ever hauls it back while it's thirsting, that would be a different thing in the soul from the thing that thirsts and drives it, like an animal, toward drinking. For we've agreed that the same thing cannot act in opposite ways, with the same part of itself, toward the same object, at the same time.
'Just as you wouldn't say the archer's hands push the bow away and draw it in at the same time, but that one hand pushes and the other pulls.'
It can't.
'Exactly,' he said.
Just as it's no good saying of an archer that his hands push the bow away and pull it in at the same time. The truth is that one hand pushes and the other pulls.
'Now, can a man be thirsty and yet unwilling to drink?'
Exactly right, he said.
'Yes,' he said, 'that happens all the time.'
Now, can we say that people are sometimes thirsty and yet unwilling to drink?
'And what should we say about that? Isn't there something in his soul telling him to drink, and something else, different, holding him back, something that overrules the part that's telling him to?'
Certainly, he said — many people, and often.
'I think so,' he said.

Then what should we say about them? I said. Isn't there something in their soul commanding them to drink, and something else forbidding it — a different thing, which overrules the thing that commands?
'And doesn't the part that holds him back, when it holds him back, come from reasoning, while the part that drives and drags him comes from feelings and from disorders of the body?'
So I think, he said.
'It seems so.'
And doesn't the forbidder, when it appears, appear out of reasoning — while the things that drive and drag arrive through passions and diseases?

'So we'd be right to judge them two distinct things,' I said. 'The part of the soul by which it reasons we'll call the rational part; the part by which it lusts and hungers and thirsts and is stirred by the other desires, the irrational and appetitive part, the companion of certain satisfactions and pleasures.'
It seems so.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's a fair way to think of it.'

Then it's no unreasonable claim, I said, that these are two things, different from each other. The part of the soul with which it reasons we may call the reasoning part; and the part with which it lusts and hungers and thirsts and flutters around the other appetites — that is the unreasoning and appetitive part, companion of certain feedings and pleasures.

'Then let's take it as settled that these two parts exist in the soul. Now, what about the spirited part, the part by which we feel anger? Is it a third, or is it the same in nature as one of these two?'
No, he said — it's the natural thing to think.
'It might be the same as the appetitive part,' he said.
Then let these stand, I said, as two forms marked off in the soul. Now what of spirit — the thing in us we get angry with? Is it a third, or does it share its nature with one of the two?

'There's a story I once heard,' I said, 'and I believe it. Leontius, the son of Aglaion, was coming up from the Piraeus, along the outside of the north wall, when he saw the public executioner's corpses lying there. He wanted to look at them and at the same time was disgusted and turned himself away. For a while he fought with himself and covered his eyes, but in the end his desire got the better of him, and he ran over to the bodies, forcing his eyes wide open and crying, "There, curse you, feast yourselves on the lovely sight!"'
Maybe with the second, he said — the appetitive.
'I've heard that story too,' he said.

But I once heard a story, I said, and I trust it. Leontius, the son of Aglaion, was coming up from the Piraeus along the outside of the north wall when he noticed corpses lying on the ground beside the public executioner. Part of him craved to look at them; part of him recoiled and turned away. For a while he fought himself and kept his face covered — but at last, overpowered by the appetite, he wrenched his eyes wide open, ran up to the corpses, and cried out at his own eyes: There, you wretches — drink your fill of the beautiful sight!
'And its point,' I said, 'is that anger sometimes makes war on the desires, as though it were one thing and they were another.'
I've heard the story too, he said.
'That is the point,' he said.
Now what it points to, I said, is that anger sometimes makes war on the appetites — one thing against a different thing.

'And don't we notice, in plenty of other cases, that when a man's desires force him against his reasoning, he rails at himself and his anger rises against the part of him that's forcing him? It's as if there were two factions at war, and his spirit takes the side of his reason. But when his spirit sides with the desires against what reason has decided shouldn't be done, that's a thing I think you've never noticed happening in yourself, or, I'd guess, in anyone else.'
It does point to that, he said.
'No, never,' he said.

And don't we notice the same elsewhere, all the time? When appetites force a man against his reasoning, he curses himself and rages at the thing inside him that's doing the forcing; and in this faction-fight, as between two parties, the man's spirit takes up arms for his reason. But for spirit to make common cause with the appetites, when reason has ruled they must be resisted — that, I think you'd say, you have never seen happen in yourself, nor in anyone else either.

'And take a man who believes he's done wrong. The finer his nature, the less he's able to feel anger when he suffers hunger or cold or any other pain at the hands of the man he wronged, because he thinks it's deserved. His spirit, as I say, refuses to rouse itself against it.'
No, by god, he said.
'True,' he said.

And what about when a man thinks he himself is in the wrong? I said. Isn't it true that the nobler he is, the less he can manage anger at going hungry, or cold, or suffering anything else of the kind at the hands of the man he believes has a right to inflict it? His spirit simply refuses to rise against that man — that's my claim.

'But when a man believes he's the one being wronged, then his spirit boils and rages and fights on the side of what he takes to be just. Through hunger and cold and every other suffering it holds out and wins, and his noble spirit won't be quieted until it has either won through or died, or until, like a dog called off by its shepherd, it is called back and calmed by the reason within him.'
True, he said.
'A perfect comparison,' he said. 'And it fits what we said about our city, that the auxiliaries were to be like dogs, obeying the rulers, who are like the shepherds of the city.'

But when a man believes he is the one wronged? Then his spirit boils and turns fierce, and enlists on the side of what seems to him just; and through hunger, through cold, through every suffering of the kind, it holds out and it conquers, and it will not give up the noble fight until it wins, or dies — or until the reason within calls it back and gentles it, the way a shepherd calls back his dog.
'You understand me exactly,' I said. 'But there's one more thing to consider.'
That's the very image of it, he said. And in fact, in our city we made the auxiliaries exactly that — dogs, obedient to the rulers, who are the shepherds of the city.
'What's that?'
You've caught my meaning beautifully, I said. But there's one thing more — have you noticed it?

'That the spirited part has turned out to be the opposite of what we just thought. We supposed it was a kind of desire, but now we say that, in the soul's civil war, it takes up arms on the side of reason.'
What?
'Definitely,' he said.

That the spirited part now shows us the opposite face from the one it showed a moment ago. Then we thought it something appetitive; now we say it's anything but — that in the civil war of the soul it sets its arms far rather on the side of the reasoning part.

'But is it then different from reason as well, or only a kind of reason? In that case there wouldn't be three parts of the soul but two, the rational and the appetitive. Or just as the city was held together by three classes, the money-makers, the auxiliaries, and the rulers, is there in the soul too this third thing, the spirited part, the natural helper of reason, as long as it hasn't been ruined by a bad upbringing?'
Absolutely.
'There must be a third,' he said.

Then is it different from reason too? Or is it some form of reason — so that the soul holds not three forms but two, the reasoning and the appetitive? Or is the soul like the city, which was held together by three classes — the money-makers, the auxiliaries, the deliberators — so that in the soul as well the spirited is a third thing, the natural auxiliary of reason, unless bad rearing has ruined it?
'Yes,' I said, 'provided it turns out to be distinct from reason, just as we showed it was distinct from desire.'
It must be a third, he said.

'That's easy to show,' he said. 'You can see it in small children. They're full of spirit from the moment they're born, while some of them, in my view, never come to reason at all, and most do so only late.'
Yes, I replied — if it shows itself different from the reasoning part, the way it showed itself different from the appetitive.

'A fine point,' I said. 'And you can see the same in animals, which is further proof of what you say. And we can call again on the line of Homer we quoted before, where he says, "He struck his breast and rebuked his heart." There Homer clearly treats the part that reasons about better and worse as different from the part that feels unreasoning anger and is rebuked by it.'

That's not hard to see, he said. Look at small children: they're full of spirit from the moment they're born; but as for reason — some of them, to my eye, never come into any at all, and most only late in the day.
'Exactly right,' he said.
Beautifully put, by god, I said. And in animals, too, you can see what you mean. And besides all that, there's the witness of Homer — the line we quoted earlier:
'So,' I said, 'after a hard swim we've reached land, and we're fairly agreed that the same three kinds are in the soul that are in the city.'
"He struck his chest and rebuked his own heart,"
'Just so.'
for there Homer has plainly made one thing rebuke another — the part that has reasoned out better and worse scolding the part that rages without reason.
'Then doesn't it follow at once that the individual is wise in the same way and by the same part that makes the city wise?'
Exactly right, he said.
'Certainly.'

Well, Glaucon, I said — we've swum through all that with some hard strokes, and made it to shore. We're decently agreed that the same kinds that are in the city live also in the soul of each single man, and that they're equal in number.
'And that the part that makes the individual brave is the same that makes the city brave, and so on, the individual matching the city in every virtue?'
So we are.
'It must be so.'
Then doesn't this follow at once: the individual man is wise in the same way, and by the same thing in him, that made the city wise?
'And we'll say a man is just, Glaucon, in the same way the city is just.'
Of course.
'That follows too, of course.'
And what makes a man brave, and the way it makes him brave, is what makes the city brave, and in the same way — and everything else that bears on virtue holds alike in both?
'And we haven't forgotten that the city was just because each of its three classes did its own work?'
It has to.
'I don't think we've forgotten,' he said.
And a just man, Glaucon — we'll say he is just, too, in the very way the city was just.
'Then we must keep in mind that each of us, too, will be just, and do his own work, when each of the parts in him does its own.'
That follows, no escaping it.
'Yes,' he said, 'we must keep that in mind.'
And surely we haven't forgotten that the city was just by each of the three classes in it doing its own work.
'And isn't it for the rational part, since it is wise and looks after the whole soul, to rule, and for the spirited part to be its subject and its ally?'
I don't think we've forgotten that, he said.
'Certainly.'
Then we must remember this too: each of us will be just — a man who does his own work — when each of the parts within him is doing its own work.

'And, as we said, won't the blend of music and physical training bring these two into accord, tightening and feeding the reason with fine words and learning, and loosening, soothing, and taming the spirited part with harmony and rhythm?'
Yes, he said — we'd better remember it.
'Just so,' he said.
So: to the reasoning part it belongs to rule, because it is wise and carries the forethought for the whole soul; and to the spirited part it belongs to obey it and fight beside it.

'And these two, so nourished and truly taught their own work, will govern the appetitive part, which in each of us is the largest part of the soul and by nature the greediest for money. They'll watch it closely, in case it grows fat and strong on the so-called pleasures of the body and stops keeping to its own work, and tries instead to enslave and rule the parts it has no business ruling, and so wrecks the whole life of the man.'
Certainly.
'Quite so,' he said.

And won't it be, as we said, the blend of music and physical training that draws these two into tune — tightening the one and feeding it on fine words and fine learning, while it slackens the other, calming it with gentle words, taming it by harmony and rhythm?

'And wouldn't these two be the best guardians of the whole soul and the whole body against enemies from outside, the one taking counsel, the other doing battle, following its ruler and carrying out by its courage what reason decides?'
Perfectly so, he said.
'Yes.'

And these two, reared that way — truly taught their own work, truly educated — will stand watch over the appetitive part, which in each of us is the largest part of the soul and by nature can never have enough of possessions. They'll keep guard over it, so that it doesn't gorge itself full of the so-called pleasures of the body, grow big and strong, stop doing its own work, and set about enslaving and ruling the parts it has no birthright to rule — overturning the whole of everyone's life.
'And we call a man brave, I think, when his spirited part holds onto what reason declares is and isn't to be feared, through pleasure and through pain alike.'
Very true, he said.
'Rightly,' he said.

And wouldn't the same two mount the finest guard against enemies outside as well, on behalf of the whole soul and the whole body — the one deliberating, the other doing the fighting, following its ruler and carrying out its decisions with courage?

'And we call him wise by that small part of him that rules and gives those declarations, the part that has in it the knowledge of what's good for each of the three parts and for the whole they make together.'
They would.
'Certainly.'
Brave, then, I think, is what we call each man by this part — when his spirit carries safe through pains and pleasures alike what reason has declared to be fearful, and not.
'And don't we call him temperate by the friendship and harmony of these same parts, when the ruler and the two ruled agree that the rational part should rule and don't make war on it?'
Rightly so.
'That's exactly what temperance is,' he said, 'in a city or in a man.'

And wise by that small part, the one that ruled in him and issued those declarations — holding in itself, in turn, the knowledge of what benefits each of the three, and the whole community of them together.
'And of course a man will be just by what we've now said so many times, and in the way we've said.'
Yes, exactly.
'Necessarily.'

And self-commanded — isn't a man that by the friendship and concord of these same parts: when the ruler and its two subjects agree together that the reasoning part must rule, and raise no faction against it?
'Now,' I said, 'is justice in the individual any blurrier than it was in the city? Does it come out as something different there, or the same?'
Self-command is that and nothing else, he said — in a city or in a single man.
'The same, I'd say,' he replied.
And just, at last — a man will be just by what we've now said so many times, and in exactly that way.
'Because, if any doubt is still hanging in our minds, we can settle it for certain with a few ordinary examples.'
It must be so.
'What sort of examples?'
Well then, I said. Has justice gone blurry on us at all? Does it look like anything different from what it showed itself to be in the city?

'Suppose someone asked us about that just city and a man brought up in its spirit, whether such a man would embezzle a deposit of gold or silver entrusted to him. Who would think he'd be more likely to do it than men of the other sort?'
Not to me, he said.
'No one,' he said.
If any part of our soul still wants to argue, I said, we can settle it for good with a few everyday tests.
'And wouldn't such a man be the last to commit temple-robbery, or theft, or betrayal, whether of his friends in private or of his city in public?'
Which are?
'He would.'

Take our city, for instance, and the man whose nature and training match it — and suppose a deposit of gold or silver had been placed in his hands. Do you think anyone would expect him, sooner than men of a different sort, to make off with it?
'And he'd never be faithless to an oath or any other agreement?'
No one would, he said.
'How could he?'
And temple-robbery, theft, betrayal — of friends in his private life, or of the city in public — wouldn't he be beyond them all?
'And adultery, neglect of his parents, failure in his religious duties, no one would be less likely to fall into any of these than he.'
Beyond them all.
'No one,' he said.
Nor would he ever be faithless, in any way, to an oath or to any other agreement.
'And isn't the reason for all this that each part of him is doing its own work, in ruling and in being ruled?'
Never.
'Yes, exactly that, and nothing else.'
Adultery, neglect of parents, gods left unserved — all of that belongs to any man sooner than to him.
'Then are you still looking for justice to be something other than this power that produces such men and such cities?'
Any man sooner, he said.
'No, by Zeus, I'm not,' he said.
And isn't the cause of all of it this — that each of the parts within him does its own work, whether its work is ruling or being ruled?

'So our dream has come true. The hunch we had at the very start of building the city, that by some god's help we'd hit from the beginning on a kind of origin and pattern of justice, has now been borne out.'
That's the cause, and nothing else.
'It certainly has.'
Then are you still hunting for justice to be anything more than this power — the power that produces men like that, and cities like that?
'So the principle that the carpenter and the shoemaker and the rest should each do their own work and not another's, that was a kind of image of justice, which is why it was useful.'
No, by god, he said — not I.
'Plainly.'

Then our dream has come completely true — the suspicion we spoke aloud the moment we began founding the city, that by some god's grace we had likely stumbled, right at the start, onto the origin and pattern of justice.

'But in truth justice was something of this sort, only it isn't concerned with a man's outward doings but with what's inside him, with his true self and what truly belongs to him. The just man doesn't let any part of his soul do another part's work, or meddle with the others. He sets his own house in order, takes command of himself, brings himself into tune, and becomes a friend to himself. He binds together the three parts, like the three fixed notes of a scale, the highest and the lowest and the one between, and any others there may be in between those, and from being many he becomes entirely one, temperate and in harmony. Only then does he act, whether in getting and spending, or in caring for his body, or in some matter of politics or private dealing, and through it all he believes and calls just and fine any action that preserves this inner harmony and helps produce it, and the knowledge that oversees such action he calls wisdom. And he calls unjust any action that breaks this harmony down, and the belief that oversees that, ignorance.'
It has, absolutely.
'That is the exact truth, Socrates,' he said.

So it really was an image of justice, Glaucon — and that's why it was so useful — the rule that the man born a cobbler had better make shoes and do nothing else, and the born carpenter build, and so on down the line.
'Good,' I said. 'So if we claimed to have found the just man and the just city, and what justice is in each, I don't think we'd be lying.'
So it appears.
'We certainly wouldn't.'

But in truth, it seems, justice was something of this kind — only not about a man's outward doing of his own work, but about the inward doing of it: about himself, in the truest sense, and what is truly his own. The just man does not allow any part of himself to do another part's work, or the kinds within his soul to meddle in one another's business. He sets his own house in order — literally his own. He rules himself. He puts himself in order, becomes his own friend, and tunes the three parts of him together exactly like the three fixed notes of a scale — low, high, and middle, and whatever happens to lie between — binding them all until, out of many, he has become entirely one: a man of self-command, in harmony with himself. Then, and only then, he acts — if he acts at all — whether he's making money or tending his body, in politics or in private business. And through all of it, the action he holds and names as just and beautiful is the one that preserves this condition and helps complete it, and the knowledge that presides over such action he calls wisdom; while the action that breaks this condition down, at any point, he names unjust, and the opinion that presides over it, ignorance.
'Shall we say it, then?'
That's the whole truth, Socrates, he said.
'Let's say it.'
Well then, I said. If we claimed to have found the just man, and the just city, and what justice actually is in them — I don't think we'd be counted liars.
'So be it,' I said. 'And now we have to look at injustice.'
By god, no, he said.
'Plainly.'
Shall we claim it, then?

'Won't it have to be a kind of civil war among the three parts, a meddling and interfering in one another's work, a rising up of one part of the soul against the whole to seize a rule that isn't its by right, the rule of a part whose nature is to be a subject of the part that ought to rule? Disorder and confusion of that kind, I think, is what we'll call injustice, along with license and cowardice and ignorance, in a word, every form of vice.'
Claim it.
'Exactly so,' he said.
So be it, I said. Next in line, I suppose, is injustice.
'Then if we know clearly what injustice and justice are, we also know clearly, don't we, what acting unjustly and being unjust come to, and likewise acting justly?'
Obviously.
'How do you mean?' he said.

Then injustice must be a kind of civil war among these same three — a meddling, an interfering in one another's work, an uprising of one part of the soul against the whole: the part rebelling so that it can rule inside the soul when rule is not its place, because its nature made it fit to serve what is of ruling stock. Something like this is what we'll say, I think — that this confusion and wandering of the parts is injustice, and lack of restraint, and cowardice, and ignorance: in one word, the whole of vice.
'They're just like the healthy and the unhealthy,' I said. 'What health and disease are in the body, justice and injustice are in the soul.'
That's what it is, he said — exactly.
'How so?' he said.
Then acting unjustly and being unjust — and acting justly, for that matter — all of that now stands in plain view too, doesn't it, if injustice and justice do?
'Healthy things produce health, and unhealthy things produce disease.'
How so?
'Yes.'
Because, I said, they're no different from the healthy and the diseased: what those are in the body, these are in the soul.
'And just actions produce justice, unjust actions injustice?'
In what way?
'They must.'
What's healthy breeds health, and what's diseased breeds disease.

'And producing health means setting up among the parts of the body a natural order, in which one rules and another is ruled, while producing disease means setting up an order against nature, in which one part rules and another is ruled contrary to nature?'
Yes.
'True.'
And doesn't doing just things breed justice, and doing unjust things injustice?
'And isn't producing justice the same, setting up among the parts of the soul a natural order of ruling and being ruled, while producing injustice means an order against nature?'
It must.
'Exactly so,' he said.

Now, to produce health is to set the elements of the body so that they master, and are mastered by, one another according to nature — and to produce disease is to set them ruling and being ruled contrary to nature.
'So virtue, it seems, is a kind of health and beauty and good condition of the soul, and vice a disease and ugliness and weakness of it.'
It is.
'That's right.'

Then producing justice, in turn, is setting the parts of the soul to master, and be mastered by, one another according to nature — and producing injustice is setting them to rule and be ruled contrary to it?
'And don't fine practices lead to virtue, and shameful ones to vice?'
Exactly.
'They must.'
So virtue, it seems, would be a kind of health and beauty and good condition of the soul — and vice its disease, its ugliness, its weakness.

'So now, it seems, all that's left is to ask which pays better, to do what's just, to follow fine practices and be just, whether anyone notices or not, or to do what's unjust and be unjust, provided one isn't punished and so forced to improve.'
That's so.

'But Socrates,' he said, 'to me that question has become ridiculous. When the body's nature is ruined, we think life isn't worth living, even with all the food and drink and wealth and power in the world. So when the very nature of the thing by which we live is disordered and ruined, are we really going to say life is worth living, as long as a man can do whatever he likes, except the one thing that would free him from vice and injustice and win him justice and virtue, now that we've seen what each of them is?'
And don't fine practices lead a man toward virtue, and shameful ones toward vice?
'Yes, the question is ridiculous,' I said. 'But still, now that we've come to the point where we can see the truth of all this as clearly as anything, we mustn't give up.'
They must.
'No,' he said, 'least of all now.'

Then what's left for us to examine, it seems, is this: whether it pays to act justly, to practice what is fine, and to be just — whether or not anyone knows you are — or to do injustice and be unjust, provided you never pay the penalty and are never made better by punishment.
'Then come up here,' I said, 'and look down at how many forms vice has, the ones worth looking at, at any rate.'

But Socrates, he said, that question has turned ridiculous now. When the body's nature is wrecked, we think life isn't worth living — not with every food and every drink, not with all the money and all the power there is. And when the nature of the very thing we live by is deranged and wrecked, life is going to be worth living, is it — as long as a man can do whatever he pleases except the one thing that would free him from vice and injustice and win him justice and virtue? Now that both have shown themselves to be what we've described?
'I'm right behind you,' he said. 'Go on.'
Ridiculous, yes, I said. But still — now that we've climbed high enough to see as sharply as we ever will that this is how things stand, we mustn't get tired.

'From the height the argument has climbed to,' I said, 'it's like standing on a watchtower. From here you can see that virtue is one, but the forms of vice are countless, though four of them are worth singling out.'
The last thing in the world to do, he said, is tire now.
'What do you mean?' he said.
Then come up here, I said, and see how many forms vice has — the ones worth looking at, anyway, as I see it.
'I mean,' I said, 'that there seem to be as many types of soul as there are distinct types of city worth naming.'
I'm right behind you, he said. Just tell me.
'How many is that?'

Well, I said, from up here — as from a watchtower, now that the argument has carried us this high — there appears to be one single form of virtue, and unlimited forms of vice; and among them, some four that are worth mentioning.
'Five kinds of city,' I said, 'and five of soul.'
What do you mean?
'And what are they?' he asked.
It's likely, I said, that there are as many types of soul as there are types of constitution with distinct forms of their own.

'The first kind of city,' I said, 'is the one we've been describing, and it could go by either of two names. Where one outstanding man rules, you'd call it a monarchy; where several rule, an aristocracy.'
How many is that?
'True,' he said.
Five of constitutions, I said, and five of the soul.
'But I count these as a single form. Whether the rulers are one or many, as long as they've been brought up and educated the way we've laid down, they won't disturb the city's fundamental laws.'
Tell me which, he said.

One of them, I say, is the constitution we've just described — though it could carry two names. If one outstanding man arises among the rulers, it will be called a kingship; if more than one, an aristocracy.
True, he said.

This, then, I count as a single form, I said. Whether it's several who arise or only one, they won't shake any law of the city worth mentioning — not if they've had the rearing and the education we described.
No, he said — it isn't likely.
'No, they won't,' he said.
spine.label: Book V
spine.title: The Three Waves
Women, Children, and the Philosopher-King
spine.text: A city like this, then — a constitution like this — I call good and right, and so is a man of the same pattern. And if this one is right, the others are bad and mistaken: bad in how they run their cities, bad in how they build the souls of the people who live in them. Their badness comes in four forms.

So this is the kind of city and the kind of man I call good and right; and if this one is right, then every other is wrong. The badness is one thing, but it shows up in the running of a state and in the ordering of a single soul alike, and it takes four different forms.
What are they? he asked.
'And what are those?' he asked.

I was about to describe the four, in the order they seemed to me to grow out of one another, when Polemarchus — he was sitting a little way from Adeimantus — reached out his hand, caught his cloak up by the shoulder, pulled him close, and leaned in to whisper something in his ear. All I caught of it was: Do we let him off, or what do we do?

I was about to lay out the order in which these four bad forms seemed to me to arise out of one another, when Polemarchus, who was sitting a little way off, just beyond Adeimantus, reached out, took hold of Adeimantus's cloak up by the shoulder, and pulled him close. Leaning in, he whispered something in his ear. I caught only the words, 'Shall we let him off, or what do we do?'
Certainly not, said Adeimantus — out loud now.
'Absolutely not,' said Adeimantus, this time out loud.
Who is it, I said, that you're not letting off?
'Let whom off?' I asked. 'Who is it you won't release?'
You, he said.
'You,' he said.
And why me, I asked, in particular?
'And why me especially?' I asked.

Because we think you're slacking, he said — cheating us out of a whole branch of the argument, and not the smallest one, so you won't have to go through it. You thought we wouldn't notice when you tossed it off lightly — as if it went without saying — that where women and children are concerned, 'friends will hold everything in common.'

'Because,' he said, 'we think you're being lazy. You mean to cheat us out of a whole stretch of the argument, an important one, and you imagine we won't notice you skating past it, as though it were obvious to everyone that, where women and children are concerned, friends hold everything in common.'
And wasn't that right, Adeimantus?
'But isn't that right, Adeimantus?' I said.

Yes, he said. But this 'right,' like everything else, needs an explanation — what kind of common holding? There could be many. So don't skip past the one you mean. We've been sitting here a long time expecting you to say something about how our citizens will produce children, how they'll rear them once they're born, this whole community of women and children you mentioned. We think it matters enormously — whether it's handled rightly or wrongly makes all the difference to the city. So now, when you're starting in on another constitution before settling these questions, we've resolved — as you heard — not to let you go until you've gone through all of it the way you went through everything else.

'Yes,' he said, 'but "right" here, like everything else, needs explaining. There's more than one way to hold things in common, so tell us which one you mean. We've been waiting a long time for you to say something about how your citizens will have children, and how they'll raise them once they're born, and in general what this whole business of holding women and children in common amounts to. We think the way these things are handled, well or badly, makes an enormous difference to a state, for better or for worse. And now, just as you're starting up another city instead, we've decided, as you heard, not to let you go until you've given a full account of all this.'
Put me down, said Glaucon, as voting for that resolution.
'You can count me in on that resolution,' said Glaucon.
In fact, Socrates, said Thrasymachus, take it as carried unanimously.
'And without further ado,' said Thrasymachus, 'take it that we're all of one mind about it.'

You don't know what you're doing, I said, ambushing me like this. Just as I was finishing with the constitution, glad to have that question laid to rest, content that you'd accepted what was said — now you're starting the whole argument over from the beginning. What a swarm of arguments you're stirring up! I saw it coming, and steered around it at the time to spare us the ordeal.

'You don't realize what you're doing, ganging up on me like this,' I said. 'What an argument you're stirring up about the state! Just when I thought I was finished and was glad to have gotten that question to lie down quietly, congratulating myself that you'd accepted what I said, you make me start over from the very foundations. You have no idea what a hornet's nest of words you're poking. I saw this trouble coming, which is exactly why I steered around it.'
And what do you think we came here for, said Thrasymachus — to prospect for gold, or to listen to an argument?
'What do you think we came here for,' said Thrasymachus, 'to dig for gold, or to hear a discussion?'
An argument, I said — one with a limit.
'To hear a discussion,' I said, 'but within reason.'
