For anyone with sense, Socrates, said Glaucon, the limit for listening to arguments like these is a whole lifetime. So never mind us. Just don't you get tired of answering the question your own way: what will this community be like, this sharing of women and children among our guardians — and the rearing of the children while they're still young, in the stretch between birth and schooling, which people consider the most demanding of all? Try to tell us how it's supposed to go.

'Socrates,' said Glaucon, 'a sensible man sets no limit on hearing this kind of discussion short of his whole life. But never mind us. Don't lose heart on our account. Just answer the question your own way: what is this community of women and children that's to hold among our guardians? And how will we handle the stretch between birth and the start of education, which seems to call for the most care of all? Tell us how these things are to go.'

It's not an easy subject to go through, my innocent friend, I said. It invites even more disbelief than everything we covered before. People will doubt that what I say is possible; and even if it came fully to pass, they'll doubt it would be for the best. That's why I'm reluctant to touch it, my dear comrade — for fear the whole thing looks like a daydream.

'It isn't an easy thing to explain, my friend,' I said. 'There's even more room for doubt here than in what we settled before. People will question whether what I'm proposing is even possible; and even granting it could be done, they'll still doubt whether it would be for the best. That's why I hold back from the subject, afraid the whole idea may turn out to be nothing but a daydream.'
Don't be, he said. Your audience isn't unfeeling, or skeptical, or hostile.
'Don't be afraid,' he said. 'Your listeners won't be hard on you. We're not skeptics, and we're not hostile.'
My good friend, I said — are you saying that to encourage me?
'My good friend,' I said, 'I suppose you say that to encourage me.'
I am, he said.
'I do,' he said.

Then you're achieving the opposite, I said. If I trusted myself to know what I'm talking about, the encouragement would be fine. Among intelligent friends who love you, a man who knows the truth about the greatest and dearest things can speak it securely. But to make the argument while you're still unsure, still searching — which is what I'm doing — is a frightening, slippery business. Not because I might get laughed at; that's childish. But if I slip on the truth just where a man most needs solid footing, I won't fall alone — I'll drag my friends down with me. So I bow to Nemesis before I say what I'm going to say. Because I honestly believe it's a lesser crime to kill a man by accident than to deceive people about what is beautiful and good and just in the laws. That's a risk better run among enemies than among friends — so thanks very much for the encouragement.

'Then you're doing the opposite,' I said. 'Your encouragement would be fine if I were sure I knew what I was talking about. A man who knows the truth about things he cares about and holds dear can speak it among wise friends who love him with no fear and no faltering. But to push ahead with an argument while you're still a hesitant, searching man yourself, which is my condition, that's a dangerous, slippery business. Not because I'd be laughed at, that fear would be childish, but because I might miss the truth on the very questions where I most need to keep my footing, and drag my friends down with me in the fall. So I pray to Nemesis to forgive what I'm about to say. For I honestly believe it's a lesser crime to kill a man by accident than to deceive people about what is fine, or good, or just, especially when laws are at stake. That's a risk I'd rather run among enemies than among friends, so your encouragement does me no favors.'
Glaucon laughed. Socrates, he said, if the argument does us any harm, we release you as in a homicide case: acquitted in advance, your hands clean of deceiving us. So take heart and speak.
Glaucon laughed. 'Well then, Socrates,' he said, 'if your argument does us any harm, we acquit you in advance, as if of manslaughter. You won't be charged with deceiving us. So take heart and speak.'
Well, I said, the man acquitted in court is clean — the law says so. And if there, then probably here too.
'Fine,' I said. 'The law does say that a man acquitted is free of guilt, and if it holds in court it ought to hold in argument too.'
Then on that score, he said, speak.
'Then speak,' he said, 'and don't hold back.'

Now I have to go back, I said, to something that maybe should have been said in its place earlier. Though perhaps this is the right way after all: the men's drama has been played to its end, so the women's takes the stage — especially with you calling for it.

'Well,' I said, 'I'll have to go back and pick up what I probably should have said earlier, in its proper place. Perhaps it's fitting this way: the men have played their part, and now it's the women's turn. I'll speak of them, all the more gladly since you've asked.'

In my opinion, for people born and educated as we described, there's no right acquisition and use of children and women except along the road we started them down at the beginning. In the argument, remember, we set out to make the men watchdogs guarding a flock.

'For men born and raised as our citizens are, the only right way I can see to settle how women and children are to be had and handled is to follow the path we set out on at the start, when we said the men were to be guardians, watchdogs of the flock.'
Yes.
'True.'
Then let's stay with that, and give the women a birth and rearing to match, near enough, and see whether it suits us or not.
'Then let's go on and assume that the birth and upbringing of our women follow the same rules, or nearly the same, and see whether the result fits our design.'
How?
'What do you mean?'

Like this. Do we think the females of our watchdogs should stand guard alongside the males, and hunt with them, and share everything else they do? Or should they stay inside, on the theory that bearing and nursing the puppies leaves them unfit, while the males do the work and carry the whole care of the flock?

'Let me put it as a question,' I said. 'When it comes to dogs, do we split them into males and females, or do both share equally in hunting and standing guard and the other work of dogs? Do we hand the whole care of the flock over to the males alone, and leave the females at home on the grounds that bearing and nursing the pups is work enough for them?'
They share everything, he said — except that we treat the females as weaker and the males as stronger.
'No,' he said, 'they share the work alike. The only difference is that the males are stronger and the females weaker.'
And can you use any animal for the same work as another, I said, if you don't give it the same rearing and training?
'And can you use any animal for the same work as another unless you raise and feed it the same way?'
You can't.
'You can't.'
So if we're going to use the women for the same tasks as the men, we have to teach them the same things.
'So if women are to do the same work as men, they have to be given the same upbringing and the same education?'
Yes.
'Yes.'
The men were given music and gymnastics.
'Now the education we gave the men was music and physical training.'
Yes.
'Yes.'
Then the women get those same two arts, and the work of war as well — and are used the same way.
'Then we'll have to give women music and physical training too, and train them in war as well, and put them to the same use as the men.'
It follows from what you're saying, I suppose.
'That follows, I suppose.'
Probably, I said, next to what we're used to, a lot of what we're proposing would look laughable if it were carried out as described.
'I expect,' I said, 'that quite a few of our proposals, just because they break with custom, will look ridiculous if they're actually carried out.'
It certainly would.
'No doubt of it.'

And what's the funniest thing in the picture? Isn't it obviously the women exercising naked in the wrestling schools alongside the men — and not just the young ones, but the older women too, like the old men in the gyms who keep at their exercise wrinkled and none too pleasant to look at?

'And what will look most ridiculous of all? The sight of women exercising naked alongside the men in the gymnasium, especially the older ones. They'll hardly be a vision of beauty, any more than the eager old men who keep showing up at the gym in spite of their wrinkles and their looks.'
By Zeus, he said — that would look ridiculous, at least by present standards.
'Yes,' he said, 'by today's standards that would seem absurd.'

Well, I said, now that we've launched into it, we can't fear the jokes of the clever set — all the kinds of things they'll say about a change like this hitting the gymnastics, and the music, and not least the bearing of arms and the riding of horses.

'But since we've made up our minds to speak plainly,' I said, 'we mustn't be frightened off by the jokes the clever wits will make at this kind of innovation, all the things they'll say about women in the gym and the music room, and above all about women in armor, riding horses.'
You're right, he said.
'Very true,' he said.

But since we've set out, we have to march into the rough country of the law — after asking these wits to drop their own business and try being serious for once, and reminding them that it wasn't so long ago that Greeks found it shameful and ridiculous, as most of the barbarian world still does, for men to be seen naked; and that when first the Cretans and then the Spartans opened their gymnasiums, the sophisticates of the day were free to make a comedy of it all. Don't you think so?

'But having started, we have to push on over the rough ground of the law, and just for once ask these gentlemen to be serious. We can remind them that not so long ago the Greeks themselves thought, as most foreigners still think, that the sight of a naked man was ridiculous and shameful. When the Cretans first, and then the Spartans, took up the practice of exercising naked, the wits of that day could have mocked it just the same.'
I do.
'No doubt.'

But once experience showed, I think, that stripping is better than covering all such things up, then what was laughable to the eye melted away before what argument revealed as best. And that showed something more: it's a fool who finds anything ridiculous but what's bad — who tries to raise a laugh looking at any spectacle but the spectacle of folly and vice, or who aims seriously at any mark of beauty but the good.

'But once experience showed it was better to strip than to keep everything covered up, the eye's first sense of the absurd faded before the better principle that reason laid down. And it became clear that the real fool is the man who aims his ridicule at anything other than folly and vice, or who seriously tries to measure beauty by any standard but the good.'
Absolutely.
'Very true,' he said.

First, then, we have to come to an agreement about whether these proposals are workable or not — and give the challenge its opening, whether it comes in jest or in earnest: is the female of the human species capable of sharing in all the work of the male, or in none of it, or in some things and not others? And the business of war — where does that fall? Isn't that the best beginning, and likely to lead to the best conclusion?

'So first, whether we put the question in jest or in earnest, let's come to an understanding about woman's nature. Is she capable of sharing in all of man's work, or only part of it, or none? And is war one of the things she can share in, or not? That's the best way to begin the inquiry, and it'll probably bring us to the fairest conclusion.'
Much the best.
'By far the best way.'
Then shall we make the argument against ourselves, on the objectors' behalf, so the other side of the case doesn't sit under siege undefended?
'Shall we argue the other side ourselves, then, and make the case against our own position? That way the opposing view won't go undefended.'
Why not? he said.
'Why not?' he said.

Then let's say this on their behalf: 'Socrates and Glaucon, you need no outside opponent — you convicted yourselves. At the founding of your city, you agreed that each person must do the one job nature suits him for.' We did agree, I think — of course. 'And doesn't a woman differ from a man by nature — enormously?' We'll have to admit the difference. 'Then isn't it proper to assign each a different job, matched to that nature?' Certainly. 'Then how are you not wrong — how are you not contradicting yourselves — when you now say that men and women must do the same jobs, their natures being poles apart?' There's the charge. Can you make any defense to it, my remarkable friend?

'Then let's put a speech in our opponents' mouths. They'll say: "Socrates, Glaucon, no outsider needs to refute you. You did it yourselves. Right at the founding of the state you agreed that each person should do the one job that suits his nature." And we did agree to that, if I'm not mistaken. "And don't the natures of men and women differ a great deal?" Of course they do, we'll say. "Then shouldn't the work given to men and to women differ too, each suited to their different natures?" Certainly. "But then, haven't you fallen into a flat contradiction, saying that men and women, whose natures are so completely different, ought to do the very same things?" Now, my friend, what defense will you make for us against an objection like that?'
It's not so easy on the spot, he said. So I'll ask you — I'm asking now — to be the voice for our side of the case too, whatever that case is.
'That's not an easy thing to answer on the spot,' he said. 'So I ask you, and I'm asking in earnest, to make the case for our side yourself.'
This, Glaucon, I said — this and a lot more like it — is what I saw coming all along. That's why I was afraid and reluctant to touch the law about how wives and children are to be gotten and reared.

'These are the objections, Glaucon,' I said, 'and many others like them, that I saw coming long ago. They're what made me afraid and reluctant to lay down any law about the having and raising of women and children.'
By Zeus, he said, it doesn't look like an easy problem.
'By Zeus,' he said, 'this is anything but easy to solve.'
It isn't, I said. But it's like this: fall into a small swimming pool or into the middle of the widest sea — either way, you swim.
'It isn't,' I said. 'But the fact is, when a man falls into the water, whether it's a little swimming pool or the open sea, he has to swim all the same.'
You do.
'Very true.'
Then we swim too, and try to come out of this argument alive — hoping some dolphin takes us on its back, or some other rescue past reasonable hope.
'So we have to swim too, and try to reach the shore, hoping that some dolphin of Arion's or some other piece of luck will carry us across.'
It seems we'd better, he said.
'I suppose so,' he said.

Come on, then, I said — let's find the way out, if we can. We've agreed that different natures should have different pursuits, and that a woman's nature and a man's are different. And now we're saying that these different natures should have the same pursuits. That's the indictment, isn't it?

'Then let's see if we can find a way out. We agreed, didn't we, that different natures should have different pursuits, and that the natures of men and women differ. And yet now we're saying that these different natures should have the same pursuits. That's the inconsistency we're charged with.'
Exactly.
'Exactly.'
Glaucon, I said, the power of the art of contradiction — what a noble thing it is!
'Glaucon,' I said, 'what a glorious power there is in the art of contradiction!'
Why do you say that?
'Why do you say that?'

Because so many people seem to fall into it even against their will, I said. They think they're reasoning when they're really just scoring points — because they can't examine a statement by dividing it into its kinds, they chase the contradiction in the mere words. It's wrangling they practice on each other, not dialectic.

'Because I think plenty of people fall into it without meaning to. They think they're reasoning when really they're just quarreling over words, because they can't carve up a subject and look at it part by part. So they go after a merely verbal disagreement, in a competitive spirit rather than a fair one.'
That happens to plenty of people, he said. But surely not to us, here and now?
'Yes,' he said, 'that does happen often. But what's it got to do with us, right now?'
It absolutely does, I said. We're in real danger of doing contradiction-work without meaning to.
'A great deal,' I said, 'because there's a real danger we've slipped into a verbal dispute without realizing it.'
How?
'How so?'

We keep insisting, bravely, combatively, on the letter of it — that unlike natures must not have the same pursuits — but we never once examined what kind of unlikeness and what kind of likeness we meant, or what our rule was aiming at when we assigned different pursuits to different natures and the same to the same.

'We've been bravely and stubbornly insisting on the bare verbal point that different natures shouldn't have the same pursuits. But we never stopped to ask what we even meant by sameness or difference of nature, or in what respect we were distinguishing them when we assigned different work to different natures and the same work to the same.'
No, he said, we never looked at that.
'No,' he said, 'we never looked into that.'

Then by that logic, I said, we're free to ask ourselves whether the bald and the long-haired have the same nature or opposite ones — and once we agree they're opposite, then if bald men make shoes, forbid the long-haired to make them, and if the long-haired do, forbid the bald.

'Then take this for an example,' I said. 'Suppose we asked whether bald men and long-haired men have opposite natures. And once we'd agreed they do, then if bald men were shoemakers we'd have to forbid the long-haired ones to make shoes, and the other way around.'
That would be a joke, he said.
'That would be a joke,' he said.

A joke for one reason only, I said: back then we didn't mean 'same nature' and 'different nature' absolutely, in every sense. We had our eye on the one kind of unlikeness and likeness that bears on the work itself. We meant, for instance, that a man with a doctor's mind and a woman with a doctor's mind have the same nature. Don't you think?

'Yes, a joke,' I said. 'And why? Because when we built the state we never meant that opposite natures should differ in every way, only in the ways that bear on the particular work in question. We'd have said, for instance, that a man with a doctor's soul and a man who actually is a doctor have the same nature.'
I do.
'True.'
But a doctor and a carpenter — different natures?
'Whereas a doctor and a carpenter have different natures?'
Completely different.
'Of course.'

So with the two sexes, I said: if one of them shows itself different from the other for some art or practice, we'll say that work should go to the one it suits. But if they turn out to differ only in this — that the female bears the young and the male begets them — we'll say it hasn't been shown at all that a woman differs from a man for the purposes we're talking about, and we'll keep thinking our guardians and their women should do the same work.

'So,' I said, 'if the male and female sex turn out to differ with respect to some art or pursuit, then we'd say that pursuit ought to be assigned to one or the other. But if the only difference is that the female bears children and the male begets them, that's no proof at all that a woman differs from a man in the way that matters for the education she should get. So we'll go on maintaining that our guardians and their women should have the same pursuits.'
And rightly, he said.
'And rightly so,' he said.
Next, don't we tell the man who says otherwise to instruct us: for which art, which pursuit that goes into the framing of a city, is a woman's nature different from a man's?
'Next, we'll ask our opponent to name a single one of the arts or pursuits of civic life in which a woman's nature differs from a man's.'
That's fair.
'That's a fair challenge.'
And maybe he'll say what you said a moment ago — that it's hard to answer well on the instant, but not hard after some thought.
'And maybe he'll say, as you did, that it isn't easy to answer on the spot, but with a little thought it's no great difficulty.'
He might.
'He might.'
Then shall we ask him to follow us, and see if we can show him there's no pursuit in the management of a city that is peculiar to women?

'Then suppose we invite the man who raises this objection to walk through the argument with us. Maybe we can show him there's nothing in the makeup of a woman that bears specially on running a state.'
By all means.
'By all means.'

Come then, we'll say to him, answer us this: when you say one person is naturally gifted for something and another isn't, do you mean the one learns it easily, the other with difficulty? That the one, from a short course of study, discovers far beyond what he was taught, while the other, after long study and practice, can't even keep hold of what he learned? That in the one, the body serves the mind well; in the other, it fights it? Are these the marks — or are there others — by which you define the naturally gifted for each pursuit, and the ungifted?

'Let's say to him: come now, answer us this. When you spoke of one man being gifted by nature for something and another not, didn't you mean this, that one man picks a thing up easily and another with difficulty; that a little instruction sets one of them discovering a great deal on his own, while the other, after much study and effort, can't even hold on to what he learns; that the body of the one serves his mind well, while the body of the other gets in his way? Aren't these the sorts of things that mark off the naturally gifted from the ungifted?'
Nobody will claim there are others, he said.
'No one would deny it.'

Now: do you know of any human occupation at which the male sex doesn't beat the female on all these counts? Or should we drag it out — talking about weaving, and minding the cakes and the stews, where the female sex is thought to be really something, and where getting beaten is the most laughable defeat of all?

'And is there any human pursuit in which men, as a sex, don't surpass women in all these respects? Need I waste time on weaving, and the management of pancakes and preserves, the things women really do seem to shine at, where to be beaten by a man would be the most absurd thing of all?'

It's true, he said — the one sex is bested by the other across the board, you could say. Plenty of individual women are better than plenty of individual men at plenty of things — but on the whole it's as you say.
'You're right,' he said, 'that on the whole one sex is far outdone by the other. Many women, to be sure, are better than many men at many things, but taken altogether it's as you say.'

Then, my friend, there is no pursuit in the running of a city that belongs to a woman because she's a woman, or to a man because he's a man. Natural gifts are scattered through both alike: by nature the woman shares in every pursuit, and the man in every one — only in all of them the woman is weaker than the man.

'Then, my friend,' I said, 'there's no occupation in running a state that belongs to a woman because she's a woman, or to a man because he's a man. The natural gifts are scattered alike through both. By nature a woman has a share in every pursuit, and so does a man, though in all of them a woman is the weaker.'
True.
'Quite true.'
So shall we assign everything to men, and nothing to a woman?
'Then are we to lay all the work on men and none on women?'
How can we?
'That would never do.'
No — because, as we'll say, one woman is born for medicine and another isn't; one is born musical, another unmusical.
'No, because one woman has a gift for medicine and another doesn't; one is musical by nature and another isn't.'
Of course.
'Certainly.'
And one for gymnastics and war, while another is unwarlike and no lover of the gym?
'And one woman has a turn for athletics and war, while another has no fight in her and no taste for the gym?'
I'd say so.
'No doubt.'
And one loves wisdom, another hates it? One is spirited, another spiritless?
'And one woman loves wisdom and another hates it; one has spirit and another has none?'
That too.
'That's true as well.'
Then one woman has a guardian's nature and another doesn't. Wasn't that the very nature we picked our male guardians for?
'So one woman has the temperament of a guardian and another doesn't. Wasn't it just this sort of nature we looked for when we picked out the male guardians?'
The very one.
'It was.'
So for guarding a city, the nature of woman and man is the same — only weaker in her, stronger in him.
'Then men and women have the same nature when it comes to guarding the state. They differ only in being stronger or weaker.'
So it appears.
'So it seems.'
Then women of that kind must be chosen to live with men of that kind and stand guard with them — they're up to it, and their natures are kin.
'And the women with the right qualities are to be chosen to live and work alongside the men who have them, since they're alike in ability and alike in character?'
Certainly.
'Certainly.'
And the same natures get the same pursuits?
'And the same natures should have the same pursuits?'
The same.
'They should.'
Then we've circled back to where we began, and we agree: it's nothing against nature to give the guardians' wives music and gymnastics.
'Then we've come back around to where we were: there's nothing unnatural in giving the guardians' women the same music and physical training as the men.'
No — nothing.
'Nothing at all.'
So the law we were laying down wasn't impossible, wasn't wishful — it stands in line with nature. It's the present arrangement, it seems, that stands against it.
'So the law we laid down was in accord with nature, not impossible and not a mere wish. It's the contrary practice, the one in force now, that turns out to go against nature.'
So it seems.
'It looks that way.'
Now, our task was to check whether our proposals were possible, and whether they were best?
'Now, we set out to ask two things: first, whether our proposals were possible, and second, whether they were for the best.'
It was.
'We did.'
That they're possible stands agreed?
'And we've agreed they're possible?'
Yes.
'Yes.'
Then next we need agreement that they're best?
'Then the next thing is to settle that they're also greatly beneficial?'
Clearly.
'Clearly.'
Well — for making a woman fit to guard, we won't have one education that makes guardian men and another that makes guardian women, will we? Especially when it receives the same nature to work on?
'You'll grant that the same education that makes a man a good guardian will make a woman one too, since their underlying nature is the same?'
No — the same for both.
'Yes.'
Then here's a question I'd like your opinion on.
'Then let me ask you something.'
What?
'Go ahead.'
Do you hold that one man is better and another worse? Or do you think all men are equal?
'Would you say all men are equal in excellence, or that one man is better than another?'
Hardly equal.
'That one is better than another.'
Then in the city we were founding, who do you think turned out better men — the guardians, given the education we described, or the shoemakers, educated in shoemaking?
'And in the city we're founding, who do you suppose come out the better men, the guardians who've had the upbringing we described, or the shoemakers whose education has been in shoemaking?'
A ridiculous question, he said.
'What a ridiculous question.'
I take your point, I said. So — the guardians are the best of the citizens?
'I take your point,' I said. 'And aren't the guardians the best of our citizens?'
By far.
'By far.'
And these women will be the best of the women?
'And won't their women be the best of the women?'
That too — by far.
'By far, yes.'
And is anything better for a city than to have in it the best possible women and the best possible men?
'And can anything be better for a state than that its men and its women should be as good as they can possibly be?'
Nothing.
'Nothing.'
And that is what music and gymnastics, applied as we described, will bring about?
'And that's exactly what music and physical training will bring about, present in the way we've laid out?'
Of course.
'Of course.'
Then the arrangement we've laid down is not only possible; it's the best thing for the city.
'So the law we've enacted is not only possible but as beneficial to the state as anything could be.'
It is.
'It is.'

Then the guardians' women must strip — since they'll wear excellence in place of robes — and take their share of war and the whole guarding of the city, and do nothing else; though within all that, the women get the lighter duties, because of the weakness of their sex. And the man who laughs at naked women exercising for the sake of what's best — his laughter plucks

'Then let the guardians' women strip for exercise, since their excellence will be their clothing, and let them share in war and in the defense of the country. Only in dividing up the work, the lighter tasks should go to the women, because they're the weaker, but otherwise their duties are the same. And as for the man who laughs at the sight of women exercising naked for the best of reasons, he's a man harvesting',
'the unripe fruit of wisdom,'
'"the unripe fruit of his own wit,"',
and he doesn't know, it seems, what he's laughing at or what he's doing. For it is, and always will be, the finest of sayings: what helps is beautiful, and what harms is ugly.
'and he has no idea what he's laughing at or what he's doing. For it always has been, and always will be, the best of sayings: what's useful is fine, and what's harmful is shameful.'
Absolutely.
'Very true.'

Say, then, that we've escaped one wave of our law about women — and weren't altogether drowned for decreeing that our guardian men and guardian women must share every pursuit. The argument stayed in agreement with itself: what it proposes is possible, and beneficial too.

'So here's one wave in our law about women that we can say we've now ridden out. It hasn't swallowed us alive for laying down that the guardians, men and women alike, should share all their pursuits. The argument's own consistency bears witness both that the thing is useful and that it's possible.'
It was no small wave you escaped, either.
'Yes, that was a mighty wave you've gotten past.'
You won't call it big, I said, once you see the one after it.
'And you'll think it was nothing,' I said, 'once you see the one that's coming.'
Go on, then — show me.
'Go on, then. Let me see it.'

This law follows from that one, I said, and from everything that came before. Here it is: these women are to belong to all these men in common; no woman is to live privately with any man; and the children are to be common too — no parent to know his own child, no child his parent.

'The law that follows from this one, and from everything before it, runs like this: that these women are all to be shared in common among these men, and none is to live privately with any man; and the children too are to be shared in common, and no parent is to know his own child, nor any child his parent.'
That's a far bigger wave than the other, he said. Whether it's even possible — and whether it would do any good — both invite real disbelief.
'That,' he said, 'is a far bigger wave than the other. There'll be much more doubt both about whether it could be done and about whether it would do any good.'

On the good of it, I said, I don't think anyone would argue — deny that sharing the women and sharing the children would be the greatest of goods — if it were possible. But whether it's possible or not: that, I expect, is where the fight will be.

'As to its doing good,' I said, 'I don't think there can be much dispute that having women and children in common would be an enormous benefit, if it were possible. The possibility is the other matter, and that's where the real argument will be.'
Both points, he said, could be fought over quite well.
'I think there's plenty of room for doubt on both counts.'
You mean I face the arguments in coalition, I said. I thought I'd slip away from one of them — if you agreed the thing was beneficial, I'd be left with only the question of possibility.

'You mean we have to fight on two fronts at once,' I said. 'I was hoping to slip away from one of them, by getting you to grant the usefulness, so that only the question of possibility would be left.'
You were spotted making your getaway, he said. Defend both.
'Well, your little maneuver's been spotted,' he said. 'So you'll have to defend both.'

Then I'll take my punishment, I said. But do me this one kindness: let me have a holiday of the mind, the way lazy-minded men feast on their own thoughts when they walk alone. Men like that don't wait to discover how their desires might actually come true. They skip all that, to spare themselves the labor of deliberating over what's possible and what isn't; they assume they have what they want, and go straight to arranging everything else — happily rehearsing all they'll do when it's real — making an idle soul idler still. Well, I'm going soft the same way. I want to put off the question of whether it's possible until later; for now, assuming it's possible — with your permission — I'll examine how the rulers will arrange it all when it comes about, and show that nothing could be more beneficial to the city and its guardians than these arrangements in practice. That's what we'll examine together first, and the other question after — if you allow it.

'All right, I accept my sentence,' I said. 'But do me one small favor. Let me feed my mind on the dream a while, the way people daydream as they walk along alone. Before they've worked out any means of getting what they want, which is a question that never troubles them, they'd rather not tire themselves wondering whether it's possible. They simply assume they already have what they're after and go straight on planning, delighting in spelling out everything they'll do once the wish has come true, the way idle minds go slack instead of doing any real good. I'm starting to go soft myself, so with your permission I'd like to put off the question of possibility for now. I'll assume the thing can be done and go straight to how the rulers would carry it out, and I'll show that nothing would do more good for the state and its guardians. I'll work through the benefits first, with your help, if you don't mind, and come back to the question of possibility afterward.'
Permission granted, he said — proceed.
'I don't mind. Go ahead.'

I think, I said, that if our rulers are worthy of the name — and their auxiliaries likewise — the auxiliaries will be willing to carry out orders, and the rulers willing to give them: obeying the laws themselves in some things, and imitating their spirit in whatever we leave to their judgment.

'Well then. If our rulers, and their helpers under them, are to deserve the names they carry, the one must be willing to obey and the other able to command. The rulers themselves must obey the laws, and in whatever details are left to their own judgment they must act in the laws' spirit.'
That's fitting, he said.
'That's right.'

Then you, their lawgiver, I said, will do with the women just what you did with the men: select them — as near as possible of the same nature — and hand them over to them. And since their houses and mess-tables are common, and no one owns anything of that private kind, they'll be together — mingled in the gymnasiums and in the whole of their upbringing — and driven by an inborn necessity, I think, toward coupling with one another. Or doesn't 'necessity' sound right to you?

'You, then, as their lawgiver,' I said, 'having picked out the men, will pick out the women in the same way and assign them to the men, matching them as far as possible in nature. And since they share common houses and common meals, with no one owning anything privately, they'll live together, mingle together in the gymnasium and the rest of their daily life, and so be drawn together by an inner necessity to mate with one another. Or doesn't "necessity" seem to you the right word?'
Not a geometer's necessity, he said, but a lover's — which is probably sharper than the other at compelling and persuading the run of mankind.
'Necessity,' he said, 'not the geometer's kind, but the kind lovers know, which is far better at persuading and compelling most people.'
Much sharper, I said. But next point, Glaucon: disorder in the couplings, or in anything else, is an unholy thing in a city of the blessed, and the rulers won't allow it.
'Quite so,' I said. 'But Glaucon, all this, like everything else, has to go in an orderly way. In a city of the blessed, promiscuity would be an unholy thing, and the rulers won't allow it.'
No, he said — because it isn't just.
'No,' he said, 'it shouldn't be allowed.'
Then clearly our next task is to make the marriages as sacred as we can. And the sacred ones will be the ones that do the most good.
'Then clearly the next step is to make marriage as sacred as we can, and the most beneficial marriages will be the ones counted most sacred.'
Absolutely.
'Exactly.'

So how will they do the most good? Tell me this, Glaucon — I see hunting dogs at your house, and a whole yard of fine game-birds. Have you, by Zeus, paid attention to their matings and their breeding?

'And how do we make marriages most beneficial? Tell me this, Glaucon, I ask because I see hunting dogs in your house, and quite a few fine birds. Have you ever paid attention to how they pair and breed?'
What about them? he said.
'In what way?' he asked.
First: among them, though they're all fine stock, aren't there some that are, and prove to be, the best?
'Well, first of all, even though they're all of good stock, aren't some of them better than the rest?'
There are.
'They are.'
And do you breed from all of them alike — or take care to breed from the best?
'And do you breed from all of them alike, or are you careful to breed only from the best?'
From the best.
'Only from the best.'
And from the youngest? The oldest? Or, as far as you can, from those in their prime?
'And do you breed from the youngest, or the oldest, or those in their prime?'
From those in their prime.
'Those in their prime.'
And if they weren't bred that way, you'd expect your birds and your dogs to turn out far worse stock?
'And if you didn't breed carefully, you'd expect your dogs and birds to deteriorate badly?'
I would.
'Certainly.'
And horses, I said, and the other animals? Any different?
'And it's the same with horses, and animals in general?'
It would be strange if it were.
'Of course.'
Ye gods, my dear friend, I said — then what surpassingly skilled rulers we're going to need, if the same holds for the human race.
'Good heavens, my friend,' I said. 'If the same holds for human beings, what consummate skill our rulers are going to need.'
It does hold, he said. But why the surpassing skill?
'It does hold,' he said. 'But why does it call for any special skill?'

Because, I said, they'll be forced to use a great deal of medicine. With bodies, you know, when they don't need drugs and will submit to a regimen, we think an ordinary doctor will do. But when drugs are required, we know a bolder doctor is called for.

'Because,' I said, 'our rulers will have to dose the body of the city with a good deal of medicine. You know that when patients don't need drugs but only need to follow a regimen, we think even a second-rate doctor will do. But when drugs have to be given, we know it takes a bolder physician.'
True. But what are you driving at?
'True, but what are you driving at?'

This, I said: it looks as if our rulers will have to use falsehood and deception on a large scale — for the benefit of the ruled. And we said, remember, that all such things are useful in the way a drug is useful.

'I mean,' I said, 'that our rulers will probably have to use a fair dose of falsehood and deception for the good of those they rule. We did say, didn't we, that such things, used as medicine, could be useful.'
And we were right.
'And we were right.'
Well, in the marriages and the making of children, this 'right use' turns out to be no small thing.
'Well, it looks as if this lawful use of them will be needed often, in arranging marriages and births.'
How so?
'How so?'

It follows from what we've agreed, I said, that the best men must lie with the best women as often as possible, and the worst men with the worst women as rarely as possible; and the children of the best must be reared, and the children of the worst must not — if the flock is to stay at the peak of its quality. And all this has to happen with no one knowing but the rulers themselves — if the guardians' herd is also to stay as free of infighting as possible.

'It follows from what we've agreed,' I said, 'that the best men should mate with the best women as often as possible, and the inferior with the inferior as seldom as possible; and that the children of the first sort should be raised, but not the children of the second, if the flock is to stay first-rate. And all this has to happen without anyone knowing but the rulers themselves, if our herd of guardians is to be kept as free as possible of strife.'
Completely right, he said.
'Very true.'

Then we'll have festivals established by law, where we'll bring the brides and grooms together — with sacrifices, and hymns our poets will compose to fit the weddings. The number of the marriages we'll put in the rulers' hands, so that — reckoning in wars and disease and everything of the kind — they can hold the number of men as steady as they can, and our city, as far as possible, grows neither great nor small.

'So we'll need to establish certain festivals at which we bring the brides and grooms together, with sacrifices, and wedding songs composed by our poets to fit the occasion. The number of marriages we'll leave to the rulers, so they can keep the population as steady as possible, taking into account losses from war and disease and the like, and keep the city, as far as they can, from growing too large or too small.'
Right, he said.
'Right.'
Then I think we'll have to invent an ingenious kind of lottery, so that at every pairing our inferior man blames his luck, and not the rulers.
'And we'll have to devise some clever system of lots, so that on each occasion the less worthy man, when he ends up unmatched, blames his bad luck and not the rulers.'
Very much so, he said.
'Of course.'

And the young men who prove themselves in war or elsewhere — among the honors and prizes we give them, I think, should be a freer license with the women; that way, under cover of the prize, we get the most children sown from men of that sort.

'And I should think that among the other honors and prizes we give our braver and better young men, we'll grant them more frequent permission to lie with the women. It will look like a reward for their courage, and at the same time it gives us an excuse for fathering as many children as possible on such men.'
Right.
'Right.'
And the officers appointed over these matters — men or women or both, since offices, I take it, are open to women and men alike —
'And the newborns are taken over by officials appointed for the purpose, whether men or women or both, since of course our offices are open to women as well as men.'
Yes —
'Yes.'

— will take the children of the good, I think, and carry them into the pen, to nurses who live apart in a certain quarter of the city. The children of the inferior — and any child of the others born defective — they'll hide away in a secret and unspoken place, as is fitting.

'These officials will take the children of the good parents to a sort of nursery, to nurses living apart in a separate quarter of the city. But the children of the inferior parents, and any born defective to the others, they'll quietly put away, out of sight, as is proper.'
Yes, he said — if the guardians' breed is to stay pure.
'Yes,' he said, 'if the breed of the guardians is to be kept pure.'

And they'll take charge of the feeding too — bringing the mothers to the pen when their milk comes in, while contriving every contrivance so that no mother knows her own child; and supplying other women with milk if the mothers run short. They'll watch that the mothers don't nurse too long; and the sleepless nights, and all the rest of the labor, they'll hand to the nurses and attendants.

'And these officials will see to the children's feeding, bringing the mothers to the nursery when their breasts are full, but taking every precaution that no mother recognizes her own child. They'll bring in other wet nurses if more are needed. They'll see that the mothers don't nurse too long, and hand over the night feedings and the rest of the trouble to nurses and attendants.'
You're describing a very easy sort of child-bearing, he said, for the guardians' wives.
'You're making childbearing an easy life for the guardians' women.'
As is proper, I said. Now let's take up the next point of our plan. We said the children should come from parents in their prime.
'And so it should be,' I said. 'But let's get on with the plan. We said the parents should be in the prime of life.'
True.
'We did.'
And do you agree with me that the prime lasts, at a fair estimate, twenty years for a woman and thirty for a man?
'And do you agree that the prime of life is about twenty years for a woman and thirty for a man?'
Which years?
'Which years do you mean?'
A woman, I said, bears for the city from twenty to forty. A man begets for the city from the time he's past his fastest years as a runner until he's fifty-five.

'A woman,' I said, 'should bear children for the state from the age of twenty to the age of forty; a man should beget them from the time he's past his sharpest speed, around twenty-five, until he's fifty-five.'
In both, at least, he said, that's the prime of body and of mind.
'Yes,' he said, 'those are the years of physical and mental prime in both.'

Then if a man older or younger than that puts his hand to the making of children for the commonwealth, we'll call it an offense — unholy and unjust. He is raising up for the city a child that, if it escapes notice and gets born, will have been conceived without the sacrifices and without the prayers that priestesses and priests and the whole city will offer at every wedding festival — that from good parents, better children may be born, and from useful parents, more useful ones. This child is begotten in darkness instead, the fruit of a terrible failure of self-command.

'So if a man older or younger than this takes part in fathering children for the community, we'll call it an offense against religion and against right. The child he's gotten, if it slips into life, will have been conceived without the sacrifices and prayers that priestesses and priests and the whole city offer at every marriage festival, praying that the new generation may be better and more useful than their good and useful parents. His child, instead, will be the offspring of darkness and lawless lust.'
Right, he said.
'Very true.'

The same law holds, I said, if a man still of begetting age touches a woman of bearing age without a ruler joining their hands. We'll say he's foisting a bastard on the city — unsanctioned and unconsecrated.

'The same law applies if a man still within the proper age touches one of the women in her prime without a ruler's sanction. We'll say he's foisting a bastard on the state, unauthorized and unconsecrated.'
Completely right, he said.
'Very true.'

But when the women and the men pass beyond the age of breeding, I imagine we'll set them free to couple with whomever they please — except a daughter or a mother, a daughter's daughters or a mother's line before her; and the women likewise, except a son or a father and their line down or up — and all this only after we've charged them to be careful, above all, that not a single conception, if they can help it, ever sees the light; and if one forces its way through, to dispose of it on the understanding that there is no rearing for such a child.

'But this holds only while they're within the prescribed ages. After that, we'll let men and women associate freely with whomever they like, except that a man may not touch his daughter or his daughter's daughter, his mother or his mother's mother, and a woman may not touch her son or his son, her father or his father, and so on in either direction. And we grant this freedom only on the strict condition that they do everything they can to see that no child comes of these unions; or if one forces its way to birth, they must understand that no provision will be made for raising it, and act accordingly.'
That's all reasonably said, he replied. But fathers and daughters, and the kin you just named — how will they tell each other apart?
'That too is reasonable,' he said. 'But how are they to tell who's father and daughter, and the rest, if no one knows?'

They won't, I said. Instead: counting from the day a man becomes a bridegroom, whatever children are born in the tenth month after — or the seventh — he will call his sons and daughters, boys and girls, and they will call him father; their children in turn he'll call grandchildren, and they'll call his generation grandfathers and grandmothers. And all the children born in the season when their mothers and fathers were making children will call one another brothers and sisters — which is exactly what will keep them from touching one another, as we just said. Though the law will let brothers and sisters live together, if the lot falls that way and the oracle at Delphi confirms it besides.

'They won't,' I said. 'But it'll work like this. Counting from the day of any marriage festival, a man will call all the children born in the seventh and tenth month after it his sons and daughters, and they'll call him father; he'll call their children his grandchildren, and they'll call him and his generation grandfathers and grandmothers; and all the children conceived in the same season, when their fathers and mothers were paired, will count as brothers and sisters, and these, as I said, won't intermarry. The law won't forbid brothers and sisters absolutely, though: if the lot falls their way and the oracle at Delphi consents, it will allow it.'
Completely right, he said.
'Quite right,' he said.

This, then, Glaucon, is how the guardians of your city hold their women and children in common. That it's consistent with the rest of the constitution — and by far the best arrangement — is what the argument has to establish next, isn't it? Or how shall we proceed?

'So that, Glaucon, is how the guardians of our state are to hold their women and children in common. Now we need the argument to confirm that this arrangement fits the rest of our constitution, and that nothing could be better. Isn't that the next thing?'
That way, by Zeus, he said.
'Yes, certainly.'

Then isn't this the first step toward agreement — asking ourselves what we can name as the greatest good in the framing of a city, the thing a lawgiver aims at when he lays down the laws, and what as the greatest evil; and then examining whether what we've just gone through walks in the tracks of the good, and out of the tracks of the evil?

'Then let's start by asking ourselves this: what should a lawmaker aim at, above all, in framing laws and ordering a state? What's the greatest good, and what's the greatest evil? Then we can ask whether what we've described bears the stamp of the good or of the evil.'
By all means.
'By all means.'
Well then: do we know a greater evil for a city than whatever tears it apart and makes it many instead of one? Or a greater good than what binds it together and makes it one?
'Is there any greater evil for a state than what splits it apart and makes it many instead of one? Or any greater good than what binds it together and makes it one?'
We don't.
'There isn't.'
And the sharing of pleasure and pain binds it — when, as far as may be, all the citizens rejoice and grieve alike at the same gains and the same losses?
'And isn't a state bound into one when its citizens share their pleasures and pains, all glad together and all grieved together over the same gains and losses?'
Absolutely, he said.
'No doubt of it.'
While making such feelings private dissolves it — when at the same event, striking the city or its people, some are in agony and others celebrate?
'Whereas it's torn apart when feeling isn't shared but private, when the same events in the city or among the citizens leave one set of people overjoyed and another plunged in grief?'
Of course.
'Certainly.'
And doesn't that begin here — when the citizens no longer say the words 'mine' and 'not mine' together, about the same things? And the same with 'somebody else's'?
'And doesn't that kind of split come from people not saying "mine" and "not mine" about the same things, and the same with "his" and "not his"?'
Exactly so.
'Exactly.'
Then the best-run city is the one in which the most people say 'mine' and 'not mine' about the same things, in the same way?
'So the best-ordered state is the one where the largest number of people apply the words "mine" and "not mine" in the same way to the same thing?'
By far.
'Quite true.'

And such a city stands closest to the condition of a single human being. Think of what happens when one of our fingers is hurt. The whole partnership stretched from body to soul, ordered into one system under its ruling part, feels the hurt — the whole of it aches together with the aching part — and so we say the man has a pain in his finger. And the same account holds for any part of a man: pain when a part suffers, pleasure when it mends.

'The state, in other words, that comes closest to a single person. When one of us hurts a finger, the whole partnership of body and soul, organized as one thing under the ruling part within it, feels the hurt and suffers along with the part that's hurt, and we say the man has a pain in his finger. It's the same with any other part of him, whether it suffers pain or finds relief.'
The same, he said. And to your question: the best-governed city lives closest to that condition.
'It is,' he said. 'And I agree, the best-ordered state comes nearest to this shared feeling you describe.'
Then whenever one citizen meets with anything good or bad, a city like that will above all call the experience its own — and the whole of it will rejoice with him, or hurt with him.
'So when anything good or bad happens to one of its citizens, a state like this will take his case as its own, and the whole city will rejoice or grieve with him?'
Necessarily, he said — in a well-governed one.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's what happens in a well-run state.'
Time now, I said, to go back to our own city and check it against the argument's terms — whether it fits them best, or some other city fits them better.
'Then it's time,' I said, 'to go back to our own state and see whether it, or some other arrangement, best matches these principles.'
Let's.
'Very good.'
Well: in our city, as in every other, there are rulers and there are the people?
'Our state, like every other, has rulers and ruled?'
There are.
'It does.'
And they all call one another citizens?
'All of whom call one another citizens?'
Of course.
'Of course.'
But besides 'citizens,' what do people in other cities call their rulers?
'But in other states, what do the people call their rulers, besides citizens?'
In most, masters; in the democracies, exactly this name — rulers.
'In most they call them masters; in democracies they just call them rulers.'
And the people in ours? Besides citizens, what will they call the rulers?
'And in our state, what name do the people give the rulers besides citizens?'
Saviors, he said, and helpers.
'Saviors and protectors,' he said.
And the rulers — what will they call the people?
'And what do the rulers call the people?'
Their paymasters and providers.
'Their providers and supporters.'
And in other cities, what do rulers call the people?
'And in other states, what do rulers call the people?'
Slaves.
'Slaves.'
And rulers there — what do they call each other?
'And what do rulers in other states call one another?'
Fellow rulers.
'Fellow rulers.'
And ours?
'And in ours?'
Fellow guardians.
'Fellow guardians.'
Now, in other cities: can you name a ruler who addresses one colleague as family and another as an outsider?
'Now, in other states, can a ruler speak of one of his colleagues as a friend and another as no friend of his?'
Yes — plenty do.
'Yes, often enough.'
And the family one he thinks of and speaks of as his own; the outsider as not his own?
'And he thinks and speaks of the friend as one of his own, and the other as an outsider, no concern of his?'
Just so.
'Exactly.'
And your guardians? Could any of them think of a fellow guardian as an outsider — or address him as one?
'But would any of your guardians ever think or speak of a fellow guardian as an outsider?'
Never, he said. In everyone he meets he'll see a brother or a sister, a father or a mother, a son or a daughter — or the children or the parents of these.
'Never,' he said. 'Everyone he meets he'll regard as a brother or sister, a father or mother, a son or daughter, or the child or parent of one of these.'

Beautifully said, I replied. But tell me this too: will your laws give them only the names of kinship, or every act that goes with the names? Toward the fathers, everything custom commands toward fathers — the respect, the care, the obedience owed to parents — on pain of standing badly with gods and with men, since anything else would be neither holy nor just? Will these be the sayings that ring in the children's ears from the whole city, from earliest childhood, about the men pointed out as their fathers, and about the rest of their kin — or something else?

'Well put,' I said. 'But tell me one more thing. Will they be family in name only, or will they back the name up in everything they do? Take the word "father." Will it carry with it a father's care, and the reverence and obedience the law commands toward a parent, so that a man who fails in these is seen as godless and unjust, the kind no one expects much good of from gods or men? Are these to be the refrains the children hear from everyone, from the moment they're told who their parents and kin are, or not?'
These, he said. It would be laughable if kinship names were only mouthed, with none of the acts behind them.
'These and no others,' he said. 'For what could be more ridiculous than mouthing the names of family ties without living up to them?'
Then in our city more than any other, when a single citizen fares well or badly, they'll all say the words together — the concord we named just now: 'mine is doing well,' or 'mine is doing badly.'
'So in our city, more than in any other, when things go well or badly with one of them, all will say with one voice, "It goes well with me" or "It goes badly with me."'
Completely true, he said.
'Very true.'
And didn't we say that shared pleasures and pains follow along with this conviction, and with this way of speaking?
'And we said this way of speaking and thinking goes hand in hand with sharing their pleasures and pains?'
We did — and rightly.
'Yes, and so they will.'
Then our citizens, more than any others, will hold one and the same thing in common, the thing they call 'mine' — and holding it so, they'll share, more than any others, one pain and one pleasure?
'They'll share a common interest in the same thing, which they'll all call their own, and sharing it, they'll share the same pleasure and pain?'
Much more.
'Far more than in other states.'
And the cause of it — over and above the rest of the constitution — is the guardians' having women and children in common?
'And the cause of this, on top of the rest of the constitution, is the guardians' holding women and children in common?'
The chief cause by far, he said.
'That, above all.'
But we agreed this sharing is the greatest good for a city — comparing a well-run city to a body, and the way it stands toward the pain and pleasure of its parts.
'And we agreed this unity of feeling is the greatest good for a state, comparing a well-ordered state to a body sharing in the pleasure and pain of its parts?'
And rightly agreed, he said.
'We did, and rightly.'
Then the cause of the greatest good to our city has shown itself: the community of children and women among its defenders.
'Then the community of women and children among our guardians is clearly the source of the greatest good to the state?'
Completely, he said.
'Certainly.'

And notice — this agrees with what we settled before. We said, didn't we, that they must have no private houses, no land, no possessions at all; that they'd take their keep from the other citizens as wages for their guarding, and spend it all in common — if they were going to be guardians in fact.

'And this fits what we said before, that the guardians were to have no houses or land or any other property; their pay was to be their keep, provided by the other citizens, and they'd have no private expenses, so that they could stay true guardians.'
Right, he said.
'Right.'

Then isn't it as I say: the earlier rules and these new ones together make them even more truly guardians — keeping them from tearing the city to pieces by calling 'mine' not the same thing but each a different thing, one man hauling into his own private house whatever he can get apart from the others, another into his different house, to a different wife and different children, breeding private pleasures and private griefs over private things? Instead, sharing one conviction about what is their own, and straining toward the same mark, they'll all feel — as far as human beings can — one pain and one pleasure together.

'So both arrangements, the shared property and the shared family, make them more truly guardians. They won't tear the city apart by disagreeing over what's "mine" and "not mine," each man hauling whatever he's gotten off into his own private house, with his own private wife and children and his own private pleasures and pains. No, they'll all be moved as far as possible by the same pleasures and pains, because they're all of one mind about what's near and dear to them, and so they all pull toward a single goal.'
Exactly so, he said.
'Just so.'

And what about lawsuits and prosecutions? Won't they all but vanish among them, since they own nothing but their bodies and hold everything else in common? Every quarrel people fall into over money or children or kin — our guardians will be clean of all of it.

'And since they have nothing they can call their own but their bodies, there'll be no lawsuits and no accusations among them. They'll be free of all the quarrels people fall into over money, children, and relatives.'
They'll be well rid of it.
'They'll have to be.'
Nor could suits for violence or assault fairly arise among them. Between men of an age, we'll say, defending yourself is fine and just — imposing on them the necessity of keeping their bodies fit.

'Nor will there be any prosecutions for assault or insult among them. We'll say it's a fine and proper thing for a man to defend himself against an equal, and that protecting one's own body is a duty.'
Right, he said.
'That's good,' he said.
And there's another good in the law: a man whose temper flares and is satisfied on the spot, one on one, is less likely to push the quarrel on to something bigger.
'And there's a further benefit in this law: if a man does get angry with another, he'll vent his anger then and there, and it won't grow into something more dangerous.'
Certainly.
'Certainly.'
The older, meanwhile, will be charged with ruling and disciplining all the younger.
'The older man will be given authority to rule and discipline the younger.'
Clearly.
'Clearly.'

And a younger man will never lay hands on an elder or strike him — unless the rulers command it — nor, I think, dishonor him any other way. Two guards stand in his way, and they're enough: shame and fear. Shame bars him from touching anyone who might be his parent; fear tells him the others will come to the victim's aid — some as his sons, some as his brothers, some as his fathers.

'And it's plain the younger man won't strike an elder or do him any other violence, unless the rulers order it, and won't show him disrespect either. Two guardians will hold him back, shame and fear: shame, which keeps a man from laying hands on those who stand to him as parents; and fear that the injured man's many defenders, his brothers and sons and fathers, will rush to his aid.'
That's how it works out, he said.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's how it would go.'
Then under these laws, every way you look at it, the men will keep the peace with one another?
'So in every way the laws will help these men keep peace with one another?'
Deep peace.
'Yes, there'll be plenty of peace.'
And with no quarrel among the guardians themselves, there's no fear that the rest of the city will ever split against them, or against itself.
'And since the guardians won't quarrel among themselves, there's no danger the rest of the city will break into factions, either against them or against each other.'
No fear at all.
'None at all.'

As for the pettiest of the evils they'd be rid of, I hesitate even to mention them — they're so unseemly. The poor flattering the rich. All the strain and ache of raising children and scraping up the money a household devours: borrowing here, defaulting there, getting it any way they can and handing it over to their wives and slaves to manage. Everything men suffer on that front, my friend — it's obvious, and ignoble, and not worth the words.

'There are smaller miseries they'll be rid of too, though I'm almost ashamed to mention them, they're so petty: the flattery of the rich by the poor, the whole grind of raising a household and scraping together money, the borrowing and then denying the debt, the getting of cash by any means and handing it over to wife and slaves to manage. All the many indignities people put up with in this line are obvious and beneath mention.'
Obvious to a blind man, he said.
'Obvious indeed,' he said. 'A man doesn't need eyes to see them.'
Rid of all that, they'll live a life more blessed than the life of Olympic victors.
'They'll be freed from all of it, and their life will be blessed, more blessed even than the life of victors at the Olympic games.'
How so?
'How so?'

The Olympic victor is counted happy for a small part of what our guardians have. Their victory is finer, and their keep at the public expense more complete. The victory they win is the preservation of the entire city; the crown they wear — they and their children too — is food and everything else a life requires. They take honors from their own city while they live, and when they die, a worthy burial.

'The Olympic victor,' I said, 'is counted happy for winning only a fraction of what's secured to our citizens. Their victory is the finer one, and their keep at the public expense more complete. For the prize they've won is nothing less than the salvation of the whole state, and the crown set on them and their children is everything life needs. They're honored by their country while they live, and given an honorable burial when they die.'
Fine prizes, he said.
'Yes,' he said, 'those are glorious rewards.'

Do you remember, I said, that earlier in the argument somebody's objection — never mind whose — hit us: that we weren't making our guardians happy, since they could have everything the citizens have and yet had nothing? And we answered, didn't we, that we'd look into that later if occasion arose, but for now we were making our guardians guardians and the city as happy as we could — we weren't shaping one class in it for happiness at the expense of the whole.

'Do you remember,' I said, 'how earlier on someone, who shall stay nameless, accused us of making our guardians miserable, men who could have owned everything and instead owned nothing? And we answered that we'd take that up another time if the chance came, but for now we were making our guardians true guardians, and shaping the state with a view to the greatest happiness not of any one class but of the whole?'
I remember, he said.
'Yes, I remember.'

Well then — now that the life of our defenders shows itself far finer and better than any Olympic victor's, is there any comparing it with the life of the shoemakers, or the other craftsmen, or the farmers?

'Well, now that the life of our protectors turns out to be far better and nobler than an Olympic victor's, is there any comparing it with the life of a shoemaker, or any other craftsman, or a farmer?'
I'd say not, he said.
'Certainly not.'

Still, it's fair to repeat here what I said back then: if a guardian ever tries to be happy in a way that unmakes him as a guardian — if this measured, steady life, the best there is by our account, doesn't satisfy him, and some senseless, boyish notion of happiness gets into his head and drives him to use his strength to grab everything in the city for himself — he'll learn that Hesiod was truly wise when he said the half is somehow more than the whole.

'Still, I'll repeat here what I said before: if any of our guardians tries to be happy in a way that stops him being a guardian, if he isn't content with this safe and harmonious life, which we judge to be the best of all, but gets some foolish, youthful notion of happiness into his head and tries to seize the whole state for himself, he'll learn how wise Hesiod was when he said that, somehow, the half is more than the whole.'
If he asks my advice, he said, he'll stay with this life.
'If he asked my advice,' he said, 'I'd tell him to stay where he is, with a life like that on offer.'

Then you accept it, I said — this partnership of the women with the men that we've gone through: education, children, and the guarding of the other citizens; that whether they stay in the city or go out to war, they guard together and hunt together like hounds, and share everything in every way they can; and that in doing all this they'll be doing what's best, and nothing contrary to the nature of female and male, nothing against the way the two are naturally made to partner with each other.

'You agree, then,' I said, 'that the men and women are to share their whole way of life, as we've described, sharing their education, sharing their children, and sharing the work of guarding the citizens, whether at home or out at war, keeping watch and hunting together like dogs, and in all things, as far as they're able, the women sharing with the men? And in doing this they'll do what's best, and won't violate the natural relation of the sexes but preserve it.'
I accept it, he said.
'I agree.'
Then what remains, I said, is to settle whether it's actually possible — among human beings as among the other animals — for this partnership to come about; and if so, how.
'Then what's left to ask,' I said, 'is whether such a community is even possible among human beings, as it is among other animals, and if so, how.'
You beat me to it, he said — I was about to say exactly that.
'You've taken the words out of my mouth,' he said.
As for their conduct of war, I said, I think the way of it is plain to see.
'As for the war part,' I said, 'there's no difficulty seeing how they'll manage that.'
How?
'How do you mean?'

They'll campaign together, men and women alike — and take the children with them to war, the sturdy ones, so that like every other craftsman's children they can watch the work they'll do themselves when they're grown. And beyond watching, they'll fetch and serve in everything the war requires, and attend on their fathers and their mothers. Haven't you seen how it goes in the trades — how the potters' children spend a long time watching and helping before they ever put hand to a pot?

'They'll go on campaign together, of course, and take along any of their children who are old enough, so the young ones can watch the work they'll have to do as adults, the way an artisan's child watches the trade. And besides watching, they'll help out and make themselves useful in war, and wait on their fathers and mothers. Haven't you noticed in the crafts how a potter's boys watch and assist for a long time before they ever touch the wheel?'
I have.
'I have.'
And should potters train their children more carefully than the guardians train theirs — with hands-on experience and a full view of what their work will be?
'And should potters take more care than our guardians to school their children by letting them watch and practice their work?'
That would be laughable, he said.
'That would be absurd.'
Besides, every living thing fights harder with its young looking on.
'Besides, every creature fights harder in the presence of its young, and the same goes for our guardians.'

So it does. But there's no small risk, Socrates. If they're beaten — and war is full of defeats — they'll lose their children's lives along with their own, and the rest of the city will never recover.
'True, Socrates. But there's a real danger here, the kind that often comes in war: if they're defeated, they lose the children along with themselves, and the state can never recover.'
True, I said. But tell me first: do you think our aim should be to arrange that they never risk anything at all?
'True,' I said. 'But would you have them run no risk at all, ever?'
Not at all.
'Far from it.'
Well — if they're ever to take risks, shouldn't it be the kind where success makes them better?
'Well, then, if they're ever to face danger, shouldn't it be the kind that, if they come through it, leaves them the better for it?'
Clearly.
'Clearly.'
And you think it makes little difference — not worth a risk — whether boys who are to be men of war see war as boys, or don't?
'And isn't it important enough, whether men who are to be soldiers see war in their youth or not, to be worth running some risk for?'
No — it matters, in the way you mean.
'Yes, very important.'
Then start from this: the children are to be spectators of war, and we're to contrive their safety — and then all's well, isn't it?
'So our first step is to make our children spectators of war. But we must also see to it they're kept safe, and then all will be well.'
Yes.
'Right.'
Now first, I said, their fathers won't be ignorant of war; they'll know, as far as human beings can, which campaigns are dangerous and which are not.
'Now their parents, presumably, won't be blind to the dangers of war, but will know as well as human foresight allows which campaigns are safe and which dangerous?'
Likely so, he said.
'We can assume that.'
So they'll bring the children to the safe ones, and think hard before bringing them to the others.
'So they'll bring the children along on the safe ones and steer clear of the dangerous?'
Right.
'Yes.'
And they'll set commanders over them — not the most expendable men, but those fit by experience and age to lead children and look after them.
'And they'll put them under the command of seasoned veterans, fit to be their leaders and teachers?'
As is proper.
'As they should.'
Still, we'll say — the unexpected has happened to many men, many times.
'Still, the dangers of war can't always be foreseen; there's a lot of chance in it.'
Very much so.
'True.'
Then against such chances, my friend, we should wing the children from the first — so that when it comes to it, they can fly away and escape.
'Then against just such chances, the children should be fitted with wings from the start, so they can fly off and escape if the need arises.'
What do you mean? he said.
'What do you mean?' he asked.

We must mount them on horses, I said, as young as possible; and once they're taught to ride, bring them to the watching on horseback — not on spirited or warlike animals, but on the fastest and most obedient we have. That way they'll get the best look at their own future work, and, if it's needed, the surest escape — following their older leaders to safety.

'I mean we should put them on horseback in their earliest years, and once they've learned to ride, take them mounted to see the fighting. The horses mustn't be spirited war-horses, but the gentlest we can find that are still fast. That way the children get a good look at what will one day be their own work, and if danger comes they only have to follow their elder leaders and ride to safety.'
I think you're right, he said.
'I think you're right,' he said.

Now to the war itself, I said. How should your soldiers deal with one another, and with the enemy? Tell me if I see it rightly. Any of them who deserts his post, or throws away his weapons, or does anything else of that cowardly kind — shouldn't he be demoted to craftsman or farmer?

'Now as for war itself, how should your soldiers behave toward one another and toward the enemy? I'd suggest that any soldier who deserts his post, or throws away his weapons, or shows any other cowardice, should be demoted to the rank of farmer or craftsman. What do you say?'
By all means.
'By all means.'
And a man taken alive by the enemy — shouldn't we make a present of him to his captors, to do with their catch whatever they please?
'And the man who lets himself be taken alive, we may as well make a gift of him to his captors; he's their lawful prize, to do with as they please.'
Exactly.
'Certainly.'

But the man who wins distinction — who proves his worth — don't you think that first, on campaign itself, he should be crowned by his comrades in arms, by each of the young men and boys in turn? Or no?
'But the hero who has distinguished himself, what's to be done with him? First, while still on campaign, he should be crowned in turn by each of the young men who served beside him. What do you say?'
I do.
'I approve.'
And greeted with the right hand?
'And what about each of them clasping his hand?'
That too.
'That too.'
But this next one, I said, I don't think you'll go along with.
'But you'll hardly approve my next proposal.'
What?
'What is it?'
That he kiss, and be kissed by, each of them.
'That he should kiss and be kissed by each of them.'

That above all, he said — and I'll add my own clause to the law: for as long as that campaign lasts, no one he wants to kiss may refuse him; so that any soldier who happens to be in love, with a boy or with a girl, will be all the hungrier to carry off the prize for valor.

'Most of all,' he said. 'And I'd add to the law that, for as long as the campaign lasts, no one he's minded to kiss may refuse him, so that if a man is in love with someone in the army, man or woman, he'll be all the keener to win the prize of valor.'

Good, I said. And we've already said that the brave man will have more marriages ready for him than the others, and be chosen for them oftener than the others, so that the most children possible come from such a man.

'Excellent,' I said. 'And we've already settled that the brave man is to have more marriages than the rest, and to be chosen for them more often than others, so that as many children as possible may be fathered on such a man.'
We did say that.
'We have.'
