And by Homer's rule too, it's just to honor the brave among the young. Homer says that when Ajax distinguished himself in the war, he 'was honored with the long cut off the chine' — the proper honor for a brave man in his prime, being tribute and added strength in one.

'And there's another way, on Homer's authority, that brave young men should be honored. Homer tells how Ajax, after distinguishing himself in battle, was rewarded with the long cut of the chine, a fitting tribute, it seems, to a hero in his prime, since it's both an honor and a thing to build his strength.'
Completely right, he said.
'Quite right.'

Then in this at least we'll follow Homer, I said. At the sacrifices and every occasion like them, we'll honor the brave — in the measure that they've proved brave, women as well as men — with hymns, and with the privileges we just named, and beyond these with

'Then in this,' I said, 'we'll take Homer as our teacher. At sacrifices and the like, we'll honor the brave according to their courage, men and women alike, with hymns and the other distinctions we mentioned, and also with',
'the seat of honor, the best of the meat, and the cup kept full,'
'"seats of honor, and meat, and brimming cups,"',
so that in honoring our brave men and women, we're training them at the same time.
'and in honoring them this way, we'll be training them at the same time.'
Excellent, he said.
'Excellent,' he said.
Good. And of those who die on campaign — whoever falls with glory, won't we say, first, that he belongs to the golden race?
'And when a man dies gloriously in war, won't we say first of all that he belongs to the golden race?'
Above all.
'Surely.'
And won't we believe Hesiod, that when men of that race die,
'And don't we have Hesiod's word for it that when men of that race die,',
'they become pure spirits dwelling upon the earth, noble beings, protectors against evil, guardians of mortal men'?
'"they become holy spirits upon the earth, doers of good, wardens against evil, guardians of mortal men"?'
We'll believe him.
'Yes, and we accept his word.'
Then we'll ask the god how the dead of that divine and golden kind ought to be buried, and with what distinctions — and bury them exactly as he directs?
'Then we'll ask the god how we're to bury these godlike, heroic men, and what special honors to give them, and we'll do as he directs.'
Of course.
'By all means.'

And for all time after, we'll tend their graves and kneel at them as at the tombs of divine spirits. And we'll keep the same customs for any who die of old age, or in any other way, when their lives are judged extraordinarily good.

'And forever after we'll revere their graves and kneel at their tombs as at the tombs of spirits. And the same honors will go to any others judged outstandingly good, who die of old age or in any other way.'
That's only just, he said.
'That's quite right,' he said.
Next: how will our soldiers deal with their enemies?
'Next, how should our soldiers treat their enemies?'
Meaning what?
'In what respect?'

First, enslavement. Does it seem just for Greeks to enslave Greek cities? Or should they refuse — as far as it's in their power — and hold the other cities to the same custom: to spare the Greek kind, and be on guard against the whole race falling enslaved to the barbarians?

'Take slavery first. Do you think it right for Greeks to enslave Greek cities, or to stand by while others do it, if they can prevent it? Shouldn't their rule be to spare them, mindful of the danger that the whole Greek race might one day fall under the yoke of foreigners?'
Sparing them, he said, is better — wholly and entirely.
'Sparing them is infinitely better.'
Then they'll own no Greek slave themselves, and counsel the other Greeks the same?
'So they'll hold no Greek as a slave, and advise the other Greeks to do the same.'
By all means, he said. That way they'd turn their force outward, against the barbarians, and keep their hands off one another.
'Certainly,' he said. 'That way they'll stand together against the foreigner and keep their hands off one another.'

And stripping the dead, I said — is it right, after a victory, to strip the fallen of anything besides their weapons? Doesn't it give cowards an excuse not to close with the enemy still fighting — as if crouching over a corpse were the performance of a duty? Many an army has been lost to that kind of plunder.

'And the slain, should the victors strip them of anything but their armor? Doesn't the habit of plundering the dead give cowards an excuse not to face the living? Many an army has been lost before now to this love of loot, with men skulking over corpses, pretending they're doing their duty.'
Many indeed.
'Very true.'

And doesn't it seem grubby and money-grasping — the mark of a small and womanish mind — to strip a corpse: to treat the dead body as your enemy when the real foe has flown off and left behind the tools he fought with? Is it any different from the dog that bites the stone that hit it and never touches the man who threw it?

'And isn't there something low and greedy in robbing a corpse, something mean and womanish in treating the dead body as the enemy when the real enemy has flown off and left only his fighting gear behind? It's like a dog that can't reach the man who threw the stone, and snaps at the stone instead.'
Not a bit different, he said.
'Very like a dog,' he said.
So — no robbing of corpses; and no preventing the enemy from taking up their dead?
'So we'll have nothing to do with stripping the dead, or refusing to let them be buried?'
None, by Zeus, he said.
'Nothing whatever,' he said.

Nor will we carry weapons to the temples as offerings — least of all the weapons of Greeks — not if we care at all for the goodwill of the other Greeks. Sooner, we'll fear pollution in bringing to a shrine spoils stripped from our own kind — unless, of course, the god says otherwise.

'Nor will we hang up captured arms in the temples as offerings, least of all the arms of Greeks, if we mean to keep on good terms with the other Greeks. In fact we have reason to fear that offering up spoils taken from our kinsmen would be a kind of pollution, unless the god himself commands it.'
Completely right, he said.
'Very true.'
And the ravaging of Greek land, the burning of Greek houses — what will your soldiers do to their enemies on that score?
'And what about ravaging Greek land or burning Greek houses? How should our soldiers behave?'
I'd enjoy hearing your opinion, he said.
'I'd be glad to hear your view,' he said.
In mine, I said, they do neither. They take the year's harvest — nothing more. Do you want to know why?
'My judgment is that both should be forbidden, and that they should carry off only the year's harvest. Shall I tell you why?'
Very much.
'Please.'

It looks to me like this: we have these two names, war and civil strife — two names, and two things, sitting on two different kinds of quarrel. The two I mean are the kindred and one's own, on one side; the foreign and alien on the other. Hatred inside the kin is called civil strife; hatred toward the alien is called war.

'It's this. There are two different words, "discord" and "war," and I think they answer to two different things. One names what's internal and at home among kin, the other what's foreign and against outsiders. The strife among one's own we call discord; only the strife with outsiders do we call war.'
Nothing off the mark in that, he said.
'That's a sound distinction.'
Then see if this is on the mark as well. I say the Greek race is its own kin — one household — and to the barbarian world it is foreign and alien.
'And isn't it just as sound to say that the whole Greek race is bound together by blood and kinship, and is foreign and alien to the non-Greek world?'
Well said, he replied.
'Quite right.'

Then when Greeks fight barbarians and barbarians fight Greeks, we'll say they're at war — enemies by nature — and that hatred is to be called war. But when Greeks fight Greeks, we'll say they're friends by nature; that Greece, in such a case, is sick and torn against itself; and that hatred is to be called civil strife.

'So when Greeks fight non-Greeks, and non-Greeks Greeks, we'll say they're at war, being enemies by nature, and this kind of conflict should be called war. But when Greeks fight Greeks, we'll say Greece is sick and torn by discord, since they're friends by nature. That kind of enmity should be called discord.'
I'm content, he said, to see it that way.
'I agree.'

Then look at what we now agree to call civil strife, I said — wherever a city splits and each side wastes the other's fields and burns the other's houses, how abominable the strife seems, and how little either side loves its city. Otherwise they would never have dared shear their own nurse and mother to the bone. The measured thing is for the winners to take the losers' harvest — and to remember that they'll be reconciled someday, that they won't be at war forever.

'Then consider,' I said, 'what happens in a case of what we're calling discord, when a city is divided against itself: if each side lays waste the other's land and burns its houses, how monstrous the feud appears. No true patriot could bring himself to tear at his own nurse and mother. It's bearable for the winners to take the losers' harvest, so long as they remember they mean one day to be reconciled, and don't intend to go on fighting forever.'
That thought belongs to far gentler men, he said, than the other.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's a far better spirit than the other.'
Well then, I said — this city you're founding: won't it be Greek?
'Now the city you're founding will be a Greek city, won't it?'
It has to be, he said.
'It will have to be.'
So its people will be good, and gentle?
'And its citizens will be good and civilized?'
Very much so.
'Very civilized.'
And lovers of Greece? They'll count Greece their own, and share in the shrines all Greeks share?
'And won't they love their fellow Greeks, and think of Greece as their own land, and share in its common shrines?'
Very much that too.
'Most certainly.'
Then any quarrel with Greeks — their own kind — they'll treat as civil strife, and won't even give it the name of war?
'So any conflict with other Greeks, since they're their own people, they'll treat as discord and not call war?'
They won't.
'They won't call it war.'
So they'll quarrel like people who expect to be reconciled?
'And they'll quarrel as men who mean some day to be reconciled?'
Certainly.
'Yes.'
They'll correct their opponents with goodwill — chastening them, not punishing them with slavery and destruction; correctors, not enemies.
'They'll bring their opponents to their senses in a friendly way, not punish them with slavery or destruction; they'll be correctors, not enemies.'
Just so, he said.
'Just so.'

Then, being Greeks, they won't ravage Greece or burn its houses; and they won't accept that everyone in a city is their enemy — men, women, children alike — but only the few who caused the quarrel, always a minority. On all these counts they'll refuse to waste the land or raze the houses of a people who are mostly their friends; and they'll press the conflict only until the guilty are forced to pay by the innocent, who are the ones suffering.

'And being Greeks themselves, they won't lay waste Greek land or burn Greek houses, and they'll never suppose that a whole city, men, women, and children alike, is their enemy. They know the guilt of any quarrel always falls on a few, and that most of the people are their friends. So they'll be reluctant to ruin the land or raze the houses, and they'll press the conflict only until the guilty few are forced by the many innocent sufferers to make amends.'
I agree, he said — that's how our citizens should deal with their opponents; and with the barbarians, the way Greeks now deal with each other.
'I agree,' he said, 'that our citizens should treat their Greek enemies this way, and treat non-Greeks the way Greeks now treat each other.'
Then we lay down this law too for the guardians: no ravaging of land and no burning of houses.
'Then let's lay down this law too for our guardians: they're not to ravage land or burn houses among the Greeks.'
Laid down, he said. It's good — and so is everything we enacted before it.
'Agreed,' he said. 'And we may agree, as with all our earlier provisions, that these are good.'

But Socrates — I think if we let you go on like this, you'll never remember the question you shoved aside to say all of it: whether this constitution can come into being, and how it possibly could. Because if it existed, everything would be splendid for the city that had it. I'll even add advantages you've left out: fighting their enemies they'd be the best of soldiers, because they'd never desert each other — these men who know one another as brothers and fathers and sons and call each other by those names. And if the women campaigned alongside, whether in the line itself or arrayed behind as a terror to the enemy and a reserve for whenever it's needed — I know all this would make them unbeatable outright. And at home I see all the goods they'd have that you haven't mentioned. Take it that I grant it all — these advantages and ten thousand others, if this constitution came to be — and say no more about the thing itself. Let's just try now to convince ourselves of this one point: that it's possible, and how — and let the rest go.

'But I have to say, Socrates, that if you're allowed to go on like this, you'll forget the question you brushed aside at the start of all this: whether such a state is even possible, and if so, how. I'm quite ready to grant that your plan, if it could be realized, would do the state every kind of good. I'll even add what you left out: your citizens will be the bravest of soldiers, since they all know one another and call each other father, brother, son; and if the women march with them, whether in the same line or behind it, to terrify the enemy or to reinforce them in a pinch, I'm sure they'll be utterly unbeatable. And there are many advantages at home you haven't mentioned, which I freely grant as well. But since I'm granting all of these, and as many more as you like, on the one condition that the state actually exists, let's say no more about them. Let's just assume it exists, and now turn to the one thing left: whether it's possible, and how.'

That was sudden, I said — this raid you've launched on my argument, with no mercy for a man dragging his feet. Maybe you don't understand: I barely got out from under the first two waves, and now you're bringing on the third — the monster of the set, the biggest and hardest of the three. When you've seen it and heard it, you'll forgive me entirely: no wonder I hesitated, no wonder I was afraid to state so paradoxical a proposal, let alone undertake to examine it.

'You spring on me the moment I pause,' I said, 'and give me no quarter. I've barely escaped the first and second waves, and now, without seeming to notice, you're bringing down on me the third, the biggest and most crushing of all. When you've seen and heard it, you'll understand my hesitation, and forgive me for being slow to take up a proposal so strange as the one I now have to state and examine.'
The more of this we hear, he said, the less any of us will release you from saying how this constitution can come to be. Speak — and no more stalling.
'The more you talk like that,' he said, 'the less we'll let you off telling us how such a state is possible. So out with it, and quickly.'
Then first let's remember, I said, that we arrived here searching for what justice is, and what injustice is.
'Let me begin by reminding you,' I said, 'that we came to all this in the course of searching for justice and injustice.'
We did, he said. What of it?
'True. But what of it?'

Nothing — only this: if we find what justice is, will we insist that the just man differ from it in nothing — match justice itself exactly, in every respect? Or will we be satisfied if he comes as close to it as can be, and has more of it in him than anyone else?

'Only this. Suppose we've found what justice is. Are we then to demand that the just man fall short of perfect justice in nothing, or will we be content if he comes close, and has more justice in him than other men?'
That will satisfy us.
'Coming close will be enough.'

Then it was for the sake of a model, I said, that we were searching for what justice itself is, and for the perfectly just man — whether he could exist, and what he'd be like if he did — and likewise injustice and the perfectly unjust man. We wanted to look at them and see how they stood with respect to happiness and its opposite, so that we'd be forced to agree about ourselves: whoever comes nearest to them will have the portion nearest theirs. We were not out to prove that these things could exist.

'We were looking for justice itself, then, and for what the perfectly just man would be like, and for injustice and the perfectly unjust man, so that we'd have a pattern to measure ourselves against. We meant to look at these in order to judge our own happiness or unhappiness by how far we resembled them, not to prove that such people could actually exist.'
That's true, he said.
'True.'

Do you think a painter is any less good, then, who paints a model of what the most beautiful human being would be — rendering everything in the picture as it should be — but can't prove that such a man could exist?
'Would a painter be any worse a painter if he drew a perfectly beautiful man with consummate skill, but couldn't prove such a man could ever exist?'
By Zeus, no, he said.
'Not in the least.'
Well — weren't we, by our own account, making a model in words of a good city?
'Well, weren't we doing the same, drawing in words a pattern of a good state?'
We were.
'We were.'
Then is our account any less good, do you think, because we can't prove that a city can be governed as we described?
'Then is our account any worse because we can't prove that a state ordered as we've described could actually come to be?'
Surely not, he said.
'Of course not.'

Then that's the truth of it, I said. But if, to please you, I must push on and show how, exactly, and on what terms it comes nearest to being possible — then for that demonstration, grant me the same admissions over again.

'That's the truth of it,' I said. 'But if, to please you, I'm to try to show how, and on what conditions, it could come closest to being possible, then I have to ask you to grant me, with that aim in view, the same admissions as before.'
Which?
'Which admissions?'
Can anything be carried out exactly as it's spoken? Or is it the nature of things that doing grips truth less firmly than talking does — whatever some people think? Do you agree, or not?

'This one: can anything ever be realized in practice exactly as it's described in words? Doesn't the word always reach beyond the fact, so that the actual thing, whatever anyone thinks, must in the nature of things fall a little short of the truth? What do you say?'
I agree.
'I agree.'

Then don't force me to exhibit the thing realized in deed, precisely as we spelled it out in words. If we can find how a city might be run closest to what we've said, then say that we've found what you demanded — that it's possible. Won't you be content with that? I know I would.

'Then don't insist that I prove the actual state will match the pattern in every detail. If we can show how a city might be governed in the way nearest to what we've described, you'll admit we've found the possibility you demanded, and be satisfied. I would be. Wouldn't you?'
So would I, he said.
'Yes, I would.'

Then next, it seems, we should try to find and show what's done badly in cities today — the thing that keeps them from being run our way — and the smallest change that would carry a city over to our kind of constitution. One change, for preference; failing that, two; failing that, the fewest in number and the mildest in force.

'Then let me try to point out what flaw it is in states that keeps them from being governed this way, and what smallest change would let a state cross over into the better form, one change if possible, or if not, two, but in any case as few and as slight as can be.'
By all means, he said.
'By all means.'
Well, there is one change, I said, that I think would carry it over. Not a small change, and not an easy one — but possible.
'I think,' I said, 'that the state could be transformed by a single change, though not a slight or easy one, still a possible one.'
What is it? he said.
'What is it?' he asked.

Here I stand, I said, at the thing we likened to the greatest wave. But it shall be said, even if the wave breaks over me — a real breaker of laughter and disgrace — and washes me away. Mark what I'm about to say.
'Here, then,' I said, 'I come to the thing I likened to the greatest wave. Yet it shall be spoken, even if the wave breaks over me in a flood of laughter and contempt and drowns me. Listen closely.'
Say it.
'Go on.'

Unless philosophers become kings in our cities, I said, or the men now called kings and rulers become philosophers — genuinely, thoroughly — so that political power and philosophy meet in the same hands, while the many natures that now chase one without the other are barred from both by force, there will be no rest from evils for our cities, my dear Glaucon, nor, I think, for the human race. And until then, this constitution we've been building in words will never grow into what it could be, never see the light of the sun. This is what made me so slow to speak: I could see how far it runs against belief. It's hard to accept that there is no other road to happiness — for a city, or for a single life.

'Unless philosophers become kings in their cities, or those we now call kings and rulers take genuinely and adequately to philosophy, so that political power and wisdom meet in the same person, while the many natures who now pursue one apart from the other are forcibly barred from doing so, there will be no rest from evils, Glaucon, for cities, nor I think for the human race; and our city, the one we've been describing in words, will never come into being and see the light of day. This is what I shrank from saying so long, seeing how very strange it would sound; for it's hard to face the fact that there's no other road to happiness, public or private.'

Socrates, he said — you've hurled out a sentence, an argument, after which you can expect a great many men — and no negligible men either — to fling off their coats, so to speak, right where they stand, snatch up whatever weapon is nearest, and come at you at a dead run, ready to do wonders. If you don't build your defense in argument and make your escape, you'll pay the penalty — jeered at in earnest.

'Socrates,' he said, 'after a statement like that, you'd better expect a great many people, and not unimpressive ones, to come at you. Picture them throwing off their coats on the spot, stripped for action, snatching up whatever weapon's nearest, and rushing at you full tilt, ready to do who knows what. If you don't have an argument ready to hold them off, you'll be cut to pieces by their scorn, and serve you right.'
And whose doing is that, I said, if not yours?
'And it was you,' I said, 'who got me into this scrape.'

And a fine thing I did, he said. But I won't betray you: I'll defend you with what I have. What I have is goodwill and encouragement — and maybe I'd answer your questions more carefully than another man would. So with a helper like that, try to show the doubters that it is as you say.

'And I was right to,' he said. 'But I won't abandon you. I'll do what I can, which is to offer goodwill and encouragement, and maybe answer your questions a bit more obligingly than someone else would. With an ally like that, do your best to show the doubters you're right.'

I must try, I said, since you offer so great an alliance. If we're going to slip past the men you describe, it seems to me essential to define for them which philosophers we mean when we dare to say that philosophers must rule. Once that's clear, a defense is possible: we can show that some people are fitted by nature to take hold of philosophy and to lead in a city, and the rest are made to leave philosophy alone and follow the leader.

'I'll have to try,' I said, 'since you offer such priceless help. And I think the first thing we need, if we're to have any hope of escape, is to explain to them exactly whom we mean when we dare to say that philosophers should rule. Once that's clear, we can defend ourselves by showing that some natures are born for philosophy and for leading the state, while others aren't, and are meant to follow rather than lead.'
This would be the moment to define them, he said.
'Then it's time for a definition,' he said.
Come along, then — let's see if we can somehow lay it out adequately.
'Follow me,' I said, 'and let's see if somehow we can lay it out properly.'
Lead on.
'Lead on.'
Will you need reminding, I said, or do you remember: when we say a man loves something — if the word is used rightly — he can't love part of it and not the rest. He has to cherish the whole of it.

'I'll have to remind you of something, or rather, you'll remember it without my help: if we call a man a lover of something, and the name fits, he must love not one part of that thing but the whole of it.'
You'll have to remind me, it seems, he said. I don't quite follow.
'I'm afraid I don't follow. You'll have to jog my memory.'

That answer, Glaucon, would suit somebody else, I said. A man of your amorous history has no business forgetting that every boy in his bloom finds some way to sting and stir a lover of boys — a man of your sort — and every one of them seems worth his devotion and attention. Isn't that how you people deal with the beautiful? One boy has a snub nose: you'll call it charming and praise it. Another's hook of a nose is regal, you say. The one in between has perfect proportions. The dark ones look manly; the pale ones are children of the gods. And 'honey-pale' — who do you think coined that phrase but a lover talking baby-talk, happily excusing a sallow cheek as long as youth is on it? In one word: there's no excuse you won't invent, no sound you won't make, to avoid losing a single boy in the flower of his spring.

'That answer would suit someone else, Glaucon,' I said, 'but a man with your eye for these things should know that everyone in the bloom of youth somehow stirs and stings a lover's heart, and strikes him as worthy of his attention. Isn't that how you all treat your favorites? One has a snub nose, and you call it charming; another's is hooked, and you say it has a royal look; the one in between, you praise for perfect proportion. The dark are manly, the fair are children of the gods, and even "honey-pale," what is that but a lover's pet name for sallow skin, forgiven so long as it's on the cheek of youth? In a word, you'll seize on any excuse and say anything rather than let a single flower of that springtime go by.'
If you insist on using me to make your point about lovers, he said — fine; for the argument's sake, I'll go along.
'If you want to make me your example of how lovers behave,' he said, 'I'll go along with it, for the argument's sake.'
And the wine-lovers? Don't you see them doing the same — welcoming every wine, on any pretext?
'And lovers of wine,' I said, 'don't you see them doing the same? Any excuse will do to drink any wine.'
I do.
'Of course.'

And the lovers of honor — you've watched them, I think. If they can't command an army, they'll command a battalion; if they can't be honored by the great and important, they'll settle for being honored by the small and negligible. Honor, of one size or another, they must have.

'And it's the same with ambitious men. If they can't command an army, they'll command a company; if they can't be honored by the great and important, they're glad to be honored by lesser, meaner people. Honor of some kind they must have.'
Exactly so.
'Exactly.'
Then tell me yes or no: when we say a man has an appetite for something, do we mean he has an appetite for the whole kind — or for one part of it and not another?
'Then tell me this. When a man desires something, do we say he desires the whole of that kind of thing, or only a part?'
The whole, he said.
'The whole.'
So the philosopher too — the lover of wisdom — we'll say has an appetite for wisdom: not for this piece and not that, but for the whole of it?
'Then shall we say of the philosopher too that he loves not part of wisdom but the whole of it?'
True.
'The whole.'

Then someone who's picky about his studies — especially while he's young and can't yet tell what's useful from what isn't — we won't call a lover of learning, or a philosopher. As we don't call the picky eater hungry: he has no appetite for food. He's a bad eater, not a good one.

'And the man who turns up his nose at learning, especially while he's young and can't yet judge what's worth knowing, we'll deny is a philosopher or a lover of learning, just as we'd say a man who has no appetite for his food isn't hungry, but has a poor appetite rather than a good one?'
And we'll be right.
'Quite right.'
But the one who's game to taste every kind of learning, who goes to his studying gladly and can't get his fill — him we'll rightly call a philosopher, won't we?
'Whereas the man who's eager for every kind of learning, curious and never satisfied, him we may fairly call a philosopher, a lover of wisdom. Don't you agree?'

Then you'll have a strange crowd on your hands, said Glaucon. All the lovers of spectacles are what they are, I suppose, because they delight in learning things. And the lovers of listening would be the oddest people to file among philosophers — men who'd never willingly come near a discussion or any such pastime, yet who run around to every chorus at the festivals of Dionysus as if their ears were under contract, never missing one, in town or village. Are we to call all these people philosophers — them, and the students of every other petty craft?

'If that's all it takes,' said Glaucon, 'curiosity, then you'll find a great many odd characters claiming the title. All the lovers of spectacles delight in learning, after a fashion, so they'd have to count. And the music lovers are a strange lot to file under philosophers, the very last people you could drag to anything like a serious discussion, yet they run from one Dionysian festival to the next as though they'd hired out their ears to hear every chorus, and miss none, in town or country. Are we really going to call all these people philosophers, along with the dabblers in every trifling art?'
Not at all, I said — though they do have a look of philosophers about them.
'Certainly not,' I said. 'They're only an imitation of the real thing.'
And the true ones? he said. Who do you mean by those?
'Then who are the true philosophers?' he asked.
The lovers of the sight of truth, I said.
'Those,' I said, 'who love the sight of truth.'
Right enough, he said — but what does it mean?
'That's well said too,' he replied. 'But what do you mean by it?'
It wouldn't be easy to explain to just anyone, I said. But you, I think, will grant me the starting point.
'It wouldn't be easy to explain to just anyone,' I said. 'But you, I'm sure, will grant me something I'm about to propose.'
Which is?
'What's that?'
That since beautiful is the opposite of ugly, they are two things.
'That since beauty and ugliness are opposites, they're two things?'
Of course.
'Of course.'
And being two, each of them is one?
'And since they're two, each of them is one?'
That too.
'That too.'

And the same account holds of just and unjust, good and bad, and all the forms: each of them is, in itself, one thing; but because they show up everywhere in company with actions and bodies and one another, each appears to be many things.

'And the same holds for just and unjust, good and bad, and every other such kind: each, taken by itself, is one. But because they show up everywhere, mixed in with actions and bodies and one another, each of them appears as many.'
That's right, he said.
'That's true.'

Well then, this is my dividing line, I said. On one side I put the lovers of spectacles you just mentioned — the lovers of crafts, the practical men. On the other, the people our argument is about — the only ones rightly called philosophers.

'And this is the line I draw between the two groups: on one side those lovers of spectacle and craft and practical affairs you spoke of, and on the other those I'm calling the only ones who really deserve the name of philosopher.'
How do you mean? he said.
'How do you mean?' he asked.

The lovers of sounds and sights, I said, delight in beautiful voices and colors and shapes and everything crafted from them. But the beautiful itself — their thought can't see its nature, can't delight in it.

'The lovers of sounds and sights,' I said, 'are devoted to beautiful tones and colors and shapes, and everything fashioned out of them, but their minds are unable to see beauty itself, or to love it.'
That is how it is, he said.
'True.'
And the ones able to approach the beautiful itself and see it as it is, by itself — won't they be rare?
'And those able to reach beauty itself, and to see it as it is in itself, aren't they rare?'
Very rare.
'Very rare.'

Then a man who believes in beautiful things but not in beauty itself — who couldn't follow if someone tried to lead him to the knowledge of it — do you think he's living awake, or dreaming? Look at it this way. What is dreaming, if not this: that a man, asleep or awake, takes the likeness of a thing not for a likeness, but for the thing itself?

'So a man who recognizes beautiful things but not beauty itself, and who can't follow if someone tries to lead him to the knowledge of it, do you think he's living awake, or only dreaming? Think about it: isn't a dreamer, asleep or awake, exactly the man who takes the likeness of a thing for the thing itself?'
I'd certainly call that man a dreamer, he said.
'I'd certainly say such a man is dreaming.'

And the opposite man — the one who holds that there is a beautiful itself, and can look upon both it and the things that share in it, and doesn't mistake the sharers for it or it for the sharers — is he awake, or dreaming?

'But the other, who recognizes that there is a beauty itself and can see both it and the things that share in it, without mistaking the things for it or it for the things, is he awake, or dreaming too?'
Wide awake, he said.
'Wide awake.'
Then this man's state of mind, since he knows, we'd rightly call knowledge — and the other's opinion, since he opines?
'So we'd be right to say his state of mind is knowledge, since he knows, and the other man's is opinion, since he only forms opinions?'
Certainly.
'Certainly.'
And what if the man we say opines gets rough with us and disputes the claim? Is there any way to soothe him — to talk him around gently, while keeping quiet the fact that he isn't in his right mind?

'But suppose this second man, the one we say only has opinions and not knowledge, takes offense and disputes what we're saying. Can we find some way to soothe him and win him over gently, without letting on that he isn't quite well in the head?'
We'd better find one, he said.
'We ought to try.'

Come, then — think what we'll say to him. Or shall we question him like this? We'll tell him first that nobody begrudges him anything he knows — we'd be delighted to see that he knows something. Then we'll say: tell us this, though. Does the man who knows, know something — or nothing? You answer for him.

'Come, then, let's think of what to say to him. Or rather, let's question him, assuring him that if he knows anything we hold no grudge against him, in fact we'd be glad to find he knows something. But we'll ask him: this man who knows, does he know something, or nothing? Answer for him, Glaucon.'
I'll answer that he knows something.
'I'll answer that he knows something.'
Something that is, or something that is not?
'Something that is, or something that is not?'
That is. How could a thing that is not be known?
'Something that is. How could anything that is not ever be known?'
Then are we sure of this — from however many angles we look at it: what fully is, is fully knowable; what in no way is, is in every way unknowable?
'So we're satisfied, however many ways we look at it, that what fully is can be fully known, and what in no way is must be wholly unknown?'
Completely sure.
'Nothing could be more certain.'
Good. Now if something is so placed that it both is and is not — won't it lie between what purely is and what wholly is not?
'Good. Now if there's something that both is and is not, won't it lie somewhere between what purely is and what utterly is not?'
Between them.
'It will.'

Then since knowledge is set over what is, and ignorance, of necessity, over what is not — over this in-between we'd have to look for something between ignorance and knowledge, if there is any such thing?

'And since knowledge was set over what is, and ignorance, necessarily, over what is not, then for this in-between thing we'll have to find something in between ignorance and knowledge, if there is any such thing?'
Certainly.
'We will.'
Well — do we say opinion is something?
'Now do we admit there's such a thing as opinion?'
Of course.
'Of course.'
A power the same as knowledge, or a different one?
'A different power from knowledge, or the same?'
A different one.
'A different one.'
So opinion is stationed over one thing and knowledge over another — each according to its own power.
'So opinion is set over one thing, and knowledge over another, each according to its own power?'
Yes.
'Yes.'
And knowledge is naturally set over what is, to know it as it is? — though hold on: first I think we need to draw a distinction.
'And knowledge is set over what is, to know that what is, is. But first I'd better draw a distinction.'
What distinction?
'What distinction?'

Powers, I said. We'll say powers are a class of things that are — the things by which we can do whatever we can do; we, and everything else that can do anything. Sight and hearing, I mean, belong among the powers — if you follow the kind I want to describe.

'I'll set down powers as a class of their own. They're what enables us, and everything else, to do whatever we can do. Sight and hearing, for instance, I'd call powers, if that makes the class I mean clear to you.'
I follow, he said.
'Yes, I understand.'

Then hear how they strike me. In a power I see no color, no shape, none of the features so many other things have — the ones I can look at to tell one thing from another for myself. In a power I look at one thing only: what it is set over, and what it accomplishes. That's how I came to call each of them a power. The one set over the same thing, accomplishing the same thing, I call the same power; the one set over something different, accomplishing something different, I call a different one. What about you — how do you do it?

'Then hear how I think of them. In a power I can't see any color or shape or anything of the sort, the kind of feature that lets me tell many things apart. With a power I look only to what it's set over and what it accomplishes, and on that basis I call one power the same as another, and another power different. What has the same field and the same result I call the same power; what has a different field and a different result I call different. Is that how you'd put it too?'
The same way, he said.
'It is.'
Then back to you, my excellent friend, I said. Knowledge — do you say it's a power, or what class do you put it in?
'Then, my friend, answer me this. Do you count knowledge as a power, or in what class do you put it?'
A power, he said — the strongest of them all.
'A power,' he said, 'and the mightiest of them all.'
And opinion — a power, or shall we file it under some other kind?
'And opinion, is that a power too, or some other kind of thing?'
A power, he said. Opining is exactly what opinion enables us to do.
'A power as well,' he said. 'It's just that by which we're able to form opinions.'
But a little while ago you agreed that knowledge and opinion are not the same.
'But a moment ago you agreed that knowledge and opinion aren't the same.'
Of course, he said. How could anyone with any sense count the infallible and the fallible as one thing?
'How could anyone in his right mind treat the infallible as the same as the fallible?'
Well said, I answered — plainly we're agreed that opinion is one thing and knowledge another.
'Well said,' I replied. 'So we plainly agree that opinion is one thing and knowledge another.'
Another thing entirely.
'We do.'
So each of them, being a different power, is naturally set over a different object?
'So each of them, having a different power, is set over a different thing?'
Necessarily.
'It must be.'
Knowledge over what is — to know what is, as it is?
'Knowledge is set over what is, to know what is, as it is?'
Yes.
'Yes.'
And opinion, we say, opines?
'And opinion, we say, forms opinions?'
Yes.
'Yes.'
The same object knowledge knows? So the knowable and the opinable will be the same thing? Or is that impossible?
'About the same thing knowledge knows? Can the field of opinion and the field of knowledge be one and the same?'

Impossible, he said — by what we've agreed. If different powers are naturally set over different things, and both opinion and knowledge are powers — each different from the other, as we said — then it follows: the knowable and the opinable can't be the same.

'No,' he replied, 'that's been ruled out already. If different powers are set over different fields, and opinion and knowledge are different powers, as we've agreed, then the field of knowledge and the field of opinion can't be the same.'
Then if what is, is the knowable, the opinable has to be something other than what is?
'So if what is, is the field of knowledge, the field of opinion must be something other than what is?'
Something other.
'Yes, something else.'

Then does opinion opine what is not? Or is even that impossible — to opine what is not? Think about it: doesn't the man who opines bring his opinion to bear on something? Or is it possible to opine — but opine nothing?

'Is it, then, what is not? Or rather, can there even be an opinion about what is not? Think: when a man holds an opinion, isn't his opinion about something? Can anyone have an opinion, yet have it about nothing?'
It's impossible.
'Impossible.'
No — the man who opines, opines some one thing?
'So the man who holds an opinion holds it about some one thing?'
Yes.
'Yes.'
But what is not isn't 'some one thing.' Speaking strictly, it's nothing at all.
'But what is not couldn't rightly be called some one thing; it's nothing at all.'
Quite.
'True.'
And we assigned ignorance, of necessity, to what is not — and to what is, knowledge?
'And we were forced to assign ignorance to what is not, and knowledge to what is?'
And rightly, he said.
'Rightly so,' he said.
Then opinion opines neither what is, nor what is not?
'Then opinion is set over neither what is nor what is not?'
Neither.
'Over neither.'
So opinion can be neither ignorance nor knowledge?
'So opinion is neither ignorance nor knowledge?'
So it seems.
'It seems not.'
Then does it lie somewhere beyond them — outdoing knowledge in clarity, or ignorance in darkness?
'Then does it lie outside both, surpassing knowledge in clarity, or falling below ignorance in darkness?'
It does neither.
'Neither.'
Then opinion looks to you, I said, like something darker than knowledge and brighter than ignorance?
'Then opinion seems to you darker than knowledge, but brighter than ignorance?'
Very much so, he said.
'Much, in both directions.'
Lying inside the two boundaries?
'And to lie inside the two, between them?'
Yes.
'Yes.'
So opinion would be between the two?
'So opinion would be the in-between thing?'
Exactly that.
'No question.'

Now, didn't we say earlier that if something turned up which at once is and is not, it would lie between what purely is and what altogether is not — and that neither knowledge nor ignorance would be set over it, but whatever turned up, in its turn, between ignorance and knowledge?

'Now didn't we say earlier that if something turned up that both is and is not at once, it would lie in between what purely is and what utterly is not, and that the power set over it would be neither knowledge nor ignorance but whatever turned up in between the two?'
Right.
'We did.'
And what has turned up between them is the thing we call opinion?
'And now, in that in-between space, what has turned up is what we call opinion?'
It has.
'It has.'

Then what remains to be found, it seems, is the thing that shares in both — in being and in not-being — and can't rightly be called either one, pure and simple. If it comes to light, we can justly call it the opinable: the extremes matched to the extremes, the in-between to the in-between. Isn't that so?

'So what's left to find is the thing that shares in both, in being and in not-being, and can't rightly be called purely one or the other. If we find it, we can fairly call it the object of opinion, assigning the extremes to the extreme powers and the in-between to the in-between power.'
It is.
'Right.'

With all that laid down, I'll say: let him step up and answer me — that good fellow who denies there is any beautiful itself, any form of beauty itself that stays forever the same in all respects, but who does believe in the many beautiful things — the spectacle-lover, who won't stand it if anyone says the beautiful is one, and the just is one, and so on. My friend, we'll say to him: of all these many beautiful things, is there one that won't ever show itself ugly? Of the just things, one that won't show itself unjust? Of the holy, one that won't show unholy?

'With that settled, I'd like to put a question to our friend, the good fellow who denies there's any beauty itself, any unchanging form of the beautiful, and holds instead that the beautiful is a many, the lover of spectacles who can't endure being told that the beautiful is one, or the just is one, or that anything at all is one. I'd say to him: my good man, of all these many beautiful things, is there one that won't also turn up ugly? Of all the just things, one that won't turn up unjust? Of all the holy, one that won't turn up unholy?'
No, he said — it's inevitable that they show up beautiful from one angle and ugly from another; and so with everything else you're asking about.
'No,' he said. 'Each of them is bound to look both beautiful and ugly, somehow, and the same with the rest.'
And the many doubles? Do they show up as halves any less than as doubles?
'And the many doubles, aren't they just as much halves? Doubles of one thing, halves of another?'
No less.
'Just so.'
And bigs and smalls, and lights and heavies — will those names hold to them any more firmly than the opposite names?
'And things we call great or small, heavy or light, won't they answer just as well to the opposite names?'
No, he said — each of them hangs on to both, always.
'Yes, each of them always belongs to both.'
Then is each of the many what somebody says it is — any more than it is not what he says it is?
'So with each of these many things, is it any more what we call it than not what we call it?'

They're like the double-edged jokes at a banquet, he said, or the children's riddle about the eunuch and his throw at the bat — the one that riddles what he hit it with, and what the bat was sitting on. These many things equivocate the same way, and you can't fix any of them firmly in your mind as being, or as not being, or as both, or as neither.

'They're like those punning riddles people trade at dinner parties,' he said, 'or the children's riddle about the eunuch and the bat, what he threw and what it was sitting on. These things are riddles in the same way, with a double face. You can't fix any of them firmly in your mind as being, or as not being, or as both, or as neither.'

Then can you do anything better with them, I said, than set them between being and not-being? Surely they can't turn up darker than what is not — by not-being more than it — or brighter than what is, by being more.
'Then what will you do with them?' I said. 'Where could they sit better than between being and not-being? They're surely no darker than what is not, no more real than what is.'
Completely true, he said.
'Quite true,' he said.
So we seem to have found it: the many conventional beliefs of the many, about the beautiful and the rest, are tumbling about somewhere between what is not and what purely is.
'So we seem to have found that the mass of conventional notions the many hold about beauty and the rest go tumbling about somewhere in between pure being and pure not-being.'
We have.
'We have.'
And we agreed in advance that whatever turned up like this would have to be called the opinable, not the knowable — the wanderer in between, caught by the power in between.
'And we agreed beforehand that anything of that sort should be called an object of opinion, not of knowledge, the wandering, in-between thing caught by the in-between power.'
We did.
'We did.'

Then as for those who gaze on the many beautiful things and don't see the beautiful itself — and can't follow another man who'd lead them to it — who see the many just things and not the just itself, and so on all the way through: we'll say they opine everything, but know nothing of what they opine.

'So those who feast their eyes on many beautiful things but can't see beauty itself, or follow anyone who'd lead them to it, who see many just things but not justice itself, and so on, of all of them we'll say they have opinion but not knowledge of the things they opine about.'
That's what we have to say.
'That's certain.'
And what about those who gaze on each thing itself — the things that stay forever the same in every respect? Won't we say they know, and don't merely opine?
'But those who can see each thing itself, the things that stay always the same, unchanging, we'll say they know, and don't merely have opinions.'
That follows too, necessarily.
'That can't be denied either.'

And won't we say these men embrace and love the things knowledge is set over, and the others the things opinion is set over? We do remember, don't we, saying of the latter that they love and gaze at beautiful sounds and colors and the rest, but the beautiful itself — they won't even allow that it's anything at all?

'And we'll say the one group loves and embraces the objects of knowledge, the other the objects of opinion. For these last, you'll remember, are the ones we said were in love with beautiful sounds and colors and the like, but couldn't bear the thought that beauty itself is anything at all.'
We remember.
'Yes, I remember.'
Then we won't be off-key, will we, calling these people lovers of opinion rather than lovers of wisdom? Will they be very angry with us for saying it?
'So we won't be out of line, will we, in calling them lovers of opinion rather than lovers of wisdom? And will they be very angry with us for it?'
Not if they listen to me, he said. Nobody has a right to be angry at the truth.
'Not if they take my advice,' he said. 'No one should be angry at the truth.'
But those who embrace, in each case, the thing itself that is — those we must call lovers of wisdom, not lovers of opinion?
'And those who love each thing as it truly is, them we must call lovers of wisdom, and not lovers of opinion?'
Absolutely.
'Without a doubt.'
spine.label: Book VI
spine.title: The Sun and the Divided Line
The Philosopher, the Good, and the Divided Line
spine.text: So there, Glaucon: it took a long stretch of argument, and some struggle, but the true philosophers and the false have finally shown themselves for what they are.
And so, Glaucon, after a long and weary stretch of argument, the true philosophers and the false have finally come into view.
I doubt the road could have been any shorter, he said.
'I don't see how the road could have been any shorter,' he said.

Probably not, I said. Though I think we would have seen them both more clearly if this had been the only subject before us — if there weren't so many questions still waiting, which anyone who wants to see how the just life differs from the unjust has to work through.

'Probably not,' I said. 'And yet I think we'd have gotten a clearer view of both kinds if we could have kept to this one subject, instead of having all these other questions still waiting for us—the ones anyone has to face who wants to see exactly how the life of the just man differs from the life of the unjust.'
So what comes next? he asked.
'So what comes next?' he asked.

Whatever follows in order, I said. Since philosophers are the ones able to grasp what always holds the same, unchanging, while those who cannot — who wander lost among the many things that shift and vary — are not philosophers, the question is this: which of the two should lead our city?

'Surely the question that follows in order,' I said. 'Since only philosophers are able to grasp what is eternal and unchanging, while those who drift about among the many changing things are not philosophers, which of the two should be the rulers of our city?'
And how do we answer that sensibly?
'How should we answer that?'
Whichever of them proves able to guard the laws and the ways of the city — make those the guardians.
'Whichever group is better able to guard the laws and institutions of our city—let them be our guardians.'
Good.
'Fair enough.'
And here's a question that answers itself, I said: should a watchman set to guard anything have sharp eyes, or be blind?
'And surely there's no question,' I said, 'that a guardian set to watch over something should have eyes rather than no eyes?'
It answers itself.
'No question at all.'

Then what about people who genuinely lack knowledge of what each thing is — who carry no clear pattern of it in their soul, and cannot do what a painter does: fix their eyes on what is most true, refer back to it constantly, study it as exactly as possible, and only then lay down the standards of the beautiful, the just, and the good here below — laying down new ones where needed, and standing guard to preserve the ones already in place? Aren't such people, frankly, blind?

'Now, men who truly lack any knowledge of what each thing really is—who carry no clear pattern in their souls, and so can't look, the way a painter looks, toward the absolute truth, return to that original again and again, see it with perfect clarity, and from it set in order our laws about what is beautiful and good and just, where they aren't ordered already, and then keep guard and preserve them—aren't men like that simply blind?'
Honestly, he said, that's more or less their condition.
'Pretty much blind, yes,' he said.
Then shall we make them our guardians — when there are others available who know what each thing truly is, who match them in experience, and who fall short of them in no part of virtue?
'Then shall we make them our guardians, when there are others who match them in experience and fall short of them in no virtue, and who also know the truth of each thing?'
It would be absurd to pass over men who have that — the greatest advantage of all. They should hold first place, unless they fail somewhere else.
'It would make no sense,' he said, 'to pass over men who have this greatest of all advantages. As long as they don't fall short in some other way, they have to come first.'
Then let's spell out, I said, how the same men can have both — the knowledge and the other qualities.
'Then suppose we work out how the same men can have both this knowledge and the other excellences too.'
By all means.
'By all means.'

First, as we said at the start of all this, we have to grasp the philosopher's nature. Once we agree on that, I think we'll also agree that the combination is possible — and that no one else should lead a city but these.

'As we said when we started, the first thing is to settle what the philosopher's nature really is. Once we've come to an understanding about that, then—if I'm not mistaken—we'll also agree that this combination of qualities is possible, and that the people who have them, and only they, should rule the city.'
How so?
'How do you mean?'
Let's agree on this much about philosophic natures: they are always in love with any learning that shows them the being that always is — the reality that doesn't drift about between birth and decay.
'Let's agree that philosophical minds always love the kind of knowledge that reveals to them the eternal—what doesn't shift with coming-to-be and passing-away.'
Agreed.
'Agreed.'
And further, that they love the whole of it, and won't willingly give up any part, small or large, more honored or less — just as we said before about lovers and about men who chase honors.

'And let's also agree,' I said, 'that they love all of that true being, that there's no part of it, great or small, more honorable or less, that they're willing to give up—just as we said before about the lover and the man hungry for honor.'
True.
'True.'
Now consider: if they're going to be what we described, mustn't there be something else in their nature too?
'And if they're to be what we've been describing, isn't there another quality they have to have as well?'
What?
'What quality?'
Truthfulness — a refusal ever to accept a lie into themselves willingly. They hate the false and love the true.
'Truthfulness. They will never willingly let a falsehood into their minds—they hate it—and they love the truth.'
That seems a safe thing to say of them.
'That's safe to say of them.'
Not just safe, my friend — necessary. A man in love with anything by nature has to love everything that belongs to it, everything akin to what he loves.
'"Safe to say" isn't the word, my friend,' I replied. '"Must be said" is the word. A man whose nature is in love with something can't help loving everything that belongs to it or is akin to it.'
Right, he said.
'Right,' he said.
And could you find anything more akin to wisdom than truth?
'And is there anything more akin to wisdom than truth?'
How could there be?
'How could there be?'
Then can the same nature love wisdom and love the false?
'Can the same nature love wisdom and love falsehood at once?'
Never.
'Never.'
So the genuine lover of learning must, from earliest youth, reach for truth of every kind, with everything in him?
'So the genuine lover of learning must, from his earliest youth, reach out for all the truth he can?'
Absolutely.
'Absolutely.'
But we also know from experience that when a man's desires run strongly in one channel, they run weaker everywhere else — like a stream diverted into a single bed.
'But we know from experience that when a man's desires run strong in one direction, they run weaker in the others, like a stream that's been drawn off into another channel.'
Of course.
'True.'

So when a man's desires flow toward learning and everything like it, he'll be absorbed in the pleasure of the soul itself, by itself, and let the body's pleasures fall away — if he's a true philosopher and not a counterfeit one.

'So a man whose desires flow toward knowledge in every form will be absorbed in the pleasures of the soul itself and will hardly notice the pleasures of the body—that is, if he's a real philosopher and not a fake.'
That follows necessarily.
'Quite certainly.'
A man like that will be temperate, and the last man alive to be greedy. The reasons other people chase money and spend it grandly have no purchase on him.
'A man like that is bound to be temperate, the very opposite of greedy. The motives that drive other men to grab and spend have no place in his character.'
Very true.
'Very true.'
And there's something else to check when you're sorting the philosophic nature from the unphilosophic.
'Here's another mark of the philosophical nature to consider.'
What's that?
'What's that?'
Watch for any hidden streak of smallness. Pettiness is the exact opposite of a soul that means to keep reaching for the whole of things — everything divine, everything human.
'There must be no hidden streak of pettiness in him. Nothing could be more at odds than smallness of mind with a soul that's always reaching out toward the whole of things, both divine and human.'
Very true, he said.
'Very true,' he said.
And a mind of that scale, which looks out over all time and all being — do you think human life can seem a great thing to it?
'And how could a man with greatness of mind, who looks out on all of time and all of being, think human life is much of anything?'
It can't.
'He can't.'
Then such a man won't count death as something terrible either?
'Or count death as something to fear?'
Not at all.
'Not at all.'
So a cowardly, small nature has no share in true philosophy?
'So the cowardly, petty nature can have no share in true philosophy?'
None.
'Certainly not.'
And a well-balanced man — not money-loving, not petty, not a boaster, not a coward — could he ever drive a hard bargain, or deal unjustly?
'And again: a man who is well-balanced—not greedy, not mean, not a braggart, not a coward—could such a man ever be unjust or hard to deal with?'
Impossible.
'Impossible.'
So when you're sorting the philosophic soul from the other kind, you'll look for this too, and early: whether a man is just and gentle, or savage and hard to deal with.

'So when you're looking at a soul, you'll quickly see whether it's just and gentle or harsh and unsociable. Even in the young, these are the signs that mark off the philosophical nature from the rest.'
Certainly.
'True.'
And you won't leave out one more thing, I think.
'There's one more point to watch for.'
What?
'What's that?'
Whether he learns with ease or with pain. You can't expect anyone to love a task that hurts him, where enormous effort buys almost no progress.
'Whether he takes pleasure in learning. No one loves what gives him pain and where, after great labor, he makes little headway.'
No.
'Of course not.'
And if he can hold nothing of what he learns — if he's all forgetting — can he help ending up empty of knowledge?
'And if he's forgetful, and holds on to nothing of what he learns, won't he end up an empty vessel?'
He can't.
'He certainly will.'
Then, laboring for nothing, won't he be forced in the end to hate himself and the whole business? — Yes.
'Laboring for nothing, he's bound to end up hating himself and hating the work?'
So a forgetful soul never makes the list of genuinely philosophic natures. We have to insist on a good memory.
'Yes.'
Certainly.
'So a forgetful soul can't be counted among the genuine philosophical natures. We have to insist that the philosopher have a good memory.'
And a nature with no music in it, no grace — where does it get dragged but toward what's out of all measure?
'Certainly.'
Nowhere else.
'And a nature that's clumsy and out of tune can only tend toward things being out of proportion?'
And is truth kin to measure, or to the lack of it?
'No doubt.'
To measure.
'And do you take truth to be akin to proportion, or to the lack of it?'
Then along with everything else, we're looking for a mind that is measured and graceful by nature — one whose native bent carries it easily toward the way each thing really is.
'To proportion.'
Certainly.
'So along with the rest, we have to look for a mind that's naturally well-proportioned and gracious, one that moves of its own accord toward the true being of each thing.'
Well then — don't all these qualities hang together? And aren't they, every one of them, necessary to a soul that is going to take hold of being fully and completely?
'Certainly.'
Absolutely necessary, he said.
'Well now—don't all the qualities we've been listing belong together, and aren't they, in a way, all necessary to a soul that's going to share fully and completely in being?'

Then can you find any fault with a pursuit that no one can practice well unless he is by nature retentive and quick to learn, large-minded and graceful — a friend and kinsman of truth, justice, courage, and temperance?
'They're absolutely necessary,' he replied.
Not even Momus, he said — the god of faultfinding himself — could find fault with that.

'And isn't this a study without reproach, one that only a man can pursue who has the gift of a good memory, is quick to learn, noble, gracious, and a friend to truth, justice, courage, and temperance—his own kindred?'
Then when age and education have brought men like that to completion, I said — wouldn't you hand the city to them, and to them alone?
'Even the god of envy himself,' he said, 'could find no fault with such a study.'

Here Adeimantus broke in. Socrates, he said, nobody can argue with you about any of this. But here is what happens to your hearers every time you talk this way. They feel that because they're inexperienced at this game of question and answer, the argument bends them a little off course at each step — nothing much, each time — but when all the littles are added up at the end of the discussion, the fall is a big one, and their first position has been turned upside down. Like weak checkers players cornered by expert ones until at last they have no move left, your hearers are cornered in this other game, played with words instead of pieces, until at last they have nothing left to say — and yet the truth isn't a bit more on your side for that. I say this looking at the present case. Because right now any one of us would admit he can't oppose you at any single question, and yet look at the facts: of the people who take up philosophy — not the ones who touch it young as part of their education and then drop it, but the ones who stay with it far too long — most turn out to be complete cranks, not to say utterly rotten, while even the ones who seem best are still left useless to their cities by this very pursuit you're praising.
'And it's to men like this,' I said, 'once they're brought to maturity by years and education, and to these alone, that you'll hand over the city.'
And do you think the people who say that are wrong?

Here Adeimantus broke in. 'Socrates,' he said, 'no one can argue against these statements of yours, point by point. But here's what happens to the people listening when you talk this way: they feel that, because they aren't skilled at asking and answering questions, they're being led just a little off course at each step of the argument, and the littles pile up, until at the end of the discussion they find themselves badly beaten—everything they used to think turned completely upside down. It's like a game of draughts: unskilled players are finally cornered by the better ones until they've no move left to make. So too your listeners are finally cornered, with nothing to say, in this other game where the counters are words instead of pieces—and yet they feel that all along the truth is on their side. I say this because of what's happening right now. Anyone of us might admit that, although in words he can't meet you at each step, he sees as a plain fact that the people who take up philosophy—not just briefly in their youth as part of an education, but as the pursuit of their mature years—most of them turn into very strange creatures, not to say downright scoundrels, and that even the best of them are made useless to the world by the very study you're praising.'
I don't know, he said. I'd like to hear what you think.
'Well,' I said, 'do you think the people who say this are wrong?'
Then hear it: I think they're telling the truth.
'I can't tell,' he replied. 'I'd like to hear your opinion.'
Then how can it be right to say that cities will have no rest from their troubles until philosophers rule in them — when we've just agreed philosophers are useless to cities?
'Here's my answer: I think they're quite right.'
That question, I said, needs an answer given in a picture.
'Then how can you be justified in saying that cities will never be free of evil until philosophers rule them, when we ourselves admit that philosophers are useless to those cities?'
And you, of course, said he, never talk in pictures.
'The question you're asking,' I said, 'can only be answered with an image.'

Very funny, I said — mock the man you've just pushed into an argument this hard to win. Hear the picture, then, and you'll see all the better how greedy for pictures I am. What the most decent men suffer at the hands of their cities is so hard to describe that no single thing is like it; to plead their case you have to assemble the likeness from many parts, the way painters paint goat-stags and other composite creatures. Imagine it happening on a fleet of ships, or on one. The shipowner is bigger and stronger than everyone else on board, but a little deaf, a little short-sighted, and his knowledge of seafaring runs about as deep. The sailors are quarreling over the helm: every one of them is convinced he should steer, though not one has ever learned the art — none can name his teacher or point to the time he studied it — and beyond that they insist it can't be taught at all, and stand ready to carve up anyone who says it can. They crowd around the shipowner himself, begging, doing anything to make him hand them the tiller; and whenever they fail and other men get his ear instead, they kill those others or pitch them overboard, and then — after knocking out the worthy owner with mandrake, or drink, or something else — they take command of the ship and help themselves to her stores, drinking and feasting as they sail the way you'd expect such men to sail. And there's more: the man clever at helping them seize control — at working the owner by persuasion or force — they praise as a seaman, a real helmsman, a man who knows ships; the one who won't, they damn as useless. As for the true helmsman, it never so much as enters their heads that he must study the seasons of the year, the sky, the stars, the winds — everything that belongs to his art — if he's genuinely to be fit to command a ship; and as for how he's to steer, whether the crew likes it or not, they don't believe there's any art or discipline of that to be mastered along with the helmsman's craft. With all this going on aboard, don't you think the sailors on ships run that way would call the true helmsman a stargazer, a babbler, of no use to them at all?
'And of course,' he said, 'that's something you never do.'
They certainly would, said Adeimantus.

'I see you're enjoying yourself, having dragged me into a discussion that looks hopeless. Now hear the image, and you'll be even more amused at how poor my imagination is—because the way the best men are treated by their own cities is so harsh that nothing on earth quite matches it. So if I'm going to plead their case, I'll have to put my picture together out of many things, the way painters make those mongrel creatures, half goat and half stag. Picture, then, a fleet, or a single ship, set up like this. There's a shipowner, taller and stronger than anyone else aboard, but a little deaf, a little short-sighted, and his knowledge of navigation is about on the same level. The sailors are all quarreling with one another over the steering, each one convinced he has the right to take the helm, though he's never learned the art, can't say who taught him or when he studied it, and will even insist that it can't be taught—and is ready to cut to pieces anyone who says otherwise. They crowd around the shipowner, begging and pleading with him to hand over the tiller; and when they don't get their way and someone else is chosen instead, they kill the rivals or throw them overboard. Then they drug the noble owner with wine or some narcotic, or knock him out some other way, take command of the ship, help themselves to the stores, and so go drinking and feasting their way along on a voyage you'd expect from men like that. On top of this, they call "sailor," "navigator," "master of the craft," any man who's clever at helping them seize the ship from the owner, by force or by persuasion, and they sneer at anyone else as useless. As for the real navigator—that he has to pay attention to the year and the seasons, the sky, the stars, the winds, and everything else that belongs to his art, if he's truly going to be fit to command a ship—they have no idea. They don't see how anyone could combine the skill of steering with the actual command, whether the rest like it or not; they've never even made that part of their trade. With all this going on aboard ship, don't you think the crew of such a vessel would write off the true navigator as a useless babbler, a stargazer, a good-for-nothing?'
I don't think you need the picture taken apart, I said, to see that it's the image of the cities and how they treat true philosophers. You take my meaning.
'Of course they would,' said Adeimantus.
I do.
'Then I don't suppose you need me to spell out what the image means—that this is the philosopher's situation in relation to the city. You see it already.'
Then offer the picture first to that man who keeps marveling that philosophers get no honor in their cities, and try to persuade him it would be far more of a marvel if they did.
'Clearly.'
I will.
'Then take this image to the man who's surprised that philosophers get no honor in their cities. Explain it to him, and try to convince him that it would be far more surprising if they were honored.'

And tell him he's right that the best people in philosophy are useless to the many — but tell him to blame the uselessness on those who make no use of them, not on the decent men themselves. It isn't in the nature of things for the helmsman to beg the sailors to be governed by him, or for the wise to wait at rich men's doors — whoever coined that clever saying lied. The natural truth is that a sick man, rich or poor, must go to the doctor's door, and everyone who needs governing to the door of the man who knows how to govern; a ruler worth anything doesn't go begging his subjects to accept his rule. But today's political leaders — go ahead and liken them to the sailors we just described, and the men they call useless stargazers to the true helmsmen.
'I will.'
Exactly right, he said.

'Tell him he's right to think the best of the philosophers are useless to the rest of the world—but tell him to blame their uselessness on the people who refuse to use them, not on the philosophers. It isn't natural for the navigator to beg the sailors to be ruled by him. And as for the clever saying that "the wise go to the doors of the rich"—whoever coined it was lying. The truth is the other way around: when a man is sick, rich or poor, it's he who must go to the doctor, and anyone who needs to be governed must go to the man who can govern. It's not for the ruler who's any good to plead with his subjects to be ruled—though the people who govern us now are a different breed, and they really do deserve to be compared to those mutinous sailors, while the true pilots are exactly the ones those sailors call useless stargazers.'

So for these reasons, and in these conditions, philosophy — the noblest pursuit there is — can hardly expect honor from men whose whole practice runs the other way. But the far greater and heavier slander falls on her from those who claim to practice her — the ones your critic has in mind when he says that most of philosophy's followers are utterly rotten and the best of them useless. And I agreed that you were right.
'Just so,' he said.
Yes.

'And for these reasons, and among men like these, philosophy—the noblest pursuit of all—is unlikely to be held in much honor by those on the opposing side. But the worst and most lasting damage isn't done to her by her enemies. It's done by her own self-proclaimed followers—the very ones your accuser had in mind when he said that the greater number of them are out-and-out rogues, and the best of them useless. And I agreed.'
And we've now seen why the decent ones are useless?
'You did.'
We have.
'And we've now explained why the good ones are useless?'
Shall we take up next why most of them inevitably go bad, and try to show that philosophy is no more to blame for that than for the other?
'True.'
By all means.
'Then shall we go on to show that the corruption of the majority is also unavoidable, and that this too is no more philosophy's fault than the other was?'

Let's start our questions and answers by going back to the nature we described — the man born fine and noble. Truth led him, you remember; he had to follow her wholly and everywhere, or be a fraud with no share at all in genuine philosophy.
'By all means.'
Yes, that was said.

'Let's take it in turn, asking and answering, going back first to our description of the gentle and noble nature. Truth, you'll remember, was his leader; he followed her always and in everything. Fail in that, and he was a fraud, with no part or share in true philosophy.'
Well, that one point alone runs violently against current opinion of him, doesn't it?
'Yes, that's what we said.'
It does, he said.
'And isn't this one point alone, to name no others, badly at odds with the way people picture him now?'

Then won't a fair defense of him run like this? — that a genuine lover of learning is born to strive toward what is; he doesn't settle among the many particular things that only seem to be, but presses on, the edge of his desire never dulled, his longing never spent, until he touches the nature of each thing that really is — touches it with the part of the soul fit to touch it, the part that is its kin — and drawing near through that kinship, coupling with true being, begetting intelligence and truth, he knows; and then he truly lives, is truly nourished, and then, and only then, is he released from his labor pains.
'Certainly,' he said.
No defense could be fairer, he said.

'And don't we have every right to say in his defense that the true lover of knowledge is always straining after being—that this is his nature; that he won't linger among the many individual things that are only appearances, but will press on, the keen edge of his desire never blunted, never slackening, until he has grasped the real nature of each thing with the part of his soul that's fit to grasp it, the part akin to it; and that, drawing near to real being and merging with it through that kinship, he begets intelligence and truth, and so comes to know, and to live and grow truly, and only then—not before—is released from the labor of his striving?'
Then will a taste for lies have any part in him? Just the opposite — won't he hate the lie?
'Nothing could be more just than that description of him,' he said.
He will.
'And will any love of falsehood be part of such a man's nature? Won't he hate a lie with all his soul?'
And with truth leading the way, we'd never expect a chorus of vices trailing along behind her?
'He will.'
Never.
'And when truth is the leader, we can't suspect any evil in the band she leads?'
Rather a sound and just character, with temperance following in its train?
'Impossible.'
Right, he said.
'Justice and soundness of mind will be in that company, and temperance will come along behind?'

Then there's no need to muster the whole choir of the philosopher's nature again from the top. You remember: courage, largeness of mind, quickness at learning, memory — all these belonged to him. And you objected that while no one could contradict any of it, still, if a man dropped the arguments and looked at the actual people they point to, he'd say that some are plainly useless and most of them bad through and through.
