Hunting the cause of that slander, we've arrived at the present question — why are most of them bad? — and that is why we took up the true philosopher's nature again and were forced to define it.
'True,' he replied.
That's it.

'There's no need for me to line up the philosopher's virtues all over again—you'll remember that courage, greatness of mind, quickness to learn, and memory were his natural gifts. And you objected that, while no one could deny what I said then, still, if you set words aside and look at the facts, some of the men so described are plainly useless and most of them thoroughly corrupt. So we set out to look into the grounds for these charges, and we've now reached the question of why the majority are bad—which forced us back, of necessity, to examining and defining the true philosopher.'

Now we have to look at how that nature gets ruined — how it's destroyed in most men, while a small number escape: the ones people call not wicked, only useless. And after that, the natures that imitate the philosophic nature and set themselves up in its occupation — what sort of souls they are, that reach for a pursuit too high for them, beyond their strength, and by striking false notes everywhere fasten onto philosophy, in all men's mouths everywhere, the reputation you describe.
'Exactly.'
What sorts of ruin do you mean? he said.

'And we have to consider next how the philosophic nature gets corrupted—why so many are ruined and so few escape ruin. I mean the ones we called useless but not wicked. After that, we'll talk about the imitators of philosophy, the men who push into a calling that's beyond them and unworthy of them, and who, by all their inconsistencies, bring down on philosophy and on every philosopher the bad name we're talking about.'

I'll try to walk you through it, I said. This much, I think, everyone would grant us: a nature with everything in it that we just demanded of the man who's to be a philosopher is a rare growth, and appears seldom among human beings.
'What are these corruptions?' he asked.
Extremely rare.
'I'll try to explain. Everyone will agree that a nature with all the qualities we required in a philosopher, brought to perfection, is a rare growth, seldom found among men.'
Then consider how many great forces are working to destroy those few.
'Rare indeed.'
What forces?
'And think how many powerful forces work to destroy these rare natures!'
Strangest of all, every one of the very qualities we praised in that nature — courage, temperance, all the things we went through — ruins the soul that has it and tears it loose from philosophy.
'What forces?'
That does sound strange, he replied.

'In the first place, their own virtues—their courage, their temperance, and the rest. Each one of these praiseworthy qualities (and here's the strangest thing of all) can ruin the soul that has them and drag it away from philosophy.'

And besides these, all the so-called goods corrupt it and pull it away: beauty, wealth, bodily strength, powerful family connections in the city — everything of that kind. You have the general shape of it.
'That is very strange,' he replied.
I do, he said; but I'd gladly learn more exactly what you mean.

'Then there are all the ordinary good things of life—beauty, wealth, strength, family connections, influence in the city, you know the sort of thing—and these too have a corrupting, distracting effect.'
Grab hold of the thing as a whole, I said, in the right way, and it will come clear — nothing strange about what was said before it.
'I understand. But I'd like you to say more exactly what you mean.'
How, then? he asked.
'Take hold of the truth as a whole, in the right way,' I said, 'and you'll have no trouble with what I just said; it won't seem strange anymore.'

Take any seed or growing thing, plant or animal: we know that if it doesn't get the food, the weather, or the soil that suits it, then the more vigorous it is, the more it suffers from the lack — for the bad is more the enemy of what's good than of what's merely middling.
'And how am I to do that?' he asked.
Of course.

'We know,' I said, 'that any seed or any growing thing, plant or animal, that fails to get the food, climate, and soil that suit it, is—the more vigorous it is—all the more harmed by the lack of what it needs; for what is good is more an enemy to evil than what is merely indifferent.'
So it stands to reason that the finest nature, under conditions foreign to it, comes off worse than a second-rate one.
'Very true.'
It does.
'So it stands to reason that the finest natures, under unsuitable conditions, suffer more harm than ordinary ones, because the gap between them and their surroundings is greater.'

Then, Adeimantus, shall we say the same of souls: the best-endowed, when they get a bad upbringing, turn out exceptionally bad? Or do you think great crimes and unmixed wickedness spring from a feeble nature, and not from a vigorous one wrecked by its rearing — while a weak nature never manages anything great, for good or for evil?
'Certainly.'
No, he said, you have it right.

'And mustn't we say, Adeimantus, that the most gifted minds, when they're badly educated, turn out exceptionally bad? Don't the great crimes and the spirit of sheer evil spring from a rich nature ruined by its upbringing, rather than from any weakness, while feeble natures are scarcely capable of any great good or any great evil?'

So the nature we gave the philosopher: with the right teaching, I think it has to grow into every virtue. But if it's sown, planted, and raised in the wrong ground, it grows into the exact opposite — unless some god happens to rescue it. Or do you believe, with the crowd, that any young men worth mentioning are corrupted by sophists — that private teachers corrupt them to any degree worth the name? Isn't it the very people who say this who are the greatest sophists of all — schooling young and old, men and women, most thoroughly, and molding them into exactly what they want them to be?
'There I think you're right.'
When do they do that? he said.

'And our philosopher follows the same pattern. Given the right nurture, he must grow up into the fullness of every virtue; but if he's sown and planted in the wrong soil, he becomes the most poisonous of all weeds—unless some divine power saves him. Do you really believe, as people so often say, that it's the Sophists who corrupt our young men, or that private teachers of the art do them any real harm worth mentioning? Isn't the public itself the greatest Sophist of all? Doesn't the public train young and old, men and women alike, to perfection, and shape them after its own heart?'

Whenever the many pack themselves into assembly seats, or courtrooms, or theaters, or army camps, or any other mass gathering, and with a huge racket blame some of what's said and done and praise the rest — both beyond all measure — shouting and banging, while the rocks and the whole place echo them back and double the roar of the blame and the praise. In a scene like that, what state do you suppose a young man's heart is in, as the saying goes? What private education will hold firm and not be washed out by that flood of blame and praise, swept downstream wherever the current runs — until he calls the same things beautiful and ugly the crowd calls, practices what they practice, and becomes one of them?
'And when does that happen?' he asked.
The pressure leaves him no choice, Socrates.

'When they crowd together,' I said, 'and the people sit packed in an assembly, or a courtroom, or a theater, or a camp, or wherever the crowd gathers, and with a great uproar they shout their praise of some things being said or done and their blame of others, both overdone, roaring and clapping their hands—and the rocks and the place they're in echo back and double the noise of their praise and their blame. In a scene like that, won't a young man's heart, as they say, leap inside him? What private training could possibly let him stand firm against such an overwhelming flood of popular opinion? Won't he be swept away on the current, taking up the public's notions of good and bad, doing what they do and becoming what they are?'
And we still haven't named the greatest pressure of all, I said.
'He's bound to, Socrates,' he said.
Which is?
'And yet,' I said, 'there's a still greater compulsion we haven't mentioned.'
What these educators and sophists add in deed when their words fail to persuade. You know, surely, that they discipline the disobedient with loss of civic rights, with fines, with death?
'What's that?'
They certainly do — in dead earnest.
'The gentle persuasion of disenfranchisement, confiscation, and death, which, as you know, these new Sophists and teachers—the public—bring to bear when their words fail.'
So what other sophist, what private man's arguments, do you think can pull against all that and win?
'They certainly do, and they mean it.'
None, I think, he said.
'So what teaching, from any other Sophist or any private man, could be expected to win out in such an unequal contest?'

None, I said — even to try is deep folly. A character trained to virtue against the education the public itself provides doesn't exist, hasn't existed, and won't exist — a human character, I mean, my friend; the divine, as the proverb goes, we leave out of the account. Because you should understand this clearly: whatever is saved and turns out well under the present condition of cities, you won't be wrong to say a god's dispensation saved it.
'None,' he replied.
That's how it looks to me too, he said.

'No indeed,' I said. 'Even to try is great folly. There neither is, nor has been, nor ever will be, a character formed in any virtue other than the one the public's training supplies—I'm speaking of human virtue, my friend; what is more than human, as the proverb says, isn't included. For I'd not have you forget that, in the present wretched state of government, whatever is saved and comes out well is saved by the power of God—and we can say that truly.'
Then let one more thing look that way to you as well.
'I quite agree,' he replied.
What?
'Then let me ask you to agree to one more thing.'

That every one of those private wage-earners — the ones the public calls sophists and treats as rivals — teaches nothing but the opinions of the many, the very things the crowd believes when it sits down together. That is what they call wisdom. It's exactly as if a keeper were raising a great, powerful beast, and made a study of its moods and appetites — how to approach it, how to handle it, when it turns most dangerous and when most mild, and what makes it so; the meaning of its various cries, and which tones of voice soothe it or set it raging. Then imagine that, having learned all this by living alongside the animal, he calls it wisdom, packages it as an art, and sets up to teach — knowing nothing, in truth, about which of these opinions and appetites is honorable or shameful, good or bad, just or unjust, but fitting all these names to the great beast's reactions: what pleases the beast he calls good, what irritates it he calls bad. He has no other account of them; whatever is merely necessary he names just and noble, because he has never seen — and couldn't show anyone else — how vast the difference really is between the nature of the necessary and the nature of the good. Wouldn't a man like that, by Zeus, make a strange sort of educator?
'What are you going to say?'
He would.

'That all those hired men whom the many call Sophists and treat as their rivals in fact teach nothing but the opinions of the many—the very views the crowds form in their assemblies—and they call this wisdom. It's as if a man kept a great, strong beast and made a study of its moods and appetites: how to approach it, how to handle it, when and why it's dangerous and when it's tame, the meaning of its various cries, and which sounds from another soothe it and which enrage it. Suppose that, by attending on it constantly, he became perfect at all this, and called his knowledge wisdom, and made of it a system and an art he could teach—though he hasn't the faintest real notion which of the creature's moods and desires is honorable or shameful, good or bad, just or unjust. He simply applies the words as the great beast's tastes dictate, calling "good" whatever delights it and "bad" whatever it dislikes, with no other account to give—he calls the necessary "just" and "noble," never having seen, and being unable to show anyone else, how vast the real difference is between necessity and goodness. Heaven help us—wouldn't a man like that be a strange sort of teacher?'

Well, is he any different from the man who thinks wisdom is having sized up the moods and pleasures of the assembled crowd — in painting, in music, or, for that matter, in politics? Whoever mixes with the many to show them a poem or some other piece of work, or a service to the city, making the crowd his master beyond anything forced on him, is under what people call the necessity of Diomede — no choice at all — to produce whatever they praise. But that what the crowd praises is really good and beautiful — have you ever heard one of them give an argument for that which wasn't laughable?
'He certainly would.'
No, he said, and I don't expect to.

'And how does he differ from the man who thinks wisdom is just knowing the moods and tastes of the mixed-up multitude—in painting, say, or music, or, in the end, in politics? For when a man goes among the many and shows off his poem or some other work of art, or some service he's done the city, and makes them his judges when he isn't forced to, then the "necessity of Diomede," as they call it, will compel him to produce whatever they happen to praise. And yet the reasons they give to back up their notions of what's noble and good are utterly absurd. Have you ever heard one that wasn't?'

With all of that in mind, remember our earlier point: can the many possibly tolerate or believe that there is a beautiful itself, as against the many beautiful things — that each thing itself exists, as against the many particulars?
'No, and I don't expect to.'
Not in the least.

'Then keeping all this in mind, recall the earlier question: will the world ever be brought to believe in the existence of beauty itself, rather than the many beautiful things—of each thing in itself, rather than the many particulars?'
Then the many can't be philosophers?
'Certainly not.'
They can't.
'So the world can't possibly be a philosopher?'
So the men who do philosophize are bound to be sneered at by them?
'Impossible.'
Bound to be.
'And so philosophers are bound to be condemned by the world?'
And by the private operators who hang on the crowd and ache to please it?
'They are.'
Obviously.
'And condemned, too, by the private individuals who keep company with the mob and try to please it?'

Given all that, what rescue do you see for a philosophic nature — any way it stays in its calling and reaches the end? Think it through from what came before. We agreed that quickness at learning, memory, courage, and largeness of mind belong to this nature.
'Obviously.'
Yes.
'Then do you see any way the philosopher can be kept safe in his calling to the end? Remember what we said about him—that he was to have quickness, memory, courage, and greatness of mind.'
Then from boyhood on, won't a boy like that be first in everything — especially if his body is born to match his soul?
'Yes.'
Why wouldn't he be? he said.
'Won't a man like that, from his earliest childhood, be first among them all in everything—especially if his body matches his mind?'
And as he gets older, his relatives and his fellow citizens will want to use him for their own affairs?
'He certainly will,' he said.
Of course.
'And as he grows older, his friends and fellow citizens will want to use him for their own purposes?'
So they'll grovel at his feet with requests and honors, staking their claim early, flattering in advance the power that's on its way to him.
'No question.'
That's usually how it goes, he said.
'They'll fall at his feet, begging favors, heaping him with honors and flattery, trying to lay hold in advance of the power that will one day be his.'

And what do you expect a young man to do in that position — especially if he's from a great city, rich and well-born in it, and good-looking and tall besides? Won't he fill up with impossible hopes, sure he'll be competent to run the affairs of Greeks and barbarians alike, and lift himself sky-high on the strength of it, stuffed with posturing and empty pride, and no sense in him at all?
'That often happens,' he said.
He certainly will.

'And what is a man like that likely to do under these conditions—especially if he's a citizen of a great city, rich and well-born, and a tall, handsome youth? Won't he be filled with boundless ambition, fancying himself fit to manage the affairs of Greeks and barbarians alike, swelling up and giving himself airs, full of empty pomp and senseless pride?'

Now suppose that while he's in that state, someone quietly comes up and tells him the truth — that there's no understanding in him, that he needs it, and that it can't be had except by slaving for it. Do you think it will be easy for him to hear, through all that noise around him?
'He's bound to.'
Anything but.

'Now, while he's in that frame of mind, suppose someone comes to him quietly and tells him the truth—that he has no sense and badly needs it, and that it can only be won by working like a slave for it. Do you think, against such odds, he'll find it easy to listen?'

But suppose, I said, that thanks to a good nature and a native kinship with reason, one such young man does take the point — bends, and lets himself be drawn toward philosophy. What do we imagine the others will do, when they see they're losing his use and his friendship? Is there a deed they won't do, a word they won't say — about him, so he won't be persuaded, and about the man persuading him, so he won't be able to persuade — plotting in private, hauling them into court in public?
'Far from it.'
It's inevitable.

'And even if, through some inborn goodness and natural good sense, one such young man has his eyes opened a little, and is humbled, and won over by philosophy—how will his friends behave when they think they're about to lose the use they hoped to make of him? Won't they do and say anything to keep him from giving in to his better nature, and to make his teacher powerless—plotting against him in private and prosecuting him in the courts?'
Then is there any way that young man becomes a philosopher?
'There's no doubt of it.'
Not really.
'And how can a man in that position ever become a philosopher?'

So you see we weren't wrong to say that even the very components of the philosophic nature, when the rearing is bad, are in their own way a cause of a man's falling out of the pursuit — they, and the so-called goods, wealth and all its apparatus?
'He can't.'
No, he said — it was said rightly.

'Then weren't we right to say that the very qualities that make a man a philosopher can, if he's badly brought up, turn him away from philosophy just as much as wealth and everything that goes with it and the other so-called goods of life?'

There, my remarkable friend, is the ruin — that, and that large — of the best nature aimed at the best of all pursuits; a nature rare enough at any time, as we keep saying. And from these same men come the ones who do the greatest harm to cities and to individuals — and the greatest good, if the current happens to carry them that way. A small nature never does anything great, to a man or to a city.
'We were quite right.'
Very true, he said.

'So this, my excellent friend, is the whole story of how the natures best suited to the best of all pursuits are ruined and lost—natures we say are rare to begin with. And it's out of this very class that the men come who do the greatest harm to cities and to individuals—and the greatest good, too, when the current carries them that way. A small nature never did anything great, for an individual or a city.'

So the men who belong to her most fall away and leave philosophy abandoned, her marriage unmade, while they live a life that is false and none of theirs; and she, orphaned of her kin, is set upon by other men — unworthy ones — who disgrace her, and hang on her the reproaches you say her detractors use: that of those who keep her company, some are worth nothing, and most deserve every bad thing they get.
'Very true,' he said.
Yes, that's what gets said.

'And so philosophy is left forsaken, her marriage rite unfinished. Her own kin have fallen away and abandoned her, and while they live their false and unbecoming lives, other men, unworthy of her, see that she has no relatives to protect her, and move in and dishonor her—and fasten on her the very reproaches her critics throw at her, that her followers are some of them good for nothing and most of them deserve the harshest punishment.'

And no wonder, I said. Other little men look over and see the ground open — a field thick with fine names and showy pretensions — and like convicts bolting out of prison into a sanctuary, the ones who happen to be cleverest at their own petty trades leap gladly out of those trades and into philosophy. Because even faring as she does, philosophy still keeps a standing prouder than any other calling — and that's what draws the crowd of stunted natures: bodies mangled by their crafts and trades, souls cramped and crushed by the same drudgery. Isn't that unavoidable?
'That's certainly what people say.'
It is.

'And what else would you expect,' I said, 'when you think of the puny little men who, seeing this field open before them—a field full of grand names and impressive titles—come bolting into philosophy like convicts breaking out of prison and dashing into a temple? They jump straight out of their trades into philosophy, and the ones who do are usually the cleverest at their own shabby crafts. For even in her present sorry state, philosophy keeps a dignity that the other arts don't have, and many a man is drawn to her whose nature is stunted, whose soul is as cramped and disfigured by his mean little trade as his body is. Isn't that bound to happen?'

And do they look any different, I said, from a little bald tinker who's come into money — just out of his chains, fresh from the bathhouse, wearing a brand-new coat, done up like a bridegroom — about to marry his master's daughter, because she's poor and there's no one to protect her?
'Yes.'
No different at all, he said.

'Aren't they exactly like a bald little tinker who's come into some money, just out of prison, freshly bathed and in a new coat, all dressed up like a bridegroom to marry his master's daughter, now that the family has fallen on poverty and ruin?'
And what will a marriage like that breed? Won't the children be bastards — poor, mean things?
'A perfect parallel.'
They can't be anything else.
'And what will the offspring of such marriages be—won't they be base and bastard?'

So when men unworthy of education come courting philosophy and pair with her above their station, what kind of thoughts and opinions shall we say they father? Won't they be exactly what deserve the name sophisms — nothing legitimate in the litter, nothing that belongs to real intelligence?
'There's no question of it.'
Exactly that, he said.

'And when men unworthy of education come up to philosophy and make an alliance with her, who is so far above them, what kind of ideas and opinions are they likely to produce? Won't they be sophisms that flatter the ear, with nothing genuine in them, nothing worthy of true wisdom or akin to it?'

That leaves a very small remnant, Adeimantus, of those who keep philosophy's company worthily. Maybe a fine, well-raised character caught by exile, who for want of anyone to corrupt him stays with her according to his nature. Or a great soul born in a small city, who looks at the city's politics and looks straight past them. And a gifted few may come over to her from some other craft they rightly despise. Some might be held back by the bridle of our friend Theages — Theages had everything else set to pitch him out of philosophy and into public life, but his sickly body reins him in and keeps him out. My own case — the divine sign — is hardly worth mentioning; it has come to almost no one before me, maybe no one at all. Now, the men of this little band have tasted how sweet and blessed a possession philosophy is, and they've watched the madness of the many long enough. They've seen that practically no one in politics does anything sound, and that there's no ally left with whom a man could march to the defense of justice and survive. He'd be like a man dropped among wild animals — refusing to join the pack in its crimes, unable single-handed to hold off the whole snarling circle, certain to be torn apart before he could do his city or his friends any good, useless to himself and everyone else. Once he's reckoned all that, he keeps quiet and minds his own work, like a traveler in a storm who steps behind a wall while the wind drives the dust and the sleet past; and watching everyone else fill up with lawlessness, he is content if he can somehow live this life clean of injustice and unholy acts, and make his exit graciously, in good temper, with fair hope.
'No doubt,' he said.
Well, he said, that's no small thing to have accomplished before leaving.

'So then, Adeimantus,' I said, 'the worthy followers of philosophy will be only a small remnant. Maybe some noble, well-bred soul kept by exile from the corrupting influences, who stays loyal to her; or some lofty mind born in a small city, whose politics he looks down on and ignores; or a gifted few who leave behind the crafts they rightly despise and come to her. And perhaps a few are held back by the bridle that held our friend Theages: everything in his life conspired to drag him away from philosophy, but bad health kept him out of politics and so kept him in it. My own case—the inner sign that holds me back—is hardly worth mentioning, since such a guide has rarely if ever been given to anyone else. Now those who belong to this small class have tasted how sweet and blessed a thing it is to possess philosophy, and they've also seen clearly enough the madness of the crowd. They've seen that hardly anyone in public life acts honestly, and that there's no ally at whose side a man might fight for justice and come through alive. Such a man is like someone fallen among wild beasts: he won't join in their wrongdoing, but he can't hold out alone against all of them in their savagery, and so, seeing that he'd be no use to the city or to his friends and would only throw his life away without helping anyone, he keeps quiet and goes his own way. He's like a man caught in a driving storm of dust and hail who takes shelter behind a wall. Watching the rest of mankind brimming with lawlessness, he's content if only he can keep his own life clean of injustice and unholy deeds, and at the end depart in peace and good will, with bright hopes.'
But not the greatest either, I said — not without a city that fits him. In one that fits, he'll grow to his full height himself, and save the commonwealth along with his own soul.
'Well,' he said, 'that's no small thing for him to have done before he goes.'
Well then: why philosophy has a bad name, and how unjustly — that seems to me fairly laid out by now. Unless you have something to add?
'No small thing,' I said, 'but not the greatest, unless he finds a city that suits him. In a city that suits him, he'll grow to his full stature and save his country along with himself.'
Nothing more on that, he said. But which of today's regimes do you say is the one that fits her?
'The reasons philosophy is so badly spoken of have now been explained well enough,' I said, 'and the injustice of the charges against her has been shown. Is there anything more you'd like to add?'

None whatsoever, I said. That is exactly my complaint: no city as constituted now is worthy of the philosophic nature. That's why the nature twists and changes — like a foreign seed sown in strange ground, which fades, is overpowered, and passes into the local strain, this stock too fails under present regimes to keep its own power and degenerates into an alien type. But if it ever meets the best regime, being itself the best, then it will show that it was truly divine all along, and everything else — every other nature and pursuit — merely human. And now, obviously, you're going to ask what that regime is.
'Nothing more on that,' he replied, 'but I'd like to know which of the existing forms of government you think suits her.'
Wrong, he said. I wasn't going to ask that — I was going to ask whether it's the city we've been founding in our talk, or some other one.

'None of them,' I said. 'And that's exactly my complaint against them: not one is worthy of the philosophic nature, and so that nature gets warped and changed. Just as foreign seed sown in alien ground loses its character and is overpowered and absorbed into the new soil, so this growth of philosophy, instead of keeping its own strength, degenerates into something else. But if philosophy ever finds the perfection that matches her own in a city, then it will be clear that she is truly divine, and that everything else—all human natures and institutions—is merely human. And now, I know, you're going to ask me what that city is.'

Ours, I said, in every other respect. But you may remember my saying even then that there would always have to be some authority alive in the city, holding to the same account of the constitution that you, the lawgiver, followed when you laid down the laws.
'No,' he said, 'there you're wrong. I wasn't going to ask that. I was going to ask whether you mean the city we ourselves founded, or some other.'
You did say it, he said.

'Ours,' I replied, 'in most respects—though you may remember I said before that there would always have to be some living authority in the city, holding the same conception of the constitution that guided you when, as legislator, you laid down the laws.'
But not clearly enough, I said — you all scared me off with your objections, which showed the proof would be long and hard. And what's left is hardly the easiest part to go through.
'That was said,' he replied.
What's left?
'Yes, but not as fully as it should have been. You scared us off by raising objections that showed the discussion would be long and hard—and what's left is the hardest part of all.'
How a city can take philosophy in hand without being destroyed by it. Everything great is precarious, and the fine things really are hard, as the saying goes.
'What's left?'
Even so, he said, settle this too, and the demonstration is complete.
'The question of how a city can take up the study of philosophy without destroying itself. Every great venture is risky—"hard is the good," as the saying goes.'

If anything stops me, I said, it won't be lack of will — lack of ability, maybe. You'll see my eagerness firsthand. In fact, look how eagerly, how recklessly, I'm about to declare that a city ought to take up this pursuit in exactly the opposite way from now.
'Still,' he said, 'let's get this cleared up, and then the inquiry will be complete.'
How?

'It won't be any lack of will that stops me,' I said, 'but, if anything, a lack of power. You'll see my eagerness for yourselves. Notice, now, how boldly and without hesitation I say that cities ought to take up philosophy—not the way they do now, but in a completely different spirit.'

Today, I said, the ones who touch philosophy at all are boys barely out of childhood. In the interval before household and moneymaking close in, they get a taste of its hardest part and then quit — and these pass for the most philosophical of men. By the hardest part I mean argument itself, dialectic. Later in life, if they're invited when others are doing it, they condescend to sit in the audience of a lecture and count it a great favor, since they think philosophy should be a side pursuit. And toward old age, all but a very few of them go out more completely than Heraclitus' sun — they are never lit again. (Heraclitus said the sun is put out each evening and kindled new each morning.)
'In what way?'
And what should they do instead?

'As things stand,' I said, 'the people who study philosophy are very young—boys barely past childhood—and they give it only the scraps of time left over from money-making and managing a household, and then they drop it, just when they come up against the hardest part of the subject, dialectic, even those reputed to have the most philosophic spirit. Later in life, if someone else invites them, they may go and hear a lecture, and they make a great fuss about it, since they don't regard philosophy as their proper business. And in the end, when they grow old, in most cases their philosophic fire is snuffed out—snuffed out more completely than Heraclitus' sun, since it never lights up again.'

Exactly the reverse. As boys and adolescents they should get a boy's education and a boy's philosophy, and take particular care of their bodies through the years when the body is growing and knitting, securing it as a servant for philosophy later. Then, as the age comes on in which the soul begins to reach its full growth, they should stiffen its exercises. And when strength fails and politics and soldiering are behind them, then let them range loose at pasture at last and do nothing else in earnest, except as a sideline — these men who are to live happily here, and crown the life they've lived with a matching portion there.
'And what should their course be instead?' he asked.
I really do believe you're in earnest, Socrates, he said. But I think most of your hearers will oppose you even more earnestly, and won't be persuaded at all — starting with Thrasymachus.

'Just the opposite. In childhood and youth they should be given the study and the philosophy suited to their age. While they're growing toward manhood, the chief care should go to the body, so they'll have it ready for the service of philosophy. Then, as life goes on and the mind begins to mature, they should step up the exercise of the soul. And when their strength fails and they're past the duties of citizen and soldier, then let them range freely and take on no serious labor, since we mean them to live happily here and to crown this life with a like happiness in the next.'

Don't set Thrasymachus and me quarreling, I said — we've just become friends, and we weren't enemies even before. We will spare no effort until we either persuade him and the others, or accomplish something they can use against the day when they live again and meet arguments like these in another life.

'How truly in earnest you are, Socrates!' he said. 'I'm sure of it. And yet I think most of your hearers will be even more in earnest in opposing you, and will never be convinced—Thrasymachus least of all.'
Just a little while off, then, he said.

'Don't start a quarrel between me and Thrasymachus,' I said. 'We've just become friends—though in fact we were never enemies. I'll keep at it with all my strength until I either win him and other men over, or at least do something to profit them against the day when they're born again and have a conversation like this one in another life.'

Nothing at all, I said, measured against the whole of time. Still, it's no wonder the many don't believe what we're saying — they have never seen the thing we're describing. What they've seen is phrases like these deliberately rhymed with one another, not falling together on their own the way ours just did. But a man balanced and matched with virtue itself, to the limit of the possible, in word and in deed, holding power in a city of the same quality — that they have never seen. Not one such man, let alone many. Do you think they have?
'You're talking about a time that's not exactly close at hand.'
No.

'Rather,' I replied, 'about a time that's nothing at all compared with eternity. Still, I'm not surprised the many don't believe it, since they've never seen what we're talking about come true. They've only seen an artificial imitation of philosophy, words strung together by design, not, like ours, having a natural unity. A human being who, in word and deed, is shaped as perfectly as a man can be into the proportion and likeness of virtue, and who rules a city built in the same image—that they've never seen, not one such man, and not many. Do you think they ever have?'

Nor, my dear friend, have they listened often enough to talk that is fine and free — the kind that strains after truth flat-out, by every means, for the sake of knowing, and keeps a polite distance from the clever quibbles whose only aim is reputation and quarrel, in the courts and in private company alike.
'No, never.'
No, he said, they haven't heard that either.

'No, my friend, and they've rarely if ever even heard free and noble talk—the kind of talk men use when they're seeking the truth with all their power, for the sake of knowing, while they hold themselves coldly aloof from the clever wrangling whose only aim is reputation and victory, whether they run into it in the courts or in private company.'

It was because of all this — we saw it coming — that, frightened as we were, the truth compelled us to say: no city, no regime, and likewise no man will ever reach completion until some chance necessity forces this small band of philosophers — the not-wicked ones, the ones now called useless — to take charge of a city whether they want to or not, and forces the city to obey; or until a true passion for true philosophy falls, by some divine breath, on the sons of the men now holding power and kingship, or on those men themselves. That either or both of these is impossible — I say there's no reason to think it. If there were, we'd deserve the laughing at, as men mouthing wishes and daydreams. Isn't that so?
'They're strangers to such talk,' he said.
It is.

'And this is exactly what we foresaw, and why the truth forced us to admit, not without fear and hesitation, that no city, no state, and no individual will ever reach perfection until the small class of philosophers we called useless but not corrupt are compelled by some providence, willing or not, to take charge of the city, and the city is compelled to obey them—or until kings, or the sons of kings and rulers, are seized by some divine inspiration with a true love of true philosophy. I see no reason to claim that either of these is impossible. If they were, we'd deserve to be laughed at as dreamers and idle visionaries. Am I not right?'

So if, somewhere in the boundless reach of time gone by, men at the peak of philosophy have been forced to take charge of a city — or are now, in some barbarian land far beyond our horizon — or ever will be, we are ready to insist on this to the last: the constitution we've described has existed, does exist, and will exist whenever this Muse of philosophy gains control of a city. It isn't impossible; we're not describing impossibilities. That it's hard, we admit ourselves.
'Quite right.'
I think so too, he said.

'Then if ever, in the endless ages of the past, or now in some distant land far beyond our knowledge, or someday in the future, the perfect philosopher has been or will be compelled by a higher power to take charge of a city, we're ready to argue to the death that our constitution has existed, and does exist, and will exist whenever this Muse of Philosophy is mistress of a city. There's nothing impossible in it. That it's difficult, we ourselves admit.'
But the many, you're about to say, don't agree?
'I agree,' he said.
They probably don't, he said.
'But are you going to tell me that the multitude don't think so?'

My friend, I said, don't be so hard on the many. They'll change their opinion if, instead of picking a fight, you soothe them and clear away the slander on the love of learning — by pointing out whom you mean by philosophers, and defining, as we just did, their nature and their pursuit, so the many see you don't mean the people they think you mean. Once they view him that way, you'll grant they'll take on a different opinion and answer in a different key. Or do you think anyone answers gentleness with harshness, or envies where no envy is shown — someone himself unenvious and mild? I'll answer for you: a temper that harsh turns up in a few people somewhere, not in the majority.
'I imagine not,' he replied.
Count me convinced, he said.

'My friend,' I said, 'don't be so hard on the multitude. They'll change their minds if, instead of attacking them, you gently set out to soothe them and to clear away their prejudice against the love of learning. Show them the philosophers as they really are, describe their nature and their calling as you were just now doing, and people will see that the man you're talking about isn't the creature they imagined. Looked at in this new light, surely they'll change their opinion of him and answer in a different tone. Who could be at war with a man who shows him no ill will, who's himself gentle and free of envy—who'd be jealous of one who has no jealousy in him? Let me answer for you: in a few you may find this harsh temper, but not in the majority of mankind.'

Then agree with this too: what has set the many against philosophy is that crowd from outside who came crashing in where they don't belong — trading insults, quarreling, forever talking about personalities — behavior nothing could suit philosophy less.
'I quite agree,' he said.
Nothing less, he said.

'And don't you think too, as I do, that the harsh feeling the many have toward philosophy comes from the pretenders—the ones who barge in uninvited, forever abusing one another, finding fault, and making people, rather than ideas, the subject of their talk? Nothing could be more unbecoming in a philosopher than that.'

Because, Adeimantus, a man whose thought is truly set on the things that are has no leisure to look down into the little wars of men, and fight them, and fill himself with envy and spite. He looks at things ranged in order, always the same — nothing wronging or wronged there, everything in pattern and proportion, arranged according to reason — and these he imitates, and grows as like them as a man can. Or do you think there's any way to keep company with what you admire and not imitate it?
'Nothing could be more unbecoming.'
There isn't.

'For the man whose mind is truly fixed on being, Adeimantus, has no time to look down at the petty affairs of men, or to fill himself with malice and envy by fighting with them. His gaze is always on things fixed and unchanging, things that neither wrong one another nor are wronged, but stand in order, all moving according to reason; these he imitates, and to these he makes himself as like as he can. Can a man help imitating that with which he keeps reverent company?'
So the philosopher, keeping company with the divine and the orderly, becomes as orderly and divine as a human being can become. Though there's plenty of slander to go around, for everyone.
'Impossible.'
Completely true.
'And so the philosopher, keeping company with the divine and orderly, becomes orderly and divine himself, as far as a man can—though, like everyone else, he'll have his slanderers.'

Now suppose some necessity forces him, I said, to practice putting what he sees up there into human characters, private and public — to shape more than just himself. Do you think he'll prove a poor craftsman of temperance and justice and the whole of civic virtue?
'Of course.'
The least poor there is.

'And if he were forced to take what he sees up there and work it into the characters of men, both in their public and their private lives, instead of just shaping himself, do you think he'd be a poor craftsman of temperance and justice and all civic virtue?'

And if the many ever realize we're telling them the truth about him, will they still be savage toward philosophers? Will they still doubt us when we say a city can never be happy unless it's drawn by the painters who work from the divine pattern?
'Anything but poor.'
They won't stay savage, he said, once they realize it. But what kind of drawing do you mean?

'And if people come to see that what we're saying about him is true, will they still be angry with philosophy? Will they refuse to believe us when we tell them no city can be happy unless its plan is drawn by artists working from the divine pattern?'

They'd take the city and the characters of its people like a painter's panel, I said, and first they'd wipe it clean — not easy at all, but you see right away that this alone separates them from every other lawgiver: they refuse to touch an individual or a city, refuse to draft a single law, until they've received a clean surface or made one themselves.
'They won't be angry, if they understand,' he said. 'But how exactly will these men draw out the plan you speak of?'
And rightly so, he said.

'They'll start by taking the city and the characters of its people as their canvas, and the first thing they'll do is wipe it clean. That's no easy task. But here, easy or not, is where they'll differ from every other lawgiver: they won't touch an individual or a city, or write a single law, until they've either found a clean surface or made one themselves.'
After that, wouldn't they sketch the outline of the constitution?
'And they'll be right to,' he said.
Surely.
'Once they've done that, won't they sketch the outline of the constitution?'

Then, as they fill in the work, I imagine they'd keep glancing both ways — toward what is by nature just and beautiful and temperate and all the rest, and toward what they're producing in mankind — blending and mixing, out of men's ways of life, the true color of a man, judging it by that very thing which Homer too, when it appears in human beings, calls the form and likeness of a god.
'No doubt.'
Right, he said.

'And then, as they fill in the picture, I imagine they'll keep glancing back and forth—looking, on the one side, at justice itself, beauty itself, temperance, and the rest, and on the other at the human copy they're shaping—blending and tempering the various elements of life into the image of a man, guided by that other image which, when it appears in human beings, Homer too called godlike and the likeness of God.'
And they'd rub one feature out, I suppose, and paint another in, until they had made human characters as dear to God as human characters can be.
'Very true,' he said.
No painting could be more beautiful, he said.
'And they'll rub out one feature and paint in another, until they've made human characters as dear to God as human characters can be?'

Well then, I said — the people you described as charging us at full stretch: are we starting to persuade them that this is the constitution-painter we were praising to their faces? They bristled because we were handing cities over to him — are they any calmer, hearing it now?
'They could make no fairer picture than that,' he said.
Much calmer, he said, if they have any sense.

'And now,' I said, 'are we beginning to win over the men you described as charging at us full force? Are we persuading them that the painter of constitutions is just the sort of man we've been praising—the one they were so furious at us for putting in charge of the city—and are they growing a little calmer now that they've heard this?'
What could they still dispute? That philosophers are lovers of what is, and of truth?
'Much calmer,' he said, 'if they have any sense.'
That would be absurd, he said.
'Why, what ground for objection could they still have? Will they doubt that the philosopher is a lover of truth and being?'
Or that the philosopher's nature, as we went through it, is close kin to the best?
'They couldn't be so unreasonable.'
Not that either.
'Or that his nature, as we've drawn it, is akin to the highest good?'
Well then — will they say that such a nature, given the practices that suit it, won't grow perfectly good and philosophic, if any nature ever will? Or that the ones we ruled out will do it better?
'They can't doubt that either.'
Surely not.
'Or will they say that such a nature, set in favorable conditions, won't turn out perfectly good and wise, if any nature ever could? Will they prefer the men we rejected?'

Then will they still snarl when we say that until the philosophic kind takes control of a city, neither city nor citizens will have rest from evils, and the constitution we've been telling like a story will never be completed in fact?
'Surely not.'
Less, maybe, he said.
'Then will they still be angry when we say that until philosophers rule, neither cities nor individuals will have any rest from evil, and this city of ours in words will never be realized?'
Not just less, if you don't mind, I said — let's say they've gone completely tame and been persuaded, so that shame, if nothing else, makes them agree.
'I think they'll be less angry.'
Certainly, he said.
'Shall we say, then, that they're not just less angry but completely won over—that they've come around, and out of shame, if nothing else, can't refuse to make peace?'
Take them as persuaded of that, then, I said. Next: will anyone contend that kings and rulers could never have sons born with philosophic natures?
'By all means,' he said.
No one, he said.
'Then suppose the reconciliation is made. Will anyone deny the other point—that there could be sons of kings or rulers who are philosophers by nature?'

And once born, can anyone claim they must inevitably be corrupted? That saving them is hard, we concede ourselves. But that in the whole of time not one out of all of them could ever be saved — would anyone press that?
'Surely no one,' he said.
How could they?

'And once such men are born, will anyone insist that they must necessarily be corrupted? That they're hard to save, even we don't deny—but that in the whole course of the ages not one of them could ever escape—who would dare to claim that?'
But surely one is enough, I said. One man, with a city that obeys him, and everything now disbelieved comes to pass.
'Who indeed!'
One is enough.
'But one is enough,' I said. 'Let there be a single such man, with a city ready to obey him, and he could bring into being the whole ideal state the world finds so hard to believe in.'
Because if a ruler establishes the laws and the practices we've described, it's surely not impossible that the citizens would be willing to live by them?
'Yes, one is enough.'
Not at all impossible.
'For if the ruler lays down the laws and institutions we've described, surely the citizens might be willing to carry them out?'
And is it any wonder, any impossibility, that what seems right to us should seem right to others too?
'Certainly.'
I don't think so.
'And it's no miracle, no impossibility, that others should approve of what we approve?'
And that these arrangements are best, if they're possible — I think we showed that well enough already.
'I think not.'
We did.
'And we've shown well enough already, in what came before, that all this, if only it's possible, is also for the best.'
So the upshot of our lawgiving is this: what we propose is best if it can be done; and doing it is hard, but not impossible.
'We have.'
That's the upshot.
'So now we can say not only that our laws would be best if they could be enacted, but also that enacting them, though hard, is not impossible.'

So — that struggle behind us, we take up what remains: in what way, through what studies and practices, the preservers of the constitution will be formed in our city, and at what ages they should take each subject up.
'Very good.'
Yes — we have to say.

'And so, after all this labor, we've come to the end of one subject. But there's more to discuss: how, and by what studies and pursuits, are the saviors of our constitution to be produced, and at what ages are they to take up their various studies?'

My earlier cleverness gained me nothing, I said — putting off the awkward business of acquiring wives, and begetting children, and appointing the rulers, because I knew how unpopular the full truth would be, and how hard to bring about. It all had to be gone through anyway. The women and children are settled; the rulers we must now pursue from the very beginning. We were saying, if you recall, that they had to prove themselves lovers of their city, tested in pleasures and in pains — shown to keep that conviction through hardships, through fears, through every reversal of fortune — and whoever broke was to be rejected, while whoever came out clean everywhere, like gold tried in fire, was to be installed as ruler and given honors and prizes, in life and in death. Something like that is what was being said, while the argument slipped past with her face veiled, afraid to stir up exactly what now lies in front of us.
'Yes, there is.'
True, he said. I remember.

'I dodged the troublesome business of how the women are to be shared, and the begetting of children, and the choosing of rulers, because I knew the whole arrangement would be looked at with envy and was hard to bring about. But that bit of cleverness did me little good, since I've had to discuss them all the same. The women and children are settled now, but the question of the rulers we'll have to take up again from the very beginning. We said, if you remember, that they had to be lovers of their country, tested by pleasures and pains, and that in no hardship, no danger, no critical moment must they ever let their loyalty slip—whoever failed was to be rejected, and whoever came through pure, like gold tried in the fire, was to be made a ruler and given honors and rewards both in life and after death. That was the sort of thing we were saying, when the argument turned aside and veiled her face, not wanting to stir up the very question that has now come up.'
I balked, my friend, at saying what we've now dared, I said. So let the daring stand: the most exacting guardians must be philosophers.
'I remember perfectly,' he said.
Let it stand, he replied.
'Yes, my friend,' I said, 'I shrank then from saying the bold word. But now let me dare to say it: the perfect guardian must be a philosopher.'
Then notice how few of them you can expect. The parts of the nature we specified rarely consent to grow together in one person; mostly the nature comes up scattered — one piece here, another there.
'Yes,' he said, 'let that be settled.'
Meaning what? he said.
'And don't imagine there will be many of them. The gifts we decided were essential rarely grow together in one nature; they usually come in scattered bits and pieces.'

You know how it goes: quick learners with good memories, shrewd, fast, and everything that follows from that — youthful fire, large ambitions — don't usually also come with a willingness to live an orderly, quiet, steady life. Men like that are carried by their quickness wherever chance takes them, and all the steadiness drains out of them.
'How do you mean?' he asked.
That's the truth, he said.

'You know that quickness of mind, good memory, shrewdness, cleverness, and the like don't often grow together, and that the people who have them, and who are also spirited and high-minded, aren't by nature inclined to live in an orderly, calm, and settled way. Their impulses carry them every which way, and all steadiness deserts them.'

And the settled characters, the steady dependable ones — the men you'd trust anywhere, who in war stand unmoved in the face of fear — are just as unmoved in the face of a lesson. They're numb where learning is concerned, as if the part had frozen, and they yawn and doze the moment there's mental work to do.
'Very true,' he said.
So it is.

'On the other hand, the steady, dependable natures, the ones who can't be moved by fear in battle and hold their ground, are just as immovable when it comes to learning. They're sluggish, always half-asleep, yawning their way through any intellectual effort.'
But we insist that a man have a good, generous share of both, or he gets no part of the highest education, no honor, no office.
'Quite true.'
Rightly, he said.
'And yet we said both sets of qualities were needed in the men who are to get the higher education and to share in any office or command.'
So don't you think that combination will be rare?
'Certainly,' he said.
Very rare.
'And won't such men be rare?'

Then the candidate must be tested in the labors, fears, and pleasures we named before — and also in something we passed over then and add now: he must be exercised in many studies, while we watch whether his nature can bear the greatest of them, or will flinch and fail, the way men fail in athletic trials.
'Very rare indeed.'
It's certainly right to look, he said. But which studies do you call the greatest?

'Then the candidate must be tested not only in the labors, dangers, and pleasures we mentioned before, but in another way we didn't mention—he must be exercised in many kinds of knowledge too, to see whether his soul can endure the highest of all studies, or whether it will flinch from them, the way some men flinch from other trials.'
You remember, I said, that we distinguished three forms in the soul, and worked out from them what justice, temperance, courage, and wisdom each are?
'Yes,' he said, 'you're quite right to test him. But what do you mean by the highest of all knowledge?'
If I'd forgotten that, he said, I'd deserve to hear none of what's left.
'You'll remember,' I said, 'that we divided the soul into three parts, and from that worked out the natures of justice, temperance, courage, and wisdom?'
And do you remember what was said just before it?
'If I'd forgotten that,' he said, 'I wouldn't deserve to hear any more.'
What?
'And do you remember the warning that came before that discussion?'

We said, roughly, that to see these matters at their finest, a longer road had to be traveled — walk it, and they become plain — though it was possible to attach demonstrations on the level of what had already been said. You all said that would do, and so the account went forward with, by my standards, less than exactness. Whether it satisfied you is yours to say.
'What warning?'
I thought you gave us fair measure, he said; apparently the others did too.

'We said, if I'm not mistaken, that to see those virtues in their full beauty a man would have to take a longer way around, at the end of which they'd come clear, but that we could tack on a popular account of them, on the level of the discussion that had gone before. And you said that account would do for you—and so the inquiry went on in what seemed to me a very imprecise way. Whether it satisfied you is for you to say.'

My friend, I said, in things like this, no measure that falls short of what is — in any respect — is fair measure at all. Nothing incomplete is the measure of anything. Though people sometimes decide the incomplete is already plenty, and that further search is wasted effort.
'It did,' he said. 'I thought, and so did the others, that you gave us a fair measure of truth.'
Plenty of people feel that way, he said — out of laziness.

'But, my friend,' I said, 'a measure of such things that falls short, even a little, of the whole truth is no fair measure. Nothing incomplete is the measure of anything—though people are often content with it, and think they needn't look any further.'
And it's the last feeling permitted, I said, in a guardian of a city and its laws.
'That's a common thing,' he said, 'when people are lazy.'
Fair enough.
'Yes,' I said, 'and it's the very last fault that should be allowed in a guardian of the city and its laws.'

Then a guardian, my friend, must go round by the longer road, and must labor as hard at learning as at the gymnasium — or, as we were just saying, he will never carry the greatest and most fitting study through to the end.
'True.'
So these aren't the greatest? he said. There's something greater still than justice and the virtues we described?

'Then the guardian must be made to take the longer way around, and to work as hard at learning as at physical training—or he'll never reach the highest knowledge of all, which, as we've just said, is his proper concern.'

Something greater, I said. And even the virtues themselves — we must not go on looking at a sketch of them, as we do now, and cheat ourselves of the most finished rendering. Isn't it ridiculous to strain every nerve for maximum precision and clarity about small things, and then not demand the highest precision for the greatest?
'What,' he said, 'is there a knowledge still higher than this—higher than justice and the other virtues?'
A worthy thought, he said. But do you imagine anyone will let you go without asking what this greatest study is — and what it's about?

'There is,' I said. 'And even with the virtues, we mustn't be satisfied with the outline we have now—nothing less than the most finished picture should content us. Isn't it absurd that when small things are worked out with endless pains so they'll appear in their full clarity and beauty, we should think the highest truths don't deserve the highest precision?'

Not at all, I said — ask away. Though you've heard the answer plenty of times; right now either it's slipped your mind, or you intend to make trouble for me by objecting. I suspect the latter. You have heard, many times over, that the greatest study is the idea of the good — the thing that just things and everything else must borrow before they become useful and beneficial. You knew more or less that this is what I was going to say — and, on top of it, that we don't know it adequately. And if we don't know it, you realize that even knowing everything else as fully as possible profits us nothing without it — exactly as owning everything profits us nothing without owning the good. Or do you think there's any gain in possessing everything except what's good? Or in understanding everything else minus the good — grasping nothing beautiful and good at all?
'A fine thought,' he said. 'But do you suppose we'll let you off without asking what this highest knowledge is, and what it's about?'
By Zeus, I don't.

'Ask, by all means,' I said. 'Though I'm sure you've heard the answer many times, and now either you don't follow me or, as I rather think, you mean to make trouble for me. For you've often been told that the Form of the Good is the highest object of knowledge, and that it's by their relation to it that just things and the rest become useful and beneficial. You can hardly be unaware that this is what I was about to speak of—the thing we know so little about, as you've often heard me say, and without which any other knowledge or possession does us no good at all. Do you think there's any value in possessing everything else, if we don't possess the good? Or in knowing everything else, with no knowledge of the beautiful and the good?'
And you certainly know this too: to the many, the good is pleasure; to the more refined, it's knowledge.
'Certainly not.'
Of course.
'And you know, too, that most people say the good is pleasure, while the more sophisticated say it's knowledge?'
And, my friend, that the ones who say this can't point to what kind of knowledge they mean — in the end they're forced to say: knowledge of the good.
'Yes.'
Which is ridiculous.
'And that the ones who say knowledge can't tell us what knowledge they mean, but are forced in the end to say "knowledge of the good"?'

Ridiculous is right, I said. They scold us for not knowing the good, then turn around and talk to us as if we did know it — the good, they say, is knowledge of the good, as though we understand the phrase the moment they pronounce the word.
'How absurd!'
Perfectly true, he said.

'Yes,' I said—'first they reproach us with not knowing the good, and then they turn around and talk to us as though we did, since they define the good as knowledge of the good, as if we understood them when they say the word "good." That, of course, is ridiculous.'
And the ones who define the good as pleasure — are they any less lost? Aren't they forced to admit, in their turn, that some pleasures are bad?
'It certainly is,' he said.
They certainly are.
'And those who define the good as pleasure are in just as much of a tangle, since they're forced to admit there are bad pleasures as well as good ones.'
Which lands them, I think, in conceding that the same things are good and bad. True?
'Certainly.'
It does.
'And so to admit that the same things are both good and bad?'
So the disputes about it are many and large — that much is plain?
'True.'
It is.
'There's no doubt this question is wrapped in difficulties.'

And here's another plain thing. With the just and the beautiful, many people would choose the appearance — doing it, having it, seeming it, without the reality. But with the good, nobody settles for owning the appearance; here everyone hunts the real thing, and the seeming is despised by all.
'None at all.'
Completely, he said.

'And don't we see this too: that with the just and the honorable, many people are happy to seem to have them, or to be thought to do them, even without the reality—but with the good, no one is content with the mere appearance. Everyone wants the real thing; here, appearance is despised by all?'

Here, then, is what every soul pursues — the thing for whose sake it does everything it does. The soul divines that the good is something, but it is baffled: it can't grasp adequately what it is, or trust it with the steady confidence it has about other things, and because of that it loses whatever benefit those other things might have carried. On a matter of that kind and that magnitude — are we to say that the best men in the city, the ones we'll put everything into the hands of, must stay in the dark?
'Very true,' he said.
Anything but, he said.

'This, then—which every soul pursues and for the sake of which it does all that it does, sensing somehow that there is such a thing, yet baffled, never quite able to grasp its nature or to feel about it the steady confidence it has about other things, and so losing whatever good there might be in those other things—this, of all things, is what the best men in our city, the men to whom everything is entrusted, must not be left to grope after in the dark. Should they be?'

At any rate, I said, just things and beautiful things won't have found much of a guardian in a man who doesn't even know in what way they are good. And I have a hunch that no one will know them adequately before he knows that.
'Certainly not,' he said.
A sound hunch, he said.
'I'm sure,' I said, 'that a man who doesn't know how the beautiful and the just are also good will make a poor guardian of them. And I suspect no one will truly know them until he knows the good.'
So our constitution will be in perfect order only if the guardian watching over it is a man who knows these things?
'That,' he said, 'is a shrewd guess.'
Necessarily, he said. But you, Socrates — do you say the good is knowledge, or pleasure, or some third thing?
'And if we have a guardian who has this knowledge, our city will be perfectly ordered?'
That's you all over, I said. You've made it perfectly clear for a while now that other people's opinions on this weren't going to satisfy you.
'Of course,' he replied. 'But I wish you'd tell me—do you think this supreme good is knowledge, or pleasure, or something else again?'
Well, Socrates, he said, it doesn't seem right for a man who has spent this long on these questions to be able to recite everyone else's convictions and never his own.
'There you are,' I said. 'I knew all along that a fastidious man like you would never be content with other people's opinions about these things.'
And does it seem right to you, I said, for a man to talk about what he doesn't know as though he knew it?
'It doesn't seem right, Socrates,' he said, 'for a man who's spent his whole life on philosophy to keep repeating other people's views and never give his own.'
As though he knew it, no, he said — but he ought to be willing to say what he thinks, as his thinking.
'Well,' I said, 'has anyone the right to speak with confidence about what he doesn't know?'

Really? I said. Haven't you noticed that opinions without knowledge are all ugly things? The best of them are blind. When men hold a true opinion without understanding, are they any different from blind men who happen to take the right road?
'He has no right,' he said, 'to speak as though he were certain. But he may say what he thinks, as a matter of opinion.'
No different.

'And don't you know,' I said, 'that opinions cut off from knowledge are all worthless, and the best of them blind? You wouldn't deny that people who hold some true notion without understanding are like blind men who happen to be on the right road?'
Then do you want to look at ugly things — blind and crooked — when you could be hearing bright and beautiful ones from other people?
'Very true.'
By Zeus, Socrates, said Glaucon, don't pull up now, with the end in sight. It will satisfy us if you go through the good the way you went through justice and temperance and the rest.
'And do you really want to gaze at what's blind and crooked and dim, when you can hear from others about what's bright and beautiful?'

It would more than satisfy me too, my friend, I said. But I'm afraid I won't be up to it, and that in my eagerness I'll cut a ridiculous figure. No, gentlemen — let's leave aside, for now, what the good itself is; to reach what I currently think about it looks like more than this push of ours can manage. But what appears to be a child of the good, its closest likeness — that I'm willing to describe, if you'd like. If not, we drop it.

'For heaven's sake, Socrates,' Glaucon said, 'don't quit just as you're reaching the finish line. We'll be satisfied if you'll give us an account of the good like the one you gave of justice and temperance and the other virtues.'
Tell us, he said. You'll pay off the account of the father another time.

'And I'd be just as satisfied myself, my friend,' I said. 'But I'm afraid I'll fall short, and that my clumsy eagerness will make me look foolish. So, gentlemen, let's set aside for now the question of what the good actually is. To reach what I have in mind about it would be too great an effort for me as I am. But I'm willing to tell you about the child of the good, the thing most like it—if you'd care to hear it. If not, we'll leave it.'

I wish I could hand over the full payment, I said, and you could collect it, instead of just the interest. Collect this interest, then — this child of the good itself. Only be careful I don't somehow deceive you against my will, and pass you a counterfeit account of the offspring.
'Tell us about the child, by all means,' he said. 'You can still owe us the account of the parent another time.'
We'll be as careful as we can, he said. Just go on.

'I only wish,' I replied, 'that I could pay that debt now, and you collect it—the account of the parent and not just of the offspring. Take this one, then, as interest in the meantime. But be on your guard that I don't cheat you with a false account of the interest, even though I've no intention of deceiving you.'
First let me get your agreement, I said, and remind you of what was said earlier in this discussion — and often enough before now.
'We'll be as careful as we can,' he said. 'Go on.'
What is it?
'I will,' I said, 'but first let me reach an understanding with you, and remind you of something I've said in the course of this discussion and on many other occasions too.'
That there are many beautiful things, I said, and many good things, and so on for each kind — that's how we speak of them, how we mark them out in words.
'What's that?'
Yes, we do.
'The old point that there are many beautiful things and many good things, each of which we describe and define as such, applying the word "many" to them.'

And there is the beautiful itself, and the good itself — and likewise for everything we were just now calling many: turning around, we posit a single idea for each, as though each were one, and we call it what each thing is.
'True,' he said.
That's so.
'And that there is also beauty itself and good itself, and so for all the things we called "many"—for each set of them can be gathered under a single Form, which we call what each really is.'
And the many, we say, are seen but not thought, while the ideas are thought but not seen.
'Very true.'
Exactly.
'And we say the many are seen but not known, while the Forms are known but not seen.'
Now, with what part of ourselves do we see the things that are seen?
'Exactly.'
With sight, he said.
'Now, with what part of ourselves do we see the things that are seen?'
And with hearing what is heard, I said, and with the other senses everything else that's perceived?
'With our sight,' he said.
Of course.
'And with our hearing we hear, and with the other senses perceive everything else that's perceived?'
Then have you noticed, I said, how extravagantly the craftsman of the senses built the power of seeing and being seen — how much more it cost him than the rest?
'True.'
Not really, he said.
'But have you noticed,' I said, 'that the craftsman who fashioned the senses made the power of sight and being seen by far the most lavish and complex of them all?'

Then look at it this way. Do hearing and sound need some third kind of thing before the one can hear and the other be heard — something whose absence means hearing won't hear and sound won't be heard?
'No, I never noticed that,' he said.
They need nothing, he said.

'Then think about it this way. Do hearing and sound need any third thing, so that the one may hear and the other be heard—some extra nature, without which the one won't hear and the other won't be heard?'
Nor do most of the other senses, I said — maybe none of them. Can you name one that does?
'Nothing of the kind.'
I can't.
'No,' I said—'and the same is true of most of the other senses, if not all. You wouldn't say any of them needs such an addition?'
But the power of sight, and of being seen — haven't you noticed that it does demand one?
'No, I wouldn't.'
How so?
'But don't you notice that sight and the things seen do need exactly that—some additional nature?'

Sight may be present in the eyes, and its owner may set out to use it, and color may be right there in things — but unless a third kind of thing is present, made by nature for exactly this purpose, you know that sight will see nothing and the colors will stay unseen.
'How do you mean?'
What thing do you mean?

'Suppose sight is in the eyes, and the man who has it is trying to use it, and color is present in the things—still, unless there's a third thing, of a kind made specially for the purpose, you know that the eyes will see nothing, and the colors will stay invisible.'
The thing you call light, I said.
'What is this thing you're talking about?' he asked.
True, he said.
'What you call light,' I replied.
Then no small nature joins them: the yoke between sight and visibility is a more precious yoking than any other pairing — by a wide margin, unless light is a thing without honor.
'True,' he said.
And it's very far from that, he said.
'So no small thing links sight and the power to be seen—a bond more precious by far than any that ties the other senses to their objects, since light is no mean thing.'
Then which of the gods in heaven can you name as master of all this — the one whose light makes our sight see, as beautifully as sight can see, and makes the seen things seen?
'No,' he said, 'light is far from a mean thing.'
The same one you would, he said, and everyone else: obviously you're asking about the sun.
'And which of the gods in heaven would you name as the lord of this light, the one whose light makes our sight see, and makes visible things appear?'
Now, sight stands to this god in the following relation, doesn't it?
'The same one you and everyone names,' he said. 'You mean the sun.'
Which?
'And isn't this how sight stands in relation to that god?'
Sight is not the sun — neither sight itself nor the place where it lives, which we call the eye.
'How?'
No.
'Neither sight itself, nor the eye in which it lives, is the sun.'
But of all the organs of sense, I think, the eye is the most sun-like.
'No.'
By far.
'But of all the organs of sense, the eye is surely the most sunlike?'
And the very power it has, it holds as a kind of allowance dispensed from the sun — an overflow streaming in.
'By far the most.'
Just so.
'And the power the eye has, it draws as a kind of overflow from the sun's store?'
So the sun is not sight; but it is the cause of sight, and sight itself sees it.
'Exactly.'
That's right, he said.
'So the sun is not itself sight, but it's the cause of sight and is seen by the very sight it causes?'

Then here is what I meant by the child of the good, I said. The good begot the sun as its own analogue: what the good is in the intelligible region, to intelligence and the things that are thought, the sun is in the visible region, to sight and the things that are seen.
'True,' he said.
How? he said. Take me through it.

'Well, this is what I meant by the child of the good—the one the good begot in its own likeness. What the good is in the intelligible world, in relation to intelligence and the things known, the sun is in the visible world, in relation to sight and the things seen.'

You know what eyes do, I said, when you turn them on things whose colors the light of day no longer holds — things lit only by the gleams of the night: they go dim, they seem nearly blind, as if there were no clear sight in them.
'Will you explain that a little more?' he said.
Very much so.

'You know,' I said, 'that when the eyes are turned toward things no longer lit by daylight, but only by the moon and stars, they see dimly and are nearly blind, as though there were no clear sight in them.'
But turn them on what the sun is shining on, and the same eyes see distinctly — the sight is plainly in them after all.
'Very true.'
Certainly.
'But when they're turned toward things the sun shines on, they see clearly, and the same eyes plainly have sight in them.'

Think of the soul the same way. When it settles on what truth and being shine upon, it understands, it knows, and it shows that it has intelligence. But when it settles on what is mixed with darkness — on what comes to be and passes away — it opines and goes dim, changing opinions up and down, and looks, this time, like a thing with no intelligence in it.
'Certainly.'
It does.

'It's the same with the soul. When it fixes itself on what truth and being shine upon, it understands and knows it and is plainly full of intelligence. But when it turns toward what is mixed with darkness, toward what comes to be and passes away, then it only has opinions, and it grows dim, shifting its opinions back and forth, and seems to have no intelligence at all.'

Then this is what you should say the idea of the good is: the thing that gives truth to what is known and the power of knowing to the knower. It is the cause of knowledge and of truth insofar as truth is known; and beautiful as both of these are — knowledge and truth — you'll be right to think the good is something else again, more beautiful still than either. As in the other realm it was correct to consider light and sight sunlike, but wrong to think them the sun, so here it is correct to consider knowledge and truth both good-like, but wrong to think either of them is the good. The standing of the good must be honored higher yet.
'Just so.'
