That's a beauty past reckoning you're describing, he said — it provides knowledge and truth, and outdoes them both in beauty. You certainly can't mean pleasure.

'Now, what gives truth to the things known, and the power of knowing to the one who knows, is what I want you to call the Form of the Good. Think of it as the cause of knowledge and of truth, in so far as truth is known. Beautiful as both knowledge and truth are, you'll be right to regard the good as different from them, and more beautiful still. And just as in the other case it was right to call light and sight sunlike, but not to call them the sun, so here it's right to call knowledge and truth good-like, but wrong to call either of them the good. The good holds a place of honor higher still.'
Watch your tongue, I said. Better to examine its image a little further, like this.
'You're speaking of an extraordinary beauty,' he said, 'if it produces knowledge and truth and yet surpasses them in beauty. You surely don't mean that it's pleasure?'
Like what?
'Heaven forbid,' I replied. 'But let me press the image a little further.'
The sun, I think you'd agree, gives visible things more than the power of being seen: also their generation, their growth, their nourishment — though the sun itself is not generation.
'In what way?'
Of course not.

'You'd say, wouldn't you, that the sun gives visible things not only the power of being seen, but also their coming-to-be, their growth, and their nourishment—though the sun is not itself a coming-to-be?'

Then say the same of the things that are known: the good not only gives them their being-known; it also confers on them their existence and their being — though the good is not being. It stands beyond being, surpassing it in rank and in power.
'Of course.'
Glaucon burst out laughing. Apollo! he said. What an unearthly exaggeration!

'In the same way, you should say that the things we know not only get their being known from the good, but also their very being and existence, while the good is not itself existence, but lies even beyond existence, surpassing it in dignity and power.'
Blame yourself, I said. You're the one who forced me to say what I think about it.
And here Glaucon said, with a comic earnestness, 'Good lord! What a staggering height!'
And don't stop, he said — at the very least, go through the sun comparison again, if you're leaving anything out.
'You brought it on yourself,' I said. 'You're the one who made me say what I think.'
Oh, I'm leaving out plenty, I said.
'And don't stop now,' he said. 'Go on—at least finish telling us about the likeness to the sun, if there's anything more.'
Then don't skip a bit of it.
'There's a great deal more,' I said.
I suspect a great deal will get skipped, I said. Still, as far as it's possible at the moment, I won't leave anything out on purpose.
'Then leave nothing out, however small.'
Don't, he said.
'I'll do my best,' I said, 'though I think a great deal will have to be left out.'

Think of it, then, as we've said: there are two of them — two kings, one reigning over the intelligible kind and region, the other over the visible. I don't say 'over the heavens,' or you'll think I'm playing on the word. (Ouranos, the heavens; horatos, the visible.) Either way, you have the two kinds before you, visible and intelligible?
'I hope not,' he said.
I have them.

'Picture, then, two ruling powers, one set over the intelligible world and the other over the visible—I won't say "the heavens," or you'll think I'm playing on the words. So you have these two before your mind, the visible and the intelligible?'

Then take a line cut into two unequal segments — one for the visible kind, one for the intelligible — and cut each segment again in the same ratio. Now rank the subsections by their relative clearness and obscurity. In the visible half, the first subsection is images. By images I mean, first, shadows; then reflections in water and in every surface that is dense, smooth, and polished; and everything of that sort. Do you see?
'I do.'
I see.

'Now take a line cut into two unequal parts. Then cut each part again in the same ratio—one part standing for the visible world, the other for the intelligible—and compare the sections by their clearness and dimness. The first section in the visible world will be images. By images I mean, first, shadows, and then reflections in water and on smooth, polished surfaces, and everything of that sort. Do you follow?'
Now set down the second subsection: what the first is a likeness of — the animals around us, everything that grows, and the whole class of things that are made.
'I follow.'
Done.
'Now let the second section stand for the things the first section was an image of—the animals around us, and every growing thing, and everything made by hand.'

And would you also say, I asked, that the visible half divides by truth and its lack — that as the likeness stands to what it's a likeness of, so the realm of opinion stands to the realm of knowledge?
'Very good.'
I would, he said — emphatically.
'And would you agree that these two sections differ in their degree of truth, and that the copy stands to the original as the realm of opinion stands to the realm of knowledge?'
Then look next at how the intelligible segment is to be cut.
'Most certainly.'
How?
'Now consider how the intelligible part of the line is to be divided.'

Like this. In its first subsection, the soul is forced to conduct its search from hypotheses, using as images the things that were themselves originals a moment ago — and it travels not toward a beginning but toward an end, a conclusion. In the second, the soul moves from hypothesis toward a beginning that is above hypothesis, without the images the first subsection used, making its way through forms themselves, by means of them alone.
'How?'
I didn't quite follow that, he said.

'Like this. In the lower of its two sections, the soul uses as images the very things that were originals before—the things in the visible world—and is forced to work from assumptions, not traveling up toward a first principle but down toward a conclusion. In the higher section, the soul moves from an assumption up toward a principle that needs no assumption, and it makes no use of images, as it did below, but works through the Forms themselves and by means of them alone.'

Then again, I said — it will be easier after this preface. You know how people who work at geometry and calculation and their kin proceed. They lay down the odd and the even, the figures, the three kinds of angle, and whatever else belongs to each inquiry, as hypotheses — as things they know. They give no account of them, to themselves or to anyone, as if they were plain to everybody; they simply start from them, and go through the remaining steps until they arrive, all consistently, at the thing they set out to examine.
'I don't quite follow you,' he said.
Yes, he said — that much I know.

'Then let me try again,' I said. 'You'll understand me better after a few preliminary remarks. You know that students of geometry and arithmetic and the kindred sciences take for granted the odd and the even, the various figures, the three kinds of angles, and the like, each in their own branch. They treat these as assumptions, as things everyone already knows, and so they don't think they owe any account of them, to themselves or anyone else, but start from them and go on, step by consistent step, to the conclusion they set out to reach.'

Then you also know that they use visible figures and build their arguments about them, while thinking not about these but about what these are like: their arguments are for the sake of the square itself, the diagonal itself — not the diagonal they've drawn. And so on throughout. The very things they mold and draw — which have shadows and reflections in water of their own — those they use in turn as mere images, seeking to see the things themselves, which can be seen by nothing but thought.
'Yes,' he said, 'I know that.'
True.

'And you also know that, although they use visible figures and reason about them, they aren't really thinking about those figures, but about the things the figures resemble. They reason about the square itself and the diagonal itself, not the particular square they've drawn; the figures they draw or model—which themselves cast shadows and reflections in water—they now treat in turn as mere images, while they're really trying to see the things themselves, which can be seen only by thought.'

This, then, is the kind I called intelligible — yes; but the soul is forced to use hypotheses in going after it, and does not travel back to a beginning, because it can't climb out above its hypotheses; and it uses as images the very objects that the things below copy — objects which, next to their own shadows, are reputed brilliant and prized for their clarity.
'That's true.'
I understand, he said. You mean what happens in geometry and its sister arts.

'This, then, is the kind of thing I called intelligible—but with the qualification that, in studying it, the soul is forced to use assumptions, and doesn't travel up to a first principle, since it can't rise above its assumptions. It uses as images the very things below, the things of which the shadows are themselves resemblances—things that, compared with their shadows and reflections, count as clear and are valued accordingly.'

Then by the second subsection of the intelligible, understand me to mean what reason itself grasps by the power of dialectic: treating its hypotheses not as first principles but as hypotheses in the true sense — footholds and springboards — so that it can rise all the way to what needs no hypothesis, the first principle of everything. And having touched that principle, it turns and holds to what follows from it, and comes down in that way to a conclusion — using nothing sensible at all, only forms: moving through forms, into forms, and ending in them.
'I understand,' he said. 'You mean the province of geometry and the related arts.'

I follow, he said — not adequately, since this sounds to me like an enormous undertaking — but this much I take you to be laying down: the slice of being and the intelligible that dialectic's knowledge studies is clearer than what the so-called arts study, whose starting points are hypotheses. Students of the arts are compelled, true, to study their objects with thought rather than the senses; but because they examine them without climbing back to a first principle — from hypotheses only — you judge that they don't exercise intelligence upon them, even though the objects themselves are intelligible when taken together with a first principle. And the state of mind of geometers and their kind you call, I think, thought and not intelligence — thought sitting somewhere between opinion and intelligence.

'And by the other section of the intelligible, you must understand me to mean what reason itself grasps by the power of dialectic. Here it treats its assumptions not as first principles but truly as assumptions—as stepping-stones and springboards—so that, rising above them, it may reach what needs no assumption, the first principle of everything; and having grasped that, it holds fast to whatever follows from it, and so comes down again to a conclusion, using no sensible thing at all, but moving through Forms, by way of Forms, to Forms, and ending in Forms.'

You've taken it in perfectly adequately, I said. Now, matching the four segments, accept these four conditions that arise in the soul: intelligence for the highest; thought for the second; assign conviction to the third; and to the last, imaging — the reading of shadows and likenesses. And set them in proportion: as the objects they're set over share in truth, so the conditions share in clearness.

'I follow you,' he replied, 'though not perfectly—you seem to me to be describing an enormous task. But I do understand you to say that the knowledge of being and of the intelligible that dialectic gives us is clearer than what the so-called sciences give, which start from assumptions; that those sciences, too, are grasped by the understanding and not by the senses; but that because the men who study them start from assumptions and don't rise to a first principle, you think they don't truly exercise reason on their objects, even though those objects, with a first principle added, would belong to reason. And the habit of mind that goes with geometry and the related sciences, I take it you'd call understanding rather than reason—something between opinion and reason.'
I understand, he replied. I agree, and I arrange them as you say.

'You've grasped my meaning exactly,' I said. 'And now, to match these four divisions, let there be four states in the soul: reason answering to the highest, understanding to the second, conviction to the third, and the perception of images to the last. Arrange them in order, and grant each one as much clearness as its objects have truth.'
'I understand,' he replied, 'and I agree, and I accept your arrangement.'
spine.label: Book VII
spine.title: The Cave
The Allegory of the Cave
spine.text: Next, I said, compare our nature — how far it is educated, how far not — to a condition like this. Picture people in a home under the earth, a kind of cave, with a long entrance rising toward the daylight, as wide as the cave itself. They have been there since childhood, legs and necks in chains, so that they stay put and look only at what is in front of them — the chains keep them from turning their heads. Their light comes from a fire burning far above and behind them, and between the fire and the prisoners, higher up, there runs a road, with a low wall built along it, like the screen a puppeteer sets between himself and his audience, over which he shows the puppets.

'Next,' I said, 'I want you to picture the difference between an educated nature and an uneducated one, and to do it with an image. Imagine human beings living underground in a kind of cave. It has a long entrance open to the light, as wide as the cave itself. The people have been here since childhood, with their legs and necks chained so that they can't move. They can only look straight ahead; the chains keep them from turning their heads. Above and behind them, some way off, a fire is burning, and between the fire and the prisoners there is a raised path. Picture a low wall built along this path, like the screen that puppeteers set up in front of themselves, over the top of which they show their puppets.'
I see.
'I'm picturing it,' he said.

Then see also men carrying things along that wall — all kinds of objects that stick up over it: vessels, and statues of people and animals in stone and wood and every sort of material. Some of the carriers, as you would expect, are talking; others are silent.

'Now picture people walking along behind that wall, carrying all sorts of things that stick up above it. Statues of men and animals made of stone and wood, and every kind of object. Naturally, some of the people carrying them are talking and some are silent.'
A strange image, he said, and strange prisoners.
'That's a strange image,' he said, 'and strange prisoners.'
Like us, I said. Because first of all, do you think such men would have seen anything of themselves and one another except the shadows the fire throws on the cave wall in front of them?
'They're like us,' I said. 'For one thing, do you suppose such people would ever have seen anything of themselves and one another except the shadows the fire throws on the wall in front of them?'
How could they, he said, if they were forced to keep their heads still their whole lives?
'How could they,' he said, 'if they were forced to keep their heads still their whole lives?'
And the things being carried past — isn't it the same? They would see only the shadows?
'And what about the objects being carried past? Wouldn't it be the same? They'd only see the shadows.'
Of course.
'Of course.'
So if they could talk with one another, don't you think they would take the shadows they saw for the real things they were naming?
'So if they could talk with one another, don't you think they'd assume that the names they used referred to the things passing in front of them?'
They would have to.
'They'd have to.'
And suppose the prison had an echo from the wall facing them. Whenever one of the men passing behind spoke, do you think they would take the voice to be anything but the passing shadow's?
'And suppose the prison had an echo coming off the wall in front of them. Whenever one of the people behind them spoke, wouldn't the prisoners be certain the voice belonged to the passing shadow?'
Nothing else, he said.
'Absolutely,' he said.
Then to men like that, I said, the truth would be nothing else than the shadows of the carried objects.
'Then for these people,' I said, 'the truth would be nothing but the shadows of those carried objects.'
It would have to be.
'That's certain.'

Now watch, I said, what their release from the chains and their cure from this folly would be like, if something of the sort naturally happened to them. Suppose one of them were set free and suddenly made to stand up, turn his neck, walk, and lift his eyes toward the light. Every movement would hurt, and the glare would leave him unable to make out the things whose shadows he used to see. What do you think he would say if someone told him that all this time he had been looking at rubbish — that now he is closer to what is, turned toward things that are more real, and seeing more truly? And if his instructor pointed to each of the things passing by and pressed him to answer what it was — don't you think he would be at a loss, and believe that what he saw before was truer than what is being shown to him now?

'Now think about what their release and their cure would be like, if it ever happened. Suppose one of them is set free and suddenly forced to stand up, turn his neck around, walk, and look toward the light. Every one of these movements would hurt. The glare would dazzle him, and he wouldn't be able to make out the things whose shadows he'd been seeing all along. What do you think he'd say if someone told him that what he'd been looking at all this time was worthless, but that now he was closer to what is real, turned toward things that have more being, and seeing more truly? And suppose that someone pointed at each of the objects passing by and made him say what each one was. Don't you think he'd be at a loss, and convinced that the shadows he used to see were truer than the things now being shown to him?'
Much truer.
'Far truer,' he said.

And if he were forced to look at the light itself, wouldn't it hurt his eyes? Wouldn't he turn and run back to the things he can see, convinced that those really are clearer than what is being shown to him?

'And if he were forced to look straight at the light itself, wouldn't his eyes hurt? Wouldn't he turn away and run back to the shadows he could actually make out, certain that they were clearer and more real than what he was being shown?'
He would.
'He would,' he said.

And suppose, I said, someone dragged him out of there by force, up the rough, steep climb, and did not let go until he had hauled him into the light of the sun. Wouldn't he suffer, and resent being dragged? And when he came into the light, his eyes flooded with the glare, he would not be able to see a single one of the things now called real.

'And suppose someone dragged him out of there by force, up the rough, steep slope, and didn't let go until he'd hauled him out into the sunlight. Wouldn't that be painful? Wouldn't he resent it? And once he reached the light, with the sun filling his eyes, he wouldn't be able to see a single one of the things we now call real.'
Not at first, anyway, he said.
'No, not right away,' he said.

He would need time to adjust, I think, before he could see the things above. At first he would make out shadows most easily; then the reflections of people and other things in water; then the things themselves. After that he would find it easier to look at what is in the sky, and at the sky itself, by night — the light of the stars and the moon — than at the sun and the sun's light by day.

'He'd need time to get used to it before he could see anything up there. At first he'd find it easiest to look at shadows, then at the reflections of people and other things in water, and only later at the things themselves. After that he'd be able to look at the heavenly bodies and the sky itself by night, gazing at the light of the stars and the moon more easily than at the sun and its light by day.'
Of course.
'Of course.'
And last of all, I suppose, he would be able to look at the sun — not its reflection in water or in some borrowed place, but the sun itself, by itself, in its own region — and see it as it is.
'And finally, I imagine, he'd be able to look at the sun itself. Not at reflections of it in water or anywhere else, but the sun on its own, in its own place, and see it as it truly is.'
Necessarily.
'Necessarily,' he said.

And by then he would be reasoning about it: that this is what gives the seasons and the years, and governs everything in the visible world, and is in a way the cause of all the things he and his companions used to see.

'And at that point he'd begin to reason about it. He'd conclude that this is what governs the seasons and the years, what oversees everything in the visible world, and that in a sense it is the cause of all the things he and his fellow prisoners used to see.'
Clearly, he said, that is where he would come next.
'Clearly,' he said, 'that's where his reasoning would lead him after all this.'
Well then. When he remembered his first home, and the wisdom of that place, and his fellow prisoners, don't you think he would count himself happy in the change, and pity them?
'And when he remembered where he'd lived at the start, and what passed for wisdom down there, and his fellow prisoners, don't you think he'd count himself lucky for the change, and pity the others?'
Very much so.
'Very much so.'

And if they had held honors and prizes among themselves back then — awards for whoever saw the passing shadows most sharply, and best remembered which of them usually came first, which later, and which together, and so was best at guessing what would come next — do you think he would crave those prizes, or envy the men the prisoners honored and put in power? Wouldn't he rather feel what Homer says — that it is

'Now suppose that down in the cave they handed out honors and praise to one another, with prizes for whoever was sharpest at spotting the passing shadows, and best at remembering which ones usually came first, which came after, and which came together, so that he was best at predicting what would come next. Do you think the freed man would want those prizes, or envy the ones who held power and honor down there? Wouldn't he feel, with Homer, that it's far better to "slave on the land for some other man, a man with no land of his own and not much to live on," and put up with anything at all rather than hold the opinions they hold and live the way they live?'
'better to work the earth as a hired hand for some other man, a man with nothing of his own,'
'Yes,' he said, 'I think he'd put up with anything before he'd live that way.'
and endure anything at all, rather than believe what they believe and live the way they live?
'And here's something else to consider,' I said. 'Suppose this man went back down and sat in his old seat. Coming in suddenly out of the sun, wouldn't his eyes be swimming in the dark?'
Yes, he said. I think he would suffer anything rather than live like that.
'They certainly would,' he said.
Then think about this too, I said. If a man like that went back down and sat in his old seat, wouldn't his eyes be filled with darkness, coming suddenly out of the sun?

'And if he had to compete with the prisoners who'd never left, judging those same shadows, while his eyes were still weak and hadn't readjusted (and getting used to the dark again might take quite a while), wouldn't he look ridiculous? Wouldn't they say he'd gone up and come back with his eyesight ruined, and that it wasn't even worth trying to go up there? And if they could get their hands on the man who kept trying to free them and lead them up, wouldn't they kill him?'
They certainly would.
'They certainly would,' he said.

And suppose he had to compete again at judging those shadows, against men who had never left their chains, while his sight was still dim and his eyes had not yet settled — and the resettling might take no short time. Wouldn't he be laughed at? Wouldn't they say he had gone up and come back down with his eyes ruined, and that it is not worth even trying the climb? And the man who tried to free them and lead them up — if they could somehow get their hands on him and kill him, wouldn't they kill him?

'Now take this whole image, dear Glaucon, and lay it alongside everything we said before. The cave, the prison, is the world we see with our eyes. The light of the fire in it stands for the sun. And the climb up out of the cave, and the sight of the things above, is the soul's ascent into the world the mind grasps. That, at least, is how I understand it, since that's what you wanted to hear. Whether it's right, only god knows. But this is how things look to me: at the very top of the knowable world is the Form of the Good, and it's hard to see, but once seen it has to be reckoned the cause of everything right and beautiful. In the visible world it gives birth to light and to the lord of light; in the intelligible world it is itself the lord, and the source of truth and understanding. And anyone who means to act wisely, in private or in public, has to have seen it.'
They would, he said.
'I agree with you,' he said, 'as far as I'm able to follow.'

Now this whole image, dear Glaucon, I said, must be fitted to everything we said before. The world our eyes show us is the prison home, and the firelight inside it is the power of the sun. If you set the climb upward and the sight of the things above as the soul's ascent into the intelligible world, you will have my hope of it right — since that is what you wanted to hear. Whether it is true, a god knows. But this is how it appears to me: in the world of what can be known, the form of the good is seen last, and seen only with effort; and once it is seen, the conclusion must be that it is the cause of everything right and beautiful in anything — in the visible world it fathers light and the lord of light, and in the intelligible world it is itself sovereign, the source of truth and understanding — and that anyone who means to act sensibly, in private or in public, must have seen it.

'Then come and agree with me on one more thing,' I said. 'Don't be surprised that the people who get up there don't want to come back down and deal with human affairs. Their souls long to spend their time above. And that's only natural, if our image holds.'
I agree, he said, as far as I can follow you.
'Quite natural,' he said.

Then come agree with me on this too, I said, and don't be surprised that those who have climbed that high are unwilling to busy themselves with human affairs — their souls keep pressing to spend their time above. That is natural, if our image holds.

'And here's another thing that shouldn't surprise you. When a man comes back down from those divine contemplations into the wretched human world, of course he looks clumsy and absurd. His eyes are still adjusting to the dark, and before he's used to it he's forced into court, or somewhere like it, to fight over the shadows of justice, or the images that cast those shadows, and to wrangle about how these things are understood by people who have never seen justice itself.'
It is, he said.
'That's not surprising at all,' he said.

And is it any wonder, I said, if a man who comes from divine contemplations to the miseries of human life cuts a poor figure and looks completely ridiculous — while his eyes are still blinking, before he has grown used to the darkness around him — when he is forced to fight, in law courts or anywhere else, about the shadows of justice, or the statues that cast those shadows, and to argue over how these things are understood by people who have never seen justice itself?

'But anyone with sense,' I said, 'will remember that eyes get confused in two ways and for two reasons: passing from light into darkness, and from darkness into light. He'll know that it's the same with the soul. So when he sees a soul confused and struggling to see something, he won't just laugh thoughtlessly. He'll ask whether it has come from a brighter life and is dimmed because it isn't yet used to the dark, or whether it has come up out of ignorance into the light and is dazzled by the glare. He'll count the first soul happy in what it has come to and the way it lives, and pity the second. And if he does feel like laughing at the second, his laughter will be less ridiculous than if he laughed at the soul that has come down from the light above.'
No wonder at all, he said.
'That's a very fair way of putting it,' he said.

But anyone with sense, I said, would remember that the eyes are confused in two ways, from two causes: moving from light into darkness, and moving from darkness into light. He would realize that the same holds for the soul, and when he saw one confused and unable to make something out, he would not laugh mindlessly. He would ask first whether it had come from a brighter life and was dark from being out of its element, or had come out of deeper ignorance into a brighter place and was dazzled by the flood of light. The first he would count happy in what it had lived and seen; the second he would pity — and if he did want to laugh, the laugh would fall less absurdly on the soul coming up from below into the light than on the one coming down from above.

'If all this is true,' I said, 'then we have to draw a conclusion about education. It isn't what some people claim it is. They say they can put knowledge into a soul that doesn't have it, as if they were putting sight into blind eyes.'
That is a fair way to put it, he said.
'Yes, that's what they say,' he replied.

Then if this is true, I said, we have to conclude that education is not what some of the people who profess to teach it say it is. They claim, more or less, that there is no knowledge in the soul and that they put it in — like putting sight into blind eyes.

'But our argument shows that the power to learn is already present in everyone's soul. It's like an eye that can't turn from darkness to light without the whole body turning. The whole soul has to turn away from the world of change until it can bear to look at what is real, and at the brightest thing that is real, which is what we call the Good. Isn't that so?'
So they claim, he said.
'Yes.'

But our argument shows, I said, that the power to learn is already in every soul, along with the instrument each of us learns with. Just as an eye cannot be turned from darkness to light except together with the whole body, so this instrument must be wheeled around, together with the whole soul, away from the world of becoming, until it can bear to look at what is — and at the brightest of what is, which we say is the good. Isn't that so?

'Then education is the art of turning this power around: the craft of doing it as easily and effectively as possible. It isn't a matter of putting sight into the eye, since the eye already has it. It's a matter of turning the eye the right way, when it's looking in the wrong direction and not where it should be.'
Yes.
'So it seems,' he said.

Then wouldn't there be an art of just this, I said — of the turning around: how the soul can be turned most easily and effectively? Not an art of putting sight into it — it has sight already — but it faces the wrong way, looking where it should not, and that is what this art would work on.

'Now the other so-called virtues of the soul do seem close to the virtues of the body. If they aren't there to begin with, they can be put in later by habit and practice. But the virtue of understanding belongs, more than anything, to something more divine, it seems, which never loses its power. Depending on which way it's turned, it becomes useful and beneficial, or useless and harmful. Haven't you noticed how sharp and clear-sighted the little soul of a scoundrel can be, the kind people call clever? Notice how keenly it sees the things it's pointed at. Its sight isn't weak. It's just forced into the service of evil, so the sharper its vision, the more harm it does.'
So it seems.
'I've certainly noticed,' he said.

Now the other so-called virtues of the soul do seem close to the virtues of the body — where they are absent at first, they really can be built in later by habit and practice. But the virtue of understanding, it seems, belongs to something more divine, which never loses its power, and which becomes useful and beneficial, or useless and harmful, depending on which way it is turned. Haven't you noticed, in men called clever but vicious, how sharply their little soul sees, how keenly it makes out the things it is turned toward? Its sight is not weak. It has been forced into the service of vice, so the sharper it sees, the more harm it does.

'But suppose,' I said, 'that a nature like that had been hammered into shape from childhood, and the leaden weights of indulgence had been cut away. I mean the cravings for food and drink and pleasures of that sort, which from birth are fastened to the soul and drag its vision downward. Suppose the soul had been turned away from all that and toward the truth instead. Then the very same soul, in the very same people, would see the truth just as sharply as it now sees the things it's pointed at.'
I certainly have, he said.
'That seems likely,' he said.

And yet, I said, if a nature like that had been pruned back in earliest childhood — cut free of the leaden weights of becoming, the weights that feasting and gluttony and pleasures of that kind bolt onto the soul and that drag its vision downward — if it had been freed of all that and turned toward what is true, the very same faculty in the very same men would have seen the truth as sharply as it now sees the things it is turned to.

'And isn't this likely too,' I said, 'in fact, doesn't it follow from what we've said, that people without education and without experience of the truth could never govern a city well, and neither could people who are allowed to spend their whole lives in study? The first have no single goal in life to aim all their actions at. The second won't act at all unless they're forced to, because they think they've already moved to the Isles of the Blessed while they're still alive.'
Very likely.
'True,' he said.

And here is another thing that is likely, I said — in fact it follows necessarily from what we have said: a city will never be well governed by the uneducated, who have no experience of truth, nor by men who are allowed to spend their whole lives in education. Not the first, because they have no single target in life at which everything they do, in private and in public, must aim. Not the second, because they will not act if they can help it — they think they have already moved out to the Isles of the Blest.

'So it falls to us, the founders of this city,' I said, 'to compel the best natures to reach the knowledge we called the greatest of all: to see the Good, and to make that climb. But once they've climbed up and seen enough, we mustn't let them do what they're allowed to do now.'
True, he replied.
'What's that?' he asked.

Then it is our job, I said — the job of the founders — to compel the best natures to reach the study we said before was the greatest: to see the good, to make that climb; and once they have climbed and seen enough, not to allow them what is allowed now.
'Stay up there,' I said, 'and refuse to go back down to the prisoners in the cave, to share their labors and their honors, whether those are worth much or not.'
What is that?
'But then,' he said, 'aren't we wronging them? Are we going to make them live a worse life when a better one is open to them?'
Staying up there, I said — refusing to go back down among the prisoners, or to share their labors and their honors, whether those honors are worth much or little.

'You're forgetting again, my friend,' I said, 'that the law isn't concerned with making any one class in the city especially happy. It aims at the happiness of the city as a whole. It binds the citizens together by persuasion and by necessity, and makes them share with one another whatever benefit each is able to bring to the community. The law itself produces such men in the city, not so that each can go his own way, but so that the lawgiver can use them to bind the city into one.'
But won't we be wronging them? he said. Won't we make them live a worse life, when a better one is open to them?
'You're right,' he said. 'I'd forgotten.'

You have forgotten again, my friend, I said, that the law is not concerned with making any one class in the city especially happy. It works to bring happiness about in the whole city, holding the citizens together by persuasion and by necessity, making them share with one another the benefit each can bring to the community. The law itself makes men like this in the city — not so that each can turn wherever he pleases, but so that the law can use them to bind the city into one.

'So consider, Glaucon,' I said, 'we won't be wronging the philosophers we produce when we make them care for the others and watch over them. We'll tell them something true: in other cities, men like them are right not to share in the city's labors, because they sprang up on their own, against the will of the regime there. And it's only fair that what grows of its own accord, owing its upbringing to no one, should feel no obligation to pay anyone back for it. But you we brought into being, for your own sake and the city's, to be like kings and leaders in a hive: better and more fully educated than the rest, and better able to share in both ways of life. So each of you, in turn, must go down to live with the others and get used to seeing in the dark. Once you're used to it, you'll see a thousand times better than the people down there. You'll know each image for what it is and what it's an image of, because you've seen the truth about beautiful, just, and good things. And so the city will be governed by us and by you in waking reality, not in a dream, the way most cities are governed now, by men who fight one another over shadows and quarrel about ruling as though it were some great good. The truth is this: the city where those who are to rule are least eager to rule will be the best and the most free of strife, and the city with rulers of the opposite kind will be the opposite.'
True, he said. I had forgotten.
'Quite true,' he said.

Then notice, Glaucon, I said, that we won't be wronging the philosophers who grow up among us — we will be saying only what is just when we compel them to care for the others and stand guard over them. We will tell them: in other cities, men of your kind can reasonably refuse a share in the city's labors, because there they spring up on their own, against the will of the regime; and what grows by itself, owing its food to no one, is right to feel no debt for its upbringing. But you we bred deliberately — for yourselves and for the rest of the city, like leaders and kings in a hive — educated better and more completely than the philosophers elsewhere, and more able to take part in both lives. So each of you in turn must go down to the common dwelling of the others and get used to seeing in the dark. Once you are used to it, you will see ten thousand times better than the people down there; you will know each of the images for what it is and what it is an image of, because you have seen the truth about the beautiful and the just and the good. And so the city — ours and yours — will be governed awake, not in a dream, the way most cities are governed now, by men fighting one another over shadows and quarreling over rule, as if rule were some great good. The truth is surely this: the city where the men who are to rule are least eager to rule is of necessity the best and most quietly governed, and the city that gets the opposite kind of rulers, the worst.

'And do you think our pupils will refuse us when they hear all this? Will they be unwilling to take their turns at the labors of the city, when they're allowed to spend most of their lives together in the pure light above?'
Exactly so, he replied.

'They can't refuse,' he said. 'We're laying a just command on just men. Still, each of them will go into office as something that has to be done, the very opposite of the way rulers do now in every city.'

Then do you think our pupils will disobey us when they hear this, and refuse to share the city's labors, each group in its turn, while living most of their time with one another in the clear air above?

'That's right, my friend,' I said. 'If you can find, for those who are going to rule, a life better than ruling, then you can have a well-governed city. Because only in that city will the rulers be truly rich, not in gold, but in the good and wise life that real wealth consists of. But if men go after public office poor and hungry for private gain, thinking that's where they'll snatch the good, then good government is impossible. They'll fight over ruling, and that war among kinsmen, that civil war, will destroy them and the whole city with them.'

Impossible, he said. We will be laying a just command on just men. But there is no doubt each of them will go to office as an unavoidable thing — the very opposite of the men who rule in every city now.
'Very true,' he said.

That is how it is, my friend, I said. If you can find a life better than ruling for the men who are going to rule, a well-governed city becomes possible for you. Only in that city will the rulers be truly rich — not in gold, but in what a happy man must be rich in: a good and sensible life. But if beggars come to public office, men starved for goods of their own, expecting to snatch their good from there, it cannot work. Rule becomes a thing to fight over, and a war like that — domestic, inside the walls — destroys the fighters and the rest of the city with them.
'And is there any life,' I asked, 'that looks down on political power except the life of true philosophy? Do you know of one?'
Most true, he replied.
'No, I don't,' he said.
And do you know of any life that looks down on political office, I said, other than the life of true philosophy?
'And the men who go to rule mustn't be lovers of ruling. Otherwise rival lovers will fight over it.'
No, by Zeus, I do not, he said.
'Of course.'
But surely the ones who go to rule must not be lovers of ruling. Otherwise the rival lovers will fight.

'So who else will you compel to take up the guardianship of the city than the men who understand best what makes a city well governed, and who have other honors and a better life than the political one?'
Of course.
'No one else,' he said.
Then whom else will you compel to go and guard the city but the men who understand best how a city is best governed, and who have honors of another kind, and a better life than the political one?
'Then do you want us to look at how such men will be produced, and how someone will lead them up into the light, the way some are said to have gone up from Hades to the gods?'
No one else, he replied. Those are the men I will choose.
'Of course I do,' he said.
Then do you want us to consider next how such men will come to exist, and how we will lead them up to the light — the way some are said to have gone up from Hades to the gods?

'But this, it seems, isn't a matter of flipping a shell in a children's game,' I said. 'It's a turning of the soul around, away from a day that is really a kind of night, toward the true day. It's that ascent into the real that we say is true philosophy.'
Of course I do.
'Exactly,' he said.

This, it seems, is not a matter of flipping a shell, as in the children's game; it is the turning around of a soul, from a day as dark as night toward the true day — the climb up into being, which we say is true philosophy.
'So shouldn't we ask which studies have the power to do this?'
Quite so.
'We should.'
Then shouldn't we ask which studies have the power to do this?

'What study, then, Glaucon, draws the soul away from the world of change and toward what truly is? And here's a thought that just occurred to me. Didn't we say that these men have to be athletes of war in their youth?'
Certainly.
'We did say that.'
So what study, Glaucon, would draw the soul from becoming toward being? And here is something else that occurs to me as I speak: didn't we say these men had to be athletes of war in their youth?
'Then the study we're after has to have one more quality besides the others.'
We did.
'Which one?'
Then the study we are looking for needs one more quality.
'It mustn't be useless to men going to war.'
What quality?
'It mustn't, if that's possible,' he said.
It must be useful in war.
'Now we trained them earlier with physical exercise and with the arts, didn't we?'
Yes, if possible.
'We did,' he said.
Earlier, we educated them in two arts, didn't we?
'And physical training is concerned with what comes to be and passes away. It oversees the growth and decay of the body.'
Just so.
'So it seems.'
And gymnastics is busy with what comes to be and passes away — it presides over the growth and decay of the body.
'Then that can't be the study we're looking for.'
Apparently.
'No.'
So that cannot be the study we are looking for.
'What about the arts and music, the way we described them before?'
No.

'But those,' he said, 'were just the counterpart of physical training. They educated the guardians through habit. Harmony made them harmonious and rhythm made them rhythmical, but they didn't impart any real knowledge. The stories in them, whether myth or something closer to the truth, had a kindred rhythm and harmony of their own. But there was nothing in any of it that led to the kind of good you're looking for now.'
Then is it music, as we described it before?
'Your memory is exact,' I said. 'There really wasn't anything of that sort in it. But then, my dear Glaucon, what study would have it? We set aside all the manual crafts as beneath us.'

But music, he said — if you remember — was the counterpart of gymnastics. It educated the guardians through habit: its harmonies gave them a kind of harmoniousness, not knowledge; its rhythms, a rhythmic grace; and its stories, whether fable or nearer truth, carried kindred qualities of the same sort. There was nothing in it leading to the kind of good you are looking for now.
'We did. And if we leave out the arts and physical training and the crafts, what's left?'
Your memory is exact, I said. There really was nothing of that kind in it. But then, my dear Glaucon, what study would do it? The crafts, we agreed, were all beneath free men.
'Well,' I said, 'if we can't find anything beyond those, let's take something that runs through all of them.'
Obviously. And yet if music and gymnastics are out, and the crafts are out, what is left?
'What's that?'
Well, I said, if we cannot take anything outside those, let us take something that runs through all of them.
'Something common, that every art and every kind of thought and knowledge makes use of, one of the first things everyone has to learn.'
What sort of thing?
'What is it?' he asked.
This common thing, for instance — what every art and every form of thought and every science uses, and one of the first things everyone must learn.
'That small matter,' I said, 'of telling the difference between one, two, and three. In a word, number and counting. Doesn't every art and every science have to share in those?'
What is it?
'It certainly does,' he said.
The trivial business, I said, of telling one from two from three. I mean, in short, number and calculation. Isn't it true of them that every art and every science must have a share?
'Including the art of war?'
It is.
'It has to,' he said.
Then the art of war too?

'In the tragedies, at any rate, Palamedes is forever making Agamemnon look like a ridiculous general,' I said. 'Haven't you noticed? He claims that by inventing number he marshaled the troops at Troy and counted the ships and everything else, as though none of it had been counted before, and as if Agamemnon, not knowing how to count, didn't even know how many feet he had. What kind of general do you suppose that would make him?'
It has no choice.
'A very strange one,' he said, 'if that were really true.'

Then Palamedes, I said, makes Agamemnon look like an utterly absurd general — every time the tragedians put him on stage. Haven't you noticed? He claims that by inventing number he laid out the positions of the army at Troy and counted the ships and everything else — as if before him nothing had been counted, and Agamemnon apparently did not even know how many feet he had, since he could not count. What kind of general do you make of that?
'So we'll set down as necessary for a soldier,' I said, 'the ability to count and to reckon with numbers?'
A strange one, he said, if that is true.
'More necessary than anything,' he said, 'if he's to understand even a little about ordering troops. Really, if he's to be a human being at all.'
Then can we deny, I said, that a man of war must learn to calculate and count?
'Now do you see this study the way I do?' I asked.
He must, more than anything — if he is to understand anything at all about ordering troops; or rather, if he is even to be a human being.
'How do you mean?'
Now do you notice, I said, what I notice about this study?
'It seems to me to be one of the studies we're after, one that naturally leads toward thought, though no one uses it rightly, as a way of drawing the soul toward what truly is.'
What?
'Explain what you mean,' he said.
It looks like one of the studies we are after — one that naturally leads toward thought — but no one uses it rightly, though it genuinely draws the soul toward being.

'I'll try,' I said. 'But I'd like you to join me in thinking it through, and to agree or disagree as I try to work out, for myself, which studies have this power to draw us. That way we'll have clearer proof that number really is one of them, as I suspect.'
What do you mean? he said.
'Go on,' he said.

I will try to explain how it seems to me, I said. As I sort out for myself which things lead toward thought and which do not, look at them with me — agree or disagree — so we can see more clearly whether this is what I suspect it is.

'Then look,' I said. 'Among the things we perceive, some don't summon the mind to look further, because the senses judge them well enough. Others positively demand a second look, because the senses give no sound result.'
Show me, he said.
'You're talking about things seen from far off,' he said, 'and about shadow-painting.'

Here is what I mean, I said. Some things the senses report do not summon the understanding to examine them, because the sense judges them adequately by itself. Others absolutely demand that examination, because the sense yields nothing sound.
'No,' I said, 'that's not at all what I mean.'
You obviously mean things seen at a distance, he said, and paintings done in light and shadow.
'Then what do you mean?'
No, I said — you haven't quite caught my meaning.

'By things that don't summon thought,' I said, 'I mean ones that don't strike the sense with two opposite impressions at once. The ones that do strike that way, I call summoners, when the sense gives no clearer impression of the thing than of its opposite, whether the thing is near or far. Let me show you what I mean. Here are three fingers: the little finger, the next one, and the middle finger.'
Then what do you mean?
'All right,' he said.

The ones that do not summon thought, I said, are those that do not spill over into the opposite perception at the same time. The ones that do spill over, I count as summoners — whenever the sense reports a thing no more than its opposite, whether it strikes from near or far. You will see my meaning better this way: here, we say, are three fingers — the little one, the second, and the middle.
'Suppose I'm looking at them up close. Now here's my point about them.'
Right.
'What is it?'
And assume I am talking about them seen up close. Now consider this about them.

'Each of them looks equally a finger, whether it's in the middle or at the end, whether it's pale or dark, thick or thin, and so on. In none of these cases is the ordinary person forced to ask the mind what a finger is, because sight never signals to it that the finger is, at the same time, the opposite of a finger.'
What?
'No, it doesn't,' he said.

Each of them appears equally a finger, and in this respect it makes no difference whether it sits in the middle or on the end, whether it is pale or dark, thick or thin, and so on. In all this, the ordinary soul is not forced to ask the understanding what a finger is — sight nowhere signals to it that the finger is at the same time the opposite of a finger.
'So naturally,' I said, 'there's nothing here to summon or wake the mind.'
No, it does not.
'There isn't,' he said.
So a perception like that, I said, naturally does not summon or wake the understanding.

'But what about the bigness and smallness of the fingers? Does sight see those well enough? Does it make no difference whether a finger is in the middle or at the end? And does touch report thickness and thinness, or hardness and softness, well enough? Don't all the senses fall short on these? Take the sense that deals with hardness: doesn't it have to deal with softness too, and report to the soul that the same thing strikes it as both hard and soft?'
Naturally not.
'Yes,' he said.

But what about the bigness and smallness of the fingers? Does sight see those adequately, and does it make no difference to it whether the finger sits in the middle or at the end? And the same for touch with thick and thin, soft and hard? And the other senses — don't they report such things defectively? Doesn't each of them work like this: the sense set over hardness is forced to be set over softness too, and it passes the word to the soul that it feels the same thing as both hard and soft?

'And in cases like that, isn't the soul bound to be puzzled? It's asking what this sense means by hard, if it calls the same thing soft as well. And the sense of light and heavy, what does it mean by light and heavy, if it reports the heavy as light and the light as heavy?'
That is right, he said.
'Those messages really are strange,' he said, 'and they do call for examination.'

Then in such cases, I said, isn't the soul bound to be puzzled about what this sense means by hard, if it calls the same thing soft as well — and what the sense of light and heavy means by light and heavy, if it reports the heavy as light and the light as heavy?
'So naturally,' I said, 'in cases like these the soul first calls in reasoning and the mind, and tries to work out whether each of the things reported to it is one or two.'
Yes, he said — those are strange reports for the soul to receive, and they call for examination.
'Of course.'
So it is likely, I said, that in cases like these the soul first calls in calculation and understanding, and tries to make out whether each of the things being reported is one or two.
'And if there seem to be two, each of them seems to be one and different from the other?'
Of course.
'Yes.'
And if they appear to be two, each of the two appears as one and distinct?
'And if each is one, and together they're two, the soul will think of the two as separated, since it couldn't think of them as two if they weren't separated, but only as one.'
Yes.
'That's right.'
Then if each is one and the pair of them two, the soul will think the two as separated — because if they were inseparable, it would not be thinking two, but one.
'Now sight, we say, saw bigness and smallness too, but not as separate. It saw them all jumbled together.'
Right.
'Yes.'
Now sight, we say, saw big and small too — but not separated: run together. Yes?
'And to clear up the confusion, the mind is forced to do the opposite, to look at bigness and smallness as separate and distinct, the reverse of how sight delivered them.'
Yes.
'True.'
And to get this clear, the understanding was forced to see big and small the other way around — separated, not run together — the opposite of what sight did.
'And isn't this where we first start asking, what really is bigness, and what is smallness?'
True.
'Exactly.'
And isn't it from here that the question first comes to us — what is the big, then, and what is the small?
'And so we came to call the one the visible and the other the intelligible.'
Absolutely.
'Quite so,' he said.
And that is how we came to call one thing the intelligible and the other the visible.

'That, then, is what I was trying to get at just now when I said that some impressions summon thought and others don't. The ones that strike the sense together with their opposites are summoners; the ones that don't, aren't.'
Exactly right, he said.
'Now I understand,' he said, 'and I agree.'

This is what I was trying to say just now — that some things summon the intellect and others do not. The ones that strike the sense together with their opposites, I count as summoners; the ones that do not, do not wake the understanding.
'Well then, which class do number and the one belong to?'
Now I understand, he said, and I agree.
'I can't say,' he replied.
Well then — number and the one: which side do they fall on?

'Reason it out from what we've already said,' I told him. 'If the one is adequately seen by itself, or grasped by some other sense by itself, then it wouldn't draw us toward what truly is, just as we said about the finger. But if some contradiction is always bound up with it, so that it looks no more like one than like the opposite, then we'd need something to decide the matter. The soul would be forced into perplexity, stirring up the thought within it and asking what the one itself really is. And so the study of the one would be one of the things that lead and turn the soul toward the contemplation of what truly is.'
I cannot tell, he replied.
'Yes,' he said, 'and seeing the one does exactly that, in a striking way. We see the very same thing as one and as an unlimited multitude at once.'

Work it out from what we have said, I said. If the one, by itself, is adequately seen — or grasped adequately by any other sense — it would not pull the soul toward being, any more than the finger did. But if some contradiction is always seen along with it, so that it appears no more one than the opposite of one, then something would be needed to judge; the soul would be forced into puzzlement, forced to search, stirring the thinking inside itself, and to ask what the one itself actually is. And so the study of the one would be among the studies that lead and turn the soul toward the contemplation of what is.
'And if that's true of the one,' I said, 'isn't it true of every number?'
Well, he said, the sight of the one certainly has that feature — as much as anything does. We see the same thing as one and as unlimited in multitude at the same time.
'Of course.'
And if that is true of the one, I said, isn't it true of all number?
'And counting and arithmetic are entirely about number.'
Of course.
'Very much so.'
And calculation and arithmetic are entirely about number?
'And clearly they lead us toward truth.'
Certainly.
'Yes, remarkably so.'
And they plainly lead the soul toward truth?

'Then this is one of the studies we've been looking for. A soldier has to learn it, to be able to draw up his troops, and a philosopher has to learn it, to rise out of the sea of becoming and lay hold of being, or he'll never become a true reckoner.'
Extraordinarily well.
'That's so,' he said.

Then this, it seems, is one of the studies we are looking for. A soldier must learn it to marshal his troops; a philosopher, because he must rise up out of the sea of becoming and take hold of being, or never become a reasoner at all.
'And our guardian happens to be both soldier and philosopher.'
That is so.
'Of course.'
And our guardian happens to be both soldier and philosopher.

'Then it would be fitting, Glaucon, to lay this study down by law, and to persuade those who are going to share in the highest offices of the city to take up arithmetic and pursue it, not as amateurs, but until they reach the contemplation of the nature of numbers with the mind itself. Not the way merchants and shopkeepers study it, for buying and selling, but for war, and for the soul's own turning, the easiest way for it to pass from becoming to truth and being.'
Of course.
'Beautifully put,' he said.

Then it would be fitting, Glaucon, to make this study law, and to persuade the men who are going to share in the city's greatest affairs to take up calculation — and not as amateurs. They must stay with it until they arrive at the contemplation of the nature of numbers by thought alone, practicing it not for buying and selling, like merchants and shopkeepers, but for war, and for the ease of the soul's own turning, away from becoming and toward truth and being.

'And now that we've mentioned the study of calculation,' I said, 'it strikes me how refined it is, and how useful it is for our purpose, provided one pursues it for the sake of knowing and not for buying and selling.'
Beautifully said, he replied.
'How so?' he asked.

And now that the study of calculation has been mentioned, I said, I realize how fine a thing it is, and how many ways it serves our purpose — as long as a man pursues it for the sake of knowing, and not for shopkeeping.

'It draws the soul powerfully upward,' I said, 'and forces it to reason about numbers themselves. It won't put up with anyone bringing visible or touchable bodies into the discussion and reasoning about those. You know how the experts in this study behave: if you try to divide the one itself in an argument, they laugh at you and won't allow it. If you chop it into pieces, they multiply it back, on guard against the one ever appearing to be anything but one, with no parts inside it.'
How so?
'That's quite true,' he said.

In just the way we were saying. It pulls the soul powerfully upward somewhere, and forces it to talk about the numbers themselves, never tolerating anyone who holds up numbers attached to visible or touchable bodies and argues from those. You know how the masters of the subject are: if you try to cut up the one itself in argument, they laugh at you and will not allow it. If you divide it, they multiply — standing guard so that the one never shows up as many pieces instead of one.

'So suppose someone asked them, Glaucon: "My good friends, what kind of numbers are you talking about, the ones with the one you mean in them, where every unit is equal to every other, with no difference at all, and not a single part inside it?" What do you think they'd answer?'
Very true.
'I think they'd say they're talking about numbers that can only be thought, and can't be grasped any other way.'

Then what do you think, Glaucon? Suppose someone asked them: 'My remarkable friends, what numbers are these you are talking about — numbers in which the one is what you demand it to be, each unit equal to every other, without the smallest difference, and containing no parts?' What do you think they would answer?
'So you see, my friend,' I said, 'this really does seem to be a study we can't do without, since it plainly forces the soul to use thought itself to reach the truth itself.'
This, I think: that they are talking about numbers which can only be thought — numbers there is no other way to handle.
'It certainly does that,' he said.
Then you see, my friend, I said, that this study looks genuinely indispensable to us, since it plainly forces the soul to use thought itself to reach truth itself.

'And have you noticed this too? People who are naturally good at calculation are quick at just about every study, and even slow ones, if they're trained and drilled in arithmetic, all improve and grow quicker than they were, even when they get nothing else out of it.'
It certainly does do that.
'That's so,' he said.

And here is another thing — have you noticed how those born to calculate are naturally quick at practically every study, while the slow, if educated and trained in it, still gain this much even if they gain nothing else: they all become quicker than they were?
'And I don't think you'll easily find many studies that take more effort to learn, or are harder.'
That is so, he said.
'No, you won't.'
And I think you will not easily find many studies that cost the learner and the practicer more labor.
'So for all these reasons we mustn't leave this study out. The best natures have to be educated in it.'
No.
'I agree,' he said.
Then for all these reasons the study must not be dropped, and the best natures must be educated in it.
'Then let that be one of our subjects settled,' I said. 'And let's look at the next one, which is related to it, and see whether it suits us.'
I agree, he said.
'You mean geometry?' he asked.
Let that stand, then, as our first subject, I said. Second, let us consider whether the study that borders on it suits us.
'Exactly,' I said.
Which? You mean geometry?

'The part of it that bears on war obviously concerns us,' he said. 'When it comes to pitching camp, taking a position, drawing the troops in or spreading them out, and all the other formations an army uses, in battle or on the march, it makes all the difference whether a man knows geometry or not.'
That very thing, I said.

'But for that sort of thing,' I said, 'a little geometry and calculation would do. What we have to ask is whether the larger and more advanced part of it tends to make it easier to see the Form of the Good. And what tends that way, we say, is everything that forces the soul to turn toward the region where the most blessed part of what is lives, the part the soul has to see at any cost.'

As much of it as bears on war obviously suits us, he said. For pitching camp, taking up ground, pulling an army together and stretching it out, and all the other formations armies take in battle and on the march, it makes all the difference whether a man is a geometer or not.
'You're right,' he said.

But for that much, I said, a small share of geometry and calculation would be enough. What we must examine is the greater and more advanced part of it — whether it tends toward our goal, toward making it easier to see the form of the good. And everything tends that way, we say, that forces the soul to turn itself toward the region where the most blessed part of what is resides — the part the soul must see at any cost.
'So if geometry forces us to look at being, it suits us; if only at becoming, it doesn't.'
You are right, he said.
'That's what we're saying.'
So if geometry forces the soul to look at being, it suits us; if at becoming, it does not.
'Now anyone with the slightest experience of geometry won't dispute this: the science contradicts the very language the people who practice it are forced to use.'
So we say, at least.
'How so?' he asked.
Well, I said, no one with even a little geometry will dispute this much: the science itself is the direct opposite of the way the men who work at it talk about it.

'They talk in a way that's quite absurd, but they can't help it,' I said. 'They're always speaking of squaring and applying and adding and the like, as though they were doing something and all their talk were aimed at action. But the whole study is really pursued for the sake of knowledge.'
How so?
'Absolutely,' he said.

They talk about it, I said, in a way that is laughable and beggarly. Everything they say sounds like business — 'squaring,' 'applying,' 'adding,' and so on — as if they were men of affairs and every proof were for use. But the whole study, surely, is pursued for the sake of knowing.
'And mustn't we agree on one more thing?'
Absolutely, he said.
'What?'
And must we agree on one thing more?
'That it's pursued for knowledge of what always is, not of what comes to be and passes away.'
What?
'That's easy to grant,' he said. 'Geometry is knowledge of what always is.'
That it is knowledge of what always is — not of something that comes to be at one moment and perishes at another.
'Then, my noble friend, it would draw the soul toward truth and shape the philosophical mind, turning upward what we now wrongly keep turned down.'
That is easy to agree to, he said. Geometry is knowledge of what always is.
'It does that as much as anything could,' he said.
Then, my noble friend, it would pull the soul toward truth, and produce a philosopher's cast of mind — directing upward what we now wrongly direct down.
'So as much as anything,' I said, 'we must insist that the people in your beautiful city not neglect geometry. And its side benefits aren't small.'
As surely as anything can, he replied.
'Which ones?' he asked.
Then as surely as anything can be ordered, I said, the men of your beautiful city must be ordered not to neglect geometry in any way. Even its side effects are not small.

'The ones for war that you mentioned,' I said. 'And besides, when it comes to grasping any study more readily, we know there's a world of difference between someone who's done geometry and someone who hasn't.'
What side effects?
'A world of difference, by heaven,' he said.
The ones you named — its uses in war, I said. And beyond that, for taking in any study better, we know it makes all the difference everywhere whether a man has grasped geometry or not.
'Then shall we make this the second subject for our young men?'
All the difference in the world, by Zeus, he said.
'Let's do that,' he said.
Then shall we set this down as the second study for the young?
'And shall we make astronomy the third? Or do you disagree?'
Let us, he replied.
'It suits me,' he said. 'A sharper sense of the seasons, the months, and the years is useful not only for farming and sailing but just as much for generalship.'
And what about astronomy as the third? Or do you think not?

'You amuse me,' I said. 'You seem afraid that people will think you're prescribing useless studies. But it's no small thing, and hard for most people to believe, that through these studies a certain instrument in everyone's soul is cleansed and rekindled, an instrument that other pursuits destroy and blind, and one worth saving more than ten thousand eyes, since it's the only one with which truth is seen. People who agree with you about this will think your words wonderfully true; people who've never grasped it will think you're talking nonsense, since they see no other benefit worth mentioning in these studies. So decide now which of the two you mean to speak to. Or perhaps to neither. Perhaps you're carrying on this discussion mainly for your own sake, though you wouldn't grudge anyone else whatever good he could get from it.'
Fine with me, he said. Keeping close track of the seasons and the months and the years suits not only the farmer and the sailor — it suits the general just as much.
'That's it,' he said. 'I'd rather speak, and ask, and answer, mainly for my own sake.'

You amuse me, I said. You seem afraid of the crowd — afraid of looking like a man who prescribes useless studies. Yet it is no small thing, and it is hard to believe, that in these studies a certain instrument in every man's soul is scoured clean and rekindled, after other pursuits have ruined and blinded it — an instrument more worth saving than ten thousand eyes, since only by it is truth ever seen. People who share that conviction will think you are speaking wonderfully well. People who have never noticed any such thing will naturally think you are talking nonsense, since they can see no other profit in these studies worth naming. So decide, here and now, which of the two you are arguing with. Or is it neither — are you making your arguments mostly for your own sake, though you would not begrudge anyone else whatever he can take from them?
'Then step back a little,' I said, 'because we've just taken the studies in the wrong order.'
That is what I choose, he said: to speak, ask, and answer mostly for my own sake.
'How?' he asked.
Then step back, I said — just now we set the wrong study after geometry.

'After plane geometry,' I said, 'we jumped straight to solids in motion, instead of taking solids on their own first. The right order is: after the second dimension, take the third, which has to do with cubes and everything that has depth.'
How did we go wrong? he said.
'That's true, Socrates,' he said. 'But these things don't seem to have been worked out yet.'

After plane surfaces, I said, we took up solids already in revolution, before taking them by themselves. The right way is to take the third dimension straight after the second — the dimension of cubes, of everything that has depth.

'For two reasons,' I said. 'First, no city honors them, so they're pursued without much energy, and they're hard. Second, the people studying them need a director, and without one they won't discover anything. But for one thing, such a director is hard to find. And even if there were one, as things stand now the people studying these subjects are too proud to follow him. That would change, though, if the whole city honored the subject and shared the director's lead. Then they'd take direction, and with steady, serious inquiry the truths would come to light. Even now, dishonored and stunted as it is, studied by people who can't say what it's good for, the subject forces its way forward by its own charm. It wouldn't surprise me if its truths did come to light eventually.'
That is true, Socrates, he said. But those questions do not seem to have been worked out yet.
'There's certainly an extraordinary charm in it,' he said. 'But explain again what you meant just now. You put plane geometry first.'

For two reasons, I said. No city holds these studies in honor, so they are pursued feebly — and they are hard. And the searchers need a director, without whom they will not make their discoveries; but such a man is hard to come by in the first place, and even if he appeared, as things now stand the men who search in this field are too full of themselves to obey him. If a whole city stood behind the work and honored it, though, they would obey, and steady, earnest inquiry would bring the answers to light. Even now — despised by the many, cut back by the very men who pursue it and cannot say what it is good for — the subject keeps growing all the same, forced up by its own charm; and it would be no surprise if it came fully to light.
'Yes,' I said.
The charm is there, certainly — exceptional charm, he said. But explain the order to me more clearly. First you set down the geometry of plane surfaces.
'And then you put astronomy after it, and then went back.'
Yes, I said.

'Yes,' I said. 'In my hurry to get through it all, I'm slowing us down. The next subject in order would have been the study of solids, but because it's in such a ridiculous state, I skipped over it and went straight from geometry to astronomy, which is the motion of solids.'
Then astronomy after it — and then you stepped back?
'You're right,' he said.

Yes, I said. In my hurry to get through everything quickly, I have made slower going. The study of depth came next in order; but because its investigation is in such a laughable state, I skipped past it and named astronomy — solid bodies in motion — right after geometry.
'Then let's make astronomy the fourth subject,' I said, 'and suppose that the one we're leaving out now will exist once a city takes it up.'
That is right, he said.

'That's reasonable,' he said. 'And since you scolded me before, Socrates, for praising astronomy in a vulgar way, let me praise it now the way you would. It's surely plain to everyone that astronomy compels the soul to look upward and leads it away from the things here to the things above.'
Then let us put astronomy fourth, I said, assuming the study we are passing over will exist the moment a city takes it up.
'Plain to everyone but me, maybe,' I said. 'I don't see it that way.'

That is reasonable, he replied. And since you scolded me just now, Socrates, for praising astronomy in a vulgar way, let me praise it your way instead. It is obvious to anyone, I think, that astronomy compels the soul to look upward, and leads it from things here to things there.
'How do you see it?' he asked.
Obvious to everyone but me, perhaps, I said — because that is not how I see it.
'The way it's handled now, by the people who try to lift it into philosophy, it makes the soul look down, not up.'
Then how? he said.
'What do you mean?' he asked.
The way it is handled now, by the men who would raise it into philosophy, it makes us look straight down.

'You seem to me to have a generous notion of what it means to study "the things above,"' I said. 'If somebody leaned his head back and studied the patterns on a ceiling and picked up a thing or two that way, I suppose you'd say he was contemplating with his mind and not with his eyes. Maybe you'd be right and I'm being foolish. But as I see it, the only study that makes the soul look upward is the study of what is, and what is can't be seen. Whether a man gapes upward with his mouth open or squints down at the ground, if he's trying to learn something about the things of sense, I say he never really learns, because none of those things can be known. And his soul is looking down, not up, even if he does his learning floating on his back in the sea or lying on the ground.'
What do you mean? he asked.
'You've got me,' he said, 'and your rebuke is fair. But how did you mean astronomy should be learned, in a way that's actually useful for the kind of knowledge we're talking about?'

You have a generous notion, I said, of what the study of the things above really is. Apparently if a man tipped his head back and studied the decorations on a ceiling, you would say he was contemplating with his understanding and not with his eyes. Maybe you are right and I am the simpleton. But I cannot count any study as making the soul look upward except the one that concerns what is and what cannot be seen. Whether a man gapes at the sky or squints at the ground, if what he is trying to learn is something the senses can reach, I say he will never learn it — no such thing admits of knowledge — and his soul is looking down, not up, even if he does his learning floating on his back at sea or lying flat on the land.

'Like this,' I said. 'These ornaments in the sky, since they're worked into a visible surface, may be reckoned the most beautiful and most precise of visible things. But they fall far short of the true ones: the real motions, in which true number and every true figure move, the motions of real speed and real slowness in relation to one another, carrying along everything they contain. Those are grasped by reason and thought, not by sight. Don't you agree?'
A fair hit, he said — the rebuke is deserved. But then how did you mean astronomy should be learned, differently from now, if learning it is to serve our purposes?
'Certainly,' he said.

Like this, I said.
