These embroideries in the sky — since they are stitched onto something visible, let them be counted the most beautiful and the most exact of visible things; but they fall far short of the true ones: the true motions, in which real speed and real slowness, in true number and in all the true figures, are carried in relation to one another and carry what is inside them. Those are grasped by reason and thought, not by sight. Or do you think otherwise?

'So we should treat the patterns in the sky as models to help us study those true things, the way we'd treat diagrams we happened to come across that were beautifully drawn and worked out by Daedalus or some other artist or painter. A geometer who saw such diagrams would think them exquisitely made, but he'd think it absurd to study them seriously expecting to find in them the truth about equals or doubles or any other ratio.'
Not at all, he replied.
'Of course that would be absurd,' he said.

Then, I said, we should use the embroidered sky as a set of model diagrams for the study that aims at those true things — just as if we had come across diagrams drawn and worked out with exceptional care by Daedalus or some other craftsman or draftsman. A man who knew geometry would look at them and admire the beauty of the workmanship; but he would think it laughable to study them in earnest, expecting to find in them the truth about equals or doubles or any other proportion.

'And don't you think a true astronomer will feel the same way when he looks at the motions of the stars?' I said. 'He'll grant that the maker of the heavens arranged them and everything in them as beautifully as such things can be arranged. But as for the ratio of night to day, or of these to a month, or of a month to a year, or of the other stars to these and to one another, don't you think he'll consider it strange to believe that these things, which are bodily and visible, are always the same and never deviate at all, and strange to go to any length trying to grasp their truth?'
Of course it would be laughable, he replied.
'I do, now that I hear you say it,' he said.

Then don't you think a real astronomer will feel the same when he looks at the movements of the stars? He will hold that the sky and everything in it have been framed by their maker as beautifully as such works can be framed. But the ratio of night to day, of these to the month, of the month to the year, and of the other stars to all of these and to one another — don't you think he will find it strange to believe that these always hold the same and never deviate anywhere, when they are bodies and visible — and stranger still to strain every nerve hunting the truth in them?

'So we'll pursue astronomy by means of problems, the way we do geometry,' I said, 'and we'll let the things in the sky alone, if we really mean to do real astronomy and to turn the soul's natural intelligence from useless to useful.'
I think so, he said — now that I hear you say it.
'You're prescribing a task,' he said, 'many times harder than astronomy as it's done now.'

Then we will pursue astronomy the way we pursue geometry, I said — by means of problems — and leave the things in the sky alone, if we mean to take real hold of astronomy, and to turn the naturally intelligent part of the soul from useless to useful.
'And I think we'll prescribe the rest the same way,' I said, 'if we're to be of any use as lawgivers. But can you suggest any other suitable study?'
The task you are laying down, he said, is many times heavier than anything astronomy does now.
'Not on the spur of the moment,' he said.
And I think our prescriptions will run the same way elsewhere too, I said, if we are to be any good as lawgivers. But can you suggest any other suitable study?
'Motion,' I said, 'presents not just one kind but several, I think. A wise man could probably name them all; even we can see two.'
Not right now, he said — not offhand.
'Which two?'
Well, motion offers not one form but several, I said. A wise man could probably name them all; but two are plain even to us.
'Besides the one we've just named,' I said, 'there's its counterpart.'
What are they?
'What's that?'
Besides astronomy, I said, its counterpart.

'It looks as if,' I said, 'just as the eyes are made for astronomy, the ears are made for harmonious motion, and these are sister sciences, as the Pythagoreans say, and as we agree. Don't we, Glaucon?'
What is that?
'We do,' he said.
It seems that as the eyes are fixed on astronomy, I said, so the ears are fixed on harmonic motion — and that these are sister sciences, as the Pythagoreans say, and as we, Glaucon, agree. Don't we?
'Then since the work is large,' I said, 'we'll ask them what they have to say about it, and whether there's anything else besides. But through all of it we'll keep our own aim in view.'
We do, he replied.
'What aim?'
Then since the work is large, I said, we will ask them what they say about it, and whether there is anything else besides. But through all of it we will guard our own principle.

'That the people we're raising should never try to learn any of these subjects in an incomplete way, one that doesn't always arrive at the point everything ought to reach, the point I just spoke of in the case of astronomy. Don't you know that people handle harmony the same useless way? They measure the chords and notes they hear against one another, and so, like the astronomers, they labor in vain.'
Which one?

'Heaven knows they do,' he said. 'They're absurd, with their talk of "close-packed" notes, pressing their ears up to the strings as though they were eavesdropping on the neighbors. One group claims it can still hear a note in between, and that there's the smallest interval, which should be the unit of measure. Another insists the two notes have already become the same. Both groups put their ears ahead of their minds.'

That the men we are raising never try to learn any of these studies in an incomplete form — a form that fails to arrive where everything must arrive, as we were just saying about astronomy. Don't you know they do the same thing with harmony? Measuring the heard concords and notes against one another, they labor — like the astronomers — to no purpose.

'You mean those fine fellows,' I said, 'who torment the strings and rack them on the pegs. I could draw out the image, the blows of the plectrum, the strings accused of holding back or running on, but I'll let it drop. Those aren't the people I mean. I mean the ones we just said we'd ask about harmony. They do the same thing the astronomers do. They look for the numbers in the harmonies they hear, but they never rise to the level of problems, never ask which numbers are harmonious and which aren't, and why each is what it is.'

By the gods, yes, he said — and absurdly too. They talk about their 'close-packed intervals,' and lay their ears alongside the strings as if hunting a voice from the neighbor's house. Some say they can still make out a note in between — the smallest interval, they claim, the proper unit of measure. Others insist the two sounds are already the same. Both parties set their ears ahead of their understanding.
'That,' he said, 'would be a superhuman undertaking.'

You mean those good souls, I said, who harass the strings and put them to the question, racking them on the pegs. I could keep the image going — the blows of the plectrum, the strings charged with denial and bluster and refusing to speak — but I will drop it and say that these are not the men I mean. I mean the ones we just said we would question about harmony: the Pythagoreans. They do the same as the astronomers. They hunt for the numbers in the concords that are heard; they never climb up to the problems — to examining which numbers sound together and which do not, and why each is so.
'A useful one, though,' I said, 'in the search for the beautiful and the good, though useless if pursued any other way.'
A superhuman undertaking, he said.
'Quite likely,' he said.
A useful one, I said, when it is sought for the sake of the beautiful and the good — though pursued in any other spirit, useless.

'And I think,' I said, 'that if the study of all these subjects we've gone through arrives at what they share with one another and how they're related, and draws together what's akin in them, then the labor contributes to what we want and isn't wasted. Otherwise it is.'
That is likely, he said.
'I have the same hunch,' he said. 'But you're talking about an enormous amount of work, Socrates.'

And I would think, I said, that if the pursuit of all these studies we have described reaches the point where their community and kinship with one another come into view, and it is worked out how they are akin, then the labor spent on them contributes to what we want and is not wasted — and otherwise it is.

'You mean the prelude?' I said. 'Or what? Don't you realize that all this is just the prelude to the song itself, the one we have to learn? Surely you don't think the people who are good at these subjects are already skilled in dialectic.'
So I would prophesy too, he said. But it is an enormous work you are describing, Socrates.
'Heavens, no,' he said. 'Apart from a very few, none of the ones I've met are.'

What do you mean, I said — the prelude, or what? Surely we know that all of this is only the prelude to the song itself, the song that has to be learned. Because you do not think that men who are clever at these studies are dialecticians?
'And do you really think,' I said, 'that people who can't give and take an account of things will ever know what we say they have to know?'
No, by Zeus, he said — except a very few of the ones I have met.
'No again,' he said.
But men who cannot give an account and take one — did you ever think they would know any of the things we say must be known?

'Then, Glaucon,' I said, 'isn't this at last the very song that dialectic sings? It belongs to the realm of thought, but the power of sight imitates it. Remember how sight, we said, tries at last to look at the living creatures themselves, then at the stars themselves, and finally at the sun itself. In just the same way, when someone sets out, by means of dialectic, without any of the senses, by reason alone, and presses on toward what each thing itself is, and doesn't give up until he grasps by thought alone what the Good itself is, then he arrives at the very end of the intelligible world, just as the other arrived at the end of the visible.'
No again.
'Absolutely,' he said.

Then isn't this at last, Glaucon, I said, the song itself, the one dialectic performs? It belongs to the intelligible; but the power of sight imitates it. Sight, we said, at last tries to look at the animals themselves, and the stars themselves, and finally at the sun itself. In the same way, when a man tries by argument — without any of the senses — to press through to what each thing itself is, and does not give up until he grasps by thought itself what the good itself is, he arrives at the very end of the intelligible, as the prisoner, in our image, arrived at the end of the visible.
'And this journey is what you call dialectic?'
Absolutely, he said.
'Of course.'
Well — don't you call that journey dialectic?

'Now think back to the prisoner being freed from his chains,' I said, 'and turned away from the shadows toward the firelight and the objects casting the shadows, and then dragged up out of the cave into the sunlight, where at first he still can't look at the animals and plants and the light of the sun, only at their divine reflections in water and the shadows of real things (not, as before, the shadows of mere images thrown by a light that is itself only an image of the sun). This whole pursuit of the studies we've described has the very same power: it leads the best part of the soul upward, to the contemplation of the best among the things that are, just as before the clearest part of the body was led up to the sight of the brightest thing in the bodily and visible world.'
What else?

'I accept that,' he said. 'It's hard to accept, but, looked at another way, it's just as hard to deny. Still, since we'll have to come back to it more than once and not just speak of it now in passing, let's take it as settled, whatever the truth turns out to be, and move on from the prelude to the song itself, and go through it in the same way. So tell me: what is the nature of the power of dialectic? Into what kinds does it divide? And what are its roads? Because those, it seems, are the very ones that lead to the place where a traveler can rest at last from the road and reach his journey's end.'

And the release from the chains, I said, and the turning from the shadows to the images and the firelight; the climb out of the cave into the sun; and up there, the inability at first to look at animals and plants and the sun's light, and looking instead at divine reflections in water, and at shadows of the things that are — no longer shadows of images, thrown by another light that is itself a kind of shadow beside the sun — all of this is what the practice of the arts we have described can do: it leads the best part of the soul up toward the sight of the best among the things that are, just as, in our image, the clearest organ of the body was led up to the sight of the brightest thing in the bodily, visible world.

'You won't be able to follow me any further, my dear Glaucon,' I said, 'though not for any lack of eagerness on my part. What you'd see then would no longer be an image of what we're talking about, but the truth itself, at least as it appears to me. Whether it's exactly so or not, I can't be sure. But that there's something of that kind to be seen, of that I'm sure. Isn't that right?'

I accept it, he said — though it seems very hard to accept, and then again, from another side, hard to deny. Still, since this is not something to be heard once today and never again — we will have to come back to it many times — let us assume it stands as stated, and go on to the song itself, and work through it the way we worked through the prelude. Tell us, then: what is the character of the power of dialectic, into what kinds does it divide, and what are its roads? For these, it seems, are the roads that lead at last to the place of rest at the end of the journey.
'Of course.'

You will not be able to follow me there, my dear Glaucon, I said — though there would be no lack of willingness on my part. What you would see would no longer be an image of what we are describing, but the truth itself, as it appears to me. Whether it is exactly so or not is not worth insisting on yet; but that there is something of the sort to be seen — that we must insist on. Yes?
'And that only the power of dialectic could reveal it, and only to someone trained in the studies we've gone through, and that it can't be revealed any other way.'
Of course.
'You can be sure of that too,' he said.
And this too: that only the power of dialectic can reveal it, and only to someone experienced in the studies we have described — no other way is possible?

'At least no one will dispute us when we say this,' I went on. 'No other approach even tries to grasp, in any orderly way and for every thing, what each thing itself is. The other arts are mostly concerned either with human opinions and desires, or with coming-to-be and putting-together, or with the care of what grows and is put together. As for the rest, the ones we said do lay hold of something real, geometry and the studies that go with it, we see that they only dream about what is. They can't see it wide awake, as long as they leave their starting assumptions untouched and can't give an account of them. For when a man's starting point is something he doesn't really know, and his conclusion and everything in between are woven out of what he doesn't know, how could agreement of that kind ever amount to knowledge?'
That too is worth insisting on, he said.
'It couldn't,' he said.

At any rate, I said, no one will dispute us when we say this: there is no other method that undertakes, systematically and in every case, to grasp what each thing itself is. The other arts are all turned toward human opinions and desires, or toward generation and assembly, or toward the care of things grown and assembled. And the rest — the ones we said lay hold of something of what is, geometry and the studies that follow it — we can see that they only dream about what is. They cannot see it awake as long as they use hypotheses and leave them untouched, unable to give any account of them. When the starting point is something a man does not know, and the conclusion and everything in between are woven out of what he does not know, what device could ever turn agreement like that into knowledge?

'So dialectic is the only inquiry,' I said, 'that travels this road, doing away with its assumptions and going up to the first principle itself, to make itself secure. When the eye of the soul is truly sunk in a kind of barbaric mud, dialectic gently draws it out and leads it upward, using the studies we've described as helpers in the turning. Out of habit we've often called those studies sciences, but they need another name, something clearer than opinion and dimmer than knowledge. Earlier we called it thought, I think. But I don't suppose we'll quarrel about a name when we have such great matters to examine.'
None, he said.
'No indeed,' he said. 'Any name will do, so long as it makes the state of the soul clear.'

Then only the dialectical method, I said, travels this road: doing away with the hypotheses, it goes straight to the starting point itself, to make it secure. It finds the eye of the soul literally buried in a barbarian bog, and gently pulls it out and leads it upward, using the arts we have listed as helpers in the turning. We have called those arts sciences more than once, out of habit; but they need some other name — brighter than opinion, dimmer than science. Somewhere earlier we settled on 'understanding.' But men with an inquiry as large as ours in front of them do not quarrel about a name.

'Then it's enough, as before,' I said, 'to call the first part knowledge, the second thought, the third belief, and the fourth imagination; and to call the last two together opinion, and the first two together understanding. Opinion has to do with becoming, understanding with being. And as being is to becoming, so understanding is to opinion; and as understanding is to opinion, so knowledge is to belief, and thought is to imagination. But let's leave aside the proportion between the things these correspond to, and the splitting of each of the two parts, opinion and understanding, into two, so we don't drown ourselves in arguments many times longer than the ones we've already gone through.'
No indeed, he said — any name will do, so long as it says clearly what is meant.
'I agree about the rest,' he said, 'so far as I can follow.'

Then it will satisfy us, I said, to call them what we called them before: the first section science, the second understanding, the third belief, and the fourth the imaging of shadows — the last two together opinion, the first two together intellect; opinion concerned with becoming, intellect with being. And to set it out as a proportion:

'And do you agree to call a man a dialectician if he can grasp an account of the being of each thing? And to say that, in the measure that someone can't give such an account, to himself and others, he falls short of understanding the thing?'
As being is to becoming, so intellect is to opinion; and as intellect is to opinion, so science is to belief, and understanding is to the imaging of shadows.
'How could I say otherwise?' he replied.

But the ratio between their objects, and the division of each realm into two — the opinable and the intelligible — let us leave alone, Glaucon, so it does not bury us in arguments many times longer than the ones already behind us.

'And the same goes for the Good. If someone can't mark off the Form of the Good in his account, separating it from everything else, and fight his way through every objection, as in a battle, eager to test what he says against what truly is rather than against mere opinion, and come through it all with his account standing, then you'll say he knows neither the Good itself nor any other good. If he lays hold of some image of it, he does so by opinion, not by knowledge; and he sleeps and dreams his way through this life, and before he ever wakes here he'll go down to Hades and fall finally and fully asleep.'
Well, he said, as far as I can follow, I agree about the rest.
'By heaven,' he said, 'I'll say all of that, emphatically.'

And do you call a man a dialectician when he grasps the account of the being of each thing? And the man who has no account — insofar as he cannot render one, to himself or to anyone else — to that extent you deny he has understanding of the thing?

'And surely, if you ever really did raise these children of yours, the ones you're now raising and educating in word, you wouldn't let them rule in the city and decide the greatest matters while they were as irrational as lines drawn at random.'
How could I not deny it? he said.
'Of course not,' he said.

And the same goes for the good. A man who cannot mark off the form of the good in his account, cutting it out from everything else; who cannot fight his way through every test of it, as in battle, pressing to test it by being rather than by opinion; who cannot come through all of that with his account still on its feet — a man like that, you will say, knows neither the good itself nor any other good. If he lays hold of some image of it, he holds it by opinion, not knowledge. He dreams and dozes through his present life, and before he ever wakes up here, he arrives in Hades and falls asleep for good.
'Then you'll lay it down by law that they have to take up the kind of education that lets them ask and answer questions with the greatest skill.'
Yes, by Zeus, he said — I will say all of that, and emphatically.
'I'll lay it down,' he said, 'with you.'

Well then, your own children, the ones you are raising and educating in our argument — if you ever raised them in fact, I do not suppose you would let them rule the city and decide its greatest affairs while they were as irrational as the incommensurable lines the geometers talk about.
'Then doesn't dialectic stand at the very top of our studies, like a coping-stone, so that no other study could rightly be set above it? Doesn't it complete the whole course of learning?'
Certainly not, he said.
'It does,' he said.
Then you will lay it down as law that they get, above all, the education that will make them able to ask and answer questions with the greatest possible knowledge?
'It only remains to settle who should receive these studies, and how.'
I will lay it down, he said — with you.
'Clearly,' he said.

Then doesn't it seem to you, I said, that dialectic sits above all the studies like a coping-stone — that no other study could rightly be set higher, and that the account of the studies has now reached its end?
'You remember the kind of men we chose as rulers earlier?'
It does, he said.
'Of course,' he said.
Then what remains for you, I said, is the distribution: to whom we will give these studies, and how.

'Well, in other respects we have to choose the same natures. We have to prefer the steadiest, the bravest, and as far as possible the best-looking. And on top of that we have to look not only for nobility and toughness of character, but for the natural gifts that suit this education.'
Clearly.
'And what are those?'
Do you remember the earlier selection of the rulers — what kind of men we chose?

'A keen edge for these studies, my friend,' I said, 'and learning that comes without agony. Souls flinch from hard study far more than from hard exercise, because the toil is more their own, not shared with the body.'
Of course, he said.
'True,' he said.

In most respects, then, the same natures must be chosen, I said. Preference goes to the steadiest and the bravest and, as far as possible, to the best-looking. But beyond that, we must look not only for noble and hardy characters — they must also have the natural gifts this education needs.

'And we must look for a man with a good memory, hard to discourage, a lover of work in every form. Otherwise, how could anyone endure both the labor of the body and so much study and practice besides?'
Which gifts, exactly?
'No one could,' he said, 'unless he were gifted in every way.'

Sharpness for study, my friend, I said, and no trouble learning. Souls flinch far sooner in hard study than in gymnastics: the labor is closer to home — it belongs to the soul alone and is not shared with the body.
'The mistake people make now,' I said, 'and the reason philosophy is held in such low regard, is that the wrong people take her up. She ought to be approached by her true kin, not by bastards.'
True, he replied.
'What do you mean?' he asked.

And the man we are looking for must have a good memory, be unbreakable, and love labor of every kind. How else would anyone consent to work through the body's toils and complete so much study and practice on top of them?

'In the first place,' I said, 'whoever takes her up mustn't be lame in his love of work, half hardworking and half lazy. That's what happens when a man loves exercise and hunting and every kind of bodily exertion, but is no lover of learning or listening or inquiry, and shirks all that work. He's also lame who limps the other way.'
No one would, he said, unless his nature had every gift.
'Very true,' he said.

The mistake nowadays, I said — and the disgrace that has fallen on philosophy through it, which I mentioned before — is that she is taken up by men who are not worthy of her. Bastard sons should not have taken her up; trueborn ones should have.

'And when it comes to truth,' I said, 'won't we count a soul maimed in the same way if it hates a deliberate lie, can't bear it in itself, and grows furious when others lie, yet cheerfully puts up with lies it falls into by accident? When it's caught in its own ignorance it isn't troubled, but wallows in it contentedly, like a pig in the mud.'
How do you mean? he said.
'Absolutely,' he said.

First, I said, the man who takes her up should not limp in his love of work — half of him work-loving, half work-shy. That is what you get when a man loves gymnastics and hunting and every labor of the body, but does not love learning or listening or inquiring, and hates the labor in all of that. And the man whose love of labor runs all the other way is lame too.

'And as for self-control, courage, generosity, and every other virtue,' I said, 'we have to watch just as closely for the bastard and the true-born. When a person or a city doesn't know how to look for such things, they unknowingly make use of the lame and the bastard for whatever they need: a city for its rulers, a private man for his friends.'
Very true, he said.
'That's exactly how it is,' he said.

And with respect to truth, I said, won't we likewise count a soul maimed if it hates the willing lie — cannot stand it in itself and boils with anger when others lie — and yet calmly accepts the unwilling lie, and is not distressed when it is caught knowing nothing, but wallows in its ignorance as contentedly as a pig in mud?

'So we have to be careful about all of this,' I said. 'If we bring people who are sound in body and mind to so great a study and so great a training, justice herself will have no complaint against us, and we'll preserve both the city and its constitution. But if we bring the wrong people to it, we'll do the opposite, and pour an even greater flood of ridicule over philosophy than she suffers now.'
Absolutely, he said.
'That would be a shameful thing,' he said.

And with respect to temperance, I said, and courage and largeness of spirit and every part of virtue, we must watch just as carefully for the bastard and the trueborn. When a city or a private man does not know how to look into all this, they end up leaning on the lame and the bastard without noticing — as friends in the one case, as rulers in the other.
'It would,' I said. 'But I think I'm being a little ridiculous myself at this very moment.'
That is exactly how it goes, he said.
'How so?' he asked.

So we must take every care in these things, I said. If the men we bring to so great a study and so great a training are sound of limb and sound of mind when we educate them, justice herself will find no fault with us, and we will keep the city and its constitution safe. Bring men of another stamp, and we will accomplish the exact opposite — and pour an even greater flood of ridicule over philosophy.

'I forgot,' I said, 'that we're only amusing ourselves, and I got carried away and spoke too vehemently. As I was speaking I looked toward philosophy, and seeing her so undeservedly trampled, I think I lost my temper. In my anger at the men responsible, I spoke with too much heat.'
That would be shameful, he said.
'You did, by heaven,' he said, 'or at least so it sounded to me, the listener.'
It would, I said. But something laughable seems to have just happened to me.

'But not to me, the speaker,' I said. 'Still, let me remind you of this. In our earlier selection we chose old men, but here that won't do. We mustn't trust Solon when he says that as a man grows old he can learn many things. He can no more do that than he can run a race; the great and many labors belong to the young.'
What?
'They have to,' he said.

I forgot we were playing, I said, and I spoke rather too intensely. As I talked, I was looking at Philosophy, and seeing her dragged through the mud — undeservedly — I think I lost my temper at the men responsible, and said what I said too much in anger.

'So calculation and geometry and all the preliminary studies that prepare the way for dialectic should be put before them while they're still children, but not in a form that forces the learning on them.'
No, by Zeus, he said — not to this listener.
'Why not?'

But too much for this speaker, I said. And here is something we must not forget: in the earlier selection we chose old men, but in this one that will not do. We must not believe Solon that a man growing old can learn many things — he could sooner learn to run. All great and repeated labors belong to the young.
'Because a free person should never learn any subject like a slave,' I said. 'Forced labor does the body no harm, but nothing learned under compulsion stays in the soul.'
Necessarily, he said.
'True,' he said.

Then calculation and geometry and all the preparatory studies that must be taught before dialectic should be set in front of them while they are children — and not with the shape of forced instruction.
'So don't bring up children in their studies by force, my friend. Let them learn through play instead. That way you'll also see better what each of them is naturally suited for.'
Why not?
'There's sense in that,' he said.
Because a free man, I said, should learn nothing like a slave. Bodily labors done under force do the body no harm; but no forced study stays in the soul.
'And do you remember,' I said, 'that we said the children should be taken to watch war on horseback, and brought up close, where it's safe, to taste blood like young hounds?'
True, he said.
'I remember,' he said.
Then don't raise the children in their studies by force, my excellent friend, I said, but through play — and you will also see better what each of them is naturally fit for.
'In all these things, then, the labors, the studies, the dangers, whoever shows himself quickest should be enrolled on a select list.'
That makes sense, he said.
'At what age?' he asked.
And do you remember, I said, that we said the children were to be taken to war too, as spectators on horseback — and where it was safe, brought up close and given a taste of blood, like young hounds?

'When the compulsory physical training is over,' I said. 'During that period, whether it's two or three years, they can do nothing else, since exhaustion and sleep are enemies of study. And how each one bears himself in the exercises is itself one of the most important tests.'
I remember, he said.
'Of course,' he said.
Then in all of this, I said — labors, studies, dangers — whoever proves nimblest is to be enrolled on a select list.

'After that,' I said, 'the ones chosen from among the twenty-year-olds will be given greater honors. And the studies they learned piecemeal as children will now be drawn together into a single view, so they can see how the studies are related to one another and to the nature of what is.'
At what age? he said.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's the only kind of learning that holds firm in those who get it.'

When they are released from the required gymnastics, I said. That stretch — two years or three — is useless for anything else: exhaustion and sleep are the enemies of study. And at the same time, how each of them shows up in the gymnastics is itself one of the tests, and not the least.
'And it's the greatest test, too, of who has the nature for dialectic and who doesn't,' I said. 'The one who can take a synoptic view is a dialectician; the one who can't, isn't.'
Clearly, he replied.
'I agree,' he said.

After that, I said, from the age of twenty, those who are chosen out will receive greater honors than the rest; and the studies that came to them scattered through their childhood education must now be gathered together, into one view of how the studies are akin to one another and to the nature of what is.

'So these are the things you'll have to watch for,' I said. 'And the ones who show the most of this, who are steadiest in their studies and in war and in their other appointed duties, these you'll have to select again once they've passed thirty, promote to still higher honors, and test by means of dialectic, to see which of them can let go of his eyes and the other senses and rise, in the company of truth, to what is itself. And here, my friend, great care is needed.'
At least, he said, that is the only learning that holds firm in the ones who take it in.
'Why so?' he asked.
And it is also the greatest test, I said, of who has a dialectical nature and who does not. The man who can see things together is a dialectician; the man who cannot, is not.
'Haven't you noticed,' I said, 'how much harm there is in the way dialectic is practiced now?'
I agree, he said.
'What harm?' he asked.

These, then, are the things you will have to watch, I said. Those who show most of this capacity, and who stay steady in study and steady in war and in the other duties the law lays down — these, once they have passed thirty, you will choose out of the chosen and raise to greater honors, and you will test them by the power of dialectic, to see which of them can let go of the eyes and the other senses and travel, with truth, toward what is itself. And here, my friend, is work that calls for great caution.
'The people who take it up are filled with lawlessness,' I said.
Why caution, particularly? he said.
'Very true,' he said.
Haven't you noticed, I said, the evil that infects dialectic today — how great it has grown?
'Do you think there's anything surprising about that?' I said. 'Won't you make some allowance for them?'
What evil? he said.
'How do you mean?' he asked.
Its students, I said, are filled up with lawlessness.

'Picture it like this,' I said. 'Imagine a supposed son brought up in great wealth, in a large and powerful family, surrounded by flatterers. Suppose that, when he grows up, he finds out that the people he calls his parents aren't really his parents, and that he can't discover who his real parents are. Can you guess how he'd treat his flatterers, on the one hand, and his supposed parents, on the other, first while he didn't know the truth, and then once he found out? Or shall I tell you my guess?'
Very much so, he said.
'Please do,' he said.
Well, do you find anything astonishing in what happens to them? I said. Don't you find it forgivable?

'My guess,' I said, 'is that as long as he didn't know the truth, he'd honor his father and mother and the rest of his supposed family more than the flatterers. He'd be less likely to neglect them in need, less likely to do or say anything against them, and less likely to disobey them in anything important.'
How forgivable, exactly?
'Probably,' he said.

Take a parallel, I said. Imagine a changeling son, raised in a great and wealthy house, in a large family, surrounded by flatterers, who discovers when he has grown to manhood that he is not the child of the couple who call themselves his parents — and cannot find the ones who actually are. Can you divine how he would feel toward the flatterers, and toward his supposed parents, first in the years when he did not know about the substitution, and then in the years when he did? Or would you rather hear my guess?

'But once he found out the truth, I imagine he'd slacken in his honor and care for them and grow more attached to the flatterers. He'd give them more weight than before, start living the way they do, openly keeping their company, and, unless he were unusually decent by nature, he'd stop caring at all about that supposed father and the rest of his made-up family.'
I would rather hear it, he said.
'It would happen just as you say,' he said. 'But how does this image apply to people who take up arguments?'

Then my guess is this, I said. As long as he does not know the truth, he will honor his father and his mother and the rest of his supposed family more than the flatterers; he will be less willing to see them go without; less willing to say or do anything improper to them; and less willing to disobey them in the things that matter.
'Like this,' I said. 'We hold from childhood certain convictions about what's just and fine, and we're brought up under them as under parents, obeying and honoring them.'
Likely enough, he said.
'We are.'

But once he has learned the truth, I would guess that his honor and attention slacken toward the family and quicken toward the flatterers. He listens to them now as he never did before; he begins to live by their standards and keeps their company openly; and unless his nature is exceptionally decent, he cares nothing anymore for that father of his, or the rest of the old supposed family.

'But there are other ways of living, full of pleasures, that flatter the soul and try to draw it to themselves. They don't win over anyone with a sense of decency; such a person keeps honoring and obeying the convictions of his fathers.'
It would all happen just as you say, he said. But how does the image bear on the men who take up arguments?
'True.'
This way. We have, from childhood, convictions about what is just and what is honorable; we are raised in them as by parents, obeying them and honoring them.

'Now suppose this man is asked, "What is the fine?" and he answers as the lawgiver taught him, and then the argument refutes him. Suppose it refutes him again and again, in many ways, until it knocks him into thinking that what he called fine is no more fine than shameful, and the same with the just and the good and everything he honored most. After that, how do you think he'll go on honoring and obeying those convictions?'
We are.
'He can't, the way he did before,' he said.

And there are other practices, opposite to those and carrying pleasure with them, which flatter the soul and pull at it — though they do not persuade men of any decency, who go on honoring their fathers' convictions and obeying them.
'And when he stops thinking these things honorable and akin to him as he did before, and can't find the true ones, is there any life he's likely to turn to except the one that flatters his desires?'
So it is.
'No,' he said.

Well then, I said. A question comes to a man in that condition and asks: what is the honorable? He answers what he heard from the lawgiver, and the argument refutes him. Refuted again and again, in many ways, he is beaten down into the opinion that the honorable is no more honorable than shameful — and the same with the just, and the good, and everything he held most in reverence. After that, what do you think he will do about honoring and obeying them?
'So out of a law-abiding man he becomes a lawless one.'
He cannot possibly, he said, go on honoring and obeying them as before.
'Necessarily.'
Then when he no longer holds those convictions to be honorable and his own, I said, and cannot find the true ones, is there any life he can plausibly turn to except the life that flatters him?
'Isn't all this only natural,' I said, 'for people who take up arguments this way, and, as I said just now, doesn't it deserve a great deal of allowance?'
There is not, he said.
'And pity, too,' he said.
And so, I suppose, he will appear to have become an outlaw, where he was law-abiding before.
'Then so that your thirty-year-olds don't become objects of pity in this way,' I said, 'mustn't you go about introducing them to arguments with every possible caution?'
He must.
'Very much so,' he said.
Now all of this, I said, is what naturally happens to men who take up arguments in that way — and, as I said just now, it deserves a great deal of forgiveness.

'And isn't one great precaution this: not to let them taste arguments while they're young? You've surely noticed how young people, once they get their first taste of argument, misuse it as a game. They use it only to contradict, imitating the ones who refute them by refuting others in turn, and like puppies they delight in dragging and tearing, with their arguments, at anyone who comes near.'
Yes, he said — and pity too.
'They love it beyond anything,' he said.
Then so that you will not have to pity your thirty-year-olds, mustn't every kind of care be taken in how they take up arguments?

'And when they've refuted many people and been refuted by many themselves, they fall hard and fast into believing nothing they believed before. And because of that, they and the whole pursuit of philosophy are slandered in the eyes of the rest of the world.'
Very much so, he said.
'Very true,' he said.

And isn't one great precaution this: that they not taste arguments while they are young? I suppose you have noticed how boys, when they get their first taste of arguments, treat them as a game and use them for nothing but contradiction. Imitating the men who refute them, they refute others in turn, delighting like puppies in dragging and tearing with the argument at anyone who comes near.

'But an older man,' I said, 'won't want to take part in that kind of madness. He'll imitate the one who wants to argue in order to look for the truth, not the one who plays at contradiction for sport. He'll be more measured himself, and he'll make the pursuit more respected, not less.'
Delighted beyond measure, he said.
'Quite right,' he said.

Then when they have refuted many and been refuted by many, they crash — fast and hard — into believing nothing they believed before. And with that, they and the whole business of philosophy get a bad name with everyone else.

'And wasn't everything we said before said with this same caution in mind: that the natures we admit to these arguments should be orderly and steady, and that we shouldn't, as people do now, let just any chance comer, with no fitness for it, approach them?'
Very true, he said.
'Absolutely,' he said.

An older man, though, I said, will not be willing to share that madness. He will imitate the man who wants to converse and examine what is true, rather than the one who contradicts for sport and play; and being more measured himself, he will make the practice more honored instead of more despised.
'Then is it enough to spend twice as many years steadily and intensely on dialectic, and nothing else, as we spent on the body?'
Right, he said.
'Do you mean six years or four?' he asked.
And wasn't everything said before this said as a precaution too — that the natures we let near arguments must be orderly and steady, and not, as now, whoever wanders in, however unfit?

'Put it at five,' I said. 'After that you'll have to send them back down into the cave again and compel them to take command in war and to hold the other offices suited to the young, so they won't fall short of the others even in experience. And in these offices, too, they have to be tested, to see whether they'll stand firm when they're pulled every which way, or give ground.'
Certainly, he said.
'And how much time do you allow for that?' he asked.
Is it enough, then, to stay at arguments continuously and intensely, doing nothing else — training in them as the counterpart of the bodily training — for twice as many years?

'Fifteen years,' I said. 'And when they reach fifty, the ones who have come through and shown themselves best in every way, in action and in knowledge, have to be led at last to the goal. They have to lift up the eye of the soul and fix it on the very thing that gives light to all things; and once they've seen the Good itself, they have to use it as a pattern for the rest of their lives, ordering the city and the citizens and themselves by it, each taking his turn. They'll spend most of their time on philosophy, but when their turn comes, each of them will toil at politics and take his turn at ruling, for the city's sake, doing it not as something glorious but as something that simply has to be done. And after they've brought up others like themselves to take their place as guardians of the city, they'll depart to the Isles of the Blessed and dwell there. The city will set up memorials and sacrifices to them at public expense, and honor them as spirits, if the Pythia approves, or, if not, at least as men blessed and divine.'
Do you mean six, he said, or four?
'Socrates,' he said, 'you've made our rulers as beautiful as a sculptor makes his statues.'

No matter, I said — call it five. After that, you will send them back down into the cave, and they must be compelled to hold command in war and every other office that suits the young, so that they will not fall short of the others in experience either. And in those offices too they must be tested, to see whether they hold their ground when they are dragged in every direction — or flinch.
'And our women rulers too, Glaucon,' I said. 'Don't imagine for a moment that anything I've said applies to men more than to women, to any woman who is born with the right nature for it.'
And how much time do you give that? he said.
'That's only right,' he said, 'since we agreed they should share everything equally with the men.'

Fifteen years, I answered. And when they reach fifty, those who have come through it all and proved best in everything — in every labor and every branch of knowledge — must be led at last to the goal. They must be compelled to lift the light of the soul upward and look toward what gives light to everything; and when they have seen the good itself, they must use it as their pattern for setting in order the city, the citizens, and themselves, each in his turn, for the rest of their lives — spending most of their time in philosophy, but when the turn comes, laboring at politics and ruling for the city's sake, treating it not as something splendid but as something necessary. And so, having educated others of the same kind in each generation and left them in their place as guardians of the city, they will depart to the Isles of the Blest and make their home there; and the city will set up memorials to them and offer sacrifices at public expense — as to divinities, if the Pythian oracle consents; and if not, then as to men blessed by fortune, and divine.

'Well then,' I said, 'do you agree that what we've said about the city and its constitution isn't merely a wish? It's hard, but in some way possible, and possible only in the way we described, when one or more true philosophers come to power in a city, men who despise the honors people prize now, thinking them unworthy of a free man and worth nothing, who prize what's right above everything, and the honors that come from doing right, and who treat justice as the greatest and most necessary thing of all, serving and increasing it as they set their own city in order.'
Like a sculptor, Socrates, he said, you have finished your rulers — and they are beautiful.
'How will they do it?' he asked.
And the women who rule as well, Glaucon, I said. Do not suppose that anything I have said applies to men any more than to women — those among them whose natures are equal to it.

'They'll send out into the countryside everyone in the city who is over ten years old,' I said. 'They'll take charge of the children, away from the habits of their parents, and raise them in their own ways and laws, the ones we've described. That's how the city and constitution we've been talking about would most quickly and easily come into being, and be happy, and bring the greatest gain to the people who possess it.'
Rightly so, he said, if they are to share everything equally with the men, as we described.
'By far the easiest way,' he said. 'And I think, Socrates, that you've described well how it would come to be, if it ever did.'

Well then, I said, do you agree that what we have said about the city and its constitution is not mere wishing? Hard, yes — but possible in a certain way, and in no other way than the one described: when true philosophers, one or more of them, come to power in a city; when they despise the honors of today as slavish and worthless, and prize above everything what is right and the honors that come from it; when they treat the just as the greatest and most necessary thing of all, serving it and building it up as they set their own city in order?
'Then haven't we now said enough about this city,' I said, 'and about the man who resembles it? Because it's clear by now what sort of man we'll say he should be.'
How will they do it? he said.

Everyone in the city over ten years old, I said, they will send out into the countryside. They will take the children in hand, out of reach of the habits their parents live by now, and raise them in their own ways and their own laws — the laws we have described. That is the quickest and easiest way for the city and the constitution we have discussed to be established, to prosper, and to bring the greatest good to the people among whom it comes to be.
Much the quickest, he said. And I think you have described well how it would come into being, Socrates — if it ever does.
Then haven't we said enough at last, I said, about this city, and about the man who matches it? For it is clear, surely, what kind of man we will say he must be.
It is clear, he replied. And as for your question — I think we have reached the end.
'It is clear,' he said. 'And as for your question, I think we've reached the end.'
spine.label: Book VIII
spine.title: The Decay of Regimes
How Cities and Souls Decay: The Four Faulty Regimes
spine.text: Good, Glaucon. So we're agreed: in the city that's going to be governed at the highest level, wives are common, children and their whole upbringing are common, the pursuits of war and peace are common — and its kings must be the men who have proved best in philosophy and in war.

'So then, Glaucon, we've reached this conclusion: in the perfect state, wives and children are to be shared in common, and so is all education, along with the pursuits of war and peace; and the best philosophers, together with the bravest soldiers, are to be their kings.'
We're agreed, Glaucon replied.
'Yes,' said Glaucon, 'we agreed to that.'

Yes — and we also agreed that once the rulers are installed, they'll lead the soldiers into the kind of housing we described: nothing private in it, nothing anyone's own, common to all. And beyond housing, you remember what we agreed about property?

'And we also agreed,' I said, 'that once these rulers are appointed, they'll take their soldiers and settle them in the kind of housing we described, which belongs to all in common and holds nothing private or personal. And as for their property, you remember what we decided?'

I remember. None of them was to own anything that other people own. They were to be athletes of war and guardians, drawing their maintenance from the other citizens as the wage of their guarding — a year's keep, nothing more — and their business was to look after themselves and the whole city.

'I remember. None of them was to own any of the ordinary possessions other people have. They were to be warrior-athletes and guardians, and in return for their year-round service they'd receive nothing but their keep from the rest of the citizens. Their job was to look after themselves and the whole state.'
That's right. But now that we've finished with all that, let's fix the point where we turned off the road, so we can go back the way we came.
'Right,' I said. 'Now that we've finished with that part, let's find the place where we wandered off the road, so we can get back on it.'

That's not hard. You were talking then, much as you are now, as if you had finished describing the city. You were saying that the city you'd described was good, and so was the man who matched it — though as it turns out, you had a still finer city and a still finer man to tell us about. At any rate, you said that if this one was right, the others were mistaken; and of the mistaken regimes, as I remember, you said four kinds were worth discussing — worth seeing where they go wrong — along with the men who match them, so that once we'd seen them all and agreed on the best man and the worst, we could ask whether the best is also the happiest and the worst the most miserable, or whether it's otherwise. I was asking which four regimes you meant when Polemarchus and Adeimantus broke in — and that's when you took up the argument that has brought us here.

'That's easy enough,' he said. 'Just as you're doing now, you were talking back then as if you'd finished describing the state. You said that this kind of state was good, and so was the man who matched it — though, as it turns out now, you had even finer things to say about both. And you said that if this was the right form, then the others were flawed. There were four main flawed forms, you said, and it was worth examining their defects and the defects of the men who corresponded to them. Once we'd seen all the types and finally agreed on who was best and who was worst, we were going to ask whether the best man wasn't also the happiest, and the worst the most miserable. I asked you what those four forms of government were, and then Polemarchus and Adeimantus broke in, and you took up the thread again, and that's how we've come to where we are now.'
Your memory is exact, I said.
'Your memory is exact,' I said.
Then do what a wrestler does, he said: give me the same hold again. I'll ask the same question, and you try to give me the answer you were about to give then.
'Then,' he said, 'like a wrestler, get back into your old hold and let me put the same question again, and you give me the answer you were about to give back then.'
I will if I can, I said.
'I will, if I can,' I said.
Then in particular, I want to hear which four regimes you meant.
'What I especially want to hear is what those four constitutions were that you mentioned.'

That's easily answered, I said. The four I mean are the ones that have names. First, the Cretan and Spartan type, which most people praise. Second — and second in most people's esteem — the one called oligarchy, a regime riddled with evils. Next its adversary, democracy, which follows out of it. And then the noble tyranny itself, outstripping all of them — the fourth and final sickness of a city. Can you think of another kind that forms a distinct type? There are hereditary lordships and purchased kingships and other regimes of that sort in between, but they're hybrids — you find them among Greeks and barbarians alike.

'That's an easy question,' I said. 'The four forms I meant — at least the ones that have proper names — are these. First, the kind you find in Crete and Sparta, which most people praise. Next comes what's called oligarchy, which isn't as well thought of and is a form riddled with troubles. Third is democracy, which naturally comes after oligarchy though it's its opposite. And last comes tyranny, that grand and famous thing, unlike all the rest — the fourth and the worst sickness a state can have. Can you name any other constitution that has a character of its own? I can't. There are petty lordships and princedoms that get bought and sold, and various in-between arrangements, but those are odd hybrids you find just as much among foreigners as among Greeks.'
Yes, he said — one hears of plenty of strange ones.
'Yes,' he said, 'we certainly hear of plenty of strange forms of government.'

And do you realize, I said, that there must be as many types of human character as there are types of regime? Or do you suppose regimes grow out of ‘oak and rock’ somewhere, and not out of the characters of the people in the cities — which tip the scale, so to speak, and drag everything else after them?

'And you realize,' I said, 'that there must be as many kinds of government as there are kinds of human character, since the two go together? We can't suppose states spring from "oak and rock," rather than from the characters of the people in them — characters that, so to speak, tip the scales and pull everything else along with them.'
No, he said — they come from nowhere else. The cities are as the people are; the regimes grow out of their characters.
'Yes,' he said, 'states are as their people are; they grow out of human character.'
Then if there are five forms of city, there will be five conditions of soul in individuals as well?
'So if there are five kinds of state, there'll be five kinds of individual soul as well?'
Certainly.
'Certainly.'
The man who matches aristocracy — rule of the best — we've already described, and we rightly call him good and just.
'We've already described the man who corresponds to aristocracy, the one we rightly call just and good.'
We have.
'We have.'

Then next we should walk through the worse men: the lover of victory and honor, who corresponds to the Spartan type of regime; then the oligarchic man; then the democratic; then the tyrannical. That way we can set the most unjust beside the most just, and finish our inquiry — how pure justice stands against pure injustice, in the happiness or misery of the man who has it — and either follow Thrasymachus and pursue injustice, or follow the argument as it's coming to light, and pursue justice.

'Then let's go on now and describe the lower types: first the contentious, honor-loving man who answers to the Spartan order, and then the oligarchic, the democratic, and the tyrannical. We'll set the most just side by side with the most unjust, and once we can see them clearly we'll be able to compare the happiness or misery of the man who leads a life of pure justice against the man who leads a life of pure injustice. Then our inquiry will be complete, and we'll know whether we ought to pursue injustice, as Thrasymachus urged, or follow where the argument leads and choose justice instead.'
That's exactly what we must do, he said.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's exactly what we have to do.'

Shall we do what we did before, then — start with the regime rather than the individual, since it shows up more clearly there? On that plan the honor-loving regime comes first. I know of no name in common use for it; call it timocracy, or timarchy. We'll examine the matching man beside it; then oligarchy and the oligarchic man; then democracy, and a look at the democratic man; and fourth, having come to the city under tyranny and seen it, we'll look in turn into a tyrannical soul — and try to become competent judges of the question we set ourselves.

'Shall we keep to the method we adopted for the sake of clarity — taking the state first and then the individual — and begin with the government of honor? I don't know a better name for it than timocracy, or maybe timarchy. We'll compare it with the matching character in a man; then we'll look at oligarchy and the oligarchic man; then we'll turn to democracy and the democratic man; and last of all we'll go and inspect the city of tyranny and take another look into the tyrant's soul, and try to reach a satisfying verdict.'
That would be a reasonable way to see it and judge it, he said.
'That's a very fitting way to look at it and judge it,' he said.

Come, then, I said — let's try to say how timocracy arises out of aristocracy. Or is it simply this: every regime changes from within, from the part of it that holds office, when that part splits against itself; and so long as that part is of one mind, however small it is, the regime cannot be shaken?

'First, then,' I said, 'let's ask how timocracy — the government of honor — arises out of aristocracy, the government of the best. The thing is plain enough: every political change begins with a split inside the ruling power itself. As long as that power stays united, no matter how small it is, it can't be shaken.'
Yes, that's so.
'Very true,' he said.

Then how, Glaucon, will our city be shaken? How will the auxiliaries and the rulers fall into faction with each other, or among themselves? Shall we do what Homer does, and pray the Muses to tell us ‘how faction first fell upon them’? Shall we say they answer us in high tragic style — playing with us, teasing us as if we were children — while pretending to be in dead earnest?

'So how will our city be shaken? In what way will its two classes — the auxiliaries and the rulers — fall out, either among themselves or with one another? Shall we do as Homer does and pray the Muses to tell us "how strife first arose"? Shall we imagine them speaking to us in mock solemnity, playing and joking as if we were children, putting on a lofty, tragic tone and pretending to be in earnest?'
Saying what?
'And how would they put it?'

Something like this. ‘A city so composed is hard to move. But everything that comes into being must decay, and even a constitution like this will not hold forever; it will be dissolved. And this is its dissolution. Not only for plants in the earth but for animals on it, there come seasons of fruitfulness and barrenness, of soul and body alike, whenever the revolutions of each complete their circuits — short orbits for the short-lived, the opposite for their opposites. And for your own race: the men you have educated to lead the city, wise as they are, will not hit the seasons of fruitfulness and barrenness by calculation joined with perception; the seasons will slip past them, and they will beget children at the wrong time. For a divine creature there is a period embraced by a perfect number. For a human creature it is the first number in which increases of root and square, taking three distances and four limits of the like and the unlike, the waxing and the waning, render all things commensurable and rational with one another. Of these, the base of four-thirds, wedded to five and three times increased, yields two harmonies: one a square, so many times a hundred; the other of equal length one way but oblong — a hundred squares of the rational diameters of five, each diminished by one, or of the irrational, diminished by two, and a hundred cubes of three. This whole geometric number is lord of better and worse begettings; and when your guardians miss it, and join brides to bridegrooms out of season, the children will not be favored by nature or by fortune. Their elders will install the best of them in office; but being unworthy all the same, and come into their fathers’ powers, they will begin to neglect us Muses, guardians though they are — undervaluing music and poetry first, and gymnastic after it — and so your young will grow up less cultivated. From them will come rulers with little of the guardian left in them, rulers who fail at testing Hesiod’s races and yours — gold, silver, bronze, and iron. Iron will be alloyed with silver, and bronze with gold, and from the mixture will come unlikeness and jarring inequality; and wherever those arise, they always breed war and hatred. This is the ancestry of faction, wherever it breaks out — so the Muses declare.’ [Trans. note: This is the famous ‘nuptial number,’ the most disputed passage in Plato. The Greek is deliberately oracular — the Muses are half-teasing — and no reconstruction of the arithmetic has ever won the field. Lectio renders the riddle as a riddle.]

'Something like this. A city set up the way ours is can hardly be shaken — but since everything that has a beginning also has an end, even a constitution like yours won't last forever; in time it too will dissolve. And here is how the dissolution comes. In plants that grow from the earth, and in animals that move across its surface, there are seasons of fertility and barrenness of soul and body alike, and these come round whenever the cycles of each complete their revolution — a short course for short-lived creatures, a long one for the long-lived. But the cycle of human fertility and barrenness — that your rulers, for all their wisdom and training, will not manage to calculate; the law of it will slip past an intelligence mixed with sense-perception, and so they'll bring children into the world at the wrong times. The cycle of the divinely begotten is governed by a perfect number, but the cycle of human births is governed by a more elusive one — a number reached by raising the base figures to higher powers, working through three intervals and four terms, with numbers that increase and decrease until everything is made commensurate and concordant. (This is the famous "nuptial number," a knot of arithmetic and geometry whose exact value has never been agreed; the point of it for the argument is simply that the timing of breeding is governed by a hidden law, and that once the rulers lose track of it, the whole order begins to fail.) For when your guardians, ignorant of this law, pair bride and bridegroom out of their proper season, the children will be neither well-favored nor fortunate. The best of them may still be picked out by their elders, but even so they'll be unworthy to take their fathers' places. And once they come to power as guardians, they'll soon be found wanting in their care of us, the Muses — first by undervaluing music, then letting that neglect spread to physical training, so that the young men of your state grow less cultivated. The next generation of rulers will have lost the guardian's gift for testing the metal in each of the races, which, like Hesiod's, are of gold and silver and bronze and iron. Iron will get mixed with silver and bronze with gold, and out of this will come unlikeness, inequality, and disharmony — which, always and everywhere, breed hatred and war. This, the Muses declare, is the stock from which strife springs up, wherever it appears. And that is their answer to us.'
And we can take it their answer is true, he said.
'And we may take it,' he said, 'that they answer truly.'
It has to be, I said — they're Muses. How could Muses speak falsely?
'Of course they answer truly,' I said. 'How could the Muses speak falsely?'
And what do the Muses say next?
'And what do the Muses say next?'

Once faction had broken out, the two strains pulled against each other: the iron and bronze strain toward moneymaking and the owning of land and houses, of gold and silver; the gold and silver strain — not poor, but rich by nature in their souls — back toward virtue and the old order. They wrenched and strained against one another until they settled on a middle course: they distributed the land and the houses as private property, and the people they had guarded till then as free men — their friends, the ones who fed them — they now enslaved, holding them as dependents and servants, while they occupied themselves with war, and with standing guard over them.

'Once strife had arisen, the two races were pulled in opposite directions. The iron and bronze leaned toward making money and acquiring land, houses, gold, and silver; while the gold and silver races, not wanting money — since the true wealth was in their own nature — inclined toward virtue and the old order of things. The two sides struggled, and in the end they struck a bargain: they'd divide up the land and houses into private holdings, and they'd enslave the very people they'd once protected as free men, the friends who had supported them, turning them into subjects and servants — while they themselves took on the business of war and standing guard against them.'
I think that's exactly where the change comes from.
'I think you've got the origin of the change exactly right,' he said.
And this regime will be something midway between aristocracy and oligarchy?
'And the new government that comes out of this will be something between oligarchy and aristocracy?'
Very much so.
'Very true.'

That's how the change will happen, then. And once it's happened, how will they live? Isn't it obvious that, lying midway between the earlier regime and oligarchy, the city will imitate partly the one and partly the other, and have some features all its own?

'That's how the change happens. And after it's made, how will they go on? Plainly, this new state, standing midway between oligarchy and the perfect state, will follow each of them in part and will also have features of its own.'
It will, he said.
'True,' he said.

In honoring its rulers; in its fighting class keeping clear of farming, of crafts, of moneymaking in general; in common meals and the devotion to athletics and the training for war — in all this it will imitate the earlier city?

'In the honor it pays its rulers, in keeping its warrior class clear of farming, crafts, and trade in general, in its common meals, and in its devotion to gymnastics and military training — in all these respects it will resemble the state that came before it.'
Yes.
'True.'

But it will be afraid to bring the wise into office, because the wise men it has now are no longer simple and single-minded but mixed; it will lean instead toward spirited, simpler men, made more for war than for peace; it will hold the tricks and stratagems of war in honor, and it will spend its whole life making war. Most of that will be its own.

'But it will be peculiar in this: it will be afraid to put philosophers in power, because the simple, wholehearted sort are no longer to be had; the ones it has are made of mixed stuff. It will turn instead to fierier, less complicated men, the kind better suited by nature to war than to peace. It will prize military tricks and stratagems, and it will be forever at war. In most of this it will stand apart from the others.'
Yes.
'Yes.'

Men of this stamp will be greedy for money, I said, like the men in oligarchies — nursing a fierce, secret reverence for gold and silver, now that they own storehouses and private treasuries where they can hide what they keep, and walled compounds around their houses, real private nests, where they can spend lavishly on women and on whomever else they please.

'And men of this stamp,' I said, 'will be greedy for money, like the men of oligarchies. They'll have a fierce, secret hunger for gold and silver, which they'll hoard away in hidden places, keeping private storerooms and treasuries to stow it out of sight; and they'll build themselves walled houses, real little nests for their eggs, where they'll spend lavishly on their wives, or anyone else they please.'
Very true, he said.
'Very true,' he said.

They'll be stingy with money too, since they prize it and can't acquire it openly — yet love spending other people's, when appetite calls. They'll pluck their pleasures in secret, running from the law the way boys run from a father, because they were educated not by persuasion but by force: they neglected the true Muse, the companion of argument and philosophy, and honored gymnastic above music.

'And they'll be tight-fisted, because they have no way of acquiring openly the money they love; so they'll squander other people's money to satisfy their cravings, stealing their pleasures and slipping away from the law like children running from a father. For they've been schooled not by gentle persuasion but by force, since they've neglected the true Muse — the companion of reason and philosophy — and honored gymnastics above music.'
The regime you're describing is a thorough mixture of bad and good, he said.
'The government you're describing,' he said, 'is certainly a mixture of good and bad.'
It is mixed, I said. But because the spirited part is in charge, one thing stands out in it above everything else: the love of victory and the love of honor.
'It is a mixture,' I said. 'But one thing stands out in it above all the rest: the spirit of contention and ambition, which comes from the dominance of the high-spirited, fighting element.'
Strongly, he said.
'No doubt about it,' he said.

That, then, is how this regime comes to be, and that's what it's like — an outline, no fine detail, because even a sketch is enough to show us the most just man and the most unjust; and to go through every regime and every character, leaving nothing out, would be an unmanageably long road.

'Such is the origin and such is the character of this state — sketched only in outline, since a fuller portrait isn't needed; the rough drawing is enough to show us the most perfectly just and the most perfectly unjust types. To go through every state and every kind of man, leaving none out, would be an endless task.'
Fair enough, he replied.
'Very true,' he replied.
Then who is the man who matches this regime? How does he come about, and what sort of man is he?
'Now, what sort of man corresponds to this kind of government? How does he come to be, and what is he like?'
I think, said Adeimantus, that as far as love of victory goes, he's not far from Glaucon here.
'I'd say,' Adeimantus put in, 'that in his love of a fight he's not unlike our friend Glaucon here.'
In that one point, maybe, I said. But in others the resemblance fails.
'In that one respect, perhaps,' I said. 'But in others he's quite different.'
Which others?
'How so?'

He'd have to be more stubborn, I said, and somewhat less cultivated — though a lover of culture, and fond of listening, while no kind of speaker himself. A man like that is harsh with slaves, instead of merely looking down on them the way a properly educated man does; gentle with the free-born; sharply obedient to authority. He loves office and loves honor, and stakes his claim to rule not on his speaking or anything of that kind, but on his deeds in war and everything to do with war — a lover of his exercise, and of the hunt.

'He'd have to be more self-assertive and less cultivated than Glaucon, though still a friend to culture — a good listener but no speaker. He's the sort to be rough with slaves, the way an educated man, too proud for that, never is; but he's courteous to free men and strikingly obedient to those in authority. He loves power and he loves honor. He claims the right to rule not because he's eloquent or anything of that kind, but because he's a soldier who has done feats of arms; and he's fond of gymnastics and hunting.'
Yes, that's the character that matches the regime.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's the character that goes with timocracy.'

As for money: a man like this despises it while he's young, but the older he grows the more he welcomes it, because he has a share of the money-lover's nature — and because he isn't pure toward virtue. He's lost the best of guardians.

'A man like this will look down on money only while he's young. But as he gets older he'll be drawn to it more and more, because there's a streak of the money-grubber in him, and he isn't single-minded in his pursuit of virtue — he's lost his best guardian.'
Which guardian? said Adeimantus.
'And who was that?' said Adeimantus.
Reason, I said, blended with music. It's the only thing that, once it moves in, stays with a man his whole life as the preserver of his virtue.
'Philosophy,' I said, 'tempered with music. She comes and takes up residence in a man, and she's the one thing that keeps his virtue safe all his life.'
Well said.
'Well said,' he replied.
That, I said, is the timocratic youth — the image of the timocratic city.
'Such, then,' I said, 'is the timocratic young man, and he matches the timocratic state.'
Exactly.
'Exactly.'

And he comes about something like this. Sometimes he's the young son of a good father who lives in a badly governed city — a father who avoids its honors and offices and lawsuits and all the usual busyness, and is willing to be shortchanged rather than have the trouble.

'And here's how he comes to be. He's often the young son of a good father who lives in a badly governed city, a father who turns down its honors and offices, won't go to law, won't put himself forward in any way, and would rather give up his rights than be bothered with the trouble.'
Then how does the son turn out this way?
'So how does the son turn out the way he does?'

It starts when he listens to his mother. She's aggrieved: her husband isn't one of the rulers, and the other women slight her for it. Then she sees he isn't much concerned about money, doesn't battle and brawl in the courts and the assembly but takes everything of that kind quietly, and keeps his attention always on his own thoughts — treating her, meanwhile, with neither much reverence nor much disrespect. All of it makes her resentful, and she tells the boy his father is unmanly and far too slack — along with the whole litany women love to chant on that theme.

'His character starts to take shape when he hears his mother complaining that her husband holds no office, so that she gets no precedence among the other women. She sees him caring little about money, never battling or trading insults in the courts or the assembly, just taking whatever comes his way calmly; she notices that his attention is always on his own thoughts, and that he treats her with no great regard. All this irritates her, and she tells her son that his father is only half a man, far too easy-going — and then she adds all the other grievances about her own ill-treatment that women so love to dwell on.'
Plenty of refrains, said Adeimantus, and just like the singers.
'Yes,' said Adeimantus, 'they give us plenty of those, and the complaints are very much in character.'

And you know, I said, that the house servants — the ones who seem loyal to the family — sometimes say the same kinds of things to the sons in private. If they see the father failing to prosecute a man who owes him money or has wronged him some other way, they urge the boy: when you're grown, punish all people of that sort, and be more of a man than your father. And when he goes out, he hears and sees more of the same — the men who mind their own business in the city are called simpletons and counted for little, while the meddlers are honored and praised. The young man hears and sees all this; and he also hears his father's words, and watches his way of life at close range beside the ways of the others; and the two pull him opposite directions — his father watering the reason in his soul and making it grow, everyone else feeding appetite and spirit. And because he isn't a bad man by nature, only fallen into bad company, he's dragged by the two of them to a middle place, and hands over the rule of himself to the middle part — the contentious, spirited part — and becomes a proud and honor-loving man.
