'And you know,' I said, 'that the old servants too — the ones supposed to be loyal to the family — sometimes have a quiet word with the son in the same vein. If they see someone who owes the father money, or has wronged him in some way, and the father lets it slide without going after them, they tell the boy that when he grows up he must pay such people back and be more of a man than his father. And he has only to step outside to see and hear the same thing: men who mind their own business in the city are dismissed as fools and counted for nothing, while the meddlers and busybodies get honored and applauded. The result is that the young man, taking all this in — and also hearing his father, and watching his way of life close up, and comparing him with others — is pulled two ways. His father waters and nourishes the reasoning part of his soul, while the others feed its passionate and appetitive parts. Since he isn't bad by nature, but has fallen into bad company, the two influences together drag him to a middle point: he hands over the kingship within himself to the middle element — to contentiousness and high spirit — and becomes a proud, ambitious man.'
You've described exactly how he comes about, I think.
'I think you've described his origin perfectly,' he said.
Then we have our second regime, I said, and our second man.
'So now we have our second form of government and our second type of character?'
We have.
'We do.'
Next, then, shall we say with Aeschylus,
'Next, let's look at another man who, as Aeschylus says,
‘another man, stationed against another city,’
"Is set against another city" —
— or rather follow our plan, and take the city first?
or rather, as our plan requires, let's begin with the city.'
By all means.
'By all means.'
Next in order, I believe, comes oligarchy.
'I think oligarchy is next in line.'
And what arrangement do you mean by oligarchy?
'And what kind of government do you mean by oligarchy?'
The regime founded on a property assessment, I said: the rich rule, and the poor man has no share in office.
'A government based on a property assessment, in which the rich hold power and the poor man is shut out of it.'
I see, he replied.
'I understand,' he said.
Shouldn't I start with how timocracy first changes into oligarchy?
'Shouldn't I start by describing how the change from timocracy to oligarchy comes about?'
Yes.
'Yes.'
Well, I said, even a blind man could see how it changes.
'Well,' I said, 'you don't need eyes to see how the one passes into the other.'
How?
'How does it happen?'

That treasury each man keeps filling with gold, I said — that is what destroys the regime. First they invent expenses to indulge themselves, and bend the laws to allow it; they and their wives simply stop obeying.

'It's the piling up of gold in private treasuries that ruins timocracy. They start inventing ways to spend illegally, and they bend the law to their own ends — for what do they or their wives care about the law?'
Likely enough.
'Quite so.'
Then, I suppose, one man watches another grow rich and wants to match him, until they've made the great mass of citizens just like themselves.
'And then one of them, seeing another grow rich, tries to outdo him, and so the great mass of citizens become money-lovers.'
Likely.
'Likely enough.'

From there they sink deeper into moneymaking; and the more honor they give money, the less they give virtue. Isn't virtue set against wealth like the two pans of a scale, each forever tipping opposite the other?

'And so they grow richer and richer, and the more they fix their minds on making a fortune, the less they think of virtue. Put riches and virtue on the two pans of a balance, and as one rises the other always sinks.'
Very much so.
'True.'
So when wealth and the wealthy are honored in a city, virtue and the good are honored less.
'And as wealth and the wealthy come to be honored in the state, virtue and the virtuous are dishonored.'
Clearly.
'Plainly.'
And what is honored gets practiced, and what is dishonored gets neglected.
'And whatever is honored gets cultivated, while whatever earns no honor gets neglected.'
It does.
'Obviously.'
So in the end, instead of lovers of victory and honor, they become lovers of moneymaking and money; they praise the rich man and admire him and bring him into office, and the poor man they despise.
'So in the end, instead of loving competition and glory, men become lovers of trade and money. They look up to the rich man and make him their ruler, and they despise the poor.'
Exactly.
'They do.'

Then they pass a law that draws the boundary line of the oligarchic regime: a fixed amount of property — larger where the oligarchy is tighter, smaller where it's looser — and they announce that no one whose wealth falls short of the assessment may hold office. They push this through by force of arms, or else they've already installed the regime by fear. Isn't that how it goes?

'The next thing they do is pass a law fixing a sum of money as the qualification for citizenship — higher in one place, lower in another, depending on how exclusive the oligarchy is — and they let no one whose property falls below that line have any share in the government. They push these changes through by force of arms, unless intimidation has already done the work for them.'
It is.
'Very true.'
That, broadly speaking, is how it's established.
'And this, broadly speaking, is how an oligarchy gets established.'
Yes, he said. But what's the character of the regime? What are the defects we said it had?
'Yes,' he said. 'But what are the characteristics of this kind of government, and what are those defects we were talking about?'
First, I said, the very line that defines it. Think what would happen if ships' pilots were appointed by property assessment, and the poor man never given the helm even if he were the better pilot —

'First of all,' I said, 'consider the nature of the property qualification itself. Just imagine if ships' pilots were chosen by their wealth, and a poor man were refused the helm even though he was the better pilot.'
A sorry voyage they'd make of it, he said.
'You mean they'd be shipwrecked.'
And isn't the same true of ruling anything else?
'Yes. And isn't the same true of governing anything whatever?'
I'd think so.
'I'd think so.'
Except a city? Or does it hold for a city too?
'A city included? Or would you make an exception of a city?'
For a city most of all, he said — the greater and harder the rule, the more it holds.
'No,' he said, 'a city is the strongest case of all, since governing one is the greatest and hardest task there is.'
So that's one defect of oligarchy, and a large one.
'So that's the first great defect of oligarchy?'
So it appears.
'Clearly.'
And here's another, hardly smaller.
'And here's a second defect, just as bad.'
What?
'What defect?'
That a city like this is necessarily not one city but two: a city of the poor and a city of the rich, living on the same ground and forever plotting against each other.
'The inevitable split. Such a state isn't one state but two — one of the poor, one of the rich — living on the same ground and forever plotting against each other.'
Every bit as large, he said.
'That, surely, is at least as bad.'

Nor is this a handsome trait: they're probably incapable of fighting a war. Arm the multitude, and they must fear it more than the enemy; leave it home, and they arrive on the battlefield oligarchs in earnest — few to fight, as they are few to rule. And all the while, being money-lovers, they're unwilling to pay for the war.

'Another disgraceful feature is that, for the same reason, they can't really wage war. Either they arm the common people, and then they're more afraid of them than of the enemy; or, if they keep them out of the fighting, they show themselves to be true oligarchs, with as few to fight as to rule. And on top of that, their love of money makes them unwilling to pay the taxes.'
Not handsome at all.
'How shameful.'
And what about the thing we condemned long ago — the same men in such a regime farming, making money, and making war, all at once? Does that look right?
'And then, as we said before, under this kind of constitution the same people take on too many jobs at once — farmer, trader, soldier, all in one man. Does that look right to you?'
Not in any way.
'Anything but.'
Now see whether this regime is the first that admits the greatest of all these evils.
'There's another evil, perhaps the greatest of all, and this is the first kind of state to be liable to it.'
Which?
'What evil?'

Letting a man sell everything he has, and letting another man acquire it — and letting the seller go on living in the city while belonging to no part of it: not a businessman, not a craftsman, not a cavalryman or a hoplite, just what they call a pauper, a man without means.

'A man can sell off everything he owns, and another can buy his property, and yet after the sale he goes on living in the city as no part of it — neither trader nor craftsman, neither cavalryman nor foot-soldier, but just a poor, helpless creature.'
Yes — it's the first.
'Yes, that's an evil that also first appears in this kind of state.'
At any rate nothing prevents it in oligarchies. Otherwise you wouldn't get the over-rich at one end and the destitute at the other.
'Nothing in an oligarchy holds it in check, anyway, since oligarchies run to both extremes — vast wealth and utter poverty.'
True.
'True.'

But consider this. Back when he was rich and spending, was this man of any more use to the city in the ways we just mentioned? Or did he only seem to belong to the ruling class, while in truth he was neither ruler nor servant of the city — merely a consumer of whatever was at hand?

'But think again. Back in his wealthy days, when he was spending freely, was a man like that any more use to the state as a citizen? Or did he only seem to be one of the ruling class, when in truth he was neither ruler nor subject, but simply a spendthrift?'
That's it, he said. He seemed; he was nothing but a spender.
'As you say — he seemed to be a ruler, but he was only a spendthrift.'
Shall we say, then, that as a drone grows up in its cell, a disease to the hive, this man grows up in his house, a drone and a disease to the city?
'Shall we say, then, that he's the drone of the household, the way the drone is the drone of the hive — a plague on the city as the other is a plague on the hive?'
Just so, Socrates.
'Just so, Socrates.'

And hasn't the god made all the winged drones stingless, Adeimantus, while of these walking drones some are stingless and some carry terrible stings? From the stingless kind come the men who end their days as beggars; from the stinging kind, everyone we call a criminal.

'And god has made the flying drones, Adeimantus, all without stings, while of the walking drones he's made some without stings but others with terrible ones. The stingless sort are the men who end their old age as paupers; the stinging sort are all the men we call criminals.'
Most true, he said.
'Very true,' he said.
Then wherever you see beggars in a city, somewhere close by are hidden thieves, and cutpurses, and temple-robbers, and the craftsmen of every evil of that kind.
'So clearly, wherever you see paupers in a state, somewhere nearby there are thieves hidden away, and pickpockets, and temple-robbers, and every kind of wrongdoer.'
Clearly.
'Clearly.'
Well then — in oligarchic cities, don't you see beggars?
'Well — and in oligarchical states, don't you find paupers?'
Nearly everyone but the rulers, he said.
'Yes,' he said. 'Nearly everyone who isn't a ruler is a pauper.'
Then shouldn't we suppose there are plenty of the stinging sort there too — criminals the authorities take care to hold down by force?
'And may we boldly say there are also plenty of criminals in them — rogues with stings, whom the authorities have to keep down by force?'
We should.
'We may certainly say so.'
And shall we say such men spring up there from lack of education, from bad rearing, and from a bad ordering of the regime?
'And the existence of such people is to be put down to lack of education, bad upbringing, and a badly ordered state?'
We shall.
'True.'
That, then, is the oligarchic city, and those are its evils — those, and perhaps a few more.
'So that's the shape of oligarchy, and those are its evils — and there may well be many more.'
Perhaps so.
'Very likely.'
Then let's call this regime finished as well — the one they name oligarchy, which takes its rulers by property. Next, the man who matches it: how he comes about, and what he's like once he has.
'Then we can leave oligarchy behind — the form of government in which rulers are chosen for their wealth. Let's go on now to consider the nature and origin of the individual who matches it.'
By all means.
'By all means.'
Doesn't the change from that timocratic man to the oligarchic go mostly like this?
'Doesn't the timocratic man change into the oligarchic one along these lines?'
Like what?
'What lines?'

He has a son. At first the son admires his father and follows in his footsteps. Then he watches him strike the city like a ship striking a hidden reef, and spill everything overboard — himself included. The father had held a generalship or some other great office; then he was dragged into court by informers, and put to death, or exiled, or stripped of his rights with all his property confiscated.

'A time comes when the timocratic man has a son. At first the boy admires his father and walks in his footsteps. Then he watches his father suddenly run aground against the state, as if on a hidden reef, and lose himself and everything he had. Maybe his father was a general, or held some other high office, and was hauled into court on charges trumped up by informers, and then put to death, or exiled, or stripped of his citizenship, with all his property confiscated.'
Likely enough.
'Nothing more likely.'

The son sees it all, my friend — suffers it, loses the estate — and takes fright, I imagine, and throws love of honor and spirit headfirst off the throne in his soul. Humbled by poverty, he turns to moneymaking; and greedily, little by little, by scrimping and hard work, he piles up a fortune. Don't you think a man like that then seats appetite — the money-loving part — on the empty throne, and makes it the Great King within him, girded with tiaras and collars and scimitars?

'And the son has seen all this and lived through it — he's a ruined man, and fear has taught him to knock ambition and high spirit headlong from the throne of his heart. Humbled by poverty, he turns to making money, and by stingy, grubbing savings and hard work he scrapes a fortune together. Isn't a man like this likely to set the greedy, money-grubbing part of himself on the empty throne and let it play the great king inside him, decked out in tiara and chain and scimitar?'
I do, he replied.
'Very true,' he replied.

And reason and spirit, I imagine, he sets on the ground beneath it, one on either side, and teaches them their place as slaves. The first he allows to calculate and study nothing but how money will breed more money; the second to admire and honor nothing but wealth and the wealthy, and to take pride in nothing whatever but the owning of money and whatever brings it in.

'And he makes reason and high spirit sit on the ground on either side of this sovereign, obediently, teaching them to know their place. He forces reason to think of nothing but how smaller sums can be turned into larger ones, and he won't let spirit admire or worship anything but riches and rich men, or be ambitious for anything except getting wealth and the means of getting more.'
There's no other change, he said, so quick and so sure as the honor-loving young man's into the money-loving one.
'There's no change,' he said, 'so quick or so sure as the turning of the ambitious youth into the money-grubbing one.'
And this, I said, is the oligarchic man?
'And the money-grubber,' I said, 'is the oligarchic man?'
Well — the man he changed out of was like the regime that oligarchy itself came out of.
'Yes,' he said. 'At any rate the man he grew out of resembles the state that oligarchy grew out of.'
Then let's see whether he's like oligarchy.
'Then let's see whether there's a real likeness between them.'
Let's see.
'Good.'
First, then, he's like it in prizing money above everything?
'First, they resemble each other in the high value they place on wealth?'
Of course.
'Certainly.'
And in being thrifty and hardworking — satisfying only his necessary desires, allowing himself no other spending, and holding the rest of his desires down as so much waste.

'And in their stingy, hard-working character. The man satisfies only his necessary appetites and keeps his spending to those; his other desires he holds down, on the grounds that they're a waste of money.'
Certainly.
'True.'
A squalid sort of man, I said, wringing a profit out of everything, laying up treasure — the very type the crowd applauds. Isn't this the man who matches that regime?

'He's a shabby fellow who skims something off everything and squirrels it away into a hoard — just the sort of man the common run of people admire. Isn't he a true picture of the state he stands for?'
So it seems to me. Money, at any rate, is what's honored — by the city and by him alike.
'He seems so to me. At any rate, money is prized as much by him as by his state.'
Because culture, I take it, was never part of his upbringing.
'You see he's not a cultivated man,' I said.
I'd say not, he said — or he wouldn't have set a blind god, wealth, at the head of his chorus and given him first honors.
'I should think not,' he said. 'If he'd been educated, he'd never have put a blind god in charge of his chorus and given him pride of place.'
Good, I said. But consider this: won't we say that from that same lack of culture, drone desires live in him too — some beggarly, some criminal — held down forcibly by his general carefulness?

'Excellent,' I said. 'But consider this too. Because of his lack of cultivation, won't we find in him drone-like desires — the desires of the pauper and the rogue — which his whole way of life forcibly keeps down?'
We will.
'True.'
And do you know where to look, I said, if you want to catch those criminal desires at work?
'And do you know where to look if you want to catch his roguery in the act?'
Where?
'Where should I look?'
Watch him where he's guardian of an orphan's estate — anywhere he gets a free hand to do wrong.
'You should watch him where he has some great chance to act dishonestly — say, when he's been made the guardian of an orphan.'
True.
'Just so.'

Doesn't that make it plain that in his other dealings — the ones that earn him his reputation for seeming just — he's holding his bad desires down by a kind of decent compulsion? Not persuading them they're wrong, not taming them with argument, but with necessity and fear, because he trembles for the rest of his estate.

'It'll be plain enough then that in his ordinary dealings, the ones that earn him a name for honesty, he's only keeping his bad impulses in check by a forced and grudging virtue — not by showing them they're wrong, or taming them with reason, but by sheer necessity and fear, because he's trembling for his money.'
It's quite plain.
'No doubt about it.'
And believe me, my friend: when it's someone else's money to be spent, you'll find the drone's desires are in him after all.
'Yes, indeed, my friend — and you'll find the natural desires of the drone alive in him all the same, whenever he gets the chance to spend what isn't his own.'
And strong in him, too.
'Yes,' he said, 'and strongly alive in him too.'
A man like this, then, isn't free of faction inside himself. He isn't one man but somehow two — though for the most part his better desires master his worse ones.
'So this man will be at war with himself; he'll be two men, not one. But on the whole his better desires will get the upper hand over his worse ones.'
True.
'True.'
And for that reason he'll be more presentable than many. But the true virtue of a soul in harmony with itself, one and undivided, escapes him by a long way.
'For that reason he'll be more respectable than most people — though the true virtue of a soul at one with itself, in harmony, will flee far away and never come near him.'
I'd expect so.
'I'd expect so.'

And the thrifty man makes a feeble competitor, in his own person, for any prize of victory in the city or any other honorable distinction. He won't spend money for the sake of glory — he's terrified of waking his spending desires and calling them in as allies for the contest — so he fights like a true oligarch, with a small part of his forces, and mostly loses. And stays rich.

'And the miser, taken on his own, will be a feeble competitor in the state for any prize of victory or other prize of honorable ambition. He won't lay out his money in the contest for glory, so afraid is he of waking his expensive appetites and inviting them to join the struggle as his allies. In true oligarchic style he fights with only a small part of his resources, and the usual result is that he loses the prize but keeps his money.'
He does.
'Very true.'
Then can we still doubt, I said, that the thrifty moneymaker takes his place beside the oligarchic city as its likeness?
'Can we have any further doubt, then, that the miser and money-maker is the man who answers to the oligarchic state?'
Not at all.
'No doubt at all.'

Next, it seems, we should look at democracy — how it comes about, and what it's like once it has — so that when we know the character of the matching man in his turn, we can bring him up for judgment.
'Next comes democracy. We still have to consider its origin and its nature, and then we'll look into the ways of the democratic man and bring him up for judgment.'
That would keep to our method, he said.
'That's our method,' he said.

Well then, I said, doesn't the city change from oligarchy to democracy in some such way as this — through the insatiable pursuit of the good it set before itself, the demand to become as rich as possible?

'Well then — how does the change from oligarchy into democracy come about? Isn't it like this? The good that such a state sets its heart on is getting as rich as possible, and that's a craving with no limit.'
How so?
'What of it?'

Since the men who rule it rule because they own so much, I suppose they're unwilling to restrain by law those of the young who turn profligate — unwilling to stop them spending and wasting what they have — because it's by buying up such men's property and lending against it at interest that they become richer and more honored still.

'The rulers, knowing their power rests on their wealth, refuse to curb the extravagance of the spendthrift young men by law, because they make money off their ruin. They lend at interest and buy up their estates, and so add to their own wealth and importance.'
Nothing plainer.
'Certainly.'
And isn't it plain by now that honoring wealth and having any adequate self-command can't coexist in the citizens of a city? One or the other has to be let go.
'And surely it's clear that the love of wealth and a sense of moderation can't both flourish in the same citizens at once; one or the other has to give way.'
Fairly plain, he said.
'Clear enough.'
So in oligarchies, by this indulgence — this license — men of good family are sometimes driven all the way down to poverty.
'So in oligarchic states, with carelessness and extravagance spreading everywhere, men of good family are often reduced to beggary.'
Often.
'Often, yes.'

And there they sit in the city, I suppose — stung, and armed: some in debt, some stripped of their rights, some both — hating the men who now hold what was theirs, plotting against them and against everyone else, hungry for revolution.

'And there they stay in the city — armed, ready to sting, some of them in debt, some stripped of their citizenship, some in both predicaments — hating and conspiring against the men who got hold of their property, and against everyone else too, and hungry for revolution.'
That's so.
'That's true.'

Meanwhile the money-men, hunched over their business, seeming not even to see the men they've already ruined, keep injecting their silver into anyone else in the crowd who yields — wounding him with it — and collecting interest, that many-times-multiplied child of the parent sum, they make the drone and the beggar swarm in the city.

'Meanwhile the men of business, walking with their eyes on the ground, pretending not even to notice the ones they've already ruined, sink their sting — that is, their money — into anyone else who isn't on guard against them, and recover the original loan many times over in a swarm of offspring; and so they make the drone and the pauper multiply in the state.'
Swarm they do, he said.
'Yes,' he said, 'there are plenty of them — no question about that.'

And the evil blazes on like a fire, I said, and they won't put it out — not by the one way, barring a man from doing whatever he likes with his own property, and not by the other, the law that would dissolve abuses of this kind.
'And they won't put the fire out, though it's blazing up; they won't do it by restraining a man's use of his own property, nor by the other remedy.'
What law?
'What other remedy?'

The one that's second-best after that — an ordinance that compels the citizens to care about their character. Make the rule that voluntary contracts are entered, in general, at the lender's own risk, and men would lend with less shamelessness in the city, and fewer of the evils we've been describing would grow there.

'The next best one, which has the merit of forcing the citizens to mind their characters. Let there be a general rule that everyone enters into voluntary contracts at his own risk; then there'll be less of this disgraceful money-making, and the evils we were describing will be far less common in the state.'
Far fewer.
'Far less, yes.'

But as it is, I said, for all the reasons I've named, the rulers reduce the ruled to this condition. And as for themselves and their own — don't their young grow luxurious, idle in body and mind, too soft to hold out against pleasure or pain, and lazy besides?

'As things stand, though, the rulers, driven by the motives I've named, treat their subjects badly. And they themselves, along with their dependents — especially the young men of the ruling class — get used to a life of luxury and idleness, in body and mind alike; they do nothing, and they're incapable of standing up to either pleasure or pain.'
What else?
'Very true.'
And the men themselves neglect everything but making money, and give no more real attention to virtue than the paupers do.
'They care for nothing but making money, and they're as indifferent as the pauper to the cultivation of virtue.'
No more.
'Yes, quite as indifferent.'

So they're formed. And when rulers and ruled in this condition run into one another — on the road, or in some shared undertaking, a festival embassy or a campaign, shipmates or fellow soldiers — and watch each other in the moment of danger itself, where the poor man is in no way despised by the rich; when a lean, sunburnt poor man, posted in battle beside a rich man raised in the shade and carrying plenty of borrowed flesh, watches him gasping, helpless — don't you think he concludes that men like this are rich because the poor are cowards? And when the poor meet in private, isn't the word that passes among them: ‘These men are ours for the taking. They are nothing’?

'That's the state of affairs among them. And often rulers and ruled cross paths — on a journey, or some other occasion, on a pilgrimage or a campaign, as fellow soldiers or fellow sailors — and they get to watch each other's behavior at the very moment of danger; for where there's danger, there's no risk of the poor being looked down on by the rich. And very likely the wiry, sunburnt poor man finds himself stationed in battle beside a wealthy one who's never ruined his complexion, who has plenty of useless fat on him; and when he sees this fellow puffing and at his wits' end, how can he help concluding that men like this are rich only because nobody has the nerve to take it from them? And when the poor get together in private, won't they be saying to one another, "These fine fellows of ours are no good"?'
I know very well that's what they do, he said.
'Yes,' he said, 'I know very well that's how they talk.'

Then just as a sickly body needs only a small push from outside to fall ill — and sometimes falls into disorder with no push at all — doesn't a city in this condition fall sick on the slightest pretext and go to war with itself, one side importing allies from an oligarchic city, the other from a democratic one? And sometimes doesn't faction seize it with no outsiders at all?

'And just as a body that's already sickly needs only a slight touch from outside to fall ill — and sometimes breaks into disorder all on its own, with no outside cause at all — so wherever there's weakness in a state, there's likely to be sickness too, brought on by the slightest occasion: one party calls in oligarchic allies from outside, the other calls in democratic ones, and then the state falls ill and goes to war with itself — and may be torn apart at times even when there's no external cause.'
Violently so.
'Yes, surely.'

Then democracy is born, I take it, when the poor win: when they kill some of the other side and exile others, and share the regime and its offices equally with the rest — and for the most part, the offices in it are assigned by lot.

'And democracy comes into being, I take it, once the poor have beaten their opponents — killing some, banishing others, and giving the rest an equal share in citizenship and office; and in this form of government the magistrates are usually chosen by lot.'
Yes, he said, that's how democracy is established — whether it's done by arms, or the other side takes fright and slips away.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's the nature of democracy, whether the revolution was carried through by force of arms, or whether the other side simply withdrew out of fear.'
And how do these people live? What is this regime like in its turn? Clearly the man who matches it will turn out to be the democratic man.
'And now, what is their way of life, and what sort of government is it? For as the government is, such the man will be.'
Clearly, he said.
'Clearly,' he said.
First of all, aren't they free? Doesn't the city fill up with freedom and free speech — with license to do whatever you want in it?
'In the first place, aren't they free? Isn't the city full of liberty and free speech, where a man may say and do whatever he likes?'
So it's said, at any rate.
'So they say,' he replied.
And where that license exists, plainly each man arranges his own life inside the city however it pleases him.
'And where there's that kind of freedom, plainly each man can arrange his own life as he pleases?'
Plainly.
'Plainly.'
Then this regime, I take it, would grow more varieties of human being than any other.
'So in this kind of state you'll find the greatest variety of human characters?'
Of course.
'You will.'

It may be the most beautiful of the regimes, I said. Like a many-colored cloak embroidered with every kind of flower, this city, embroidered with every kind of character, might well look the most beautiful of all. And no doubt, I said, many people would judge it so — the way women and children judge, when they see bright things in every color.

'This, then, looks like it might be the fairest of states. Like an embroidered robe spangled with flowers of every color, this state, spangled with every human manner and character, will strike a great many people as the most beautiful of all — just as women and children find a robe of many colors the most charming thing in the world.'
Many would.
'Yes.'
And it's the convenient place, my friend, to go looking for a constitution.
'And it's the very place, my good man, to go looking for a constitution.'
How so?
'Why?'

Because its license means it carries every breed of constitution in stock. Anyone wanting to found a city, as we've just been doing, should probably go to a democratic city first and browse the bazaar of constitutions, and pick out whichever style suits him — and then do his founding.

'Because of the liberty that reigns there — it carries a full assortment of constitutions in stock. Anyone who wants to set up a state, as we've been doing, has to go to a democracy as if to a bazaar where constitutions are on sale, pick out the one that suits him, and then found his state on that model.'
He wouldn't be short of models, at least.
'He'd certainly have no shortage of patterns to choose from.'

And there's no compulsion to rule in this city, even if you're capable of ruling, nor to be ruled if you don't feel like it; no compulsion to be at war when the city's at war, or to keep the peace when everyone else keeps it, if you don't want peace; and if some law bars you from office or from a jury — no compulsion not to hold office and sit on juries anyway, if the mood takes you. Isn't that, for the moment, a divine and delicious way to live?

'And in this state there's no compulsion to rule, even if you're fit to rule, nor to be ruled if you don't care to be; no compulsion to go to war when the rest do, or to keep the peace when others are at peace, unless you happen to want to; and if some law bars you from holding office or sitting on a jury, there's no compulsion to keep you from doing either, if you take it into your head. Isn't this, for the moment at least, a wonderfully pleasant way to live?'
For the moment, he said, perhaps.
'For the moment, yes.'

And isn't the gentleness of the place toward convicted men exquisite? Or haven't you seen it in a regime like this — men sentenced to death or exile staying on regardless, hanging about in the middle of everything, and the man strolling the streets like a hero come back from the dead, as if no one saw and no one cared?

'And isn't its mildness toward the condemned, in some cases, quite charming? Haven't you noticed how, in a democracy, men sentenced to death or exile simply stay put and stroll about in public, with the man parading like a hero, and nobody seeing or caring?'
I've seen plenty, he replied.
'Yes,' he said, 'I've seen plenty of them.'

And its forgivingness — the total absence of pettiness — its contempt for everything we said so solemnly when we were founding our city: that unless a man's nature were exceptional, he could never become good unless from earliest childhood his play was among beautiful things and his practices all of that kind. How magnificently it tramples all this underfoot, without a thought for what practices a man was raised in before he entered public life — ready to honor him if only he says he's the people's friend.

'And look at the forgiving spirit of democracy, its breezy indifference to small matters, its contempt for all those fine principles we so solemnly laid down when we were founding our city — as when we said that no one, unless he had a rare and gifted nature, would ever grow into a good man without having played from childhood among beautiful things and made a study and a delight of them. How grandly democracy tramples all these fine notions of ours underfoot, never sparing a thought for what a man has done before he goes into politics, and heaping honor on anyone who merely claims to be a friend of the people!'
Very noble of it, he said.
'Yes,' he said, 'she's of a noble spirit.'
These traits, then, and their cousins, belong to democracy. A pleasant regime, you'd say — no one in charge, every color in the cloth, dealing out a kind of equality to equals and unequals alike.
'These and other such traits belong to democracy. It's a charming form of government — full of variety and disorder, dealing out a kind of equality to equals and unequals alike.'
Nothing you're saying is unfamiliar, he said.
'We know it well.'
Then look at the man himself, the private version. Or should we first ask, as we did with the regime, how he comes about?
'Now consider,' I said, 'what sort of man corresponds to it — or rather, as we did with the state, consider how he comes to be.'
Yes, he said.
'Very good,' he said.
Isn't it like this? He'd be the son, I take it, of that thrifty oligarchic man — raised by his father in his father's habits.
'Isn't it like this? He's the son of that stingy, oligarchic father, brought up by him in his own habits.'
Naturally.
'Exactly.'
So he too rules his pleasures by force — the spending kind, the ones that don't earn, the ones called unnecessary.
'And like his father, he keeps down by force the pleasures that spend rather than earn — the ones we call unnecessary.'
Obviously.
'Obviously.'
Then so we're not arguing in the dark, do you want us first to mark off which desires are necessary and which are not?
'Would you like us, for the sake of clarity, to draw the line between necessary and unnecessary pleasures?'
I do.
'I would.'
Wouldn't ‘necessary’ rightly mean the ones we can't turn aside, and all the ones whose satisfaction does us good? Our nature is compelled to reach for both kinds — isn't it?

'Aren't the necessary ones those we can't be rid of, and those whose satisfaction does us good? We're right to call them necessary, because we're so made by nature that we have to desire both what benefits us and what we can't do without.'
Certainly.
'True.'
So we'll be right to call these necessary.
'So we're not wrong to call them necessary?'
We will.
'We're not.'

And the ones a man could be rid of if he trained against them from youth — the ones whose presence does no good, and in some cases does real harm — if we said all of these are unnecessary, we'd be saying it well?
'And the desires a man could get rid of, if he took pains from his youth on — the ones whose presence does no good, and sometimes positive harm — these we'd be right to call unnecessary?'
Well indeed.
'Yes, certainly.'
Shall we pick an example of each, so we have a general picture of them?
'Suppose we pick an example of each kind, so we have a general idea of them?'
We should.
'Very good.'
Wouldn't the desire to eat — plain food, and something to eat it with, as far as health and fitness require — be a necessary one?
'Won't the desire for food — for plain food and seasonings, just so far as they're needed for health and strength — fall in the necessary class?'
I'd think so.
'I'd suppose so.'
The desire for food itself is necessary on both counts: it does us good, and if it goes unmet, life stops.
'The pleasure of eating is necessary on two counts: it does us good, and it's essential to staying alive.'
Yes.
'Yes.'
But the desire for relish is necessary only insofar as it serves fitness.
'But the seasonings are necessary only so far as they're good for health.'
Certainly.
'Certainly.'

And the desire that goes past that — for delicacies beyond plain fare — a desire most people can be rid of if it's checked and educated young, and that is harmful to the body, and harmful to the soul in its pursuit of wisdom and self-command: wouldn't that rightly be called unnecessary?

'And the desire that goes beyond this — for richer food, or other luxuries, which most people could get rid of if it were checked and trained in youth, and which harms the body and harms the soul in its pursuit of wisdom and virtue — that we'd rightly call unnecessary?'
Entirely rightly.
'Very true.'
And shouldn't we say the unnecessary desires are spenders, while the necessary ones earn — since they're useful for the work itself?
'And may we not say that these desires drain a man's purse, while the others actually make money, since they help him to produce?'
Surely.
'Certainly.'
And the same holds for the desires of sex, and for the rest?
'And the same holds for the pleasures of sex and all the rest?'
The same.
'True.'

And the man we just now named a drone — didn't we mean the man crammed with pleasures and desires of this kind, ruled by the unnecessary ones, while the man ruled by the necessary was the thrifty oligarch?

'And the drone we spoke of just now — wasn't he the man gorged on pleasures and desires of this kind, the slave of unnecessary desires, while the man ruled by the necessary ones was the stingy oligarch?'
We did.
'Very true.'
Now back to how the democratic man grows out of the oligarchic. It seems to me it usually happens like this.
'Now let's see how the democratic man grows out of the oligarchic one. As I suspect, it usually happens like this.'
Like what?
'Like what?'

When a young man raised the way we just described — without education, and on a tight rein — first tastes the drones' honey, and falls in with fierce and dangerous beasts who can supply him with pleasures of every color and kind and complication: there, you can be sure, is the beginning of his change, from an oligarchy inside him to a democracy.

'When a young man, raised in that crude, miserly way we just described, gets a taste of drones' honey and falls in with fierce, clever people who can supply him with every kind of refined and varied pleasure — that, as you can imagine, is where the change begins inside him, from the oligarchic principle toward the democratic.'
It can't help but be.
'Inevitably.'

And just as the city changed when one of its parties got help from like-minded allies outside, doesn't the young man change when one class of desires in him gets help from a kindred class outside — like reinforcing like?

'And just as the city was changed when an outside alliance came in to help one faction of like-minded citizens against the other, so the young man is changed when a class of desires from outside comes to reinforce the desires already inside him — kindred and alike helping kindred and alike.'
Exactly.
'Certainly.'

And if a counter-alliance comes to the aid of the oligarchic part of him — from his father, say, or the rest of his family, warning and scolding — then there's faction in him, and counter-faction, and a battle with himself.

'And if some ally turns up to back the oligarchic principle in him — say a father, or relatives, advising and scolding — then a faction and a counter-faction spring up in his soul, and he goes to war with himself.'
There is.
'It can't be otherwise.'

And sometimes, I suppose, the democratic party gives ground to the oligarchic: some of the desires are put down, others driven out; a kind of shame rises in the young man's soul, and order is restored.

'And there are times when the democratic side gives way to the oligarchic, and some of his desires die off and others are driven out; a sense of shame comes into the young man's soul, and order is restored.'
That does happen sometimes, he said.
'Yes,' he said, 'that does happen sometimes.'
But then, as the old desires are driven out, new ones — kin to them — are quietly reared in their place, and because the father doesn't know how to bring anyone up, they grow many and strong.
'And then, again, once the old desires have been driven out, fresh ones spring up akin to them, and because their father doesn't know how to bring them up, they grow fierce and many.'
That's usually the way, he said.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's the usual way of it.'
They drag him back to the old crowd, and breeding in secret, they multiply.
'They draw him back to his old companions, and in secret company with them they breed and multiply in him.'
True.
'Very true.'

Until at last, I suppose, they capture the acropolis of the young man's soul — having found it empty of learning, of beautiful practices, of true accounts: the best watchmen and guardians there are in the minds of men the gods love.

'In the end they seize the citadel of the young man's soul, which they find empty of fine learning, worthy pursuits, and true words — the very things that make their home in the minds of men dear to the gods, and stand as their best guardians and sentinels.'
By far the best.
'There are none better.'
And into the emptiness march false and swaggering words and opinions, and take the citadel in their place.
'False, boastful notions and phrases come rushing up to take their place.'
They do indeed.
'They're bound to.'

So back he goes to live among the Lotus-eaters — openly now. And if reinforcements arrive from his family for the thrifty part of his soul, those swaggering words shut the gates of the royal wall against them: they won't let the allies in, and they won't so much as receive the wise old counsel of private men sent as envoys. They win the battle themselves. Shame — which they rename silliness — is thrown out, a dishonored fugitive; self-command — which they call cowardice — is dragged through the mud and pitched over the border; and measure and orderly spending they persuade him are rustic and beneath a free man, and with the help of a mob of useless desires they drive them out of the country.

'And so the young man goes back to the land of the lotus-eaters and openly takes up residence there. If his friends send any help to the oligarchic part of him, those vain conceits bar the gates of the king's stronghold: they won't let the relieving embassy in, and they won't listen to the fatherly counsel of older private advisers or take it from them. There's a battle, and the conceits win the day; then modesty, which they call silliness, is shamefully banished into exile, and self-control, which they sneer at as cowardice, is trampled in the mud and thrown out. They convince him that moderation and orderly spending are crude and mean-spirited, and with a mob of worthless appetites to help, they drive these virtues out beyond the border.'
That they do.
'They do it with a will.'

And once they've emptied and purged the soul they hold — the soul they are initiating, now, into their great mysteries — the next step is to lead insolence and anarchy and waste and shamelessness home from exile: in torchlight, garlanded, with a great chorus behind them, singing their praises and calling them by sweet names. Insolence is now good breeding; anarchy is freedom; waste is magnificence; shamelessness is courage. Isn't that roughly how a young man raised among the necessary desires changes into one who frees and releases the useless, unnecessary pleasures?

'And once they've emptied and swept clean the soul of the young man now in their power — the soul they're initiating into great mysteries — the next thing is to bring back insolence, anarchy, extravagance, and shamelessness in shining procession, garlands on their heads, a great throng behind them singing their praises and giving them flattering names: insolence they rename good breeding, anarchy they call liberty, extravagance they call magnificence, and shamelessness they call courage. And so the young man passes out of his original nature, schooled in the school of necessity, into the liberty and license of useless and unnecessary pleasures.'
Yes, he said — you've made the change vivid enough.
'Yes,' he said, 'the change in him is plain to see.'

After that, I take it, he lives spending money and effort and time on the unnecessary pleasures no less than the necessary ones. If he's lucky, and the frenzy doesn't run through him unchecked — if, as he gets older and the great commotion has passed, he readmits some of the exiled party and doesn't surrender himself entirely to the invaders — then he settles his pleasures into a kind of equality, and lives handing the rule of himself to whichever one comes along, as though it had drawn the lot for office, until it's satisfied; then to another, despising none of them, feeding them all alike.

'After this he lives on, spending his money, effort, and time on unnecessary pleasures just as much as on necessary ones. But if he's lucky, and not too far gone in folly — once the years pass and the fever of youth burns itself out, supposing he then lets some part of the exiled virtues back into the city and doesn't surrender wholly to the newcomers — then he settles into a kind of balance among his pleasures, living in a sort of equilibrium. He hands the government of himself over to whichever desire happens to come up first and wins the turn; and when he's had enough of that one, to another. He looks down on none of them, but treats them all as equals.'
Just so.
'Very true,' he said.

And a true account, I said, he keeps outside the walls — he won't receive it, won't let it into the guardhouse. If someone tells him that some pleasures belong to fine and good desires and others to bad ones, and that the first should be practiced and honored and the second checked and enslaved, he shakes his head at all of it and says one pleasure is as good as another, and every one deserves equal honor.

'And he won't admit any true word of advice into the fortress, or let it pass. If someone tells him that some pleasures belong to good and noble desires and others to base ones, and that he ought to indulge and honor the first and discipline and master the second, he shakes his head at every mention of it and says they're all alike, and one is as good as another.'
That's exactly what a man in that condition does.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's exactly how he is.'

And so he lives out his days, I said, indulging whatever appetite comes along. One day he's drunk, with pipes playing at the party; the next it's plain water and a diet. Now it's exercise; then a stretch of idleness in which nothing matters; then a spell of what passes for philosophy. Every so often it's politics — up he jumps, and says whatever occurs to him, and does it too. If he catches admiration for military men, he swings that way; if for businessmen, then their way instead. There's no order in his life and no necessity, but he calls this life sweet and free and blessed, and he keeps it to the end.

'And so,' I said, 'he lives from one day to the next, gratifying whatever appetite turns up. One day he's deep in drink and the music of the flute; the next he drinks only water and is trying to slim down; then he takes a turn at gymnastics; sometimes he loafs and neglects everything; then again he plays at being a philosopher. Often he throws himself into politics, leaping to his feet to say and do whatever comes into his head. If he envies some soldier, off he goes in that direction; if some man of business, then that way instead. His life has no order and no law — and this scattered existence he calls pleasure and freedom and bliss, and so he keeps on living it.'
You've described the life, he replied, of a man for whom everything has equal rights.
'Yes,' he replied, 'that's the man — all liberty and equality.'

And I suppose he's a man of every color and kind, I said — stuffed with more characters than any other, beautiful and various like his city. Many a man and many a woman would envy his life, with its endless samples of constitutions and characters inside it.

'Yes,' I said. 'His life is a patchwork, a jumble, a digest of many men's lives in one — and he answers to that state we called fair and many-colored. Plenty of men and plenty of women will take him as their model, for he holds within him samples of countless constitutions and ways of living.'
That's the man.
'Just so.'
Then let him take his place opposite democracy — the one who'd rightly be called the democratic man.
'Then let him stand opposite democracy; he truly deserves to be called the democratic man.'
Let him, he said.
'Let that be his place,' he said.
Now for the most beautiful regime, I said, and the most beautiful man, still left to describe: tyranny, and the tyrant.
'Last of all comes the most beautiful of them — beautiful both as a man and as a state — tyranny and the tyrant. These we now have to examine.'
So they are, he said.
'Quite right,' he said.
Come then, dear friend — how does tyranny arrive? That it changes out of democracy is fairly obvious.
'Tell me, then, my friend — how does tyranny arise? That it springs from democracy is obvious.'
It is.
'Clearly.'
And doesn't tyranny come out of democracy somewhat the way democracy came out of oligarchy?
'And doesn't tyranny spring from democracy in much the same way democracy sprang from oligarchy — in a sort of way, I mean?'
How do you mean?
'How?'
The good that oligarchy set before itself — the thing the regime was built on — was wealth. Yes?
'The good that oligarchy set before itself, and the thing on which it rested, was excess of wealth — am I right?'
Yes.
'Yes.'
And it was the insatiable appetite for wealth, and the neglect of everything else for the sake of moneymaking, that destroyed it.
'And it was the insatiable craving for wealth, and the neglect of everything else for the sake of money-making, that ruined oligarchy?'
True.
'True.'
Then does democracy too define a good for itself — and does the insatiable appetite for that dissolve democracy in its turn?
'And democracy has its own good, the insatiable craving for which brings it down too?'
What good do you mean?
'What good?'
Freedom, I said. In a democratic city you'll hear that this is its finest possession, and that this is why it's the only city worth living in for a man who is free by nature.
'Freedom,' I said. 'In a democracy you'll be told that this is the state's chief glory — that this is the only place where a man with a free nature would deign to live.'
Yes — you hear that line everywhere.
'Yes,' he said, 'that saying is on everyone's lips.'
Well then, as I started to say: isn't it the insatiable appetite for freedom, and the neglect of everything else, that transforms this regime too — and sets it up to need a tyrant?
'Well, what I was about to say is this: the insatiable craving for freedom, and the neglect of everything else, is what brings about the change in democracy and creates the demand for tyranny.'
How?
'How so?'

When a democratic city, thirsty for freedom, gets bad cupbearers pouring for it, and drinks past the point of drunkenness on freedom taken neat, then — unless its rulers are utterly mild and hand out liberty in quantity — it punishes them, and accuses them of being filthy oligarchs.

'When a democracy, parched with thirst for freedom, gets bad cupbearers presiding over the feast, and drinks too deeply of the strong wine of liberty, then, unless its rulers are utterly compliant and keep pouring out generous draughts, it hauls them up, charges them with crimes, and punishes them, calling them cursed oligarchs.'
Yes, he said — that they do.
'Yes,' he replied, 'that happens all the time.'

And the men who obey the rulers it drags through the mud as willing slaves and nobodies; the rulers it praises and honors, in public and in private, are the ones who act like subjects — and the subjects who act like rulers. In a city like that, doesn't freedom have to run to its limit?

'Yes,' I said, 'and loyal citizens it insults as willing slaves who hug their chains, men of no account; while it demands rulers who behave like subjects and subjects who behave like rulers. These are the men after its own heart, the ones it praises and honors in private and in public. In a state like that, surely freedom can know no bounds?'
How could it not?
'It can't.'
And it seeps down, my friend, into the private houses — until in the end the anarchy takes root even in the animals.
'And little by little, the anarchy seeps into private homes, until at last it even spreads to the animals.'
What do you mean by that?
'What do you mean?'

I mean that a father gets used to being like his child, and to fearing his sons; and a son gets used to being like his father, with no respect and no fear of his parents — that's how he proves he's free. Resident alien is the equal of citizen, citizen of resident alien, and the foreigner is as good as either.

'I mean that the father gets used to coming down to the level of his sons and being afraid of them, and the son puts himself on a level with his father, with no respect or reverence for either parent — for that's his idea of freedom. The resident alien is on a par with the citizen, and the citizen with the resident alien, and the foreigner is reckoned just as good as either.'
Yes, that's how it goes.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's how it goes.'

That, and other small evils like it. In such a place the teacher fears his students and flatters them, and the students hold their teachers cheap — their tutors too. The young in general ape their elders and compete with them in word and deed; and the old lower themselves to the level of the young, brimming with wit and charm, imitating them so as not to seem disagreeable or despotic.

'And these aren't the only evils,' I said. 'There are smaller ones too. The teacher in such a society fears and flatters his pupils, and the pupils think nothing of their teachers and tutors. All in all, the young put themselves on a level with their elders and stand ready to compete with them in word and deed; and the old stoop to the young, full of jokes and good cheer, copying the manners of the young because they hate to be thought sour or domineering.'
Quite true, he said.
'Quite true,' he said.

And the far edge of the crowd's freedom is reached, my friend, when bought slaves, men and women, are as free as their buyers. And the equality of women with men and men with women — the full liberty on both sides — I almost forgot to mention.

'And the very last degree of popular liberty is reached when slaves bought with money, male and female alike, are every bit as free as those who bought them — not to mention the freedom and equality between the two sexes in their dealings with each other.'
Then, as Aeschylus says, shouldn't we ‘speak what was on our lips just now’?
'Why not,' he said, 'come right out, as Aeschylus says, with the words on the tip of our tongue?'

By all means, I said — that's what I'm doing. No one who hadn't seen it would believe how much freer even the animals under human ownership are here than anywhere else. The dogs come to be just like their mistresses — the proverb has it exactly — and there are horses and donkeys in the habit of marching down the road at full liberty and full dignity, barging into whoever meets them and doesn't step aside. And everything else is just as bloated with freedom.

'That's exactly what I'm doing,' I replied. 'And I must add that no one who hadn't seen it would believe how much more freedom the very animals under human rule enjoy here than anywhere else. The bitches, as the proverb says, are the equals of their mistresses; the horses and donkeys have taken to marching down the streets with all the rights and dignity of free men, barging into anyone who doesn't clear the way for them. And everything else is just as ready to burst with liberty.'
You're telling me my own dream, he said. It happens to me every time I walk out to the country.
'You've described my own experience,' he said. 'I often run into exactly this when I take a walk in the country. You and I have dreamed the same dream.'

And the sum of it all, when you add it up, is this: it makes the souls of the citizens so tender that at the least whiff of servitude they're furious and won't stand it. In the end, as you know, they stop caring even about the laws, written or unwritten — so that no one, in any way, will be master over them.

'And the upshot of it all,' I said, 'is that the citizens grow so touchy that they bristle at the slightest hint of authority, until in the end, as you know, they stop caring even for the laws, written or unwritten — they'll have no one set over them at all.'
I know it very well, he said.
'Yes,' he said, 'I know that all too well.'
This, then, my friend, I said — so beautiful, so full of youth — is the beginning out of which tyranny grows, as it seems to me.
'And this, my friend,' I said, 'is the fine and glorious beginning out of which tyranny grows.'
Full of youth indeed, he said. But what comes next?
'Glorious indeed,' he said. 'But what comes next?'

The same disease, I said, that broke out in oligarchy and destroyed it breaks out here too — wider and stronger, because of the license — and enslaves democracy. And in fact, doing anything to excess likes to repay us with a great swing to the opposite side: in the seasons, in plants, in bodies, and in regimes not least.

'The same disease that ruined oligarchy ruins democracy too, only magnified and intensified by its very freedom, until it masters democracy altogether. The truth is that doing anything to excess tends to provoke a violent swing in the opposite direction — and this is so in the weather, in plants and animals, and above all in forms of government.'
So one would expect.
'True.'
Too much freedom, it seems, can collapse into nothing else but too much slavery — for a man and for a city alike.
'Excess of liberty, whether in a state or in an individual, seems only to turn into excess of slavery.'
Yes — that follows.
'Yes, that's the natural sequence.'
Then tyranny, it's fair to guess, is established out of no other regime than democracy: out of the summit of freedom, the largest and most savage slavery.
'So tyranny naturally grows out of democracy — the most savage form of tyranny and slavery out of the most extreme form of liberty.'
That stands to reason, he said.
'As we'd expect.'
But that wasn't your question, I think, I said. You asked what the disease is that grows in oligarchy and in democracy alike, and enslaves the second.
'But that, I think, wasn't your question. You wanted to know what that disorder is that's bred alike in oligarchy and democracy, and ruins them both.'
True, he replied.
'Just so,' he replied.

I meant, then, that breed of idle and extravagant men — the boldest of them leading, the more timid following. We compared them to drones: the leaders to drones with stings, the followers to drones without.

'Well, what I had in mind was that class of idle spendthrifts — the bolder of whom are the leaders and the more timid the followers — the same people we compared to drones, some stingless, some with stings.'
Rightly, too.
'A very apt comparison.'

These two kinds, I said, make trouble in any regime they appear in, the way phlegm and bile make trouble in a body. And the good physician and lawgiver of a city must take his precautions far in advance, like a shrewd beekeeper — best of all so they never appear; but if they do appear, to have them cut out as fast as possible, cells and all.

'These two classes are the plague of every state where they breed, just as phlegm and bile are to the body. The good doctor and lawgiver of a state ought, like a wise beekeeper, to keep them out and prevent them from getting in at all if he can; and if they have somehow worked their way in, then to cut them and their cells out as fast as possible.'
Yes, by Zeus — completely.
'Yes,' he said, 'by all means.'

Then let's take it this way, I said, so we can see what we're after more distinctly: divide the democratic city in speech into the three parts it actually has. One part is this breed of drones, which grows in it no less than in the oligarchic city, because of the general license.

'Then, so that we can see clearly what we're doing, let's picture a democracy as divided — as in fact it is — into three classes. In the first place, freedom breeds even more drones in the democratic state than there were in the oligarchic one.'
So it does.
'That's true.'
But it's far fiercer here than it was there.
'And in the democracy they're far more aggressive.'
How so?
'How so?'

There, because it's shut out of office and kept from exercise, it stays unpracticed and weak. In a democracy, with few exceptions, this breed is the presiding class of the city: its fiercest part talks and acts, while the rest settle around the speaker's platform, buzzing, and won't tolerate a word from the other side. So in a regime like this, everything, apart from a few matters, is managed by the drones.

'Because in the oligarchic state they're shut out of office and pushed aside, so they get no exercise and never gather their strength; whereas in a democracy they're practically the whole ruling power. The keener of them do the talking and the acting, and the rest sit buzzing around the speaker's platform, refusing to let a word be said on the other side — so that in democracies almost everything is run by the drones.'
Quite so, he said.
'Very true,' he said.
Then there's a second group that keeps separating itself out of the mass.
'Then there's a second class always sorting itself out from the rest.'
Which?
'Which one?'
When everyone's busy making money, the most orderly natures generally end up the richest.
'The orderly class, which in a nation of traders is sure to be the wealthiest.'
Probably.
'Naturally.'
And there, I take it, is the deepest honey for the drones — and the easiest to squeeze out.
'They're the easiest to squeeze, and they yield the most honey to the drones.'
Well, he said, who could squeeze it out of people who have next to nothing?
'Yes,' he said. 'There's little to be squeezed out of people who have little.'
So ‘the rich’ is what this class is called — the drones' pasture.
'And this is what's called the wealthy class — the drones' feeding-ground.'
More or less, he said.
'That's pretty much it,' he said.

And the third class is the people — everyone who works with his own hands, stays out of politics, and owns very little. This is the largest class in a democracy, and once assembled, the most powerful thing in it.
'The third class is the people — those who work with their own hands and take no part in politics, owning very little. When they assemble, they're the largest and most powerful class in a democracy.'
It is, he said — but it won't assemble often unless it gets some share of the honey.
'True,' he said. 'But the multitude won't gather unless it gets a little honey.'
And it does get a share, I said — as much as its leaders can manage, stripping the haves of their property and distributing it to the people, while keeping the largest cut for themselves.
'And don't they get their share?' I said. 'Don't their leaders strip the rich of their estates and parcel them out among the people — keeping the larger share for themselves, of course?'
Yes, he said — that's the kind of share it gets.
'Why, yes,' he said, 'to that extent the people do get a share.'
And the men being stripped are forced to defend themselves, I suppose — speaking before the people, acting however they can.
'And the men whose property has been taken are forced to defend themselves before the assembly as best they can?'
What else can they do?
'What else can they do?'
For which the other side accuses them — even if they have no appetite for revolution at all — of plotting against the people, of being oligarchs.
'And then, even if they have no wish for any change, the others accuse them of plotting against the people and being friends of oligarchy?'
Of course.
'True.'

Until in the end, when they see that the people — not out of malice but out of ignorance, deceived by the men who slander them — are truly set on wronging them, then, like it or not, they become oligarchs in earnest. Not willingly: that evil too is bred by the drone's sting.

'And the end of it is that when they see the people trying to wrong them — not deliberately, but out of ignorance, because the informers have deceived them — then at last they're driven, against their will, to become real oligarchs. They don't want to, but the sting of the drones torments them and breeds revolution in them.'
Precisely.
'That's exactly the truth.'
Then come impeachments and prosecutions and trials, each side against the other.
'Then come impeachments and trials and lawsuits, with each side dragging the other into court.'
Yes.
'True.'
And isn't it always the people's way to put one man at its head as its special champion — to feed him, and grow him great?
'And the people always have some champion they set over themselves and nurse into greatness.'
It is.
'Yes, that's their way.'
Then this much is plain, I said: whenever a tyrant sprouts, it's from this root, the people's champion, and from nowhere else.
'And this, and nothing else, is the root from which a tyrant grows. When he first sprouts above ground, he's a protector.'
Very plain.
'Yes, that's quite clear.'
So how does the change begin — champion into tyrant? Isn't it obviously when the champion starts doing what the story tells of at the shrine of Lycaean Zeus in Arcadia?
'And how does a protector begin to turn into a tyrant? Plainly, it's when he starts doing what the man does in the story about the temple of Lycaean Zeus in Arcadia.'
What story?
'What story?'
That whoever tastes the one piece of human innards minced in among the innards of the other sacrifices must turn into a wolf. Haven't you heard it?
'The story goes that whoever tastes the entrails of a single human victim, minced up among the entrails of the other sacrifices, is fated to turn into a wolf. Haven't you heard it?'
I have.
'Oh yes.'

It's the same with the people's champion. Once the mob obeys him in everything, he doesn't hold back from a kinsman's blood. He hauls a man into court on the usual false charges and murders him — blotting out a human life, tasting kindred blood with unholy tongue and lips. He exiles, he kills; and all the while he drops hints about the cancellation of debts and the redistribution of land. After that, isn't such a man bound by necessity — isn't it his fate — either to be destroyed by his enemies, or to rule as tyrant: to turn from a man into a wolf?

'And the protector of the people is just like that man. With the mob entirely at his command, he doesn't hold back from shedding kinsmen's blood. By his favorite method of false accusation he drags them into court and murders them, blotting out a man's life, his unholy tongue and lips tasting the blood of his fellow citizens. Some he kills, others he banishes, all the while hinting at a cancellation of debts and a redistribution of land. And after this, what is his destiny bound to be? Either he must perish at the hands of his enemies, or turn from a man into a wolf — that is, a tyrant.'
It's inevitable.
'Inevitably.'
He, then, is the one who raises the faction against the men of property.
'This, then,' I said, 'is the man who starts the feud against the rich?'
He is.
'The very man.'
And if he's driven into exile and comes back in spite of his enemies, he comes back a finished tyrant.
'And after a while he's driven out, but he comes back in spite of his enemies — a full-grown tyrant.'
Clearly.
'That's clear.'
And if they can't manage to expel him, or to have him put to death by turning the city against him, they plot to kill him quietly, by violence.
'And if they can't expel him, or get him condemned to death on a public charge, they plot to assassinate him in secret.'
That's the usual course, he said.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's the usual move.'
And then comes the demand that everyone who has reached this stage discovers — the famous tyrant's request: a bodyguard, so that the people's helper may be kept safe for the people.
'And then comes the famous request for a bodyguard, the trick of everyone who's gotten this far in his tyrant's career: "Don't let the people's friend be lost to them!"'
Exactly.
'Exactly.'
And they give it to him, I suppose — afraid for him, and serene about themselves.
'And the people grant it readily; all their fear is for him, and none for themselves.'
Very much so.
'Very true.'
And when a man with money — money, and with it the reputation of hating the people — sees this, then, my friend, in the words of the oracle to Croesus, he
'And when a man who's wealthy, and is also accused of being an enemy of the people, sees all this — then, my friend, as the oracle said to Croesus,
‘flees along the pebbled Hermus, does not stay, and is not ashamed to be a coward.’
"Along the pebbled bank of the Hermus he flees and does not stay, and is not ashamed to be a coward."'
Quite right, he said — he'd never get a second chance to be ashamed.
'And quite right too,' he said, 'for if he stayed he'd never have the chance to be ashamed again.'
True, I said — anyone caught is put to death.
'And if he's caught, he dies.'
He has to be.
'Of course.'

As for the champion himself — obviously he doesn't lie ‘mighty in his mightiness’ in the dust. He has toppled many a rival, and he stands upright in the chariot of the city, champion no longer: the finished, absolute tyrant.

'And our protector — there he stands, not "sprawling his bulk across the plain" in death, but having toppled many another himself, upright in the chariot of state with the reins in his hands: no longer protector, but tyrant outright.'
What else, he said.
'No doubt about it,' he said.
Then shall we describe the happiness of this man, I said — and of the city in which such a mortal arises?
'And now let's consider the happiness of this man, and of the state in which such a creature is bred.'
Yes, he said, let's describe it.
'Yes,' he said, 'let's consider that.'

In his first days — his early season — doesn't he have a smile and a greeting for everyone he meets? He says he's no tyrant; he promises everything, in private and in public; he forgives debts and parcels out land, to the people and to the men around him; he plays at being gracious and gentle with all.

'In the early days of his power he's all smiles, greeting everyone he meets — this man who's going to be called a tyrant! He makes promises in public and in private, cancels debts, hands out land to the people and to his followers, and wants to seem kind and gracious to everyone.'
He has to, he said.
'Naturally,' he said.

But once he's settled with his enemies abroad — come to terms with some, destroyed the rest — and that front is quiet, his first move is to keep stirring up one war after another, so that the people will keep needing a leader.

'But once he's disposed of his foreign enemies, by conquest or by treaty, and has nothing left to fear from them, then he's forever stirring up some war or other, so that the people will keep needing a leader.'
Naturally.
'Of course.'
And for another reason too, isn't it — so that the taxes will impoverish them, force them down to the day's needs, and leave them less leisure to plot against him?
'And hasn't he another motive too — that by paying for these wars the people will be kept poor, forced to attend to their daily needs, and so less likely to conspire against him?'
Clearly.
'Plainly.'

And if he suspects certain men of free thoughts — of not intending to leave the ruling to him — hasn't he a ready pretext for destroying them: hand them to the enemy? For all these reasons a tyrant is compelled to be forever stirring up war.

'And if any of them are suspected of harboring free thoughts and resisting his rule, he'll have a fine pretext for destroying them by handing them over to the enemy. For all these reasons, the tyrant must always be getting up a war.'
He is.
'He must.'
And doing all this, he becomes, day by day, more hateful to the citizens.
'And now he begins to make himself unpopular.'
Of course.
'A necessary result.'

And then some of the men who helped raise him up — men who hold power of their own — start speaking their minds, to him and to one another, and the boldest of them criticize what's happening to his face.
'Then some of the very men who helped put him in power, and who hold positions of their own, speak their minds to him and to each other; the bolder ones throw what's being done in his face.'
Likely enough.
'Yes, that's to be expected.'
So the tyrant, if he means to keep ruling, must quietly remove them all, until he has no one left, friend or enemy, who is worth anything.
'And the tyrant, if he means to keep his rule, has to get rid of them; he can't stop until he has no friend or enemy left who's any good at all.'
Obviously.
'He can't.'

He must keep a sharp eye out, then, for who is brave, who is high-minded, who is intelligent, who is rich. And such is his happiness that he must be the enemy of all of them, whether he wants it or not, and plot against them until he has purged the city.

'So he has to keep a sharp eye out for anyone brave, or high-minded, or wise, or wealthy. Lucky man — whether he likes it or not, he's the enemy of all of them, and must scheme against them until he's purged the state of every one.'
A fine purge, he said.
'A fine sort of purge,' he said.
Yes, I said — the opposite of the one physicians give a body. They draw off the worst and leave the best; he does the reverse.
'Yes,' I said, 'the opposite of the purge the doctors perform on the body. They take away the worst and leave the best; he does the reverse.'
It seems he has no choice, he said — if he's going to rule.
'And yet, if he's to rule, I suppose he has no choice.'
A blessed necessity binds him, then, I said: live with the mob of the worthless, and be hated by them even so — or not live at all.
'A blessed predicament,' I said: 'either to live hemmed in by a crowd of worthless men who hate him, or not to live at all.'
That's his necessity.
'Yes, that's the choice.'
And the more the citizens hate him for all this, the more bodyguards he'll need, and the more loyal ones?
'And the more his deeds make the citizens loathe him, the more bodyguards he'll need, and the more devoted they'll have to be.'
Certainly.
'Certainly.'
And who are the loyal? Where will he send for them?
'And who is this devoted band, and where will he get them?'
They'll come flying on their own, he said — plenty of them — if he pays the wage.
'They'll come flocking to him of their own accord,' he said, 'if he pays them.'
By the dog, I said — drones again, I think you're telling me. Foreign ones, of every stripe.
'By the dog!' I said. 'More drones, of every sort and from every land.'
You're right; that's what I'm telling you.
'Yes,' he said, 'there are plenty of those.'
But locally — wouldn't he be willing to recruit on the spot?
'But won't he want to recruit them on the spot as well?'
Meaning what?
'How do you mean?'
To take their slaves away from the citizens, free them, and enroll them in the bodyguard around him.
'He'll rob the citizens of their slaves, set them free, and enroll them in his bodyguard.'
Absolutely, he said — since they're actually the most loyal men he has.
'To be sure,' he said, 'and those are the very men he'll trust most of all.'
What a blessed thing you make the tyrant out to be, I said, if these are the friends and the faithful he keeps once he's destroyed the ones he had before.
'What a blessed creature this tyrant must be,' I said: 'he's put the others to death, and these are the friends he relies on.'
Well, he said, these are what he keeps.
'Yes,' he said, 'they're entirely his kind of people.'
And these companions admire him, I said, and the new citizens keep his company — while the decent hate him, and keep out of his way.
'And these,' I said, 'are the new citizens he's called into being, who admire him and keep him company, while the good men hate and shun him.'
What else would they do?
'Of course.'
No wonder, I said, that tragedy has the general name of wisdom — and Euripides the name of its master.
'No wonder, then, that tragedy is reckoned a wise thing, and Euripides a great tragedian.'
Why?
'Why so?'
Because among the rest, he produced this piece of concentrated thinking:
'Because he's the author of that pregnant line,
‘tyrants grow wise by keeping company with the wise.’
"Tyrants grow wise by keeping company with the wise."'
— and he clearly meant that the wise are the company we've just seen the tyrant keeping.
'And he plainly meant that the tyrant's companions are the wise.'
Yes, he said — and he praises tyranny as ‘godlike’ too, along with much else; and the other poets do the same.
