'Yes,' he said, 'and he praises tyranny too, as something godlike — and so do the other poets, in many other lines of the same sort.'
Then surely, I said, being wise, the tragic poets will forgive us — us and everyone whose regime resembles ours — for refusing them entry into the city, seeing that they sing tyranny's praises.

'And so,' I said, 'since the tragic poets are wise men, they'll forgive us, and anyone who governs as we propose to, if we refuse to admit them into our state — seeing that they're the eulogists of tyranny.'
I think the subtle ones among them will forgive us, he said.
'Yes,' he said, 'the clever ones, at least, will forgive us.'
Meanwhile, I imagine, they'll make the rounds of the other cities, drawing the crowds, hiring voices — beautiful, big, persuasive voices — and pulling the regimes toward tyrannies and democracies.
'But they'll go on touring the other cities, drawing crowds, hiring fine, loud, persuasive voices, and pulling those cities over to tyrannies and democracies.'
So they will.
'Very true.'

And they're paid for it, and honored for it — most of all by tyrants, as you'd expect, and second by democracy. But the higher they climb up the slope of the regimes, the more their honor gives out, as if it were short of breath and could go no further.

'What's more, they get paid for it and win honor — the greatest honor, as you'd expect, from tyrants, and the next greatest from democracies. But the higher they climb the ascent of our constitutions, the more their reputation flags, until it seems too short of breath to go any further.'
Quite so.
'True.'
But we've wandered, I said. Back to the tyrant's camp — that beautiful, numerous, many-colored, ever-changing army of his. How is it fed?
'But we're straying from the subject. Let's go back and ask how the tyrant will keep up that fine, numerous, varied, ever-changing army of his.'

Obviously, he said, he'll spend whatever sacred treasure is in the city, as long as it holds out, together with the property of the men he has destroyed — so that the levies he forces on the people can stay smaller.

'Well,' he said, 'if there are sacred treasures in the city, he'll seize and spend them; and as long as the confiscated property of his victims holds out, he can keep down the taxes he'd otherwise have to lay on the people.'
And when that runs out?
'And when those run out?'
Then clearly, he said, he'll feed off his father's estate — he, and his drinking companions, his men and his mistresses.
'Then plainly,' he said, 'he and his cronies, male and female, will be kept out of his father's estate.'
I understand, I said. The people, which fathered the tyrant, will feed him and his companions.
'You mean that the people — from whom he derives his very being — will support him and his companions?'
It will have no choice, he said.
'Yes,' he said, 'they can't help it.'

And what do you say to this? I said. Suppose the people get angry, and say a grown son has no business being fed by his father — the feeding should run the other way; that a father doesn't beget a son and set him up so that, once the son has grown great, the father must serve his own slaves and feed his son along with the slaves and the whole rabble around him — but so that with this champion at its head it might be freed from the rich and the so-called gentlemen of the city. Suppose the people now order him out, him and his friends, the way a father drives a son and his rowdy drinking crowd out of the house.

'But what if the people lose their temper and declare that a grown son has no business being kept by his father, that it should be the other way around — the father kept by the son? They never brought him into the world and set him up in life so that, once he was a man, they'd become the slaves of their own slaves and have to maintain him along with his rabble of servants and hangers-on; the idea was that with him to champion them they'd be freed from the rule of the so-called rich and aristocratic. And so they order him and his companions to clear out — exactly as a father might throw a riotous son and his disreputable friends out of the house.'
Then, by Zeus, he said, the people will find out what it is — what a creature it fathered and welcomed and grew great — and that it is the weaker trying to drive out the stronger.

'Then, by heaven,' he said, 'the people will find out what a monster they've been nursing in their bosom, all this time — and when they try to drive him out, they'll discover that they're the weak ones now, and their son is strong.'
What do you mean? I said. Will the tyrant dare to lay hands on his father — to beat him if he doesn't comply?
'What do you mean?' I said. 'Surely you're not saying the tyrant will use violence — that he'll actually strike his father if his father stands in his way?'
Yes, he said — once he's taken away his weapons.
'Yes,' he said, 'he will — once he's disarmed him first.'

A father-beater, then, I said — a tyrant makes a harsh nurse of old age. And this, it seems, is tyranny now in the open, acknowledged for what it is; and the people, as the saying goes, fleeing the smoke of enslavement to free men, has fallen into the fire of a despotism of slaves. In place of that abundant, unseasonable freedom, it has pulled on the harshest and bitterest of slaveries — slavery to slaves.

'So the tyrant is a parricide, a brutal keeper of his aged parent. This, then, is what tyranny really comes to, and there can be no mistaking it any longer: the people, trying to flee the smoke of being enslaved by free men, have plunged into the fire of being enslaved by slaves. So liberty, breaking out of all measure and all reason, passes into the harshest and bitterest slavery there is.'
That's exactly what happens, he said.
'True,' he said.
Well then, I said — will anyone quarrel with us if we say we've adequately described how tyranny evolves out of democracy, and what it is once it has arrived?
'Very well, then — may we say we've dealt sufficiently with the nature of tyranny, and with the way a state passes over from democracy into tyranny?'
We've described it quite adequately, he said.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's quite enough.'
spine.label: Book IX
spine.title: The Tyrant’s Soul
The Tyrant, and Why Justice Pays
spine.text: Last comes the tyrannical man himself, I said — and we still have to ask how he emerges out of the democratic man, and, once he exists, what kind of man he is, and what kind of life he leads: miserable or happy.
'Last of all,' I said, 'comes the tyrannical man. We still have to ask the same questions about him: how does he grow out of the democratic man, and how does he live, in happiness or in misery?'
Yes, he said — he is the one still left.
'Yes,' he said, 'he's the only one left.'
But you know, I said, there is something I feel we have left out.
'But there's a question we left hanging,' I said.
What?
'What question?'
The desires. I don’t think we have adequately settled what they are and how many kinds there are — and as long as that is missing, the whole inquiry will stay blurred.
'I don't think we ever properly settled the nature and the number of our desires. Until we do, the whole inquiry will stay muddled.'
Well, he said, it’s not too late to fix it.
'Well,' he said, 'it's not too late to fill in what we left out.'

Quite right, I said. And here is what I want to see about them. Among the unnecessary pleasures and desires, some strike me as outright lawless. They are probably born in every one of us; but in some people, disciplined by the laws and by the better desires working alongside reason, they are either rooted out entirely or left few and weak — while in others they stay stronger and more numerous.

'Quite right,' I said. 'And here's the point I want to get clear. Among the unnecessary pleasures and desires, there are some I'd call lawless. Everyone seems to have them. In some people the laws and reason keep them in check, so that the better desires win out and they're either driven off altogether or left few and weak. But in others they're stronger, and there are more of them.'
Which desires do you mean?
'Which desires do you mean?'

The ones that wake while we sleep, I said — when the rest of the soul is dozing, the reasoning, gentle, ruling part of it, and the beast in us, wild and gorged with food or drink, shakes off sleep, springs up, and goes looking for a way to satisfy its own instincts. In that state, you know, it will dare anything, loosed from every shame and every scruple. It does not shrink, in fantasy, from trying to sleep with a mother — or with anyone else, man, god, or beast; it is ready for any bloodshed, and there is no food it will not eat. In a word, there is no folly and no outrage it will not commit.

'The ones that wake up when the rest of the soul is asleep, the reasoning, gentle, ruling part of us. Then the wild beast inside, gorged with food and drink, stirs, shakes off sleep, and goes off to satisfy its own cravings. At a time like that, you know, it will dare anything, since it has cut loose from all shame and all sense. It won't shrink from lying with its own mother in its imagination, or with anyone or anything else, man, god, or animal. There's no murder it won't commit, no food it won't touch. In a word, there's no folly and no shamelessness it won't go through with.'
Perfectly true, he said.
'Very true,' he said.

But take a man who keeps himself healthy and temperate, and who goes to sleep only after he has wakened his reasoning part and feasted it on good arguments and good questions, coming to a quiet agreement with himself; who has given the appetitive part neither too little nor too much, just enough for it to sleep without disturbing the best part with its pleasure or its pain, leaving that part alone, pure, by itself, free to reach out and grasp at something it does not yet know, in the past, the present, or the future; a man who has soothed the spirited part in the same way and does not fall asleep with his temper up against anyone — when he has quieted those two parts and stirred the third, where thinking lives, and only then takes his rest, you know that in that state he touches truth most nearly, and the visions of his dreams are least likely to be lawless.

'But when a man is healthy and temperate in himself, and goes to sleep only after rousing his reasoning part and feeding it on fine thoughts and questions, having come to terms with himself in reflection, and after giving his appetites neither too little nor too much, just enough to lull them to sleep so they won't trouble the best part with their joys and pains but leave it alone, pure and by itself, free to reach out after the truth and to know what it doesn't yet know in past, present, or future, and after soothing his spirited part too, so that he doesn't drop off angry at anyone, when he has quieted these two and woken up the third, the part in which wisdom lives, and so takes his rest, then, as you know, it's at such a time that the soul comes nearest to the truth, and the lawless visions of dreams least trouble it.'
I agree entirely.
'I'm sure of it,' he said.

We have wandered rather far to say all this. But the point I want is this: some terrible, wild, lawless class of desires is in every one of us — even in those of us who look thoroughly measured — and sleep is where it shows itself. Consider whether I’m talking sense, and whether you agree.

'I've gone off on a digression saying all this. The point I want us to see is just this: in every one of us, even in the most respectable, there's a lawless, wild-beast kind of desire that comes out in our sleep. Do you think that's right? Do you agree?'
I do agree.
'I do.'

Now recall the democratic man and how we said he was formed. He was raised from childhood by a thrifty father who honored only the money-making desires and had no use for the unnecessary ones, the ones that exist for amusement and show. Yes?

'Now recall the democratic man, the way we described him. He was raised, you'll remember, from his youth under a tight-fisted father who valued only the money-making desires and looked down on the unnecessary ones, the ones spent on amusement and show.'
True.
'True.'

Then he fell in with more polished company, men full of the desires we have just been describing, and out of loathing for his father’s stinginess he ran to their kind of excess and every sort of indulgence. But because his nature was better than his corrupters’, he was pulled in both directions and settled in the middle, tasting each life in what he told himself was moderation — a life neither slavish nor lawless, as he saw it. And so the oligarchic man became democratic.

'And then he fell in with more sophisticated men, men full of those lawless pleasures, and out of disgust at his father's stinginess he plunged into every kind of arrogance and excess, the very opposite of his father. But because his own nature was better than that of the men who were corrupting him, he was pulled both ways and came to rest in the middle. Living what he took to be a balanced life, neither slavish and stingy nor lawless, he became a democrat out of an oligarch.'
Yes — that was our view of him, and it still is.
'Yes,' he said, 'that was our view of him, and it still is.'
Now imagine, I said, that this man has grown older in his turn, and has a young son brought up in his father’s habits.
'Now imagine,' I said, 'that years have passed, and this man has a son of his own, raised in his father's ways.'
I’m imagining him.
'I can picture it.'

Then imagine the same thing happening to the son that happened to the father. He is pulled toward total lawlessness — which the men doing the pulling call total freedom. His father and the rest of the household throw their weight behind the middle desires; the others push from the opposite side. And when these terrible sorcerers and tyrant-makers feel their grip on the young man slipping, they contrive to plant one master passion in him, a standing champion for the idle desires that drain whatever he has — a great winged drone. What else could you call the passion of such men?

'And imagine the same thing happening to the son that happened to the father. He's drawn into total lawlessness, which the men leading him on call complete freedom. His father and the rest of his family side with his moderate desires, while these others side with the opposite ones. And when these clever wizards and tyrant-makers see no other way to keep their grip on the young man, they manage to plant in him a master passion to lead the idle desires that squander whatever's at hand, a kind of monstrous winged drone. Can you think of any other image that fits this passion?'
Nothing else, he said. That is exactly what it is.
'No,' he said, 'that's the only one that fits.'

And when the rest of the desires come buzzing around it, steeped in incense and perfume, garlands and wine, all the loose pleasures of that kind of company, and feed the drone and fatten it to its full size, then they plant in it the sting of longing. From that moment this champion of the soul takes Madness for its bodyguard and is stung into frenzy; and if it finds in the man any opinions or desires still counted decent, anything still capable of shame, it kills them and throws them out, until it has purged him of temperance and filled the emptiness with madness brought in from outside.

'And when the other desires come buzzing around it, thick with incense and perfume and garlands and wine and all the loose pleasures of that kind of company, feeding the drone and making it grow until they've planted in it the sting of longing, then at last this leader of the soul takes madness for its bodyguard and runs wild. If it finds in the man any decent opinions or desires still left, anything that still feels shame, it kills them off and drives them out, until it has purged him of all self-control and filled him up with imported madness.'
That, he said, is a complete picture of how the tyrannical man is made.
'You've described exactly how the tyrannical man comes to be,' he said.
And is this why love has been called a tyrant since the old days?
'And isn't this why love has been called a tyrant from long ago?'
It may well be.
'It looks that way.'
And a drunk man, my friend, I said — doesn’t he too have something of the tyrant’s mind in him?
'And a drunken man, my friend, has something of the tyrant's temper too, hasn't he?'
He does.
'He has.'
And the man who is truly out of his mind, deranged, undertakes to rule not only men but gods, and fully expects to manage it?
'And a man who is mad, out of his mind, will try to rule not just over men but over the gods, and think he can do it.'
He certainly does.
'He certainly will.'
Then the strictly tyrannical man, my friend, I said, appears when nature, or habit, or both together, make a man drunken, lustful, and mad. Isn’t that so?
'So a man becomes a tyrant in the full sense, my friend, when by nature, or by habit, or by both, he turns drunken, lustful, and half-mad. Isn't that so?'
Exactly.
'Exactly so.'
So that is how this man is made, and that is what he is. Now — how does he live?
'That's the man, then, and that's how he comes to be. Now, how does he live?'
As the joke goes, he said: you tell me.
'I'll leave that to you,' he said, 'as the joke goes.'
I will, I said. From then on, I think, it is feasts and revels and parties and mistresses and everything of that sort, once Love the tyrant has moved in and steers everything in his soul.
'All right,' I said. 'Next, I'd say, come the feasts and the revels and the parties and the call-girls and all the rest of it, for love has set itself up as tyrant in his soul and runs everything.'
Inevitably.
'It has to be that way,' he said.
And day and night, desires shoot up beside it — many of them, and fierce, and every one of them demanding.
'And every day and every night more and more desires grow up in him, fierce ones, with endless demands.'
They do indeed.
'Endless indeed,' he said.
So whatever income he has is quickly spent.
'So whatever income he has is quickly drained away.'
Of course.
'Of course.'
After that comes borrowing, and carving into the estate itself.
'Then come the debts and the carving up of his property.'
Naturally.
'What else?'

And when everything is gone, won’t the desires, packed close and crying in him like a nest of young birds, begin screaming for food? And won’t he — goaded on by them, and above all by Love, whose bodyguard the rest of them are — go half-mad, hunting for anyone who has anything he can take, by fraud or by force?

'And when there's nothing left, surely the swarm of desires nesting in him, thick and loud, will start to cry out, and goaded on by the rest of them, and above all by love itself leading them like a bodyguard, he'll rage and look around for anyone he can rob or cheat of his property to feed them.'
Absolutely.
'That's bound to happen,' he said.
Money has to come from every side, or his life turns to agony and torment.
'He has to get money from somewhere, by any means, or live in terrible pain and torment.'
It must.
'He does.'

And just as the new pleasures inside him beat out the old ones and stole what was theirs, so the man himself, young as he is, will claim more than his father and mother — and once his own share is spent, he will start taking a slice of theirs.

'And just as in his own soul the new pleasures kept getting the upper hand over the older ones and stripping them of what was theirs, so the man himself, being younger, will claim the right to take more than his father and mother. Once he's run through his own share, he'll start carving up theirs.'
No doubt about it.
'Of course he will.'
And if they won’t hand it over, first he’ll try theft and fraud on his own parents?
'And if they won't hand it over, won't he first try to cheat and trick them out of it?'
Certainly.
'Certainly.'
And when that fails, he’ll move on to seizing it by force?
'And if that fails, won't he take it by force and rob them?'
Probably so.
'I'd expect so.'
And if the old man and the old woman hold their ground and fight back — what then, my friend? Will he hesitate, and hold back from anything a tyrant would do?
'And if the old man and the old woman dig in and fight back, my friend, will he hold off, will he spare them, or will he tyrannize over them too?'
I wouldn’t feel very easy, he said, about that man’s parents.
'I wouldn't bet much on their safety,' he said.

But in God’s name, Adeimantus — for the sake of a girlfriend of a week, someone he has no necessary tie to at all, do you believe he would strike his mother, his oldest friend, whose tie to him nature itself made necessary? Or, for the sake of some blooming boy, the newest and least necessary of loves, raise his hand against his worn old father, the first and most necessary friend he has — and put his parents under such creatures’ rule if he brought them into the same house?

'But by heaven, Adeimantus, do you really think that for the sake of some newfound girlfriend he can do without, he'd strike the mother he's had all his life and can't do without? Or that he'd put this new love over her, under the same roof? Or that for the sake of some fresh young boyfriend he can perfectly well live without, he'd beat his worn-out old father, his oldest friend and the one he most needs?'
Yes, he said. Honestly, I believe he would.
'Yes, by Zeus,' he said, 'I believe he would.'
What a blessing, then, I said, to give birth to a tyrannical son.
'What a blessing it is, then,' I said, 'to be the father or mother of a tyrant.'
A real blessing, he replied.
'A great blessing,' he said.

And when his father’s and mother’s money runs out, and the swarm of pleasures packed inside him keeps clamoring, he starts by breaking into someone’s house, or lifting the cloak off a man walking home late; after that he’ll strip a temple clean. And all the while the old opinions he held since childhood about what is honorable and what is shameful — the ones we count as just — are overthrown by opinions newly freed from slavery, Love’s bodyguard, ruling at its side. In his democratic days, while he still lived under the laws and under his father, those desires broke loose only in sleep, in dreams. But now, under Love’s tyranny, he has become, awake and permanently, the man he used to be only rarely and in dream: he will stop at no murder, no forbidden food, no unspeakable act. The passion that lives in him as a tyrant, in total lawlessness and anarchy, sole ruler now, drives the man it possesses, as a tyrant drives a city, into any recklessness that will feed it and the noisy mob around it — the desires that bad company brought in from outside, and the ones his own bad nature loosed and set free from within. Isn’t that this man’s life?

'And when his parents' property runs out, and the swarm of pleasures crowding his soul has grown thick, won't he start by breaking into someone's house, or stripping the cloak off a late-night traveler, and then go on to clean out a temple? All the while the old beliefs he held as a child, his judgments about right and wrong, are overthrown by the ones lately set loose, the bodyguards of love that now rule along with it. In his democratic days, while he was still under the laws and under his father, these came out only in his dreams. But now that love tyrannizes over him, he becomes, awake and for good, what he used to be only now and then, in sleep. There's no terrible murder he'll shrink from, no food, no deed. Love lives in him as a tyrant, in total lawlessness and lack of restraint, and since it's a sole ruler, it leads the man it possesses, as a tyrant leads a city, into any reckless act that will keep itself and its riotous crew fed, whether that crew came in from outside, from the bad company he kept, or broke loose from within, set free by the same evils in his own nature. Isn't that the way such a man lives?'
It is, he said.
'That's it exactly,' he said.

And if there are only a few men like this in a city, I said, and the mass of the people are sound, they leave and hire on as bodyguards to some foreign tyrant, or as paid soldiers in whatever war is running. If there is no war and everything is quiet, they stay home and commit a stream of small evils right in the city.

'And if there are only a few such men in a city,' I said, 'and the rest of the people are decent, they go abroad and become some other tyrant's bodyguard, or serve as paid soldiers if there's a war on. But in peacetime, when there's no war, they stay home and do a great deal of small harm in the city.'
Such as?
'What sort of harm?'

They steal; they break into houses; they cut purses and strip travelers of their clothes; they rob temples; they sell people into slavery. Sometimes, if they can talk, they turn informer — they bear false witness, and they take bribes.
'They're its thieves, its burglars, its pickpockets and muggers, its temple-robbers and kidnappers. Or if they can talk, they turn informer, give false testimony, and take bribes.'
Small evils, he said — as long as there are only a few of them.
'Small harm,' he said, 'as long as there aren't many of them.'

Small is small next to great, I said; and all of it together, set against the tyrant, doesn’t come within a mile — as the saying goes — of the misery and rot he brings a city. Because when a city fills up with men of this kind, and with the others who follow them, and they realize how many they are, that is when they breed the tyrant — helped along by the foolishness of the people — and the man they breed is whichever of them carries the greatest and strongest tyrant in his own soul.

'Small and great are relative,' I said. 'All of this, measured against the misery and ruin a tyrant brings on a city, doesn't come anywhere close. But when men of this stamp, and their followers, grow numerous in a city and realize their own strength, then, with the foolishness of the people to help them, they make a tyrant out of the one among them whose soul holds the biggest tyrant of all.'
Naturally, he said — that man would be the most tyrannical already.
'Naturally,' he said, 'since he'd be the most fit to be one.'

If the city yields willingly, well and good. But if it resists, then — just as he once punished his own mother and father — he will punish his fatherland now, if he can: he’ll bring in his new companions, and hold his once-dear motherland, as the Cretans call it, his fatherland, in slavery to them and keep it so. And that is where this man’s desires finally arrive.

'And if the people give in quietly, well and good. But if the city resists him, then just as he once beat his own father and mother, so now, if he has the power, he'll beat his fatherland, dragging in his young cronies to lord it over what used to be his dear motherland, as the Cretans say, and his fatherland. And that's the end his desires come to.'
That is it exactly.
'That's exactly it,' he said.

Now, in private life, I said, before they ever hold power, isn’t this what such men are like? Their company is flatterers, men ready to serve them in anything; or, if they need something from someone, they do the groveling themselves — no pose of devotion is beneath them — and once they’ve got what they wanted, strangers again.

'Now while such men are still private citizens, before they get power, this is the sort they are. They keep company only with their own flatterers, men ready to do anything for them, or, when they need something themselves, they grovel and cringe and put on every show of friendship. But the moment they have what they want, they don't know you.'
Very much so.
'Very true.'
So through the whole of their lives they are never friends with anyone: always someone’s master, or someone’s slave. Real freedom and real friendship the tyrannical nature never tastes.
'So all their lives they're friends with no one. They're always either someone's master or someone's slave. The tyrannical nature never tastes real freedom or real friendship.'
Never.
'Quite so.'
Wouldn’t we be right, then, to call such men faithless?
'And wouldn't we be right to call such men untrustworthy?'
Of course.
'How could we not?'
And unjust — as unjust as men come, if we were right earlier about what justice is.
'And as unjust as men can be, if we were right earlier about what justice is?'
And we were right, he said.
'And we were right,' he said.
Then let us sum up the worst man in a sentence: he is, awake, what we described in the dream.
'Then let's sum up the worst man in a phrase,' I said. 'He's the man who, awake, is what we said the rest of us only are in our dreams.'
Exactly.
'Exactly.'
And that is what the man becomes who is most tyrannical by nature and wins sole power — and the longer he lives as tyrant, the more like this he grows.
'And this is what the man becomes who is by nature most tyrannical and gains sole power, and the longer he holds his tyranny, the more tyrannical he grows.'
Inevitably, said Glaucon, taking over the answering.
'That follows,' said Glaucon, taking his turn to answer.

And now, I said, won’t the man who shows himself the most wicked also show himself the most wretched? And the man who is tyrant longest and hardest — won’t he in truth be wretched longest and hardest, whatever the crowd may think?

'And won't the man who turns out to be the worst also turn out to be the most miserable? And won't the one who has been tyrant longest and most thoroughly be most truly and most lastingly miserable, however it may look to most people?'
That much is certain, he said.
'That has to be so,' he said.
And the tyrannical man corresponds to the tyrannized city, the democratic man to the democratic city, and so on down the line?
'And isn't the tyrannical man bound to be like the tyrannical city, and the democratic man like the democratic city, and so on for the rest?'
Of course.
'Certainly.'
And as city stands to city in virtue and in happiness, so man stands to man?
'And as city stands to city in virtue and in happiness, so man stands to man?'
Naturally.
'Of course.'
Then in virtue, how does the city under a tyrant stand against the city under kings — the one we described at the start?
'Then how does the man ruled by a tyrant compare, in virtue, with the city we first described, the one ruled by a king?'
They are opposite extremes, he said: one is the best of cities, the other the worst.
'They're complete opposites,' he said. 'One is the best, the other the worst.'

I won’t ask which is which, I said — that’s obvious. But happiness and misery: is your judgment the same there? And let’s not be dazzled into panic by staring at one man, the tyrant, or at the handful around him. We ought to go in and look at the whole city, slip down into every corner of it and see everything — and only then declare what we think.

'I won't ask which is which,' I said, 'since that's obvious. But tell me, do you judge their happiness and misery the same way? And let's not be dazzled when we look at the tyrant. He's a single man, perhaps with a few hangers-on. Let's go right into every corner of the city and look all around before we say what we think.'
A fair challenge, he said. And it’s plain to everyone that no city is more wretched than one under a tyrant, and none happier than one under kings.
'A fair request,' he said. 'And it's plain to anyone that no city is more wretched than one under a tyrant, and none happier than one under a king.'

And in judging the men, wouldn’t I be fair to make the same demand — that the verdict belong to someone who can enter a man’s character in thought and see through it, not a child gawking from outside, dazzled by the front tyrants dress themselves in for the world, but someone whose sight goes all the way in? Suppose I say we should all listen to the man qualified to judge — one who has lived under the same roof with a tyrant, watched him at home, seen how he deals with his own household, where he stands most stripped of his stage costume, and watched him again in public dangers. Shouldn’t we ask the man who has seen all that to report how the tyrant stands, for happiness and misery, against everyone else?

'And in judging the men,' I said, 'wouldn't it be just as fair to ask for a judge who can get inside a man and see him through, not one who, like a child taken in by the outside, is dazzled by the grand front a tyrant puts on for the crowd, but one who sees clearly? Suppose I had us all listen to someone competent to judge, someone who has actually lived under the same roof with such a man, watched him at home among his family with his stage costume off, and seen him too in moments of public danger. Suppose he could report to us how the tyrant's happiness compares with other men's.'
That would be the fairest demand of all.
'That would be a very fair way to do it,' he said.
Then shall we claim that we ourselves are among those who can judge — that we have met such men before — so that we’ll have somebody to answer our questions?
'Then shall we pretend that we ourselves are among those able to judge, men who've already met such people, so we'll have someone to answer our questions?'
By all means.
'By all means.'
Then look at it this way, I said. Keep the likeness of city and man in front of you, take each in turn, and tell me the condition of each.
'Come then,' I said, 'and look at it this way. Keep in mind the likeness between the man and the city, and examining each in turn, tell me what condition each is in.'
What conditions? he asked.
'What do you mean?' he asked.
Start with the city, I said. A city under a tyrant — do you call it free or enslaved?
'To start with the city,' I said. 'Would you call a city ruled by a tyrant free or enslaved?'
As enslaved as a city can be.
'As enslaved as a city can be,' he said.
And yet you can see masters in it, and free men.
'And yet you see free men and masters in it.'
I see a few, he said. But the whole of it, near enough — and certainly the most decent part of it — is degraded and enslaved, and without honor.
'I do see some,' he said, 'a few. But the bulk of it, and the best part of it, are degraded and enslaved in the most shameful way.'

Then if the man resembles the city, I said, the same order must hold in him: his soul loaded with slavishness and meanness, the most decent parts of it enslaved, while a small part — the maddest and most vicious — sits as master.

'Well, if the man is like the city,' I said, 'mustn't the same be true of him? His soul is full of slavishness and meanness. The best parts of it are enslaved, while a small part, the worst and maddest, rules.'
It must be so.
'It has to be,' he said.
So what will you call such a soul — slave or free?
'And would you say such a soul is the soul of a slave or of a free man?'
A slave, surely.
'A slave's, I'd say.'
And the enslaved, tyrannized city least does what it actually wants?
'And the city enslaved under a tyrant is least able to do what it wants?'
Far the least.
'Far from able.'
Then the tyrannized soul will also least do what it wishes — I mean the soul taken as a whole. Dragged always by the sting of the gadfly, it will be full of turmoil and regret.
'Then the soul under a tyrant, taking the soul as a whole, will also be least able to do what it wants. Driven on by a kind of frenzy, it's forever full of confusion and regret.'
Of course.
'Of course.'
And the tyrannized city — must it be rich or poor?
'And is the city under a tyrant rich or poor?'
Poor.
'Poor.'
Then the tyrannical soul, too, must always be needy and never filled.
'Then the tyrannical soul too must always be poor and never satisfied.'
So it must.
'True.'
And such a city, and such a man — mustn’t they be full of fear?
'And mustn't a city and a man of this kind be always full of fear?'
Very much so.
'They must.'
Do you expect to find more wailing and groaning, more lament and grief, in any other city?
'And is there any city you'll find more full of wailing and groaning and grief and pain?'
Nowhere.
'None.'
And in any man more than in this tyrannical one, maddened by his desires and his passions?
'And do you think there's any man more loaded with these miseries than the tyrannical man, driven wild by his desires and passions?'
There couldn’t be.
'How could there be?' he said.
It was looking at all this, I think, that made you judge the tyrannized city the most wretched of cities.
'It was looking at all these things, and others like them, that led you to judge the tyrannical city the most miserable of cities.'
And wasn’t I right? he said.
'And I was right,' he said.
Completely, I said. But looking at the same facts in the tyrannical man — what do you say now?
'You certainly were,' I said. 'And when you see the same evils in the tyrannical man, what do you say of him?'
That he is by far the most wretched of all men.
'That he's by far the most miserable of all men,' he said.
There, I said, you may be going wrong.
'There,' I said, 'I think you've gone a little wrong.'
How?
'How so?'
I don’t think this man has quite reached the extreme of wretchedness yet.
'I don't think this man has reached the very depths of misery yet.'
Then who has?
'Then who has?'
There is one you will probably think more wretched still.
'There's one I'd call still more wretched.'
Who?
'Who?'
The man who is tyrannical by nature, I said, and does not live out his life as a private citizen — the unlucky one whose bad luck runs so far that he is made an actual tyrant.
'The man with a tyrannical nature who doesn't live as a private citizen but has the bad luck to become an actual tyrant of a city.'
Going by everything we’ve said, he said, I’d guess you’re right.
'From what we've said, I'd guess you're right,' he said.

Yes, I said, but guessing isn’t good enough here. A question like this wants the hardest scrutiny we can give it — for what we are examining is the greatest question there is: the good life and the bad.
'Yes,' I said, 'but in a matter this weighty we shouldn't just guess. We should reason it out carefully, for there's no greater question than this one, about the good life and the bad.'
Quite right.
'Quite right,' he said.
Then see whether there is something in this. Here, I think, is where we have to look.
'Then consider this,' I said. 'I think it may throw light on the question.'
Where?
'What is it?'
At the private rich men in our cities who own many slaves. They resemble the tyrant in this: they rule over many. The difference is the size of his crowd.
'Think of the rich men in our cities who own many slaves. They can give us some idea of the tyrant's situation, since they too rule over many. The difference is only in the number.'
Yes, that’s the difference.
'Yes, that's the difference.'
Well — you know that these men live without fear. They aren’t afraid of their household slaves.
'Now you know these men live in security and have nothing to fear from their slaves.'
What would they be afraid of?
'What would they have to fear?'
Nothing, I said. But do you see why?
'Nothing,' I said. 'But do you see why?'
Yes: because the whole city stands ready to defend each private citizen.
'Yes,' he said. 'It's because the whole city stands ready to defend each citizen.'

Well said, I replied. But now suppose some god lifted one of these men — a man with fifty slaves or more — clean out of the city, him and his wife and children, and set him down in a wilderness with his property and his whole household, where no free man could come to his aid. What kind of fear, and how much of it, do you think he’d feel that he and his children and his wife would be killed by the slaves?

'Just so,' I said. 'But now imagine that one of these slaveowners, the master of fifty slaves or more, were lifted up by a god, along with his wife and children and property and all his slaves, and set down in some empty wilderness where no free man could come to his aid. Wouldn't he be in terror that he and his wife and children would be killed by his slaves?'
Total fear, I should think.
'In the greatest terror,' he said.

Wouldn’t he be forced, from that moment, to fawn on some of his own slaves — to promise them all sorts of things and set them free with nothing requiring it? Wouldn’t he stand revealed as a flatterer of his own servants?
'So that now he'd be forced to fawn on some of those very slaves, promising them their freedom and a great deal more, all against his will, and to flatter the people he owns?'
He’d have to, he said, or die.
'He'd have to,' he said, 'or be destroyed.'

And now suppose the god planted neighbors all around him — a ring of them, many, who will not tolerate one man claiming mastery over another, and who, if they catch such a man, punish him with the extreme penalty.
'And suppose,' I said, 'the god ringed him round with neighbors who would not stand for one man owning another, and who, if they caught any such owner, would put him to death?'
Then his case is worse still, I suppose — ringed on every side by nothing but enemies.
'He'd be in an even worse spot,' he said, 'hemmed in on all sides by enemies.'

And isn’t that exactly the prison the tyrant is chained in? His nature is what we described, packed with fears and passions of every kind; and greedy as his soul is, he alone of the men in the city can never travel anywhere, never go to see any of the things every other free man is eager to see. He burrows into his house and lives there mostly like a woman kept indoors, envying every other citizen who goes abroad and sees anything worth seeing.

'And isn't this just the sort of prison the tyrant is shut up in, a man whose nature is what we've described, riddled with fears and longings of every kind? For all that his soul is greedy for it, he's the one man in the city who can't travel abroad or go and see the things other free men long to see. Instead he burrows at home like a woman shut indoors, envying any other citizen who goes abroad and sees something worth seeing.'
Exactly so.
'Very true,' he said.

Such is the harvest of evils, then, for the man badly governed within himself — the tyrannical man you just judged most wretched — when he does not live out his life in private but is forced by some accident to become an actual tyrant: unable to rule himself, he undertakes to rule others. It is as if a man sick and helpless in his own body were forced to spend his life not resting at home but competing and fighting against other bodies.

'So a man so badly governed in his own soul, the tyrannical man you just now judged the most miserable of all, is worse off still when he isn't a private citizen but is forced by chance to become an actual tyrant. He has to rule others when he can't even rule himself. It's as if a man who was sick, paralyzed in his own body, were forced to spend his life not in quiet retirement but in fighting and wrestling with others.'
The likeness is perfect, Socrates, he said — that’s it exactly.
'That's a perfect likeness, Socrates,' he said. 'Exactly right.'
So isn’t his condition wretched through and through, dear Glaucon? Doesn’t the reigning tyrant live a harder life than the life you judged hardest of all?
'Isn't his condition utterly wretched, then? And doesn't the man who is actually a tyrant live even worse than the one you judged to have the worst life of all?'
He does.
'No doubt of it,' he said.

In truth, then, whatever anyone may think, the real tyrant is the real slave — one long career of flattery and groveling, a courtier to the vilest men alive. His desires he never satisfies at all; he is needier than anyone, and genuinely poor, if you know how to look at a soul whole; loaded with fear his whole life long, full of convulsions and pains — if his condition really matches the city he rules. And it does match. Doesn’t it?

'So the truth is that the real tyrant, whatever anyone may think, is the real slave, forced to grovel and cringe more than any man, to flatter the very worst of men. He can never satisfy his desires. Look into his whole soul and you'll see how much he lacks, how truly poor he is. All his life he's filled with fear, racked by convulsions and pain, just like the city he resembles. And he does resemble it, doesn't he?'
It does.
'He does,' he said.

And on top of all this, add what we said before: power must make him — and does make him — more envious, more faithless, more unjust, more friendless, more impious than he was; host and feeder of every vice. And for all these reasons he is supremely unhappy himself, and then makes everyone near him just as unhappy.

'And on top of all this, won't the man grow even worse from holding power, won't ruling make him more envious, more faithless, more unjust, more friendless, more godless than before, the host and nurse of every kind of vice, until he is, in the end, supremely miserable, and makes everyone around him miserable too?'
No one with any sense will contradict you.
'No one with any sense would dispute it,' he said.

Come then, I said. Like the judge who decides the whole competition, give your verdict now across the field: who, in your judgment, is first in happiness, who second, and so on through the five — the kingly man, the timocratic, the oligarchic, the democratic, the tyrannical.

'Come then,' I said, 'like the judge who announces the winner at the games, you give us your decision. Who, in your view, comes first in happiness, who second, and the rest in order? There are five of them: the kingly man, the timocratic, the oligarchic, the democratic, and the tyrannical.'
The judging is easy, he said. I rank them like choruses, in the order they came on stage — by virtue and vice, by happiness and its opposite.
'That's an easy ruling,' he said. 'I rank them, like choruses, in the order they came on stage, by virtue and by vice, by happiness and by misery.'

Shall we hire a herald, then, I said, or shall I make the announcement myself? The son of Ariston has judged: the best and most just man is the happiest — and he is the most kingly man, the one who is king over himself; the worst and most unjust is the most wretched — and he, in turn, is the man who, being the greatest tyrant over himself, is the greatest tyrant over his city.

'Then shall we hire a herald,' I said, 'or shall I announce it myself, that the son of Ariston has judged the best and most just man to be the happiest, and that this is the most kingly man, the one who is king over himself, and that the worst and most unjust is the most miserable, and that this turns out to be the man who, being the greatest tyrant over himself, is also the greatest tyrant over his city?'
Announce it yourself, he said.
'Announce it yourself,' he said.
And shall I add: whether or not gods and men see them for what they are?
'And shall I add that this holds whether or not they're seen by gods and men?'
Add it.
'Add it,' he said.
Good, I said. That would be our first proof. Now the second — see if there’s anything in it.
'Good,' I said. 'So that's one proof. Now here's a second, if it seems to carry any weight.'
What is it?
'What is it?'
Since the soul, like the city, divides into three parts, I think it gives us a second demonstration.
'It comes from the nature of the soul. Since we divided the soul, like the city, into three parts, I think it gives us a fresh proof.'
What is that?
'How so?'
This. Three parts — and, it seems to me, three pleasures, one proper to each part; and likewise three kinds of desire, and three kinds of rule.
'It seems to me that as there are three parts, so there are three pleasures, one for each, and likewise three desires and three kinds of rule.'
Explain.
'Explain,' he said.

One part, we said, is what a man learns with; another is what he gets angry with; the third had so many faces that we couldn’t give it one name of its own, so we named it for its biggest and strongest member. We called it the appetitive part, for the intensity of its appetites for food and drink and sex and everything that goes with them — and the money-loving part too, because money, more than anything, is how appetites like these get satisfied.

'There's one part with which a man learns, we said, and another with which he feels anger. The third has so many forms we couldn't give it a single name of its own, so we named it from what's biggest and strongest in it. We called it the appetitive part, because of the sheer force of the appetites for food and drink and sex and the rest, and we called it money-loving too, since money is mostly the means of satisfying such desires.'
And rightly.
'And rightly,' he said.

So if we said its pleasure and its love are for profit, that would gather it best under a single head for the argument — so we know what we mean whenever we speak of this part of the soul. Call it money-loving, profit-loving: is that fair?
'So if we said its pleasure and its love are for gain, we'd be reducing it to a single heading, and could speak clearly when we called this part of the soul money-loving and gain-loving.'
It seems right to me.
'I agree,' he said.
And the spirited part — don’t we say it drives, whole and always, toward power and victory and a great name?
'And the spirited part, don't we say it's always set on mastery, on winning, on a good name?'
Very much.
'Certainly.'
So victory-loving and honor-loving would suit it well?
'So if we called it the victory-loving and honor-loving part, would that be fitting?'
Extremely well.
'Very fitting.'
But the part we learn with — everyone can see that its whole effort, always, is to know the truth as it stands, and that of the three it cares least for money and reputation.
'And the part we learn with, surely it's plain to everyone that it's wholly bent on knowing where the truth lies, and cares less than the other two about money or reputation.'
Far the least.
'Far less.'
Learning-loving, wisdom-loving — those are the names that fit it?
'Then "learning-loving" and "wisdom-loving" would be the right names for it.'
Of course.
'Of course.'
And in some souls this part rules, I said, while in others one of the other two does — whichever way it falls out?
'And in some men's souls this part rules, in others' one of the other two, however it falls out.'
Just so.
'That's so,' he said.
That is why we say there are three primary kinds of human being: the lover of wisdom, the lover of victory, the lover of gain.
'Then let's say, to begin with, that there are three kinds of men: the lover of wisdom, the lover of honor, and the lover of gain.'
Exactly.
'Exactly.'
And three forms of pleasure, one underlying each?
'And three kinds of pleasure, one matched to each.'
Certainly.
'Quite.'

Now, I said, if you asked these three men in turn which of their lives is the pleasantest, each would praise his own the loudest. The money-maker will tell you that next to making a profit, the pleasures of being honored or of learning are worth nothing — unless some of it converts to cash.

'Now you know,' I said, 'that if you asked these three men in turn which of their lives is most pleasant, each would praise his own above the rest. The money-maker will say that compared with making a profit, the pleasure of honor, or of learning, is worthless unless it pays.'
True.
'True,' he said.
And the lover of honor? Doesn’t he count the pleasure of money as vulgar, and the pleasure of learning — except where learning brings distinction — as smoke and nonsense?
'And the honor-lover, what of him? Won't he think the pleasure that comes from money is vulgar, and the pleasure of learning, if it brings no fame, mere smoke and nonsense?'
That is exactly how it is.
'Just so,' he said.

And the philosopher — what do we suppose he thinks the other pleasures are worth, next to knowing the truth and how it stands, and living always in some such state while he learns? Doesn’t he hold them far from real pleasure, and call them necessary in the strict sense — meaning he would want nothing to do with them if necessity didn’t force them on him?

'And the philosopher, the wisdom-lover, what do we suppose he thinks the other pleasures are worth, set against knowing where the truth lies and always being engaged in something of that kind while he learns? Won't he count them very far down the list, and call them necessary only because, if there were no need for them, he'd rather do without?'
We can be sure of it, he replied.
'There's no doubt of that,' he said.

So when the pleasures of each kind, and the lives themselves, are in dispute this way, I said — not over which life is nobler or more shameful, or worse or better, but simply over which is more pleasant and freer of pain — how do we know which of the three men speaks truest?

'Now since the pleasures of these three kinds of life are in dispute, and the men along with them, and the question isn't which life is more honorable or more shameful, or better or worse, but simply which is more pleasant and freer from pain, how are we to know which of them speaks most truly?'
I honestly can’t say, he said.
'I can't say,' he said.

Well, look at it this way. What should things be judged with, if they are to be judged well? Is there anything better than experience, and intelligence, and reasoned argument? Could you find a better standard than these?
'Well, think about it. What ought we to judge by, if we want to judge well? Isn't it by experience, by intelligence, and by reasoning? Could we find any better standard than these?'
Hardly, he said.
'How could we?' he said.

Then look. Of our three men, which has the widest experience of all the pleasures we named? Do you think the lover of gain, by studying what truth itself is, gains more experience of the pleasure of knowing than the philosopher has of the pleasure of gain?

'Then consider. Of our three men, which has the most experience of all three pleasures? Does the lover of gain have more experience of the pleasure of knowing the truth itself than the philosopher has of the pleasure of making money?'

There’s no comparison, he replied. The philosopher had no choice: from childhood on he has tasted the other pleasures. But the lover of gain — not only is there nothing forcing him to learn how things really are and taste how sweet that pleasure is; even if he were eager to, he’d find it hard going.

'There's no comparison,' he said. 'The philosopher has the great advantage. He can't help having tasted the other two pleasures from childhood on. But the lover of gain isn't bound to taste the sweetness of knowing the nature of things, isn't bound to gain experience of that pleasure. Even if he wanted to, it wouldn't be easy for him.'
Then in experience of both kinds of pleasure, the lover of wisdom stands far above the lover of gain.
'So the philosopher far outdoes the lover of gain in experience of both pleasures,' I said.
Far above.
'Far indeed.'
And against the lover of honor? Has the philosopher less experience of the pleasure of being honored than that man has of the pleasure of knowing?
'And how does he stand against the honor-lover? Has the philosopher less experience of the pleasure of being honored than the honor-lover has of the pleasure of understanding?'

No, he said. Honor comes to all three of them, if each accomplishes what he set out to do — the rich man is honored by plenty of people, and so is the brave man, and so is the wise one — so the pleasure of being honored is one they’ve all tasted. But the pleasure held in the sight of what really is — no one but the philosopher can have tasted that.

'No,' he said. 'Honor comes to all three alike, as long as each achieves what he's after. The rich man and the brave man and the wise man are all honored, so all of them know by experience what the pleasure of being honored is like. But the pleasure of seeing what truly is, that's a thing only the philosopher can have tasted.'
Then as far as experience goes, I said, he is the finest judge of the three.
'Then in experience,' I said, 'he's in the best position of the three to judge.'
By far.
'Far the best.'
And he alone will have experience joined to intelligence.
'And he alone will have gained that experience together with intelligence.'
Certainly.
'Of course.'
Further: the very instrument the judging must be done with belongs not to the lover of gain or the lover of honor, but to the philosopher.
'What's more, the very instrument the judging has to be done with belongs not to the lover of gain or the lover of honor, but to the philosopher.'
What instrument?
'What instrument?'
Reasoned argument. We said the judging must be done through arguments, didn’t we?
'We said the judging had to be done by reasoning, didn't we?'
Yes.
'Yes.'
And argument is, above all others, the philosopher’s own instrument.
'And reasoning is above all his instrument.'
Of course.
'Of course.'
Now, if wealth and profit were the best standard for judging things, then whatever the lover of gain praised or condemned would necessarily be truest.
'Now if the things being judged were best judged by wealth and gain, then what the lover of gain praised or blamed would have to be truest.'
Necessarily.
'It would.'
And if honor and victory and courage were the standard, then the verdict of the honor-lover and the victory-lover?
'And if by honor and victory and courage, then the judgment of the honor-loving, victory-loving man would be truest.'
Clearly.
'Clearly.'
But since the standard is experience and intelligence and argument —
'But since they're judged by experience and intelligence and reasoning?'
Then necessarily, he said, the truest pleasures are the ones praised by the lover of wisdom and of argument.
'It follows,' he said, 'that the pleasures the philosopher, the lover of reasoning, approves are the truest.'
Then of the three pleasures, the pleasantest belongs to the part of the soul we learn with; and the man in whom that part rules has the pleasantest life.
'So of the three pleasures, the pleasantest is the one belonging to that part of the soul we learn with, and the man in whom this part rules has the pleasantest life.'
How could it be otherwise? he said. The man of understanding praises his own life with full authority.
'How could he not?' he said. 'At any rate, the man of understanding speaks with authority when he praises his own life.'
And which life and which pleasure does our judge put second?
'And which life does our judge put second,' I said, 'and which pleasure second?'
Obviously the fighter’s, the honor-lover’s — it stands closer to his own than the money-maker’s does.
'Plainly the soldier's, the honor-lover's. His pleasure is nearer the philosopher's than the money-maker's is.'
And the lover of gain comes last, it seems.
'And the lover of gain comes last?'
Of course, he said.
'Of course,' he said.

That makes two in a row, then: twice running the just man has thrown the unjust. Now the third fall — wrestled Olympic style, for Olympian Zeus the Savior. Watch: I once heard a wise man say that only the pleasure of the understanding is fully true and pure, and all the others are shadow-painting. And this fall would be the greatest and most decisive of all.

'That's twice running, then, that the just man has thrown the unjust. Now for the third fall, dedicated to Olympian Zeus the savior. Notice that, apart from the philosopher's, the pleasure of the other parts isn't altogether true or pure but a kind of shadow-picture, as I think I've heard one of the wise men say. And this will be the greatest and most decisive fall of all.'
Much the greatest. But what do you mean?
'By far. But explain how you mean it.'
I’ll trace it out, I said, if you answer while I ask.
'I'll find it out as we go,' I said, 'if you'll keep answering my questions.'
Ask away.
'Go on, then. Ask.'
Then tell me: don’t we say pain is the opposite of pleasure?
'Tell me,' I said, 'don't we say that pain is the opposite of pleasure?'
We do.
'We do.'
And there is such a thing as feeling neither enjoyment nor pain?
'And that there's a state of feeling neither?'
There is.
'There is.'
A state midway between the two — a kind of stillness of the soul with respect to both. Is that what you’d call it?
'Something in the middle between the two, a kind of rest of the soul in between? Isn't that what you mean?'
It is.
'Just that,' he said.
Do you remember what sick people say when they’re sick?
'You remember what people say when they're ill?'
What?
'What's that?'
That nothing is pleasanter than being healthy — but that they never noticed it was pleasantest until they fell ill.
'That nothing is sweeter than being healthy, though they never noticed it was the sweetest thing until they fell sick.'
I remember.
'I remember,' he said.
And people gripped by some violent pain — you’ve heard them say nothing is pleasanter than for the pain to stop?
'And you've heard people in great pain say that nothing is pleasanter than for the pain to stop.'
I have.
'I have.'
And in many other situations like these, I think, you find people in pain praising not enjoyment but the absence of pain — the rest from it — as the pleasantest thing there is.
'And there are many other situations, I think, where you'll find people in distress praising the absence of pain, mere rest from it, as the greatest pleasure, not some positive enjoyment.'
Yes, he said. Because at those moments the rest itself becomes pleasant — welcome enough to satisfy them.
'Yes,' he said. 'For in those moments the rest becomes pleasant and welcome.'
And when a man’s enjoyment stops, that rest from pleasure will be painful.
'And when a pleasure stops,' I said, 'that rest from the pleasure will be painful.'
I suppose it will.
'Probably,' he said.
So the rest we just called a state between the two will at different times be both — pain and pleasure.
'So what we just called the middle state, the rest, will turn out to be at one time pleasure and at another pain.'
So it seems.
'It seems so.'
But can what is neither of two things become both of them?
'But can what is neither of two things become both of them?'
I don’t see how.
'I don't think so.'
And pleasure arising in the soul is a kind of motion, and so is pain. Yes?
'And both pleasure and pain, when they arise in the soul, are a kind of motion, aren't they?'
Yes.
'Yes.'
But didn’t we just see that feeling neither pain nor pleasure is a stillness — a midpoint between the two?
'But what is neither pleasure nor pain, didn't we just show it to be rest, in the middle between the two?'
We did.
'We did.'
Then how can it be right to think the absence of pain is pleasant, or the absence of enjoyment painful?
'Then how can it be right to suppose that the absence of pain is pleasure, or the absence of pleasure pain?'
It can’t be.
'There's no way.'

So the stillness isn’t really pleasant or painful — it only appears so: beside what hurts, the still state looks pleasant; beside what pleases, painful. And there is nothing sound in any of these appearances, measured against true pleasure — only a kind of conjuring trick.

'So this isn't real,' I said. 'It only looks so. Beside what is painful, the rest looks pleasant, and beside what is pleasant, painful. But none of these appearances stands up against true pleasure. They're a kind of trick.'
That is what the argument says, anyway.
'That's what the argument shows,' he said.

Then look at pleasures that don’t come out of pains, I said, so you don’t keep thinking — as you may be thinking now — that pleasure is by nature the stopping of pain, and pain the stopping of pleasure.

'Then look,' I said, 'at the kind of pleasures that don't come from the stopping of pains, so you won't be tempted to think, as you might just now, that it's simply in the nature of things for pleasure to be the ceasing of pain and pain the ceasing of pleasure.'
Where should I look? he said. Which pleasures do you mean?
'Where shall I look,' he said, 'and which pleasures do you mean?'

There are plenty, I said, but the clearest case is the pleasures of smell. Out of nowhere, with no pain beforehand, they arrive at extraordinary strength; and when they end, they leave no pain behind them.

'There are many,' I said, 'but take the pleasures of smell as a good example. They come on suddenly, with tremendous intensity, without any preceding pain, and when they stop they leave no pain behind.'
Very true.
'Very true,' he said.
So let no one persuade us that pure pleasure is relief from pain, or pain relief from pleasure.
'So let's not be persuaded that pure pleasure is just the removal of pain, or pain the removal of pleasure.'
No.
'No.'
And yet, I said, the so-called pleasures that reach the soul through the body — the biggest crowd of them, and the most intense — are exactly this kind: some form of release from pain.
'Still,' I said, 'the pleasures that reach the soul through the body, the ones we usually call the strongest, are mostly of this kind, reliefs from pain.'
They are.
'They are.'
And the pleasures and pains of anticipation, the ones that run ahead of the real thing — the same kind?
'And the same goes for the pleasures and pains of anticipation, that come before the things themselves?'
The same.
'The same.'
Do you know what they are like, then, I said — what they most resemble?
'Shall I tell you an image of what they're like?'
What?
'Please do.'
You believe there is, in nature, an up and a down and a middle?
'You'd grant,' I said, 'that in nature there's an up, a down, and a middle?'
I do.
'I would.'

Then wouldn’t a man carried from below toward the middle be sure he was moving up? And standing in the middle, looking back down at where he came from, wouldn’t he be certain he was at the top — never having seen the true top?

'Now if someone were carried from the bottom to the middle, don't you think he'd be sure he was going up? And standing in the middle, looking back at where he'd come from, he'd think he was already at the top, simply because he'd never seen the real top.'
Honestly, he said, I don’t see how such a man could think anything else.
'Of course,' he said. 'How could he think otherwise?'
And if he were carried back down, he’d suppose he was moving down — and this time he’d be right?
'And if he were carried back down, he'd think, this time truly, that he was going down.'
Of course.
'Naturally.'
And all this would happen to him because he has no experience of what is truly up, in the middle, and down?
'And all of this would come from his never having known the true up and middle and down.'
Obviously.
'Clearly.'

Then is it any wonder that people with no experience of truth hold unsound opinions about pleasure and pain and the state in between, the way they do about so much else? When they’re carried toward the painful, they judge truly — they really are in pain. But when they’re carried from pain back to the middle state, they are firmly convinced they have arrived at fullness, at pleasure. Never having seen true pleasure, they compare pain against the painless and are taken in — like men who, never having seen white, compare gray against black. Can any of that surprise you?

'Then can you be surprised that people with no experience of truth have unsound views about a great many things, and about pleasure and pain and the state between them too? When they're carried toward what's painful, they feel pain, and they're right to think it real pain. But when they pass from pain to the middle state, they're firmly convinced they've reached fullness and pleasure. Like people who've never seen white and judge gray by comparing it with black, they have no experience of true pleasure, and so they're deceived when they set pain beside the absence of pain. Can you wonder at it?'
No indeed — I’d be far more surprised if it weren’t so.
'No, by Zeus,' he said. 'I'd wonder far more if it weren't so.'
Then think of it this way, I said. Hunger and thirst and everything like them — aren’t they emptyings of the body’s condition?
'Then look at it this way,' I said. 'Aren't hunger and thirst and the like a kind of emptiness in the state of the body?'
Certainly.
'What else?'
And ignorance and folly — emptyings of the soul’s condition?
'And aren't ignorance and lack of understanding an emptiness in the state of the soul?'
Very much so.
'Very much so.'
And a man fills the one when he takes in food, the other when he comes to understand?
'And a man is filled when he takes in nourishment, or when he gains understanding?'
Of course.
'Of course.'
Now, which filling is the truer: filling with what has less being, or with what has more?
'And which is the truer filling, the filling with what is less, or the filling with what is more?'
With what has more, obviously.
'Clearly the filling with what is more.'

Then which class of things do you think has the greater share of pure being — things like bread and drink and meat and nourishment in general, or the class of true opinion and knowledge and understanding and, in a word, all excellence? Judge it this way: what keeps company with the unchanging and immortal and true, is itself of that kind, and comes to be in what is of that kind — does that seem to you to be more, or what keeps company with the changing and mortal, is itself of that kind, and comes to be in what is of that kind?

'Now which kinds of things do you think share more in pure being: things like bread and drink and seasonings, food of every sort, or the kind that takes in true belief and knowledge and understanding, in short, all of excellence? Judge it this way. Which seems to you to have more of pure being: what clings to the unchanging, the deathless, the true, what is itself of that kind and comes to be in things of that kind, or what clings to the changing and the mortal, what is itself of that kind and comes to be in such things?'
What holds to the unchanging, he replied — by far.
'What clings to the unchanging is far superior,' he said.
And does the being of the unchanging share any less in knowledge than it does in being?
'And does the being of the unchanging share in knowledge any more than it shares in being?'
Not at all — in knowledge equally.
'Not at all more.'
And in truth equally?
'Or in truth any more?'
Equally.
'No more.'
And conversely: what has less of truth has less of being as well?
'And if less in truth, then less in being too?'
Necessarily.
'Necessarily.'
So as a whole, the kinds of thing that serve the care of the body have less share of truth and of being than the kinds that serve the care of the soul?
'So in general the kinds of things that serve the body share less in truth and in being than the kinds that serve the soul.'
Much less.
'Far less.'
And the body itself, compared with the soul — the same?
'And don't you think the body itself shares less in these than the soul does?'
Yes.
'I do.'
Then what is filled with things that have more being, and itself has more being, is more really filled than what is filled with things that have less being, and itself has less?
'Now isn't a thing that's filled with what has more being, and that itself has more being, more truly filled than a thing filled with what has less being, and that itself has less being?'
Obviously.
'Of course.'

So if being filled with what suits our nature is pleasant, then what is more really filled, and with things that are more real, would enjoy true pleasure more really and more truly; while what takes in things with less being is filled less truly and less securely, and gets a pleasure less trustworthy and less true.

'So if being filled with what suits our nature is a pleasure, then what is more truly filled, with things that have more being, will more truly and really enjoy a true pleasure, while what takes in things of less being will be less truly and surely filled, and will share in a pleasure that's less to be trusted and less real.'
Inescapably.
'That's certain,' he said.

Then those who have no experience of wisdom and virtue, who spend their whole time at feasts and everything of that sort, are carried down, it seems, and back up as far as the middle, and wander that road their whole lives. They never cross beyond it: they have never looked up toward the true top, never been carried there, never been really filled with what really is, never tasted a pleasure that is solid and pure. Like cattle they graze, eyes forever down, heads bent to the ground — to the table, that is — fattening themselves and mounting each other; and in their greed for more of these things they kick and butt one another with horns and hooves of iron, and kill one another, and can never be filled — because the part of themselves they are filling is not the real part, and holds nothing, and what they are filling it with is not real either.

'So people who have no experience of wisdom and virtue, but are forever caught up in feasting and that sort of thing, are carried down, it seems, and then back up to the middle, and they wander between these two all their lives, but they never go past that to the true upper world. They never even look that way, or are truly filled with what truly is, or taste of any pleasure that is steady and pure. Instead, like cattle, always looking down, heads bent to the ground, or rather to the table, they graze and breed and grow fat, and in their greed for more of all this they kick and gore one another with iron horns and hoofs and kill one another, because they can never be satisfied. For the part of themselves they're filling isn't real, and they're filling it with what isn't real either, and what isn't real can never be held fast.'
Socrates, said Glaucon, you describe the life of most men like an oracle.
'Socrates,' said Glaucon, 'you describe the life of the many like an oracle.'

And doesn’t it follow that the pleasures they live among are mixed with pains — mere images of the true pleasure, shadow-paintings that take their color from being set side by side, so that both look intense; pleasures that breed insane desires for themselves in fools, and get fought over, the way Stesichorus says the shadow of Helen was fought over at Troy by men who did not know the truth?

'And aren't their pleasures necessarily mixed with pains, mere shadow-pictures of true pleasure, colored by being set side by side, so that they take on an intensity at each end and breed in foolish men a frantic love of themselves, and are fought over the way Stesichorus says the men at Troy fought over the phantom of Helen, in ignorance of the truth?'
Something exactly like that must be the case.
'Yes,' he said, 'something of that sort is bound to happen.'

And the spirited part — mustn’t the same story hold wherever a man works to fill it: envy driving his love of honor, violence his love of victory, temper his sullenness, as he chases his fill of honor and victory and anger without calculation and without sense?

'And won't the same hold for the spirited part? Whenever a man lets his spirit drive him, whether he's full of envy and ambition, or violence and quarrelsomeness, or anger and discontent, chasing the satisfaction of his honor and his victory and his rage without reasoning or intelligence, won't he get just such shadow-pleasures?'
The same story must hold there too.
'Yes,' he said, 'the same thing happens with that part too.'

Then may we say this with confidence, I said? Even the desires of the gain-loving and honor-loving parts — whenever they follow knowledge and argument, and pursue with their help the pleasures that understanding prescribes, they will get the truest pleasures they are capable of getting, because they are following truth, and the pleasures that are properly their own — if indeed what is best for each thing is also what is most its own.

'Then we may say it boldly,' I said. 'When the lover of gain and the lover of honor pursue their pleasures under the lead and in the company of knowledge and reasoning, taking the pleasures that wisdom points them to, they'll have the truest pleasures open to them, since they follow truth, and the pleasures that are their own, if indeed what is best for each is what is most truly its own.'
And it certainly is its own.
'And it surely is,' he said.

So when the whole soul follows the wisdom-loving part and there is no faction in it, each part can do its own work and be just in everything — and, in particular, each reaps its own pleasures, the best pleasures and, as far as possible, the truest.

'So when the whole soul follows the wisdom-loving part, and there's no faction within it, then each part can not only do its own work and be just, but also reap its own pleasures, the best and, so far as may be, the truest.'
Exactly.
'Exactly so.'
But when one of the other two takes control, it fails to find even its own pleasure — and it forces the other parts to chase a pleasure that is alien to them and false.
'But when one of the other two parts rules, it fails to find its own pleasure, and it forces the others to chase a pleasure that isn't theirs and isn't true.'
True.
'That's right,' he said.
And the farther a thing stands from philosophy and argument, the more surely it produces effects like these?
'And wouldn't the parts furthest from philosophy and reasoning bring this about most of all?'
Much the farther.
'Very much so.'
And what stands farthest from argument is what stands farthest from law and order?
'And whatever is furthest from reasoning is furthest from law and order too?'
Clearly.
'Clearly.'
And the desires that stand farthest, as we saw, are the lustful and tyrannical ones? — Yes.
'And we saw that the lustful, tyrannical desires are furthest of all?'
And the kingly, orderly ones stand nearest?
'By far.'
Yes.
'While the kingly and orderly desires are nearest?'
Then the tyrant, I think, will stand at the greatest distance from true pleasure — pleasure that is a man’s own — and the king at the least.
'Yes.'
Necessarily.
'Then the tyrant will live furthest of all from true and proper pleasure, and the king nearest to it.'
So the tyrant will live the least pleasant life, I said, and the king the most.
'Necessarily.'
Absolutely.
'So the tyrant will live the most unpleasantly, and the king the most pleasantly.'
And do you know, I said, just how much less pleasantly the tyrant lives than the king?
'That's bound to be so.'
Tell me.
'And do you know,' I said, 'just how much more unpleasantly the tyrant lives than the king?'

There are three pleasures, it seems — one legitimate, two bastard. The tyrant has fled beyond even the bastard ones. He has run from law and argument out past the border, and lives with a bodyguard of slave pleasures; and how far he has sunk is not easy to state — except perhaps like this.
'Tell me,' he said.
How?

'There seem to be three pleasures, one genuine and two counterfeit. The tyrant has run clear off the end of even the counterfeit ones. He's fled from law and reasoning altogether and taken up with a crowd of slave-pleasures for a bodyguard, and just how far below the king he falls is hard to put into words, except perhaps with a number.'
The tyrant stood third from the oligarch, counting down — the democrat sat between them.
'How do you mean?'
Yes.
'The tyrant, I take it, stands third from the oligarch, with the democrat in between?'
Then if what we said earlier is true, the pleasure he lives with is a phantom three times removed from the oligarch’s, as truth goes.
'Yes.'
It is.
'And if what we said is true, isn't he wedded to an image of pleasure that, measured by truth, is third removed from the oligarch's?'
And the oligarch in turn stands third from the king, if we count kingly and aristocratic as one.
'He is.'
Third, yes.
'And the oligarch in turn is third from the kingly man, if we count the kingly and the aristocratic as one.'
So the tyrant is removed from true pleasure, I said, by a number that is three times three.
'Third, yes.'
Apparently.
