'So the tyrant stands from true pleasure at a distance of a number that is three times three.'
Then the phantom of tyrannical pleasure, taken by the number of its length, is a plane figure.
'Plainly.'
Quite.
'Now the shadow of the tyrant's pleasure, going by its length, seems to come out as a plane figure, the number three times three.'
But take the square, and then the cube, and it becomes plain how great the distance is that separates them.
'Just so.'
Plain, at least, he said, to a man who can calculate.
'And by squaring and cubing it, it becomes clear how great the distance is.'

Then turn it around: if you want to say how far the king stands from the tyrant in truth of pleasure, finish the multiplication and you will find the king lives seven hundred and twenty-nine times more pleasantly, and the tyrant, by the same interval, more painfully.
'Clear to anyone who can do the arithmetic,' he said.
You have poured out a prodigious calculation, he said, of the distance between the two men — the just and the unjust — in pleasure and pain!

'And turning it around, if you ask how far the king stands from the tyrant in truth of pleasure, you'll find, once the multiplication is finished, that he lives seven hundred and twenty-nine times more pleasantly, while the tyrant lives that much more painfully.'
And yet the number is true, I said, and it fits human lives too — if days and nights and months and years fit human lives. (729 is close to the number of days and nights in a year.)
'What an extraordinary calculation,' he said, 'for the difference between the two men, the just and the unjust, in pleasure and in pain.'
They certainly do fit.

'And yet it's a true number,' I said, 'and one that fits human life closely, if human life is measured out in days and nights and months and years.' (Seven hundred and twenty-nine is nearly the number of days and nights in a year.)
Then if the good and just man beats the bad and unjust man by that much in pleasure, how incalculably further will he outstrip him in grace of life, in beauty, in virtue?
'It certainly is measured that way,' he said.
Incalculably indeed, he said.
'Then if the good and just man surpasses the bad and unjust man by this much in pleasure, won't he surpass him beyond all measure in the grace of his life, in beauty, and in virtue?'

Good, I said. And now that we have come this far in the argument, let us go back to the claims that started it. Wasn’t it said that injustice pays for the completely unjust man who is reputed to be just?
'By all means, beyond all measure,' he said.
It was.

'Good,' I said. 'And now that we've reached this point in the argument, let's go back to what was said at the start, the thing that brought us here. Wasn't it claimed that injustice pays for the man who is perfectly unjust but is thought to be just?'
Now, then, is the moment to have a word with the man who says so — now that we have settled what doing injustice and doing justice each accomplish.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's what was claimed.'
What shall we say to him?
'Then now that we've settled what justice and injustice each can do, let's have a word with the man who said it.'
Let us mold an image of the soul in words, so that the man who says such things can see what he is actually saying.
'What shall we say to him?'
What kind of image?
'Let's mold an image of the soul in words, so he can see what his own claim really comes to.'
One like those natures the old myths tell of, I said — the Chimera, Scylla, Cerberus, and all the others where many shapes are said to have grown together into one.
'What kind of image?'
So the stories go.
'One of those creatures the old stories tell of,' I said, 'like the Chimera, or Scylla, or Cerberus, where many different natures are said to have grown together into one.'
Then mold a single creature: a beast of many colors and many heads, wearing a ring of heads of animals tame and wild, able to change them and sprout new ones out of itself at will.
'Yes,' he said, 'there are such stories.'
That would take a clever sculptor, he said. Still — since words are easier to shape than wax, consider it molded.
'Then mold one form of a many-colored, many-headed beast, ringed all around with the heads of animals tame and wild, able to grow them and change them out of itself at will.'
Now a second form, a lion; and a third, a man. Make the first by far the biggest, and the second next.
'That takes a skilled craftsman,' he said. 'But since words are more easily molded than wax and the like, take it as molded.'
That’s easier, he said. Done.
'Now mold a second form, of a lion, and a third, of a man. Make the first by far the biggest, the second smaller.'
Now join the three into one, so that they somehow grow together.
'That's easier,' he said. 'It's done.'
Joined.
'Now join the three into one, so they grow together.'
And around the outside of them mold the likeness of one of the three — the man — so that anyone who cannot see inside, who sees only the outer shell, takes it for a single animal: a human being.
'They're joined,' he said.
It is molded.
'Then mold around the outside of them the single shape of a man, so that to anyone who can't see what's inside and sees only the outer shell, it looks like one creature, a human being.'

Now, to the man who says it pays this creature to do injustice, and that doing justice brings no advantage, let us say: he is claiming nothing more than that it pays the creature to feast the many-formed beast and make it strong, and the lion and everything lion along with it, while starving the man inside and weakening him, until the other two drag him wherever either of them pleases — and never to get any of them used to the others or make them friends, but to leave them to bite and fight and devour one another.
'It's done,' he said.
That, he said, is exactly what the praiser of injustice is saying.

'Now, to the man who says it pays this creature to be unjust and does it no good to be just, let's reply that he's simply saying it pays him to feed and strengthen the many-headed beast and the lion and all that's lion-like in him, but to starve the man inside and leave him so weak that he's dragged wherever the other two lead, and never to get the parts used to one another or on good terms, but to leave them to bite and fight and devour each other.'

And the one who says justice pays is saying that a man should do and say only what will give the man inside the fullest mastery over the whole human creature — that he should tend the many-headed beast like a farmer, feeding and taming the gentle heads and blocking the growth of the wild ones, making the lion’s nature his ally, and, caring for all of them in common, bring them up to be friends with one another and with himself.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's exactly what the man who praises injustice is saying.'
Yes — that is exactly what the defender of justice means.

'While the one who says justice pays would answer that we should so speak and act as to give the inner man the firmest possible control over the whole human creature. He should tend the many-headed beast like a farmer, raising and taming its gentle heads and checking the growth of the wild ones, and he should make the lion's nature his ally, so that, caring for them all in common, he keeps them friends with one another and with himself.'

From every angle, then, the man who praises justice speaks the truth, and the man who praises injustice speaks falsely. Judge it by pleasure, by reputation, by advantage: the praiser of justice is right, and the fault-finder has nothing sound to say — he doesn’t even know what it is he is condemning.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's just what the man who praises justice means.'
Nothing sound at all, I’d say.

'So from every side the man who praises justice speaks the truth, and the man who praises injustice speaks falsely. Whether you look to pleasure, or to reputation, or to advantage, the one who approves of justice is right and the one who condemns it is wrong and knows nothing of what he's condemning.'

Then let us persuade him gently — he isn’t wrong on purpose — and ask him: ‘Friend, wouldn’t we say this is what the customary standards of noble and shameful come from? The noble is what brings the beast in our nature under the human — or better, perhaps, under the divine; the shameful is what enslaves the tame in us to the wild.’ Will he agree, or not?
'He knows nothing at all,' he said.
He will, if he takes my advice.

'Then let's gently bring him round, since he goes wrong without meaning to. Let's ask him, "My friend, isn't this how the customs of the noble and the base have come about, that the noble are whatever subjects the brutish parts of our nature to the human, or rather perhaps to the divine, while the base are whatever enslaves the gentle part to the wild?" Won't he agree? Or what do you think?'

Then on this argument, can it pay any man to take gold unjustly, when it works out like this: in the act of taking the gold, he hands the best part of himself into slavery under the worst? If it would pay no one to sell a son or a daughter into slavery for gold — and slavery under savage, evil men at that — no matter how enormous the price, then what happens when a man enslaves the most divine thing in him to the most godless and polluted thing, and feels no pity for it? Isn’t he wretched — bribed with gold toward a ruin more terrible than Eriphyle’s, when she took the necklace as the price of her husband’s life?
'He'll agree, if he takes my advice,' he said.
Far more terrible, said Glaucon — I’ll answer for him.

'And on this showing,' I said, 'could it ever pay a man to take gold unjustly, if by taking it he enslaves the best part of himself to the worst? If a man took money to hand his son or daughter into slavery, into the hands of cruel and wicked masters, no sum could make that a good bargain. And if he remorselessly enslaves the most divine part of himself to the most godless and polluted, isn't he wretched, and isn't the gold a far more terrible bribe than the necklace Eriphyle took to betray her husband?'
And why do you think self-indulgence has been condemned from the old days? Because in such a man that terrible thing — the great, many-formed beast — is let loose further than it should be.
'Far more terrible,' said Glaucon. 'I'll answer for him.'
Clearly.
'And don't you think this is why the loose-living man has long been blamed, because in him that huge and many-formed beast is given too much freedom?'
And willfulness and bad temper are condemned when the lion-and-snake part of us grows and strains out of all proportion?
'Clearly,' he said.
Certainly.
'And why men blame stubbornness and bad temper, because the lion and the serpent in us are stretched and strengthened out of all proportion?'
And luxury and softness are condemned because they slacken and unstring that same part, and breed cowardice in it?
'Just so.'
Of course.
'And why luxury and softness are blamed, because they slacken and loosen this same part until they make a coward of it?'

And flattery and servility, when a man puts this same spirited part under the mob of a beast, and for the sake of money and the beast’s bottomless appetite trains the lion, from youth up, to take abuse — until it becomes a monkey instead of a lion?
'Of course.'
Just so.

'And why flattery and meanness are blamed, when a man puts his spirited part under the unruly beast and, for the sake of money and the beast's endless greed, trains it from youth up to be a monkey instead of a lion?'

And why do you think menial and manual work carries a stigma? Shall we say it is only this: when the best part in a man is naturally so weak that it cannot rule the creatures inside him, but has to wait on them instead, and can learn nothing except how to flatter them?
'Very much so,' he said.
It seems so, he said.

'And why do you think working at a low trade carries a kind of reproach? Isn't it just because, in such a man, the best part is naturally so weak that it can't rule the beasts within him but can only serve them and learn how to flatter them?'

Then in order that such a man may be ruled the way the best man is ruled, we say he ought to be the servant of that best man — the man with the divine ruler inside him. Not that the servant should be ruled to his own harm, as Thrasymachus thought about the ruled; but because it is better for everyone to be ruled by what is divine and intelligent — best of all by his own, living inside him; failing that, set over him from outside — so that as far as possible we may all be alike, and all friends, steered by the same pilot.
'It seems so,' he said.
Yes, he said — and rightly.

'So if we want such a man to be ruled by something like what rules the best man, we say he ought to be the slave of that best man, in whom the divine rules. Not, as Thrasymachus thought about the ruled, that this is to the slave's harm. It's better for everyone to be ruled by the divine and wise, best of all by something divine within himself, but if not that, then by something set over him from outside, so that, as far as possible, we may all be alike and friends, all steered by the same thing.'

And the law shows the same intention — the law that is every citizen’s ally. So does our rule over children: we do not allow them to be free until we have set up a constitution inside them, as inside a city — until, by tending the best in them with the best in us, we have installed in the child a guardian and ruler like our own. Then, and only then, we let them go free.
'And rightly so,' he said.
Yes — that is what the law shows.

'This is plainly what the law intends, too, the law that stands ally to everyone in the city. It's plain in our rule over children, in not letting them be free until we've set up a constitution in them, as in a city, and by tending the best part in them have set up in its place a guardian and ruler like our own in ourselves. Only then do we let them go free.'

On what ground, then, Glaucon, and by what argument, can we say it pays a man to be unjust or self-indulgent or to do anything shameful that makes him a worse man, even if it brings him more money or more power?
'Yes,' he said, 'that's plain.'
On no ground at all.

'On what ground, then, Glaucon, and by what argument can we say it pays a man to be unjust, or self-indulgent, or to do anything shameful that makes him a worse man, even if he gets money or power out of it?'

And how can it pay to do injustice and escape — to go unpunished? Doesn’t the man who escapes simply become worse? While in the man who is caught and punished, the beast in him is calmed and tamed and the gentle part set free; the whole soul, restored toward its best nature, wins temperance and justice together with understanding — a condition more precious to it than strength and beauty and health are to the body, exactly as the soul is more precious than the body.
'On no ground at all,' he said.
Absolutely.

'And how can it pay him to do injustice and not be caught and punished? The man who gets away with it only grows worse, while in the one who's caught and punished the brutish part is calmed and tamed, the gentle part is set free, and his whole soul, settling into its best nature, gains something more precious in gaining self-control and justice along with wisdom than the body gains in gaining strength and beauty and health, as much more as the soul is more precious than the body.'
Then a man with any sense will bend every effort of his life toward this end. First, he will honor the studies that shape his soul this way, and despise the rest.
'Without any doubt,' he said.
Clearly.
'Then the man of sense will bend all his life to this. First, he'll prize the studies that shape his soul this way, and think little of the rest.'

Next, I said, his bodily condition and training: he will not hand them over to beastly, irrational pleasure and point his life that way. He won’t even make health his object — won’t rank being strong or healthy or handsome as things that matter — unless temperance comes with them. You will find him always tuning the harmony of his body for the sake of the concord in his soul.
'Clearly,' he said.
He certainly will, if he means to be truly musical.

'Next, when it comes to the condition and care of his body, he won't hand himself over to brutish, unreasoning pleasure and aim his life that way. He won't even make health his chief concern, or count it the great thing to be strong or healthy or handsome, unless these bring temperance with them. He'll always be found tuning his body to keep the harmony in his soul.'
And in acquiring money, the same order and concord? He won’t be dazzled by what the crowd congratulates itself on, and pile up wealth without limit, and bring limitless troubles on himself.
'Yes,' he said, 'if he's to be truly in tune.'
I think not.
'And in getting and spending money he'll keep the same order and harmony. He won't be carried away by the crowd's idea of happiness and pile up endless wealth, with endless trouble for himself.'

He will keep his eye instead on the constitution inside him, I said, and stand guard against disturbing anything there through having too much or too little; steering by that, he will add to his wealth, or spend it, as far as he is able.
'I think not,' he said.
Exactly so.

'He'll keep his eye on the constitution within him,' I said, 'and guard against disturbing anything there, whether by having too much property or too little. On that principle he'll govern what he has, adding to it or spending it as best he can.'

And honors — the same rule. He will taste, even gladly, the ones he judges will make him better; but the ones he thinks would break down his settled condition he will avoid, in private and in public alike.
'Just so.'
Then if that is what he cares about, he said, he won’t be willing to enter politics.

'And with honors, too, the same. He'll gladly take and enjoy the ones he thinks will make him a better man, but the ones he thinks would upset the order in him, in private or in public life, he'll avoid.'
By the dog, I said, he will — very much so, in his own city. Though perhaps not in the city of his birth, unless some divine stroke of luck intervenes.
'Then if that's his care,' he said, 'he won't be willing to go into politics.'
I understand, he said. You mean the city we have just founded and described — the one that exists in words. I don’t think it exists anywhere on earth.
'By the dog,' I said, 'in his own city he certainly will, though perhaps not in the city of his birth, unless some divine luck should bring it about.'

But perhaps, I said, there is a pattern of it laid up in heaven for the man who wants to see it — and, seeing it, to found that city in himself. Whether it exists anywhere, or ever will, makes no difference. He will act in the politics of that city, and of no other.
'I understand,' he said. 'You mean he'll take part in the city we've been founding, the one that exists only in our words. For I don't think it exists anywhere on earth.'
Most likely, he said.

'But perhaps,' I said, 'there's a pattern of it laid up in heaven, for anyone who wants to look and, looking, to found himself. It makes no difference whether it exists now or ever will. This is the only city in whose politics he could take part, and no other.'
'That seems right,' he said.
spine.label: Book X
spine.title: Poetry and the Myth of Er
Poetry, the Immortal Soul, and the Myth of Er
spine.text: And really, I said, among the many things about our city that convince me we built it right, none pleases me more, when I think it over, than our rule about poetry.
'There are many things about the way we've ordered our city that please me,' I said, 'but the one I think about most, when I look back, is what we decided about poetry.'
Which rule do you mean?
'What do you mean?' he asked.
Refusing to admit any poetry that works by imitation. Now that we have distinguished the parts of the soul, I see more clearly than ever that such poetry must not be let in.
'That we refused to admit any of the part of it that works by imitation. Now that we've distinguished the different parts of the soul, it seems clearer than ever that this was exactly right.'
What do you mean?
'How so?'

Between ourselves — you won't report me to the tragedians and the rest of the imitative tribe — all that kind of thing seems to me to maim the minds of those who hear it, unless they carry the antidote: knowing what it actually is.

'Between ourselves,' I said, 'and don't go repeating this to the tragedians and the rest of that imitative crowd, all such poetry seems to me to cripple the minds of those who listen to it, unless they have the antidote, which is knowing what these things really are.'
What are you thinking of?
'Tell me what you're getting at.'

I'll tell you, I said, though a certain love and reverence for Homer, which I have carried since I was a boy, makes the words stick in my throat. He seems to have been the first teacher and captain of this whole splendid tragic company. But no man is to be honored above the truth. So I'll say it.

'I will, though there's a love and reverence for Homer I've had since I was a boy, and even now it almost ties my tongue. He is, after all, the first teacher and the captain of that whole noble company of tragic poets. But no man should be honored ahead of the truth, so I'll say what I have to say.'
By all means, he said.
'Go on,' he said.
Then listen — or better, answer.
'Then listen, or rather, answer me.'
Ask away.
'Ask away.'
Can you tell me what imitation is, altogether? I don't entirely grasp it myself — what it's supposed to be.
'Can you tell me what imitation is, in general? Because I'm honestly not sure myself.'
Then what chance, he said, do I have of grasping it?
'And I'm supposed to know, when you don't?'
None too strange a thing. Dim eyes often spot what sharp ones miss.
'There'd be nothing strange in that,' I said. 'A duller eye often spots a thing before a sharper one does.'
So they do, he said. But with you here I couldn't bring myself to speak up, even if I did see something. Look for yourself.
'That's so,' he said, 'but with you here, even if I had some glimmer of an idea, I wouldn't have the nerve to say it. You do the looking.'
Then shall we start our inquiry the usual way? Our practice, you remember, is to posit a single form for each set of many things that we call by the same name. Do you follow me?
'All right then, let's begin the way we usually do. Whenever a number of things share a single name, we suppose there's also a single form, or idea, that goes with them. Do you follow me?'
I do.
'I do.'
Then take any example you like. There are many beds in the world, and many tables — plenty of them, no?
'Then take any example you like. There are plenty of beds and tables in the world, aren't there?'
Yes.
'Of course.'
But only two forms for them — one form of the bed, one of the table.
'But there are only two forms behind them, one of a bed and one of a table.'
True.
'Yes.'

And we usually say that the craftsman who makes either one looks toward the form while he makes the beds or tables we use, and the same with everything else. For no craftsman makes the form itself. How could he?

'And we say that the craftsman who makes either of them looks to the form when he makes the bed or table we use. That's how we talk about it. No craftsman, after all, makes the form itself. How could he?'
He couldn't.
'He couldn't.'
Now consider another kind of maker, and tell me what you would call him.
'Now there's another kind of craftsman I'd like to ask you about.'
Who is he?
'Who's that?'
The one who makes everything — every single thing that each of the other craftsmen makes separately.
'One who makes everything that every other craftsman makes.'
That's a formidable, marvelous man you're describing.
'What an extraordinary man!'

Wait — you'll say so with better reason in a moment. This same craftsman can make not only furniture of every kind but everything that grows from the earth; he produces every living thing, himself included; and on top of that he makes earth and sky and the gods, everything in heaven and everything under the earth.

'Wait, you'll have even more reason to say so. This same craftsman can make not only every kind of furniture, but every plant that grows and every animal, including himself; and on top of that the earth and the sky and the gods, and everything in the heavens and everything in the world below.'
An utterly amazing wizard, he said.
'He must be some kind of wizard.'

You don't believe me? Tell me — do you think there is no such maker at all, or that in one sense a person could make all these things, and in another sense not? Don't you see that there is a way you could make them all yourself?

'You don't believe me?' I said. 'Tell me, do you think there's simply no such maker at all, or that in one sense there could be a maker of all these things, and in another sense not? Don't you see that there's a way in which you yourself could make every one of them?'
What way?
'What way?'

An easy one — or rather many, and quick. Quickest of all: take a mirror and carry it around with you everywhere. In no time you'll make the sun and everything in the sky, the earth, yourself, the other animals and plants and furniture — everything we were just talking about.

'An easy one,' I said. 'In fact there are several ways to bring it off quickly, but none quicker than taking a mirror and turning it this way and that. In no time you'll have made the sun and the heavens, the earth, yourself, and all the animals and plants and everything else we were just talking about.'
Yes, he said — appearances, though nothing that really is.
'Yes,' he said, 'but they'd only be appearances, not real things.'
Good, I said — you've come straight to the point. For the painter, I take it, is another maker of just this kind. Isn't he?
'Exactly right,' I said. 'Now you're getting to the heart of it. And the painter, I take it, is another maker of just this kind, isn't he?'
Of course.
'Certainly.'
But you'll say, I suppose, that what he makes isn't real. And yet in a certain way the painter, too, makes a bed. Doesn't he?
'You'll say, I suppose, that what he makes isn't real. And yet in a way the painter does make a bed too, doesn't he?'
Yes, he said — the appearance of one.
'Yes,' he said, 'but not a real bed.'
And what about the carpenter? Weren't you just saying that he doesn't make the form — which is what we say a bed really is — but only a particular bed?
'And what about the carpenter who makes the bed? Weren't you saying a moment ago that he too makes not the form, which on our view is what a bed really is, but only some particular bed?'
I was.
'I was.'

Then if he doesn't make what a bed is, he isn't making the real thing — only something like the real thing, which isn't quite it. So if anyone claimed that the work of the carpenter, or of any other craftsman, is completely real, he would probably not be telling the truth.

'Then if what he makes isn't the thing that truly is, he isn't making something that truly is, but only something that resembles it, something that is, without quite being. And if anyone claimed that the work of the carpenter, or of any other craftsman, fully and truly exists, he'd be wrong, wouldn't he?'
So it would seem, he said — at least to people who spend their time on arguments like ours.
'At least,' he said, 'anyone used to arguments like ours would say so.'
Then we shouldn't be surprised if the carpenter's bed, too, turns out to be a dim thing next to the truth.
'No wonder, then, that even the carpenter's bed is only a dim, secondhand version of the truth.'
No.
'No wonder.'
Then shall we use these examples to hunt down what this imitator really is?
'So, with these examples in front of us, suppose we ask who exactly this imitator is.'
If you like.
'Go ahead.'
We have three beds, then. One exists in nature — the bed itself — and I suppose we would say the god made it. Who else could?
'We have three beds, then. One exists in nature, and we'd say, I think, that a god made it, for who else could?'
No one.
'No one.'
A second is the work of the carpenter.
'A second is the one the carpenter makes.'
Yes.
'Yes.'
And the painter's is a third?
'And a third is the one the painter makes.'
Yes.
'Yes.'
So three beds, and three masters set over them: the god, the carpenter, the painter.
'So there are three sorts of beds, and three makers in charge of them: the god, the carpenter, and the painter.'
Yes — three.
'Yes, three.'
Now the god, whether by choice or because some necessity was on him, made only that one bed in nature — the one that is what a bed is. Two such beds, or more, he never produced and never will.
'Now the god, whether he chose to or had no other choice, made just one bed in nature, and only one. Two or more such beds the god never made and never will.'
Why not?
'Why is that?'
Because if he made even two, a third would show up behind them — the one whose form both of the others would share — and that one, not the two, would be what a bed is.
'Because even if he'd made only two, a third would show up behind them, the one whose form they'd both share, and that third would be the real bed, not the other two.'
Right, he said.
'True,' he said.
The god knew this, I think, and wanting to be the real maker of the real bed — not some carpenter making some bed — he made it one in nature, and one only.
'The god knew this, I think, and since he wanted to be the maker of a bed that really is a bed, and not just some maker of some particular bed, he made the one that by its own nature is single.'
So it seems.
'So it seems.'
Shall we call him, then, its maker in nature — something like that?
'Shall we call him the natural maker of the bed, then, or something like that?'
That would be just, he said, since by nature he has made this and everything else.
'That would be fair,' he said, 'since by nature he made this and everything else.'
And the carpenter? Shall we call him the craftsman of a bed?
'And the carpenter? Shall we call him the maker of the bed?'
Yes.
'Yes.'
And the painter — is he a craftsman and maker of a bed too?
'But would you call the painter its maker, the one who fashions it?'
Not at all.
'Certainly not.'
Then what will you say he is, in relation to the bed?
'Then what is he, in relation to the bed?'
The fairest name for him, I think, he said, is imitator — an imitator of what the others make.
'I think,' he said, 'the fairest thing to call him is the imitator of what the others make.'
Very well, I said. So the man whose product stands third from nature — him you call an imitator?
'Good,' I said. 'So the one who is third in line from nature, you call an imitator?'
Exactly, he said.
'Just so.'
Then the tragedian too, if he is an imitator, will be someone third in line from the king and from the truth — and so will every other imitator.
'Then the tragic poet, since he's an imitator too, is like all the rest of them: three removes from the king and from the truth.'
It looks that way.
'It looks that way.'
Then we are agreed about the imitator. Now tell me this about the painter. Do you think he tries to imitate the thing itself, there in nature — or the works of the craftsmen?
'So we're agreed about the imitator. But now tell me about the painter. Do you think he tries to imitate the thing as it is in nature, or only the works that craftsmen make?'
The works of the craftsmen.
'Only the works of craftsmen.'
As they are, or as they appear? Draw that distinction too.
'As they are, or as they appear? You still have to settle that.'
How do you mean?
'What do you mean?'
This: a bed, looked at from the side, or head-on, or from any angle you like, doesn't differ from itself at all — it only appears different. And so with everything else.

'I mean this: look at a bed from the side, or straight on, or from any angle at all, and the bed looks different each time, though it doesn't actually become any different. And the same goes for everything else.'
Just so, he said. It appears different, but isn't.
'That's right,' he said. 'It looks different without being different.'
Then consider this very point. What is painting aimed at, in each case — imitating what is, as it is, or imitating what appears, as it appears? Is it imitation of appearance, or of truth?
'Then here's my question. When the painter paints, is he setting out to reproduce the thing as it is, or as it appears? Is his imitation of the appearance, or of the reality?'
Of appearance, he said.
'Of the appearance.'

So the art of imitation is a long way from the truth. And that, it seems, is how it can make everything — because it touches only a small part of each thing, and that part an image. The painter, we say, will paint us a cobbler, a carpenter, any craftsman at all, though he understands nothing of their crafts; and yet, if he is a good painter, he might paint a carpenter, show it from a distance, and fool children and foolish men into thinking it is a real carpenter.

'Then imitation is a long way from the truth,' I said. 'And the reason it can reproduce anything and everything is that it gets hold of only a little of each thing, and even that little is just an image. Take the painter. He'll paint us a cobbler, a carpenter, any craftsman you like, though he knows nothing of any of their trades. Still, if he's a good painter, he can fool children and simple people by showing them a painted carpenter from a distance, so that they take it for a real one.'
Of course.
'No doubt.'

Then here, my friend, is how we should think about all such cases. When someone tells us he has met a man who knows every craft, and everything else that anyone knows, each thing more precisely than anybody else — the only answer to give is that he is a simple fellow. It seems he has run into some wizard or impersonator and been taken in, and thought the man all-wise because he himself cannot tell knowledge from ignorance from imitation.

'And whenever somebody tells us he's met a man who knows every trade, and indeed everything else there is to know, each thing more exactly than any specialist, we should suspect that he's a simpleton who has run into some sorcerer or impersonator and been taken in, so that the man struck him as all-knowing, only because he himself couldn't tell knowledge from ignorance from mere imitation.'
Absolutely true, he said.
'Very true.'

Then next, I said, we have to examine tragedy and its captain, Homer — since some people tell us these poets know every craft, everything human that touches on virtue and vice, and everything divine besides. A good poet, they say, must know his subject if he is to compose about it well, or he could not compose at all. So we must ask whether these people have run into imitators and been fooled — whether, looking at the poets' works, they fail to notice that these stand at the third remove from what is, and are easy to make without any knowledge of the truth, since they are appearances and not realities. Or is there something in what they say, and do good poets really know the things the crowd thinks they describe so well?

'So when people tell us that the tragic poets, and Homer at their head, know all the crafts and all human affairs, virtue and vice and the things of the gods besides, on the grounds that a good poet can't write well about his subject without knowing it, we should ask ourselves whether these people too haven't been taken in. Maybe they've run into imitators and been fooled, and when they looked at the work they failed to notice that it was three removes from what truly is, and easy to make without any knowledge of the truth, since it's only an appearance and not the reality. Or are they right, after all, and do the good poets really know the things they seem, to most people, to speak about so well?'
We certainly have to examine it, he said.
'That's certainly worth looking into,' he said.

Do you think, then, that if a man could make both — the thing imitated and the image — he would seriously give himself over to crafting images, and set that up as the best thing in his life, as if he had nothing better in him?

'Now do you suppose that if a man could actually make the real thing, and not just the image of it, he would devote himself in earnest to making images? Would he let imitation rule his life as if he had nothing better in him?'
I do not.
'I wouldn't think so.'

If he truly understood the things he imitates, I imagine he would put his effort into deeds rather than imitations of them. He would try to leave behind many fine works as memorials of himself, and would rather be the man praised than the man writing the praise.

'No. A man who really knew the things he was imitating would put his heart into the things themselves, not into the imitations. He'd want to leave behind him many fine deeds as monuments, and he'd rather be the one praised than the one writing the praises.'
I should think so, he said. The honor and the profit are of a different order.
'Yes,' he said, 'there'd be far more honor and benefit in that.'

Then let's not demand an account from Homer or the other poets on most subjects. Let's not ask whether any of them was really a doctor, rather than an imitator of the way doctors talk — whether any poet, old or new, is said to have healed the sick as Asclepius did, or to have left behind students of medicine as he left his sons. Let's not press them about the other crafts either; let those go. But about the greatest and finest things Homer undertakes to speak of — wars, generalship, the founding of cities, the education of a man — about these it is surely fair to question him. 'Dear Homer,' we'll say, 'if you are not third from the truth about virtue, a maker of images — what we defined as an imitator — but even second, and able to tell which pursuits make men better or worse in private and public life, then name one city that was governed better because of you. Sparta has Lycurgus; many cities, great and small, have their own men. Italy and Sicily name Charondas, and we name Solon. Who names you?' Will he have any city to name?

'Well then,' I said, 'there are some things we won't bother asking Homer about, like medicine, or any of the crafts his poems only touch on in passing. We won't ask whether he cured anyone, as Asclepius did, or left behind a school of healers as the sons of Asclepius did, or whether he just talks about medicine and the other crafts at secondhand. But on the greatest and finest subjects he takes up, war and the command of armies, the running of cities, the education of a man, on these we have every right to question him. "Homer, my friend," we'll say, "if when it comes to virtue you really are not at the third remove from the truth, a mere maker of images, but at the second, and you can see what makes men better or worse in private and in public life, then tell us: which city was ever better governed thanks to you? Sparta has Lycurgus to thank for its good order, and many other cities, large and small, owe theirs to others. But who credits you with being a good lawgiver, who says you ever did them any good? Italy and Sicily boast of Charondas, and we have our Solon. But who has anything of the kind to say about you?"' Could he name a single city?
I think not, said Glaucon. Even the Homeridae themselves claim nothing of the sort.
'I don't think so,' said Glaucon. 'Even his own admirers, the Homerids, don't claim he was a lawgiver.'
Well, is any war in Homer's day remembered as being won under his command, or by his counsel?
'Well then, is there any war we're told he won, or helped to win with his advice, in his own lifetime?'
None.
'None.'
Then is he credited with many ingenious inventions for the crafts or for practical life, the way a man wise in his works would be — like Thales of Miletus or Anacharsis the Scythian?
'Or is there some invention of his, some clever device useful in the crafts or in daily life, the way we hear of Thales of Miletus or Anacharsis the Scythian and other ingenious men?'
Nothing of the kind at all.
'Nothing whatsoever of that kind.'

Then if there is no public service, is Homer said to have been a guide in private to any men who loved his company in his lifetime and handed down a Homeric way of life to those who came after — the way Pythagoras was loved for exactly that, and his followers even now call their way of life Pythagorean and seem set apart by it?

'Well, if he did no public service, was he at least, in his private life, a guide and teacher to anyone? Did he have, while he lived, companions who loved his company and handed down to later generations a Homeric way of life, the way Pythagoras was so deeply loved for his wisdom, and his followers to this day are famous for the way of living that still bears his name?'

No, nothing like that is told of him, Socrates. Homer's own companion Creophylus — the name means something like 'son of the Meat-clan,' and people laugh at it — would look even more ridiculous for his education than for his name, if the stories about Homer are true. They say Creophylus barely took notice of Homer while the man was alive.

'No, nothing like that is recorded of him,' he said. 'In fact, Socrates, Homer's companion Creophylus would look even more ridiculous than his name already makes us laugh, the "child of the meat-tribe," if the stories are true that Homer was badly neglected by him and the rest in his own lifetime.'

That is the tradition, I said. But Glaucon, if Homer had really been able to educate men and make them better — if he had genuine knowledge of these things and not just a power of imitating them — do you think he wouldn't have made many companions, who honored and loved him? Look at Protagoras of Abdera and Prodicus of Ceos and the rest: each of them can convince the men of his day, in private conversation, that they will never manage their house or their city unless he supervises their education — and for this wisdom they are loved so fiercely that their students all but carry them around on their shoulders. If Homer or Hesiod had really been able to help men toward virtue, would their contemporaries have let them wander from town to town reciting? Wouldn't they have held onto them harder than onto gold, and forced them to stay home? And if the masters wouldn't stay, wouldn't the disciples have followed them anywhere, until they had gotten education enough?

'Yes,' I said, 'so the tradition goes. But can you imagine, Glaucon, that if Homer had really been able to educate people and make them better, if he'd had knowledge of these things and not just been an imitator of them, he wouldn't have gathered crowds of followers who honored and loved him? Look at Protagoras of Abdera and Prodicus of Ceos and all the rest. They have only to whisper to their pupils that they'll never manage their own households or their cities until they put themselves under their teaching, and they're loved for this so much that their companions all but carry them about on their shoulders. So are we to believe that the people of Homer's day, or of Hesiod's, would have let them wander about reciting poems for a living, if they had really been able to make men more virtuous? Wouldn't they have clung to them harder than to gold, and made them stay home? Or if the master wouldn't stay, wouldn't the students have trailed after him wherever he went until they'd gotten their fill of his teaching?'
Socrates, he said, I think that is exactly true.
'I think that's quite true, Socrates,' he said.

Then shall we settle it: all the poets, beginning with Homer, are imitators of images — of virtue and of everything else they write about — and they never touch the truth. As we were just saying, the painter will make what passes for a cobbler, though he knows nothing of cobbling, for viewers who know nothing of it either and judge by colors and shapes.

'So mustn't we conclude that all these poets, beginning with Homer, are only imitators? They copy images of virtue and the other things they write about, but they never reach the truth itself. It's just as we said: the poet is like a painter who can produce the likeness of a cobbler though he knows nothing about cobbling, a likeness good enough for people who know no more than he does and judge only by shapes and colors.'
Quite so.
'Exactly.'

In the same way, I suppose, the poet lays down colors of a sort — his words and phrases — over each of the crafts, understanding nothing of them except how to imitate; so that to others like him, who see things only through language, his talk of cobbling or generalship or anything else seems very fine, as long as it comes with meter and rhythm and melody. That is how strong an enchantment these things carry by nature. Strip the poets' works of their musical coloring and say them plain, and you know how they look — you have surely seen it.

'In the same way, I'd say, the poet uses words and phrases to lay on the colors of each of the crafts, though he understands no more than how to imitate them. And other people, just as ignorant as he is, judging only by his words, think he speaks beautifully whenever he talks about cobbling or commanding an army or anything else in meter and rhythm and harmony, so natural is the charm these things have. You must have noticed, I think, what poets' tales look like when they're stripped of their musical coloring and said in plain prose. You've seen what becomes of them.'
I have, he said.
'I have,' he said.
Like the faces of the young who were never beautiful, only fresh — once the bloom has left them.
'They're like the faces of young people who were never really beautiful but only fresh, once that first bloom has left them.'
Exactly.
'Exactly.'
Then come, consider this. The maker of the image — the imitator, we say — understands nothing of what is, only of what appears. True?
'Here's another point. The imitator, the maker of the image, knows nothing of what truly is, only of how things appear. Isn't that so?'
Yes.
'Yes.'
Then let's not leave the point half-made; let's see it whole.
'Then let's get this fully clear and not leave it half-explained.'
Go on.
'Go on.'
A painter, we say, will paint reins and a bit?
'The painter, we say, will paint reins and a bit.'
Yes.
'Yes.'
But it is the leatherworker and the smith who will make them.
'But it's the leatherworker and the metalworker who actually make them.'
Certainly.
'Of course.'
Then does the painter understand what the reins and the bit ought to be like? Even the makers hardly do — the smith and the leatherworker. Only the man who knows how to use them: the horseman.

'Now does the painter know the right form for the reins and bit? Come to that, do even the men who make them, the metalworker and the leatherworker, really know it? Doesn't the one who knows their right form turn out to be the horseman, the one who uses them?'
Very true.
'Very true.'
And won't we say it is the same with everything?
'And can't we say the same of everything?'
How?
'How do you mean?'
That for each thing there are three arts: one that will use it, one that will make it, one that will imitate it.
'That with anything there are three crafts: one that uses it, one that makes it, and one that imitates it.'
Yes.
'Yes.'
And the excellence, the beauty, the rightness of every implement and creature and action — don't they all come back to the use for which each was made, or for which nature made it?
'And the goodness, the beauty, the rightness of any object, living or made, or of any action, is measured by the use for which it was made or born.'
That is so.
'That's so.'

So it is an absolute necessity that the user of each thing has the most experience of it, and reports to the maker how his product performs, well or badly, in actual use. The flute player, for instance, tells the flute maker which flutes serve him in the playing; he prescribes how they should be made, and the maker obeys him.

'Then the one who uses a thing must be the one with the most experience of it, and he's the one to tell the maker how well or badly it performs in use. The flute-player, for instance, tells the flute-maker which of his flutes serve the player well, and lays down how they ought to be made, and the maker does as he's told.'
Of course.
'Of course.'
So the one has knowledge, and pronounces on good and bad flutes; the other trusts him, and makes them accordingly.
'So the user knows, and speaks with authority about which flutes are good and which bad, while the maker, taking the user on trust, ends up with a correct belief about them.'
Yes.
'True.'

So for one and the same instrument, the maker will have correct belief about its excellence and its faults — from keeping company with the one who knows, and having to listen to him — while the user has knowledge.

'It's the same instrument, but about its goodness or badness the maker can reach only a correct opinion, which he gets by talking with the one who knows and being made to listen to him, whereas the user has actual knowledge.'
Quite.
'Yes.'

And the imitator? Will he have knowledge, from use, of whether the things he paints are fine and right? Or correct opinion, from having to keep company with the one who knows and being told what he should paint?

'But the imitator, now, will he have either? Will he know, from using the thing, whether what he paints is right and good? Or will he even have a correct opinion, from being forced to keep company with the one who knows and to do as he's instructed?'
Neither.
'Neither.'
So the imitator will neither know nor rightly judge what he imitates — neither its excellence nor its faults.
'So the imitator will have neither knowledge nor even correct opinion about whether the things he imitates are good or bad.'
Apparently not.
'It seems not.'
A lovely position for the poetic imitator to be in — so wise about the things he makes.
'A fine state of understanding the imitator will be in, then, about the things he makes.'
Not exactly, he said.
'Hardly a fine one.'
And still he will imitate anyway, without knowing what makes each thing good or bad. What he will imitate, it seems, is whatever looks fine to the crowd — to people who know nothing.
'And still he'll go on imitating without knowing what makes each thing good or bad. He'll imitate, it seems, whatever strikes the ignorant crowd as beautiful.'
What else?
'What else can he do?'

So we are fairly agreed on this much: the imitator knows nothing worth mentioning about what he imitates; imitation is a kind of game, not serious work; and the tragic poets, whether they write in iambics or in epic lines, are imitators to the last degree.

'So far, then, we seem fairly agreed: the imitator has no knowledge worth mentioning of the things he imitates; imitation is a kind of game, not a serious thing; and those who write tragic poetry, in iambics or in epic verse, are imitators through and through.'
Very true.
'Quite so.'
Then tell me, in heaven's name: this business of imitating is concerned with something at the third remove from the truth. Isn't it?
'And now, in heaven's name, this imitation we've been talking about, isn't it concerned with what stands at the third remove from the truth?'
Yes.
'It is.'
And the power in a human being that it works on — what kind of thing is that?
'And which part of a person is it that imitation works on?'
What sort of power do you mean?
'What do you mean?'
This kind. The same object doesn't look the same size to the eye from close up as it does from far away.
'I'll explain. The same object looks one size up close and another size from far off, doesn't it?'
No, it doesn't.
'Yes.'

And the same things look bent in water and straight out of it, concave or convex as the eye is misled by colors — clearly there is every kind of confusion of this sort in our soul. It is this weakness in our nature that trick painting preys on, and conjuring, and every sleight of that family; nothing short of sorcery.

'And a straight stick looks bent when it's half in the water, and what's curved looks the other way, because of the trick the eye plays with colors. Clearly our soul is full of this kind of confusion. And it's just this weakness in our nature that scene-painting and conjuring and all those other clever tricks of light and shadow exploit, working on us like sorcery.'
True.
'True.'

And measuring, counting, and weighing have proved to be our most gracious helpers here — so that what rules in us is not the apparent bigger or smaller, the apparent more or heavier, but the part of us that has calculated, measured, weighed.

'But measuring and counting and weighing came to the rescue of just this weakness, and a fine thing they are. They make sure it isn't the apparent bigger or smaller, more or heavier, that rules us, but what has been counted and measured and weighed.'
Certainly.
'Certainly.'
And that is the work of the reasoning part of the soul.
'And this must be the work of the reasoning, calculating part of the soul.'
It is.
'It must.'
But often, when this part has measured, and reports that one thing is bigger or smaller than another, or equal to it, the same soul sees the opposite at the same moment about the same things.

'Yet often, when this part has done its measuring and reports that some things are bigger than others, or smaller, or equal, the very same things appear to it, at the same moment, to be the opposite.'
Yes.
'Yes.'
And didn't we say it is impossible for the same part to hold opposite judgments about the same things at the same time?
'But didn't we say it's impossible for the same part of us to hold contrary opinions about the same thing at the same time?'
We did, and rightly.
'We did, and rightly.'
Then the part of the soul that judges against the measurements cannot be the same as the part that judges with them.
'So the part of the soul whose opinion runs against the measurements can't be the same as the part whose opinion agrees with them.'
No.
'No, it can't.'
And the part that trusts measure and calculation would be the best part of the soul.
'And the part that trusts to measurement and calculation must be the best part of the soul.'
Of course.
'Certainly.'
Then what opposes it is one of the weak things in us.
'While the part that contradicts it is one of the inferior parts in us.'
Necessarily.
'It has to be.'

This is what I wanted agreed when I said that painting — and imitation as a whole — does its own work far from the truth, and keeps company with the part of us that is far from wisdom: a companionship and friendship with nothing healthy or true about it.

'This is exactly the conclusion I was driving at when I said that painting, and imitation generally, does its work far from the truth, and keeps company with the part of us that is far from intelligence, with nothing healthy or true to gain from the friendship.'
Exactly.
'Just so.'
So imitation is a poor thing that mates with a poor thing and breeds poor offspring.
'So imitation is a paltry thing that consorts with a paltry thing and breeds paltry offspring.'
So it seems.
'It seems so.'
Only the imitation we look at, I said? Or also the kind we listen to — the kind we call poetry?
'And does this apply only to what we see, or to what we hear as well, the thing we call poetry?'
Probably that too, he said.
'Presumably to hearing too.'
Well, let's not lean on 'probably' just because it matches painting. Let's go straight to the very part of the mind that poetic imitation keeps company with, and see whether it is trivial or serious.
'Let's not just rely on the likeness to painting,' I said. 'Let's go straight to the part of the mind that poetic imitation deals with, and see whether it's a worthless thing or a worthy one.'
Yes, we should.
'Yes, let's.'

Put it this way. Imitation, we say, imitates human beings in action — acting under compulsion or by choice, judging that they have done well or badly by how it turns out, and through it all feeling grief or joy. Was there anything beyond that?

'Put it this way. Imitation, we say, imitates people acting, whether under compulsion or of their own free will, who think they've done well or badly as a result, and who feel pain or pleasure accordingly. Is there anything more to it than that?'
Nothing.
'No, nothing.'

And in all of this, is a person of one mind with himself? Or, just as with sight — where he was divided, holding opposite judgments about the same things at the same moment — is he divided in his actions too, at war with himself? But actually I remember: we don't need to settle this now, because in the earlier arguments we settled it well enough — the soul is crowded with ten thousand oppositions of this kind, arising all at once.

'And through all of this, is a person at one with himself? Or, just as with sight there was conflict and he held contrary opinions about the same things at once, is there strife and self-contradiction here too, in how he acts? Though I needn't really raise the question again, since we settled all this earlier and agreed that the soul is full of countless contradictions of this kind, all occurring at the same moment.'
Rightly settled, he said.
'We were right to agree to it,' he said.
Rightly, I said. But what we left out then, I think we now have to work through.
'We were,' I said. 'But there's something we left out then which we need to add now.'
What did we leave out?
'What's that?'
A decent man, we said, who meets some misfortune — losing a son, or something else he holds most dear — will bear it more easily than other men.
'Didn't we say, somewhere back, that a good man who suffers some great loss, of a son, or of anything else he holds dearest, will bear it more easily than other people would?'
Certainly.
'We did.'
But now consider: will he feel no grief at all? Or, since that is impossible, will he keep some measure in his pain?
'But will he feel no grief at all? Or, since that's impossible, will he at least keep his grief within bounds?'
The second, he said, is nearer the truth.
'That's nearer the truth,' he said. 'He'll keep it in bounds.'
Then tell me this about him. Do you think he will fight the grief and resist it more when his equals can see him — or when he is alone with himself, in some empty place?
'Now tell me. Will he be more likely to fight down his grief and hold out against it when his equals are watching him, or when he's alone by himself?'
Far more when he is watched, he said.
'He'll hold out far better when he's being seen.'
Alone, I imagine, he will let himself say much that he would be ashamed to have heard, and do much that he would never let anyone see.
'But when he's alone, I imagine, he'll let himself say and do all sorts of things he'd be ashamed to have anyone hear or see.'
That is so.
'That's so.'
Now, what commands him to resist is reason and law; what drags him toward the grief is the suffering itself.
'And what bids him resist is reason and the law, while what drags him toward his grief is the suffering itself.'
True.
'True.'
And when opposite pulls arise in a man about the same thing at the same time, we say there must be two things in him.
'And when a man is pulled in two opposite directions at once over the same thing, we say there must be two distinct parts in him.'
Of course.
'Of course.'
One of them ready to obey the law wherever it leads?
'One of them ready to obey the law, wherever the law leads.'
How so?
'How do you mean?'

The law says, roughly, that it is finest to stay as calm as we can in misfortune and not cry out — because the good and evil in such things is not clear; because taking it hard gains nothing for the future; because nothing human deserves great seriousness; and because grief blocks the very thing we need to arrive quickest of all.

'The law tells him that it's finest to keep calm under misfortune as far as he can, and not to chafe against it. For one thing, you can never be sure such things are good or bad; for another, taking it hard gets you nowhere, and nothing in human affairs is worth that much earnestness; and grief, besides, blocks the very thing we need most at such a moment.'
What thing? he asked.
'And what is that?' he asked.

Deliberation, I said. We should think about what has happened, and — as at a throw of the dice — set our affairs against the way they have fallen, however reason picks out as best. Not like children who have taken a fall, clutching the hurt place and spending our time howling; we should train the soul to turn as fast as it can to healing and setting upright what fell and what sickened — letting medicine drive out lamentation.

'To take counsel about what's happened, and, as the dice have fallen, to arrange our affairs by the light of reason in whatever way seems best. We shouldn't behave like children who've taken a tumble, clutching the hurt place and wasting time wailing. We should be training the soul always to turn at once to healing, to set right and raise up whatever has been struck down and made sick, and to silence the cry of grief with the cure.'
That would certainly be the rightest way to face fortune, he said.
'Yes,' he said, 'that's the right way to meet whatever fortune sends.'
And the best part of us is willing to follow this reasoning.
'And it's the best part of us, we say, that's willing to follow this guidance of reason.'
Clearly.
'Clearly.'
While the part that pulls us back to the memory of the suffering, back to the wailing — the part that can never get enough of it — won't we call that unreasoning, idle, a friend of cowardice?
'While the part that keeps dragging us back to the memory of our suffering and can never have enough of weeping, that part we may call unreasoning, idle, and a friend to cowardice.'
We will.
'We may indeed.'

Now, the fretful part of us offers rich and varied material for imitation. But the wise and steady character, always nearly the same as itself, is not easy to imitate — nor, when imitated, easy to understand, least of all for a festival crowd, all sorts of people packed into a theater. What is being imitated is an experience foreign to them.

'Now this fretful, rebellious part gives the poet plenty of varied material to imitate. But the wise and quiet temperament, always more or less the same in itself, is neither easy to imitate nor, when imitated, easy to take in, especially before a packed festival crowd in a theater, since the feeling shown is one they've never lived.'
Absolutely.
'Quite so.'

Then plainly the imitative poet is not made for this reasoning part of the soul, and his skill is not set on pleasing it — not if he wants fame with the many. He is made for the fretful, changeable character, because it is easy to imitate.

'So the imitative poet, the one who's out to please the crowd, plainly isn't made by nature to reach the rational part of the soul, nor is his craft framed to please it. He turns instead to the excitable and volatile temper, because it's so easy to imitate.'
Plainly.
'Obviously.'

So at this point we can fairly take the poet and stand him beside the painter. He resembles him in making things that are worthless by the measure of truth, and he resembles him in this too: he consorts with a part of the soul that is not the best. So we are now justified in refusing to admit him into any city that is to be well governed — because he wakes this part of the soul, feeds it, makes it strong, and destroys the reasoning part. Just as in a city, when someone strengthens the vicious and hands the state to them, betraying the better sort — the imitative poet, we will say, does the same thing: he plants a bad constitution in the private soul of each man, gratifying the part that has no judgment, the part that cannot tell larger from smaller but calls the same things now big, now little — an image-maker whose images stand a very long way from the truth.

'So now we're in a position to set him alongside the painter, for he resembles him in two ways. First, what he makes is of a low order of truth. Second, the part of the soul he deals with is a low one, not the best. And so we're right to refuse him entry into a city that's to be well governed, because he awakens this part of the soul and feeds it and strengthens it, and so destroys the rational part. It's just like handing a city over to wicked men and ruining the good: in the same way the imitative poet plants a bad government in the soul of each of us, by gratifying its foolish part, which can't tell big from little but calls the same thing now great, now small, a manufacturer of images standing very far from the truth.'
Exactly.
'Just so.'
But we haven't yet brought the heaviest charge against poetry. Its power to damage even good men — with very few exceptions — is surely the frightening thing.
'But we haven't yet brought our gravest charge against poetry. Its power to harm even decent people, all but a very few, is surely the most alarming thing of all.'
Frightening indeed, if it really does that.
'It certainly would be, if it really does that.'

Listen, and judge. When the best of us hear Homer, or one of the tragedians, imitating some hero in grief, stretching out a long speech of lamentation, or singing and beating his breast — you know how we enjoy it. We give ourselves over; we follow, suffering along with him; and in all seriousness we praise as a fine poet whoever does this to us most.

'Then hear me out and judge for yourself. When the best of us listen to Homer, or to one of the tragedians, imitating some hero in mourning, drawing out his grief in a long lament, or beating his breast and singing his sorrow, you know how we surrender to it. We follow along, we suffer with him, and in all earnest we praise as a fine poet the one who can move us most deeply this way.'
I know it. Of course.
'I know it well.'

But when private grief comes to one of us, you notice we pride ourselves on the opposite — on staying calm and bearing it — as if that were a man's part, and the thing we praised in the theater a woman's.

'But when one of us suffers a grief of his own, you'll notice we take pride in just the opposite, in staying calm and bearing up, as if that were the manly thing, while the other behavior, the one that thrilled us in the theater, we count womanish.'
I do notice it, he said.
'I've noticed that,' he said.
Then is that praise really in order? Looking at a man behave as we would refuse — would be ashamed — to behave ourselves, and instead of being disgusted, delighting in it and praising it?
'Now is it right, this praise? When we watch a man behaving in a way we'd be ashamed and disgusted to behave ourselves, instead of being repelled we enjoy it and praise it?'
No, by Zeus, he said — it doesn't look reasonable.
'No, by heaven,' he said, 'that doesn't seem reasonable.'
Yes it does, I said — if you look at it this way.
'It does, though,' I said, 'looked at a certain way.'
Which way?
'What way?'

Consider it like this. The part of us that in our own misfortunes is held down by force — the part that has hungered for tears, for a good long cry, for its fill of grief, because that is what it naturally desires — this is exactly the part the poets fill up and delight. And our best part, insufficiently trained by reason and habit, slackens its watch over this mournful part, on the grounds that the sufferings it is watching belong to someone else; there is no shame, it thinks, in praising and pitying another man who calls himself good while he grieves without measure — and the pleasure feels like pure gain, not to be thrown away by despising the whole poem. Only a few, I think, ever reckon that what we take in from the feelings of others comes home to our own — that after feeding the pity there until it is strong, it is not easy to hold it down in our own sufferings.

'Consider this. In our own misfortunes there's a part of us that hungers to cry its fill and pour out its grief, since that's what it naturally craves. This is the part the poets feed and satisfy. Meanwhile the best part of us, not yet properly trained by reason and habit, slackens its guard over this weeping part, on the excuse that the sorrow it's watching belongs to someone else, and that there's nothing shameful in praising and pitying another man who claims to be good and grieves beyond all measure. It thinks the pleasure pure gain, and isn't willing to throw it away by condemning the whole poem. For very few, I think, ever reckon that what we catch from others must spread to ourselves: once you've fed and fattened your pity on someone else's troubles, it's not easy to hold it down in your own.'
Very true, he said.
'Very true.'

And doesn't the same argument hold for laughter? There are jokes you would be ashamed to make yourself, yet in a comic imitation — or in private — they delight you enormously, and you don't hate them as vulgar. Isn't this the same thing as with pity? The part of you that wants to play the clown, which you used to hold back by reason for fear of being thought a buffoon, you let loose there; and having made it frisky in the theater, you are carried off unawares, and end up the comedian at home.

'And doesn't the same hold for what's funny? Things you'd be ashamed to clown at yourself you'll laugh at heartily in a comedy, or even just hearing them in private, with no disgust at all at how low they are. It's exactly like pity. There's a part of you that itches to raise a laugh, which you used to hold back by reason for fear of looking like a buffoon; now you give it free rein, and once you've roused that appetite for laughter in the theater, before you know it you find yourself playing the comedian at home.'
Exactly so, he said.
'Quite true.'

And with sex, and anger, and every appetite and pain and pleasure in the soul — the ones we say follow every action of ours — poetic imitation works the same effects on us. It waters them when they should be left to dry; it sets them to rule over us when they should be ruled, so that we might become better and happier instead of worse and more wretched.

'And it's the same with desire and anger, and with all the appetites, the pleasures and pains that we say go with everything we do. Poetry feeds them and waters them when it ought to dry them up. It sets them up as our rulers when they ought to be ruled, if we're ever to grow better and happier instead of worse and more wretched.'
I can't say otherwise, he said.
'I can't deny it,' he said.

Then, Glaucon, when you run into men who praise Homer — who say this poet educated Greece, that for the management and refinement of human life he is worth taking up and studying, your whole life arranged according to him — you should love them and greet them as the best people they know how to be, and grant them that Homer is the most poetic of poets and first of the tragedians. But hold fast to this: the only poetry to be admitted into our city is hymns to the gods and praises of good men. Once you let in the honeyed Muse, in lyric or in epic, pleasure and pain will be kings in your city, in place of law and of the reasoning that the community in each case judges best.

'So, Glaucon, whenever you meet admirers of Homer who tell you he educated Greece, that for the management of human affairs and for our schooling we should take him up and study him and order our whole lives by his teaching, you may welcome them and treat them with affection, since they're as good as their understanding allows; you may even grant that Homer is the greatest of the poets and the first of the tragedians. But you must hold firm to this: that the only poetry to be admitted into our city is hymns to the gods and the praises of good men. For once you let in the honeyed Muse, in lyric or in epic, then pleasure and pain will be kings in your city in place of law and the principle that, by common consent, has always been held best, which is reason.'
Very true, he said.
'Very true,' he said.

So let this be our defense, now that we have come back to the subject of poetry: given her nature, we were reasonable to banish her from the city then. The argument compelled us. And let us say to her — so she can't accuse us of harshness or bad manners — that there is an ancient quarrel between philosophy and poetry. There are the old taunts: 'the yelping bitch shrieking at her master,' and 'great in the empty talk of fools,' and 'the mob of over-wise heads that rules,' and 'the subtle thinkers who are beggars after all' — countless signs of the old feud. Even so, let it be said that if poetry made for pleasure, imitative poetry, can give any argument that she belongs in a well-governed city, we would be delighted to take her back. We know her spell on us first-hand. But it would be impious to betray what we hold true. Come, my friend — doesn't she charm you too, especially when you watch her through Homer?

'There, then,' I said, 'since we've come back round to the subject of poetry, let this stand as our defense: that we were right, back then, to send such an art out of our city, given the kind of thing it is. Reason compelled us. But so that poetry won't accuse us of being harsh and unmannerly, let's tell her there's an old quarrel between philosophy and poetry. There are plenty of signs of it: "the bitch that yelps and snarls at her master," "a giant in the empty chatter of fools," "the mob of know-it-alls who lord it over Zeus," "the deep thinkers who haven't got a coin," and no end of other tokens of their ancient feud. All the same, let it be said plainly that if poetry, the imitative kind made for pleasure, can give us some argument to show she belongs in a well-run city, we'd be glad to bring her back, for we're well aware of her spell on us. But it would be wrong to betray what we take to be the truth. Aren't you yourself, my friend, under her spell, especially when it's through Homer that you see her?'
Very much, he said.
'I am, deeply.'
Then it is just to let her come home from exile on these terms: that she plead her own defense, in lyric or whatever meter she likes.
'Then is it fair to let her come home from exile, but only once she's made her defense in lyric or some other meter?'
By all means.
'Certainly.'

And we would allow her champions too — those who aren't poets themselves but love poetry — to speak for her in prose: to argue that she is not only sweet but useful, to cities and to human life. And we will listen kindly. We stand to gain, surely, if she turns out to be not only pleasant but good for us.

'And we'd allow her champions, too, the ones who love poetry without being poets themselves, to speak in prose on her behalf, to show that she isn't only sweet but useful to cities and to human life. We'll listen to them kindly, for we'll be the gainers if poetry turns out to be useful as well as delightful.'
Of course we stand to gain, he said.
'Of course we'll be the gainers,' he said.

But if not, my dear friend — then like men who have fallen in love, and who judge the love is doing them no good, and force themselves away from it — we will do the same. Reared as we are in the love of this kind of poetry by the upbringing our fine cities give, we will be glad for her to prove as good and true as can be; but as long as she cannot make her defense, we will listen to her while chanting this argument of ours to ourselves as a counter-charm, taking care not to fall back into the boyish passion for her that most men never leave. One thing we know: such poetry is not to be taken seriously, as if it were a serious thing laying hold of truth. The listener must be on his guard against her, fearing for the city inside himself, and must hold to what we have said about poetry.

'But if her defense fails, then, my friend, we'll have to do what people do who have fallen in love but see that the love is doing them harm: hold ourselves back from it, however hard it is. The love of this kind of poetry, bred in us by the upbringing our fine cities give, is in us too, so we'd be glad for poetry to prove herself the best and truest thing there is. But so long as she can't make her case, we'll listen to her chanting this argument of ours to ourselves like a charm against her, on our guard not to slide back into that childish love of her that grips the crowd. At any rate we'll know not to take such poetry seriously as a thing that lays hold of truth; whoever listens to her must be wary, afraid for the city within himself, and must take what we've said as his law.'
I fully agree, he said.
'I'm entirely with you,' he said.

Yes, dear Glaucon — because the stakes are great, greater than they look: whether a man becomes good or bad. So neither honor nor money nor any office — no, and not poetry either — is worth neglecting justice for, and the rest of virtue with it.

'Yes, my dear Glaucon,' I said, 'for great is the stake, far greater than people think, whether a man turns out good or bad. So neither honor nor money nor power, nor poetry either, should ever tempt us to neglect justice and the rest of virtue.'
The argument has convinced me, he said. I think it would convince anyone.
'After all we've gone through,' he said, 'I agree with you, and I think anyone else would too.'
And yet, I said, we haven't even mentioned the greatest wages of virtue, or the prizes waiting for it.
'And yet,' I said, 'we still haven't gone through the greatest rewards and prizes that are laid up for virtue.'
Then they must be unimaginably great, he said, if they are greater than the ones we've named.
'They must be of an inconceivable size,' he said, 'if there are any greater than the ones we've already named.'
What could ever grow great in a little time? I said. And this whole span from childhood to old age is little, next to all of time.
'And what,' I said, 'is ever really great in a short span of time? This whole stretch from childhood to old age is a small thing set beside all of time.'
It is nothing at all, he said.
'It's nothing at all,' he said.
Well then: should an immortal thing take this little interval so seriously — instead of the whole?
'And do you think an immortal thing should take such a brief span seriously, rather than the whole of time?'
The whole, of course, he said. But why do you ask?
'The whole, of course,' he said. 'But why do you ask?'
Haven't you realized, I said, that our soul is immortal, and is never destroyed?
'Haven't you realized,' I said, 'that our soul is immortal and never perishes?'
He looked at me, astonished. By Zeus, no, he said. Are you actually prepared to claim that?
He looked at me in amazement and said, 'No, by heaven, I haven't. Can you really maintain that?'
I am — or I'd be in the wrong. And so could you. It isn't hard.
'I'd be wrong not to,' I said, 'and so would you, for there's nothing difficult about proving it.'
It is for me, he said. But I would gladly hear from you this thing that isn't hard.
'It seems very difficult to me,' he said. 'But I'd be glad to hear this proof you make so light of.'
Then listen.
'Then listen.'
Just speak.
'I'm all attention.'
You call something good, and something evil?
'There's something you call good, and something you call bad?'
I do.
'There is.'
And do you think of them the way I do — evil is everything that destroys and corrupts, good is what preserves and benefits?
'And do you think of them as I do? The thing that corrupts and destroys is the bad, and the thing that preserves and benefits is the good.'
Yes.
'I do.'

And each thing has its own evil and its own good? Eye disease for the eyes, sickness for the whole body, blight for grain, rot for timber, rust for bronze and iron — for almost everything, as I say, its own natural evil and its own sickness.
