'And you'd agree that everything has its own peculiar good and its own peculiar evil, the way the eyes have inflammation, the whole body has disease, grain has mildew, timber has rot, bronze and iron have rust. In nearly everything, that is, there's some inborn evil, some disease that belongs to it.'
Yes.
'There is,' he said.
And when one of these evils gets into a thing, it makes what it touches bad — and in the end dissolves the whole of it and destroys it.
'And when one of these evils attaches itself to a thing, it makes the thing bad, and in the end breaks it down entirely and destroys it.'
Of course.
'Yes.'

So each thing is destroyed by its own natural evil and its own badness; and if that doesn't destroy it, nothing else will. The good will never destroy anything, and neither will what is neither good nor evil.

'So it's each thing's own inborn evil and its own disease that destroys it; and if that doesn't destroy it, nothing else will. For the good will surely never destroy anything, and neither will what is neither good nor bad.'
How could they?
'Of course not.'
Then if we find something that has an evil which makes it worse, but which cannot dissolve it or destroy it — won't we know at once that a thing of such a nature cannot be destroyed at all?
'Then if we find some thing that has an evil of its own which makes it worse but can't break it down and destroy it, won't we know at once that a thing of that nature simply cannot be destroyed?'
That seems likely.
'That seems right.'
Well then — does the soul have something that makes it evil?
'Well then, isn't there an evil that belongs to the soul?'
Very much so, he said — everything we were just going through: injustice, self-indulgence, cowardice, ignorance.
'There certainly is,' he said. 'All the things we ran through just now: injustice, lack of self-control, cowardice, ignorance.'

Then does any of these dissolve and destroy it? Think carefully here, so we aren't tricked into supposing that when the unjust and foolish man is caught, he has been destroyed by his injustice — by badness of soul. Do it this way instead. Disease, the badness of the body, wastes a body, dissolves it, brings it to the point of not being a body at all; and everything we listed just now is brought to nonexistence by its own particular evil settling into it and inhabiting it. Isn't that so?

'And does any of these break the soul down and destroy it? Be careful here. Let's not be misled into thinking that when an unjust and foolish man is caught out, he perishes through his own injustice, which is an evil of the soul. Look at the parallel with the body. The body's own evil, disease, wastes it and shrinks it and finally destroys it altogether, until it's no longer a body at all; and all the other things we mentioned are destroyed, in the same way, by the evil proper to each, which fastens on it, settles in it, and ruins it. Isn't that so?'
Yes.
'Yes.'

Then look at the soul the same way. When injustice and the rest of vice inhabit it, do they — by settling in and dwelling there — waste the soul and wither it, until they bring it to death and split it from the body?

'Now consider the soul in the same light. Do the injustice and the other evils that lodge in the soul, simply by being in her and clinging to her, waste her away and destroy her, until they bring her to death and cut her off from the body?'
That they never do, he said.
'No, they certainly don't do that.'
But surely it is unreasonable that a thing could be destroyed by the badness of something else, when its own badness cannot destroy it.
'And yet,' I said, 'it would be absurd to suppose that a thing could be destroyed by an evil that belongs to something else, when it can't even be destroyed by an evil of its own.'
Unreasonable, he said.
'It would be absurd,' he said.

Think, Glaucon: we don't suppose the body has to be destroyed by the badness of food itself — staleness, rottenness, whatever it might be. If the food's own badness breeds bodily evil in the body, we will say the body was destroyed through the food, but by its own evil — by disease. But by the badness of food, which is one thing, the body, which is another, will never be destroyed — not unless that alien evil implants the body's own natural evil in it.

'Consider, Glaucon,' I said. 'We don't suppose that the body is destroyed by the badness of food, the staleness or rot or whatever it may be, simply as a quality of the food. If the bad food breeds a corruption of the body in the body itself, we say the body has been destroyed by an evil of its own, by the disease the food brought on. But that the body, which is one thing, should be destroyed directly by the badness of food, which is another thing, without any disease of the body's own being set off, this we'll flatly deny.'
That is exactly right, he said.
'And rightly,' he said.

By the same argument, then: unless the body's badness breeds the soul's own badness in the soul, let's never suppose the soul is destroyed by an alien evil apart from its own — one thing by another thing's evil.

'On the same principle, then, unless some evil of the body can breed an evil in the soul, let's never suppose that the soul, which is one thing, is destroyed by an evil that belongs to another, by an evil from outside her.'
That makes sense, he said.
'There's reason in that,' he said.

Then either let us refute this argument — or, as long as it stands unrefuted, let us never say that fever, or any other disease, or the knife at the throat, or chopping the whole body into the smallest possible pieces, brings a soul one step nearer to being destroyed — not until someone proves that through these sufferings of the body the soul itself becomes more unjust and more unholy. As long as it is an alien evil arising in a thing, and its own evil is absent, let no one be allowed to say that a soul, or anything else, is destroyed.

'So either we refute this argument and show it's wrong, or, as long as it stands unrefuted, let's never say that the soul is destroyed by fever or any other disease, or by the knife at the throat, no, not even if the whole body were cut into the smallest pieces, until someone proves that these things done to the body make the soul herself more unjust and unholy. But that the soul, or anything else, when no evil of its own is destroying it, can be destroyed by an evil belonging to something else, let no one claim.'
Well, he said, no one will ever prove that — that the souls of the dying become more unjust because of death.
'And surely,' he said, 'no one will ever prove that the souls of the dying are made more unjust by death.'

But suppose someone dares to close with the argument, and says that the dying man does become worse and more unjust — just so he won't be forced to admit that souls are immortal. We will hold, I suppose, that if he is telling the truth, injustice must be deadly to its possessor, like a disease: the thing itself kills those who catch it, the worst cases fastest, the milder more slowly — instead of what happens now, where the unjust die of injustice only because other people execute them for it.

'But suppose someone, rather than admit the soul is immortal, has the boldness to dispute this and say that a dying man does become worse and more unjust. Then, if he's right, we'd have to say that injustice is fatal to its possessor, like a disease, and that those who catch it are killed by the natural deadliness of the evil itself, which destroys them sooner or later, instead of their being put to death by others as a penalty for their crimes, the way it actually happens.'

By Zeus, he said, then injustice would turn out not so terrible after all, if it were fatal to whoever caught it — that would be a release from troubles. But I think it will prove the exact opposite: a thing that kills other people if it can, while making its owner positively lively — lively, and wide awake besides. So far from being deadly, it has pitched its camp a long way from death.

'But in that case,' he said, 'injustice wouldn't be so very terrible after all, if it were fatal to the one who has it, since it would set him free from his troubles. No, I rather suspect we'll find the opposite: that injustice murders others if it can, but keeps the unjust man himself very much alive, and wide awake too. So far is its dwelling, it seems, from being anywhere near death.'

Well said, I replied. For when the soul's own badness, its own evil, cannot kill or destroy it, then an evil assigned to destroy something else will hardly destroy a soul — or anything except the thing it was assigned to.

'Well said,' I replied. 'For if the soul's own inborn evil and its own wickedness can't kill it and destroy it, an evil appointed to destroy something else is hardly going to destroy the soul, or anything else, except the very thing it was meant to destroy.'
Hardly — so it seems, at least.
'Hardly,' he said.
Then since it is not destroyed by any evil at all, its own or another's, clearly it must be something that always exists. And if it always exists, it is immortal.
'Then since the soul isn't destroyed by any single evil, whether its own or another's, plainly it must always exist; and if it always exists, it's immortal.'
Necessarily.
'It must be,' he said.

Let that stand, then. And if it does, you see that the souls will always be the same souls. They can't grow fewer, since none is destroyed — and they can't grow more numerous either. For if anything immortal increased, you know its increase would have to come out of what is mortal, and in the end everything would be immortal.

'So much for that,' I said. 'And if it's true, then the same souls must always exist, the same in number. None being destroyed, they can't grow fewer; and they can't grow more either, since any increase in the immortal could only come from the mortal, and in the end everything would become immortal.'
True.
'True.'
But we won't believe that — the argument won't permit it — and we won't believe either that the soul in its truest nature is a thing packed with variety, unlikeness, and difference from itself.
'But we mustn't believe that, reason won't allow it, any more than we should believe that the soul, in her truest nature, is a thing full of variety and difference and disagreement with herself.'
How do you mean? he said.
'What do you mean?' he said.
It isn't easy, I said, for a thing to be everlasting when it is composite — put together out of many parts — and not put together in the finest way; yet that is how the soul appeared to us just now.
'It's not easy,' I said, 'for a thing to be everlasting that's compounded out of many parts and not put together in the finest way, which is how the soul has just now appeared to us.'
No, probably not.
'No, it isn't likely.'

That the soul is immortal, then, this argument and the others would force us to admit. But to know what it is like in truth, you must see it not as we see it now, maimed by its partnership with the body and by other evils, but as it is when it has become pure — that you must gaze at, and thoroughly, with reasoning. You will find it a far more beautiful thing, and you will see through to justice and injustice and everything we have gone through. What we have said so far is true of the soul as it appears at present. But we have been looking at it the way men look at the sea-god Glaucus: they can hardly make out his original nature, because the old parts of his body have been broken off or ground down and altogether disfigured by the waves, and other things have grown onto him — shells and seaweed and stones — so that he looks more like any beast at all than what he naturally was. That is the state we see the soul in, disfigured by ten thousand evils. But we must look elsewhere, Glaucon.

'Well, that the soul is immortal the present argument compels us to admit, and other arguments would too. But to see her as she really is, we mustn't look at her as we do now, marred by her union with the body and by other evils. We have to look with the eye of reason at her love of wisdom, and see what she lays hold of and what company she longs for, since she's akin to the divine and immortal and everlasting. We must see what she'd become if she gave herself wholly to that, and were carried by this longing clear out of the sea she's now sunk in, and had knocked off her the stones and shells that have grown over her. Because she feeds on earth, a wild crust of earthy, rocky, savage stuff has crusted over her from the so-called good things of this life. Then, and only then, would you see her true nature, and whether she has many forms or one, and how she's really made. For now we've described well enough, I think, what she's like and what she undergoes in this human life.'
Where?
'We certainly have,' he said.

At its love of wisdom. Notice what the soul reaches for, what company it craves — kin as it is to the divine and immortal and everlasting — and what it would become if it followed that kinship whole and entire, lifted by the impulse out of the sea it now lives in, the stones and shells knocked away: all that wild, earthy overgrowth crusted onto it from the so-called happy feasting here, because it feeds on earth. Then you would see its true nature — whether it has many forms or one, and how it stands. But for now, I think, we have described well enough what happens to it in human life, and the shapes it wears.

'Then haven't we cleared away the other objections to the argument? And we've done it without dragging in the rewards and reputation that justice brings, the way you said Homer and Hesiod do. We've found that justice in itself is best for the soul in herself, and that the soul ought to do what's just whether or not she has the ring of Gyges, and the cap of Hades on top of the ring.'
We certainly have, he said.
'That's perfectly true,' he said.

Well then, I said. We have cleared the rest of the case, and we haven't invoked the wages or reputations of justice, as you said Hesiod and Homer do. We found justice itself best for the soul itself — found that the soul should do what is just whether or not it owns the ring of Gyges, and the cap of Hades on top of the ring.

'And now, Glaucon,' I said, 'surely there can be no objection if, on top of this, we give back to justice and the other virtues all the rewards they win for the soul from gods and men, both in life and after death?'
Very true.
'None at all,' he said.

Then, Glaucon, can there be any objection now to our giving back to justice and the rest of virtue their wages too — all the wages, in their number and kind, that they win for the soul from men and from gods, while a man still lives and after he has died?
'Then will you give me back what you borrowed from me during the argument?'
None whatever, he said.
'What did I borrow?'
Then will you give me back what you borrowed in the argument?

'I granted you, for the sake of the argument, that the just man might be thought unjust and the unjust man just. You both asked for this, even though you agreed it could never really escape the eyes of gods and men, so that justice in its pure state could be weighed against pure injustice. Don't you remember?'
What, exactly?
'I'd be much to blame if I didn't,' he said.

I granted you that the just man could seem unjust, and the unjust man just. You asked for it: even if no one could actually hide the truth from gods and men, still it should be conceded for argument's sake, so that justice itself could be judged against injustice itself. Don't you remember?

'Well, now that the case has been judged, I ask, on justice's behalf, that we hand back to her the reputation she actually has among gods and men, and let us admit she deserves it. She's been shown to confer real benefit and never to deceive those who truly possess her, so let her be given back the prize of appearance too, the one she wins, and which she awards to her own.'
It would be unjust of me not to, he said.
'That's a fair demand,' he said.

Well, they have now been judged — so on behalf of justice I demand back her reputation. She must be given the esteem she actually enjoys with gods and with men, so that we agree she also carries off the prizes of appearing — the prizes she wins by seeming, and gives to those who hold her — now that she has clearly given the goods of being, and does not cheat those who truly take hold of her.
'Then the first thing you'll give back is this: that the gods, at least, are never deceived about which man is just and which unjust.'
A just demand, he said.
'We'll grant that.'
Then first give this back: neither of them is hidden from the gods — what each of the two really is.
'And if neither is hidden from them, the one will be loved by the gods and the other hated, as we agreed at the start.'
We give it back.
'Just so.'
And if neither is hidden, then one is loved by the gods and one is hated — as we agreed at the very start.
'And won't the gods grant to the man they love every good thing that comes from them, except for whatever harm he's bound to suffer as the necessary consequence of some earlier wrong?'
That is so.
'Certainly.'
And won't we agree that everything that comes from the gods to the man they love comes as the best it can be — unless some evil was already owed him from an earlier fault?

'Then this must be our view of the just man: that whether he falls into poverty or sickness or any of the things that look like misfortunes, all of it will turn out, in the end, for his good, whether in life or in death. For the gods never neglect a man who is in earnest about becoming just and, by the practice of virtue, growing as like to a god as a human being can.'
Certainly.
'It stands to reason,' he said, 'that one who's like the gods won't be neglected by them.'

Then this is how we must think about the just man: whether poverty comes to him, or sickness, or any other seeming evil, it will end in some good for him, living or dead. For the gods never neglect a man whose heart is set on becoming just — on becoming, through the practice of virtue, as much like a god as a human being can.
'And of the unjust man we must suppose the opposite.'
It stands to reason, he said, that such a man is not neglected by what he resembles.
'Most certainly.'
And of the unjust man we should think the opposite?
'So those, then, are the prizes the gods award the just man.'
Emphatically.
'In my view, yes,' he said.
From the gods, then, these are the victor's prizes for the just man.

'And what does he win from men? Look at the thing as it really is. The clever unjust are like runners who run well from the start to the turning-post but not back again. They sprint off the line at a great pace, but at the end they're a laughingstock, slinking off uncrowned with their ears drooping on their shoulders. The true runners, though, reach the finish and carry off the prizes and the crowns. And isn't this how it usually goes with the just? At the close of every undertaking, every dealing, every life, they come away with a good name and the prizes their fellow men can give.'
That is certainly my view, he said.
'It is.'

And from men? What does he get there? Isn't the truth of it this, if we are to say what actually happens: your clever unjust men are like runners who run the first leg well but not the return — off the mark at a sprint, but by the finish they look like fools, ears drooping on their shoulders as they slink off uncrowned. True runners come in at the end, take the prizes, and wear the crown. And isn't that how it usually goes with the just? Toward the end of every action, every partnership, and of life itself, they carry the honors and take the prizes men have to give.

'Then you'll let me say of the just the very things you were saying of the unjust. I'll say that as they grow older the just become rulers in their own city if they want the office; they marry into whatever family they please and give their daughters where they like; everything you claimed for the others I now claim for these. And of the unjust I say that most of them, even if they get away with it in their youth, are caught at the finish and made fools of, and in a bitter old age are mocked by foreigners and citizens alike, beaten and racked, and made to suffer those things you rightly called unfit for polite ears, branded and their eyes burned out. Just imagine I've recited the whole catalogue of horrors you described. But may I take it, without listing them, that all this is so?'
Very much so.
'You may,' he said, 'for what you say is true.'

Then will you bear it if I say about the just what you yourself said about the unjust? This is what I'll say: the just, when they are older, hold office in their own city if they want office; they marry where they choose, and give their children in marriage where they please — everything you said of the one lot, I now say of the other. And the unjust — most of them, even if they go unnoticed while they are young, get caught at the end of the race and are laughed at; by the time they are old they are miserable, insulted by foreigners and citizens alike, whipped — and then everything you rightly called too savage for polite ears: they will be racked, their eyes will be burned out. Consider the whole catalogue recited; I have repeated it. See whether you will bear with me.
'These, then, are the prizes and wages and gifts that the just man receives from gods and men while he's still alive, on top of the good things that justice gives him by herself.'
Easily, he said. What you say is just.
'Yes,' he said, 'and they're fair ones, and lasting.'
So these are the prizes, the wages, the gifts the just man receives while he lives, from gods and from men — over and above those goods that justice provided of herself.

'And yet,' I said, 'all of these are nothing, in number or in size, beside what waits for the just and the unjust after death. And you ought to hear it, so that each of them may receive in full the payment the argument owes him.'
And they are beautiful and lasting things, he said.
'Tell it,' he said. 'There's little I'd rather hear.'

Yet all of that, I said, is nothing in number or size next to what awaits each of the two after death. And it ought to be heard, so that each of them can take away, in full, what the argument owes him.

'It isn't, though,' I said, 'a tale of Alcinous I'll tell you, but the tale of a brave man, Er the son of Armenius, a Pamphylian by birth. He was killed in battle, and when the dead were gathered up ten days later, already decaying, his body was found untouched by decay and was carried home to be buried. On the twelfth day, as he lay on the funeral pyre, he came back to life, and once revived he told what he had seen in the other world. He said that when his soul left him, it journeyed in a great company until they came to a strange place where there were two chasms side by side in the earth, and opposite them, above, two more in the sky. Between them sat judges, who, when they had given their judgment, ordered the just to take the road to the right that led up into the sky, fixing on them in front the tokens of the judgment passed; and they sent the unjust down the road to the left, and these too bore tokens, but on their backs, of all that they had done. When Er himself came forward, they told him that he was to be the messenger to mankind about that other world, and bade him listen to and watch everything in the place. So he watched the souls departing, after sentence, by one or other chasm of the sky and the earth; and at the two other chasms he saw souls arriving, some coming up out of the earth caked with dust and travel-worn, others coming down out of the sky clean and bright. And as they kept arriving, they seemed to have come from a long journey, and they turned gladly aside into the meadow and camped there as at a festival. Those who knew each other embraced and fell to talking, the souls from the earth eagerly asking about the things above, and the souls from the sky about the things below. And they told each other their stories, the ones from below weeping and groaning as they remembered all they had suffered and seen on their journey under the earth, a journey of a thousand years, while those from above described the joys of heaven and visions of unimaginable beauty. It would take too long, Glaucon, to go through it all, but the sum of it, he said, was this. For every wrong a soul had ever done anyone, it paid the penalty ten times over, once in every hundred years, a hundred being reckoned the span of a human life, so that the price of the wrong was paid tenfold over the thousand years. If a man had been the cause of many deaths, by betraying cities or armies and dragging people into slavery, or had taken part in any other such crime, for each and every wrong he suffered tenfold; and in the same proportion, the doers of good and the just and the holy were rewarded. About those who died as infants, almost as soon as they were born, he said things not worth repeating. And for piety and impiety toward gods and parents, and for murder done by one's own hand, he told of still greater wages, both of reward and of punishment. He said he was there when one soul asked another, "Where is Ardiaeus the Great?" This Ardiaeus had been tyrant of some city in Pamphylia a thousand years before, and was said to have killed his old father and his elder brother and to have done many other unspeakable things. And he heard the other soul answer, "He isn't here, and he never will come here." And this, said Er, was one of the terrible sights they themselves saw. When they had been through all their punishments and were near the mouth of the chasm, about to go up, suddenly Ardiaeus appeared, and others with him, most of them tyrants, though there were some private men too who had committed great crimes. Just as they thought they were about to climb out, the mouth would not take them, but gave a roar whenever one of these incurable sinners, or anyone who had not yet paid enough, tried to come up. And then, Er said, fierce men of fiery aspect, standing ready and understanding the sound, seized some of them and led them away; but Ardiaeus and the rest they bound hand and foot and neck, flung down, flayed with whips, and dragged off along the road, raking them on thorns like carded wool, and telling the passers-by what their crimes were and that they were being carried off to be thrown into Tartarus. And of all the many terrors they had felt, he said, the worst by far was the fear that the mouth would roar as each of them tried to go up, and the greatest joy was to climb out in silence. Such, said Er, were the punishments and penalties, and the blessings answered to them.'
Then speak, he said. There are few things I would rather hear.

'Each soul spent seven days in the meadow, and on the eighth they had to rise and go on, and after four days more they reached a place from which they could see, stretched through the whole heaven and the earth, a shaft of light, straight as a pillar, very like a rainbow but brighter and purer. They reached it after another day's journey, and there, at the middle of the light, they saw the ends of its bonds let down from heaven; for this light is what binds the heaven together, holding the whole revolving vault as the undergirding ropes hold a trireme. And from these ends hung the spindle of Necessity, by which all the revolutions are turned. Its shaft and hook were of adamant, and its whorl partly of adamant and partly of other materials. The whorl was shaped like the ones we use here, but from what he described you must picture it as if one great hollow whorl had been scooped right out, and into it a second, smaller one had been fitted, and into that a third, and a fourth, and four more, eight in all, nested one inside another like bowls. Their rims showed as circles from above, but underneath they all formed one continuous whorl around the shaft, which was driven straight through the center of the eighth. The first and outermost whorl had the widest rim; next widest was the rim of the sixth, then the fourth, then the eighth, then the seventh, then the fifth, then the third, and the second whorl had the narrowest rim of all. The rim of the largest was spangled, that of the seventh was the brightest, that of the eighth took its color from the seventh shining on it, those of the second and fifth were like each other and yellower than the rest, the third was the whitest, the fourth was reddish, and the sixth was second in whiteness. The whole spindle turned with one motion, but within the turning whole the seven inner circles slowly revolved the opposite way, and of these the eighth went fastest; next, and all together, the seventh, sixth, and fifth; third in speed, it seemed to them, ran the fourth; the third was fourth in speed, and the second was fifth. And the spindle turned on the knees of Necessity. On the top of each circle stood a Siren, carried round with it and singing one single note, one pitch, and all eight notes together made a single harmony. And round about, at equal distances, sat three more, each on a throne, the daughters of Necessity, the Fates, robed in white with garlands on their heads: Lachesis, Clotho, and Atropos. They sang to the Sirens' harmony, Lachesis of what had been, Clotho of what is, and Atropos of what is to come. And from time to time Clotho, with a touch of her right hand, helped turn the outer circle of the spindle, while Atropos with her left hand turned the inner ones, and Lachesis laid hold of each in turn, first with one hand and then with the other.'

Well, I said, it isn't the long tale told to Alcinous that I'm going to tell you, but the tale of a brave man — Er the son of Armenius, a Pamphylian by birth. He was killed in battle. On the tenth day, when the dead were taken up already decaying, he was taken up whole; he was carried home for burial, and on the twelfth day, laid out on the pyre, he came back to life — and once alive again, he told what he had seen there. He said that when his soul went out of him, it traveled with a great company until they came to an uncanny place, where two openings stood in the earth, side by side, and opposite them, above, two others in the sky. Judges sat between. When they had passed judgment, they ordered the just to take the right-hand road, upward through the sky, hanging signs of the judgment on their chests; and the unjust the left-hand road, downward, wearing on their backs the signs of everything they had done. When Er himself came forward, they told him he was to be a messenger to mankind of the things in that place, and they charged him to hear and watch everything there. So he watched: through one opening of the sky and one of the earth, the souls departing after judgment; and out of the other two, souls returning — from the earth, dusty and caked with the road; from the sky, clean and bright. The souls kept arriving, looking glad to be done with a long journey, and they turned aside into the meadow as if to a festival and camped there. Those who knew one another embraced, and they traded questions — the ones from the earth asking about the things above, the ones from heaven about the things below. The souls from under the earth wept and wailed as they told what they had suffered and seen on their journey beneath the ground — a journey of a thousand years — while the souls from heaven told of joys, and of sights beautiful past telling. The whole account, Glaucon, would take a long time; but the sum of it, he said, was this. For every wrong a soul had ever done, and every person it had wronged, it paid the penalty in turn, ten times over for each — that is, once every hundred years, a hundred years being the length of a human life — so that the price of each wrong was paid tenfold across the thousand years. If, say, men had caused many deaths, betraying cities or armies, or throwing others into slavery, or had a hand in any other crime, they suffered ten pains for every one of them; and if they had done good deeds and been just and holy, they carried off rewards in the same proportion. About those who died at birth or lived only a short while, he said other things not worth recording. And for piety and impiety toward gods and parents, and for murder by one's own hand, he described wages greater still. He said he was standing there when one soul asked another, 'Where is Ardiaeus the Great?' This Ardiaeus had been tyrant in a city of Pamphylia a thousand years before: he had killed his old father and his elder brother, and done many other unholy things, so the story went. And the soul who was asked said: 'He has not come. He will not come. For this was one of the terrible sights we saw. When we were near the mouth, about to come up with all the rest of it behind us, suddenly we saw him — Ardiaeus, and others with him, most of them tyrants, though there were private men among them too, great sinners. They thought they were finally about to go up, and the mouth would not take them: it bellowed whenever one of the incurables, or anyone who had not paid in full, tried to ascend. Wild men stood by there, fiery to look at, who understood the sound; and they seized some and carried them off — but Ardiaeus and the others they bound hand and foot and head, threw them down, flayed them, and dragged them along the roadside, carding them on thorn-bushes like wool, telling everyone who passed why this was done, and that they were being taken to be hurled into Tartarus.' And of all the many fears they had felt there, he said, this one rose above them all: that the mouth would bellow when each of them went up. When it stayed silent, each climbed out with utter joy. Such were the penalties and punishments, he said — and the blessings were their equal and opposite.

'When the souls arrived, they had to go straight to Lachesis. First a kind of spokesman set them in order; then he took from the lap of Lachesis the lots and the patterns of lives, climbed onto a high platform, and spoke: "This is the word of Lachesis, the maiden daughter of Necessity. Souls that live but a day, here begins another round of life that ends in death. No guardian spirit will be assigned to you by lot; you will choose your own. Let the one who draws the first lot be the first to choose a life, and that life will be his by necessity. Virtue has no master; each will have more of it or less according as he honors or dishonors her. The blame belongs to the one who chooses. God is blameless." When he had said this, he scattered the lots among them all, and each picked up the one that fell beside him, all but Er, who was not allowed; and each, as he took his lot, saw what number he had drawn. After that the spokesman laid out before them on the ground the patterns of lives, far more of them than there were souls present, and of every kind. There were lives of all the animals and every sort of human life. Among them were tyrannies, some that lasted out the tyrant's days and others that collapsed halfway and ended in poverty and exile and beggary. There were the lives of men famous for their looks and beauty, or for their strength and their victories in the games, or for their high birth and the deeds of their ancestors, and the lives of men unknown for all these things, and of women too. But there was no fixed character of soul in any of them, because a soul must change as it takes up a different life. All the other qualities were there, mixed with one another and with wealth and poverty, with sickness and health, and with the states between. And here, my dear Glaucon, it seems, is the whole danger of being human, and this above all is why each of us must do everything to set aside every other study and seek out and learn this one thing: to find the man who can give him the knowledge and the power to tell a good life from a bad one, and so always and everywhere to choose the better as far as he is able. He must weigh all the things we've been speaking of, both as they stand alone and as they combine, to see how they bear on a good life; he must understand what beauty does to a soul when it's mixed with poverty or with wealth, and what comes, for good or ill, of high or low birth, of private or public station, of strength and weakness, of quickness and slowness of mind, and of all the gifts of soul a man is born with or acquires, and how they work when joined together. From all of this he will be able to reason it out, keeping his eye on the nature of the soul, and to name as worse the life that will make his soul more unjust, and as better the one that will make it more just, and let everything else go. For we've seen that this is the best choice both in life and after death. A man must hold to this belief like adamant as he goes down into the world below, so that even there he won't be dazzled by riches or any of the other evils, won't fall into tyrannies and the like and do irreparable harm to others and suffer still worse himself, but will know always how to choose the life that lies in the middle and to shun the extremes on either side, in this life so far as he can and in every life to come. For this is how a human being grows happiest."'

Now when the souls in the meadow had each spent seven days there, on the eighth they had to rise and march; and on the fourth day out, he said, they reached a place from which they could see a straight light stretched from above through the whole of heaven and earth, like a pillar — most like the rainbow, but brighter and purer. Another day's march brought them into it, and there, at the middle of the light, they saw the ends of its bindings stretched down from heaven. For this light is what ties heaven together: as the undergirding cables hold a trireme, so it holds the whole turning frame of the universe in one. And from the ends hangs the spindle of Necessity, by which all the revolutions are turned. Its shaft and hook are of adamant, and its whorl of adamant mixed with other stuffs. The whorl's nature is this. In shape it is like an ordinary whorl here on earth; but from his account you must picture one great hollow whorl, scooped clean through, and a second, smaller one fitted snugly inside it — like those jars that nest into one another — then a third inside that, and a fourth, and four more. Eight whorls in all, set one within another, their rims showing from above as circles, and forming together the continuous back of one single whorl around the shaft, which is driven straight through the center of the eighth. The first, outermost whorl has the broadest rim; the sixth is second in breadth, the fourth third, the eighth fourth, the seventh fifth, the fifth sixth, the third seventh, and the second last. The rim of the largest is spangled — these are the fixed stars; the seventh, the sun, is brightest; the eighth, the moon, takes its color from the seventh's light falling on it; the second and fifth, Saturn and Mercury, are like each other, and yellower than the others; the third, Venus, carries the whitest light; the fourth, Mars, is reddish; the sixth, Jupiter, is second in whiteness. Now the whole spindle revolves as one; but within the whole as it turns, the seven inner circles wheel slowly the opposite way. Of these the eighth moves fastest; next the seventh, sixth, and fifth, keeping pace together; third in speed, it appeared to them, moved the fourth, in this counter-wheeling course; fourth came the third, and fifth the second. And the spindle turns on the knees of Necessity. On top of each circle rides a Siren, carried around with it, sounding one single note, one pitch; and all eight notes together make a single harmony. Around them, at equal distances, three others are seated, each on a throne: the Fates, daughters of Necessity, robed in white with garlands on their heads — Lachesis, Clotho, and Atropos — singing to the Sirens' harmony: Lachesis of what has been, Clotho of what is, Atropos of what is to come. Clotho, from time to time, lays her right hand on the outer rim of the spindle and helps turn it; Atropos with her left hand does the same for the inner circles; and Lachesis takes hold of each in turn, first with one hand, then with the other.

'And here is what the messenger from that world reported the spokesman as saying at the time: "Even for the one who comes forward last, if he chooses with intelligence and lives in earnest, a life is laid up that is to be loved, not a bad one. Let not the first to choose be careless, nor the last lose heart." When he had said this, Er told us, the one who had drawn the first lot came up and at once seized the greatest tyranny. In his folly and greed he chose without examining the whole of it, and failed to see that it was fated, among its other evils, to include the eating of his own children. When he looked at it more closely, he beat his breast and bewailed his choice, going back on the warning the spokesman had given; for he blamed not himself for his troubles but chance and the gods and anything but himself. Now this was one of those who had come down from the sky, having lived his former life in a well-ordered city, but with a virtue that was only habit, untouched by philosophy. And in fact, of those caught out this way, the greater number came from the sky, since they had never been schooled by suffering; whereas most of the souls that came up out of the earth, having suffered themselves and seen others suffer, did not snatch at their choice. And because of this, and because of the luck of the draw, many souls traded a good destiny for an evil one, or an evil for a good. For if a man, whenever he came into this life, would always take up sound philosophy from the start, and if the luck of the draw didn't put him among the very last to choose, then, by Er's account, the odds are not only that he'd be happy here, but that his journey from this world to the other and back again would be smooth and along the road of heaven, not rough and underground. It was a sight worth seeing, he said, how the several souls chose their lives, a thing pitiful and laughable and strange, for the most part choosing according to the habits of their former life. He saw the soul that had once been Orpheus choosing the life of a swan, out of hatred for womankind, unwilling to be born of a woman because women had murdered him. He saw the soul of Thamyras choosing the life of a nightingale, and a swan, with other songbirds, choosing in turn to change over into the life of a man. The soul that drew the twentieth lot chose the life of a lion; it was the soul of Ajax the son of Telamon, who shrank from being a man again, remembering the judgment over the arms. After him came Agamemnon, his soul too at enmity with the human race because of what it had suffered, and he took the life of an eagle. Somewhere in the middle came the turn of Atalanta's soul, which, catching sight of the great honors paid to an athlete, could not pass them by but took that life. After her he saw the soul of Epeus the son of Panopeus passing into the nature of a woman skilled in crafts; and far off among the very last, the soul of Thersites the buffoon putting on the body of an ape. By the luck of the draw the soul of Odysseus had come last of all to make its choice; and the memory of its old toils had cured it of ambition, so it went about a long time looking for the life of a private man who minds his own business. With some trouble it found one lying somewhere, neglected by all the rest, and when it saw it, it said it would have done the same even if it had drawn the first lot, and chose it gladly. And there were other crossings too, from beasts into men and from one kind of beast into another, the unjust changing into the savage animals and the just into the gentle ones, every sort of mixture coming about.'

When they arrived, they had to go straight to Lachesis. And first a kind of spokesman arranged them in order; then he took from the knees of Lachesis lots and patterns of lives, climbed onto a high platform, and spoke: 'The word of Lachesis, maiden daughter of Necessity. Souls of a day, here begins another round of death-bearing life for mortal kind. No guardian spirit will draw you by lot; you will choose your guardian spirit. Let the one who draws the first lot be first to choose a life — a life that will then be his by necessity. Virtue has no master: as each honors her or dishonors her, he will have more of her or less. The blame belongs to the chooser. God is blameless.' With that he flung the lots out over them all, and each soul picked up the one that fell beside it — all except Er, who was not allowed. And as each picked up its lot, it saw what number it had drawn. Next the spokesman set out on the ground before them the patterns of lives — far more than the souls present, and of every kind: lives of every animal, and every human life. There were tyrannies among them, some running the full term, others cut down midway, ending in poverty and exile and beggary. There were lives of famous men — famous for beauty of form, for strength and victory in the games, or for their birth and the virtues of their ancestors — and lives of men obscure for the opposite reasons; and lives of women, the same way. But no rank of soul was fixed in them, since a soul necessarily becomes different according to the life it chooses. Everything else was there, mixed together — wealth with poverty, sickness with health — and the middle conditions too. And here, dear Glaucon, it seems, is the whole danger for a human being. This is why each of us must set aside every other study and care most for this one: to seek and find whether there is anyone who can give him the power and the knowledge to tell a good life from a bad one — anyone to learn it from — and to choose, always and everywhere, the best life that is possible. He must reckon what everything we have said tonight, taken together and taken separately, contributes to virtue in a life: what beauty does when mixed with poverty or wealth, and joined to which condition of soul; what noble and humble birth do, private station and public office, strength and weakness, quickness and slowness of mind, and everything of that sort the soul has by nature or takes on — what they work when combined with one another. Out of all this he will be able to reason, keeping his eye on the nature of the soul, and to choose between the worse life and the better — calling worse whatever leads the soul toward becoming more unjust, and better whatever leads it toward becoming more just. Everything else he will let go. For we have seen that this is the sovereign choice, for a man living and for a man dead. And he must go down to the house of the dead holding this conviction hard as adamant, so that there too he will not be dazzled by wealth and evils of that kind, will not stumble into tyrannies and doings of that sort — working many incurable wrongs on others, and suffering worse himself — but will know how to choose, always, the life that keeps the middle way, fleeing the extremes on either side, in this world as far as he can and in all the life to come. For this is how a human being becomes happiest.

'When all the souls had chosen their lives, they went forward in the order of their choosing to Lachesis. To each she sent the guardian spirit it had chosen, to go with it through life and bring its choices to pass. This spirit led the soul first to Clotho, passing it beneath her hand and beneath the whirling of the spindle, to ratify the destiny it had chosen by lot; and after it had touched the spindle, the spirit led it on to Atropos, who spun the thread to make the fate unalterable. From there each soul passed, without turning back, beneath the throne of Necessity. When they had all gone through, they marched on across a terrible, stifling heat to the plain of Forgetfulness, a barren waste with no tree or growing thing; and as evening came on they camped by the river of Unmindfulness, whose water no jar can hold. Of this water all of them were forced to drink a certain amount, and those who weren't kept safe by good sense drank more than the measure; and each, as he drank, forgot everything. When they had fallen asleep, in the middle of the night came thunder and an earthquake, and all at once the souls were swept up and away, this way and that, to their births, shooting off like stars. Er himself was not allowed to drink the water; but by what road, and in what way, he came back to his body, he could not tell. He only knew that, opening his eyes suddenly at dawn, he found himself lying on the pyre.'

And then, according to the messenger from that world, the spokesman spoke as follows: 'Even for the last to come forward, if he chooses with sense and lives with effort, a life worth loving is laid out here — not a bad one. Let the first chooser not be careless, and let the last not lose heart.' The moment he had spoken, Er said, the man who drew the first lot strode up and chose the greatest tyranny. Out of folly and greed he took it without examining it all, and missed the fate folded inside it — that he was destined, among other horrors, to eat his own children. When he studied it at leisure, he beat his breast and wailed over his choice, forgetting everything the spokesman had proclaimed; for instead of blaming himself for his troubles, he blamed fortune, and the spirits, and everything rather than himself. He was one of those who had come down from heaven — a man who had lived his former life in an orderly city, and had taken his share of virtue by habit, without philosophy. Indeed, broadly speaking, more than half of those caught out this way were of the company come down from heaven, because they had never been trained by suffering; while the ones up from the earth, who had suffered themselves and watched others suffer, were in no rush to make their choice. Because of this — and because of the luck of the lot — most of the souls traded a good destiny for an evil one, or an evil for a good. Yet if a man, every time he entered this life, practiced philosophy soundly, and the lot for choosing did not fall to him among the very last, then, from what Er reported, the odds are fair not only that he would be happy here, but that his journey from here to there and back again would run not underground and rough, but smooth, and through heaven. The sight itself, he said, was worth seeing — how the several souls chose their lives — pitiable to watch, and laughable, and astonishing. For the most part they chose by the habits of their former life. He saw the soul that had once been Orpheus choosing the life of a swan: hatred of womankind, because women had been his death, made him unwilling to be conceived and born of a woman. He saw the soul of Thamyras choosing a nightingale's life; and a swan changing over to choose a human life, and other musical animals doing the same. The soul that drew the twentieth lot chose the life of a lion: it was the soul of Ajax the son of Telamon, who shunned becoming a man because he remembered the judgment of the arms. After him came Agamemnon: he too hated the human race because of what he had suffered, and traded into the life of an eagle. The soul of Atalanta had drawn a lot toward the middle: she caught sight of the great honors of a male athlete's life, and could not pass them by, and took it. After her he saw the soul of Epeus, son of Panopeus, entering the nature of a craftswoman; and far off among the last, the soul of the clown Thersites putting on an ape. And as chance had it, the soul of Odysseus had drawn the last lot of all, and came forward to choose. The memory of his old labors had cured him of ambition, and he went around a long time looking for the life of a private man who minds his own business — and found it at last, lying somewhere, passed over by everyone else. When he saw it, he said he would have done the same if his lot had come first, and he chose it gladly. And it went the same way with the animals: they passed into men and into one another — the unjust changing into the wild kinds, the just into the tame — mixed in every combination.

When all the souls had chosen their lives, they went before Lachesis in the order of their lots; and she sent with each the guardian spirit it had chosen, to watch over the life and fulfill the choice. The spirit led the soul first to Clotho — under her hand as it turned the whirling spindle — ratifying there the destiny it had drawn and chosen; and after touching her, the spirit led it on to the spinning of Atropos, who made the threads unalterable. From there, without turning back, each soul passed beneath the throne of Necessity; and when all had come through, they marched together to the plain of Forgetting, through terrible, stifling heat — for the plain is bare of trees, bare of everything the earth grows. Evening was coming on, and they camped beside the river of Heedlessness, whose water no vessel can hold. All of them were required to drink a measure of that water; and those not saved by good sense drank past the measure; and as each one drank, he forgot everything. When they had gone to sleep, at midnight there came thunder and an earthquake, and suddenly they were swept up and away, this way and that, to their births, like shooting stars. Er himself had been prevented from drinking the water. But how and by what way he came back to his body, he could not say: he simply opened his eyes at dawn and found himself lying on the pyre.

And that, Glaucon, is how the tale was saved and not lost. And it can save us, if we believe it: then we will cross the river of Forgetting safely, and our soul will not be stained. So here is my counsel: let us hold forever to the upward road, and practice justice with wisdom in every way — believing the soul immortal, and able to endure every evil and every good — so that we may be friends to ourselves and to the gods, both while we remain here and when we carry off the prizes justice wins, like victors in the games making their round to gather the gifts. And both here, and on the thousand-year journey we have described, may we fare well.

'And so, Glaucon, the tale was saved and was not lost. And it can save us too, if we'll believe it: we shall cross the river of Forgetfulness safely and keep our soul undefiled. So this is my counsel, that we hold forever to the upward road and pursue justice together with wisdom by every means, believing the soul to be immortal and able to bear every evil and every good. Then we shall be dear to one another and to the gods, both while we stay here and afterward, when we gather in the rewards of justice like victors going round to collect their prizes; and we shall do well, both here and on that thousand-year journey we've been describing.'
